HOUSE OF COMMONS.

---

Tuesday, 8th
March, 1938, pursuant to the Resolution
of the House of 2nd December, 1937,
provided that if it appears to the satisfaction of Mr. Speaker, after consultation
with the Government, that the public
interest requires that the House shall
meet at any earlier time during the
Christmas adjournment, Mr. Speaker
may give notice that he is so satisfied,
and thereupon the House shall meet at
the time stated in such notice and shall
transact its business as if it had been
duly adjourned to that date.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
A PROCLAMATION
FOR DISSOLVING THE FOURTH
PARLIAMENT OF NORTHERN
IRELAND AND DECLARING THE
CALLING OF ANOTHER.
WHEREAS it is provided by section.
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said
Act, that the Governor of Northern
Ireland shall, in His Majesty's name,
summon, prorogue and dissolve
Parliament of Northern Ireland:
the
And whereas it is desirable that the
present Parliament of Northern Ireland
should be dissolved and that a new
Parliament should be called:
Now therefore I, James Albert
Edward, Duke of Abercorn, Knight
of the Most Noble Order of the Garter,
Knight of the Most Illustrious Order of
Saint Patrick, Governor of Northern
Ireland, by this Proclamation do publish
and declare His Majesty's Pleasure that
the said Parliament be, as from the date
of this Proclamation, dissolved, and that
the Senators and Members of the House
of Commons be discharged from further
Attendance thereat :
And I do Hereby make known to all
His Majesty's loving subjects His Royal
Will and Pleasure to call a new Parliament of Northern Ireland, and do
further declare that I have taken Order
that Writs shall be issued forthwith in
His Majesty's name under the Great
Seal of Northern Ireland, in due Form
and according to Law, for calling a
Parliament of Northern Ireland to meet
at Stormont, Northern Ireland,
Tuesday the First day of March next,
and for causing the Senators and
Commons who are to serve in the said
Parliament to be duly returned to and
give their Attendance in His Majesty's
said Parliament on Tuesday the First
day of March next, which Writs are to
be returnable in due course of Law.
on
Given this Twentieth day of January,
in the year of our Lord one thousand
nine hundred and thirty-eight.
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
INDEX.

Monday, 3rd October, 1938.
The Contractor whose Tender is
accepted must undertake to commence
the work within 7 days from the written
notice to proceed.
The Council do not bind themselves
to accept the lowest or any Tender.
V. M. CONRAN,
Town Clerk.
City Hall, Armagh,
September, 1938.
1843 Belfast County Borough Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Nixon]
That is a very specific and proper advertisement. They had to
to be qualified
contractors, they had to lodge £3 3s, and
the tenders had to be in by a certain date.
There was one gentleman named Hogg
who put in a tender, and it was the
lowest tender, which was in order.
George B. Hanna, on the day of the
meeting, brought in a letter in his pocket
from Messrs. Lees, Hyman & Lees, Ltd.,
Corporation Street, Belfast. It was
lower than Hogg's tender because Mr.
Hyman had seen Mr. Hogg's tender the
night before. I do not say that George B.
Hanna saw it; I say Hyman saw it.
Lees, Hyman & Lees tender was accepted,
although it was not on the proper form,
and in spite of the fact that they were
only furniture contractors and that the
£3 3s Od had not been paid. Mr.
Frederick J. Hogg, who is organist in
Ballysillan Presbyterian Church, is a
most respectable man. Here is his statement, taken down by Head-Constable
Glass:
Statement by Frederick James Hogg,
40 years,
builder and contractor,
Glenside Parade, Ballysillan, Belfast.
I am a partner in the firm of Hogg
Brothers, with premises situate at Glenside Parade, Ballysillan, Belfast.
Early in September, 1938, I met Mr.
Hyman, of Messrs. Lees, Hyman &
Lees, Ltd., Corporation Street, Belfast,
furniture manufacturers. Mr. Hyman
told me that there was a contract
shortly to be placed in Armagh in connection with repairs to the City Hall,
and asked me if I would be inclined to
tender for it. I replied that I would
when the advertisement for tenders
""
appeared. The advertisement duly
appeared in the "Northern Whig,
and I went to Armagh, and after depositing £3 3s Od received the plans
and specifications. The next day, when
I examined the premises, I was handed
a typewritten sheet (attached hereto
and marked "a") by Mr. Conran, the
town clerk. This sheet contained the
names of persons recommended by
them to carry out the sub-contracts—
namely, painting and
three items were recommended to be
supplied by Messrs. Lees, Hyman &
Lees, Ltd.,
Ltd., of Corporation Street,
Belfast. I approached these subcontractors and got their price to carry
out their portion of the work. Messrs.
Lees, Hyman & Lees gave me their
price verbally, the others I got in
writing.
a most unusual and improper thingnamely, painting and decorating, electric installations, heating, steel work,
seating, carpets and curtains; the last
had my price drawn up and
On these figures which I obtained I
drew up my estimate, but had to confirm two items with Mr. Hyman before
submitting my price. I called with
Mr. Hyman on Saturday, 1st October,
regarding these two items. In the
course of conversation he asked me if
I
told him I had when I had
fixed up with him regarding the
two items I came to see him about. We
agreed as to the price of the two items.
He informed me that there were only
three contractors tendering for the
work to be done to the City Hall, two
Armagh firms and my firm. He asked
me my price, and I told him it came to
£4,172 19s Od. When I arrived back
at my office after my interview with
Mr. Hyman, I found an amended price
from the plumber increasing his contract, which would add to my price and
brought it up to £4,202 0s 0d, and this
was the sum I submitted to the
Armagh Council.
During the course of my conversation
with Mr. Hyman on Saturday, 1st
October, he said to me that someone
else would have to be looked after, not
in the form of money but with a substantial present which would be highly
appreciated. I said that I had not
counted on anything of that description, that my price was a keen contract
price, but he insisted that it would
have to be done, and I agreed, in the
event of the other contractors also
agreeing, to subscribe. I said I could
allow between £20 and £25 in the
event of the other sub-contractors also
subscribing. He discussed with me
various details concerning the contract,
and he said that he had not got the
plans or specifications from Armagh.
I gave him any details which he asked
for. The reason I gave him these
details was that he seemed to be in very
close touch with any work that there
was to be done in the hall, and I was
under the impression that the infor-
1845 Belfast County Borough Bill-
2 JULY 1942

Second Reading
mation might be required for someone
else not in my line of business. He
also told me that he was not sure if
they would go ahead with the job or
not, as the council had only asked for
a loan of £3,500. He impressed upon
me very strongly not to submit my
tender before 4 o'clock on Monday the
3rd October, at which time tenders
were to be considered, and when handing it in to ask for either Mr. Conran
or Mr. Hanna.
On Monday, the 3rd October, I took
the tender to Armagh and asked for
Mr. Conran, but the clerk told me that
the meeting had just started, and that
Mr. Conran was inside at the meeting.
I handed the tender to the clerk who
went forward and handed in the tender
to some person who was in the room in
which the meeting was being held.
When he came back I asked him for a
receipt, and he suggested that I should
wait and hear the result. I did so,
and in the course of conversation with
the clerk I asked him how many were
tendering for the job and he also told
me three, two Armagh firms and my
own firm. After about twenty minutes
there was a knock on the door of the
room in which the meeting was being
held and the clerk went to answer it.
He came back and said, "Congratulations, you have got the job; there were
no names mentioned, but they said the
Belfast firm has got it, and you are the
only Belfast firm tendering."
I then left for home. I did not call
at my office that night, but in the
morning I saw a telephone message
which had been received at 5-50 p.m.
on Monday night to say there had been
a mistake made and the job had been
given to a builder named "Lee."
On Tuesday night, the 4th October,
I noticed in the "Telegraph" that the
job had been given to Messrs. Lees,
Hyman & Lees at £4,150. I might
add that I am aware that Messrs. Lees,
Hyman & Lees never did any work in
connection with building contracting;
they are solely furniture manufacturers.
On Wednesday morning, the 5th of
October, I immediately got in touch.
with the various sub-contractors, and
was informed by them that they had
not been asked for prices by Messrs.
Lees, Hyman & Lees.
On Thursday, the 6th October, Mr.
Hyman's typist 'phoned me at my
office and asked me if I could arrange
an appointment with Mr. Hyman at 11
or 12 that day. I said I had no intention of going to see him at any time.
On Sunday, the 9th October, at about
4-30 p.m. Mr. Hyman rang me up at
my home, 48 Ballysillan Road, Belfast.
He said he understood that I had got a
wrong impression of his actions, and he
wanted to make an explanation.
I
replied that I did not think there was
any explanation necessary as in my
opinion it was as dirty an action as one
man could play on another. He suggested that he should meet me at my
office on Monday, the 10th October,
at 11 oclock to make an explanation,
but I refused to meet him and replaced
the receiver.
On or about Thursday, the 13th
October, I was approached by a man
who told me he had been in touch with
Mr. Hyman, who had asked him to get
in touch with me. He told me that
Mr. Hyman was willing to give me our
portion of the work to do at our
contract price if I did not cause any
trouble. I replied that I would not be
willing to work under Mr. Hyman on
any conditions.
On the attached memo marked "B"
is a list of articles recommended to be
supplied by Messrs. Lees, Hyman &
Lees. The articles enumerated were
included in my estimate. Since making
inquiries I am of the opinion that the
prices quoted for these articles are
approximately one hundred per cent.
too high.
I also attach copy of a letter which
I sent to the Ministry of Home Affairs
(marked C), Stormont, Belfast, on the
15th October, and I attach hereto copy
of their reply marked "D."
I might mention that throughout
all my time in business I have never
been asked to give a present or subscribe to one, nor have I ever done so.
I have heard this statement read
over and it is all true.
(Signed) F. J. HOGG.
Statement taken by Head-Constable
J. Glass at office of J. A. Leighton &
Son, Solicitors, Donegall Chambers,
Donegall Place, Belfast, at 11 a.m.,
25-10-38.
1847 Belfast County Borough Bill-
HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. Nixon]
I drew your attention at the outset to
the terms of the advertisement in the
"Whig," which laid it down that no one
but a qualified contractor should enter.
Hyman, as I explained, got the contract;
he never put in a tender, and he only
lodged the three guineas after he got the
contract, a thing that was wholly and
totally irregular. Furthermore, in Mr.
Hogg's statement, you will see that he
got a list of sub-contractors, firms on the
list, in Armagh, and that the prices were
100 per cent. too high. There was an
inquiry, and one Gentleman from the

Anyone who is familiar with deeds
knows that the purchaser of an estate gets
a solicitor if he wants to keep himself
right, and that solicitor draws up the
deed. After it is drawn up it is sent to
the solicitor for the vendor, who examines
it to see if it is in order, and if it is in
order he gets the vendor to execute it by
signing it. That signature is usually
witnessed by a clerk in the office of the
solicitor who acts for the vendor. That
signature has to be attested by affidavit.

can claim that my right hon. Friend

I am fully satisfied that the right hon.
Gentleman fulfils the qualifications of a
Speaker. The office of Speaker contains

The Speaker is the guardian of the rights
and privileges of the House of Commons,
and although in these days that may
seem merely a method of speech, nevertheless in the long and checkered history
in which our Parliamentary institutions
have risen that aspect of the Speaker's
office played an important-indeed, I may
say a paramount-part, because in the
long constitutional struggles across the
water between the House of Commons
and the King, in which the House of
Commons was naturally and properly
victorious, the Speaker of the House of
Commons was the gentleman upon whom
devolved the duty of asserting against
the Crown the rights and privileges of
Parliament.
The Right Hon. Henry George Hill
Mulholland from my past experience is
tolerant, is possessed of the gift of unfailing patience and a desire to give fair
play to all, and last but not least he
possesses charity that charity that
suffereth long and is kind. It is the duty
of the Speaker to act impartially towards
every section of the House, and it is
because I believe and have no doubt that

The PRIME MINISTER: It is one of
the privileges of my office to have the
extreme pleasure of congratulating, on
behalf of all parties, the newly-elected
Speaker of this House. Having been
in the Imperial Parliament for some
years and having studied the procedure
there and being very jealous of a
democratic institution such as the Mother
of Parliaments in our Empire, I have
always felt that Mr. Speaker plays a
predominant part in carrying on, from
year to year and generation to generation, the high traditions associated with
British institutions.
I can only say from my heart that we
owe you a deep debt of gratitude for
the fairness and, if I may say so, the
sense of humour you have shown in
carrying on in so dignified a manner the
duties of Mr. Speaker for some years
past. The mover and seconder have
borne eloquent tribute to the capabilities
you possess in every way to preside over
this assembly, and it is indeed, after
seventeen years here,
a very much
esteemed pleasure on my part once again
to tender you very deep felicitations from
all sides of the House on again being
placed in the Chair. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Mr. HENDERSON: It is not my
intention to utter one discordant note
to-day. I would like to associate myself
with the remarks made by the hon.
Member for Duncairn in regard to seeing
the Prime Minister once more in this
House. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I hope his health will continue to
improve and that he will be able to work
in the interests of Ulster.
I cannot, however, allow this occasion
to pass without entering my protest
in no uncertain manner. I cannot
altogether agree with what the
mover and seconder have said in
nominating Mr. Speaker. As one of
Election of Speaker
Election of Speaker
1 MARCH 1938
those representing independent thought
in this country I feel I have a grievance
about many things that have happened.
We have felt that we were not getting
as fair play as we ought to have got. As
a matter of fact another Independent
Member decided to remain away this
morning because he said if he had been
present he might have said something
he did not want to utter.
I cannot allow this occasion to pass
without reference
reference to something that
happened-something that is unprecedented in the history of any Parliament.
I had occasion to write to Mr. Speaker
a letter asking him if he would be kind
enough to put on the Order Paper a
question which I think is of paramount
importance to the loyalists of Northern
Ireland. To my amazement I got a
letter from Mr. Speaker, a letter that.
might have come from the principal of
a school to a scholar. I want to be quite
frank on this matter. As long as I am
in this House I intend to uphold my
rights. I care not about anyone so long
as I am in order. I will respect Mr.
Speaker just as much as any Member.
I do not wish to destroy the good feeling
that exists in this House, but I will
reserve my right to speak for the people
I represent and the tens of thousands of
people of independent thought all over
Ulster.
I have a great regard for Mr. Speaker.
I may have given trouble on a good
many occasions, and exhausted the
patience of Members in listening to me
for a long time, but I must say there
were times when one would have thought
there was no Parliament here at all,
because
very few Members ever
attempted to take part in the debates.
It was left on a good many occasions to
the Members on this side to continue the
debates on the different Bills. I want it
to be understood that I will speak here
as long as I like, so long as I am in
order, on behalf of the tens of thousands
of loyalists and Independent Unionists
in this area.
I may have read into the letter I have
referred to something wrong, but in my
opinion the Speaker of this House has
done something no other Speaker would
have done to any private Member of a
Parliament. I felt this very much this
morning, and I regret to have to make
these comments. I do not want to
.
""
divulge the contents of the letter, but
I say it was the duty of the Speaker,
when a Member of Parliament, elected
by the votes of the people, wants to put
a question in the House, to say "The
question is in order, I will see it is put
on the Order Paper in due form, and
give an opportunity for it to be asked
in the House.' That was his duty, and
his duty should have ended there. But
what I was told, to all intents and purposes, was that in future it would be
better if I was not to make lengthy
speeches. As long as I am in this
House, whether or not it pleases Mr.
Speaker or the Prime Minister, I am
going to talk and talk about the poor
of this country who are starving. Starvation is worse to-day than it was when
this Government was established. I will
speak on behalf of all these people as
long as I get the opportunity from the
Speaker of this House.
As representing people of independent
thought in this country we expect to get
justice from Mr. Speaker. That is only
what we are entitled to. I want nothing
more and nothing less than the justice
I am entitled to. If I make long speeches
it is for the benefit of the people I represent, and with God's help I am going
to continue to try to get for the people
who sent me here those loyal peoplethe justice they are entitled to receive.
I am sorry I have had to utter this
protest, but I feel that when Mr. Speaker
considers the contents of the letter he
sent me he will see that he overstepped
the mark. In my opinion he said something he ought not to have said, and I
feel I am justified, as the person who
received that letter, in making my
protest.

Oral Answer to Question.
THE ANGLO-EIRE NEGOTIATIONS.
Mr. HENDERSON (by private notice)
asked the Prime Minister whether it is a
fact that during the week ending 19th
February, 1938, the Minister of Finance
was summoned to London by the
Imperial Cabinet to discuss the position.
of Ulster in relation to the present
Anglo-Eire trade negotiations; whether
he again received an urgent summons to
London on Thursday last; whether he
crossed immediately to London to continue the discussion with the Imperial
Cabinet, and, if so, whether he can give
the House any information on the
matter; and whether the question of
partition was discussed at this conference.
The PRIME MINISTER: With regard
to the first three parts of the question
the answer is in the affirmative. With
regard to the fourth, it would not be in
the public interest to make any statement
at present, but when it is appropriate
and he is in a position to do so my right
hon. Friend will immediately inform the
House. With regard to the fifth, the
answer is in the negative.
SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Election for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return or Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such bribery or other corrupt
practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved That if it shall appear that
any persons hath been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,
the same is declared to be a high crime
or misdemeanour; and this House will
proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in
any case before this House or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take
care that, during the Session of Parliament the passages through the streets
leading to this House be kept free and
open, and that no obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members
to and from this House, and that no
disorder be allowed in the precincts of or
in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts, and that the Serjeant-at-
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear his Grace's Speech on
behalf of his Majesty to both Houses of
Parliament, of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The speech
is as follows:
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
On the occasion of the opening of
this, the first session of the fifth Parliament of Northern Ireland, I feel confident that wisdom and zeal will
characterise your deliberations on the
important matters entrusted to your
control.
It is with sincere regret that my
Ministers have to report that the
volume of employment in 1937, which
showed a steady increase until the
month of September, began to diminish
substantially until January of this
year. This was undoubtedly a reflection of the set-back in trade activity
throughout the United Kingdom which
marked those months. The linen
industry and its ancillary trades, in
particular, felt the full effect of unsettled conditions in the markets of
the Far East, America and the
Continent. Notwithstanding this
recent decline in business and commerce, it is noteworthy that in 1937
comparable employment in insured
industries reached the highest level for
seven years, and that there were on
the average over thirty thousand more
persons in such employment in that
year than in 1931.
My Ministers will continue the policy
of fostering trade in the Home and
Over-seas markets, thereby assisting in
the expansion of the volume of employment in Northern Ireland.
My Government is taking all the
steps within its power to stimulate the
establishment of new industries and
the extension of existing undertakings
likely to provide additional employment of a permanent nature, and I am
gratified to learn that the measures
taken to make more widely known the
extended facilities now available to
new industrial undertakings have
aroused considerable interest in the
United Kingdom. It is my earnest
hope that a substantial contribution
towards the solution of the unemployment problem will
will eventually
achieved along these lines.
be
While strife and uncertainty abroad
have unfortunately checked the forward movement of the linen trade, I
trust, as a result of the negotiations
now about to begin between His
King's Speech
1 MARCH 1938
King's Speech
Majesty's Government in the United
Kingdom and the Government of the
United States of America, that the
industry may once again be started
upon an upward curve of production
by widening the scope of what has
always been its principal Overseas
market.
I am gratified that local authorities
and public bodies are co-operating with
my Government in promoting works of
public utility which provide useful employment, and that during last year
forty-four schemes were approved,
involving a total capital expenditure
of over nine hundred thousand pounds.
I am glad to know that substantial
assistance is being rendered to building and allied industries by reason of
the large programme of works which
the Government has in hand, both
directly for its own departmental
activities and for departments, such as
the Post Office Department, which are
not under its control but are of
intimate concern to the community.
I learn with pleasure that the programme of providing suitable accommodation for our Police Force is
steadily proceeding, although a few
years must elapse before the programme
is completed. Again in our provincial
towns I observe the provision of
Employment Exchanges in conformity
with modern standards of building and
comfort. The success of the Bann
Drainage Works, also, I am informed,
is assured, even though their final completion is still some time off. Large
areas have been saved from the flooding to which they would have been
subjected but for the amelioration provided by these works.
I also see everywhere new elementary
schools being constructed on up-to-date
lines, and for this activity our local
authorities are to be congratulated,
the Government having also given substantial assistance in financing and in
some cases desigining these works.
You will be invited to consider a
Measure to amend and consolidate the
law regulating conditions in factories
and workshops on lines similar to the
Bill on this subject which was introduced in the last Parliament.
Proposals will also be laid before
you to amend the law relating to Unemployment Insurance and National
Health Insurance, and to extend the
statutory provisions for the welfare of
the blind, including the lowering by
ten years of the age of qualification for
pension.
A Bill will be introduced authorising my Government to give financial
assistance to urban authorities to
enable them to provide houses for our
industrial workers at reasonable rents
and also to facilitate the issue of loans
to the owners of working-class houses,
both in towns and in rural areas, for
the repair of such houses as can be
made fit for human habitation.
A Measure will be laid before you to
enable local authorities to prepare and
carry out schemes for the protection of
life and property in the event of attack
from the air in time of war.
A Bill will be submitted for your
consideration to amend the Exported
Animals (Compensation) Acts (Northern Ireland), 1928 and 1932, in order
give shippers of
of cattle from
Northern Ireland ports greater protection in the case of foot and mouth
disease discovered or suspected at a
British landing centre.
to
You will be invited to consider proposals for the amendment of the
Marketing of Potatoes Acts (Northern
Ireland), 1928 and 1934, providing
further powers for the purpose of
maintaining a reasonable price level
in respect of potatoes for shipment.
It was impracticable in the last Parliament to proceed with the Bill
designed to encourage and assist the
provision of facilities for physical
training for young persons still at
school and for adult members of the
population who wish to take advantage
of them. Consequently this matter
will be brought forward for your consideration during the forthcoming
Session.
My Government will also lay before
you a Measure to ensure that every
boy and girl shall, subject to necessary
exemptions on account of beneficial
employment, such as farm work, industrial occupation, or other reasonable cause, continue his or her education in an appropriate manner until at
least fifteen years of age.
The proposals which were contemplated in the last Parliament to

enable teachers on retirement to

Members of the House of Commons.
The Estimates for the Public
Services will be laid before you in due
course.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I am glad to learn that preparations
are well advanced for the representatation of Northern Ireland at the
Empire Exhibition to be held this year
in Glasgow, and I am confident that
this Exhibit will enhance the industrial
prestige of the Province and make its
attractions to the tourist even more
widely known.
It is a great tribute to all concerned
with the conduct of industry in Northern Ireland that industrial relations
between employers and employed have
been so harmonious, and the steady
development of voluntary machinery
for adjusting by amicable negotiations
such points of difference as may arise
from time to time gives me great
satisfaction.
I am gratified to know that facilities
for the instruction and training of unemployed persons are being extended
on practical lines and that increased
opportunities for physical training are
being provided for those who are out
of work.
The report of the Departmental
Committee which has been investigating the question of the protection of
the young and the welfare of
young offenders has now been received
and will be given full and sympathetic
consideration by my Government.
I have observed with interest the
results of the Census of Northern Ireland which was taken exactly a year
ago to-day and I am sure that the

There is just one aspect of this question

of unemployed. A very large number of

have been out of employment for long
periods. It is true that the longer a man
is out of employment the greater difficulty he has in getting back. When some
of these men have been out a year or
two years or even longer from one of
those great commercial undertakings
which employ labour on a large scale they
are frequently rejected because they are
unable to do a full day's work for a full
day's pay or because their labour would
slow down the squad with whom they

I hope that serious consideration will
be given to the condition of those out of
employment for prolonged periods,
because the physical deterioration which
is a necessary consequence of enforced
idleness is bad enough, but in the case of
people in no way to blame for their misfortune the social deterioration which
attacks some of them is far more serious.
I hope it will be possible to prevent any
fall in the morale of those who are suffering from unemployment through no fault
of their own. I beg to move.

us.
But then I asked myself what more
can this Government or any Government
do. That is the problem which lies before
In the first instance no Government
can with safety intrude upon the privacy
of the business which is carried on and
which has been the making of our great
city of Belfast and of Ulster itself. No
Government can intrude upon the

Mr. NIXON: Hear, hear.
The PRIME MINISTER: We cannot
dictate to them, nor have we any desire
to do so. It is open to the public, to
all classes and creeds, to criticise the
Government, but it is a different thing
for the Government to criticise the way in
which business is carried on. That is my
first observation. My second is that it
is the duty of the Government to give
trade and industry all possible assistance
in struggling through bad times, to place
as little restriction on them as possible
on the one hand, and on the other to
encourage and attract into our midst new
industries in order that we may not rely
entirely upon the agricultural, linen
and shipbuilding industries. The
more industries of a diversified
nature we have scattered through
the Province the more solid the
foundations upon which we can build.
The Government have made two vigorous
attempts by passing two Bills dealing

justified in years to come.
There are very satisfactory indications.
as far as I can judge of tentative

The North of Ireland man who is transferred to England or Scotland is asked

am going to keep him to the step-by-step

Not one word has appeared in the
Gracious Speech in regard to the high
cost of living. We are now 18 points
higher than we were in October, 1933.
That means that the purchasing power of
the £ is equal only to 14s 8d as compared with the purchasing power of 1933.
In other words, the purchasing power of
old-age pensioners, of widows and
orphans, of the unemployed, of those who
are obtaining public assistance, has been
reduced to that extent. That involves a
reduction in the purchasing power of over
300,000 consumers. You must remember
that one out of every three of our insured
population in Northern Ireland is out of
employment at the moment. If we take
that fact, and consider the average
number of a family, we see that there
are 300,000 persons in Northern Ireland
dependent on unemployment benefit and
public assistance. If their purchasing
power has been reduced, as I suggest, that
involves a curtailment of the business of
the shopkeepers. It means that the home
market cannot buy the goods from the
producers, the farmers. It means the
throwing out of employment of an
additional number of people who are at
present in employment.
Therefore, the Government have got to
tackle this question of unemployment.
They have got to tackle it in a way that
is likely to be beneficial to those who are
looking to the Government for a solution
of the problem. The Government should
not accept the suggestion of my hon. and
learned Friend, the Member for St.
Anne's (Mr. Warnock), that there is no
such thing as a cure for unemployment.
The subject of new industries is
mentioned in the Speech. I do not think
we are going to have any assistance from
new industries in Northern Ireland,
because all the modern industries that
are required are being established in
England and Scotland by the assistance
of the British Government, and are
making plans to supply the market in

no new industry that I know of, with

Sir ROBERT JOHNSTONE:
rising to support the Motion for an
Address I commence by congratulating
the mover and seconder of this Address
on the speeches they delivered to this
House yesterday. We all expected a
good deal from them and I think the
highest compliment I can pay them is
to say they did not fall below the level
of what we had expected. They have
had already pointed out to them by the
Member for Pottinger the joints in their
armour, but I am sure that when they
have received from him the instruction
that he was good enough to offer them
they will be of very great assistance to
us in the debates in this House.
I will now go on to consider the Gracious
Speech. When I listened to the debate.
yesterday I thought we were in for one
of those hardy annuals, a debate on
unemployment. And we certainly heard
a great deal about unemployment yesterday. One remark was made about the
pessimistic condition of the minds of
those who spoke in regard to unemployment. I will not say that I do not share
in that pessimism, and one of my main
reasons for sharing in that pessimism is
that unemployment, which ought to be,
and is, definitely an economic question,
has become a political question. It is
now the weapon with which the party
in opposition hope to belabour the party
that happen to be in power. It is a
very sad thing that a question which is an
economic question and can only be solved
by economic measures should be used as
a political weapon, and that one party
should point with triumph to the fact
that unemployment has fallen by a few
thousands and that the other party
should hail with unholy glee the fact
that unemployment has risen by 10,000.
I think that it is time we took unemployment out of the political arena
altogether and all put our heads together
to endeavour to find a solution for this
very serious and terrible problem that
lies before us. I shall say no more about
unemployment.
I do not quite agree with the mover
of the Address that the Gracious Speech
of the King does not afford any prospect
of any very important legislation. I
understood him to say that it was rather
in the form of amending legislation than
in the form of new legislation. Because
when I looked through the King's Speech
I found one thing which, to my mind,
is of very great importance. The King's
Speech definitely adumbrates that we are
going to turn our attention to the people
whom it is really worth while turning
attention to, that is, the children and
young people also, because if we
improve the lot of the children and young
people of Ulster we shall do the best
thing we can towards building up a new
and better Ulster than we have at the
present time.
the
can
a
And I see in the King's Speech that
we have, first of all, promised a measure
to assist in the provision of facilities for
physical training, and, secondly,
measure to ensure that every boy and
to
girl shall, subject
necessary
exemption, be kept at school until 15
years of age. We are not promised a
measure, but it is definitely adumbrated
that there will be a
measure coming
from the Government, in regard to
another very important thing, that
is, with regard to the
of
dealing
protection
the young and
with
the welfare of young offenders. It
seems to me that if this Session of Parliament do nothing else than pass Acts
which will ensure that we get these
things which are directly for the benefit
of the young of the Province we shall
have done a very considerable deal for
the benefit of our country.
Yesterday there was a remark made in
regard to the facilities for the physical
training of children to the effect that
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir R. Johnstone]
these children would be better off if
better fed than physically trained. I am
quite sure that the hon. Member for
Pottinger, who made that remark, has
in his bailiwick, as most of us have in
our bailiwick-I mean those of us who
are not University Members-a number of
children who are under-nourished, but
I had the opportunity last year when the
King was here on his day's visit of
driving through the Ormeau Park
immediately after the King's procession.
In the Ormeau Park were massed the
school children of Belfast.
That day
will ever be memorable to me.
It was a
day well worth living for the sake of
seeing such a number of healthy, happy
looking children, who were evidently enjoying themselves and at the top of
physical health. Although I admit and
deplore the fact that there are a number
of children who are under-nourished,
still we have quite a large number
of well-nourished children in the North
of Ireland, and it is for us to see that
they get every possible opportunity of
maintaining and increasing their physical
health.
I hope that this Measure, when it does
come before us, will not confine itself to
physical training. Physical training is
all very well. I think somebody remarked yesterday that it was supposed to
provide cannon fodder for the next war.
When we talk about war, aeroplanes,
cannon fodder, and all sorts of things
like that I should point out that we are
engaged in warfare every day. We are
engaged in a warfare against want,
starvation, colds, dirt and disease. It is
for that warfare we want to strengthen
the younger generation. It is a warfare
we have to undertake right away from
the time they once leave their parents'
houses. We should not be content with
physical training. I hope this Measure
will enable the local authorities who will
undertake the responsibility for physical
training to provide proper playgrounds
for the children, where they can divert
themselves and engage in games. I think
it is much better to engage in games
than to take part in organised exercises.
The Measure for increasing the school
age is one that will, I am sure, meet with
the support of every Member of this
House. I do not quite share in the
criticism made in regard to this Measure,
that because some boys and girls would
be exempted on account of being employed
it would really mean that the Measure
would be a dead letter in Northern
Ireland. I do not agree with that. I
am sure that a considerable number of
boys and girls will remain at school until
the age of 15. I cannot altogether agree
either that even if they go into employment at the age of 14 they will have
ceased their education. After all, the
most important factor in education is not
the things we learn from the teacher or
a book, but it is our experience of life.
If these children commence their experience of life that does not mean that
their education is finished. I do not
agree that education is regarded as
finished when a boy or girl leaves school.
I am quite sure as time goes on parents
will see the advantage of keeping their
children at school for a year longer.
More and more children will be kept at
school until 15 instead of being taken
away at 14.
I go back on the King's Speech, and I
read another announcement which I feel
will meet with the approval of every
Member of this House-that is, the
announcement that the statutory provisions for the welfare of the blind are
to be improved, and in particular that
there is to be a lowering of the age of
qualification for pension. I have got a
copy of the Bill, but did not follow Mr.
Speaker's advice yesterday to go over it
carefully. I hope to read that Bill soon,
and I hope also that when that Measure
comes before the House for approval the
Government will be persuaded to extend
their care for the blind to another class
of afflicted persons.
I refer to the deaf
and dumb. While blindness is, perhaps,
the most feared and most dreadful of all
defects, those who are deaf and dumb
suffer also very considerable disability.
I do think when we are very careful of
the blind and do our best to improve their
lot we might also do something for the
deaf and dumb, who are to a great extent
prevented from taking their place in the
world in the way they ought to be able
to do.
We come back to the question of the
children. Towards the end of the
Gracious Speech I see a statement that
the Report of the Departmental Committee which has been investigating the
question of protection of the young and
the welfare of young offenders has been
received, and will be given full and
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
2 MARCH 1938
sympathetic consideration by the Government. As a member of that committee
who was not able to attend as many of
the meetings as I should have liked, I
would like to commend to the attention
of Members the report of the committee,
which was issued yesterday. I can
assure them if they read that report, as
I hope they will, they will find it an
extremely interesting document. It is
the result of a large amount of hard work
on the part of some members of the committee, whose chairman was the Chairman of Ways and Means (Sir Robert
Lynn). If you look over the list of
authorities who were consulted in the
preparation of that report, the visits
made to institutions, and the interviews
held with experts on this subject, you
will agree, whether you approve or not
of the conclusions reached, they were not
arrived at without having a very considerable amount of excellent evidence
before the committee and without a very
considerable amount of deliberation on
the part of the committee itself.
The question of juvenile offenders has
become a very serious one. One of the
first things that struck the committee was
the fact that the number of juvenile
delinquents was increasing at a remarkably rapid rate in Northern Ireland, as
indeed it is across the water as well.
This very important question should
engage the very closest attention of Parliament. After all, the juvenile offender,
if he is wrongly treated or neglected,
is apt to turn into
an anti-social
member of the community. While the
recommendations made by the committee
will, undoubtedly, cost a good deal of
money, I think it is very much better
that the money should be spent on
juvenile offenders so as to endeavour to
make him into a decent citizen, rather
than that more money should be spent
later on, when he has become an adult

recommendations of the committee are
adopted even in part they will go a long
way towards solving the problem of the
juvenile offender, which is becoming every
day more important and greater in its
extent.
When I am on the question of Departmental Committee, I may say that I am
a member of another Departmental Committee, which I hope will send in its
report to the Minister of Home Affairs
a
in a short time. I refer to the Departmental Committee on maternity services
in Northern Ireland. We have
number of recommendations to make. I

as we are promised in the case of this
report in regard to
regard to the welfare of
children. I have great pleasure in supporting the Motion.
Mr. HENDERSON: Yesterday when

The only thing I see of any importance in

pray that the blessing of Almighty God
may rest upon your deliberations.'
"" The
rest of the Speech is most hopeless and
most useless. It is the worst document

Before dealing with some of the things

would like to ask the Prime Minister, on

area, is partition going to be removed?
Mr. SPEAKER: I do not want to

When he saw the monster he had created

They are Members belonging to the Prime

they would not overawe me, because I

Member for Woodvale is not afraid. If

we were afraid, the gunmen you let loose

The hon. Member for the University

a political question. Who made it a

the Minister of Finance dispute that?

Is it not true that America, which previously depended on Northern Ireland.
for linen, is manufacturing linen herself?

Mr. HENDERSON: To-day America

right hon. Gentlemen to counteract that?
Was anything done? Not at all. Is it

opposite are more interested in foreign

Northern Ireland? Can that be dis-

tunity of proving conclusively that that

I do not see mentioned in the Speech

I think it is a most pessimistic speech.
I must humbly apologise for an

reference to physical training.
his
Might I refer him to the people whom

In my constituency is a married woman
who secured employment as her husband

was unemployed. She received 30s a
week. Her husband was receiving 11s
transitional benefit. Immediately the
wife got that employment and 30s a week
the husband's transitional benefit was
reduced from 11s to 2s 6d per week. I
would suggest that the hon. and learned

to take up physical culture, especially

Speaking yesterday the Prime Minister said that these people in Ulster were
receiving the same benefits as the people
across the water. Let me give another
case, so that the hon. and learned Member for St. Anne's may take it up,
because he has pledged himself to look
after the interests of the working people.
One of my constituents, a disabled ex-
Service man, fought with the hon. and
learned Member for St. Anne's in the
Great War. He is a hopeless cripple and
has to be lifted out of his bed and carried
down to the kitchen every morning and
back to his bedroom at night. He was
receiving £2 2s a week from his country
for wounds received. His son received
unemployment benefit, but owing to the
means test-and there is no mention of
the means test in the Gracious Speech
from the Throne-that benefit was
reduced to 3s a week.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): May I correct the hon.
Member? There is no means test in connection with unemployment benefit.
Mr. HENDERSON: I want to tell
the right hon. Gentleman that the transitional benefit was reduced, which is a
means test.
Mr. ANDREWS: That is not unemployment benefit.
Mr. HENDERSON: There is no use
in the Minister of Finance trying to
hedge. He knows exactly the position
in this country. This man's brother was
also in receipt of transitional benefit.
He, too, is an ex-Service man who
suffered for his King and country, and
his transitional benefit was reduced to
2s 6d a week. He told me that if it was
not for his brother he would have to
go to the poorhouse. There are thousands
of cases such as that in all parts of
Northern Ireland, even in Sandy Row,
where the True Blues come from. If the
Prime Minister says that is the gracious
treatment that is being meted out by the
Mother of Parliaments to its subjects
across the water all I have to say is that
I wish I were a Member of that Parliament. I would do my utmost to put
an end to conditions like that.
Looking at the whole situation from
whatever angle you like, you must come
to the conclusion that the present Government have failed hopelessly in the
past, and are going to fail hopelessly
in the future, in grappling with the
worst evil a country can be infested
with. They have no solution. They
will go on and on, day in and day out,
and in five years' time the Prime Minister will come along and say, "You must
return us again because the Border is in
danger."
It is not my intention to take up much
of the time of the House this afternoon,
but I want to say that the Prime
Minister has created a Frankenstein
monster, in other words, a monster that
is going to destroy the foundations of
this Parliament that he has built up.
He may think, because he got returned to power quite recently on
account of a scare which frightened the
lives out of some of the loyalists, that
it will continue. Five years will soon
go in.
Some of the right hon. Gentlemen on the other side may not be here.
I may not be here. But the seeds of
discontent have been sown, and if between Independents and Progressives
twenty-three candidates stood at the last
election that number will be greatly increased next time unless something is
done towards solving this vital problem
which is destroying the youth of the
country.
If you travelled through any country
in the world you could not find worse
conditions than those existing in Northern Ireland. It has been stated that the
Government intend to take steps to
establish new industries. They have
been taking those steps for seventeen
years, and where are the new industries?
I expected the Minister of Finance to
roar at me "Short & Harland's." But
I know a little about them. The Government had nothing to do with bringing
Short & Harland's to Ulster.
Mr. ANDREWS: That statement is
wrong.

Mr. HENDERSON: Short & Harland's were brought to Northern Ireland
through the great influence of Mr.
Rebbeck and one of the directors of
Short's. It is quite true to say that the
Government gave the firm assistance, but
that is not the same thing as bringing
the industry to Belfast.
The Labour
and Independent Members on this side.
of the House suggested for eight years
that there should be an aircraft factory
here, and it was only within the last two
or three years that the Government took
action. It was the Members on this side
of the House who raised that very
important question. It is quite true
that that firm has given employment to
1,400 or 1,500 men, but what other
industries have been established?
I will tell you what is wrong. Instead
of putting this reference to new industries into the King's Speech the Government should have tried to save the old
industries. What is the cause of the old
industries disappearing from Northern
Ireland? Was any attempt made by this
Government to prevent the closing of
Highfield Factory, which gave employment to 800 or 900 persons? The linen
machinery of that firm was purchased
quite recently by an English syndicate,
and they send scrap breakers with sledge
hammers to smash it. The tactics that
were adopted in the Highfield Factory
were also employed by the shipbuilding
companies to break up Workman & Clark's.
That was a very serious matter for the
country. Workman, Clark & Company's
was one of the greatest shipbuilding yards
in the world, and the Government made no
attempt to save it, but, on the contrary,
deliberately let those people come from
across the water to close the concern.
There was not one word of protest from
the right hon. Gentlemen on the other
side of the House. The result is that
thousands of workmen who were employed
by Workman & Clark's are being exploited
in shipyards in other parts of the British
Isles, owing to the action of this
Government.
The hon. Member for Pottinger (Mr.
Beattie) pointed out yesterday the conditions that prevail among the skilled
workers of Northern Ireland who have
been compelled to go across the water.
Those men are denied subsistence allowances because they come from loyal
Ulster. What has the Government done
to see that those men get the justice to
which Ulstermen are entitled ? Another
matter of grave importance is that no
action has been taken with a view to
getting an armaments factory established
here. Mr. Lavery, who is one of the
staunchest supporters of the Prime
Minister-if the Prime Minister said that
orange and purple were green Mr. Lavery
would agree with him-went to the War
Office, and was there told that no representations had been made by the Government of Northern Ireland on the subject.
That statement was made by Mr. Lavery
at a conference in the Law Courts, and
it has not been disputed. It has been
repeated at numerous public meetings.
He is an official Unionist from Ballymacarrett. Is it not strange that one of
the members of the Government's own
party should find out at the War Office
that no representations had been made
by the Northern Government with the
object of getting a share of the rearmament work? The Government have not
taken action, notwithstanding that there
are 100,000 unemployed persons, some of
these the best skilled workmen to be
found anywhere in the world.
I was surprised, therefore, when I saw
in the King's Speech that the Government are going to take steps to have new
industries established here. I have
pointed out that the Government have
done Ulster a great disservice by their
inaction. Is it not rather strange that all
the friends of the right hon. Gentlemen
opposite have severed their connection
with Ulster? Is it not true to say that
Robinson & Cleaver's now belongs to an
English syndicate? Is it not true to say
that Workman & Clark's was sold for
breaking-up purposes a long time ago?
Is it not true to say that one of the
greatest Unionist firms in the country,
Thomas Dixon & Sons, has sold all its
chattels to an English syndicate? Why
are all these blue-blooded supporters of
the Government selling their businesses
in Northern Ireland? (An hon. Member: Even Dunville's.) Yes, and they
made the best whisky in the world. The
Government are not concerned about the
old industries. I wish I only had the
power to do something. If I had had the
power I could have brought new industries to Northern Ireland. All that
these people do is prate about their
loyalty to this country, but it would be
a much better form of loyalty to invest

their money in their own country. They
are investing their money in foreign

I have listened with great attention to
a description of the terrible conditions

keep their eyes closed and vote blindly
at General Elections. I could go on for
a long time, but I understand that two
hon. Members wish to make their maiden
speeches. I think the people have been
sadly let down. Mr. Stewart, one of
your own standard-bearers, has repeatedly
pointed out that nothing has been done.
to get rearmament work here, and because
he raised that question he has been coldshouldered for the past two or three
years. (An hon. Member: What about
Mr. Kirk) He was living in the Grand
Central Hotel during
during the General
Election. Agriculture is mentioned in
the King's Speech, but no encouragement
has been given to the farmers of Northern
Ireland. There was a great ado about
Mr. Stewart bringing Belgian bricks
here, but when I look at the other side
of the House I see half-a-dozen Members
who import Belgian and Russian flax
every day in the week, notwithstanding
the fact that there are thousands of acres
of fertile land in Northern Ireland available for the growing of flax. If the
farmers of this area were given encouragement they could grow flax, and help to
give employment to the agricultural
workers who are in a state of starvation
at the present time.
I notice that the Government are
gratified by the fact that the local
authorities are carrying out work for the
relief of unemployment, and that right
hon. Gentlemen opposite are praising
themselves because 44 schemes, involving
a total capital expenditure of over
£900,000, were approved last year. What
are the facts? The ratepayers throughout the length and breadth of the country
have been reduced to the verge of bankruptcy by the Government of this country
refusing to make unemployment a
national question and to tackle the
problem themselves. The Government
have deliberately foisted the responsibility for unemployment on the shoulders
of the local authorities. The Government, for instance, struck an education
levy, which hit the local authorities very
severely. The Government have also put
an unemployment levy on the city of
Belfast, with the result that the rates
to-day are 10s in the £. The rates were
reduced to that figure from 10s 4d. It
was proposed that the rates should be
fixed at 10s 2d. Had that been done 400
men would have been employed in useful
work during the coming summer. But
the rates were reduced to 10s, and in consequence there will be 300 fewer men
employed on street works, 30 fewer men
in other work, and 20 to 30 fewer men in
the parks and playgrounds.
It is not the duty of the local authorities to look after the unemployed of this
country. They have tried to do it, but
they cannot continue to do so without
increasing the burden borne by the ratepayers all over the country. The ratepayers are clamouring for a reduction of
rates. Nearly every board in Northern
Ireland is composed of official Unionists,
and outside the city of Belfast I do not
think many of them have any regard for
the poor. They are all clamouring for a
reduction of rates, and if the Government wish to avoid criticism they must
make unemployment a national question.
If they continue to foist the responsibility for unemployment on the local
authorities the ratepayers and shopkeepers all over the country will find
themselves in bankruptcy.
I do not wish to say much more about
unemployment. I sincerely regret that
the Minister of Labour is not present on
this occasion. There is no Member of
this House for whom I have a higher
regard. I know that his case will be
looked after by the Minister of Finance.
The Government have five years of office
ahead of them, and they have an army
behind them. The Government supporters, especially the hon. and gallant
Member for Cromac (Captain Sinclair),
tell the outside public what they are going
to do for the unemployed. When the
testing time comes it will be found that
those Gentlemen will vote blindly with
the Government. Will the Minister of
Finance, who will be the spokesman for

the Prime Minister, tell us what the

the streets; they are a burden on their
The Minister of Finance will
parents.
tell the House that the Government are

They were born to work, and if allow
you
the youth of the country to rot you will

an
asset to the country if only our

I notice there is one suggestion in the
King's Speech that I would never expect
to hear of outside Honolulu, where they
used to turn out quoit champions in days
gone by. It says:
A Bill will be introduced authorising
my Government to give financial
assistance to urban authorities to
enable them to provide houses for our
industrial workers at reasonable
rents . . .
I agree with that, and it should have
stopped there, but it goes on to say:-
and also to facilitate the issue of loans
to the owners of working-class houses,
both in towns and in rural areas, for
the repair of such houses as can be
made fit for human habitation.
My opinion is that you are simply proposing to do that in order to assist your
estate agent friends. Does the Prime
Minister or the Minister of Finance think
for one moment that you could reconstruct or repair the houses in Urney
Street or Weir Street, where I used to
live, and put them in a proper sanitary
condition? Those houses were built
almost eighty years ago. The best thing
that can be done by the Government is
to re-house these people. You have numbers of skilled craftsmen who are unemployed and who could be utilised to
demolish slum property and build new
houses to accommodate the people.
A more monstrous suggestion than that
contained in the King's Speech I never
heard of. Every one of those houses that
were built eighty years ago was erected
on an earth foundation, because there
was no such thing as a damp course in
those days, and to give money to owners
of property of that kind is nothing less
than a scandal. It would take almost as
much to put in a damp course as it would
to build a fairly decent new house.
When
take into consideration the
you
fact that the floors and rafters have been
in these houses for seventy or eighty
years the suggestion that they should be
patched up is monstrous, and could only
emanate from the minds of such
antiquated politicians as sit on the front
Government benches.
Immediate steps should be taken to
embark upon a housing policy. Instead
of foisting this responsibility on to the
local authorities the Government should
itself take it upon its own shoulders
In the past the Government gave handsome subsidies for the building of houses,
but in ninety-nine cases out of every
hundred their rich friends put the subsidy of £140 into their own pockets.
Why should not the Government start to
build houses not only in Belfast but in
every part of the country. You would
not see worse hovels in Timbuctoo than
are to be seen in some of the constituencies represented by agricultural
Members in this House. If the Government's suggestion is carried out there
will be nothing to hinder the owners of
these dilapidated cottages from going to
the local authorities to get a loan for the

that were originally built of mud and
ordinary kidney paving stones. If that
is the only suggestion the Government is
capable of making God pity the electors
of Northern Ireland for returning such
a Government to power. I hope some of
the Members on the Government side of
the House will support the Members on
this side who have protested against this
iniquitous suggestion.

The Speech goes on to say :—
A Measure will be laid before you to
enable local authorities to prepare and
carry out schemes for the protection of
life and property in the event of attack
from the air in time of war.
That Measure is to be introduced
during the present Session, but before it
becomes effective in Northern Ireland we
will probably have to wait three or four
years. We on this side of the House have
been clamouring for something to be done
in this direction for the past three or four
years, and when they do provide this
financial assistance to local authorities I
hope they will be as
as liberal as the
Imperial Government have been. Up to
now there has been nothing done in
Northern Ireland in the way of providing
gas masks and underground chambers for
the protection of human life in case of
air raids. If this matter had been taken
up three or four years ago
there
would now be thousands of men employed
on the construction of these underground
chambers for the protection of the people
of this country.
I notice we are to have more Bills and
more Boards in connection with the
marketing of potatoes in order to maintain a reasonable price level in respect of
potatoes for shipment. That will mean
more hordes of officials and more jobs
for your political friends. Everything
you put your hands to means that the
taxpayers of this country have to pay for
more officials. You have more Bills dealing with the shipment of potatoes than
any other Parliament of a similar size in
the world. You have more legislation
regarding potatoes than the Mother of
Parliaments.
Mr. GRANT: We have more potatoes.
Mr. HENDERSON: We do not grow
enough potatoes to feed the people of
Southampton for a week. There could
be hundreds of thousands of tons more
potatoes grown in this country if the
farmers were getting justice, and if the
farm labourers were getting justice. If
this additional legislation will help the
farmers to stop exploiting the agricultural labourers, who have to starve on a
wage of 10s a week, I will give it my
whole-hearted support, notwithstanding
the fact that it may create another horde
of officials. The Government propose to
keep children at school until they are
fifteen years
of age. You can keep them
at school in the industrial areas as well
as in agricultural areas not only until
they are fifteen but until they are twentyfive because there is nothing for them to
do. There is no work for them, so that,
providing you make arrangements to
assist their parents, you can keep them
at school. It would be far better if the
Government gave their fathers and
mothers a handsome sum every week to
enable them to keep their boys and girls
at school until they are twenty, because
when they leave school to-day they get a
job for about two years and then their
employers throw them into the street,
and there is nothing for them but to
parade the streets day in and day out.
I could go on talking for quite a long
time, but it would make no difference so
far as
the Government is concerned.
Even if we talked for years nothing would
be done to assist the unemployed of this
country. I am sorry that in the King's
Speech not one reference is made to
making the Border safe for the Ulster.
loyalists. Not one reference is made to

Yesterday in this House the Prime Minister stated that when they were on the
hustings some Members of this House

pensions increased to £1 per week. I for
one did so, and if I was in power in this
House I would increase old age pensions
to £1 per week without any trouble, and
you can do it if you like.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
will have to put down a Motion on that

Mr. HENDERSON: Widows, orphans,

£2,000 a year for doing six weeks' work

as you get the money for the payment of

suggestion as to how you can partially

if the people see a red light and he tells
them it is a blue light they will believe

stated time and again that Ulster's credit
is known all over the world. I do not
agree with him, because it is not even
known in London. Last year the hon.
Member for Pottinger and myself were
stopping in an hotel in Tottenham Court
Road. As I always like to advertise
Ulster I asked the attendant if he knew
where Ulster was, and he replied that
there was nobody of that name stopping
at the hotel. Apparently Ulster has not
been advertised in London. You should
start with London and try to get the
friends who gave you £30,000 or £40,000
to run your election to invest anything
up to twenty millions pounds in Ulster
in order that new industries may be
created. The credit of Ulster is good
for twenty or thirty million pounds, and
the loan could be spread over 40 or 50
years.
This King's Speech is the most amazing document presented to any Parliament. It is stated with a flourish of
trumpets that the Government is making
its labour exchanges more modern. The
Prime Minister stated yesterday that he
addressed a meeting on the Shankill
Road at which there were 2,000 or 3,000
men, and he asked all those who wanted
work to stand up and all the men stood.
It was the first time in history that I
ever heard of a Prime Minister going
to a free supper. You were at a supper
given in the Albert Hall, and the people
on that occasion shouted that it was not
talk they wanted but work. Matters
have got worse since the Prime Minister
was up the Shankill Road. It was the
Rev. Henry Montgomery who gathered
the men into one huge building in order
to give them a free supper. The unemployed in Northern Ireland to-day are
being kept by charitable organisations
because the Government has failed them.
In order to help the people I suggest,
first of all, that you get your rich friends
to invest their money in Ulster, and,
secondly, that you float a loan of twenty
million pounds. The Minister of Labour
stated in this House that he spends four
million pounds on unemployment benefit.
Would it not be a good idea if the Minister of Finance added two millions to the
four millions which he will be paying
out next year, and with the six millions
at his disposal built forty or fifty
thousand workers' houses all over the
country? That would give employment
to every skilled worker-bricklayers,
hodsmen, plasterers, painters, joiners,
and others. It would also provide employment for the semi-skilled artisans. If
you did that you would be able to say:
"We do not pay dole in our country.
We borrow money, add to it the money
we would be giving away in unemployment benefit and build houses with it.
If we did not do that the people would
be running about idle and drawing the
dole."
Is there any other country so backward in so far as roads are concerned?
The roads outside the main arteries are
terrible. On many of them two buses
cannot pass. I suggest that you employ
another 10,000 Ulstermen reconstructing
these roads and make them 150 feet wide.
Is there any reason why that should not
be done? Adjoining all the main roads.
throughout Northern Ireland you have
large quarries, and the Transport Board
-I had better not say anything about
that Board because it would be like
shaking a red rag at a bull-could be
utilised to draw the stones to the roads.
You could get millions of tons of stones
on the County Down coast, and with
these stones the roads could be widened.
The Crown, if the Prime Minister used
his influence, would allow you to gather
all the boulders from Donaghadee to Kircubbin.

Mr. BROWN: As one sent from the
largest constiuency in County Down to

taken to banish the grim spectre of unemployment and to relieve our sorelypressed farmers from the plight that so
many of them are in to-day, although, I
must confess, these references fall short

urgent necessity for these steps we are, I

numerous diametrically-opposed but none
the less honestly-held views, and I avail

once, with the grievous ills of industrial

I most profoundly disagree with the
hon. and learned Member for St. Anne's
when he stated, in moving the Address in
Reply to the King's Speech, that there
is no immediate cure for unemployment.
I say that this statement is a slander on
the genius of our race. The spirit of our
people, which built the great industries
that were the envy of the globe and converted this once rock-strewn land into
fertile fields, must not, and will not, fail
to find a panacea for this demoralising
evil. If the old confidence and determination of our people, that regarded
difficulties only as something to be overcome, is not still there-and I do not
admit it is not still there-this House
must re-create it. There is the grave
danger of our becoming so accustomed to
a third of our working-class people being
unemployed that we will unconsciously
drift into the position of regarding it as
a permanent feature of our existence, and
allowing apathy and inertia to fasten such
a grip upon us as we will not be able
to free ourselves from in this generation.
The statement of the hon. and learned
Member of St. Anne's will have a most
unfortunate psychological effect at this
critical juncture, and I am glad that the
hon. and youthful Member for Enniskillen, who seconded the Address, did not
share the gloom of the proposer. Unemployment can and will be cured, and
I am going to give you the basis of the
cure here to-day.
Before I proceed to give you the details
of my schemes let us consider for a
moment how closely related are the

some
depressions in commerce and agriculture,

Let the economic and social fabric and

to the country. Unfortunately, the
whole tendency of recent years has been
to centralise big undertakings and industries in the city to the grievous loss of
the provincial towns, but not even the

Road transport amalgamation. has
given us higher fares, and higher charges
for farm and industrial freightage, and
fewer facilities, and deprived many hard
workers of livelihoods, so much so that a
Commission has had to be set up to review
the whole present very unsatisfactory
position.
Shipping combines have resulted in
depriving South Down of no less than
four passenger steamship services with
Cross-Channel ports, and have left us
without a single solitary link of the kind
with England, Wales or Scotland. It is
the duty of this Government to make
possible by subsidies, as the British
Government has done across the water in

and a cross-Channel port, which would
not only greatly aid tourist development

but would also provide much and greatly
needed expedition in the Northern Ireland cross-Channel mail service.
Multiple shops are gradually ousting
our small, hard-working individual
traders, who require an immediate consideration of their precarious position.
And now this disastrous policy of
swallowing up small enterprises in the
towns, on the roads and on the seas, in
the craze for trusts, combines, monopolies
and amalgamations, threatens to breakout

very glad the Minister of Agriculture is
because

If
I totally disagree with the suggestion

it does I for one must strenuously oppose

Experience has shown in the numerous
depressions or economic blizzards that have
swept over the world that small concerns
were able to defy such depressions when
many big trusts and combines were going
down in the storm, and I know of my
own knowledge, gained in visits paid at
different times to America, Canada,
Belgium, France, Switzerland and
Germany, that the intensively-cultivated small holding yielded much
more happiness of mind and financial
security than the immense tracts of graingrowing lands in the States and Canada,
where on my visits I heard of many full
asylums because of the intolerable loneliness and strain involved in running such
huge and isolated undertakings.
a
Wipe out the small holdings of our
country and you wipe out one of the
greatest nurseries of one of our greatest
possessions a sturdy spirit of selfreliance and self-help,
spirit of
integrity, industry, thrift and perseverance, a spirit of reality and recognition
and appreciation of true values that
springs from contact with the simple and
essential things of life. The Bible tells
us more than once of the ideal state on
earth, when they shall sit every man
under his vine and under his fig tree and
none shall make them afraid, and history
and literature since then is full of praise
of the humble agriculturist and of warnings of the woes that follow any interference with a country's peasantry.
"The small landowners are the most
precious part of the State," wrote Thomas
Jefferson, and Emerson tells us that the
first farmer was the first man, and that
all historic nobility rests on possession
and use of land, and that all trade rests
at last on the primitive and creative
activity of agriculture, which, says
Edward Gibbon, is the foundation of
manufactures, since productions of
nature are the materials of art. Bryant
tells us that
"Far back in the ages,
The plough with wreaths was
crowned;
The hands of kings and sages
Entwined the chaplet round."
Our own countryman, Dean Swift, tells
us that "Whoever could make two ears
of corn, or two blades of grass, to grow
upon a spot where only one grew before,
would deserve better of mankind, and
do more essential service to his country,
than the whole race of politicians put
together." Another distinguished Irishman, Oliver Goldsmith, has told us in
words that no one can mistake the
meaning of, that
"A bold peasantry, their country's pride,
When once destroyed, can never be
supplied;"
and that
"A time there was, ere England's griefs
began,
When every rood of ground maintained
its man.

the

potatoes has been left unaided, and

The drop in last year's flax crop of 6,377
acres is another warning. In South
Down and in Mourne I have witnessed
the tragedy of hundreds of tons of good
potatoes being thrown into the sea or
buried in the ground as useless, because
no market could be found for them, and today, although they are nominally quoted
in the market reports at 1s 6d to 2s per

What is the remedy against such violent
fluctuations in price and against gluts of
potatoes in general? It is this: Let the
Government erect factories for making industrial spirit and motor spirit from our
surplus stocks of potatoes and thus maintain a stable price, and let them insist on
such spirit being used in all vehicles in
Government service, such as police cars
and lorries, etc., and in all vehicles and
factories of such semi-Government concerns as the Transport Board, the Pigs.
Marketing Board, etc.
Newry as the centre of the most important farming district in Northern
Ireland has an irresistible claim to one at
least of such potato spirit factories, just
as it has an unanswerable priority to one
of the Pigs Marketing Board's pork
factories by virtue of the fact that Newry

bacon curing factory, and seventy-five per
cent. of our once great granite industry,
and where to-day we have a total of
3,621, or almost a third of the population

a

workless, spoke yesterday of hope of

our portion of the factories
necessitated by the Imperial Government's huge rearmament expenditure of

Drainage of large tracts of periodically

Before concluding my references to

imposed thirty years ago, which prevent
the farmers of Newry, Warrenpoint,
Rostrevor, and Kilkeel districts from

because of the harm it would do our commerce, and if this argument holds good

As well as my scheme for bringing
about the salvation of agriculture, I have
a scheme too for putting the fishing industry on its feet. In October last I was
a saddened spectator of 127,000 excellent,
freshly-caught herrings being dumped
back into the sea on one night alone at

for them, or because the people were not

Queen to eat more wholesome herrings,

Government can save a once fine industry

our appalling unemployment figures.
Financial facilities to the fishing industry in general must also be increased
and simplified. Although this industry
