Housing is also mentioned in the
King's Speech, and I am much gratified
to learn of the probability of greatly increased Government aid for the erection
of more houses at cheaper rents for the
working classes, because in the town of
Newry alone we have still 207 human
beings condemned to exist in hovels
officially described as unfit for human
habitation, with, in some cases, as many
as seven, six, or five people in one room
without segregation of the sexes or isolation of tuberculosis cases, which are
exacting a greater toll than any war.
In conclusion, let me say that I am
well aware of the regrettable fact that
unemployment and lean times in agriculture and industry in general are world
wide, but there is no reason why Northern Ireland should not lead the world
with a solution or even a partial solution
of these problems of our age, just as we
have led the world with the best ships,
the best linen and the best farm produce
in the universe. Are we who have been
noted for our enterprise to sit down and
in a spirit of defeatism await the end, or
are we going to make a characteristic
fight for our continued industrial and
agricultural existence? As for me, I am
going to fight. If we all prefer the latter
course, as I think we do, let us make a
start right here and now with the
schemes and suggestions I have detailed
and give the world another example of
our statesmanship and our leadership, and
better days for all will have already
begun and the nightmare of no work for
willing workers will slowly but surely
become only a memory of the unhappy
past.
Mr. AGNEW: On reading the King's
Speech I was sorely disappointed, from
the Labour standpoint, at the items
which have been put forward by the Government who have been returned by a
large majority and who have been carrying on the machinery for the past 17
years. As one affected by unemployment, I understand from personal experience what unemployment really is.
I would like to ask the members of the
Government do they really understand
unemployment as we have found it, or
do they understand the terrible evils
which spring from it?
I
I would like to place unemployment
under three headings. We have those
who are idle and in receipt of unemployment benefit, which only lasts for a
short period. They are living a mere
existence. We have others affected by
what I would call an inhuman system of
unemployment assistance. It brings the
unemployed down to what I would term
the border line of starvation. We now
come to the third and last degree of unemployment as enshrined in the Poor
Relief Act, the administration of which
is carried out by boards of guardians,
which are relics of former days.
say the Government have neglected their
duty in dealing with this situation,
seeing that we have over 100,000 unemployed. I have watched the state of
affairs in my own county, Armagh.
have been personally in contact with the
unemployed for the last ten years, dealing with their grievances and trying to
assist them to the best of my ability.
Their lives are lives of uncertainty, and
we who are engaged in the working-class
movement issue a strong challenge to the
Government to declare that they have
honestly tried to find a solution.
I
Such things as are outlined in the
King's Speech are only small matters,
Facing us who know the actual state of
affairs, the Government should come
forward with a constructive policy in
order to solve this great problem. They
have been lacking in constructive policy
during the last seventeen years.
If we
look at the linen industry, which is
mentioned in the King's Speech, in my
own area we find that that industry
which was once a source of employment
is practically non-existent to-day. I say
it is a disgrace that the Government
should not have considered that state of
affairs many years ago, because since
1931 we have found that the situation in
Armagh has become exceedingly worse.
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Agnew]
Taking my own constituency, South
Armagh, I find that in Bessbrook and
Keady, the only areas in which the linen
industry operated, it is not in a very
prosperous state. We know the reaction
from the loss of the linen industry. It
means an additional army of unemployed
struggling for other employment and
making the lot of the other workers
harder. I say the Government are not
immune from criticism in regard to the
industrial situation as we find it to-day
in Northern Ireland. Surely it should
not take them seventeen years to make
up their minds in order to get to the
bottom of this question, because the depression has not existed only a matter
of days or months. It has been a matter
of years.
This problem must be faced
in a spirit that will place it on a better
and sounder basis.
I come now to the question of new
industries. It has been the Labour
policy all along to visualise what the
British Government have done in regard
to what are known as distressed areas.
We cannot say the same of the Northern
Government. They have not SO far
appointed a Commission to consider what
we would call the distress that is found
in Northern Ireland, and particularly
industrial depression, which causes distress. If the British Government can
send their Minister of Labour to South
Wales in order to find out the facts, we
in the Labour movement suggest that
the Northern Government should have
sent from their Department those responsible to see the actual state of affairs for
themselves. If such had been done there
would have been greater results.
If we take South Armagh we find
scutch mills, where flax was scutched in
the raw state, and corn mills studded all
over the country; and in my opinion
they are a strong reminder to the Government of their inability to govern in so
far as the industrial life of Northern
Ireland is concerned. The delay in
tackling those problems has left the
position very difficult, because those flax
mills and corn mills are ruined, and
financial assistance would be needed to
place them on a better footing. The
people who feel the pinch are not always
the owners, but the people who have
been employed. They are the sufferers
at all times.
One of my greatest ambitions in life
has been the furtherance of schemes of
public utility. At our local authority in
Armagh I have always on every occasion
struggled to see Armagh City placed in
a fitter and more healthy state.
If we
take South Armagh, from the point of
view of water supply, I find it in a very
backward state. It is also very backward in regard to sanitation, that is, as
to a sewerage system, and in regard to
town planning and town improvement.
There is a serious unwillingness on the part
of the Government and the local authorities to deal with the situation, but I am
glad to say that representations have been
made through the Labour movement that
those very serious problems should be
tackled, and there are hopes that
through this pressure something will be
done.
By
Now we come to the question of roads.
The roads in South Armagh are, I
believe, the worst roads in Ireland. The
first-class roads there are no better than
thrid-class roads, and even where there
is bus traffic it is very difficult for a
motor-car to pass a bus on a road. It
can only do so at great danger. That
is a job that should be tackled.
widening these roads, taking away bad
corners, and providing the necessary
work something would be done to help
to solve the unemployment problem.
Schemes of public utility are essential
for that purpose.
I notice in the King's
Speech that we are going to have more
palatial and up-to-date employment
exchanges. If the best the Government
can do is to build employment exchanges
they have absolutely no solution for unemployment. Labour exchanges do not
always augur well for prosperity. They
are the relic of a disease which ought
to be removed and not encouraged. The
Government ought not to build labour
exchanges as they do not stand for prosperity or progress.
Then the Bann drainage is mentioned
in the King's Speech. There are many
other areas affected by flooding throughout County Armagh. To have them
drained would be of great service to the
public.
I come now to the question of new
schools. One thing which strikes me
very forcibly in regard to the building
of new schools is, does the Government
ever consider the state of affairs affect-
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
2 MARCH 1938
ing those sending their children to the
schools. Under present-day conditions
children attend school under-fed and
under-nourished and their parents are
not in a position to provide even the
necessary books. Do the Government
ever think of following step by step with
the British Government on the question
of free books and free meals? Those are
things which we in our day have tried
to obtain. From my experience in Great
Britain I find that the system of free
books has been in operation for many
years. Outside Belfast, as far as I
know, free books are only provided to
necessitous children. I say it is not too
much to ask for free books for every
child at school.
In regard to conditions in factories,
it is time that something was done in
order to end the sweated conditions which
prevail. But that should not only apply
to certain industries. It is the duty of
the Government to pass the necessary
legislation so that all factories should
come within its scope in order to see that
the workers are properly housed and
in healthy surroundings.
I am somewhat bewildered regarding
the coming changes in Unemployment
and National Health Insurance. In view
of the existing anomalies under the Unemployment Insurance Act, owing to the
abnormal depression in Northern Ireland,
there are some people who may find it
possible to get one or two days per week.
They cannot find any further employment, and the inevitable result is that
they automatically become classified as
being only normally employed for two
days a week. That is a grave injustice
in an abnormal time. This should
receive the serious consideration of the
Department concerned, because it is
affecting many of our people. I have
experience in appearing before courts of
referees, and in these cases the result isdisallowed. That disallowance means
that they will be disallowed by the Unemployment Assistance Board as being
only normally insurable for that particular time, two days a week, and then
they become the victims of what I call the
pauper state, the poor law system, which
is the last resort, and should be abolished.
We come to the question of blind
pensions. I may be wrong, but as far as
I can remember, under British administration, as in Glasgow and other places,
blind pensioners are assisted sufficiently
to be guaranteed a better standard of life.
I believe that in Belfast a little stretch
is given to people who suffer the terrible
affliction of blindness and poverty. Are
the Northern Government satisfied that
persons afflicted with blindness and
poverty can exist on 10s a week? This is
a reminder to the Government that they
have been lacking in regard to finding
their feet in so far as these people are
concerned.
Now we come to the very important
question of housing. That is a problem
that has faced us in Armagh for many
years. We have many premises-there
are 400 houses in Armagh to-day-unfit
for human habitation. The Government
have been lacking in their duty so far
as that area is concerned. In South
Armagh the housing conditions, both
urban and rural, are, I believe, worse
than in any other part of Northern
Ireland. I have inspected some of the
houses myself, and I would be ashamed
to give an honest opinion of the actual
situation as I find it there. The time
has come for building decent homes for
the people. In regard to the question of
houses, the quantity is all right, it is a
question of the quality. We want to see
the workers housed with ample accommodation, sufficient air space for their
children, and at a rent in accordance
with their means. I am afraid there are
regulations in force to-day which permit
only a certain type of house.
should be wiped out. We want houses
fit for the people in accordance with the
family requirements. We say, up with
the houses and down with the slums.
They
The next question is what are called
air raid precautions. It is a terrible
thought that in this age of progress we
find the Northern Government prepared
to think out a plan to provide precautions for their citizens in case of war.
We thought the last war was a war to
end war. Now the destruction of
humanity seems to be the ideal of all
nations, and we are a party to it. That
science should serve humanity and not
destroy it should be the great ideal of
all. Air raid precautions will be taken
throughout Northern Ireland simply
because the statesmen and those concerned have not the wisdom to bring
peace.
Peace can be obtained when war
is over. All the nations can agree to
Debate on the Address
Adjournment
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Agnew]
discuss it then, but they cannot find the
time to do so prior to the blood bath.
To-day we stand for freedom, peace and
security.
Next we come to the question of
physical training for our youth. I would
like to see the average unemployed
husband, wife, and family doing their
daily dozen, but before anything is done
as regards physical training it would be
a far sounder investment for the Government to consider the giving of food, clothing and shelter. That is the main issue.
After all, I would like to know what is
behind this physical training, and where
it will lead to.
We come now to the question of the
raising of the school-leaving age.
Exemptions will be made. If we are
going to have exemptions as far as
the raising of the school age is concerned, the Act will be an absolute
farce. That is what it amounts to. It
should be made compulsory for children
to attend school until they are fifteen
years of age, with certain additional help
given to those responsible. Exemptions
will mean that industry will be overcrowded again by the youth leaving the
schools, and the result will be that those
who to-day are walking the streets will
never find work. Cheap labour will
always be carried on by the youth. That
is a terrible monopoly in Northern
Ireland to-day.
I now come to the operations of the
Loans Guarantee Acts. There is one
thing I am not clear about. Does this
Measure apply to the small peasant
farmers of Northern Ireland? I say that
the small farming community are in a
very terrible plight. Take South
Armagh. It would be a splendid place
for tourists to see the actual conditions
that prevail in the rural areas of Northern Ireland. It is what I would call
the Connemara of the North, wild
mountainous, and rocky, where farmers
with four, five or six-acre holdings are
trying to exist. It is a matter for the
Ministry of Agriculture to see that the
small farming community are not completely wiped out, because they form the
backbone of the community. I think
the Government have failed to come to
the aid of the small farmers.
I come now to the question of the
Exhibition in Glasgow. Seeing that we
are likely to have a stall there, it would
be a good thing to adopt some of the
ideals of the Corporation which has
promoted that great undertaking. We
know who constitute the Corporation
that to-day is trying to build up an
Exhibition to show the products of the
Empire. It would do Northern Ireland
a good turn if the Government would
only try to follow some of the other social
ideals of that body, for the benefit of
the common people.
When I, as a workers' representative,
view the position as it stands to-day, I
find nothing to make me enthusiastic in
regard to the King's Speech. It contains what I would call a very meagre
allowance for a stricken people. It is
the duty of the Government to guarantee
security to the citizens and to look after
the unemployed, who constitute the
problem with which we are most concerned to-day. Whilst poverty and unemployment remain, it is an indication
that the Government are unable to tackle
the problem after so many years in
office. They evade their responsibilities,
and I, as a representative of the Labour
movement, demand justice and security
for my class.

THIRD DAY.
Order read for resuming Adjourned
Debate on Question (1st March),
"That an humble Address be presented to the His Grace the Governor
of Northern Ireland, as follows:
:-
"Your Grace,
"We, His Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Commons of
Northern Ireland, in Parliament
assembled, beg leave to offer our
humble thanks to Your Grace for the
speech which Your Grace has addressed
to both Houses of Parliament."-(Mr.
Warnock).
Question again proposed.
Mr. NIXON: I would like, with your
permission, to follow the example of the
Prime Minister and extend a welcome to
all new Members to this Protestant Parliament for a Protestant people. I also want
to congratulate the mover and seconder of
the Address. It was my privilege on
former occasions in other places to listen
to the eloquence of the mover of the
Address. He had a rather difficult task
to perform here. I noticed that when
he began to speak on the question of
unemployment he got into a most
despondent mood-into an attitude of
despair. He said, among other things,
that he was not going to make promises,
but the hon. and learned Member is the
very man who made promises not long
ago, if the papers reported him correctly.
I am sure, being a loyalist-there are no
official Unionists now, they are all
loyalists that they did report him correctly. I read in a speech he made in
St. Anne's Division, subsequent to his
election-I do not profess to quote the
words exactly, but I am quoting the substance of what the hon. and learned
Member did say he said that he would
insist on something being done for the
unemployed. When he got on his feet
here he did not insist on that; he rather
despaired.
The hon. and learned Member was
followed by an hon. Member from
Enniskillen. By the way, I think I may
congratulate the Government on having
such a lot of members of the legal profession in Parliament. Personally, I
always liked them. If you get a proper
legal man you will undoubtedly get a
squarer deal from him than any other
man. At the same time, I do not see
where the Government are going to get
jobs for them all. I do not think they
come into Parliament for their own
benefit; they come into Parliament for
the good of the people and of the
country. Everyone knows that. The
hon. Member for Enniskillen had not
much to tell us, except that he did not
agree with the mover of the Address that
nothing could be done. At all events,
we know that nothing has been done up
to the present. Then we had a speech
from another new Member from Newry.
I cannot congratulate the Chief Whip
on that speech. The Chief Whip no
doubt will bring the hon. Member into
line. He thought when he had got the
hon. Member for South Down a seat on
that side he had him, but when the hon.
Member got on his feet he found he had
not got him. We saw that he would
have to get another touch, and I am sure
he will.
The hon. Member for Windsor made
a speech in Windsor the other night on
the question of unemployment, and it
was such a speech as I would make myself. I noticed yesterday the Chief Whip
sat beside him for an hour. He was talking him over; he was bringing him into
line. I am about the only one he cannot manage. I told him yesterday that
I have just as many tricks as he has, and
that is a good many. Anyhow, here we
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
3 MARCH 1938
are back again, and I propose to deal with
the question of unemployment, but I will
leave it over until later, as I want to
speak on one or two other matters first.
We know there is leglsiation promised
in the King's Speech to enable local
authorities to take measures for protection in case of air raids. I want to say
something about that. A great many
people think there might be no air raids
here, but I would not like to assume
that. I am giving away no secret when
I tell the House that if three bombs were
dropped on the power house-every
technical man in Europe knows what is
in the power house-Ulster would be
paralysed, as power for industry all over
the Province is drawn largely from that
power house. What this Bill proposes
to do or what has been done up to the
present does not satisfy me. All we have
got up to the present are lectures. We
have been told how the ambulance would
take us away and how we would be buried
when we were killed.
That is good enough in its own way,
but that was never my way of dealing
with a thing. I would like to see as
many guns here as would make it impossible for aircraft to have any considerable success. I cannot see why there
should not be at least one hundred antiaircraft guns mounted round the city in
suitable places. I know as well as anyone there is no need to tell me that
the Imperial authorities are responsible
for our defences. At the same time, it
is up to the Northern Government, who
are responsible for the lives of the people
and the industry of the country, to see,
not exactly how we are going to be buried
if we were poisoned or where gas-masks
are to be got, but what guns there are to
drive off the aeroplanes. If I was in
power myself I would start this evening,
because if there were plenty of modern
guns available the aeroplanes would not
be likely to take a very good aim.
Some people think that to come here
the aeroplanes would have to cross Great
Britain. Not necessarily. We know
that a great many cruisers carry aircraft
which can be launched from places other
than Great Britain, and if Great Britain
vas properly protected they would be
more likely to come across here, where
there would be a lot of work being done
for the Admiralty. I am not making any
criticism, but I would like to see more
done. I would like to see the precautions and the defence taking the nature
of counter-attack. That is always the
best defence. It does not matter if it
is only in an election, counter-attack is
far better than defence. I know that,
and that is why I succeed.
There is another question I want to
refer to before I come to unemployment,
but I will not spend long on it. Legislation for the building of new houses is
foreshadowed that is all right-and for
the lending of money to the owners of
slum property for the repair of old
houses that is all wrong. Some of the
kitchen houses are being sold at as low
as £50, or even less. I do not see why
the public health and other authorities
should not compel the owners of slum
property to put the houses in proper
repair. I certainly object to public
money being voted into the pockets of
owners of slum property for the purpose
of repairing and doing up houses.
never heard such a proposal in my life.
It was brought forward one time in the
City Council, and I proved that the man
who brought it up had a quarter of an
acre of the worst slum property in the
city. I object to that part of the proposal altogether. You might as well
give a man money to repair a private
house. I know this is talked of as a loan,
but I know where these loans go in the
end. I hope that matter will get more
consideration before it goes any farther.
I
What has been done and what is going
to be done about unemployment? The
Prime Minister in his speech-I may not
quote it properly, but I give the substance of it-said that when the new
Minister of Labour was appointed he was
so overcome with the conditions of the
unemployed that it preyed on his health,
and that he is now ill. We all regret
the absence of the Minister through
illness. He is a most courteous gentleman, who never said an unkind word in
this House and who never struck below
the belt. But on the high authority of
the Prime Minister he found things in
such a state that it upset his health.
Who is going to reply to the debate this
evening? The Minister of Finance, who
left unemployment in such a condition
that when his successor took up office
what he had to look at, on the authority
of the Prime Minister, so upset his health
that he became ill.
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
That is what the Minister of Finance
did when he was Minister of Labour for
so many years. Now he is going to windup this debate.
I hope he will not leave
the Ministry of Finance in the same
state. It is bad enough, as we were told
from that side of the House, for the
health of the unemployed to be undermined by starvation, but when a Minister, who is appointed to look after them.
and take charge of the Department, is
so kind-hearted that it upsets his health
things are bad indeed. Yet the Minister
of Finance thinks he is the most competent Minister in the world.
The Prime Minister told us that no
Government should interefere with
industry. I subscribe to that. But who
interfered with it more than the Prime
Minister and the Government? Who
interfered with the transport industry
and made it the laughing stock of
Europe? A similar proposal was turned
down in the Imperial Parliament. I told
the Prime Minister, and several other
Members told him, that he should not
interfere with it, and now he is coming
round to our way of thinking, that no
one should interfere with industry, and
that no one should make promises about
unemployment.
Another hon. Member
-he is not here to-day-told us that unemployment should not be a political
question. Who made it a political
question? Who covered the walls of
Belfast with posters telling us what the
Government had done for the unemployed
and about all the ships they got built
in Belfast, and all the great work they
did, when, as a matter of fact, instead
of helping the shipbuilding industry they
permitted one shipyard to close?
The Prime Minister gave us an account
of his famous promise made in West
Belfast Orange Hall on 28th November,
1923. The noble Lord's memory is
greatly at fault. He told us that the
meeting was largely composed of men,
and that he invited them to stand up if
they wanted work. They did so, and
then he made the promise that if the
Imperial Government would not solve the
unemployment question he would. That
promise was made at a political meeting
held in support of the present hon.
Member for North Antrim. At about
four o'clock in the afternoon a telephone
message came to Brown Square Barrack
to provide a guard of honour of "B"
Specials to accompany the Prime Minister
to West Belfast Orange Hall. They met
him at Peter's Hill and marched up with
him, step for step, to the Orange Hall.
There was a meeting at the hall. They
were not all men, but were mostly women.
Anyone who goes up there knows that it
is the women who go to these political
meetings, as the men have too much
sense.
I would not mind if that was the only
promise made. Prior to that the Prime
Minister said there was a period of unprecedented prosperity before Ulster, and
then later, in the People's Palace, on
26th November, 1927, he said that
neither the Minister of Labour nor he
would rest until every man who desired
work had an opportunity to work in
Ulster. They have no opportunity to
work in Ulster. There are thousands of
them working in Great Britain. When
the Prime Minister made his statement
on 28th November, 1923, the unemployment roll-I am speaking from memory
-was about 43,000 odd, and now we know
it is over 100,000. Unless I am a false
prophet, if nothing is done next winter
it will be 115,000.
What has been done, or what is going
to be done? You have a perfect right to
ask me what I would do, and I have no
right to stand here and denounce you if
I cannot answer that question. I can
answer it, and I have answered it before.
With the country in the state it is in at
present, instead of calling an election you
should have called Parliament together
and passed a resolution declaring this a
distressed or special area. I think the
technical expression is a special area.
You should have applied for a grant and
got it. It was not necessary to rush away
to smash that Independent Association.
I knew myself they were not strong, and
it was not necessary to do that at all.
What was necessary was to get something
done for the unemployed. But nothing
has been done, and nothing is going to be
done. Not alone that, but I charge the
Prime Minister-I do not say he does
it deliberately-with preventing work
from coming to Ulster by his policy.
What is the proof in support of that
charge? Does not the Prime Ministe
every four years raise a hullabaloo that
we are not safe. that we are going to be
overrun from the Free State? That is

Nobody would.
That is one way the Prime Minister

is not permitted in other countries is
that the Cabinet Ministers, if they were

might be in possession of information

directors. In addition to that, there is

reported to the Ministry of Commerce.
I want to say at the outset I know as well

As late as November last we were told

in Ulster. On 2nd November Sir Wilson

The Northern Government had

That was
established a short time
ago when
Western Australia wanted to cede from

people who might think of coming here.
for the purpose of investing money.
I do not think I will say much more at

He is the only man who could tell you

ago. When the right hon. Gentleman

thousands who are out of work. I do not

But if a full-blooded Roman Catholic is 99

must be 49 per cent. disloyal. They

They know the religion of everybody, and

But, what are you going to do for the

Rev. ROBERT MOORE: If I may I

work which our fathers did to teach the

The
In regard to unemployment, I am concerned very much with the increase in
unemployment amongst agricultural
labourers. I fear that of the thousands
who to-day are classified as agricultural
labourers on the unemployment list 90
per cent. within the next twelve months
or a little more will take steps to be no
longer classified as agricultural labourers,
but as industrial workers, and thus to
qualify for the higher rate of unemployment benefit. I am up against the constant tendency to drift away from the
land, and something will have to be done
to counteract it. To my mind we could
take those thousands of agricultural
workers, or 90 per cent. of them,
multiply the number by the days they
have been unemployed this winter, and
the result would about represent the
amount of work that has not been done
on the farms of the Six Counties this
winter. That is work that should have
been done, such as reclamation, improvement of fences, improvement of lanes and
roadways, and so on, for want of which
farms in many instances are steadily deteriorating and going back to their
natural state.
I wonder if it would not be possible
for the Government to help by making it
easier to obtain the grant which is available in certain cases for drainage and
improvement work on the land. I do not
see why some of the conditions governing
this grant should not be removed. If by
doing so the Government would enable
the farmers to absorb these unemployed
farm workers it would be all to the good.
If it would help to keep the land of the
Six Caunties in good arable condition we
would be creating or maintaining an
asset which is surely invaluable to the
people of Northern Ireland. There is a
reference in the King's Speech to an
amendment of the Marketing of Potatoes
Acts, which will be introduced with the
object of enabling the Ministry of Agriculture to take steps to see that the
prices fixed from time to time for
potatoes are adhered to.
Unfortunately the prices fixed for
potatoes this year have been far below
the cost of production. One explanation,
to my mind, of the very large numbers
of farm workers unemployed is the very
low prices received for potatoes. This is
the main cash crop on which the average
farmer has to depend to carry on during
the winter, and this winter he has not
had enough money available from this
source. He has had, therefore, to allow
his men to drop off one after another and
thus they become unemployed. If something more than merely safeguarding the
prices which are fixed could be done,
something which would make the price an
economic one to the producer that, to my
mind, would go a long way towards
the
solving
unemployment problem
amongst agricultural workers.
The question of flax has not been
referred to in the King's Speech, but I
should like the Minister of Agriculture
some time to inform the House what is
the position in regard to this crop. Could
he tell us if anything has been achieved,
or is likely to be achieved, with the Imperial authorities to get this crop brought
under the Inskip Committee from the
point of view of Imperial defence. I do
not know whether anything has been done

along that line, but I say flax is a crop
that gives a maximum of employment, and
something should be done to set this crop
on its feet again by guaranteeing a
reasonable price to the producer. If that
were done it would help to solve the unemployment problem both on the farm
and in industry, because the ramifications
of this crop run far beyond the farm.
With regard to pensions for blind
people I merely wish to say that I am in
sympathy with the lowering of the age
qualification.
I should like to say a word with regard
to the proposal to make it possible for
teachers to forego part of their personal
pension in favour of a small pension payable to a named beneficiary such as a
wife or a daughter. I believe that is a
step in the right direction. I have in
mind another type of case-I do not
know whether hon. Members are aware
of any such cases, but I know of a teacher
afflicted with a form of sleepy sickness.
He is trying to carry on his profession in
an elementary school. Every month or
six weeks he has to leave his work and
rest for a week or ten days. He is
struggling on from year to year in the
hope of being able eventually to qualify
for a pension. I think that in a genuine
case of that kind the Government ought
to be able, through the Ministry of
Education and the Ministry of Finance,
to relieve a person who is suffering from
a disease due to causes over which he has
no control. This man is suffering and the
school and the scholars are suffering too.
No one can convince me, no matter how
inspectors may slip over a case of that
kind, that the standard of education in a
school of that sort can be what it should
be. This would only occur in an odd
case. I think the matter could be
straightened out and the teacher safeguarded. We ought to be in a position
to relieve individuals of that kind from
having to slave in order to secure a pension upon which they and their
dependents can subsist.
Regarding the proposal to raise the
school-leaving age from 14 to 15 years I
am in thorough agreement with that. It
is a splendid thing, and I hope that the
proposal will not be looked upon merely
from the point of view of keeping boys
and girls off the unemployment register.
To my mind the year between 14 and 15
is the year when something serious
ought to be attempted in building up a
sense of citizenship along the basis of
character. It should not be merely a
matter of jamming a little more
geography or a little more mathematics
into their minds during that extra year.
I do not suppose all the Members of
the House will agree with me, but it is
my personal feeling that continued legislation entailing restrictions upon the
actions and lives of the community in one
respect and another has a tendency to
create a disposition to try to get round
the restrictions. Some people are getting
exceedingly clever at evading the law,
and the moral character is not of the
same high standard as it used to be. To
give a case in point. I was told yesterday on good authority about a small
clearance sale in a provincial town with
which I am familiar. During the course
of that sale several hundreds of pounds
worth of goods were stolen and taken
away. I am afraid that some people are
out to rob the Government or to get
things whether it is right or wrong, and
boys and girls imbibe those ideas. I do
not for a moment say, nor should I like
anyone to suggest, that generally speaking the moral character of our people at
bottom is not sound, but on the surface
there is this tendency I have spoken off.
The State has a duty to the rising
generation and should see to it that the
character of the children is built
upon a sound foundation. The school
curriculum should be such that the
boys and girls, who remain at school
after the age of 14, will be taught the
fundamental principles of good citizenship.
Captain SINCLAIR: May I, first of

suffice. The hon. Member stated, if I

Enough has already been said on both

I deplore the fact that there is no

Government factory. I feel that we are
entitled to at least one such factory in
the Province for the manufacture of
shells, gas-masks, or other things. I am,

measure and that the setting up of such a
factory would not be a permanent cure
for unemployment. Desirable as rearmament work may be as a temporary
palliative, it seems to me that our best
hope of reducing our unemployment
figures-frankly the figures appal me
-is by attracting new industries of a
permanent nature. Valuable help in that
direction would be provided by a Government factory for the manufacture of
the many articles required in peace as
well as in war. Nor must we neglect the
industries already established, of which
the principal, linen and shipbuilding,
rely on export trade.
I hope that as a result of the negotiations between Great Britain and the
U.S.A., tariffs will be so adjusted as to
allow greater exports of our linen goods
to the latter country. Pending the completion of those negotiations, we cannot
hope for an improvement in demand from
America, and indeed we will probably see
trade even quieter than it is at present.
It will be obvious to the Members of this
House that importing firms in America
are not going to place orders now when
there is every prospect of their being able
to buy cheaper in the near future through
reduced tariff rates, although they would
not appear to run any grave risk if those
orders were placed for delivery after the
rates had been agreed.
Reference is made in the Gracious
Speech to a Measure for the protection of
life and property from aerial attack in
the event of war. That Measure envisages passive protection only. I venture
to hope that, through the Territorial
Army organisation, active protection, in
amplification of the Ulster Squadron of
the Royal Air Force, will be afforded by
means of anti-aircraft guns and searchlights. The response to the recruiting
appeal for the existing coast defence
units has been quite satisfactory, and I
think should encourage the Imperial
Government to consider the formation of
anti-aircraft units here. I am quite
certain the response would be equally
worthy of Northern Ireland. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) If the danger of
aerial attack is sufficiently grave to
warrant expenditure on passive protection it is grave enough to warrant the
formation of anti-aircraft gunner and
engineer units. I have much pleasure in
supporting the Motion. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)

one of those who think that the

It has been admitted on all sides of

I can well remember that some of the

Mr. NIXON: China.

if you like. I am afraid he would not

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.

a very delicate, difficult and important

Parliamentary duty with care, tact,

They have each proved that they are well

It is gratifying, I am sure, to us all
to know that His Majesty's Gracious
Speech has had such a favourable
reception during this debate. I think
only one Member has criticised it unfairly. I propose to deal with this
criticism later on. This debate, I feel,
has been mainly centered on this very
distressing and disappointing problem of
unemployment. I think, therefore, it is
desirable that my reply should chiefly
be on the same problem, because in the
first place we all recognise it is important,
and in the second place we have many
new Members in this House to-day, and
I wish frankly to endeavour to make clear
the position and the difficulties associated
with it from my point of view. I will
not approach the matter either from a
party or political point of view, because
I feel it is a great industrial, social and
human matter, which ought to be dealt
with, and I believe is generally dealt
with, in the most sympathetic way
possible.
As Minister of Labour I was daily
brought into very close contact with
the problem for 16 years, as has been
said to-day. It was a trying and anxious
experience, because I recognise that
though it is possible to narrow its scope
and lessen its chief ill-effects, yet at the
same time it has never been possible to
find a complete cure. If it were possible
to find a complete cure for the problem
I can assure you my colleagues and I
would have applied it long ago. The
reason that it is such a difficult problem
to deal with is because it is not governed
by local conditions, and the cure, therefore, cannot be entirely a local one.
is an international problem, governed
mainly, as far as we are concerned, by
international conditions. We should remember that we are mainly an exporting
community, that three out of four at least
of all those things which we produce have
got to find a market outside our shores.
It
Therefore, the difficulty of the situation
really is this, that we are affected by the
conditions in foreign countries to a very
large degree. For instance, we cannot
prevent war between one country and
another.
We cannot prevent civil wars in other
countries. We cannot bring back industrial and economic prosperity to the
United States of America or to Brazil.
We cannot place Germany or Italy in
the position to buy from us what they
used to buy, because the truth is that they
would be unable to pay for the goods
purchased. It is very regrettable, I
admit, and we all join in feeling the
regret, that there has been a back-set to
our industrial position during the past
four months and that our unemployment
figures have risen to the extent of 33,000.
I am glad, however, to be able to say
that it appears as if an improvement has
set in already, because the figures for
February show that the position has
improved to the extent of a falling in
the number registered of just over 2,000.
I agree with the hon. and gallant
Member for Cromac when he says that
we have reason to hope that when this
new trade agreement is made between
the United Kingdom and the United
States of America our linen and other
industries will benefit to a substantial extent. I know it is poor consolation to
realise that other countries are suffering
with us in connection with unemployment,
but still when we come to look at the
position, not as we would like to see it,
but as it actually is, we find that almost
every country has suffered during these
few months, some of them to a more
serious extent than we have. For instance, in the Free State they have not
the complete register that we have here
for various reasons too numerous to
mention on this occasion. There the
register of unemployed persons has increased by 39,440; in Great Britain, notwithstanding the advantage got from the
rearmament programme, the numbers
are up by 488,000, and in the United
States of America, which have been
referred to, the increase during the same
period was 2,800,000. I can assure the
House that the Government are ever
anxious to obtain from anyone any light
or leading which will improve the situation here or add to the prosperity of our
native land.

Some hon. Members have said that the
Government are doing nothing to help
the situation, and have done next to
nothing. I would point to the fact that
a few months ago we passed a New
Industries Act-and there are signs of it
bearing fruit-giving greater advantages
to new industries to come into our midst

any other country, so far as I know,
outside the United Kingdom. These
advantages take the form of free sites,
freedom from rates for a certain
period, freedom from income-tax for five
years, and large capital facilities.
addition to that, this Act will encourage
our older industries to extend in our
midst. I maintain that we have helped
the linen industry in every way possible.
Hon. Members will admit that we have
helped our farming industry in many
ways. We have supported the efforts of
the Ulster Industries Development Association, and we have co-operated with all
who are interested in extending our
tourist traffic.

£30,000,000, of which £21,000,000 was
guaranteed by our Government. The
hon. Member for South Down said that
we have given millions to shipbuilders.
Of course, we have not done so. Through
this Act we have guaranteed loans to
shipowners in consideration of their
placing their orders here in Belfast.
Then, again, in regard to the housing
problem, the Government have played a
very important part. A great many
thousand houses have been built, and a
great many more thousand houses are
going to be built. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) They will be built not
only in our rural areas in co-operation
with our local authorities, but we hope
our new Bill, when it becomes law, will
encourage local authorities to build also
in our urban areas. The Government
will not be satisfied until, as far as is
possible, every
every family in Northern
Ireland will be provided with a suitable
and comfortable home at a reasonable
rent. I do not think I could be expected to say more than that, because it
is really going the whole way.
Now, as regards relief schemes, here,
again, I maintain that the Government
have done everything possible. Last
year 44 schemes were approved by the
Ministry of Labour at a capital cost of
£900,000. In order further to encourage
local authorities and public bodies to
provide additional employment on works
of public utility, the Government has
decided to give increased financial assistance by raising the existing relief
scheme grant from 75 per cent. to 85
per cent. of the labour costs, under the
usual conditions. Whilst this increased
rate will, of course, not apply to schemes
already approved, it will apply to all
schemes approved from this date, other
than street works in urban areas, for
which special terms were authorised in
December of last year. The increase in
the rate of the grant from 75 per cent.
to 85 per cent will also apply to works
of improvement on farm holdings carried
out by farmers. Hon. Members will be
asked to agree to the necessary increased
money provision. It is expected that
this further concession to local authorities and farmers will enable a great deal
of useful work to be carried out at an
early date and will, at the same time,
give employment to many of our people.
What is not generally understood is
that the Government themselves are very
large employers of our industrial classes,
apart from the Civil Service altogether.
We have a large programme of work in
hand for accommodating our police
force, and for the erection of suitable
employment exchanges. There is also
work in connection with the Bann and
other drainage works, and in connection
with the erection, in co-operation with
local authorities, of elementary
schools not only in Our towns but
scattered through our country districts.
Then the Imperial Government are
carrying out a large programme here as
well in connection with the post offices
and army barracks accommodation, and
also at Aldergrove.

I feel that I must say a few words
about the speech of the hon. Member
for Shankill (Mr. Henderson), and I
am glad to see him in his place, because
I never like to speak of what an hon.
Gentleman has said when he is not
present. He was the hon. Member who
characterised the Gracious Speech as the
most useless and most hopeless document
ever presented to any assembly. Of
course we know that the hon. Member
always takes a despondent view, we know
that he is an extremist, and we do not
always take him too seriously. At the
same time, I do feel that it is desirable
in the public interest that I should correct some of the statements which he
made. He told us that he had read the
Speech in the bus. I think it must have
been a very dark bus, because he evidently
did not see very clearly or fully what
the Speech contained. For example, he
did not observe the steps that are being
taken to stimulate the establishment of
new industries or to help the old industries, nor did he see that the Speech contained a reference to our proposed
housing schemes, or the reduction of the
age for blind persons' pensions. He did
not observe, I think, that we intend to
extend for a further period the Loans
Guarantee Acts. Again, it is mentioned
in the King's Speech that we intend to
deal with our Unemployment Insurance
and National Health schemes with the
object of removing, as far as possible,
certain anomalies which exist. Physical
training is also referred to, and I should
have thought that that would have.
appealed to the hon. Member himself.
Mr. HENDERSON: It is empty
stomachs I am concerned with.
Mr. ANDREWS: Then, again, he
went on to talk in a most reckless way
about borrowing money. He said he
would begin by borrowing a sum of 20
millions to carry out works of public
utility, and also to increase pensions and
unemployment benefit, et cetera, et cetera.
When that was done he would go on
borrowing and borrowing and borrowing.
That sounds very brave, but I do not
think it would be practicable, because I
think he would find, before he got very
far, that for obvious reasons nobody
would lend him money.
What the hon.
Member does not understand is this, that
while you can borrow money temporarily
to meet a charge, if I may put it that
way, you cannot go on borrowing permanently, or else it is perfectly clear that
you would land yourself in national bankruptcy in a very short time, and that
nobody would lend you money at all.

Mr. ANDREWS: What the Prime
Minister did say was this: he asked the

Mr. NIXON: A Minister a director of

The difference between some of the

to help our people as far as we have the
means to do it. We have told the
electors, both at election times and at
other times, that we cannot go in advance
of Great Britain, but that we will never
drag behind. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) That is an honest statement.
Some hon. Members opposite, possibly
unintentionally, or because they do not
realise the true position, mislead the
electors by saying that it is possible for
us to go in advance of Great Britain.
The hon. Member for Shankill knows
quite well-for, in fact, he admitted it
yesterday that our revenue will not permit us to go in advance of Great Britain,
and therefore he is driven to say that he
would meet the outlay by borrowing.
But, as I have told him, he could not
do it that way, because he would very
soon find that there was nobody willing
to lend him money. Hon. Members tell
us they would borrow, but they never
tell us how they would pay back what
they borrowed. If they did they would
have to admit at the same time that they
would tax the people of Northern Ireland
more than the people across the water are
taxed, which would also, beyond a shadow
of doubt, lead to disaster.
May I just refer to one other matter
which I think is of importance. The hon.
Member for Woodvale (Mr. Nixon) said
that the Prime Minister, in appealing to
the country, had created the impression.
that the country was not safe.

country.
Do not for a moment think that I am
suggesting anything in connection with
conscription. Conscription is a bogey,
and it is talked about by people who
have an imperfect knowledge of the
British Army. When we talk about conscription we should make it clear whether
it is conscription in time of war or in
time of peace. Conscription in war is a
subject I will not touch upon. Happily
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
3 MARCH 1938
we are not at war. When people talk
about conscription in peace they refer to
it in relation to the regular Army. The
object of the British Army is to garrison
the defended ports, the Colonies abroad
and India. In passing I might say that
the great bulk of the British Army
abroad is in India and is paid for by the
Indian Government. Having decided
what is necessary to garrison these places
abroad, then under the Cardwell system
equivalent units are made up at home.
These units which are really draft finding units were gathered together by Lord
Haldane and formed into the Expeditionary Force which fought so gallantly
for us in 1914.
Take the ordinary Army recruit. He
joins his depot and is given two, three or
six months training. He then goes to a
home unit and after that is drafted
abroad. It is quite obvious that conscription would not serve any purpose,
because the minimum service a man must
complete is six years. No Government
could conscript a man for that period. I
would ask hon. Members to encourage
young lads between 18 and 25 years of
age to join the Army and thus not only
make for themselves an honourable useful
career and obtain employment, but serve
the Empire to which we have the
privilege to belong.
Lieut.-Colonel MITCHELL: I desire
to join in congratulating the Mover and
Seconder of the Address, and also to
congratulate the various other Members
on their maiden speeches. I propose
briefly to draw the attention of the House
to a point in regard to unemployment. I
refer to young lads of 16 or 17 years of
age who, after receiving the requisite
number of stamps on their cards, fall out
of work and are able to go to the bureau
and draw a certain amount of money.
These boys are at a very impressionable
age and get the idea that money can be
got for nothing. A man who has worked
for many years has learned something
about labour, but I think it is disastrous
that young fellows of 16 or 17 years of
age should be in a position to get money
handed out to them which they have not
earned.
I realise that there are serious difficulties in the way, but I think they could
be solved. These young lads should do
something. Dictatorships, much as I
despise them, have solved that problem,
and every young man and young woman
has to go to some sort of labour colony.
I do not know whether it would be possible to establish some place where these
young people would have to do some
work, and where they would receive
physical training to make them strong,
vigorous and healthy. I realise that that
would involve some degree of compulsion,
but every Act which we pass in this
House compels someone to do something
which he does not wish to do or prevents
some other person doing something he
desires to do. We cannot get away from
that fact. I realise the difficulty of
establishing extensive labour colonies for
adults, but the young people are limited
in number and the expense would not be
very great. It would be quite reasonable
to say to them: "If you are not prepared
to do some kind of work you cannot draw
unemployment money." I look upon this
as a growing evil, something which is
steadily undermining the morale of the
younger generation.
I do not wish at this stage of the debate
to take up the time of the House, but I
throw out the suggestion that the young
people who are unemployed should be
dealt with and something done which
would convert them into useful and
valuable citizens.

houses." The Government will have to

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Minford]
The only thing his wife could do was to

was engaged in a business.
I think it most unfair that people like
this man's wife who, through force of
circumstances, have to start these little
shops in order to keep the home together,
should be turned down and that their
husbands should receive no allowance in
respect of them when they are unemployed. I understand that one of these
cases happened in my own district of
Antrim, and has been adjourned to see
if the Ministry of Labour can get over
the difficulty. These anomalies are
injustices. When a man has been in
constant work and only drops out
through no fault of his own, for example,
through the depressed state of the linen
industry, surely he should not be
debarred from getting the amount to
which he is justly due. The result in the
case I have mentioned is that this poor
woman had to stop this little shop in
order to enable her husband to receive
enough benefit to keep the house together.
Surely the Minister of Labour has in his
hands the means whereby these anomalies
can be rectified.
In regard to the Bann drainage, I
admit, with other hon. Members, that it
has done a great deal of good in some
places. In my constituency we have a
river which I have mentioned here before,
and which is the cause of the flooding of
hundreds of acres of the finest arable and
grazing land in Ulster. The position we
are in is hopeless, because the County
Council say they cannot take the work
on their hands, and the District Council
say they are not going to do their share,
with the result that the farmers are
suffering year after year. Surely it is
not beyond the bounds of possibility that

Labour, or the Minister of Commerce, or
the Minister of Home Affairs-should
take steps to try to remedy this terrible
flooding. In these times, when our unemployment is so high and when we are seeking avenues whereby we can help those
people, something could surely be done.
I believe that if the Members on both
sides of this House would meet in conference we could find lots of useful work.
The removal of the valuation limit of £75
and the making of grants for drainage
would encourage the farmers to undertake more work in the cleaning of rivers.
Then the making of better roads would
also provide much work.
Nobody can have any dispute or controversy in regard to the King's Speech,
because it sets out the design of the
Government to make perfect Acts which

or fixing an economic price for

10,000, but it would be the means of

to have proper houses dotted all over

Government is taking all the steps

Ulster. Some of us who have been

modern world we have all to recognise

deal of publicity. Without publicity he
will not get votes. I think the same
thing applies to our Province here, that
without publicity you are much less
likely to attract new industries to the
Province, and to attract new business to
the old industries.
I think it is important that the Government should address their minds to
this problem. We are spending annually
a sum of, roughly, three million pounds
unemployment relief. That three
million pounds is the amount of money
spent not on curing the disease, but in
relieving the symptons of the disease. I
think it would be money well spent if
a proportion of that sum were devoted
not to alleviating the symptoms of the
disease, but in trying to get at the root
of the disease. A miserable five per
cent. of three million pounds would be
£150,000, and I think that if the Government spent £150,000 in publicity
every year they would find it money well
spent. Why do I suggest that that should
be done? The hon. and gallant Member for Clifton (Major Hall-Thompson)
has suggested that someone in the Ministry of Commerce should be set apart to
make a special study of the Province. I
would suggest that a special department
should be set up-I do not care whether
it is in the Ministry of Commerce, the
Ministry of Labour, or any other Ministry-for the express purpose of conducting publicity and propaganda on behalf
of the Province.
I know that that is already being done
to some extent by organisations such as
the Ulster Development Council, who are
doing very necessary work. That work
is being carried on by patriotic individuals who have the interests of the
community at heart, but those gentlemen
cannot give their whole time to the task
and they cannot put large sums of money

you must have a department, with a
number of officials who can devote their
whole time to the work, and there
must be an amount of money at
their disposal, not provided by private sources, but by the Government.
I recognise that the Ulster Development

money ought to be provided by the
Government.
I do not think it is sufficient to establish such a department here. I think
the Government ought to establish an

I think that five per cent. of three
million pounds would be well spent
every year in doing some such work

One other thing that was said by the

the reason for that. There must be some
reason, and the Government should
grapple with the problem, find out what
the reason is, and tackle the matter.

city? Of course,

To cure

the export trade. A period of acute

Sir BASIL BROOKE (Minister of
Agriculture): I rise to deal with some
of the matters concerning my
Department which have been raised in
this debate. I should like, first of all,
to congratulate the Proposer and
Seconder on the manner in which they
moved and seconded the Address. I
think all the new Members distinguished
themselves.
One or two matters have been discussed which intimately concern my
Department. One thing discussed does
not refer particularly to agriculture, it
is really an industrial one, that is the
question of flax. It was raised by the
hon. Member for North Armagh (Mr.
Johnston) and various agricultural Members. The hon. Member for North
Armagh will, of course, realise that the
real reason why more flax is not grown
in this country is because enough money
is not paid for it. The gentlemen connected with the industry think they pay
too much that is no concern of minebut the farmers consider they do not get
a sufficient amount. The hon. Member
has urged me, as various other Members
have done, to do something to promote a
flax marketing scheme. Although I am
perfectly willing and anxious to find a
solution, I am quite unable to find a
watertight one which would encourage a
greater acreage of flax to be grown without involving the Government in a grave
risk.
To involve the Government in a
risk of this kind is far too serious.
In most of the schemes which I have
had the honour of introducing in this
House we have been able to foresee to a
certain extent the expenditure involved.
It is improper to say that our Treasurv
has not been asked to pay any substantial
sum, but if we were to introduce a
scheme offering either subsidies to flax
growers or guaranteeing a price, the sum
might run into £400,000. It is a danger
which cannot be contemplated by this
Government, when, in point of fact, flax
only represents 1.8 per cent. of the total
agricultural output of the Province. The
Ministry and myself feel that where a
large amount of money is expended on
agriculture we would rather see it being
expended on those products of agriculture which would benefit the largest
number of farmers.
I think it was the hon. Member for
North Derry (Rev. Robert Moore) who
mentioned that potato prices had been
extremely bad this year. I am quite
aware of that fact. A potato scheme is
in existence in England and, during its
operation has done good work, but where
you get an excess of potatoes over requirements in this case I think it is only
about 5 per cent. of the requirements of
the country-it has been found that the
actual price of the potatoes may fall by
50 per cent. That is why the prices have
fallen this year.
We are linked with
that scheme, and I hope that within the
next few years we will maintain a price
something the same as last year.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Minford) raised one or two questions in
regard to drainage. I will bear in mind
what he stated in regard to the valuation
question. There is, of course, the draining of a river which comes under a major
drainage scheme, but this is a question
for his County Council. Presumably if
the County Council find they cannot raise
a sufficient sum then they will apply to
the Government Department concerned.
I should like to refer to the speech
made yesterday by the hon. Member for
South Down, because he made one or two
statements which are slightly disturbing.
He quoted from the speech broadcast by
the Secretary of my Ministry. I think
the hon. Member has misinterpreted
what the Secretary intended to convey
As I gather from his speech, he thought
that the Secretary's policy was to abolish
all small-holdings.
Mr. BROWN: I quoted from the
official report issued by the B.B.C.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have refreshed
my memory by reading the broadcast
speech. What was suggested, and is
perfectly true, was that where you have

would be possible to establish an alcohol
factory, which would obtain its alcohol
from potatoes, in Newry. In the Free
State we have a very good example of
that. A factory was built there for that
purpose and the price which they have
guaranteed, at least as far as I understand, to the producer is 35s per ton.
Thirty-five shillings per ton is an uneconomic price at which to produce
potatoes. We assume that it takes at
least £2 per ton to make the production
of potatoes economic. In addition, it is
far better and more economic for any
man who has a surplus of potatoes for
which he cannot get £2 per ton to feed
his pigs or his cattle with them.
The price at 35s and even down to 20s
a ton is obviously a perfectly hopeless
proposition. The only way you can get
a factory of that sort is either by a
Government subsidy or else inducing
motorists to use a certain proportion of
alcohol for the running of motor-cars.
It would have to be subsidised somehow
or other. If potatoes went up to the
price of last year, namely, £4 a ton,
factories would be lying idle with very
heavy overhead charges being incurred.
There was
one final point which was
made by the hon. Member for Enniskillen, in which he urged that agricultural legislation should go slowly. I
quite agree with him, but I should not
like any Member to think that the reason
why during the last Session these marketing schemes were poured out like water
was because we had nothing else better
to do. The reason we had to do that
was that we had studied the position,
not only in foreign countries, and we
were perfectly convinced that if Ulster
was to maintain her position in the
English markets we would have to take
immediate action. If we had waited
until other people had taken action in
these schemes we should have lost the
markets and the policy would have been
like that in some countries, not one of
increasing production, but rather one of
encouraging farmers to reduce their production.
Mr. MINFORD: May I put a question

between growers, spinners and others.
would do a lot of good.

Mr. SPEAKER: If the hon. Member

THE REARMAMENT PROGRAMME.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Captain Dixon.)
Mr. BROWN: I crave the indulgence
of this House to make a very brief statement on a matter of importance and extreme urgency. In view of the fact that
it is officially announced in the "Daily
Mail," a copy of which I have before me,
that the rearmament expenditure of
the British Government is to exceed
fifteen hundred million pounds, which
I alluded to in my speech yesterday, I suggest that this provides
a chance to get a share in the matter
of factories for this particular area. What
I mean is a brick-by-brick policy, similar
to the step-by-step policy now in operation in other directions. I do not want
contracts merely to be given out: I want
factories to carry out these contracts. We
want to have factories provided here in
proportion to the population of both
countries. The factories in operation
across the water are paid for by our
money as well as their money. In view
of these facts I urge on the Government
to send a deputation to the British
Government to make representations for
a brick and brick contribution of what
we are entitled to in regard to rearmament. We pay our share for every brick
used in England, Wales and Scotland. We
do not want a preference in regard to
contracts; we want factories. We want
the brick-and-brick policy. May I join
in the congratulations of other hon.
Members to the Prime Minister, who was
not here yesterday when I spoke, on his
splendid recovery from his recent illness.
and the improvement he has shown in his
health. In conclusion, I again ask
that a deputation be sent from this
Parliament to Whitehall to impress on
them the necessity of extending the brick
and brick policy to this area. We do
not want merely the matter of tendering
for contracts, but to be placed on the
same lines in proportion to the population as our friends across the water.
The PRIME MINISTER: May I say
I am only too delighted to answer the
question of the hon. Member for South
Down, and take the opportunity, which
I had not before, of congratulating him
on his maiden speech. No one knows
more than I do how very important it is
that we should get our fair share of the
rearmament programme. It is no new
question. It has been raised from time
to time on the other side by myself in
the early stages and by my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Finance quite
recently. All I can say to my hon.
Friend is that I do not think that anything more can possibly be done than
has been done with regard to the urging
of schemes for a fair share of rearmament
work. I believe it will come, but it is
slow. We will require to exercise very
great patience, and I would ask him and
other Members to bear in mind that there
is a considerable amount of work going
on quietly behind the scenes that people
do not realise or have any idea of.

The Prime Minister knows that there

have got a number of ships. I went to

OLD CAVEHILL ROAD BRIDGE.
1. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that a number of motor accidents
have occurred at the Old Cavehill Road
Bridge; whether the Ministry are taking
any action to have this old bridge
demolished, and the road made safer;
and whether any representations have
been made to the Antrim County
Council to have the old Ballysillan Road
widened.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Davison):
Since the 1st January, 1937, only one
motoring accident has occurred at the
place mentioned by the hon. Member,
and it was due to carelessness on the
part of a motor cyclist.
The local authority have had under
consideration the question of demolishing the bridge and widening the road,
and have approached the persons interested in the property which would be
benefited by such operations with a view
to secuuring a contribution from them.
At the moment no agreement has been
reached.
The position with regard to the proposal to widen the Ballysillan Road is
similar.
HIGH HEDGES ON CREGAGH
ROAD.
2. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that the hedges at the top of the
Cregagh Road are so high that numerous
accidents have occurred at this corner;
whether the ratepayers living in this
area have approached the Down County
Council to have these hedges removed,
and the dangerous corner widened;
whether the Council have refused to take
any action; and, in view of the large
number of accidents at the corner,
whether he would approach the Council
to have this dangerous corner made safe
for the public.
1st
Mr. DAVISON: Since the
January, 1937, only one motoring
accident has occurred at the road
junction mentioned by the hon. Member.
The Rural District Council have, I
understand, been approached on the
question of improving this corner, but
the matter is one of some difficulty.
Even if the hedges and shrubs at the
corner were lowered the view would still
be obscured by a wall and close timber
fence which is necessary to preserve the
privacy of a house situated there, and
if this screen were removed the value
of the property would be very substantially reduced and heavy compensation would have to be paid.
With a view to making the junction
safer, white lines and the word "Slow"
have been painted on the road surface,
and it is considered that these measures
are, in the circumstances, adequate.

THE ANGLO-EIRE NEGOTIATIONS
Mr.
HENDERSON (by private
notice) asked the Prime Minister
whether it is a fact that on Friday last
he received an urgent message from the
British Government requesting him to
cross to London for consultation with
regard to the present negotiations between the British Government and the
Irish Free State Government; whether
the Minister of Finance was deputed to
go, and in fact did go on Friday night,
and whether the question of Partition
was discussed; whether in view of the
anxiety which this third hurried visit of
an Ulster Minister to London is
creating amongst the loyalists of Ulster
he will make a public statement that
Ulster's position as part and parcel of
the United Kingdom is in no way endangered and that Ulster trade and
commerce will not be injuriously affected
in any way by any arrangement which
may be reached between the Irish Free
State and the British Government.
The PRIME MINISTER: The
answer to the first and third part of the
question is in the negative; as regards
the second part, my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Finance, was asked to
cross on Friday last and did so; as regards the fourth part, I have nothing
to add to the statement I made in the
House on this day week.
Mr. HENDERSON: Why all this
secrecy? Why do the loyalists of Ulster
not know the exact position and everything that takes place with regard to
these negotiations?
The PRIME MINISTER: The
anxiety of the Ulster people is quite
uncalled for. They may have every
reliance on the judgment of my
right hon. Friend to see that they are
properly protected.
Mr. HENDERSON: The loyalists of
Ulster are afraid of the same thing
being done to them as was done to
Cavan, Monaghan and Donegal.
The PRIME MINISTER: Oh, there
is no fear.

The first two items relate to the Lagan
Navigation. Since 1753, when work was
first commenced on the scheme of making
the River Lagan navigable and extending
it by means of a canal, the Lagan
has been brought into use as a navigable
waterway from Belfast to Lough Neagh,
which provides a link with the Tyrone
Navigation or Coalisland Canal and the
Upper Bann Navigation. The canalized
river also fulfils the useful functions of
providing water power for a number of
mills and factories situated in the Lagan
Valley, and of facilitating the drainage
of the area through which it flows.
As a result of competition from road
and rail transport the company which
carries on the navigation has reached the
end of its financial resources and, in the
absence of some form of assistance, is
likely to be forced to abandon the under-
Whatever views hon. Members
taking.
may hold regarding the merits of water
transport, they will, nevertheless, I am
sure, realise that the abandonment of the
navigation would give rise to serious difficulties regarding drainage and water
rights. These difficulties are of special
significance to the Government, as we are
advised that, if the undertaking were
abandoned, it would revert to the charge.
of the Ministry of Finance as successors
to the Commissioners of Public Works.
The various aspects of this problem are at
present being investigated and, in order
to facilitate this investigation, the
Government obtained an independent
survey of the condition of the navigation
and a report thereon from a firm of consulting engineers at a cost of two hundred
and fifty guineas.
Certain essential works of major repair
were found to be necessary to prevent the

have explained to hon. Members, the
company is not in a position to meet such
expenditure, and the authority of the

The sum of £1,000 included under this
head is intended to cover the expenditure

end of the present financial year,
securing publicity for the facilities made.
available for industrialists under the New
Industries (Development) Acts of last
year. This subhead brings me to a topic
which is one of supreme public interestand rightly so at the present time. For
while there are many well-known methods
of approaching the problem of the alleviation of the evils of unemployment, hon.
Members will, I think, agree that there
is no obvious or easy approach to the
question of effecting a permanent cure.
The Government is fully convinced that
one of the most constructive, although at
the same time an extremely difficult,
method of grappling with this question.
lies in the expansion of existing, and
the establishment of new, industries.
as
As hon. Members are aware, legislation has already been passed to encourage industrial development of this
kind. I realise, however, as much
any Member of this Committee, that the
mere existence of an Act of Parliament
is not likely to induce industrialists to
look to Northern Ireland as a field for
industrial enterprise. The essential
part of our campaign is to make as
widely known as possible, and in the
right quarters, not only the facilities
available under the new industries legislation, but also the special advantages
which Northern Ireland offers for industrial enterprise, advantages to which our
old-established linen, shipbuilding and
other leading industries bear testimony.
To this end I have
I have brought into
existence the body known as the Ulster
Development Council, with the specific
purpose of planning and obtaining the
widest possible publicity both for the
New Industries Acts and for other
matters pertaining to Northern Ireland
as a potential field for further industrial
development. The Council is representative of Municipal and Harbour
Authorities, Chambers of Commerce and
Trade, leading industries and transport
interests, and we have been fortunate
enough to secure as chairman, Senator
Sir Roland Nugent.
Information in regard to the scope
of the legislation has been widely disseminated, through the Press, through
letters and leaflets, and by personal
contact. At the moment a special
brochure is in preparation and will
shortly issue from the Council. This, it
is hoped, will bring the inducements
which Northern Ireland has to offer
forcibly and succinctly before those who
might be expected to contemplate the
establishment either of a new industry
or a branch of an existing undertaking.
While on the subject of publicity, I
would like to emphasise that the task
which we have set ourselves is one which
I am sure we are all, irrespective of
party, anxious to accomplish, and one
in which every one, to a greater or less
extent, can co-operate. While the major
portion of the work in this direction
must naturally fall to be undertaken
