working-class families due to the heavy
increase in the price of food."
We are told that this is a period of
prosperity, and from the point of view
of certain people it is true enough.
Profits were never higher. The
"Economist" index of industrial profits
for the third quarter of 1937 shows that
profits were 19.2 per cent. above the same
quarter of the previous year, while the
average ordinary dividend had risen from
7.6 in 1936 to 9.7 in 1937, and 1936 was
a record year for the volume of profits
according to Josiah Stamp's estimates.
In some industries there have been wages
advances. Registered unemployment has
decreased in Great Britain although it
has increased in Northern Ireland, and at
the moment there are over 100,000 of
the insured population of Northern Ireland unemployed or, in other words,
there are two out of every three of the
insurable workers in Northern Ireland
out of employment to-day.
Since 1935 food prices have been rising
to a startling extent. I want to give you
examples. The average price of 4lbs. of
bread is up from 72d to 94d, and a pound
of tea has risen from 1s 11 to 2s 2d,
fresh butter from 1s 2d to 1s 4d a
pound, and a pound of cheese from 8d
to 10d. Now these figures, for fear
there should be any misunderstanding,
are taken from the Ministry of Labour
Gazette. All my quotations throughout
my advocacy of this Motion will be based
on
the Ministry of Labour Gazette.
figures. As we in Northern Ireland have
no separate index figure of the cost of
living we have to accept the index figure
of the British Minister in his compilation
of these figures. There may be some misunderstanding in certain commodities
and Members might feel that I have
made a wrong quotation. All these
quotations are from the Gazette.
According to the Ministry of Labour
index prices of food have risen from 31
points above 1914 in November, 1935, to
46 points in November, 1937, a total increase of 11 per cent. since 1935 and 16
per cent. since 1933. Another explanation, from November, 1937, to March,
1938, two points have been added to the
increase of the cost of living, therefore
the figures are subject to an addition of
two points. That means that £1 to-day
will only buy as much food as 17s 8d in
November, 1935, or 16s 9d in November, 1933. That is the reduction in the
purchasing power of the £1 from the
workers' point of view. Now wages rates
are no longer keeping pace with prices.
It is quite clear from the Ministry of
Labour's figures that in 1935 full-time
wages had greater purchasing power than
they have to-day.
The figures given are based on the
Ministry of Labour's index for wage
rates. These do not cover agricultural labourers, Government employees,
domestic servants, shop assistants or
clerks. But since they include all
organised work under trade union agreements and those protected by Trade
Boards, the picture they give is rather
better than the average. That is to say
these wage rates cover organised workers,
which on the whole are generally a higher
standard than those who are not
organised. Wage rates in 1935 taken all
round were 96, in 1936 they were 98, in
1937 they were 102. That was the wage
rates increase. Now we get the cost of
living. In 1935 we have 81.9; in 1936,
83.9; in 1937, 88.9. Then we come to the
real wages. In 1935 the real wages were
117.2; in 1936, 117.4; in 1937, 115.3.
That is the real wage against the increased cost of living in respect of the
years I have quoted. In other words,
wage rates for the trades covered by the
index have risen by 1s 4d in the pound,
but the cost of living has risen during
the same period by 1s 8d in the pound.
This index does not include the heavy
price increase in October and November
of last year.
Now I do not think there is any
Government attempts to deny those
figures, and especially this Government,
because they are fathered by the British
Government, and at the present moment
you accept them as an authoritative
statement. Therefore, my quotation of
them should be accepted. Now I want to
day it down that those figures as applied
at the present moment in Northern Ireland are of such a nature that they
become startling. They are severe in
Great Britain, but the severity of them
is felt to a greater extent in Northern
Ireland, because the purchasing power of
the workers in Northern Ireland is lower
than in Great Britain for reasons I will
give. Take the fixed rates of benefit for
unemployment. Although the pound has

Mr. AGNEW: I agree very strongly

of the necessity for a general investigation of the high cost of living which has
an effect on the family life of the people
throughout Northern Ireland. The prices
of the foodstuffs which the ordinary
people buy are going up so much that it
is becoming impossible for them to obtain
them. I believe the people most affected
in the first instance, those who really feel
the pinch, are those in receipt of outdoor
relief, which is a very meagre allowance.
In some cases with which I have come in
contact I find it absolutely impossible for
them to provide the necessities of life at
the prices charged. They were allowed
only 5s a week. In other cases the
amount allowed was 7s 6d or 10s.
Generally speaking, the unemployed feel
the pinch more than any other section
of the community.
Next to those on poor relief I believe
those on assistance are feeling the
straitened circumstances caused by the
high cost of living. In the provincial
towns the rates of wages for certain work
are very low, which means that there are
certain commodities the people are not
able to obtain. That is bound to cause
under-nourishment in families. We view
the plight of the old-age pensioner with
10s a week trying to provide the necessities of life, and we must admit that it
is absolutely impossible for him to do so.
I feel the Government would be doing a
service to the community if they gave
careful consideration to the question of
the setting up of a Food Council to go in
a general way into the question of what
is spent by the working class in providing
the necessities of life.
Being in contact continually with the
ordinary people I know that on one day
in the week a serious burden is placed on
those who are responsible for spending
the cash. That is at the end of the week,
when they have to make up their budget.
and provide for the week that is coming
on. In my opinion the high cost of living
must be a nightmare to them. I honestly
believe that the setting up of a Food
Council should be delayed no longer. It
is a matter for the Government, and in

Northern Ireland the time is ripe for it.
As one belonging to the working-class

add to the burden of people who have

inflicted any longer. I hope a Food
Council will meet with their approval and
will be set up.

far as employment is concerned, to a very

the main factors of recent economic

I take it, therefore, that hon. Members do not regard rising food prices as
an evil per se, for it would obviously be

item, due to a desire on the part of distributors to profiteer under cover of the
inevitable rise in food prices generally.
Bearing this distinction in mind, I
personally am not inclined to think that
there is anything abnormal in the present
level of food prices in Northern Ireland.
Undoubtedly there has been, as I have
said, a general increase in prices due to

Northern Ireland has no control, but on

roughly corresponds with the level

opposite advocate for Northern Ireland.
Admittedly there are differences in some

prices in Northern Ireland, but in
general the result is that a higher price.
in one direction is counter-balanced by
a lower price in another.
Apart altogether from the question of
the present level of food prices, however,
is it necessary to set up new machinery
to deal with this matter when the existing machinery has not yet been tried and
found wanting? As hon. Members are
aware, there exists in Great Britain a
Food Council which, while not in a
position to fix prices, is empowered to
inquire into the reasonableness of the
prices charged for any foodstuff and,
where it is met with a refusal to lower

of Trade for presentation to Parliament.
My Ministry maintains constant
liaison with the Food Council in London,
and the latter have expressed in the past
their willingness to investigate specific

assure the hon. Members who have

open to us, and until it has been proved

machinery for Northern Ireland.

I went to this Board and placed the position before them, and I was politely told

I will have to overhaul this Board. It has

Blind Persons Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Davison): This
is a short measure which I am sure will
meet with general approval. Its object
is to improve the lot of a very helpless
class in the community, those deprived
of sight.
The number of blind
persons in
Northern Ireland cannot be stated with
exactitude. At the end of the year 1936
the local authorities had 2,165 names on
their registers, but probably the lists are
not complete; 1,166 of these persons were
in Belfast. Although exact particulars
of the numbers at different ages have not
been obtained for all areas, it would
appear from unofficial inquiries made
that about 85 per cent. of the known
blind persons are over fifty years of age.
This, of course, may be due to the fact
that the people over fifty are known
because they claim their pensions,
whereas those under that age do not
come under the notice of the authorities.
At present provision is made for assisting blind persons under the Blind
Persons Act of 1920. Under this Act
blind persons become entitled to pension
under the Old Age Pensions Act on
reaching the age of fifty. Local
authorities under this Act have also very
extensive powers of providing for the
welfare of blind persons, and the present
Bill, therefore, only proposes a few
amendments, carrying somewhat further
the principles already laid down.
The first proposal-Clause 1-is to
reduce the age at which blind persons
become eligible for pension from fifty
years to forty years. This is a concession which has been advocated for some
time by those associations, official or
otherwise, which are interested in promoting the welfare of the blind. They
have pointed out that while persons
under forty may be trained and may be
able to find a certain amount of employment, the chances after that age are
slight. It would, therefore, be a great
blessing to these people to have some
small regular income. The number to
be added to the pension list will not be
considerable. This is estimated at about
300 and the cost at £7,800 a year.
The second main alteration, Clause 2
(2), is to transfer from the poor law
authorities and place on the local
authorities under the 1920 Act the

Eire Negotiations
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
It may be recollected by hon. Members
that this question was definitely settled
by the statement made by the British
Government in answer to the publication
by Eire of its new Constitution. There
was an immediate reply by the British
Government-I am speaking entirely
from memory, because I was not aware
that this question would be raised to-day
-stating quite clearly that the alteration in the Constitution of Eire did not
in any way affect the status of Northern
Ireland. That statement was issued by
the British Government prior to their
meeting with the Ministers of Eire.
Then it is well-known that the British
Government informed our Government
that the question of a trade pact between
the two countries was about to be raised.
If I remember aright there were two
subjects on the agenda published in the
Press. The first was the actual trade
agreement, and the second was with
regard to defence. Nothing else was
mentioned at that time, nor were we
informed that anything else was about to
take place. Suddenly, however, an
announcement was made by the Prime
Minister of Eire that he was going to
super-impose something upon the other
two the question of partition.
That
was instantly turned down by the
British Government, and it was subsequently turned down in no uncertain
voice by the people of Ulster. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
That should wipe out from the mind
of the hon. Member, if I may say so,
any question whatever as to the status
of Ulster being changed in any way by
the conversations at present going on.
That closes that part.
-we
So far as defence is concernedwere naturally not interested in the
matter beyond being citizens of the
United Kingdom. Therefore, the Ministers of Eire and Great Britain are talking over this question without our
knowledge. We have no way of penetrating into the conversations on that
matter. That disposes of it too.

agreement which has existed between

past, or as it is commonly called,

the old agreement between the two

demanded, I do not like the word, but
shall asked that when an attempt
say
was being made to renew the cattle-coal
pact of the past, they might go a step

between the two countries for the purpose of promoting better trade.
It is here where we came in, because

ourselves. Instead of wasting any time
the Home Office immediately got into

own
Agriculture also came into the picture,
and my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Agriculture, accompanied the Minister of Finance on two occasions in order
that the agricultural position might be
placed before the Government of Great
Britain.
There is nothing at the moment to
report in regard to the progress being
made in this connection, nothing whatever, but I have the greatest faith in
the British Ministers, and know that
they will act fairly by this part of the
United Kingdom as they have acted
fairly by other parts of the United
Kingdom. We are all one. There is no
difference between ourselves, so far as
trade and industry and agriculture are
concerned, and
any part of Great
Britain. I will not say that the position
is exactly the same, because in Great
Britain you have a great diversity of
industries and an enormous population.
It is different here, for the reason that
most people on the other side will talk
about forty or fifty millions in a comparatively airy way, whereas, so far as
we are concerned that is a very large
Adjournment-
Eire Negotiations
9 MARCH 1938
sum of money. Our proportion is about
one to forty. That is to say, when they
talk about forty millions we talk about
one million.
In consequence of that, there is a
delicacy in dealing with matters of the
kind, because a very small give-away,
as it were, on the part of the British
Government to Eire in regard to trade
and industry might mean a great deal
to us. My right hon. Friends realise
that and also realise that, whereas agriculture in England bears a small proportion to its industrial side of life, in
Ulster it is exactly the opposite. Agriculture bears a very big proportion, a
much larger proportion to our various
industries. These are, as I have said,
entirely financial matters.
So far as I am concerned I am glad
beyond measure that we have a Minister
of Finance fit and able in every degree
to meet those on the other side. I have
no qualms whatever as to the efforts he
will make to see that we get fair play.
The only thing is that what may appear
fair play to the British Ministers may
not be exactly fair play to us, for the
reasons I have mentioned. That is the
difference between the relative positions
of industry and agriculture over there
and here, and the large influence which
agriculture has here compared to our
other industries.
So far as the British Ministers are concerned I know them all, and I trust
them. I do not think I can say any
more to-day on the subject, because even
in Eire itself nothing apparently has
leaked out as to the arrangements before
the two sides at the present moment.
Therefore, there is nothing I can reasonably say further, except that my right
hon. Friends have been kept fully
informed. They may have to go over
again.
In the normal state of affairs year by
year we are constantly crossing over to
meet the Chancellor of the Exchequer or
the Home Office or whatever Ministry
has to deal with certain matters. It is
nothing out of the way for our Ministers
to be invited over to consult about
matters affecting Northern Ireland. The
hon. Member for Shankill may rest
assured that the promise I made yesterday will be fulfilled, and that as soon
as possible the fullest information will
be given to the House.

The Bill to which I am asking the
House to give a Second Reading is a
counterpart of a Measure which has just
received the Royal Assent at Westminster, and is a fresh indication of the
Government's policy of maintaining the
uniformity of the unemployment insurance scheme in Northern Ireland with
the scheme in Great Britain. I have
reason to believe it will be warmly supported by both sides of the House.
The Bill has three principal objects,
which I propose to submit to the House.

Bill. Under Section 80 of the Unem-

and medical (including dental) inspection and treatment for juveniles attending at such courses under the same
conditions as those authorities may at
present make this provision for children.
attending at public elementary schools.

charge during instructional hours to unemployed juveniles attending at these
courses.
The exercise of these powers will be in

of the Ministry of Finance, and will be
subject to the approval of the Ministry
of Labour. The expenses incurred by

Sub-section (2) of Clause 2 of the Bill

by regulation. These classes include

of Northern Ireland at the cost of the

Shortly, the effect of this Reinsurance

in

the outstanding debt of

in
The recent examination of the finances
of the Great Britain fund by the Unemployment Insurance Statutory Committee
has enabled them to recommend that the
amount of the reserves held by the Great
Britain Unemployment Fund are
excess of its probable requirements.
Accordingly, the Committee has recommended to the Imperial Minister that
£20,000,000 out of a total reserve of just
over £60,000,000 should be used at once
to reduce the outstanding debt of the
Great Britain Fund, which now amounts
to about £103,000,000.
Under the law as it stands, this debt
is being repaid by a statutory funding
arrangement. An annuity is payable,
covering principal and interest, amounting to £5,000,000 a year, and this
annuity will extinguish the debt in 1971.
Under existing law, if the outstanding
debt is reduced by £20,000,000, as the
Statutory Committee recommends, the
effect will simply be to leave untouched
the amount of the statutory annuity but
to reduce by a number of years the period
during which that annuity will be payable. In the view of the Statutory Committee it is fairer to the existing contributors to the fund that they themselves
should have some benefit from a surplus
which their contributions have gone to
build up.
Accordingly, the Statutory
Committee recommends that no attempt
should be made to shorten the period
during which the debt is to be
tinguished, but that power should be
taken to reduce the annuity, leaving the
period unaltered. The effect of this will
be to release an annual sum, hitherto
ex-

The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount

Measure now before the House. I should

days prior to the Act of 1920, covering
the whole of Great Britain and Ireland.
Then, in consequence of the Act of 1920,
which made no differentiation between
the North and the South, the fund was
divided, so much being allocated to the
whole of Ireland and so much to Great
Britain.
Subsequently, when the Free State was
established, it had to be readjusted once
more between Great Britain on the one
hand, and Northern Ireland and
Southern Ireland on the other hand. For
carrying out that division, to the best of
my recollection, there was very little data
to go upon, and it was extremely difficult
for the officials, who were dealing with

idea as to what would happen when
the two funds were divided, nor, I think,
was it sufficiently realised that on normal
standards unemployment in Northern
Ireland was always considerably higher
than it was in Great Britain. Therefore,
the division, I believe, was really an ad
hoc settlement for which there was in-

Exported Animals (Compensation) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): At the outset it is
necessary for me to explain to the House
the existing legislation and its effect on
the export of livestock to England.
Great Britain is only responsible for
cattle moved from the various ports.
That is to say in the event of an outbreak
of foot-and-mouth disease it is necessary
for the country concerned, including
Northern Ireland, to deal with the cattle
detained in the various ports.
In 1928 an Act was passed which provided for compensation in the event of
cattle being slaughtered as a result of
foot-and-mouth disease. An Insurance
Fund was established to deal with these
payments. Levies were made in order to
create the fund. Later many
cases
occurred where cattle were detained for
periods varying from a short to a comparatively lengthy period. Investigations
were carried out by the various veterinary
officers to ensure that these cattle arrived
in a healthy state and were not being contaminated.
In 1932 an Act was passed to cover
such additional charges as lairage, the
cost of feeding and the tending of the
cattle. The Bill now before the House
goes a step further. It proposes, and,
indeed, the trade has agreed, that where
depreciation in the value of cattle takes
place as a result of their being detained
in the ports of Great Britain the owner
should be compensated. I think that is
quite fair. The trade agree that where
cattle have been exported and are
detained in a port through no fault of
the traders, the owners should be compensated for their loss.
The Bill also makes another slight
modification. At present an owner cannot receive compensation for slaughter
and also for extra lairage and feeding
charges. It is possible, however, to
visualise cases where owners might have
had their cattle in these lairages for some
time and after investigation the cattle
would be slaughtered. Therefore, it is
right that they should not only receive.
compensation for the cattle slaughtered
but also for the lairage and feeding
charges.
What the Bill sets out, briefly, is this.
The owner will in future obtain compensation in respect of slaughter, or
slaughter plus the extra lairage and feeding charges, or, thirdly, depreciation,
together with lairage and feeding costs.
There is just one other point about this
Bill. Where compensation for slaughter
is paid the owner cannot claim for depreciation as well. The whole of these
payments will be met by the Insurance
Fund which has been set up by the livestock traders of this country. The fund
has been made possible by a levy on the
various types of livestock exported.
There is a levy of 23d on every head of
cattle; 1d on every pig and d on every
sheep. When the capital sum has reached
a certain figure-one which is considered
satisfactory by the trustees and the
Ministry then the levies are suspended,
as they are at present. The fund is controlled by a body of trustees appointed
by the North of Ireland livestock trade.
I should, in conclusion, like to congratulate that body on operating so
successfully a scheme which has been and
will be of very great benefit to the traders
without calling on the Treasury for
assistance. It is obvious that the losses
incurred as a result of detention or
slaughter would eventually fall on the
farmers and I have no hesitation in
recommending this Bill to the House. I
beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

Oral Answers to Questions.
SUPPLY OF BASIC SLAG.
1. Major PANTER asked the Minister of Agriculture whether it is a fact
that farmers have been unable to purchase British basic slag under the Land
Fertility Scheme, which allowed them
a rebate of 25 per cent., and that only
two small cargoes of slag have been
imported into Northern Ireland this
year; whether farmers have been compelled to buy inferior foreign slag on
which there is no rebate, and what steps
the Ministry propose to take in order to
ensure that adequate supplies of British.
slag will be available.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): I am aware
that farmers have had difficulty in procuring British basic slag, and I am
informed that two cargoes have been
imported since October last. The total
quantity was, however, about the same
as in the 1936 season, but, of course,
owing to the subsidy the demand this
year has been abnormal. When the
shortage of British slag was first
apparent my Ministry took up the
matter with the Land Fertility Committee. It was clear, however, that no
Governmental action could alter the
position brought about entirely by the
fact that the United Kingdom supply
of slag was unequal to the increased
demand created by the Land Fertility
Scheme and that the position could only
be remedied in the course of time. I
cannot accept the suggestion that
farmers in Northern Ireland have been
obliged to turn to foreign slag. My
Ministry has repeatedly announced by
broadcast and otherwise that there is no
need to do so and have advised farmers
who have difficulty in procuring high
grade British basic slag
to obtain
ground North African phosphates which,
under the conditions in Northern Ireland, are quite as effective as highgrade slag. Ample supplies of this
reliable substitute have been and are
still available at reasonable prices, even
when allowance is made for the subsidy
payable under the scheme in respect of
British basic slag. Evidently farmers
generally are following the Ministry's
advice, so that there is really no hardship as far as agriculture is concerned.
SUBSIDIES FOR FLAX GROWERS.
2. Dr. MAGINESS asked the Minister of Agriculture whether the figure of
£400,000 mentioned by him in a recent
speech is necessary for the introduction
of a scheme either of subsidies to flax
growers or guaranteeing a price; whether
this figure is merely a conjecture, or one
which has been arrived at by computing
in detail the moneys necessary for such
a scheme, and if so, whether he will
give the details to the House.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am satisfied
that the figure of £400,000 referred to
by the hon. Member is a reasonable
estimate of the amount that might be
required to finance any scheme of subsidies or guaranteed prices that would
induce farmers to increase substantially
the acreage under flax. The figure is
not merely a conjecture and has been
calculated as follows:-
-
Let it be assumed that there is a
guaranteed price calculated to send the
flax area up to at least 40,000 acres,
which was approximately the pre-war
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
15 MARCH 1938
figure. Take an average yield of 40
stones to the acre, which is not excessive, having regard to increased yields
from pedigree strains. This would mean
a production of 1,600,000 stones of flax.
Let us assume that there would be
a guaranteed price of, say, 10s a stone,
because, having regard to cost of production, this is the lowest price that
would be likely to bring about a substantial increase in production. If,
therefore, the market price fell to 5s a
stone a very simple calculation indicates
that a subsidy of another 5s would be
required or a total of £400,000, and
even that implies a limitation of the
acreage to 40,000. There would also, of
course, be the cost of administration. It
may be considered that these figures are
fantastic, but in this connection it is
right to point out that so recently as
the season 1930-31 the average price did
in fact fall to 5s a stone, and in the
following year it was no more than 7s
a stone.

IRON ORE IN COUNTY DOWN.
3. Mr. BAILEY asked the Minister
of Commerce whether, in view of the
necessity of introducing new industries
into Northern Ireland, he will explore
the possibility of re-starting work at an
iron-ore mine situate in Dehornet,
County Down, which was worked about
sixty years ago and which was only
stopped owing to transport difficulties;
whether this mine is still capable of producing valuable iron-ore in such quantities as to make the mining a paying
concern; whether all transport difficulties
have now disappeared; whether he is
prepared to obtain a mining engineer's
report on the mine, and, if such report
be favourable, whether he is prepared to
finance or aid in the financing of a project to re-open and re-work this mine;
whether in the event of ore being
obtained from the mine he would encourage by financial support the smelting
of the ore in Northern Ireland, and
whether such mining and smelting works
would give considerable employment in
this part of County Down.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The hon. Member will
appreciate that any assistance which the
Government could give to a project of
the nature which he has in mind, must
fall within the scope of the legislation
passed by this House for the encouragement of new industries. If any person,
or body of persons, will come forward
with a proposal for the reopening of the
Dehornet mine, the hon. Member may
rest assured that my Department will
give such a proposal the fullest consideration. The hon. Member will
appreciate that any preliminary exploratory work of a detailed nature in
connection with the mine, would be a
matter for those interests which seek
eventually to secure a profit by its exploitation.

Quite recently the Highfield Factory

be taken immediately to see that new
industries are brought to Northern Ireland. Realising the responsibility that

As far as Ulster is concerned, there

It has been suggested that there should

for tourist purposes. I am glad to know
that the tourist traffic is an increasing
traffic, and that more and more visitors
are coming every year to our shores. We
want them all to come. Surely a road
round Lough Neagh, which is one of the
beauty spots of Northern Ireland, ought
not to be impossible. If the Government
spent several millions on making that road
under the Act passed some time ago, I
think it would be a better way of spending money than the way it is now being
spent. It would give the people healthy
and useful employment and assist the
whole community. It ought to be done.
That is one way in which the Government could do a great deal to relieve
unemployment from our midst.
There is another way by which they
could do something not only to help the
agricultural community, but to help to
relieve unemployment in the rural areas,
and that is by increasing the rateable
value of a farm holding on which drainage operations can be carried out. I am
grateful to the Government for increasing
the grant from 75 to 80 per cent., but I
want to say that there are a great many
farms on which much labour could be
employed in draining and reclaiming the
land. Where, however, the valuation is
more than £75 the farmer is ruled out.
A great many of the larger farms are
going without the drainage and reclamation necessary simply because the farmers
cannot afford to pay the whole cost of the
labour. They are debarred from taking
advantage of the scheme because of this
barrier that farms of over £75 valuation
do not come within the meaning of the
Act. I would like the Government to remove that barrier entirely. If a farmer
with an agricultural holding of £75 or
£175 or £275 valuation is prepared to
take advantage of the scheme and utilise
some unemployed people in draining and
reclaiming the land I think no obstacle
ought to be put in his way. I appeal to
the Government to remove this restriction
of £75, which is hampering the development of the farming community along
these lines.
There is another restriction placed on
them, that is, a man must derive his
living wholly from farming in order to
get the benefit of the scheme. I have
one man in my own constituency for
whom I can speak now. His valuation
is not above £75. He is an auctioneer
in a small way; he bought a farm of
land which was derelict and required
a great deal of money spent on it.
That man because he has a side line is
prevented from getting the benefit of
this 75 or 80 per cent. for the drainage
and improvement of his land. I think
that is not as it should be. I think it
is better to spend money in that way
than to continue paying it out all the
time and have nothing for it. I appeal
to the Government to remove not only
the restriction as far as the valuation
of farms is concerned, but also to remove
that restriction which prevents a man
who has another business, if he is prepared to comply with the necessary conditions, taking advantage of this scheme.

authorities suggesting that local authorities might usefully and reasonably
indicate their preference to firms supplying goods manufactured in Northern

Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move an
Amendment to this Motion as follows:
"That this House, fully realising the

present time, pray that its efforts to attain

That is an Amendment which is, I
think, more in keeping with the powers
of this House. This House has no right
or authority to commit its people to the
foreign policy of another Parliament. It
has no right or authority, nor has it the
voice of the people, to say that because
that Parliament may call upon the nation
for conscription we should follow on those
lines.
The commitments at the present
time of the Government mentioned in the
Motion are of such a kind that we in
Northern Ireland are in total disagreement with them.
I do not want to use any words likely
to reflect on any foreign power. I do
not intend to do it, but we in Northern
Ireland are opposed to dictatorships. We
believe the policy of certain countries in
the world is wrong. I think I can safely
say we all recognise and admire democratic government. That being so, I feel
that this is not an opportune moment for
the Prime Minister to come in with a
Motion setting out SO many commitments, as I see them, on the people of
Northern Ireland.
I have only got to recall the speech of
one of the military authorities in
Northern Ireland not so very long ago,

Ireland. It is here that the highest percentage of recruits has been got for the
British Army. Whether Members on the
other side like it or not, I say without

tendency in Great Britain to bring in

is eating into Northern Ireland. There
is a fear in my mind at any rate that if
that position arises in Northern Ireland
you will find you have worked in the

for the power which have set out to
you
support. We are in a unique position.
We are situated in an island, our nearest
neighbour being Eire. I am satisfied
there will be no conscription in Eire.
What is going to be the position in

what might happen.
I do say candidly to the Prime Minister that if ever there was a disturbing

Mr. BLACK: I rise to move this
Amendment which stands in the name of
the hon. and learned Member for St.
Anne's (Mr. Warnock) who, unfortunately, cannot be here to-day. If the
Committee will look at the Clause of the
Bill as drafted they will see that the
local authority, in determining
extent of financial assistance in the case
of a blind person, must have regard to
the rules laid down in Section 33 of the
Unemployment Act of 1934. They have
the
Blind Persons Bill-
Committee
22 MARCH 1938
to comply with those rules when computing the resources of a blind person.
When one turns to Section 33 of the
Unemployment Act of 1934 one finds that
that section provides that in computing
the resources of a person entitled to any
allowance under that Act certain
resources are to be disregarded or only
to be partially regarded. By this
Clause, as drafted, those directions are
being carried into this present Bill. The
effect is that the local authority, in computing the resources of any blind person,
is to disregard, for example, the first
£1 of any wound or disability pension.
It has, also, to disregard one-half of any
amount which a blind person is receiving by way of workmen's compensation,
and the first 7s 6d of any benefit under
the National Health Insurance Act.
The whole idea of that is that there
are certain amounts of income, such, for
instance, as those I have mentionedwounds or disability pensions, amounts
payable under the Workmen's Compensation Act, and insurance benefit-which
the local authority is not to take into
account, or fully into account, as being
part of the means of a blind person when
calculating the amount which the local
authority ought to pay under the Act.
It will be obvious to the Committee that
one matter has been omitted, that is in
regard to old-age pensions, and the object
of this Amendment is that old-age
pensions should not be taken into account
to the extent of 6s.
The practice in Northern Ireland now
is that once a person who has been
receiving an allowance from a local
authority reaches an age when he is
entitled to the old-age pension the
amount being paid by the local authority
is decreased by the amount of the old-age
pension. The result is that when a
blind person becomes entitled to the oldage pension he gets no financial benefit
whatever. The State bears the cost of
the pension and the local authority is
relieved by the amount of the pension
which the State is paying. The effect of
that is, that when people come to the
old-age pension age the State take on a
certain liability, the local authority is
relieved of that amount, and the blind
person remains where he or she was.
The object of this Amendment is to
bring old-age pensions to the extent of
6s into the same category as, for
instance, the payment of sick benefit
under the National Health Insurance
Act, and it struck me that the intention
is to provide that a blind person who
is receiving an allowance from the local
authority, when he becomes entitled to
the old-age pension, shall not get just
no benefit at all from the old-age
pension, but that the old-age pension to
the extent of 6s a week shall inure to
the benefit of the blind person. Under
the Bill as it is at present, incorporating
Section 3 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1934, a person getting a blind
person's allowance is entitled to any
benefit under the National Health
Insurance Act. The blind person is
getting the total of that benefit and it
does not just pass to relieve the local
authority. That is the Amendment
which my hon. and learned Friend put
on the Paper. I think it should commend itself to the Committee. The
Amendment is simply designed to see
that when a person who is getting the
blind person's allowance reaches the age
entitling him to the pension some of the
amount should inure to the benefit of
that person instead of inuring to the

Agricultural Labourers' Wages Board.
Mr. AGNEW: I beg to move :
"That in the opinion of this House
the Government should establish immediately an Agricultural Labourers'
Wages Board for Northern Ireland."
Northern Ireland is the one "black
spot" in the Commonwealth of Nations
because the Government have not
established a Wages Board for farm
labourers. In 1924 the Labour Government took office and without having a
Labour majority one of the first things
they did was to set up a Wages Board in
order to protect farm labourers who form
a very important section of the community. Our Minister of Finance talks
occasionally about our step-by-step policy
as far as social services are concerned.
We have no step-by-step policy in social
services for farm labourers. We are
exactly 14 years behind Great Britain in
this respect. Why is this so? It will be
interesting to know the reason.
Week after week, and month after
month, the farmers' champions are "on
the air." They are always telling us how
the farmers are being helped by past and
present legislation, and promises are
being made for future legislation. Never
once on the wireless have we had a serious
talk about the starvation wages being
paid to farm labourers. The average
wage is 15s per week. This is supposed
to provide food, clothing and shelter. It
only allows one penny per meal for each
of the labourer's dependents-three meals
per day, 21 meals per week. How they
exist on it is a mystery to me. They
must be able to perform miracles. We
still have the old antiquated system of
hiring fairs. It is time they died out
completely. I still find the old system of
fairs in many parts of the country.
If we look at the conditions in England
and Scotland we find that the average
wages of farm labourers there are from
34s to 42s a week. In Northern Ireland
the farm labourer works a week and a

Agricultural Wages Board HOUSE OF COMMONS

practically amounts to a starvation allowance. Northern Ireland's population is
1,300,000, and that of New Zealand
1,600,000. The democratic Government

We find that in Northern Ireland farm

I was always led to believe that Northern Ireland was a great agricultural

farmers

was put down the whole matter has been

needs no inquiry to convince us all that
the farm worker is not sufficiently well

There have always been unions and

a
The mover of this Motion seemed to
think that all that was necessary was to
wave a wand, and somehow these wages
that we hear about would, if they were
paid, solve the whole problem of keeping
the people on the land. He told us
about the wages that are fixed by Statute
by the Wages Boards in Great Britain,
and yet, in spite of those wages, that
seemed to satisfy even him, such
prominent public man as Sir John
Russell only a few days ago came out
with an S O S that something must be
done to prevent the drift from the land
in Great Britain. It is not merely a
question of wages, though wages, I
admit, are an important factor in the
situation. There is, in addition to that,
the fact that no one to-day wants to
work on the land. When men are going
to the employment exchanges to register
as unemployed they put themselves down.
as practically anything but what they
really are-farm workers-because when
a farmer applies for help on his farm he
finds that these men have not registered
as farm hands. The moral of it is that
no one who can possibly avoid it wants to
work on the land to-day.
It has been cast up to the farmers that
they are subsidised on every side. As a
representative of the farmers I am very
grateful for what has been done and for
what has been attempted on their behalf
by our own Ministry and by the Imperial
authorities. And yet if Members on the
other side of the House would just take
as much trouble to go out and in among
some of the small farmers, as they are
taking to prove their case in connection
with the farm labourer-and I am not
saying that one word of it is not truethey would learn something of the other
side of the story. In spite of all that has
been done, the fact remains that to-day
we have a multitude of farmers who
simply are not able to pay the wages
asked for.
I could take as an illustration-I do
not want to weary the House-the working of the Pigs Marketing Scheme.
Owing to that scheme the pig population
went up very rapidly, and as a result
it has been estimated that £1,000,000 or
£1,250,000 more money was being
circulated amongst the farmers. It is
very easy for hon. Members on the other
side of the House to run away with the
idea that all that money is going into the
farmers' pockets. I submit that in that
case, as in every case like it, the increase
in the circulation of money, owing to the
increase in the pig population, has
actually helped the towns and the cities
more than it has helped the farmers.
It has meant more money going into the
pockets of the feeding-stuffs merchants;
it has meant more money in transport;
it has meant more money to the employees of the curing establishments, and
it is evident that it has not meant very
much more money to the pig producers,
because they are ceasing to produce pigs
on the old scale.
There are endless facts that might be
advanced if one wanted to argue against
the setting up of a Wages Board. I do
not rise to oppose that principle at all,
but I should like to point out, in spite
of all the information that hon. Members
359 Agricultural Wages Board HOUSE OF COMMONS
Agricultural Wages Board 360
[Rev. Robert Moore]
claim to have gathered, that there are
endless factors in this situation that do
need an inquiry to clear up. The same
customs do not hold or prevail in any
two of the six counties of Northern
Ireland. There are arrangements as
between employers and employed in the
County of Fermanagh that were never
heard of in the County of Down. Some
of the perquisites, of which no mention
has been made by hon. Members at all
in moving and seconding this Motion, are
of such a nature that it would be almost
impossible to calculate their actual
financial value. Problems of this kind
arise immediately in connection with the
setting up of any Board of this kind, and
I do not see that any Government
Department could possibly have launched
out straight away on a scheme such as
has been proposed without making a
very exhaustive inquiry into these
matters.
I am not at all sure that even when
the inquiry has been held, and when a
Wages Board has been set up, that we
will have solved this problem. I believe
that a great deal will have to be done in
the way of lightening the nature of the
labour that has to be done on the land,
and that the position of the labourer in
the country will have to be made more
attractive. I am tempted to make an
almost wild suggestion to the House,
that is, that the Government should take
their courage in both hands and institute
for the whole of agriculture in the Six
Counties vast relief schemes, that would
enable something substantial to be done.
to induce the fine, sturdy, robust young
men and women to remain on the land
instead of drifting into other industries.
It would enable the employers to pay an
attractive wage, it would enable the
small farmers, who are not able to pay
wages or to make improvements on their
holdings, to improve the whole working
conditions on their farms.
I know that it looks wild, but I believe
that in the long run it would save the
Government a very considerable amount
of money, and it might be a greater contribution to the safety of our country
and of our Empire in the long run than
the piling up of arms. Up to now we
have simply been turning this way and

not conversant with local affairs to solve

opinion, is not the best way of tackling
them. If Sir William McLintock is not
prepared to come and conduct an inquiry
in public, which I hope this House will
approve, I do not think we will lose anything. I believe the Government will
have no trouble in finding inside Northern Ireland a very eminent man fully
qualified to undertake the inquiry, and a
man who will be prepared to carry out
the instructions of the Government.
The second party to this Act are the
Transport Board. As I said earlier in
my remarks, I opposed the Transport
Bill, but it is only fair to say that when
it became law I immediately got into
touch with the Transport Board and I
was able, after negotiations, to come to
terms with the Board. Since then my
own haulage contractor has been taken
over and I have transferred all my
business to the Transport Board. I have
no fault to find with their operation.
They have done their work well. I have
received efficient service from the Board,
and the only fault I have is that my
haulage expenses are something over 10
per cent. more than they were. I state
that to show I do not adopt a dog-in-themanger attitude, and that when the Bill
became law I did my best to help the
Transport Board to carry out the duties
imposed on it, but even with my assistance I am sorry to say it has not been a
success.
These men were asked by the Government to undertake this unsavoury job of
carrying on the business of the Transport
Board, and they have carried on to the
best of their ability for some considerable
time. They have done their very best
to do an impossible thing. They have
found out after some considerable time
that they could not do the job, and now
they come and say in an interview that
they have done their best to carry out
the duties imposed upon them, but they
found it impossible to do so, and so they
now ask for a public inquiry at which
they would have the fullest opportunity
of stating their case. They ask that, so
that they should have the fullest opportunity of repelling any attacks that
might be made upon them, and of vindicating the position they are in to-day. If
I may say so, I think it very unfair of
the Government to run away from the
men they put into that unfortunate position, and not to give them the public
inquiry they have demanded. There is
no ambiguity about the request made by
the Transport Board according to the
letter which I have in my hand and
which they sent to the Press. They say:
Early in the month of January we
felt it our duty, as trustees for the
public, appointed under the Act in the
Transport Act Tribunals
Transport Act Tribunals

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Elliott]
matter of road transport, to bring to
the attention of the Government, at an
interview, certain vital matters in connection with the working of the Act
which were causing us the gravest concern, and also certain defects in the
Act itself.
The Government representatives proposed at the interview that an impartial
Commission of Inquiry should be
appointed to go into the matter raised,
and we at once expressed our approval
of this course and our desire to place
all the information in our power before such a Commission.
Subsequently the railway companies
had an interview with the Government,
and also agreed that an inquiry should
be held.
For a considerable time past, both
before the actual appointment of the
Commission and since, we have been
pressing upon the Government our view
that it is essential to every interest that
this should be a public inquiry, if it is
to command the fullest public confidence.
There are three parties interested in
the success of the Act, namely—(1) the
public, (2) the Board, (3) the railway
companies. If we are to judge by the
opinion expressed in the Press and elsewhere, it would appear that the first
and most important party to the Act
desire that the inquiry should be
public. The Board certainly desire it.
Further, for the past 2 years the
Board has been subjected to much
criticism, which, in our view, was made
without proper appreciation of the
true facts. We feel that the time has
now come when we should have an
opportunity of stating the position
fully to the public, and affording them
an opportunity of hearing what the
parties to the scheme have to say, in the
circumstances which will enable the
statements to be properly tested and
weighed.
This letter is signed by Mr. D. L.
Clarke, chairman of the Transport Board;
Lord Enniskillen, Messrs. J. R. Haslett,
S. G. Haughton, D. W. Smyth, R. H.
Smyth and J. E. Wilson, members of the
Transport Board. I do not know whether
all the members of the Board signed the
letter, but I know that that letter, which
has been sent to the Press, is a clear claim
to the Government to give them an opportunity of vindicating themselves at a
public tribunal. I think the Government
are not playing fair by the Transport
Board, who have asked for this public
inquiry, in not acceding to their demand.
The third party to this Transport Act
is the railway companies. It seems to
me very strange that the railway companies should still have such influence
with the Government. I understand they
are doing their best to prevent a public
inquiry being held. When the Transport
Bill was brought into this House I was
bold enough to say that I believed it
originated in the minds of the railway
companies. I believed that then; I believe it now. I believe the Bill never
would have been brought in here had it
not been that the Government thought-
I think, perhaps, rightly thought-that
something ought to be done to co-ordinate
transport and to preserve to some extent
our railways.
The railway companies supported the
Bill with their whole heart. They expected something from the Bill which
they evidently did not get. I am taking
my cue from the shareholders' meetings,
the reports of which I have read.
Evidently the shareholders are not satisfied that the Transport Act has brought
success and revenue to the railway companies. The railway companies, who
were loudest in their demands for the
Transport Act, are just as loud now in
their demand that the inquiry which is
going to be held ought to be held in
private and not in public.
We
We have three parties to this arrangement under the Transport Act.
have the public, we have the Transport
Board, and we have the railway companies. Surely the demand made by the
public, backed up by the Transport

have with the Government. Perhaps I
should not say this, but I got a letter
yesterday morning which rather confirms

prevent this inquiry being held in public.

We ought to have a public inquiry. The

on the whole matter. As I said before,

It is only when we get to grips with it,

The PRIME MINISTER: I hope that
while I am explaining certain matters
to the House I will also convert my hon.
Friend (Mr. Elliott), and that he will

Mr. BEATTIE: He has said that he

The PRIME MINISTER: I do think
he can change his mind, after he has
heard what I have to say. First of all,

for the manner in which he put up the
case for the Motion? Both the Mover
and Seconder referred to three parties
that are particularly interested in the
question of road and railway transport.
There are four: in addition to those
mentioned, there is this House-Parliament. The position is that the Government, I think, anticipating the feelings
of Parliament, decided to have an inquiry into the whole matter. After that,
a question arose as to whether it should
be a public or a private inquiry. I think
I am correct in gathering that hon.
Members on both sides of the House
desired a public inquiry. They seemed
to be anxious to have the whole matter
thrashed out in public.
As soon as that desire was expressed
to me, I got busy with my colleagues to
see how we could reconcile all the elements that are involved in this matter,
and I think we have solved that question.
The hon. Member for South Tyrone (Mr.
Elliott), is mistaken in thinking that Sir
Josiah Stamp came to see me in London
in order to persuade me that there should
be no public inquiry. When Sir Josiah
Stamp came to see me he indicated that
he would welcome a public inquiry, and
there was nothing in the Press, as far
as I could see, to indicate anything else.
If I may say so, he was most helpful in
every way, as he always is when we ask
him for his help and advice. Sir Josiah
Stamp is, in the true sense of the word,
one of the biggest men in finanical as
well as in railway circles, and he is
always at the disposal of Ulster. Therefore, I hope that that will satisfy my
hon. Friend.
is
It is hairsplitting to think that there
a point of difference between the
Government and the public and the
Members of this House, because we are

Transport Act Tribunals
[The Prime Minister]
all most anxious to make a success of this
Transport Board and of the co-ordination-do not let us forget that of railway
and road transport. Therefore we should
be all working together in order to secure
that object. As to the suggestion that
the inquiry should be public, we really
could not possibly ask men of the calibre
and importance of those who are to hold
it to sit for months listening to evidence
on matters which they could pick up afterwards when the first inquiry is held. It
would be quite unfair to them. We have
no control whatever over their doing this.
Sir William McLintock and his two colleagues are doing this in order to oblige
us. The moment they were asked to
undertake this task, they indicated their
willingness to oblige, just as Sir Felix
Pole and others have done in the past
when they were asked for expert advice.
I am sorry to say that we could not get
in Ulster men who carry so much weight.
When one looks at the work that Sir
William McLintock has done-incidentally he helped us here in the unravelling
of that very complicated matter of the
shipping companies-one realises that we
could not find in England, let alone
Northern Ireland, a man more fully
equipped to take the chair at an inquiry
into financial and technical matters so
far as our transport is concerned.
I observe that in the Motion it is stated
that it will take more time and money to
hold two inquiries than to hold one. I
do not agree with that at all. I think
that the open public inquiry in the first
instance will give everybody an opportunity of appearing before the Committee
in order to give his views. That will
prevent its being said afterwards that a
single interested party was refused a
hearing. The careful way in which notes
can be taken there will very greatly help
the second Commission. My opinion is
that this course will help the House to
agree that the plan which we have in
view is the best one.
When this Road Transport Board was
set up for the purpose of co-ordinating
road transport with the railway system
everybody in Ulster realised that it was a
very big task to undertake. I am not
going back to draw attention to the condition in which many of the hauliers'
companies were at that time, as well as
the railway companies; but it was an
earnest attempt by the Government to
solve a most difficult problem, and I think
half of that problem has been solved.
I notice by the debates, by the Press,
and by general conversation, that so far
as the great bus services are concerned
there is not very much complaint left
now in the country districts. I dare say
you would find the same class of complaint here and there with regard to the
tramways. On the whole, taking it as a
broad principle, there seems to be general
agreement that that half of the work of
the Transport Board has been performed
admirably. Then we come to the other
half of the problem, and I have no doubt
whatever that by persistence, by all of
us working as hard as we can to help in
every possible way, we will be equally
successful with regard to the haulage of
goods throughout the country.
A question was raised as to how we
could have the two committees without
a clash either in connection with the
terms of reference or with the evidence
which must be heard. That seems to be
very simple indeed. The terms of reference of the public committee, which will
be held first, will be:-
To consider representations from the
public or other interests desirous of
being heard in regard to existing
transport facilities and charges.
We hope to get a very able and prominent man to act as chairman of that
committee. The terms of reference of
the other committee are:-
To investigate and report on the working of the Road and Railway Transport Act (Northern Ireland), 1935,
and to advise what improvements in
the operation of the Act or changes in
its provisions are necessary in order
to secure on a sound economic basis an
adequate and efficient transport system.
That is what we are all aiming at, that
is what the Government are determined
to attain in the end, and I think it
would be helpful if this Motion were not
pressed to a division, and if the whole
House showed that it is desirous of
helping. There are so many interests
involved that it is not easy to satisfy
everybody. I think the procedure that
my colleagues and I have worked out
ought to give absolute confidence to the
whole public that whatever should go

out to the public will go out at the

the other matters will be dealt with by
the very eminent men who are to investigate the financial and technical side.
Between the two the Government will
be able to arrive at some proposal to put
before Parliament in order that we may,
as I have said, secure in the end the

Mr. YOUNG: The Prime Minister
has naturally said a good deal that I
intended to say myself. I want to say
that I think the Government are quite
right in the object they have in view.
To my mind the first inquiry should be
a public inquiry, at which everybody in
the country who has any grievance about
fares and conditions of service may state
his objections. The second inquiry will
deal with financial and technical matters.
In my opinion, if the Government started
a public inquiry into the technicalities
and finances of the undertaking, and if
counsel were employed on both sides, and
were to make long-winded speeches as
they do in the law courts, as if they
were addressing jurors, we would never
get anything fixed at all. In the next
place, the general public would not read
all the evidence, word for word, given at
any inquiry of that kind. The newspapers are no more perfect than anything
else. They pick out tit-bits and put
them in the next day's papers, often
thereby leaving an entirely wrong impression of the evidence of a witness.
Then the next thing would be correspondence in the newspapers about the evidence
of the witness, correspondence upon
partial evidence.
Sir William McLintock and his two
colleagues would refuse to sit for months
and months at a public inquiry of that
kind. and in my opinion if the Government lost the benefit of the services of
these three gentlemen it would be a
calamity. There is nothing new in an
inquiry of this kind being held in private.
We have had the striking example a few
weeks ago of the Cadman Inquiry on
Civil Aviation. That inquiry was set
un on 1st December, 1937, and, in spite
of the Christmas holidays, it was able to
submit its report on the 10th February,
1938. When one takes the Christmas
holidays into consideration, that means
that the Committee only occupied about
two months in the entire proceedings and
they examined about seventy witnesses,
in addition to considering other statements. I think this House will admit
that the Cadman Report was drastic in
the extreme. In my opinion the
Cadman Inquiry clearly demonstrates
that facts can be arrived at much
more clearly and in a businesslike way
before a committee of experts sitting in
private than at a public inquiry with
counsel. A friendly inquiry dealing with
financial matters would arrive at a solution much better because witnesses would
say what they really thought at a private
commission. They would not be afraid
that an
extract would appear in the
Press which would, perhaps, give a wrong
impression of what they really did say.
There should not be any objection to a
person bringing counsel to a private commission. For these reasons I strongly
support the Government in their attitude
of having two inquiries.

TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Davison): I am very

the
There is no doubt that outside Belfast
proper provision has not been made for
blind persons. They have been left
almost, if not entirely, to the poor law
for relief. This Bill transfers to the
county council the duty of maintaining
the entire burden of responsibility for
their welfare and takes them out of the
poor law entirely. It does seem hard, in
the case of Belfast particularly, that the
blind persons should not get the full
benefit of Clause 1 which grants old age
pensions to blind presons at an earlier
age. Remember that what is being done
is making blind persons entitled to the
old age pension at an earlier age than
those who are not blind. This Bill
reduces to 40 the age at which blind
persons become entitled to the pension;
it simply applies the Old Age Pension
Act to blind persons at an earlier age.
This question was raised in the
Imperial House when a similar Bill was
going through there, and it was rejected
by the Government upon the ground that
blind pensions were on exactly the
same footing as the non-contributory
pensions awarded to able-bodied persons
under the Old Age Pensions Act.
This
present Amendment would really not
work out for the benefit of the blind
persons at all, because the allowance that
is made by the local authorities to the
blind persons must be taken into
account in awarding the old-age pension
in every case as the law stands at the
present time. The proposal here, not to
take into account the first six shillings
of the pension, would automatically increase the means for the purpose of
calculating the old-age pension. For
instance, if the means ascertained were
£31 a year, and the blind person were
awarded a pension of 8s a week, which
is the proper old-age pension on that
income, the disregarding of the first six
shillings of that pension by the local
authority would mean additional assistance of £15 12s a year. That would
increase the income of £31 by £15 12s,
giving a total income of £46 12s a year.
A person with means of £46 12s a year
gets a pension of only 2s, which would
reduce the pension of 8s to 2s.
There is no doubt whatever on this
point. I am informed by the Ministry
of Labour, who have control of the
awarding of old-age pensions, that that
result must necessarily follow. The
blind persons would be absolutely no
better off, and the only result of carrying
out this Amendment would be that, instead of that 6s a week being paid as
part of the old-age pension, relief to
that extent would be given to the Government and the local authority would
have to provide the 6s. The hon.
Member for Woodvale
Woodvale (Mr. Nixon)
pointed that out yesterday when this
Amendment was before the Committee.
He apparently has an intimate knowledge of the working of the Old Age
Pension Act and of the assistance given
to blind persons by the Corporation of
Belfast, and there is no doubt that his
view is correct, that the Amendment,
having regard to the Old Age Pension
Act as it stands, would be of no benefit
whatever to blind persons. My hon. and
learned Friend, the Member for St.
Anne's (Mr. Warnock), said that the
other local authorities outside Belfast do
nothing, and, therefore, they do not
matter. They do matter, because this
reduction of the age at which the pension
is payable to blind persons will be an
encouragement to them to make proper
provision for the blind persons in their
areas. For these reasons the Government cannot accept this Amendment.

The reason why I ask the Government
favourably to consider this Amendment
is that it seems to me, having regard to

have already been told by the Parliamentary Secretary that in different areas
in Northern Ireland the Act has been

In the city of Belfast, and perhaps in

been administered well in spirit, but in
other districts of Northern Ireland it has

The twelve months referred to in the
Act of 1920 expired during the time that
this Government was being set up, and
as far as I know no steps were taken to
compel the local authorities to furnish
schemes under the Act. I suggest it is
most important that that power should
now be put into effect. I do not desire
to add to the burden of local authorities,
but I think there are two good reasons
why this Clause in the Act of 1920
should be re-enacted in this Bill. The
first is the lack of uniformity in the provision made for the blind. The burden
of providing for the blind is placed on
the local authorities, and I see no reason
why the man who is blind and is in need
because he is blind should have rights
which are dissimilar according to whether
he lives in the city or in the country. It
is beyond my comprehension why the
State should leave a blind person's
benefits to depend upon whether he
lives in the city or in the country, and
that is the first reason why I suggest that
this Amendment should be made.
The second reason is that this Bill adds
considerably to the burden and duty of
local authorities with regard to the welfare of the blind. They must now look
not only to the needs of the blind person,
but must have regard to the needs of
those members of his household who are
his dependents and also in need. That
may mean very substantial expenditure
on the part of the local authorities. If
there was reason in 1920 for devising
some way of compelling local authorities
to do their duty there is far more reason
now, and there should be some method
of securing uniformity of administration
the part of all local authorities.
Various questions may possibly arise in
the administration of the further duties
cast upon local authorities, and one can
easily see that some central control is
very desirable.
