Milk and Milk Products Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): This Bill is
designed to effect a number of minor
Amendments to the code of legislation in
connection with the marketing of milk
and milk products in Northern Ireland.
The first Clause deals with the
question of processing factories, because
before this came into the industrial life
of Northern Ireland milk produced on
the farms had been used for the production of butter and cream. It is now
proposed to bring within the scope of
the Measure factories dealing with the
processing of milk. I will deal in some
detail with that question later.
Clause 2 deals with the powers of the
Joint Milk Council to fix differential
prices for milk according to the purposes
for which it is sold or used. There is
some doubt as to whether the Council
has power to charge a different price for
milk sent to hospitals, sold to ice-cream
manufacturers or sold for other purposes.
This Clause is merely to clarify the law
on that matter.
Clause 3 gives power to the Ministry's
inspectors to take samples of milk not
only at the premises of the licence
holders, but also during transit from the
producer right down to the consumer.
Up to the present the officers engaged
on the sampling of milk have not power
to sample milk on the street or in the
retailers premises. This Clause aims at
putting that matter right. It is most
important that through all the stages
from the producer to the consumer the
milk should be tested.
Clause 4 deals with the question of
refunds when butter or margarine is sold
for manufacturing purposes. Some difficulty has been experienced in effectively
checking whether these commodities
have actually gone into factories or been
used for retail purposes.
I regret to
say my Ministry has reason to believe
that there have been cases in which
butter licensed for manufacturing purposes has been used for other purposes.
Under this Clause it is proposed that a
general licence fee of 4s 6d will be paid,
but that a rebate can be claimed from
the Ministry in respect of butter or margarine for manufacturing purposes.
a
Probably the part of the Bill which
will be of principal interest to Members
is the first Clause, which, as I have
already mentioned, deals with processing. In Northern Ireland up to date all
milk which is produced, except that for
liquid consumption, has been either
turned into butter or cream. For a considerable time my Ministry has been
endeavouring to interest outside firms to
establish processing factories in Northern Ireland. I am satisfied such
factory would not only help agriculture,
but would be of inestimable benefit to
industry. I am very glad, therefore, to
be able to announce to the House that
Messrs. Nestle, one of the most famous
milk processing firms in the world, propose to establish a factory at Ballymoney. My Ministry, as the House is
aware, has been endeavouring to
encourage farmers to increase not only
the production of milk but also all other
kinds of farm produce, and the present
is undoubtedly a favourable one for this
firm to set up a factory. A land fertility scheme was started a short time ago,
and my Ministry has applied its energies
to trying to induce farmers to take
advantage of the scheme and increase the
growth of grass in the country and thus.
increase not only the production of milk,
but of beef.
There is also a beef subsidy scheme.
which guarantees to the farmer a substantial subsidy in respect of fat stock.
Not only is he given a grant, which is
made by the British Government, but
Milk Products Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke]
there is also a quota on imports of all fat
stock from foreign countries, which
stabilises prices. In addition my Ministry, a short time ago, introduced a
scheme whereby creamery suppliers supplying milk of high quality receive an
extra bonus on grades "C" and "B" of
from 1d to 2d per gallon. The only unfavourable factor at the moment is the
high cost of feeding stuffs.
I should point out to those who are
interested in agriculture that although
butter has been the mainstay of the
farmers who supply milk to creameries,
it is a very precarious business. This is
due to the fact that the Dominions have
entered this trade to a large extent, and
Great Britain is unable to apply tariff
or quantity regulations to stop imports
of this commodity. It is, therefore, extremely unlikely, even if the economic
price of butter dropped below a certain
figure, that any restriction would be
placed on this product. On the other
hand, they have placed a restriction.
upon the importation of processed or
tinned milk into the United Kingdom.
That puts manufacturers of processed
milk in the position of being able to give
a slightly better price. The Milk Board
in England has been diverting a great
deal of its milk into these processing
factories. Up to the present Northern
Ireland has not benefited from the tariff
or quantity regulations. The factory
which Messrs. Nestle's propose to establish will, if all goes well, employ from
200 to 300 persons. They will also be
in a position to take greater supplies of
milk, and I hope be able to pay a better
price.
I understand that some representatives
of co-operative creameries look upon this
new venture with a good deal of misgiving. I realise as well as anybody the
valuable work which creameries have
done in the past, and I hope that they
will continue to give valuable service to
the country in the future. Most of their
fears, I think, are unfounded because in
this particular are, namely, County
Antrim, there is a very large number of
cattle to a central creamery. There are
creameries, of course, in County Fermanagh, County Tyrone and parts of
County Armagh, but this particular area
is, in the opinion of the Ministry, a
most suitable one in which to establish
a factory of this kind.
As I have already pointed out, the Ministry have given and will continue to give
encouragement to farmers to increase the
production of cattle and milk. Having
studied the position very carefully I do
not think the creameries concerned need
have any fear. I believe that with goodwill and co-operation there will be
sufficient milk to keep the creameries
going and also to keep Messrs. Nestle's
supplied.
The agricultural Members who are
interested in co-operative creameries
need have no doubts as to the Ministry's
policy in regard to increasing the number of livestock. In four years we
have increased the pig population in
Northern Ireland to such an extent that
we are now producing, roughly, onequarter of the United Kingdom's output
of pigs. There is no reason why the
cattle population should not increase.
It will increase, and in a certain number of years I hope to see the cattle
population double what it is to-day.
When the pig scheme was brought in
fears were expressed that the roll bacon
and ham trades would suffer as a result
of the starting of the Wiltshire
factories. Those fears have proved to
be entirely groundless, and so I believe
the fears now expressed by the creameries
will disappear. This is one way in which
agriculture can help industry.
It is impossible to foresee how far
Messrs. Nestle's may develop. There is
the possibility that they may set up their
own tinning factory to enable them to
tin cream. The production of milk is
something which agriculture in Northern
Ireland can do to help industry and also
help the farmers, and if this is done
the work carried out will not have been
in vain. I beg to move.
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I move the
rejection of the Bill. It is with the
greatest diffidence and reluctance that I
do so. If the Minister of Agriculture
can see his way to adjourn the Second
Reading of this Measure for two weeks
and in the interval consult the different
interests concerned I will be quite satisfied, but in the absence of an undertaking of that kind I can do nothing
but propose the rejection of the Bill.
Milk Products Bill-
Second Reading
23 MARCH 1938
•
My first complaint is that the people
most vitally concerned have never been
consulted. So far as I understand the
Ministry have never approached the
organisation which has control over the
co-operative creameries in Northern Ireland. I am told so, and I can say with
certainty that they have never
approached or asked for any advice of
any sort or kind from the Farmers'
Union. There seems to have been a
tremendous amount of secrecy from first
to last about this whole matter. Practically the first thing the public knew
about it was that a meeting was held in
Ballymoney and representatives of the
Ministry and others came there, and
representatives of this new firm to boost
the project and ask the support of the
farming community. I cannot think the
Ministry allowed representatives of theirs
to go there and take up the attitude they
did at the meeting at a moment's notice.
There must have been negotiations going
on between the Ministry and representatives of this firm for a considerable time
previous.
The farmers' organisations
were never consulted.
Not only did the Ministry send representatives to that meeting, but I am
credibly informed the officials from the
Ministry of Agriculture at that meeting
got up and assured the representative of
Nestlé's and the farmers who were there
that certain payments would be made on
the same basis as have been made to the
creameries when as a matter of fact the
Ministry had no power at that time in
law to make any such payments. I think
we have just cause for complaint in the
attitude the Ministry has taken up on
this whole matter. I speak on these lines
with the greatest reluctance, because of
my admiration for the Minister and for
his permanent officials in the Ministry. I
submit that the Bill as drafted is simply
not worthy either of the Ministry or of
his officials. I am concerned not only
with what is in the Bill but with what is
not in the Bill.
I would like the House to understand
that I do not speak with any prejudice
against this new concern the Ministry
seems so anxious to get established in
Northern Ireland. On the other hand I
want also to make it plain that I hold no
brief for the creameries. Many a time
I have criticised them and blamed them
for lack of initiative and other qualities,
but it has taken 40 years or thereabouts
to build up the present creamery system,
and there is something like £30,000 of
farmers' money involved in one block of
creameries that is going to be affected by
the invasion from Great Britain of this
new concern.
I find fault with the Bill because there
is no provision in it whatsoever to give
any compensation to all or any of these
creameries. I oppose the Bill because from
every point of view it is giving an unfair
deal to the creameries. This new concern,
I presume, is going to be declared, if it
has not already been declared, a new
industry, which means that it will get a
free site and automatically it will be free
for a period of years-I think ten years
-from rates and income-tax. That in
itself puts the creameries at a very great
disadvantage as compared with this new
proprietary concern.
Then the Minister referred in speaking
about the last section of the new Bill to
the 4s 6d as part of the licence fee which
creameries pay
into the Milk Fund. Now
the creameries are compelled to pay that
on every hundredweight of butter, but I
do not find that in this Bill there is any
proposal that this new concern should
contribute one halfpenny to this Milk
Fund, but they are to be paid from the
Milk Fund on a basis equal to that which
the creameries derive from it. So that
from every point of view the dice is
loaded against the creameries. Not only
so, but the price that the creamery can
obtain for its cream and for its butter
made from the milk supplied to the
creamery by the farmers is fixed by the
Milk Marketing Committee or the Butter
and Cream Marketing Committee. I do
not find in the Bill anything to fix in
any way the price of the output of this
new concern or similar concerns. So that
again the advantage is going to be with
the milk products factories as opposed to
the creameries.
The Minister cast some doubt on the
future of the butter market, and he
visualised the time when the colonies
would pour so much butter of such high
standard into the British market that our
North of Ireland butter might be
absolutely shut out. We could not afford
to make it at the price obtainable for it.
Is it not a fact that Northern Ireland
butter in the last six months has been
obtaining the highest price from the
Milk Products Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Rev. Robert Moore]
British market? I believe that those
who are very good judges have said that
at no time in the history of Northern
Ireland did the creameries turn out such
a very fine product as they have been
doing in the last twelve months. It seems
to me that our position in the butter
market was never surer than it is to-day.
What is the situation with the creameries?
As things are they simply cannot get
enough milk to convert into butter and
to convert into cream, and their overhead
charges are much heavier than they
might be or than they ought to be if they
could get sufficient milk.
It is a very strange thing that in the
country from which this new company
is coming the Milk Marketing Board sets
a higher value on cream and on milk that
is going to be converted into fresh cream
than it does on milk that is going to be
turned into powder or tinned or made
into other products by this concern. The
difference in price is as much as 1½d a
gallon. Evidently the Milk Marketing
Board in Great Britain feels that everything that can be done should be done to
encourage the fresh cream trade. Why
does our Ministry in Northern Ireland
turn round and make the fresh cream
trade practically impossible by
attitude to a concern like Nestle's?
its
There is another deficiency in the Bill
on which I want to say a word, that is,
in the new Bill the Minister proposes to
give the Milk Council power to fix the
price of grades A, B, and C, a different
price for these grades of milk according
to the purpose the milk is going to be
used for. But there is no proposal in the
Bill to give the Milk Council or any other
council or committee power to fix the
price on ordinary creamery milk, grade
D. Why should not this Bill-
Sir BASIL BROOKE: It does not
come under it.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: The Minister
says it does not come under it. I want
it put under it if this Bill is going to
become law. Here is a company coming
into a creamery district. We are told
there are 20,000 cows in that particular
district and their milk is not going to the
creameries. That may be the case or it
may not. I am informed it is not the
case.
But if it is the case, why is this
company going about the suppliers of the
creameries canvassing for some of the
milk. If it is creamery milk they are
going to depend on why should there be
no provision in the Bill to fix the price
to the private proprietary concern of milk
which it is going to manufacture?
As to the last section, I can only say
that I think it is fantastic. I do not know
how often the Ministry has changed its
attitude in regard to the matters concerned in the last section of the Bill
during the last six or twelve months.
This is the last stance they have taken.
What the next will be is known only to
themselves, Are they going to post a
spy in the kitchen of every restaurant
and every hotel say in the city of Belfast
to see whether a particular pound of
butter is put into a cake or spread on
the bread that is going to be laid on the
people's tables? I submit that the last
section as it stands would take a regular
army of inspectors and officials, and even
then it would be impossible to administer
that section of the Bill with equity. I
can think of no administrative machinery
that could be devised that would make
the working of that section anything like
water-tight.
I understand that the motive is to try
to get the trade in butter and margarine
back again to the products of Northern
Ireland. I understand that some time
ago certain people in certain lines of
business were advised-it is not for me
to say by whom they were advised-or
they discovered, that they could evade
the payment of this 4s 6d or 4s 8d licence
duty by buying butter and margarine in
Great Britain. And now this section is
being devised to allure them back to buy
Northern Ireland butter and margarine
for cooking and other purposes.
submit whatever is behind that section it
is absolutely unworkable in practice and
in administration. For these reasons,
and for others which I will not take up
the time of the House with, I beg to
move the rejection of the Bill.

Mr. GAMBLE: I rise to second the
Amendment proposed by
by the hon.
Member. In doing so I would like to
express the regret I feel at having to
do so, knowing how much the Minister
of Agriculture has done for the creamery
industry in Northern Ireland in the past
number of years. I felt in listening to
Milk Products Bill-
Second Reading
23 MARCH 1938
him that he struck a very optimistic
note. I wish I could take the same view
of the whole milk industry in Northern
Ireland as the right hon. Gentleman.
He talks of the great increase in milk
production here. My idea, which is
backed up by statistics which have been
supplied, is that milk production is on
the decrease rather than on the increase.
According to these statistics I find that
in this very district where Nestle's propose to start there is a decrease of
over 260,000 gallons from 1936 to 1937.
Again, the total milk supplied to the
creameries was over 2 million gallons.
That does not go to show that there is
an increase in milk production in the
country. The creamery industry has
been built and fostered for the past fifty
years by the milk producers themselves.
They own the creameries; it is their
money that is in them; they are interested in them. The creameries are
subject to very close supervision and
inspection by the officials of the Ministry of Agriculture.
There is another point, and that is a
licence fee of 4s 6d per cwt. must be
paid on butter manufactured or sold.
This is paid into the Milk Fund, out of
which equalisation payment and bonus
is proposed to be paid to the new
factory or factories to be set up. It is
no secret that this new factory is possibly the forerunner of others to be
established in various places. What payment is it proposed that this processed
milk factory should make into this
Fund? No mention of that is made in
the Bill. What machinery is in the Bill
to ensure that such payment will be
asked for? Why are these factories not
put on equal terms with the creameries
which have worked up their industry for
the past fifty years? Why should they
be placed in a privileged position? I
do not see that they have a right to be
placed in that privileged position. I do
not think that the Minister of Agriculture has been well advised to put an
outside firm-a firm opposed to cooperation-in a particular and privileged
position. The creameries are subject to
inspection by the Ministry's officials
as regards the management, equipment
and supervision generally. No key
position in a creamery can be filled without the consent of the Ministry. No
similar inspection is indicated in regard
to processed milk factories.
All they
ask for is that the milk be supplied.
By whom? By the creamery suppliers.
It has been stated that there is the
milk of 20,000 cows in this district for
which there is no outlet, and that it does
not go to the creamery industry. I am
not prepared to say that is not so, but
I know one thing, that in Ballymoney
a very short number of years ago an
auxiliary creamery had to be closed
down. Why? For the lack of milk
supply. Where then does the Minister
propose that the milk will come from for
this new processed milk factory?. I
would like to suggest one thing to the
right hon. Gentleman, and that is,
when we talk of new industries, that a
new industry should either use for its
raw material something of which there
was a surplus or which was not already
being used economically. We have no
reason to believe there is any surplus
milk. Our creameries are working on
a lesser quantity than what they ought
to do, with the result that their overhead charges are higher, possibly, than
if they had a better supply. What is to
be the consequence if the milk supply
is to be divided amongst the creameries
and the processed milk factories? Will
it not add to the overhead charges and
to a reduction in the milk supplies to
the creameries?
Let us consider for a moment the
prices proposed to be given by the new
processed milk factory. If we take the
average price paid by creameries in this
district, without taking into consideration the equalisation grant, it has been
round about 54d or 53d per gallon, plus
a d equalisation grant, and for those
who had grade "C" 2d a gallon extra.
What does this firm propose to give?
The first price that appeared in the
paper was 6d, with no skim milk given
back. Nothing is returned to the
farmer. That was the complete price he
was to receive for the article delivered.
If we add to the 5d or 52d the equalisation grant of d, and the 2d a gallon
as the lowest value we put on skim milk,
then we in the creamery industry are
paying a higher price than the new
milk factory proposes to pay. As was
pointed out on the public platform, this
company did not come across to benefit
Northern Ireland or purely for the welfare of the milk producers; they came
for the benefit of their own shareholders,
to pay them greater dividends. The
Milk Products Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gamble]
company made no secret also that what
they wanted from the start off was
30,000 gallons a day, which meant the

Antrim and Derry, and that in a year's

Let us compare the creameries with

How are we to increase
supply? There are only two ways of

us to clear out and let these other

come in and take their places. Had he
consulted the interests concerned he
would possibly have got our views on the
subject, and after discussion we might
have agreed with him. Meantime we
hold that our co-operative movement
which has given satisfaction for the past
forty or fifty years should be fostered.
That industry should not be led away by
even the promise of d or 1d more per
gallon. I have pleasure in seconding the
rejection of the Bill.
Question proposed, "That the word
'now' stand part of the Question”.
Mr. GRANT: I rise to support the
rejection of this Bill. I do not do so
with any pleasure, but I am reminded
of the fact that after the General
Election we had a sort of understanding
from the Government that there would
not be any legislation of a contentious
nature introduced into the House, but
that there would be one or two
simple Bills introduced. This is one
of the few simple Bills introduced.
When I heard the Minister introducing this Bill I wondered if he
had a short memory, because to-day
I took the trouble to read the Hansard
of 6th June, 1934, when the Minister in
introducing the original Bill mentioned
the benefits the Bill would confer upon
the creameries of Northern Ireland.
During the course of his speech he said:
"A matter that has been exercising
my mind and that has given me a very
great deal of anxiety is the very
serious position of the creameries.
Many have been contemplating closing
down. If they were to close down it
would be one of the most disastrous
things that have ever happened to
agriculture in this country, because it
will be admitted that with the
creameries goes the improvement of
our herds. If the creameries go down
fewer cows will be kept, fewer store
cattle will be the result, and it will be
difficult to feed the pigs which we hope
are coming forward under the pigs
marketing scheme, while in addition,
would
poultry feeding
suffer."-
(Official Report-6th June, 1934, vol.
XVI, col. 2,132.)
I wonder if the Minister thought of that
speech when he got up to-day to introduce this Bill. I was one of those who
honestly believed him in 1934 when he
said that he was concerned about the
creameries and that he was going to
bring in legislation which would be their
salvation. I believe he has been fairly
successful in that way up to the moment,
but having done something to have his
name put on the scroll of honour by
the people of Northern Ireland he is
now going to destroy all that good work
by the introduction of this Bill unless
he defers to the hon. Members who have
advised him to withdraw the Measure in
the meantime and consult the interests
concerned.
The Prime Minister repeatedly in this
House and we believe the noble Lord
when he makes these statements-said that
as far as possible before any new legislation is introduced into the House all the
interests concerned would be consulted.
They have not been consulted in connection with this Bill. I am sorry for
the Minister who introduced this Bill,
because I believe it is an officials' Bill.
They are the people who are really responsible. The time has arrived in
Northern Ireland when we are not going
Milk Products Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
We
to be dictated to by civil servants.
are going to have a voice as the representatives of the people as to the sort
of legislation that is going to pass
through this House.
As regards the creameries, I believe
that they are just beginning to wash
their faces. They are able to pay their
way. Of course I can understand the
Minister listening to the appeal which
is very often thoughtlessly made to
establish new industries in Northern
Ireland, but they should not be established at the price of old industries.
That is exactly what this Bill means.
We are asked to support, and not only
support but subsidise, a new industry in
Northern Ireland that is going to wipe
out an old industry. We have had
figures produced by the Ministry.
Nobody can increase the milk supply
like the Ministry of Agriculture, but the
farmers cannot see the milk. The Ministry can increase the output by thousands
of gallons a day, but this increase is
never seen by the representatives of the
creameries nor by the people interested
in this particular business.
After all, it is facts and not fancies
that we want. We have had it stated
on most reliable authority that the milk
supply of Northern Ireland was reduced
by two-and-a-half million gallons last
year, and we also have it on reliable
authority that the output of milk in the
particular district in which the new milk
factory is to be could not do more than
supply the requirements of that factory.
If that is the fact how are the creameries
going to exist? We are told that the
new industry will employ more people.
That may be so up to a point, but it is
going to throw an equal number of
people out of employment.
The butter question is one that I want
to emphasise. We have an organisation
in Belfast, and it might seem peculiar
that I should put forward the claims of
this organisation, but like the hon.
Member who moved the rejection of the
Bill I am interested neither in creameries
nor butter factories, or in any of the
associations dealing in that kind of commodities. I am one of the unfortunate
people who have to pay for these things,
no matter who is going to get the benefit.
There is an organisation in Belfast called
the Wholesale Butter Merchants' Association which have repeatedly given
valued services to the Ministry. They
have graded butter at the railway
stations and helped the Ministry in
every possible way. This organisation
has been ignored in connection with this
Bill. Through their sales levies they
assisted the Government for a long time,
and now the result is that all the levies
that are going to be paid into the Milk
Equalisation Fund will go to help this
new factory as well as the creameries.
As has been pointed out by those better
able to deal with this question, this
money is going into the pockets of
shareholders who do not belong to this
part of the world, instead of going back
to the farmers who have been trying
to carry on this co-operative creamery
system in Northern Ireland.
The hon. Member for North Derry
(Rev. Robert Moore) referred to butter
going into a hotel or restaurant. Take,
for instance, the Grand Central Hotel in
Belfast. Who is going to find out what
proportion of the butter going into that
hotel will be put on the bread on the
tables and what proportion will go into
the kitchen to make pastry or such
things. Yet the butter used to make
pastry is exempt from this sales tax,
while on that that goes on the bread
4s 6d a cwt. has to be paid. Then the
man who is responsible for the sale to
the hotel or restaurant, that is
the wholesale man, has to keep a record
of those sales. He has to make a return
to the Ministry, and then the person
who has bought the butter has to make a
claim to the Ministry for a rebate of
the 4s 6d per cwt. on the butter used for
manufacturing purposes.
Any person will realise that the refund will not be made in a week or
two. He will have to wait until the
Ministry's officials make the necessary inquiries and certify that the claim is
correct before he can get the money.
This will give a means of escape from all
that. He can go into the Free State
and buy the butter there without having
any of this trouble, or he can butt the
butter in the English market without
having to make any returns. From that
and many other points of view I think
this is a very obnoxious Bill. It is not
in the interests of the people of Northern Ireland, and, therefore, I support
its rejection.

Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.

Ministry of Labour:
The Unemployment Insurance (Insurable Employments) Regulations (Northern Ireland), 1938. (By Act.)
Oral Answers to Questions.
FAMILY ALLOWANCE SYSTEM
OF WAGES.
'1. Professor CORKEY asked the
Minister of Labour whether he is aware
that agricultural labourers and other
lower paid workers who have families
receive more in unemployment benefit
when they are out of work than they
receive as wages when they are in work;
whether he will take such action as may
be necessary to secure the adoption in
Ulster of a family allowance system of
wages suited to the needs of our area so
as to bring this anomaly to an end; and
whether he will endeavour, in conjunction with other Ministries, to have
this system of wages applied without
delay to all lower paid workers in the
employment of the Government, so that
the Government may set an example in
this matter to other employers of labour.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): In reply to
the hon. Gentleman, cases have come to
the notice of the Ministry of Labour
where the amount of unemployment
benefit payable to low-paid agricultural
and other workers has been more than
their wages while in employment. These,
however, are exceptional, as is shown by
the fact that the weekly amount of
benefit (including dependants' benefit)
payable to an adult male worker averages
at present about 18s 6d under the Agricultural Scheme and 23s 6d under the
General Scheme.
With reference to family allowances,
I am aware that the system is being
tried in some of the Dominions, in certain foreign countries, and in a few
isolated cases by firms in Great Britain.
The general adoption of the system in
Northern Ireland would entail a complete reconstruction of the wages basis in
this Province, and for reasons that the
hon. Member will appreciate the Government is unable to commit itself to such
a drastic step in industrial policy in
advance of the rest of the United
Kinglom.
DISPENSARY DOCTORS AND
HEALTH INSURANCE.
2. Lieut.-Colonel MITCHELL asked
the Minister of Labour whether, on the
introduction of National Health Insurance into Northern Ireland, an arrangement was made under which dispensary
doctors would be paid 1s 6d less than the
standard capitation grant for patients
who selected them as their panel
doctors; whether the services which they
are required to give are exactly the same
as given by other panel doctors; whether
there is any legal justification for paying
less than the statutory fee for panel work
under the National Health Insurance
Act; whether, since the application of
the Act to Northern Ireland, many young
doctors have been appointed to dispensaries who receive: (a) normal capitation payment of 9s for panel patients;
(b) same scale of dispensary salary as
their predecessors; and whether he is
prepared to reconsider the matter, and
see that the older and more experienced
men are paid the same capitation grant
for panel work as their junior colleagues.
Mr. GORDON: The arrangement
referred to by the hon. and gallant
Member affects only insurance practitioners who held office as dispensary
doctors on the 1st October, 1930, when
medical benefit was introduced in
Northern Ireland.
This arrangement, to which statutory
effect was given, was made at the request
of the dispensary doctors themselves, as
they preferred it to a revision of their
dispensary salaries which would have had
to take place as a result of the removal
of insured persons from the scope of the
dispensary system.

Dispensary doctors appointed since the
1st October, 1930, and any others who
can show that the terms of their dispensary appointment have been altered
to such an extent that their insurance

are paid the 9s capitation fee.
As regards the last part of the hon.

The question of the capitation fee was

HOUSING OF LABOURERS IN
DOWNPATRICK RURAL DISTRICT.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether the Downpatrick Rural District Council have
taken any action in providing labourers'
cottages in that district, and, if not,
whether he will make representations to
the Council immediately to commence
building these cottages; whether it is a
fact that over twelve years ago it was
found out that hundreds of labourers'
cottages were necessary in this district;
whether he can state in how many houses
in this district there are families of 6,
8, and 10 persons living in one room
and kitchen; how many children are at
present patients in Downpatrick Fever
Hospital, and how many children were
patients in the same fever hospital
during the last six months.
The PARLIAMENTRY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Davison): The
Downpatrick Rural District Council are
preparing a scheme for the erection of
cottages under the Labourers Acts and
have advertised for representations.
Twelve years ago the Council received
representations for 139 cottages only and
the scheme as approved provided 88
cottages, the other 51 being disallowed
for various reasons, but in 1930 they
were preparing a scheme in connection
with which they had received 338 applications when operations under the
Labourers Acts were suspended for financial reasons.
I am unable to state how many
houses there are in the district with
6 to 10 persons living in one room and
kitchen.
There are at present 22 children in
Downpatrick Fever Hospital, and the
number in the hospital during the past
six months was 76.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the Parliamentary Secretary have inquiries made
to find out the number of persons from
six to ten living in one room in the area
mentioned in the question?

AND CASTLEWELLAN.

Castlewellan; whether it is a fact that
in Castlewellan nearly twenty buses

Mr. DAVISON: The erection of

Castlewellan has been under consideration by the Downpatrick Rural District
Council for some time past, and the

THE ANNSBOROUGH-
CASTLEWELLAN ROAD.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether it is a fact that
two persons were recently killed on the
road from Annsborough to Castlewellan
owing to the fact that there is no footpath on this road; whether the Government gave a promise to the hon. Member for Central almost a year ago that it
would suggest to the Down County
Council to make such a footpath; and
whether the Government will again ask
this County Council to make the footpath and prevent further fatalities.
Mr. DAVISON: In last December a
motor-cyclist collided with a pedestrian
on the road mentioned by the hon.
Member and the pedestrian and motorcyclist died in consequence.
Following representations-made by
the Ministry to the County Councilthe matter was brought before the
Council's Proposal Committee in October
last, but was postponed as it was felt
that footpaths were more urgently
needed on other roads.
I understand that another proposal
will be submitted at the Committee's
meeting next month.
It is the Ministry's policy to encourage
the provision of footpaths on public
roads, and I can assure the hon. Member
that the County Council will again be
asked without delay to make a footpath
on this road.
A DEATH IN DOWNPATRICK
MENTAL HOSPITAL.
6. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has received a
request from Mr. D. S. Thompson,
2 Rosemary Street, Belfast, for a public
sworn inquiry into the death of
his daughter, which took place in Downpatrick Mental Hospital; whether he has
seen the statements furnished by this
man in support of his request; and
whether in the interests of all concerned
he will order a public sworn inquiry into
this matter.
Mr. DAVISON: I have received a
request from Mr. D. S. Thompson for a
sworn inquiry into the circumstances of
his daughter's death and have seen the
statements submitted by him. I should
explain that immediately on receipt of
Mr. Thompson's request inquiries were
set on foot and a medical officer of the
Ministry went to Downpatrick without
notice to investigate the allegations. In
the course of this investigation he
examined all the clinical and other
records bearing on the case, and came
to the conclusion, in which I entirely
concur, that Miss Thompson had received skilled and sympathetic treatment
in her last sudden illness, and, indeed,
throughout her stay in the Mental Hospital. I am satisfied that all possible
information has been elicited and verified
and that there are no grounds on which
a sworn inquiry would be justified.
Mr. NIXON: If everything is as clean
and as clear as the Parliamentary Secretary says it is, what objection can he have
to a sworn inquiry in the interests of the
feelings of this respectable man and his
family?
Mr. DAVISON: I have every
sympathy for Mr. Thompson and his
family, but when the Ministry is satisfied
that there is no ground whatever for any
suggestion of wrong treatment or mistreatment in the institution I cannot see
that any good purpose would be served
by holding an inquiry.

I am
Mr. DAVISON: I am sure the House

glad to say that he will soon be able to

It is in no sense a payment for the

general public as to the first-aid steps to
be taken in the event of air raids and
in providing, through the machinery of
their organisation, a most important
nucleus for any scheme of air raid
precautions.
The Ministry's air raid precautions'
officer has already visited practically
every local authority in Northern
Ireland, and is always ready and available to give advice and assistance in the
preparation of schemes. While some of
the local authorities have taken considerable interest in the matter and have
done a good deal in the direction of
initiating schemes, there seems generally
a good deal of apathy in the matter, due,
perhaps, to a disposition to regard
Northern Ireland, from its geographical
position, as immune from attack. I do
not wish to appear to be an alarmist on
this subject, but it is, I think, only right
to remind the Committee that we have
been advised that under present-day conditions an air raid in Northern Ireland
is by no means outside the bounds of
possibility, and this possibility cannot
be ignored. While, therefore, it is,
perhaps, unnecessary generally throughout Northern Ireland to prepare elaborate
and expensive schemes, the preparation
of schemes suitable for the requirements
of the various local authorities is one
which should be taken in hand by all
local authorities without delay. A Bill
to give the necessary statutory powers
and to provide for assistance from
Government funds on approximately the

Another matter arising out of this
Estimate, which is of considerable
public interest, is the construction of the
Sydenham by-pass road. Some criticism
has been made that the work is proceeding too slowly, but I would remind the
Committee that any scheme of the magnitude of this road involves much difficult
and detailed preparation before work
can be commenced on an appreciable
scale. The road will include a viaduct
over the railways, an under-bridge at
Dee Street, a widening of the bridge
over the Connswater, a bridge under the
railway at Tillysburn, another before the
junction with the Holywood Road, an
extensive embankment between the railway at Tillysburn and the Holywood
Road, and a considerable amount of
piling and difficult drainage. Extensive
surveys and elaborate drawings, specifications, and other documents have been
necessary and have been progressing
steadily and without delay.
The proximity of the road to the new
airport increased our difficulties. A
bridge to take the road over the railway
did not appear at first to be open to
objection; later fears were expressed that
it would endanger aircraft, and every
point between Tillysburn and Sydenham
was tested as to its suitability for a
crossing. Eventually the idea of an
overbridge was abandoned in favour of a
bridge under the railway at Tillysburn.
The work of preparing drawings, plans,
etc., for the viaduct had to be stopped
because of doubts expressed as to the
suitability of the city-end of the proposed
route. An investigation by a traffic
expert is being undertaken to settle that
point. Meanwhile attention is being
directed to the portion of the route to
the east of Dee Street, and plans are
being prepared without delay for the
bridges, embankments, walls, etc., which
will have to be constructed. The existing roadway at Victoria Park is being
widened by direct labour, the work giving
direct employment at present to 40 men.
The accumulation of filling material has
been progressing steadily for some time.
past, and has afforded constant employment for lorry drivers and others.
avoidable delay has occurred in the carrying out of the extensive surveys needed,
and in the preparation of drawings,
specifications and other documents.
Advertisements for tenders for the first
contracts will probably be issued in about
two months' time.

With regard to public health, the local
authorities have shown themselves to be
alive to their responsibilities, and during
the past year much has been done in
the way of providing better water supplies and sewers, and improved sanitary
conditions generally. Loans amounting
to £371,000 for these purposes
sanctioned during the year. The housing of the poorer classes is not, however,
satisfactory in many towns. While the
Housing Acts have been successful in
providing houses for people able to pay
an economic rent, little has so far been
done for the less fortunate members of
the community. Many of the houses in
our towns are unft for human habitation
and a disgrace to our community.
Mr. BEATTIE: Shame.
Mr. DAVISON: It is proposed to
introduce legislation which will enable
the local authorities to provide houses at
rents which the class of tenants I have
in mind will be able to pay. In the
rural districts work under the Labourers
Eight
Acts is now proceeding steadily.
schemes have already been confirmed, two
are awaiting confirmation, and sixteen
others are in preparation. Under these
schemes about 4,000 houses are being
built.
I regret to find that the vital statistics
for the past year indicate a higher rate
of mortality than has been the case for
some time. The exceptional mortality
was due to an epidemic of influenza in
the early part of the year. But for this
epidemic the death rate for the year
would have been about normal. The
death rate from tuberculosis again shows
a decline, and the steady fall in the death
rate from this disease shows that the
special measures taken to deal with it,
assisted by the improvement of sanitary
conditions generally, are proving effective.
I am sorry that I cannot refer to a
like fall in the infantile and maternal
death rates, which still stand at too high
a level, but I think that the Departmental Committee appointed last year to
consider conditions under which midwives carry out their duties may result in
suggesting some means for reducing the
dangers incident to child-birth.
I now turn to law and order, and I am
glad to say that the improvement to
which reference was made on the introduction of the Estimates last year has
been maintained. A few isolated
instances of outrage have, it is true,
occurred, indicating that constant
vigilance on the part of the police is still
necessary if we are to avoid the possibility
of a recrudescence of organised crime. So
long as the police are maintained in their
present high state of efficiency and are
supported by the goodwill of the general
public, I think we need have no apprehensions on this score. It indeed affords
me very great pleasure to pay the usual,
but nevertheless well-deserved, tribute to
the members of the police forces-both
the Royal Ulster Constabulary and the
Special Constabulary. I think we can say
without fear of contradiction that no
finer body of men could be found in any
other country of
of the world. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)

no

Not only can the public assist the police

The duty of the police consists not only

for a
In dealing with any matter in the
world, no matter what it is, if you have
not the capacity to make up your mind
definitely, one way or the other, after
due consideration, you are not fit for the
position. It does not matter what you
are, that rule applies. A general in the
field who cannot make up his mind will
very soon retreat in disorder. A man in
business who cannot make up his mind
will end badly. No one need tell me that
it takes seven or eight years to make up
one's mind about a site for a sanatorium
in Northern Ireland. This all comes
from interfering with the expert; his
recommendation should never have been
interfered with. That is where all this
trouble originated. He knew all about
it. He could tell the amount of oxygen
that there is in the air at Downpatrick,
here, in the centre of the city, or in
Donaghadee. He has all that by him;
he knows all about it. He has experience,

Professor CORKEY: I need hardly
say that there are a great many Departments in the Ministry of Home Affairs
for which I have the highest admiration.
They have discharged their duties well.
Peace and order have been maintained
through difficult years, and many institutions have been managed with great
efficiency. I would be lacking in my
duty if I did not express my appreciation. I know the fine results achieved.
I am sorry, however, that on this
occasion I will have to blow hot and blow
cold, because there is one branch of
work carried out by this Ministry which
I think is very badly done. There is
one section of our law which is very
feebly administered, and I feel it my
duty to draw attention to the serious
failure of administration in that particular. The efforts of the police to deal
with illegal betting resorts in this city are
about the queerest piece of Government
work that you could find in any part of
the world. It is an administrative
curiosity which is not a credit to the
police or the Government. The administration by the Ministry in this particular is very defective.
Ministry of Home Affairs 446
Estimates-
24 MARCH 1938
First of all I am told they invite the
bookmakers periodically to the police
court. That is done according to a prearranged programme, which is not in
accordance with the traditions of the
police in dealing with law breakers, and
which does not suggest any desire on
their part or on the part of the Government to end this great evil. The owners
of these betting resorts are asked to
appear before the authorities three times
every two months with a regularity that
cannot altogether be accidental. When
they go along to the police court they are
always fined £5. Here is an extract
from a recent edition of the "Belfast
Telegraph":
"Nineteen bookmakers were each
fined £5 for betting offences in the
Belfast Custody Court to-day. One
defendant was making his 109th
appearance, another had been up 90
times and three others 79, 73, and 70
times respectively."
It appears to me that to bring people
up in that mild way, three times every
two months, and then fine them £5, regardless of the number of former appearances, is not the way to keep the law in
good respect or the way in which to suppress this evil. Moreover, I observe
from statistics given to me by the Ministry of Home Affairs that the number of
people convicted has decreased. However, on account of these £5 fines the
amount of money received in fines during
the past few years has increased to a remarkable extent. The number of
persons convicted in 1934 was 4,888. In
1935 the number fell to 3,500, while in
1936 it dropped to 2,754. The fines
imposed are still more remarkable. In
1934 the fines amounted to £1,254. In
1935, when the 5s fine regime prevailed,
the amount fell to £887, while in 1936,
when resident magistrates had charge of
these cases, the amount received in fines
jumped to £13,759.
The police when raiding these offices
use, I am told, the maximum amount of
civility, and cause the minimum amount
of inconvenience. I am informed that
the sergeant simply sends a telephone
message to the bookmaker, informing
him that he is due in court on a certain
day. The bookmaker then sends down
one of his clerks to represent him, or
perhaps someone he brings in from the
street, and to whom he is willing to pay
10s to appear for him in court as a bogus
bookmaker. No papers are seized in
these offices except, perhaps, a few which
are required for the purpose of the
prosecutions. No inconvenience is
caused to these people. It is a remarkable fact that the business is not interfered with in the least during or
after the conviction. The bookmaking
business goes on as briskly as ever even
during the time the bookmaker is in
court answering for his crime. It seems
to me that these are very grave defects
in the administration of the law which
exists for the benefit of the people.
The third curious feature of the
administration of this law, and one very
provocative of thought, is that no effort
is made to proceed against the owner of
the property in which the bookmaking
business is carried on. The owners of
the property are incriminating themselves all the time by leasing or renting
their premises for this purpose.
are they never proceeded against if this
cash betting business is illegal?
Why
Finally, and this is the most serious
feature of the administration, there is
apparently a very singular working
arrangement between the police authorities and the Turf Guardian Association.
If a bookmaker is a member of that
association he is allowed to carry on his
illegal business quietly provided he pays.
a fine of £5 three times every two months.
If he is not a member of the association,
or is a blackleg so to speak, then his
office is raided every other day until he
is finally compelled to close down.
I have no pleasure in bringing these
facts before the House, but they are
fairly well-known, and they are very discreditable. I respectfully submit that
the Ministry should take more cognisance
of these matters than they have done up
to the present. Such an arrangement
with a society which exists for the protection of bookmakers is very undesirable. I do not believe there is such a
thing as graft in the police force, but
an arrangement of that kind lends itself
to all sorts of suspicion.
I do not suggest that the Ministry
should make an attempt to suppress all
betting. For any Member of the House
to say I am proposing that is simply to
draw a red herring across the trail. There
are moral questions involved, but I do
not intrude them at this point. I look

Mr. GRANT: There are one or two
points I want to deal with in connection
with the Estimates. First, I would like
to congratulate the Parliamentary Secretary on his presentation of the Estimate.
As regards the police force, I think every
right-thinking person is agreed that we
have a police force of which we have
every right to be proud. Hon. Members
on all sides have paid that tribute to the
force. The men do their duty in a very
efficient manner. The point I would like
to bring to the attention of the Parliamentary Secretary refers to the traffic
police. I do not mean the ones that are
waiting round corners and watching for
the hon. Member for Pottinger. I mean
the ordinary traffic policemen in the city.
We have men who carry out their duties
to the admiration of the public and who
deserve all the credit it is possible to
award them, but there are certain traffic
points in the city I cannot understand.
Men are on duty from a certain hour in
the morning until one or half-past one,
when they go away to lunch and then
come back at two or half-past two.
Nobody is bothering about the traffic in
the interval. It seems to me that that is
all wrong. The policemen should be there
when the traffic is heaviest. That does
not apply to all areas, but it does apply
at the corner of Bridge Street and High
Street and the Albert Memorial. I hope
that some provision will be made for
relief during the period I have mentioned.

the taxpayers of the country to be told
of the maladministration that has driven
them to the verge of bankruptcy. Ulster
was never passing through
serious state of affairs than she is at the
present time, with 100,000 unemployed,

audacity to put down a sum of £900 to

car. It is time a halt was called to
this kind of extravagance. It would not
matter who was Prime Minister, I would
criticise this item just the same.
regret that some effort has not been made

He should fill his office in the way the

I wish to refer to another matter of
vital importance. I think some action
should be taken in regard to the mental
hospitals all over Northern Ireland. A
large number of deaths have taken place
in the mental hospitals. In one case, a
girl from the Shankill, a very faithful
follower of mine from she was a child,
met her death in the Belfast Mental
Hospital. The Government held
inquiry, at which I was present, but the
Ministry of Home Affairs have refused.
to issue the finding of the inspector who
held the inquiry. I think that is monsan
strous.
If a child of the Parliamentary
Secretary's died in similar circumstances
I am afraid he would be embarrassed if
the Ministry of Home Affairs refused
to give him the inspector's finding, so
that he would know the cause of death
and whether anyone was responsible for
what occurred. I hope the hon. and
learned Gentleman will make a special
note of this case, because it is my intention to raise the matter by means of a
question on Tuesday next, so that he will
then be in a position to tell the House
the nature of the inspector's report.
So far as the Mental Hospital is concerned, there must be greater supervision by the Government inspectors. I
hold that there is not half enough attention paid to these hospitals. I am
sincere when I say that I believe many
things take place there that ought not to
take place. One regrettable feature of
Government administration, both here
and elsewhere, is that warning is given
of approaching visits by inspectors. In
my opinion, when an inspector is going
to visit an institution he should go on
an unexpected day and at an unexpected
hour, in order to find out actually what
takes place. I believe a practice of that
kind would be an eye-opener. Not long
ago, when visiting a hospital, I saw a
little thing affecting a patient against
which I protested. If the inspectors
paid greater attention to the mental
hospitals that come under the Ministry
of Home Affairs they would find out
many things that could be remedied for
the benefit of the patients.
In regard to the tuberculosis hospital,
who was responsible for stopping it?
To-day any person suffering from tuberculosis in Belfast refuses point blank to
go to Whiteabbey. The Ministry agreed
to the Corporation erecting a magnificent
building there, and a large sum of money
was spent on the preparation of plans.
A deputation went across the Channel to
see most of the modern hospitals. The
Ministry, in fact, agreed to everything
the Tuberculosis Committee had done for
at least two years, and then turned down
their recommendations. Nothing has
been done for the past two years to provide accommodation for the thousands of
persons in Belfast who are dying from
tuberculosis. Owing to the laxity of the
Government and of the Corporation
hundreds of lives must have been lost
during the past two or three years. That

Another matter that concerns me very
much is that of the public health services all over Northern Ireland. One of
the hon. Members for the University
(Sir Robert Johnstone) was chairman of
a Commission that was set up by the
Government a long time ago. That
Commission brought in certain recommendations, which were published in a
blue book, showing how local government
conditions could be changed to such an
extent that hundreds of thousands of
pounds could be saved and a great deal
of overlapping prevented between the
local authorities and the poor-law
guardians. Not one of those recommendations has been put into operation.
What was the use of setting up a Commission to tell you what you ought to
do, and then ignoring its report? That
Commission was composed of legal men,
technical experts, and medical practitioners, who gave of their services free,
in order to try to put things on a better
basis, but not one solitary thing has been
done. I feel that if something had been
done thousands of pounds would have
been saved, but the Government,
apparently, are not concerned as to
whether they can save the money of the
taxpayers or not. They put down a
certain amount in these Estimates, and
never for one moment go into the
question of whether £1,500 would do
instead of £2,000. In the absence of the
Cabinet Minister responsible for this
Department, I think the Parliamentary
Secretary should go into these matters,
with the object of arriving at a better
understanding between the Corporation
and the Guardians, and of saving a great
deal of the taxpayers' money.
There is another matter that requires
a little explanation from the Parliamentary Secretary. There is a sum of
£6,500 provided for the guard at the
Governor's House. I have the greatest
respect for the Governor; I think he is
one of nature's gentlemen. But, like
the Prime Minister, who is seldom at
Stormont, the Governor is seldom at
Hillsborough, and there is no need to
have a guard to protect an empty house.
One or two men could guard that house,
whereas at present over £6,000 a year
is spent in that way. I think a considerable saving could be effected there.
I hope that, if it is not done this year,
an effort will be made next year to
bring about a reduction, because the
Governor is seldom at Hillsborough; he
is either in England or at Barons Court.
Between £2,000 and £3,000 could be
saved in this Estimate that has been
placed before us to-day. I hope when
the Belfast Corporation bring forward
their scheme for the building of a new
sanatorium immediate steps will be taken
to sanction whatever scheme they think
best. I do not altogether blame the
Ministry in this matter. In no other
country of a similar size are there so
many people suffering from tuberculosis.
It is amazing that in Belfast alone 2,000
children attending public elementary
schools are affected with some form of
tuberculosis. These children are allowed
-and this is the tragedy of the whole
thing to attend school and in all probability infect other children. The only
hope of saving the lives of these children
is by treating them in the early stages
of the disease. Instead, for the past
four years, children who are suffering
from this disease are rapidly getting
worse and it will be utterly impossible to
save them when they enter hospital. I
hope the Minister will give this matter
the attention which it deserves.
Another matter to which I would like

appointed for Northern Ireland. I am
not anxious for appointments to be
made, but you want an experienced man,

Now that you have appointed this

There are about 40,000 unemployed in Belfast at the present time, and from among
this number you could find men qualified

citizens are in destitution. I do not think

Belfastmen; it is not suitable for those

in the country because they would have
to travel too far. The Parliamentary

in Belfast. Many men have not been

and a half years. Is not that a terrible
state of affairs? If I were the engineer
in charge of that work I could find suitable men in Belfast.
The engineer has the money at his disposal, and why the delay? The work
could be started immediately. I understand it will take two years to complete
the work. Why not, in view of the large
number of men unemployed, carry on

hope now the election is over and
the Minister has been returned to Parliament that matters will be expedited.

not doing anything to modernise the

Oral Answers to Questions.
ANNVALE FACTORY, KEADY.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Commerce whether, in view of acute
industrial depression in Keady and the
loss of the linen industry, any steps will
be taken to have Annvale Factory, which
employed about 400 workers, reopened;
and whether the reopening of this factory
would give much-needed employment in
that area.
The MINISTER OF
COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The business to which
I understand the hon. Member to refer
was placed in the hands of a Receiver
in 1926. In connection with the efforts
now being made to secure the establishment of new industrial undertakings in
Northern Ireland lists of available
vacant premises have been compiled by
my Ministry, and I can readily assure
the hon. Member that the claims of
Keady to consideration will not be overlooked. The question as to the locality
of any new factory is, however, as the
hon. Member will appreciate,
primarily for determination by the industrialist concerned.
one

industries which have closed since the 1st
January, 1918.

3. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he can state the
for
number of applications received

applications refused; the total amount of

Mr. BARBOUR: Up to the present
thirty-five formal applications for assistance under the New Industries (Development) Act (Northern Ireland), 1937,
have been received by my Ministry, and
of these seven have been refused.
Advances to the amount of approximately £20,000 have SO far been
authorised in three cases, apart from
grants in respect of sites, rent of premises
and income-tax contributions, while the
remainder of the applications are still
under discussion.

has been granted are engaged, or propose
to engage in the manufacture of carpets,
toilet requisites, and in the preservation
of apples for the bakery and restaurant
trades. Two will operate in Belfast and
one in Portadown.
Apart from the thirty-five cases which
have reached the stage of a formal application, there are twelve proposals in
connection with which preliminary discussions are now proceeding.

EFFECT OF REVALUATION.
5. Mr. DOWLING asked the Minister
of Finance whether the present taxes
which have now to be paid on property
valuations in Northern Ireland are
seriously injuring trade and employment,
and whether, having regard to the
already high percentage of unemployment before revaluation took place, and
the higher percentage now, he will give
this problem his immediate consideration.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): Having regard to the fact
that industries are derated to the extent
of 75 per cent., and to the fact that
income-tax has not to be paid unless
profits are earned, I am of the opinion,
therefore, that the revaluation that took
place two years ago is in no way the
cause of the high regrettable percentage
of unemployment which exists at present.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the right non.
Gentleman say whether it is a fact that
many small householders have been
driven out of their homes owing to the
high valuation imposed upon them by
the Government of Northern Ireland.
Mr. ANDREWS: I do not think that
arises out of this question.
AMENDMENT OF THE VALUATION
АСТ.
6. Mr. DOWLING asked the Minister
of Finance whether, with a view to
stimulating trade and employment to the
utmost extent, he will amend the
Valuation Act so that any improvements
to existing house property now undertaken, and which would be subject to
an increase in valuation will not be subject to any increase for a period of ten
years.
Mr. ANDREWS: I am unable to
agree to this proposal, which, in effect,
seeks to revive the provisions of the
Valuation Act (Northern Ireland), 1924.
I feel that to give exemption for a period
of ten years in respect of improvements
to existing house property would be unfair
to other property owners, and would only
revive the anomalies which existed before
Revaluation.

PRODUCTION OF FLAX.
17. Mr. MAGINESS asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he can state
if it is a fact that the production of flax
in the year 1937 increased in almost all
the flax producing countries of Europe,
while in the same year the production of
flax in Northern Ireland decreased by
almost 20 per cent.; whether the average
price of flax in Northern Ireland is
about 9s 6d per stone, and that
guaranteed price of 10s, even if the
present production were doubled, would
cost not £400,000, but a mere £40,000
at present prices; whether the figure of
£400,000 given by the Minister was based
upon a figure of 5s per stone; and
whether he has any justification for the
assumption that the price of flax may
fall to 5s per stone.
a
Mr. GORDON: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply to this
question. It is a fact that in the year
1937 the area under flax increased in
many countries in Europe, and that the
area under flax in Northern Ireland
showed a substantial decrease as compared with 1936, but was, at the same
time, higher than in any of the years
1931-1934 inclusive. For example, the
acreage in 1937 was 19,099 acres, whereas
the acreage in 1932 was only 6,093 acres.
The figures and calculations given by the
hon. Member are also quite correct. In
making my calculation to which he
refers, in order to estimate the possible
extent of the Exchequer liabilities, I had
to take into account the price to which
flax might fall, and it will, I think, be
within the hon. Member's knowledge that
the price did, in fact, drop to 5s a stone
in the 1930-31 season.
It was,
therefore, quite natural that we should
estimate on this basis, because, while we
all hope that such a low price level will
not be reached, there is no assurance
whatever that our hopes will be fulfilled.
I desire once more to emphasise that
without a guaranteed price which will
give the farmer a reasonable return it is
unlikely that there will be a substantial
increase in the flax acreage. One difficulty I have met with in trying to secure
such a guaranteed price for farmers is
that the spinners appeared to be unable
to agree upon a scheme which would
ensure that the price paid for Northern
Ireland flax is related on a definite basis
to the price paid by them for imported
flax of corresponding quality. Another
is that any guaranteed price to be
effective clearly implies that the flax produced will be purchased. A guaranteed
price without any obligation on the part
of the spinners to take over the flax produced would mean nothing. Without
undertakings from the manufacturing
end on these points we have to face the
fact that the cost of a subsidy scheme
might be as much or even more than I
have stated, and bear in mind, too, that
any such scheme to be effective would
necessarily have to be continued over a
period of years. I can only add that I
have long been in favour of an adequate
guaranteed price for flax to the Northern
Ireland grower, if agreement can be
obtained with the manufacturers as to
necessary Exchequer safeguards. This
fact is, I think, well-known both to the
trade and to the Farmers' Union.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask whether
the hon. Gentleman can give us any idea
of the prices prevailing for flax in
Northern Ireland for the last two
months?
Mr. GORDON: Perhaps the hon.
Member would put that question down.
Mr. MAGINESS: Is it a fact that the
years to which the hon. Gentleman refers,
when the price of flax dropped to 5s a
Oral Answers

Mr. GORDON: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply to this
question. The hon. Member will, I hope,
realise that there is no close relationship
between the area under flax in Northern
Ireland and employment in spinning and
weaving factories. It is true, of course,
that a substantial increase in the area
under flax in Northern Ireland would
provide additional work of a seasonal
character at scutch mills and on farms,
but the total additional number that
would be so employed is a matter of
speculation. Needless to say, I did not,
in making the calculation to which the
hon. Member refers, take into account
speculative savings from the Unemployment Relief Fund. The hon. Member is
aware of the steps I have taken with the
Committee of Imperial Defence in regard
to increasing the home output of flax,
and in the national interest I am as concerned as he is to see a very substantial
increase in our flax area. I have, however, no means of compelling farmers to
grow flax, and the situation must be
faced that the area can only be increased
if the farmer has some security that he
will receive a remunerative price for his
crop. I need hardly remind the hon.
Member that this Government has
limited financial resources, and if a State
subsidy scheme for flax involves a considerable liability, as it well might, the
cost might have to be met by increased
taxation applicable only to Northern
Ireland.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Murphy): In view of the assertions that
have been made in the course of this
debate, with your permission, Mr.
Speaker, and if it is not out of order, I
would like to refer at the outset to some
matters connected with the original
report of the eminent gentleman who
was asked to make that report, and on
whose report the Act under which the
Transport Board was set up was passed
by this House. It will be within the
recollection of some Members that when
Sir Felix Pole was asked by the Government to report on this whole question of
transport in Northern Ireland the
Government pointed out-I am now
reading from the report itself that
"it is of great importance that we
should be able to formulate a policy
which will be fair to the interests concerned, and at the same time will
ensure an efficient system of transport
for Northern Ireland."
That was the Government's policy, and it
was in reference to that policy that Sir
Felix Pole held inquiries and made his
report. It is not correct to say, as my
hon. and learned Friend, the Member for
Iveagh (Dr. Maginess), has said in terms,
that the public interests were not consulted in connection with that report. I
do not intend to weary the House by
reading the long list of bodies and
organisations which were consulted,
which did, in fact, make reports, and the
reports of which were considered.
As some hon. Members will recollect,
it was not the railway companies only,
it was not the principal bus companies
only, but the Provincial Road Hauliers'
Association, the general carriers, the
Association of County Councils, the
Tyrone County Council, the General
Council of Municipal Authorities, the
Association of Rural District Councils and,
I may say without enumerating all the
other bodies, practically each and every
Chamber of Trade and Chamber of Commerce in Northern Ireland and, in
addition, the Railway Clerks' Association, the National Union of Railwaymen,
the Associated Society of Locomotive
Engineers and Firemen, the Amalgamated Transport and General Workers'
Union and, last but not least, the
Londonderry Employers' Federation.
Those were among the bodies and associations who were asked to make representations, and on whose recommendations,
collected together, considered and
weighed by an expert, the report was
made to the Government in 1934. On
that report the Bill, which afterwards
became a Statute, was presented to this
House. That was the policy which
underlay the Act.
That policy being expounded when the
Bill was submitted to the House for
Second Reading, I, like other hon. Members, voted in favour of that Bill. Like
other hon. Members I believed, and still
believe, that the system that was set up
under the Road and Railway Transport
Act will eventually become successful.
But I recognise we all recognise that
certain complaints have been made here
and there as to the working of this Act,
and now the question that I suggest to
the House is this. Assume that to be
the case.
There are complaints, there
are persons-if you like, many personsdissatisfied. I should like to say that at
the same time it is quite certain that
there are quite numerous bodies of

in fact, satisfied with the present system
of transport which has been set up. Even

services in his part of the world. I am

my hand.

and cultivate more excursion traffic than
they have done. They might also consider whether the preparation and organisation of the time-table has been efficient.
They might deal with a great many
matters of this sort in regard to freight.
They might consider whether the Board's

the best way of conducting transport is

Under the Act of 1935, which constituted the Transport Board, there was
set up a tribunal called the Transport
Appeal Tribunal. This tribunal is set
up under Section 40. When one reads
the Act one sees that it is a tribunal of
importance and prestige. By Sub-section
5 of Section 40 it is given the position of
a court of record. It has a prestige on
a level with the King's Court. What
are the tasks entrusted to that tribunal?
When one goes through the Sections
dealing with it you will find that the

That tribunal was set up under the Act

or should be carrying out to-day what

public and Parliament.

moved the Motion and my hon. Friend
who has just sat down for asking a point
blank question as to what the result will
be when the McLintock Committee have
reported. The report will be laid upon.
the Table of the House. A White Paper
will be issued giving a full report in
exactly the same way as was done in the
case of the inquiry held by Sir Felix
Pole in the first instance. The House
will obtain the report as it is issued by
the three gentlemen concerned. I give
my pledge that that will be done in this
case.
May I answer the hon. Member for
North Derry (Rev. Robert Moore), for
whom I have the highest regard as a
champion of the farming community?
He
says that a great deal of the difficulty
that he and others have experienced
arises from rumours. We are all, of
course, from time to time embarrassed
by rumours, and very often there is
absolutely no foundation for them whatever. However, I will give him an
assurance for Coleraine and for all the
other Members of the House, that the
Government have got nothing whatever
to hide in connection with this question.
That is one of the reasons I had to come
to the conclusion to which I did come,
knowing the value of the expert advice
we will get on the one hand, and on the
other knowing the desire among Members and others outside to have a wider
investigation by somebody on the spot
who would understand the Ulster people
and the real problems that are afoot,
and who would make a report as to the
working of the Board up to the present
time, and give a large amount of data
on which the expert Committee will work.
The hon. Member behind me expressed
the fear that this double bite at the
cherry would cost more money and time
than a single bite would involve. On
thinking the matter over I came to the
conclusion that it will really shorten the
proceedings, because the expert Committee will not be overburdened with the
sort of matters that are raised here from
time to time, and which, even with great
patience, it might take months to get to
the bottom of. Therefore, I believe this
is a solution which will suit the public
when they bear in mind, as I said before,
that the Government have got nothing
whatever to hide. The Government want
to bring out nothing but the facts. They
want to place the facts before the Members of this House as soon as possible,
and at the same time to give the Government and this House the benefit of the
very best expert advice they could
possibly get. That is the position of the
Government.
The hon. and learned Member for
Willowfield (Mr. Black), who made a
very interesting speech, narrowed things
down for us considerably. I think he
approved of the terms of reference of
the M'Lintock Committee, and I think
he admitted, as most of us do, that the
bus question was not so very urgent as
that of transport. That being so. I will
make a careful note of what he has said
-it will be in the Debates-with regard
to the terms of reference of the other
Committee. If I may say so, I do not
know any respected and esteemed class
of our citizens who differ more among
themselves more than the lawyers-
(laughter) but as I have to take the
advice of one I always take the advice
of our Attorney-General, and so far I
have not found him making a mistake.
