The Purdysburn Inquiry.
Mr. HENDERSON: I was not at all
satisfied with the answer given by the
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Home Affairs to my question regarding the death of Miss Sadie Edith
Robinson which took place in the Purdysburn Mental Hospital in August last.
This is a case where a young woman lost
her life. Her parents allowed her to go
into the Mental Hospital, thinking she
would be looked after properly. She
met a most horrible death-she
burnt all over the body. Her parents
asked for an inquiry, and I also wrote
to the Ministry of Home Affairs asking
was
The Purdysburn Inquiry 552
Adjournment-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Henderson]
that an inquiry should be held. I find
that notwithstanding the plea of the
parents the Ministry have refused to
make known the findings of their
Inspector who held the inquiry.
The evidence given on that occasion
was terrible. It was openly admitted
that the staff was insufficient to look
after the patients. There were about
60 or 70 patients and only three nurses
to attend them. No dismissals followed
the inquiry, but I believe the lady in
charge of the nurses was reprimanded.
Notwithstanding the fact that an
inquiry was held the parents of this
child have not got any satisfaction as to
how she met her death or as to who was
responsible. There is no other country
in the world, after an inquiry has been
held, that this could happen in except
Northern Ireland. This will be looked
upon in a very serious way by people
who have relatives in that Institution.
Is there any reason why the Parliamentary Secretary should hide the findings of the Inspector? I should like to
bring the case to the door of hon. Members on all sides of the House. Picture
your sisters, or one of your wives.
(Laughter.) I mean the wife of any
hon. Member, or his daughter, who
happened to be a patient in Purdysburn
being burned to death and after an
inquiry is held the findings of that
inquiry are refused. I think that is
monstrous.
May I ask the Parliamentary Secretary to say that the Inspector's finding
is that the hospital neglected its duty in
not having a sufficient number of nurses
to look after the patients and that this
girl was burnt to death through improper supervision. The girl was not
found for nearly an hour afterwards.
If there had been proper supervision
this young woman might not have met
her death. On behalf of the parents, I
protest against the Ministry refusing to
give the findings of the Inspector.
There were a large number of people
at the inquiry, which was a public one.
I was there, and also a large number of
medical men, and the father of this girl.
In these circumstances how could it be
called anything but a public inquiry?
Mr. BEATTIE: I understand the
silence of the Parliamentary Secretary
to give consent to the hon. Member's
complaint that something came out at
the inquiry-whether it was a private.
inquiry or not I do not know-that they
are afraid to disclose. If that is so, I
do not think that is the way in which
the business of the Home Office should
be conducted. As citizens and as representatives of the citizens in Northern
Ireland we should be informed as to the
result of the inquiry. The hon. Member for Shankill stated that it was a
public inquiry. Whether it was public.
or private we should be informed of the
decision arrived at.
Private inquiries have previously been
held in Northern Ireland and as Members of this House we are entitled to
know the result because it is our money
which pays for the holding of those
inquiries. I am not at the moment
making any charges, but I do demand,
as a Member of this House, to be
informed of the results of the detailed
examination. You may refuse to-day
to give the result or the details if you
feel so disposed, but if you fail we will
place you in the position in which we
placed a previous Parliamentary Secretary. In that case we got the detailed
information from the Home Office by
indirect methods, and we were able to
place the full facts of the inquiry before
the House. Why not give the hon.
Member for Shankill an answer to his
question which will satisfy every Member of this House and which will satisfy
the parents. By doing so it will show
there is nothing to be ashamed of, and
it will also give the hon. Member the
right to which he is entitled.
Mr. DAVISON: It is absolutely
ridiculous to suggest that there is anything which the Ministry of Home
Affairs is ashamed of or that they have
anything to conceal. They are not concerned with the management of Purdysburn; the management is entirely under
the control of the Committee of that
institution.
Mr. BEATTIE: You are the Government; you are the head.
Mr. DAVISON: I trust the hon.
Member will allow me to continue.
Mr. BEATTIE: You said you had
nothing to do with it. You have all to
do with Purdysburn.

Oral Answer to Question.
LABOURERS' COTTAGES IN
BALLYMONEY RURAL DISTRICT.
Mr. ELLIOTT (for Mr. Young) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether
he can state if it is a fact that the
Ballymoney Rural District Council has
decided to fix the rents of cottages,
recently erected near Rasharkin, according to applicant's income; whether the
Council has power to do this, in view of
the fact that in 1937 a public inquiry
was held by the Ministry's inspector in
Ballymoney, to which each applicant
received notification to attend, and was
asked at this inquiry if they were prepared to pay 2s 6d per week; whether
each applicant agreed to pay this
amount; whether each applicant understood this to be an agreement, and
whether the Council has now the right
to ask these same applicants to pay a
higher rent, in some cases 3s 6d per
week.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Davison): At
the last meeting of the Ballymoney
Rural District Council there was some
discussion regarding the rents to be
charged for new cottages, in the course
of which it was suggested that industrial
workers should be charged rents of 3s 6d
a week and agricultural workers 2s 6d a
week, but no decision was come to.

I am, however, to point out that rents
payable in respect of labourers' cottages
cannot be fixed by the Council without
the approval of the Ministry, and in
approving such rents the Ministry takes
into consideration not only the cost of
the erection of the cottages but also the
circumstances of the labourers.
The query put to applicants by the
inspector at the inquiry was directed to
finding out whether the applicants were
able and willing to pay a reasonable rent
in the event of the cottages being
erected. Two shillings and sixpence was
mentioned as being the probable minirent, but no undertaking was
given on behalf of the Council that this
would, in fact, be the rent finally decided upon. Obviously at that early
stage of the proceedings it would not.
have been possible to determine properly
what would be a suitable rent.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

EDUCATION (Mrs.
(Mrs. Parker): With
your permission I am taking the two
Votes together, as you have said we may
do. When presenting the Education
Estimates to the Committee last year, my
predecessor had to ask for the sum of
£2,155,849, representing the total of

subsequently, it was decided to restore

in full the cuts to the teachers, it became necessary to vote a supplementary

than that estimate by £47,462, namely,

for the Ministry's administration and
£2,158,677 for the educational services.
I would like, first of all, to deal with
Vote 1 for the salaries and expenses of
the Ministry of Education. The sum
required this year is practically the same
as last, and I am glad to inform the
Committee that there is no appreciable
increase under this head. This is really
owing to the fact that the cost of increments to the Ministry's officials has been
almost entirely off-set by savings due to
retirements.
In this connection I feel it appropriate
for me to mention that one of the most
valued officers of the Ministry, the
Assistant Secretary for Higher Education, Dr. Garrett, is now retiring on
pension. His services ever since the establishment of the Ministry have been of
the greatest benefit to education in
Northern Ireland. His long experience
of technical instruction particularly,
and of all branches of education in this
country has proved invaluable in the
establishment and development of the
new education system set up by the
Londonderry Act in 1923.
We part from Dr. Garrett with the
very greatest regret, and I would like
to add an even more personal note to
what I have already said on behalf of
the Ministry. When I first came into
touch with him on the Lynn Committee,
and, subsequently, when I was the first
chairman of the Magherafelt Regional
Education Committee set up under the
new Act, he always gave me the greatest
help and the most valuable advice.
can say truthfully that he has been a
friend and guide to all the education
authorities, and they will miss him. In
my new position I will greatly miss one.
to whom I looked for guidance and on
whom I looked, when I first took up the
position, as an old friend to welcome me.
I
I was a back bencher for a great many
years, and I sometimes wonder if my
colleagues and I always fully realised
what the country owes to the men behind the scenes-men such as he is-men
who work unceasingly and untiringly for
their fellow citizens, and who continue
to do so day in and day out—whether
Governments come or Governments go.
We have also lost by death or retirement several other valued officials during
the past year. To assist in the increasing work of higher education owing to
the extension of the secondary school

is little else in Vote 1 which calls for

The new allocation of posts and renaming of the grades under the recent
of

I now turn to Vote 2, amounting to

We cannot, however, get a comprehensive picture of the amount that education costs to public funds without adding
to the above the net expenditure raised

to approximately £180,000. The total

spending from public funds upon education reaches a sum in the neighbourhood
of £2,410,000. If we divide this sum
between the Government Vote and the
ratepayers we find that the latter contribute about £350,000, while Parliament puts up £2,060,000.
I include, of course, in the expenditure met from local rates the contributions by local authorities under Section 3
of the Finance Act, 1934, which is

and which must be set against the gross
amount of £2,228,000 which I am asking

the Committee to vote to-day.
credit the amount of the de-rating grants

This Vote indicates the gradual and
increasing development of our education.
system. It is obvious that the provision
of splendid new schools in all parts of the
Province, the gratifying developments in
our secondary and technical education
systems, the restoration of the economy
cuts made in the salaries of all classes
of teachers six years ago and the necessity
of bearing the increasing charges for

into operation without throwing an

I thought, perhaps, I might to-day
make a comparison with the expenditure
of ten years ago and examine the progress in the educational services and the
Education Vote since 1928. One of my
reasons for making this comparison is
that I ceased to be chairman of a regional
education committee in that year and,
therefore, since then I have not been in
quite such close touch with local education authorities, and I find the indications of progress and the consequential
rise in expenditure most interesting. I
hope the Committee may share my view.
one-
In the Estimates for 1928-29 the
amount put down for Vote 2 was
£1,825,650. Compare that
sum with
to-day's Estimate and you will find
an increase of £333,000, almost
third of a million pounds. How is this
increase accounted for? The largest
item, amounting to £102,000, represents
the cost of paying the annual pensions of
the teachers who have now retired from
the service. In 1928 the receipts in
teachers' premiums and interest on the
Pension Fund were sufficient to deal with
the outgoings, but as the operation of the
improved scales of salaries after the war
began to take effect the pensions grew in
consequence, and this sum of over
£100,000 is required to meet the current
payments of annual superannuation
allowances.
Another item which accounts for a
large part of the increase is the addition
to the grants paid to the local education.
authorities under Section 76 of the
Education Act which, owing to the revaluation of the Province and the greater
yield in consequence of the 8d rate, show
an increase of £86,000 on the Estimate
for this purpose in 1928. Then we find
that the grants for secondary education
have increased by £77,000, almost
entirely due to the increased numbers in
attendance at our secondary schools. The
present attendance at these schools is
approximately 50 per cent. higher than
it was ten years ago.
I am sure the
Committee will agree that it is a most
gratifying feature of my comparison, and
proves that the people of this Province
are becoming increasingly alive to the
advantages of secondary education. The
three items I have mentioned account
for over £265,000. The remaining items
include an addition of £50,000 for
elementary education, owing to the
automatic growth in the incremental cost
of teachers' salaries, and £12,000 for
technical education, due principally to
the same cause.
On the other hand, it is estimated that
the net increase from the same period in
the education charges, falling upon the
rates is represented by a sum of £60,000.
At the time I am speaking of only about
22 new schoolhouses had been erected by
the education authorities, as against the
142 which have now been constructed in
all parts of the Province. It might be
tedious to go into other comparisons with
1928, but I think I have said enough to
indicate that the increase in expenditure
has been inevitable in view of the very
great advance in our educational equipment and facilities, which has been
attained in the last ten years.
As has been pointed out already, the
possibilities of reduction of educational
expenditure are not great. The two
factors on which this expenditure chiefly
depends are first, the standard of emoluments paid to the teachers, and secondly,
the numbers of these teachers that are
employed in the schools. I am sure that
no member of the Committee is prepared
to advocate a reduction in teachers'
salaries, and I feel equally sure that
nobody would wish to see the staffs of
our elementary schools reduced in
number. As the Committee know, a
great deal has been done through the
amalgamation of redundant schools in
Ministry of Education 562

populous parts of the country, and the
economies effected in this way are not
inconsiderable. The decline in the attendance at our elementary schools which
still continues is not of sufficient extent
to lead to any great economy of teaching
staff, although it is possible that here
and there some assistant teachers have
been threatened with loss of position on

on the latter subject in a few moments.
our
With regard to the attendance at our
schools, the extreme severity of the
weather in the first quarter of last year
caused a considerable decline in the
month of January, a decline which is reflected in the figures of regularity of
attendance. In previous years
elementary schools have seldom fallen
below 85 per cent. in regularity of attendance, and have reached sometimes 87
and 88 per cent., but, unfortunately, last
year our records show that the attendance percentage was as low as 84.9, a
result which is largely ascribed to the
severity of the weather, to which I have
referred. I wish I were able to tell the
Committee that the regularity of attendance is improving, but, unfortunately,
this is not the case. There is no doubt
that our education authorities should
look further into this matter and take
steps to improve their administration of
the compulsory attendance machinery.
The school enrolment continues to fall
slightly, and the actual number of pupils
on the rolls on 31st December last was
194,347, showing a drop of nearly 3,000
as compared with the same date in 1936,
when it
was returned as 197,283.
Following a decline in the last two or
three years this means that since 1933
the enrolment in our elementary schools
has fallen by over 12,000. In this
respect our experience here is similar to
that found in Great Britain, but is not
so great in its extent.
Taking the different heads of the
Estimate the sum required this year for
training colleges shows a decrease of
£2,428. The capitation rate payable in
respect of the students is not changed,
and the decrease is almost entirely due
to a reduction in the numbers of students
in training. There are now 304 students
in our training colleges, as against 323
this time last year. This fall is due to
the policy of the Ministry aiming at a
reduction in the number of students, so
that too many candidates for the teaching profession may not be turned out in
future.
I am pleased to say that the position
in regard to unemployment of teachers is
much more favourable than a year ago.
The returns in the Ministry, made up
to the last day of January, show that on
that date there were 43 ex-students not
in employment, whereas on the corresponding date of the previous year the
number was 87. The position, therefore,
has been much relieved, and in the period
between January and July it is expected
that vacancies in the profession will
account for a substantial number of the
43 not now employed. A good deal of
relief has been obtained owing to the
measures taken by the Ministry to secure
the fuller employment of substitutes for
teachers who are absent from duty
and
through illness,
also
by the
strengthening of the teaching staffs in the
larger schools.
The refresher courses for teachers
which were held at Stranmillis Training
College last summer proved very successful, and the Ministry proposes this year
to hold similar courses on a larger scale.
The teachers attending the courses have
shown great keenness and interest, and
the Ministry is satisfied that the benefits.
of becoming acquainted with the latest
developments in the teaching methods in
different branches of the curriculum are
very great. The sum required for the
salaries of the elementary teachers is
increased by £25,450, of which £16,000
is due to the cost of the full restoration
of the cuts. The restoration, of course,
took effect from July, 1937, but its full
financial effect does not become evident
until the present year.
The balance of the increase is due
partly to the automatic effect of the addition of increments in the salary scale, but
some portion is due to the new regulations
regarding substitute teachers and also to
the increase now allowable in the staffs
of the larger schools. My predecessor last
year spoke at some length on the inadequacy of the staffs in these schools
which led to many cases of over-large
classes, and promised that the Ministry
would study the question with a view to
finding some alleviation of the difficulty.
This has been done in conjunction with
representatives of the teaching profession
and new regulations have been brought
into effect which enable the Ministry to

hardship that would be caused in such
cases has been brought to the notice of
the Ministry by the teachers' representatives. The Ministry is taking steps to
impress upon the education authorities
and managers of schools that in filling
vacancies that occur from time to time in
the schools, preference should be given
to teachers whose positions were
jeopardy owing to the cause mentioned.
Provision was made to enable this to be
done in the Education Act that was
passed in 1935, which permitted the
transfer of a redundant teacher from one
school to another in the area of a regional
committee without the necessity of advertising the post. Many of our regional
committees have refrained from making
use of this means for dealing with
teachers dispossessed of their posts
through a fall in the average attendance,
and I would urge them to look into the
matter and make use of the provisions of
the Act.
The Estimates include a small sum in
the shape of a grant towards nursery
schools for the first time, and I have
much pleasure in saying how much the
Ministry appreciates the work done by
those who have started such schools in
the city by voluntary effort. The advantages of nursery schools, particularly in
working-class quarters of the city is now
recognised everywhere, and it is gratifying to know that two new nursery schools
are likely to be aided by the Ministry in
the current year. The ladies who have
been responsible for the running of these
schools until now, have had a very uphill
task. The obvious happiness of the small
children who attend, the improvement in
their health and habits, must be a reward
in itself. I can only add my personal
note of pleasure that their efforts are
being recognised by the Ministry and the
general public. The 50 per cent. grant
made by the Ministry towards the building of voluntary schools shows an increase
of £1,735, and now amounts to £6,475
which represents the loan charge on half
the capital expenditure outstanding in
respect of this and previous years' grants.
A conference of inspectors and teachers
is at present sitting, with a view to
making improvements in the system of
teaching arithmetic and mathematics in
the elementary schools, and, in this connection the question of altering the system
of payment of extra fees is receiving
attention. A system of payment based on
examination of the pupils is now generally
considered antiquated and undesirable,
and changes are being sought which, while
preserving the teachers' legitimate
interests, will lead to a more rational
system of instruction.
The conference which has been dealing
with the question of the scholarship
system has just furnished its report which
will be in the hands of the public very
shortly and contains valuable suggestions
for the consideration of the education
authorities with a view to making this
system still more conducive of benefit to
the pupils in the elementary schools.
The Vote for secondary education continues to increase, and the estimate of
£202,140 is greater than last year's by
£7,740. Nearly half the increase is due
to the cost of full restoration of the cuts,
while the remainder arises out of the still
increasing enrolment at the secondary
schools, and also from the recognition of
a new secondary school in Downpatrick,
which was opened last August.
The enrolment in the secondary schools.
stood at 13,683 in December last, which
is the highest point ever reached, and
the development of this type of education
may be considered as one of the surest
signs of our educational progress. There
is no doubt that one of the chief factors
in this progress is the provision for a
greater number of pupils of further
education, by which I mean education
over the age of fourteen, and the more
we can induce pupils to continue their
school life, whether by attendance at
full-time secondary or junior technical
schools or by part-time
by part-time attendance at
technical classes, the more we can ensure
that the funds spent on elementary
education bear their proper fruit.
Besides the increase in the enrolment, it
is also gratifying to find that the numbers
attending the certificate examinations
move steadily upwards.
The grant for technical instruction is
estimated at £75,400, an increase of
£5,300 over last year. About £1,000 of
this increase is accounted for by the full
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
30 MARCH 1938
restoration of the cut. The balance,
which shows an increase over last year, is
partly due to the fact that owing to the
severity of the weather and epidemics in
1936-37, last year's estimate was somewhat low, so that a larger sum will mature
for payment as attendance grant in
1938-39.
A new item in the account is the special
grant of £700, which is to be made to the
Belfast College of Technology as a contribution towards the cost of trades
scholarship courses in respect of scholars
who attend from areas outside the county
borough. The grant, payable to the local

the Education Act, 1923, is estimated at
£241,000 which is slightly larger than
last year, but represents an increase of
over £60,000 on the year before. This
result is, of course, due to revaluation,
being the increased yield of the 8d rate.
The total estimated budget of the education authorities for 1938-39 amounts to
£545,000, towards which the Ministry
contributes £318,000, while derating
grants are responsible for £71,000. The
balance falling on local resources will
amount, therefore, to £156,000, and this
sum will be further diminished by the
amount collected from students in fees,
etcetera, estimated at £42,000.
Apart from technical instruction the
largest item of expenditure in the budget
of the education authorities comes under
the head of loan charges in respect of new
school buildings and reconditioning of
transferred schools. Nearly all the
authorities continue to be very active in
building work. At the end of last year
new provided schools built by the education authorities amounted to 142. The
number of transferred schools under these
authorities now in actual operation is 511,
making a total of 653 elementary schools,
with accommodation for approximately
100,000 pupils.
The number of schools that have been
transferred since the 1923 Act to the
education authorities exceeds 700, but
many of these are now closed, according
as new provided schools were erected.
There are still over 1,000 voluntary
schools, of which 387 are under management other than Roman Catholic. It will
be noted that this class of school comes
under precisely similar regulations to
those schools which are under Roman
Catholic management. The total of
elementary schools continues to decline,
and now stands at 1,727, a decrease of
The
26 compared with last year.
majority of the schools that have been
struck off were situated in Belfast and
other urban centres, and most of them
have been replaced by larger and wellconstructed new buildings. Thirteen new
provided schools were brought into operation during last year.
There is little change to record in the
progress made by the education authorities in carrying on their work. Steady
improvement continues all over the
Province. I am glad to say that practically all authorities now have suitable
schemes of medical inspection, but it
cannot yet be said that the situation in
regard to the provision of meals for
As
necessitous children is satisfactory.
in past years, Belfast and County Down
continue to pay careful attention to this
matter. Two or three other authorities
do a little to assist voluntary schemes,
but there is great need for most authorities to take up this important question
in a more serious way.
My personal knowledge of the regional
education committees of the men and
women who constitute those committees,
and of their desire to do their best for all
the children attending school in their
areas makes me feel certain that the
only reason for the delay in dealing with
the question is that there are considerable
difficulties connected with the provision
of these meals in remote rural districts.
I do not believe that the difficulties are
insuperable. I appeal to the education
authorities and I look confidently to their
action in tackling the problem in the
near future. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
I would like to deal briefly with the
special school at Haypark for mentally
deficient children. The estimate for this
school remains practically the same as
before. The school has now been in
operation for two years, and there is no
question as to the value of results that
have been gained for the pupils by their
attendance there. I have satisfied myself
by personally visiting the institution that
the pupils are well cared for and are progressing in every way in an almost
surprising degree. There is still accommodation for many more boarders than
attend at present, and I hope that as the
advantages of attendance becomes
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Parker.]
apparent to parents throughout the
country there will be less disinclination
to permit children suited for the institution to go into residence.
I hope that the education authorities
and all interested will take every opportunity to point out the advantages to be
gained by the children, with a view to
overcoming the parents' objections.
There is, I suppose, a natural reluctance
on the part of parents in the country, to
send their children away from homeparticularly so when those children are
delicate, mentally and physically.
want to give the assurance that a visit to
this institution would convince those
parents that their children will be
absolutely happy and well cared for, and,
what is equally important, they will have.
a chance of being so much improved

In this review of the Estimates I have
said little about the actual work done in
the schools, which continues to proceed
without much alteration from year to
year. As time goes on opportunities are
taken to improve the curriculum, and
the inspectors report that the general
standard of efficiency in teaching in all
types of schools continues to rise.
In our secondary schools there has been
in recent years a steady increase in the
number of teachers with honours degrees
and the certificate examinations show that
the standard of attainment and the number of pupils who reached the end of the
secondary school course are on the upgrade.
In our technical schools the actual
numbers of students in attendance remain
much as in previous years, and it would
seem that saturation point may have been
reached.
The Ministry is hopeful that coming
legislation in connection with the school
leaving age may lead to increased
activity and scope for all types of schools.
dealing with pupils from 14 upwards, and
it is probably in this direction that the
next steps in progress must be looked for.
I am happy to say that the Ministry's
relations with the education authorities
and with the teaching profession continue
to be of a pleasant and sympathetic
kind, and we are indebted to these bodies
for co-operation and assistance in every
department of the Ministry's work.
I hope that I have not unduly tried the
patience of the Committee by these
details. The great and useful work of
the Ministry is apt to be taken for
granted. May I be forgiven if I say that
it lays the foundation on which the
other Ministries are built up-because out
of its activities the mental and intellectual
life of our Six Counties is fashioned.
The sum for which I am asking the
Committee may seem large, but the value
to the State of the intellectual future of
its citizens cannot be appraised in terms
of cash. I beg to move.

Rev. PROFESSOR CORKEY:
should like, first of all, very warmly
to congratulate our new Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Education
on the very gracious and interesting
and audible way in which she has presented these Estimates. As she was
speaking, there occurred to me a story
which I heard about a message which
was sent from a native village in Africa
to the headquarters of one of the
missions there asking for a teacher.
This message, after voicing the request
of the people, said that the natives of
the village were of opinion that a
woman would be the best man for the
job. (Laughter.) We have all been
delighted with the lucidity of the explanation which has been given to us
by the Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Education in presenting
these Estimates. If I might without
presumption, I would congratulate her
and congratulate the House upon having
this arrangement made by the Cabinet.
Perhaps it would not be out of place
if I took this opportunity also of voicing
my own appreciation, and I am sure the
appreciation of other hon. Members, at
the fact that our former Member for
Queen's University now occupies the
position in the Cabinet of Minister of
Education. When he was a Member of
this House, he had the full confidence
of every Member so far as ability and
judgment were concerned. He was a
Minister who was always easy to
approach, and from whom one was
always sure of a friendly reception and
a solution of difficulties when solution
was possible at all. Mr. Robb, if I may
so speak of him now, held office during
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
30 MARCH 1938
some difficult days in the history of our
educational development, but he steered
the ship well so far as his responsibility
for the ship was concerned. I believe
that when he was a youth, owing to the
arrangement of his initials, he was
affectionately dubbed by his school
fellows by the name of a traveller in
the Old Testament who was thrown
overboard on one occasion, and who was
treated without any great ceremony by
a great fish. (Laughter.) In Mr.
Robb's later days, so far from being
thrown overboard, he has been rescued
from the seas of politics, and has been
translated to a higher and better place
where no monsters will in future be
able to catch him at all. We congratulate our former Member on his exaltation to the rank of Cabinet Minister,
and I congratulate the Cabinet also on
having such a man as their colleague.
a
When I am in this appreciative and
congratulatory mood, I should like to
make similar references to the officials
of the Ministry to whom the Parliamentary Secretary has paid such a
gracious compliment. It is always
pleasure, I may say, to go to that Ministry. They are always willing to receive
one, to hear one's statement, and to do
the best they can for disturbed and
anxious or dissatisfied individuals, of
whom I am not one, but sometimes such
people write to me, and I have got to
act as their mouthpiece.
There is a great deal to which one
might refer in speaking on these Estimates, but I do not propose to cover
the ground to-day. There are just one
or two details to which I should like to
make appreciative reference in speaking
of the work of the Ministry.
First of
all, I hope that the Ministry, so far as
possible, will keep in step in their
educational standard with the standard
set in Great Britain. We have always
tried to do so here in our social services
and in our system of education, and I
am quite sure we will make no mistake
in attempting to reach the standard of
education set for us in Great Britain.
Then I should like to express my appreciation of little services which the
Ministry renders every year in the interests of better international understanding and more efficient education in
international affairs. I am not a peace
at any price man, but I do retain some
lingering faith in the League of Nations,
and I believe it is very important that
our people should be to some extent
versed in international affairs and obtain
a sane outlook. The Ministry helps that
in a quiet way by paying part of the
expenses of two students of Stranmillis
every year to go to Geneva to see the
working of this piece of international
machinery for themselves and to hear
lectures upon the subject while they are
there. This little bit of service just
shows that the Ministry is wide awake
to world events and to the need that
there is among ourselves for education in
the principles of democracy within our
own nation and the principles of
democracy as they will eventually be
applied to the whole world.
I may also express my appreciation of
the grants made by the Ministry to the
nursery schools. I am at these schools
once in a while, and it is always a joy
to see the splendid, kindly, educative
work that is being done there. Perhaps.
I may make one other reference to the
Estimates and then I have finished.
The authorities in Queen's University
were a little bit alarmed when these
Estimates were published, because they
were hopeful that the grant to the
University would be increased a little.
this year in proportion to the increase
in the work done by the University, and
in proportion to the increase in the number of students. When I was a student
at Queen's some years before the war,
the number of students in attendance
was about 400, and now there are between 1,400 and 1,500 students, but the
grants from public sources have not increased in proportion.
I know that there are other great
claims on the Ministry of Finance and
on the Ministry of Education. For
example, we have those gentle-minded
critics of the Northern Government laying land mines over our city-those
people who are so kindly spoken of in
the "Spectator" and other journals that
are ill-informed in regard to Ulster.
When we have individuals like that
going round we feel the necessity of the
Government concentrating on other services for defence and protection. We
have also the poor and the unemployed.
But I hope that the Ministry, when
they balance their books, will be able
to do something more for Queen's

University than they have hitherto been
able to do. The congestion there is very

Mr. JOHN JOHNSTON: I venture,
with diffidence, to address the Committee on the Education Estimates,
because, unlike the previous speaker, I
am neither a graduate of the University
nor such an educational authority as he
is. Having, however, enjoyed
moderate education and having been at
a secondary school, I do appreciate the
work of the Ministry of Education. I
should like to congratulate the Parliamentary Secretary on her clear
exposition of the Votes, and if her predecessor has been translated he has left
behind him the mantle of Elijah or
Elisha-I do not know which-(laughter) and she has shown that she has
the gift of clear exposition.
There is one thing I should like to
point out I think we cannot congratulate ourselves upon the number of pupils
attending the secondary schools. If you
look at the number in Northern Ireland
you will find that we lag behind
very
alarmingly the number of secondary
school pupils in England, Scotland, and
Wales. I think I am right in saying
that we have only about one-third of
our proportion of pupils of secondary
schools in Northern Ireland as compared
with Great Britain, and in my opinion
that arises from the paucity of scholarships offered in this country. I understand that the County Councils of
England, Scotland, and Wales offer far
more scholarships to poor children than
we do, and I was very pleased to hear
the Parliamentary Secretary say that
that aspect of education would receive
attention this year.
There is another aspect of the education question to which I would like to call
the attention of the Committee. It is in
connection with technical education. I
understand that a good part of the time
of the technical school teacher is occupied
in teaching unemployed youths in the
afternoon and evening, that these classes
are more or less a farce, that no one
receives any real education, and that the
teachers themselves look upon the classes
as utterly useless. I am afraid that no
good results come from these classes of
instruction.
I think that is largely due to a want of
inspection of the classes and lack of
attention in looking for results. It is a
matter that is mixed up between two
Ministries-the Ministry of Labour and
the Ministry of Education. The Ministry of Labour sends these youths to be
taught in the technical school, and the
technical school teaches them, and that
is the end of it. There is no inspection
of the results of that teaching, and I am
informed-I hope wrongly-that these
classes are of no use at all. I would like
to ask the Parliamentary Secretary if
there is any system which would test
whether these classes are of any service
to the community at all.
I know perfectly well that these unemployed youths are better attending classes
than running about the streets, but if the
classes are not effective, and if the education that is given in them is not tested,
I am afraid the result is largely negative.
I would again like to congratulate the
Parliamentary Secretary on her clear
explanation of the Estimates, and on the
small increase in expenditure which they
show.

like to add another leaf to the laurel
wreath that has been presented to

listened, I think, to every Education
Estimate that has been presented since

That leads me to speak of two other

subjects-history, philosophy, poetry,
English, and all sorts of educational and

taken advantage of to a very large extent by working men and working

women, although not to the extent that

with the object of getting an extra

If there are adult working men and

like the claims of the Workers' Educational Association to an increased grant
to be taken into consideration.
Then my colleague in the representation of Queen's University spoke about
the grant to the Queen's University of
Belfast. I know that that is under very
careful consideration at the present time,
and while I should like to press the claims
of the University, which I believe have
every right to be pressed, I would like to
draw the attention of the Government to
a few figures. I want to talk about something that is not mentioned in these
Estimates at all, the University Grants
Committee, which is a committee
appointed by the Parliament in Great
Britain to review the claims of
universities for an increased amount of
money every year from the Government.
That committee was established under
the influence of a feeling and belief, expressed by one of the responsible
Ministers of the Crown, that university
education, had it been better and more
universal, and better endowed in Great
Britain before the war broke out, would
probably have materially contributed to
the lessening of the period of the last
Great War. Whether that is a correct
idea or not I do not know, but I do know
that after the war the Government in
Great Britain was so much impressed
with the importance of university education that they established the University
Grants Committee to go into the claims
of universities for extra money, and to
make recommendations to the Government.
I have before me the last available
report of the University Grants Committee, and I find from the figures they
give that in the year 1924-25 they advised
the Government in regard to the distribution to the universities of Great Britain
of £1,238,000; that is rather over a
million and a quarter. They receive
applications from the universities for
increased grants, and deal with them as
they think right, and in the year 1931-32,
that is seven years later, in place of distributing a million and a quarter they
distributed £1,828,000 to different
universities in Great Britain. That is to
say that inside seven years they had increased the grants by £590,000, or well
over half a million pounds. You can see
that that does not fall far short of increasing the Government's contribution
to the universities of Great Britain by
between forty and fifty per cent.
I should like to give you an example
of what they have done for universities
in many ways comparable to our Queen's
University of Belfast. Birmingham
University, which is a very similar
university to ours, or perhaps rather
larger, was receiving £55,000 in 1924-
25, and in 1931-32, £76,000, so that in
the latter year it was receiving half as
much again. The same thing happened
in the case of Leeds University, which
was receiving £46,000 at the earlier
date, and seven years later £71,000 from
the Government. Manchester University was receiving £56,000 in 1924-25,
and seven years later £81,000. I could
quote the figures for all the universities,
but I only quote these to show you that
in the case of every university in Great
Britain, including Wales, increases of
grants have taken place to an amount
that varies from 25 per cent. or 30 per
cent., up to 50 per cent., and even more.
That has nothing to do with our
educational system, but I want the Committee to understand that Queen's
Estimates-

University approached the University
Grants Committee and were informed by
them that its University Grants Committee is the Government of Northern
Ireland. Now I hope the Government
of Northern Ireland will follow the

Committee.

education. I hope they will continue to
do so and that the figures will increase.
They have increased by 50 per cent.
during the past ten years, and I trust
they will still further increase in the
near future.
With regard to the question of adult
education, which was raised by the hon.
Member who was just spoken (Sir Robert
Johnstone), I can say that the Ministry
have agreed and have received the
approval of the Ministry of Finance to
increase the grant in aid to the Workers'
Educational Association from £150 to a
maximum of £350. The new grant does
not fall due for payment until 1939-40,
as the University authorities did not.
feel able to use the grant until next
year. Consequently, the increased grant
will appear in next year's Estimates.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Minford) raised the question of free
books to necessitous children. I think I
am correct in saying that in this matter
the Ministry have the same feelings as
they have with regard to the provision
of meals to necessitous children. The
Ministry have put forward suggestions
to the educational authorities. It is
entirely a matter for them, and the
Ministry can only make suggestions and
urge upon them the necessity of looking
sympathetically into this question. I
think I am correct in saying that something like 41,475 children are provided
with books. Ten committees have
taken this matter up and I hope it will
be gone into even more fully in the
near future.
The hon. Member for Antrim also
referred to the inspection of convent
schools. He stated that these schools
are not inspected. I am very pleased to
be able to inform him that he is under a
misapprehension, and that convent
schools are inspected in the same way as
other schools in the Province.
I should like once again to thank
hon. Members for dealing so kindly
with me in regard to the presentation of
the Estimates. I am very glad they
have not found very much to criticise.
Question put, and agreed to.

ROAD TRANSPORT BOARD STAFF.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of inspectors, drivers and conductors employed by the Transport
Board; the hours per week which these
officials are required to work, and what
arrangements or facilities, if any, exist
to enable these men to attend divine
service.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Davison): I
have been informed by the Transport
Board that there are at present 40
inspectors, 481 drivers and 441 conductors in its employment. It will, of
course, be understood that the number
of drivers and conductors varies from
time to time.
The hours of work of these employees
are regulated by agreement with the
Trades Union concerned, the normal
working hours being 48 per week on a
cumulative basis. Every man has, however, one complete rest day in each
week.
Sunday duty is performed by the men.
in each depot in rotation, and each man
is, therefore, on duty on as few Sundays
as is possible throughout the year.
Mr. NIXON: Do the inspectors get
an opportunity of attending divine service on Sundays?
Mr. DAVISON: I have no further
information than what I have given to
the hon. Member, which I got from the
Transport Board. If the hon. Member
puts down another question on this point
I will have inquiries made.
Mr. NIXON: Would the Parliamentary Secretary actually inquire into
the supplementary question, leave it at
that, and give me a personal answer?
SAFETY OF POPULATION IN CASE
OF WAR.
4. Mr. CLARK asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether, in view of the
grave unrest abroad and the vulnerable
and unguarded position of Belfast, with
its Shipyards, Aircraft Factory, etc., he
can state what steps have been or are
going to be taken to ensure the safety
of the population.
Mr. DAVISON: The question of
the defence of Northern Ireland as part
of the United Kingdom is, as the hon.
Member will appreciate, a matter which.
does not lie within our jurisdiction.
However, in accordance with the general
scheme of
precautions being taken
throughout the British Isles for the protection of persons and property from
injury or damage in the event of attack
from the air in time of war, this Ministry has been in communication with the
Corporation of the City of Belfast in
connection with the preparation of a
scheme for this purpose, and I understand that arrangements to this end are
now receiving actual consideration.
Mr. NIXON: Will the Ministry or
Government make representations to the
proper authority-the Imperial Government to have provided the
proper
means of defence in case of air attacks?
The PRIME MINISTER: I think I
can answer that question. Steps in that
direction are being taken at the present
moment. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report to
the House that I have this day received
the following reply from the Prime
Minister of the Government of the
United Kingdom to your Resolution of
the 22nd of March, 1938:-
"My dear Speaker,
"It was with great pleasure that I
received the Resolution of the House
of Commons of Northern Ireland
which you were good enough to transmit to me.
"The record of the people of that
part of the United Kingdom in the
annals of the British Commonwealth
of Nations puts beyond doubt the
earnestness of their desire that peace
should be ensued throughout the
world and the fixity of their determination to defend, should the need
arise, our common inheritance at all
costs.
"Yours sincerely,
"N. CHAMBERLAIN."

CLASS VII. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF COMMERCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £15,134 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1939, to
defray the salaries and expenses of the
Ministry of Commerce." (Note-£7,000
has been voted on account).
The CHAIRMAN: I intend, as I did
yesterday, to take the two Votes and
allow discussion on both, and put the
second Vote formally after discussion.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): In presenting the
annual Estimates of my Ministry last
year, I was able to report favourably on
the general trade position of Northern
Ireland. Since that date I may say that,
taking the year as a whole, after a
favourable start a decline set in in the
autumn which has as yet shown no sign
of abatement. The fact that the present
Estimates are being presented for your
consideration earlier than is usual has
deprived me of the guidance of Northern
Ireland's trade statistics for the year
1937, the compilation of which has not
yet been completed. It is probable,
however, that the trend of the trade
statistics of the United Kingdom as a
whole will be reflected in our local returns for that year. The value of
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
31 MARCH 1938
imports into the United Kingdom in
1937 showed an increase of 20 per cent.
over the 1936 figures which, in turn, had
shown an increase of 12 per cent. over
those for 1935. For exports the increase
in 1937 was 18 per cent, as compared
with a 3 per cent. increase in 1936.
As the tonnage of goods passing through
the Port of Belfast in 1937 exceeded,
and the tonnage of vessels cleared at the
Port equalled, the record figures attained
in the previous year, there is some indication that our trade position during
1937 w was at least as good as in 1936.
As the Committee are aware, Northern
Ireland's economic position depends to a
large extent on the state of its two major
industries. Of these, shipbuilding enjoyed a considerably increased degree of
activity during 1937. While a return
to the record output of 1935 has not yet
been achieved, an increase over the previous year of about 20 per cent. in the
total tonnage launched was recorded.
Members of the Committee will, I am
sure, join with me in hoping that our
Belfast yard will continue to share in
the increased activity of the United
Kingdom industry.
Measured by the value of exports over
the whole year, the linen trade, too,
showed an improvement during 1937,
although the rate of expansion was not
maintained throughout as during the
previous year. The high level of exports
over the year as a whole is, in fact, attributable rather to the relatively active
condition of the industry in the early
part of the year than to a steady upward
trend of trade throughout the whole
period. In the latter half of the year,
the fall in the price of cotton, the hostilities in China, where considerable
quantities of our linen are shipped for
embroidering, and, particularly, the
business recession in the United States,
coupled with the anticipation of the
Anglo-American trade negotiations, led
to a serious curtailment of linen purchases. Until these adverse factors are
removed, the progress of the linen trade
will necessarily be impeded.
The unemployment which inevitably
results from the difficulties experienced.
by our major industries is a matter which
my Ministry has steadfastly endeavoured
to alleviate. I would remind the Committee, however, that our powers in this
direction are limited, inasmuch as the
prosperity of our linen and shipbuilding
industries is mainly dependent upon
world conditions over which the Government has no control. Nevertheless it has
been the consistent policy of my Ministry,
within the limit of its powers, to safeguard the interests of our manufacturers
in overseas markets. This task has been
facilitated by the spirit of co-operation
existing between my Ministry and the
Trade Departments in London. I may
go so far as to say that no trade agreement with an overseas country is concluded by the Imperial Government
without an opportunity being given to my
Department, at every stage of the
negotiations, of putting forward the particular desiderata of Northern Ireland.
Naturally, it is the task of the Board of
Trade to co-ordinate the particular requirements of all the varied trading
interests within the United Kingdom as
a whole, but we have every reason to be
satisfied with the consideration which has
been accorded us in the past, and I would
hope that, as the negotiations with the
United States develop, negotiations in
which our linen industry in particular is
vitally concerned, we shall have equal
grounds for satisfaction in the future.
Apart from the special attention which
my Ministry is able to give to trade
negotiations and specific difficulties in
overseas markets, members of the Committee are, I am sure, aware that a
highly-organised commercial intelligence
service is provided by my Ministry to all
Northern Ireland firms interested in
export trade. This service is designed to
ease the path of the exporter or prospective exporter in the conduct of his
Overseas business. Although international trade is still at a comparatively
low ebb, Northern Ireland firms, I am
glad to say, have not relaxed their efforts
to develop new markets and agents,
recommended by the Ministry, were
appointed to represent Northern Ireland
firms during 1937 in countries ranging
from Denmark to Australia.
Assistance is being rendered to
Northern Ireland industry in the home
market by the "Buy Ulster Goods"
campaign carried on by the Ulster Industries Development Association. The
miscellaneous industries of the Province
have derived undoubted advantages from
this campaign which has hitherto been
confined to Northern Ireland, but which
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
will, in the near future, be extended,
mainly through the medium of exhibitions, to the market in Great Britain.
I earnestly trust that, with the assistance of the Ulster Industries Development Association, Northern Ireland
manufacturers will not neglect to utilise
to the utmost the opportunities which
unrestricted entry into the market in
Great Britain offers to them.
Coincident with this effort to widen the
market for Northern Ireland products,
the Government is endeavouring to provide additional employment, and to
spread the risk of future unemployment
by broadening the industrial basis of the
Province. One of the last acts of the
late Parliament was to amplify the
Measure passed a few months earlier for
the attraction of new industries to
Northern Ireland. The facilities made
available by the Acts have already
aroused considerable interest. During
the last four months in particular,
numerous inquiries have reached my
Ministry, and thirty-five of these have
already crystallised in the form of actual
applications for grants and loans. The
consideration of these applications has
occupied a great deal of the time of the
three distinguished gentlemen whose
assistance in an advisory capacity I was
fortunate enough to secure. They commenced their labours towards the close of
last year and, by holding weekly meetings, have so far been able to consider
thirty-three of the thirty-five applications
received.
was
The immediate task of my Ministry, on
the passage of the Act, was to ensure that
the substantial financial facilities provided should be brought to the notice
of all interested persons. In this task
the Ulster Development Council, which,
like the Advisory Commitee,
appointed towards the close of the year,
has already rendered valuable service.
The chairman of the Council, Senator Sir
Roland Nugent, has, unfortuately, for
reasons of health, found it necessary to
take a holiday away from home during
the more trying winter months; but the
two vice-chairmen, Major Herdman, who
may be known better as the chairman of
the Linen Guild, and Sir Basil McFarland, of Derry, assisted in particular by
the members of the Publicity Committee,
have been unsparing in their efforts and
have succeeded in obtaining a considerable
amount of publicity through the Press,
through trade associations and by means
of personal contacts.
During the last few weeks, in particular, the results of their labours have
become more marked and, while it is
never safe to prophesy it can at
least be said that several of the
proposals now under consideration have in
them the germ of success. Under the
direction of the Information Committee
of the Council a mass of information has
been collected in regard to such matters as
wages and the state of employment in
various trades, freight rates, the cost of
power, vacant industrial premises and
sites for new factories, all of which is
proving of value to genuine inquirers.
I have referred to the fact that our
field of employment, and indeed our
prosperity, is largely dependent upon the
fortune of our two great staple industries,
linen and shipbuilding. But we have,
fortunately, a large number of progressive industries of a miscellaneous
nature, and with a number of these discussions are now proceeding as to how far
they may be in a position to take advantage of the facilities made available under
the new industries legislation, which, as
hon. Members will be aware, dealt not
only with the establishment of new industrial undertakings, but also with the
development and expansion of factories
already in our midst. I am glad to say
that keen interest in the possibilities of
expansion is being evinced in various
quarters.
I make no apology for again appealing
for the co-operation not only of the Members of the Committee, but also of all
Ulstermen to assist in the difficult task
we have in hand in carrying into
practical effect at the earliest possible
date our policy of broadening the basis
of our industrial life.
Whilst the Ministry's former Exhibition programme is being maintained, the
most important event of the current year
is undoubtedly the Empire Exhibition at
Glasgow, which is to be opened by His
Majesty the King on the 3rd of May
next. I am glad to be able to inform
the Committee that my Ministry's plans
for the exhibit for which we are responsible are well advanced. We have
been fortunate in securing one of the
finest sites in the Exhibition, which will
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
31 MARCH 1938
most certainly attract millions of visitors,
and I am confident that the exhibit will
be worthy of the occasion. I have had
the advantage of the assistance of a
widely representative advisory committee,
from which various sub-committees have
been formed, which have been collaborating enthusiastically with my Department
in the work of preparation. Our objective is to present an epitome of the industrial activities and tourist attractions of
the Province in such a form as I trust
will leave upon the minds of all who see
it a lasting impression of the technical
equipment of the Province, the superb
craftsmanship of our workers and those
scenic beauties of Northern Ireland which
are attracting year by year a larger
number of visitors to our shores.
CO-
The tourist industry once again provides an exceptionally bright spot in my
review of the year. With the
operation of the transport and shipping
companies, my Ministry has been able to
form an estimate of the value of the
tourist traffic. Last year I informed the
Committee that roughly one and a half
millions sterling accrued to the Province
from this traffic in 1936. I am happy to
say that the results of similar calculations for 1937 show an increase to one
and three-quarter millions.
Turning to fisheries, I am gratified to
be able to record an improvement in the
herring fishery last season, the returns
of quantity and value of the fish landed
being the highest since 1934. The total
quantity landed was 47,000 cwts., valued
at £16,000, as against 27,000 cwts.,
valued at £13,000 in 1936. The supply
at times was in excess of the demand,
with the result that, while the increase in
quantity over the previous year was about
74 per cent., the total value increased by
only 23 per cent., and the average price
fell to 7s per cwt., which is the lowest
recorded for many years. Unlike the
previous season, the bulk of the landings
were made by local boats using the drift
net. Most of the shoals were located in
mid-Channel, with the result that the
ring net proved ineffective under these
conditions and the few Scottish boats
from the Clyde who used this form of net
met with indifferent success.
These results would tend to confirm
the opinion which I expressed to the
Committee in presenting the Estimates
last year, that conditions generally, and,
particularly, the location of the herring
being incalculable in advance, the final
solution of the problem of the relative
merits of the two types of net may prove
to be the equipment of boats for both
types of fishing, leaving the selection of
the type on any particular occasion to
the circumstances of the moment. There
appears, however, to be no doubt that
the type of herring available in the early
part of
the season is unsuitable for
curing and that the capture of these
herring by ring net boats would only
tend to aggravate conditions in a market
that is frequently over-supplied.
Accordingly, the Herring Industry
Board, on the advice of the local Area
Committee, again issued a direction prohibiting the landing in Northern Ireland
ports up to 11th July of any herring
caught by ring nets.
There was a welcome revival in the
curing of herring for export, notwithstanding the difficult marketing conditions in Germany and on the Continent.
Over 5,000 barrels of herring were
cured for export at Ardglass during the
season, as against 1.969 barrels in 1936
and 2,221 barrels in 1935. As usual, a
number of our Portavogie boats took
part in the autumn herring fishing at
Maryport, but I am given to understand
that the season there was a comparative
failure, so far as these boats were concerned.
While the herring fishing for the year
1937 may be regarded as satisfactory
when compared with that of recent years,
I am sorry to say that, from the returns
we have received of the landings of other
sea fish, the substantial improvement in
value recorded in 1936 as compared with
1935 was not maintained. In fact, the
total value of the landings of white fish
has fallen by almost £8,000. The final
figure for 1937, however, will probably
be slightly above 1935, the decrease as
compared with 1936 being largely due to
the fact that no Scottish boats took part
in the whiting fishing from Ardglass.
From the returns at present available, it
would appear that the value of the whiting
landed in 1937 was more than £4,000
less than in 1936. The total for whiting
is, however, still well above that of
1935. The same fluctuation is apparent
in the landings of plaice, the 1937 figure
showing a falling-off of over £2,000, but
still being about £1,000 above the 1935
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour.]
figure. The most gratifying feature of
the white fishing operations has been the
adaptation of the Kilkeel herring luggers
for Danish seine fishing during the winter
months and the consequent creation of
remunerative employment for the crews
during what was, admittedly, a slack
season of the year.
As regards shellfish, the returns are
not yet complete but a further fallingoff in the quantity and value of
escallops landed is clearly indicated, a
fact that suggests that the escallop beds
which were discovered in the survey
undertaken by the Ministry a few years
ago off the County Down coast are now
being thinned out. With that consideration in mind, the Ministry early last
year took the precaution of issuing an
Order prohibiting the sale of escallops of
a smaller size than 4 inches measured
across the greatest width. Arrangements
were also made for a survey of
waters off the Antrim and Derry coasts,
but I am sorry to say that the results
did not disclose the presence of any new
extensive beds of escallops in these
waters.
the
With regard to inland fisheries, I am
informed that 1937 must be regarded as
a poor one from the point of view of
salmon fisheries, particularly as regards
the catches taken in drift nets and fixed
nets along the coast. Reports received
after the close of the salmon fishing
season, however, indicate that the rivers
were well stocked with breeding fish, so
that it may be hoped that the decline in
the catches of salmon is merely
temporary. As regards eel fishing in
Lough Neagh, the improvement recorded
for 1936 was not maintained, but there
has been a slight revival in the pollan
fishing.
I am glad to say that the past year
has seen further steady progress in the
development of the Government's policy
of co-ordinating supplies for the purpose
of securing to the rural districts the
benefits of a supply of electricity for all
purposes on reasonable terms. .The
Electricity Board erected a main transmission line from Armagh to Keady,
proceeding thence via Newtownhamilton
to Newry, thus linking up a number of
towns and villages that had not
previously enjoyed the amenities of a
supply as well as providing an alternative link which will improve
improve the
efficiency of the operation of the main
transmission system in this part of the
Board's area. Altogether the Board has
provided supplies in six additional districts during the year, and the sales of
current have increased from 33 million
units to 393 millions.
There has also been considerable
development in the area served by the
Antrim Electricity Supply Company and
its subsidiary the Antrim Electricity
Distribution Company, Limited, which
has resulted in the linking up of nine
new districts in the County of Antrim
and South Derry. Arrangements have
also been made for the extension of the
system from Coleraine to the village of
Castlerock. The consumption in the districts already served by the Antrim
Company's system has again shown a
substantial increase of over one million
units during the year 1937.
In the two county boroughs of Belfast
and Londonderry, the output of the
generating stations continued to show a
marked
increase apart from the increased demands from the Electricity
Board, which shows that development is
not confined to rural areas. The consumption in Northern Ireland as a whole
has risen during the year from
169,490,000 to 189,603,000, an increase
of 20,103,000, or nearly 12 per cent.
While the rate of increase is less than in
previous years, the growth in consumption may be gauged by comparison of the
total for 1937 with that of 1934 when the
total sales were 873 millions, a figure
which has been more than doubled in the
short space of four years.
Coming now to the statutory functions
of the Ministry, I may perhaps remind
hon. Members that a large volume of
work, essential to the public welfare, is
transacted from day to day. This work
includes, in addition to electricity to
which I have already referred, the administration of services in connection
with canals; harbours, docks and piers;
gas undertakings; mines and quarries;
and weights and measures. It includes
also the registration of limited companies,
business names, insurance companies, and
societies of various kinds. The general
lines of administration are now well
established and I am happy to say that
my Ministry continues to maintain
amicable and mutually helpful relationships with the interests concerned.
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
31 MARCH 1938
Perhaps I should refer particularly
once again to one statutory function of
the Ministry as being of special interest,
administration
namely, the
of the
Industrial Assurance Acts. The business
of industrial assurance is of very considerable dimensions in Northern Ireland
where a total sum of upwards of one
million pounds is collected each year in
premiums, and collected by agents in
person from door to door. The Permanent Secretary to the Ministry is also
the Industrial Assurance Commissioner
for Northern Ireland. The greater part
of the work which falls to the Commissioner is that of dealing with disputes
which arise between the policy-holders
and the companies or societies which have
issued the policies. The grounds of these
disputes are very wide, ranging from
alleged breaches of warranty as to health
and incorrect statements as to ages to
claims for damages for failure to collect
premiums and insurances outside the
permitted limits of relationship. Many
of these disputes are disposed of by advice
given verbally or in correspondence, but
a considerable number remain to be dealt
with at formal sittings held by the Commissioner or his representative. The
claimants may conduct their own cases
or may be represented by solicitors or by
counsel. The chief merits of this quasijudicial procedure are that it is informal
and that the charges for hearing are very
moderate, ranging from 2s 6d upwards,
according to the amount of the claim.
The great majority of the cases which
have come to hearing in recent years
have been dealt with on behalf of the
Commissioner by a practising barrister.
It may interest the Committee to learn
that, during the year 1937, 698 cases
were referred to the Commissioner, and
that the number of cases which fell to be
heard by the Commissioner or his representative in person during the year was
190. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That a sum not
exceeding £15,134 be granted to His
Majesty for the said Service.'
The CHAIRMAN proceeded to collect
the voices.
Mr. NIXON: You are going to put
this Vote through quickly. I would not
mind for myself, but the hon. Member
for South Down (Mr. Brown) is going
to say something about electricity in the
Newry district. Perhaps it would not be
out of order if I wish the Minister success
in his election to-day. I have little doubt
but that he will be at the top of the
poll, and if there are any celebrations—
and I know there will be-there are only
a few Members on this side of the Committee. The Minister always makes a
the
nice encouraging speech, and on
surface he is the fairest and most candid
man in the world. He is not always so
fair. For instance, on more than one
occasion there was a question addressed
to the Minister as to the number of
factories or industrial concerns in Northern Ireland that were closed, and on
both occasions, I think I am right in
saying, he declined to answer on
ground of the labour that would be incurred in collecting the information.
There would not be much labour involved
in collecting the information, and I do
not think there would be much trouble

Government Departments are overlapping

lation and fostering of the trade and

three staple

There was another very serious matter
-I might almost call it a disaster-that

Nobody could have anticipated any of

What we have to do now is to take a

Then I may touch on the fact that a

with the rest of the United Kingdom, to
send in tenders for any of the constructive work necessary for rearmament and
other things. Ulster was not cold

in rearmament came over to Belfast and
went about amongst business men and
firms, especially engineering firms, to find
out if they could undertake munition
work. A difficulty arose at once from
the fact that it was called a five-year
plan. It was feared by many of the
industrial people here that the five-year
plan meant that during those five years
they would have to concentrate on making
munitions of one sort or another, and that
their own trade might be picked up by
their competitors, and that when the five
years were up they might have to turn
the key in their own doors, having lost
touch with those who had previously
kept them in work.
It was a difficult problem. I honestly
do not know what other reasons there
might have been, but so far I have not
seen any outward or visible sign of the
engineering firms being able to adapt
themselves to the production of munitions. The blame cannot be placed on
my right hon. Friend. How could it?
We made representations; we did our
best. The people in England know our

But that popularity having
been attained the desire to supply it was
very strong in other countries who

All of us sympathise with labour and
the desire that labour should receive
adequate reward, whether it is for hard
work or the dexterity and degree of skill
which they bring to bear upon their daily
vocations. We must remember that in
the sale of our products we have to compete with the markets of the world.
The hon. Member for Woodvale (Mr.
Nixon) thought that we were barely
doing justice to our people by utilising
the cheaper wages which were available
in China to give that finishing touch
that is necessary to our materials in
order to make them saleable in the
markets. If we were to interfere with
that trade, I think hon. Members will
admit if they think it over, we would
be only paving the way for other linenproducing countries to secure a greater
share of the trade in those markets in
which we compete. However regrettable
it may be to see the embroidery of Irish

Irish linen in the markets of the world
I think it is the duty of our manufacturers to take advantage of that way
of doing business. I think they must

altogether.

So far as the home market is concerned, representations were made,
through my Ministry as a matter of fact,
to the Import Duties Committee in
London, and we were able to secure
tariff on embroidered linen coming into
the United Kingdom, so that we have
that market available to a greater extent
than heretofore. The Northern Ireland
share of the British market has benefited
very considerably by the Import Duties
which have been imposed.

Unfortunately, as is so very often
the case, what appears to be
attractive proposition at first sight
found to bristle with difficulties when
we try to study how we can put into
operation the ideas which we may have

that means the fishermen around our
coast. That is a matter which has
always enlisted the sympathy of the Government of Northern Ireland, and, as a
matter of fact, loans are available.
Many of the fishermen have already
taken advantage of those loans. Fishing
is a very hazardous business not only
in a pecuniary sense but in the risk to
human life, and in that way it commands our sympathy to a greater extent
than it otherwise might. These loans
are given on quite reasonable terms.
While I am mentioning this-and this
bears also on the very much larger subject of new industries-I may say that
I have listened with varying feelings to
a great deal that has been said this afternoon as to the degree of assistance that
might be given, whether to the fishermen or to those interested in prospective
industries who have come to us and who
wish to take advantage of the very substantial attractions which are offered
under the New Industries Act. We, on
the other hand, are faced with the grave
duty of protecting the interests of the
taxpayer. Our desire is to promote new
industries and to interpret in a very
liberal way indeed the conditions which
have to be imposed in order that there
may not be reckless use of the taxpayers'
money. While that is our duty, we are
very anxious indeed to attract these new
industries, and I may say that the gentlemen who very kindly undertook the
investigation of those propositions have
interpreted the conditions in a very
sympathetic and liberal way.

Therefore, if the administration of this
Act is confided to my care, I should
not be a bit surprised if I have to come
here some day and say, "Well, here is

Unless we risk a certain amount of
