We have
got to take a chance. I hope the most
of them will be good ones. As I have
said before, it would not be my policy
at all to be reckless with other people's
money.
I would rather take a chance
with my own, and certainly I would be
far more careful with the taxpayers'
money than I would with my own. With
the chance of getting people into employment, if we succeed, by taking a number
of people off unemployment insurance, I
think on balance we would be apt to
make very much more than we would lose
in an odd bad debt that might be made.
The fishermen in County Down are
anxious to get loans in order to help
them in procuring equipment, and if
they will come to my Ministry I am sure
they will get all the assistance to which
the law entitles them. But the mere
fact that the Government has made a
loan or an advance of a million pounds
in one direction is not sufficient to justify
the Government in giving money to any
other fellow who may not have the same
need, and merely desires to see in the
meantime what he can get.
Another matter that I am sure must
have enlisted the interest of the Committee is this: In modern life, where,
undoubtedly, there is always a certain
amount of privation and shortage of food
stuffs, why should it ever be possible that
an attractive commodity like herrings
should be thrown into the sea after being
caught? That, unfortunately, is the
case, but if the fishermen were to follow
the advice which is given them by a
Board which was recently set up in order
to control the fishing industry around
our coasts an unnecessary catch of
herrings would be avoided. Advice is
given to the fishermen when the markets
are glutted, and in some cases the Board
would actually prohibit the landing of
herrings where big landing had already
been made and where the market was
glutted. Unfortunately more than is
necessary is really an embarassment
rather than a benefit. All our big
institutions and hospitals to which we
would so gladly see supplies of cheap
food stuffs like herrings being made
available cannot depend on the chance
supply of fish of this kind. They have
their running contracts made with regular sources of supply, so that they can
count on keeping their inmates promptly
supplied. To receive more than that on
any one particular day would upset their
arrangements.
In addition to that, while we have the
herrings being thrown back into the sea
as being absolutely worthless, if the
herrings were to be disposed of as
suggested, the fisherman, seeing that his
catch was going to be turned to some
useful purpose, would say, "That is a
different matter; I am entitled to be paid
for them." The fisherman is not going
to give them away for nothing; undoubtedly he would have to be paid.
Prior information as to the landing of
these catches cannot be obtained
sufficient time to enable arrangements to
be made for the necessary transport and
retail distribution of the herrings. If
they could be dealt with in bulk in some
way by the use of a freezer or something
in

Prime Minister has already dealt with

As to the employees of the Electricity
Board, I certainly should be sorry if that
body behaved in a different way from
ordinary employers. If there is any
matter in which that is done, perhaps the
hon. Member would draw my attention to
it, and I will be glad to look into it. In
connection with the Electricity Board,
there again one is rather torn in two
ways, because I have to bear in mind that
the supply of electricity at the lowest
possible price is an immense boon to all
of our people, and to the poor more than
to the wealthier classes. Therefore it is
essential that such a necessity should be
given to them at the lowest possible price,
and I am sure the hon. Member for
Pottinger will realise that expenses must
be cut down, so long as that is not done
by treating the employees in an inconsiderate way.

The hon. and learned Member for St.
Anne's takes an interest in harbours. I
hope he showed that interest this morning. I said in the course of my remarks
that the total tonnage cleared was a

many years. I do not belittle the collapse
that has taken place in trade during the

I expect I will have to call myself a
politician-to assume too much responsibility for good or bad trade. What my
Ministry wish to do is to help those who
are in trade to carry on their business to
the best possible advantage. I am glad to
say that, while I have reason to congratulate myself upon the vocal tributes made
to my Ministry, there are many silent

Belfast and to the very valuable assistance

ability of the officials in my Ministry that

The Prime Minister has already dealt
with propaganda. The hon. and learned
Member for Iveagh (Mr. Maginess) criticised the failure of the new Act to
encourage new industries. He also
belongs to the legal profession. May I
remind him that the task to which this
Committee has set itself is not an easy
one. The Prime Minister mentioned
some of the difficulties facing industrialists anxious to branch out and
settle in the North of Ireland instead of
England or Scotland. I do not wish to
make those difficulties any more obvious
than they are. It is hard to get people
to start branch establishments in Northern Ireland however good the local
market may be. I speak from experience.
The overhead charges of the main
establishment still go on in spite of opening a branch of the industry in another
place and so manufacturers would rather
extend their existing plant than open a
separate establishment. That is one difficulty which always obtains.
May I
remind the Committee that when we talk
of expanding existing industries
attracting new ones we are doing so at
the very depth of the depression which
has overtaken us. People are mostly
anxious about securing enough business
to keep their existing establishments
going.
or
May I remind the hon. and learned
Member for Iveagh that when he talks
about the supply of flax he almost makes
the flax spinners' teeth water. It is not
a question of flax, but a question of
orders. I hope no consumer of linen will
get the idea that it is not worth while
trying to buy linen because he will not
get his orders through on account of the
scarcity of flax. I would rather stress
the fact that the present is a very good
time. I am not a bit afraid of any
orders that may come along.
As to whether we can do more in
regard to the cultivation of flax is a
matter which has my entire sympathy.
I should be glad to see more grown here,
but the climate is not good for it and the
foreign flax grower has the advantage
of being able to save his seed. That is
not done in Northern Ireland. However discouraging the problem may be,
it will continue to be very carefully
studied. The trade and the Linen Research Association at Lambeg have done
a great deal, but it is not an easy
problem to solve. I hope it will always
receive very careful study and that in
the end we may be able to accomplish
something.

Oral Answers to Questions.
PRINTING OF GOVERNMENT
PUBLICATIONS.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he can state if
quotations were asked for the printing.
of the various Government publications
issued last year, and, if so, to whom were
the tenders sent and when; whether
quotations were obtained for the recent
publication H.C. 394 and Cmd. 187;
what was the number of copies ordered
and the cost.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews) I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to reply. The Government practice is not to invite printing
contracts for individual publications, but
to ask for tenders extending over a period
of usually seven years. This practice is
the same as that followed by the
Stationery Office in Great Britain. All
printers of standing in Northern Ireland
are invited to tender, and the two publications mentioned by the hon. Member
are covered by the contract. The number of copies ordered was 250 and 500
respectively, the cost being approximately £90 and £113 respectively.

number of dismissal notices sent out to
teachers in public elementary schools
owing to declining averages for each of

the school population for the same
period.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

staffed on the basis of the year ending

relates to the year ended 31st March,
1937. In the case of other schools, the
information is available up to 31st
December, 1937.

Member's question must, therefore, be
divided into two parts. As the answer
is in the form of a somewhat lengthy
tabular statement, I shall, with the
hon. Member's permission, send a copy
to him and cause it to be circulated in
"Hansard."

FIRST QUINQUENNIAL
REVALUATION.
4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Finance whether the Government
will introduce a Bill to postpone for two
years the first quinquennial general revaluation throughout Northern Ireland
of rateable hereditaments in order to
afford time for investigation into allegations of hardship caused by the recent
general revaluation, and whether he is
aware that legislation has been laid
before the Imperial Parliament on the
recommendation of the English Central
Valuation Committee to postpone with
a like object for two years the operation
of new valuation lists which would otherwise take place in England on April 1st,
1939.
Mr. ANDREWS: The question
whether sufficient time has elapsed since
the General Revaluation of 1936 to make
it desirable to proceed with the Second
Revaluation, due to take effect on 1st
March, 1941, has been under the consideration of the Government for some
time past, and it is considered that on
the whole the balance of argument is in
favour of adhering to the statutory date.
The conditions which have led to the
proposed postponement in England and
Wales do not exist in Northern Ireland.
I have no doubt that any anomalies
which require adjustment will be corrected in the Second General Revaluation
if not at the annual revision.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Would the right
hon. Gentleman specify what are the
conditions which warrant a departure in
this case from the English practice, and
the abandonment of the step-by-step
policy?
Mr. ANDREWS: Of couse the stepby-step policy was never intended, so
far as I know, to go beyond the social
services administered by the Ministry of
Labour. As regards the direct question
which is asked, the conditions which
have caused the postponement in England and Wales do not exist in Northern
Ireland.
Mr. CAMPBELL: The question I put
was would he specify what those conditions are.
Mr. ANDREWS: I understand there
is a misunderstanding between the local
authorities and the Government in Great
Britain. I am glad to say those misunderstandings do not exist here.
Captain DIXON: Is the hon. Member
aware of the fact that the smaller houses
want revaluation at the earliest possible
moment?

Exceptional Distress (Transitional
Provisions) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This short
Bill really affects the Belfast Corporation only. Some five years ago the Corporation borrowed a sum of £156,000 for
the purpose of affording outdoor relief
to able-bodied persons. By the Exceptional Distress (Transitional Provisions)
Act (Northern Ireland), 1934, a period
of five years was allowed to local
authorities for repayment of money
borrowed under such circumstances.
That period in the case of Belfast expires on the 31st March, 1939. The
649 Exceptional Distress Bill-

5 APRIL 1938
Second Reading
balance remaining to be paid off before
that date is some £29,000, and in view
of the other heavy commitments of the
Corporation it is felt that in order to prevent the rates for the coming year being
unduly high the Corporation should be
allowed an extension of the time within
which this balance may be paid off.
Accordingly, in the Bill it is proposed to
allow a further period of five years for
repayment of the sum in question, so
that the whole amount will be paid off
within a period of ten years from the
date on which it was originally borrowed.
I beg to move.

Hydrogen Cyanide Bill-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
Hydrogen Cyanide (Fumigation)

Bill [S.].
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Bill is
intended to safeguard human life by
regulating the use of hydrogen cyanide
for fumigation purposes in enclosed
places. This substance is probably the
most efficient agent known for the destruction of vermin, and is largely used for
clearing agricultural land of rabbits and
ships of rats and cockroaches. On
account of its efficiency it is becoming
more frequently used for fumigating
vermin-infested houses. Its deadly
qualities and the fact that its presence in
small but fatal quantities is not perceptible, render it most necessary to
ensure that every precaution is taken in
its use.
Many of the leading countries, including Great Britain, have already passed
legislation controlling the use of this gas,
and the Government wish to afford
similar protection to the people of
Northern Ireland. While there have
been fatal accidents in other countries
due to the use of this gas for fumigation
purposes, up to the present no such
accidents have occurred in Northern
Ireland. The fact that such accidents
have occurred elsewhere, even when the
fumigation was carried out by experts, is
sufficient evidence of the necessity for
taking adequate steps to control the use
of this gas.
Clause 1 of the Bill confers upon
the Minister of Home Affairs a general
power to make regulations governing the
conduct of the fumigation of premises or
articles with hydrogen cyanide. The
fumigation of rabbit warrens and
fumigation carried out in the open air
is specially exempted. The reason for
this is that the gas is so volatile and unstable that its use in the open air is
practically free from danger. It is also
proposed to exempt, in the regulations to
be made, fumigation for purely agricultural or horticultural purposes of
agricultural or horticultural buildings
not used for human habitation.
Clause 2 requires notice of any accident
due to fumigation by hydrogen cyanide
to be reported to the Minister. Clause 3
applies the provisions of the Petroleum
(Consolidation) Act, (Northern Ireland),
1929, relating to inquiries into accidents
and coroners' inquests in cases of
accidents which may occur in carrying
out fumigation by hydrogen cyanide.
Clause 4 enables the provisions of the
Bill to be extended by Order in Council
to other dangerous fumigants which may
come into use. It is proposed that any
such Order in Council shall be laid in
draft-I would draw the attention of
hon. Members to this before both
Houses of Parliament, in order that any
extension of the Act may come under
review of Parliament before becoming
operative. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

hon. Gentleman may not believe it, but

journey through Committee.

for the Second Reading of this Bill.
Like other hon. Members, I hope that
when the Measure comes before the Joint
Opposed Committee the differences between the parties concerned will be
agreeably settled. I also hope that the
matters in dispute will be settled in a
very short space of time because I feel
that it is vital to the interests of the
City of Belfast that this Bill should
be passed, containing, as it does, promise
of increased employment for our workers
in the shipyard. I think that every consideration should be given to this Bill
in Committee, and that it should be
accorded a speedy passage in this House
and in another place.
Question: "That the Bill be now read
a Second time," put, and agreed to.
Ordered: That the Clerk do carry the
Bill to the Senate.
Adjournment.
Resolved: "That this House do now
adjourn." (Captain Dixon).
Adjourned accordingly at five
minutes before Four o'clock
until Tuesday, 26th April,
pursuant to the Resolution of
the House of this day.

In answer to the question, His
Majesty's Government, with a view to
promoting harmonious relations and
facilitating trade between the United
Kingdom and Eire, have entered into
an Agreement, the terms of which are
embodied in a White Paper which is
being presented at Westminster. The
Agreement deals with matters which are
not within the competence of the Government of Northern Ireland, and it will
be understood that we are therefore not
a party to it.
The negotiations, however, which led
up to the Agreement, afforded the
United Kingdom Government and our
Government opportunities of conferring
Oral Answers

upon certain questions which had been
causing us much concern in recent years.
That Government, recognising the
special difficulties of Northern Ireland
in respect of trade with Eire resulting
from the latter's tariff policy, has agreed
to make certain adjustments in its financial relations with Northern Ireland-

The PRIME
MINISTER--which
will, in other directions, provide benefits
for the Province. The Agreement provides for immediate modifications of duty
on certain goods of special interest to

that, when decisions are being taken as

I trust, too, that Northern Ireland
may reap advantages which are
bounded by the four walls of the Agreement itself. Nevertheless, should advantages fail to accrue from the Trade
Agreement with Eire, the United Kingdom Government will be prepared to
consider sympathetically any request

Ireland for dealing with the matter
under the provision of the Agreement as

the parties to the Agreement.
our
I now turn to the financial matters
which have arisen out of discussions
which have taken place between
Government and the Government of the
United Kingdom. They fall under four
heads :
Firstly, Agricultural Subsidies;
Secondly, Expenditure on Unemployment Insurance and Assistance;
Thirdly, The General Financial
Relations between the two Exchequers;
Fourthly, Northern Ireland's share of
rearmament work.
On the first point-Agricultural Subsidies Northern Ireland farmers have
in the past shared in various agricultural subsidies, such as the beef and milk
subsidies, the land fertility scheme embracing lime and basic slag, and so on.
But no general agreement has hitherto
been reached as to whether, in principle,
such agricultural subsidies should be
borne on United Kingdom Votes or on
our Votes. I am glad, therefore, to be
able to state that an amicable agreement
has been arrived at which ensures that
where agricultural subsidies are granted
in Great Britain and circumstances are
such as to justify corresponding subsidies
in Northern Ireland, no objection will
be raised to the cost being borne on
United Kingdom Votes.
Turning now to the Unemployment
Re-Insurance Agreement, it will be
recalled that the United Kingdom
Government recoup to us 75 per cent.
of the expenditure incurred by our Exchequer in maintaining our Unemployment Insurance and Unemployment
Assistance Fund in parity with the
Funds in Great Britain. It was an
understanding, however, confirmed in a
letter to the then Chancellor of the Exchequer that if the United Kingdom
contribution in any year exceeded one
million pounds, the United Kingdom
Government would be entitled to reopen
on its merits the question of the amount
of the contribution. In the year just
closed, owing in the main to the considerable balance on the right side in
the British Insurance Fund, their contribution to us in the way of parity payment reached the sum of nearly
£1,700,000 and the understanding to
which I have referred caused apprehension to our Minister of Finance. The
full payment was generously conceded
and the United Kingdom Government
have now definitely agreed that so long
as the Trade Agreement with Eire is
in force the United Kingdom Government will not exercise their right to reopen the question of the amount of the
contribution of the United Kingdom Exchequer under the Northern Ireland
Unemployment Insurance Agreement of
the 29th April, 1935, if such a contribution exceeds one million pounds.
I come now to our general Exchequer
relations. A difficult situation would
arise if at some future time our revenue
were to prove insufficient to maintain our
social services at the United Kingdom
level. Such a situation might eventuate
as a result of reductions of taxation in
the United Kingdom or the expansion of
social services. The United Kingdom
Government has recognised this possible.

difficulty and has agreed that it would

to make good this deficit in such a way

(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The fourth matter to which I have to
refer is the question of Northern Ireland's
share in the British rearmament programme. We have, to some extent,
benefited from such work in recent years,
mainly in the construction of warships.
Since April 1st, 1936, orders have been
placed by the Admiralty for work exceeding £3,600,000 in value. In the same
period orders to the value of £2,067,000
have been received from the Air Ministry
as well as considerable orders from the
War Office. We have not ceased to press
on the United Kingdom Government our
view that even these substantial orders
do not represent an adequate share of
armament work, regard especially being
serious unemployment
had to our
problem. I am glad to say that the
United Kingdom Government recognises
our position, and further rearmament
orders, subject to satisfactory tenders.
being received, are in prospect, and I
have reason to hope that, as a result of
our representations, substantial orders
will be placed in Northern Ireland by the
various Defence Departments.
We have further pressed for the establishment of a Government factory in
Northern Ireland and, in so doing, we
have not overlooked the claims of
Londonderry.
I desire to avail myself of this, the
earliest opportunity, to express my
gratitude to the Government of the
United Kingdom for their appreciation
of the difficulties with which we were confronted and the readiness they evinced to
meet our wishes in reaching a solution.
I am happy in paying this tribute to
their understanding and sympathy.
Taking the long view, Ulster will greatly
benefit, and her prospects in regard to
rearmament work be very materially
brightened. Thanks are also due to our
Ministers of Finance, Commerce and
Agriculture for the successful outcome of
the prolonged negotiations.
Apart from the matters to which I
have referred, I have further satisfactory
information to impart to the House.
Under the Coal-Cattle Pact which has been
in operation between the United Kingdom
and the Irish Free State during the past
year or so, there has been a detailed
schedule of the f.o.b. prices of United
Kingdom coal to be charged to Free State
buyers. These prices were agreed
between the United Kingdom coal owners
and the Free State importers, and one of
the conditions of application of the
original schedule was that Free State
buyers of United Kingdom coal should
receive not less favourable treatment than
that accorded to buyers in Northern
Ireland. No such assurance was enjoyed
by Northern Ireland buyers, and difficulty was experienced in the past in securing for Northern Ireland the acceptance
of the principle that the price charged in
respect of shipments of coal to Northern
Ireland should not exceed the price of
comparable coal shipped to the Irish Free
State. Owing to the persistent efforts
of our Minister of Commerce this difficulty has now been removed, and I am
glad to say that an arrangement has been
reached whereunder the schedule prices
will apply uniformly to Ireland irrespective of whether the destination of the coal
is Northern Ireland or Eire. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)

Sir DAWSON BATES: It will be
within the recollection of many Members
of this House that when this present
Government was formed
we had no
premises in Northern Ireland in which
to house criminal lunatics. Our criminal
lunatics had to be sent to a criminal
lunatic asylum in Dublin.
That was
found to be very undesirable and,
accordingly, in the Act of 1929 the
Government took power to convert part
of Derry Prison into a criminal lunatic
asylum. In that Act it was necessary to
designate the exact portion of the prison
that was to be used in future for the
purpose, but, unfortunately, we did not
take sufficient area to meet the requirements of modern conditions in the treatment of criminal lunatics.
I am glad to say that there has been
no increase in the number of criminal
lunatics; but, at the same time, the
premises which were set apart in 1929,
the ground floor tier of the main block
of the Londonderry Prison and the three
exercise yards adjacent thereto, were, in
my opinion, not sufficiently large to provide the necessary amenities for the poor
creatures who are incarcerated there and
will be incarcerated there for the rest of
their lives. We find that especially in the
winter the lunatics cannot get out into
the open air, and I think everybody in
this House will agree that we should do
all we can to try to improve their conditions. It may be that we will still
further have to enlarge the area used for
this purpose, and in order to prevent us
having to come back to the House for
power to increase the area it is proposed
that authority should be given to His
Grace the Governor to make a Ministerial
Order if at any future time it becomes
necessary still further to increase the
I beg to move.
area.

I am pleased to know that the Minister
is going to spend a sum of money in the

of prisoner, so as to bring a proper course
of treatment within their reach. That
is, treatment of an open-air kind. I
would be the last person to retard in any
way the extension of accommodation for
this type of prisoner.
I am glad to know that there has been
no noted increase in this class of prisoner
in Northern Ireland in the past year or
two; but whether we have one prisoner

or a hundred prisoners, we are in duty

Physical Training and Recreation Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): The Bill
which I am introducing to-day is one
which. I think ought to make an appeal
to all sides of the House. We have
heard a great deal in the past few months
about the physical fitness campaign, and
the keenness with which it is being
pressed in Great Britain. We have all
thought a great deal about it, and I hope
we will think a great deal more. The
importance of this movement for physical
fitness cannot possibly be over-stressed,
and it is just as vitally necessary to the
people of Northern Ireland as it is to the
people of England, Scotland and Wales.
Before I look into the future I will, if
I may, glance briefly into the past. It
seems hardly necessary to say that the
cultivation of physical fitness reached its
very highest pitch in the Greek civilisation. To the ancient Greeks the body of
man had a glory just as much as the
intellect and the spirit of man. They
believed in the discipline of the body as
well as in the discipline of the mind.
That idea has run down, if I mav put it
that way, through the different eras of
our civilisation, but it has been a verv
shadowy and very attenuated one at anv
rate in certain periods. At one time it
became a purely military glorification of
brute force; at another time it became the
almost exclusive possession of the richer
and more leisured classes. To-day this
modern awakening which has taken place
first reached-I think I am right in saying
the Scandanavian States and
Czechoslovakia. Then it went to the
totalitarian States-Germany, Italy, and
Russia.
We
I want to make it perfectly clear to-day
that the way we in this country view this
question of the universal necessity of
health and strength, and the best way to
obtain it, is quite different from that of
most other countries in the world.
here look upon it somewhat differently
from these other States. I want to
emphasise this point particularly, that
with us there is in it absolutely no
question of a military or a political spirit.
With us participation in the benefits
which we hope will come to our country
will be entirely voluntary after school
age. We, in Great Britain and Northern
Ireland, are not going to try to compel
the people to take physical exercises. We
are going to encourage them by every
means in our power to do so. We are
going to put opportunities in their way.
We are going to give them opportunties
to attain physical fitness in the very best
and most health-giving manner.
way in which we propose to do so is by
exercises specially devised for the purpose
and by organised sports and games.
The
We believe that this is the best way
in which to preserve the population in
health and strength, and we believe, as
has often been said in the past, that
bodily and mental relaxation must stimulate each other. I believe it was
Rousseau who said:
The great secret of education is to
secure that bodily and mental exercises
shall always serve to relax one another.
I might give quotations from very many
sources. I might give quotations from
the great thinkers throughout all the ages
from Plato to the present day. I might
quote from the leaders of scholastic and
medical thought. But I am not going to
weary the House in that manner. I am
merely going to give one more quotation,
and that is one which I think has a bearing upon this question, and which is expressed in very eloquent language. Mr.
Kenneth Lindsay, the Parliamentary
Physical Training Bill-

Second Reading
Secretary of the Board of Education in
England, speaking at the 26th annual
conference of the Educational Associations on the subject of "National Fitness
and the Child" used these words-he was
saying that the British people might well
realise the idea of physical fitness in 25
years-
It was no mean vision to see a great
democracy raising its stature during a
generation. Some of them believed it
to be possible and, in truth, it would
mean a rebirth of the British people.
Before I begin to explain the Bill in
detail, I would remind the House of
the words spoken by His Gracious
Majesty the King at the London Mansion House, on February 17 last, when
he warmly and earnestly stressed his
great interest in the movement for the
encouragement of physical fitness. His
Majesty said:
It is a cause of the first importance,
for while we are striving to bring the
fruits of education within the reach of
all, to improve the conditions in which
everyone may grow and live, and to
keep before our eyes the spiritual basis
and aims of human life, we must
always remember that our bodies are
the instruments with which we have
to work. They, too, need education
if we are to play our part in the life
of our family and of our country.
We have here a duty to ourselves and
to our generation which will bring
swift returns in human happiness-for
nothing adds more to the pleasure of
life and to the joy of work and play
than physical fitness.
The Physical Training and Recreation
Act passed by the Imperial Parliament
in July, 1937, was for the purpose of
enabling and assisting local authorities
in Great Britain to provide for the development and encouragement of physical training and recreation and to
establish centres for social activities
throughout the country. Following the
passing of that Act a Committee, representative of the Ministries of Education,
Labour, Home Affairs and Finance, sat
here and studied the application of a
similar Measure to Northern Ireland.
The Bill which I am introducing to-day
is the fruit of their labours. The outlines of the Measure follow the English
Act, but the conditions here are different,
and it has been found necessary to make
certain modifications in order to make
the Measure more suitable to the conditions prevailing here. The English
legislation was framed mainly with the
idea of developing and encouraging
physical training for adolescents and
adults. It had not quite so much to do
with the question of schools.
In Northern Ireland we are in a
rather different position, because so far
as schools are concerned the matter was
not so fully developed as in Great
Britain. There were not the same
facilities or the same equipment here.
For instance, we discovered that threefourths of the secondary and technical
schools were without proper gymnasiums
and more than one-fifth without playing
fields. There were very few facilities for
swimming except in the case of schools
recently built. Our public elementary
schools seldom have adequate playing
fields or physical training equipment,
and it seemed to us that you could
hardly expect adults to go in for physical training in the way in which we hope
when it had not been a feature of their
school life. We, therefore, thought it
desirable to take advantage of this
opportunity to encourage the provision
of facilities for physical training, particularly in connection with secondary
and technical schools.
There is a condition attached, that is,
that these facilities, when provided,
shall be shared, so far as is reasonably
possible, with persons who are not in
attendance at those schools.
The money
at the Government's disposal for this
purpose is naturally limited, and, therefore, although we have very great
interest in schools we feel that the claims
of the schools must not overshadow the
claims of the unemployed adults and
juveniles, who we hope will also benefit
by the increased facilities.
The primary object of the Bill is to
arouse interest throughout the country.
There must be a general growth of interest in physical training for adults,
and the Measure will assist local statutorv authorities to provide suitable
facilities wherever needed.
Clause 1 sets up an Advisory Council
much on the same lines as the British
Act and corresponding to the National
Advisory Council in England and Wales

Minister. They will be persons interested in education, in the work of

medical work and

The Council will advise the Ministry
and the Grants Committee, to which I
will refer in a moment, in regard to

to take a lead in giving publicity to the
objects of the movement. I need hardly

this Advisory Council are extremely
important. In England and Wales, in

It was
considered sufficient to appoint an

Clause 2 of the Bill establishes the
Grants Committee. It also has
counterpart in the English scheme. The
Committee will consist of a representative each from the Ministries
Education, Home Affairs, Finance and
Labour, and will have an independent
chairman, who will not be an official or
a civil servant, but who will be appointed
by the Prime Minister. I should like
to emphasise that the grants, when
decided upon, will be distributed by the
Ministry of Education. They will, however, be entirely conditional on the
recommendation received from the
Grants Committee. Except in the case
of schools, with which I will deal in a
minute, all applications for financial aid
will come through the Grants Committee. In the case of secondary and
technical schools, proposals will first be
sent to the Ministry of Education, who
will forward them, with their recommendations, to the Grants Committee.
The Grants Committee will, where they
think it necessary, refer applications to
the Advisory Council for further information and recommendation. It will be
realised that it is essential for the Grants
Committee to have all recommendations
and applications, even those connected
with schools which have been looked into
by the Ministry of Education, placed
before them.
The amount recommended in the Bill
is a limited one, and it is absolutely
essential that the Grants Committee
should be able to consider every application on its merit and distribute the
finances in accordance with the merits.
What we require and the object
we have in view are facilities for adult
training and recreation. That means the
provision of gymnasiums, playing fields,
swimming baths and bathing places,
which, I again repeat, would be freely
open to all members of the adult population who cared to make use of them.
. We consider that it would also be desirable to encourage the setting up of
holiday camps, youth hostels and so on,
these being agencies where we could
encourage young people to go in for
recreation.
Under existing
existing legislation local
authorities have certain powers for the
provision of playing fields and swimming
baths. These powers-and this is one of
the main objects of the Bill-would have
to be enlarged in order to provide the
authorities with a very much wider
scope for their activities. The Bill will
enable the Ministry of Education to give
a 50 per cent. grant, subject to the
recommendations of the Grants Committee, to help the schemes.
The education authorities, under the
Education Acts of 1923 and 1930, have
power to provide for physical training
so long as the training is given in connection with schools or classes. In many
of the technical schools they have classes
and instructors, and these instructors, it
is thought, can be allowed to extend
their activities and organisation to encourage training for persons not attending schools. So in this Bill we are
extending the powers of these different
authorities. But I think that, in
practice, the education authorities, that
is to say, the county councils acting
through the borough or regional committees will mostly be found to be most
suitable.
Physical Training Bill-

Then, in addition to the encouragement of these statutory bodies to extend
their powers, we also intend to help the
voluntary organisations when approved.
Some of these voluntary organisations
may be described as local ones and others
as central ones. Some of them are connected with churches, and many of them
have done magnificent work already in
this direction. The purpose of the Bill
is to assist, as I said, these organisations
in certain approved cases, so that they
can extend their activities and reach a
larger portion of the population. They
will be given aid towards capital expenditure on buildings and equipment, and the
central voluntary organisations might be
given aid towards their work as a whole
or towards any specified branch of their
work, provided always-this is a very
important condition of any grant which
may be given to these organisationsprovided always that they must not be
run for private profit.
Then with regard to the schools, as I
said, a 50 per cent. grant will be available
to the managers or governing bodies of
these schools to which I have referrednot public elementary schools. That I
ought to emphasise and explain will be
over and above any aid already available under the Education Act for provision and maintenance. This is a
separate grant. We will take, for
instance, a gymnasium or swimming-pond
in a technical school, which may be built
by a regional committee. The funds expended would not be taken into account
in the ordinary education finance
arrangements with the technical school.
A 50 per cent. grant over and above
these will be available. Then, of course,
it is recognised that it will be absolutely
necessary for all the authorities such as
the county boroughs and regional education committees and so forth to have
organisers and leaders if this movement
is to be taken up as it should be taken
up, an organiser of physical education, a
sort of general promoter and encourager
of the scheme within the district, and the
Ministry is allowed to pay, under this
Bill, half the salary of the officer
appointed in this respect by the local
authority, but no grant can be greater
than a 50 per cent. grant. The balance
will have to come out of local funds or
out of the rates.
Clause 4 deals very largely with the extension of powers of the local authorities.
It includes, of course, the education
authorities, and it is in order to enable
them to acquire suitable lands and buildings for physical training purposes, and
also to enable them to equip such buildings and either manage them themselves
or let them to a club, society, or organisation for carrying on such activities, and
also to provide wardens and teachers and
leaders to secure that proper use is made
of the facilities. These powers will be
given to all our local authorities, and it
is expected that the work will largely
devolve upon the regional or borough
education committee. But, of course, a
great deal will depend in this connection
upon local opinion. After all, it is that
local opinion we hope to arouse by this
Bill.
Then it is recognised that a very substantial number of instructors will be
required, and it is also recognised that
the question of the qualifications of these
instructors is a most important matter.
At the present moment in Northern
Ireland I fancy that the number of people
who would be sufficiently qualified in this
direction is somewhat limited, so that
Clause 6 enables the Ministry to make
grants to assist in training suitable
persons in one of the special colleges
being established in Great Britain, and
two-thirds of the cost of such training
would be paid to suitable applicants, and
under the Bill the choice of applicants
lies with the Grants Committee.
I will just very briefly deal with the
question of finance. In Great Britain
the Imperial Government have announced
their intention of placing a sum of
£2,400,000 at the disposal of the Grants
Committee, to be expended over three
years, as the capital expenditure that may
be incurred under their legislation. Our
Government has decided to allocate a sum
of £65,000 for a similar purpose, also to
be spread over a period of three years
from the date of the passing of the Bill.
With regard to the allocation of this
money, as I have already indicated, it
would be a matter for the Grants
Committee, which would judge each
application on its merits, and there
would have to be a date fixed in each year
before which applications must be made.
These are matters of detail, which will
be gone into later on under regulation.
There will be, it is estimated, an expenditure of something like £4,500,
Physical Training Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Parker]
which would be used towards the cost of
training instructors, the salaries of
organisers, and the increased Vote for
technical school education, because there
would be an increased number of physical
instructors.
Now I would like just to make one
reference. It may be asked by those who
will speak on this Measure whether the
Queen's University is one of the bodies or
institutions to which grants may be made,
and I felt I would like to say on this
question that the Government is quite
sensible of the importance of the part
that Queen's University can take in this
matter, and which, indeed, it has actually
taken in the promotion of a higher standard of physical fitness, especially in view
of the opportunity it possesses for implanting in the minds of the younger generation a true conception of the relation
between a healthy mind and a healthy
body, by means of organised sports and
games. But a Clause in a Bill like this
would not be the proper method of
making grants to the University. So
following the precedent of the English
Physical Training Acts we are not taking
power to do so under this Bill, but the
matter is not being lost sight of by the
Government.
It will be recognised that there will
be a great deal to be done in the way of
encouraging these new activities in
developing them and in organising them,
so it is proposed to put on the staff of
the Ministry of Education two highly
qualified persons, one to be a woman,
because it is necessary to remember that
the development of physical training for
women is one of the most important
factors with which we have to deal.
Physical fitness for women, as well as for
men, is of the most tremendous importance, and I think it will be accepted
by all who pause to think for a minute
that without health of body mothers cannot possibly bear healthy children and,
therefore, it is possible that if we can do
something in this direction for the women
of the race it may have a bearing upon
the question of maternal and infant
mortality, ill-health, and physical
troubles generally.
In this connection I should like to say
that there are already in existence many
women's organisations and physical training organisations, who believe in the
scientific training of the body and whose
aim it is to give exercises of curative
value. I understand that it is generally
recognised these exercises have got a
curative value, and those who participate
feel fitter and less tired after a course.
There is one woman's organisation to
which I would like to refer.
It is a particularly large one, and it has its main
branch in England. I am referring to
the Women's League of Health and
Beauty. I am particularly referring to
it, because there is a branch in Ulster,
and because it was founded, I believe,
by an Ulster woman. That Women's
League, which has done a tremendous
amount of good, in its literature speaks
of women as the natural race builders
of the world. Their slogan which they
have adopted is, help to train healthy
mothers to bear healthy children. I do
not propose to say any more on that
subject of developing the physical training for women, but it is a very important
side of the work. I am sure some hon.
Members who are listening will agree with
me in that respect.
In conclusion, I would like to say that
this Bill represents the Government's
contribution towards this whole movement, this tremendous work which is
taking place all over the world. The proposals which the Government are making,
the financial assistance which they are
proposing to give, and the bodies which
they are setting up in order to encourage
and interest the people, can be of very
little use without popular support from
the people and without the interest which
I do hope will be forthcoming in this
Province. This interest is absolutely
essential. It is absolutely necessary that
we should do everything in our power
to stimulate the local authorities to take
their proper share in this campaign for
the good of the people of Northern
Ireland. I would like to refer to it as
a crusade a crusade against the stigma
of unfitness and a crusade for the health,
well-being and strength of our people.
We can to-day-and I have no doubt we
will give this Bill a Second Reading,
but when it passes its final stages it will
only then be an empty shell unless the
breath of life is put into it through local
interest and enthusiasm.
I recognise that this Bill, more than
any other Bill ever passed in this House,

Professor CORKEY: I rise to say a
word or two, because I am heartily in

ideal, that is, physical fitness. It was

good animal. That is not the only condition of success which we appreciate in

cross, but some symbol such as an Indian
club or a dumb-bell.

Professor CORKEY: It indicates the

of a very practical nature which, I think,

Mr. NIXON: I rise to discuss the
statement which the Prime Minister
called an agreement, and which he read
at the opening of to-day's sitting. I may
say at the outset that I approach this
matter from the standpoint of one who

in Northern Ireland. I do that on my

who sent me here, as well as on behalf
of the 100,000 Unionists who voted Independent. That is the standpoint I
approach it from. What has taken place?
I say this is a black day for Ulster. I
will call it Black Tuesday. It is a
remarkable thing that the hon. and
learned Member for Willowfield was
selected to ask the question put to the
Prime Minister. Do not think I am
reflecting on him for doing so. I am not
permitted to mention his name, but I
think there is a black in it. I would
not have been surprised if the Prime
Minister instead of reading that statement had announced his resignation for
leading and misleading us during the past
17 years.
I know well enough I cannot debate
the settlement between the Imperial
Government and the Free State Government, and I am not going to try. It is
a remarkable thing that we got a printed
copy of that Agreement put into our
hands, but we got no copy of what the
Prime Minister read out, and what he
called an agreement. If it is an Agreement when is it going to be ratified by
the House? What were the negotiations
that led to the Agreement? Who signed
the Agreement? When will that Agreement be put on the Table? We know
well enough that everything that could
legally be given has been given. Anyone who understands our Constitution

that the position in which we now find
ourselves is due entirely to the Prime
Minister and to the betrayal of the
Counties of Cavan, Monaghan and
Donegal. It is remarkable how I have

CLASS VI. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £55,273 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge that
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1939, to
defray the salaries and expenses of the
Ministry of Agriculture.' (Note -
£36,000 has been voted on account).
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): There are
few changes of importance in the Estimates which I now submit for this year.
As hon. Members will observe, there is
a net increase of £21,000. This increase
is mainly accounted for by the provision
in the Ministry's Vote of a sum of
£17,000 in respect of milk equalisation
payment. As the Committee is aware,
the sum required for equalisation pay.
ment has up to the present been paid
into the Milk Fund by the Imperial
Government. The whole question of the
form of assistance to the milk industry
in Great Britain will shortly be considered and it has been deemed advis
able to place the sum of £17,000 on our
own Vote to cover the period of October
to March of this financial year.
The balance of the net increase is
accounted for by the provision of £2,200
for the Ministry's display at the Glasgow Exhibition; by the additional
provision of £1,000 for the purchase of
stud animals for the improvement of
herds and stock. There are also increases in the inspectorate staff to cope
with new services, and finally an increase
in the wages of the Ministry's forestry
and agricultural staff, but these, as hon.
Members will see, have been offset by
savings in other directions and by increases in appropriation-in-aid, which
are in the main payments made to the
Ministry for the services rendered.
I do not propose to deal at length
with all the activities of my Ministry,
because it would take a very long time.
It is difficult to know the points that
would interest Members and, therefore,
I will deal with two not dealt with in
previous Estimates. Last year I dealt
with the development of our pig and
milk industries. This year I propose to
deal with our egg industry, which is a
unique undertaking, and the Ministry's
forestry activities. The Egg Marketing
Act of 1936 has gradually been put into
operation, and I am glad to say that it
has met with general acceptance and is
working with most encouraging smoothness. It does, I hope, put a coping

stone on our egg legislation. It may
not be the last word, but it puts us

I mention this matter for two reasons:
first, because the poultry industry represents 20 per cent. to 25 per cent. of our
agricultural industry, and secondly,
because I doubt if we can do much more
in the perfecting of our egg marketing
organisation with the object of securing
economy and efficiency and thus enhancing the returns to the producers. Undoubtedly during the past two years the
poultry industry has had and is still
having a difficult time. Whilst the Act
of 1933 has strengthened its competing
power the increased cost of feeding stuffs
has left very little margin of profit.
Many of our producers felt inclined to
go out of the business. I would say to
them: "Carry on a bit longer in the
hope, which I think justified, of getting
a better return." The present abnormal
cost of feeding stuffs is not likely to last
much longer.
a
The next
next point is the Ministry's
forestry progress, which has not been
dealt with for
very long time.
Critics of the Ministry say we are not
doing enough. It may interest the Committee to know that the Ministry has
acquired some 21,000 acres of land. It
is being planted at the rate of 1,000
acres a year.
So far we have planted
12,000 acres, and those Members who
have passed along the road from Coleraine to Limavady, or who are familiar
with the Sperrin Mountain, the Mourne
district, or County Antrim, will have
seen the great improvement in the
countryside by the planting of trees.
The Ministry has already planted more
than 20 million trees and has sold to
farmers and others for this purpose upwards of five million trees at a reduced
rate.
We are keeping a very accurate
costing record and as far as we can see
the State will earn on the money invested 3 per cent. compound interest,
and over and above that there will be
a very substantial profit accruing to the
Government.
I should like to say something about
the Land Fertility Scheme introduced a
short time ago. By this scheme farmers
were able to buy lime at half price and
half cost of transit also. There is no
need for me to dwell upon the immense
benefit to our soils of a return to the
old practice of regular liming and the
deterioration where it is not done. The
scheme is of the utmost importance for
Northern Ireland. We have dealt with
over 5,200 applications, covering 26,500
tons of lime. That, in a comparatively
short time, is very gratifying. The
difficulty I think at the present time is
that there are insufficient kilns to deal
with the amount of lime required by
farmers, but I hope that will be put
right in a very short time.
I want to make one plea to agricultural Members in this House. In view
of this policy of increasing our stock I
appeal to them to do all they can to discourage farmers from killing their
heifers. I should like at this point to
apologise to some Members. I told them
yesterday that the percentage of heifers
in calf had increased to a very large
amount. The actual figure is 15 per
cent., and not the figure I gave yesterday.
That was an error on my part. It must
be obvious I think to everyone here that
the policy of increasing production is one
of more vital importance to Northern
Ireland than it is to any other part of
the United Kingdom. The share which
agriculture bears in the total wealth of
the country is greater here than in
England or Scotland. If we can produce
conditions under which there will be outlets for this increased production, which
will give a remunerative return to
farmers, we will have done something of
real value to Northern Ireland.
Before I sit down I should like to express my gratitude to the British Government for the manner in which they have
met us with regard to the negotiations so
far as agriculture is concerned.

that farmers in this country are placed

Mr. ELLIOTT: I rise to support the
Estimate submitted by the Minister of
Agriculture. I should like to congratulate him, and through him his Ministry,
on a great many things they have done
during the last year, but there are some
things that have been left undone. The
first thing I would like to direct attention to is the question of the Ulster Dairy
School. There have been some appointments made there within the last number
of years. I have no fault to find with
the status of the young ladies who have
been appointed to these positions.
think they are in every way qualified for
the posts, but it does seem strange that
with all the money spent on our schools
in Northern Ireland, when we come to
make an appointment we have to go to
Scotland on every occasion in order to get
a qualified young lady to take up the
position. There may be nothing sinister
in the fact that we have a strong Scotch
secretary in the Ministry of Agriculture
who can see nothing good outside Scotland, but it does seem strange that some
of our own trainees do not get an opportunity to be placed in these better paid
positions. We have had those schools in
operation for well nigh twenty years, and
if we cannot produce a properly qualified
young lady to take up a responsible
position like this the sooner we close our
Ulster dairy schools the better. I have
heard that a vacancy is about to arise
in this Ulster Dairy School again. We
have two very capable young ladies there.
I know both young ladies, who are
Scotch, very well, and I am not finding
fault with their capabilities. I hope that
when it comes to making a third appointment it will be possible to appoint a
young lady from Northern Ireland who
has been trained and qualified in some of
our agricultural schools, either Strabane
or Loughrey.
I should like to refer to the question
of creamery managers under the Ministry
of Agriculture. It seems rather peculiar
that before we can train a creamery
manager for a position he has to spend
some considerable time in an institute in
Cork, where he is compelled to learn
Irish. I think that is altogether wrong.
With our schools and creameries in
Northern Ireland we ought to be able to
provide sufficient material for the carrying on of the work of the creameries without having to get our young men from
Northern Ireland to have to go to Cork
for a period and there spend a good deal
of time learning amongst other things
the Irish language. That ought to be
remedied. I know one young man who
has served a considerable time as assistant
manager in a creamery. In my opinion
he is qualified to sit for his examination,
but he has been turned down by the
Ministry because he is not actively engaged in assisting a creamery manager,
although, to all intents and purposes, he
has been assistant manager in one of our
creameries. That young man is not in
a position to go to Cork and learn Irish
and spend a considerable time there
in order to qualify for that examination.
He ought not to be asked to do so. I
think we ought to have sufficient accommodation for our young men and young
girls in our two schools, which are costing a good deal of money and which I do
not object to-we ought to be able to
train our young men and young women
for these important appointments. I hope
the Minister will be able to assure us that
everything possible is being done to give
the young men and young women
opportunity to take up these responsible
positions.

I should like to refer for a moment to
another thing which is perturbing the
minds of agriculturists very much, that
is the question of getting agricultural
labour. The hon. Member for Pottinger
will, no doubt, tell me we will get the
labour if we are prepared to pay for it.
I want to say that the difficulty arises
with the agricultural stamps and industrial stamps. I know that many good
farm labourers are to-day refusing to
take up agricultural work because of the
fact that they only get an agricultural
stamp on their card. When they go to
draw unemployment benefit, if they
happen to be possessed of a wife and a
large family, they are likely reduced in
unemployment benefit. I know a great
many people in my own locality who were
agricultural labourers up to a short time
ago. They have now gone into employment as workers in a quarry or as carters
Ministry of Agriculture 734

at much reduced rates of wages compared with what they previously got. It
is because they now get an industrial
stamp on their card. When they go out
of employment they get increased benefit.
Mr. BEATTIE: What is the difference
in benefits?
Mr. ELLIOTT: The hon. Member
knows that much better than I do. An
agricultural labourer with a wife and
family cannot draw more than 30s a week.
I know industrial workers who can draw
over £2 a week. Naturally, a man when
getting his card stamped is anxious to get
stamps that will give him much more
benefit when he is unemployed. Farmers
should be allowed if the labourer agrees
to put on the bigger stamps on his card.
Unless something is done along these
lines, I say the time is not far distant
when it will be impossible to get agricultural labour in some districts. People in
my own constituency have told me it is
getting increasingly
increasingly difficult to get
agricultural labourers, and the stamp
question is the one obstacle in the way.
The Minister of Agriculture suggested
that we ought to increase production,
and I am with him, but a man cannot increase his production if he is going to have
a reduced quantity of labour and if it is
impossible to get labour. That is one of
the things standing in the way of increased production. I hope something
will be done to remedy it.
I do not want to anticipate the adjourned debate on the Second Reading of

the moment we on the Pigs Board have

In substance this means that the assistance which is to be given in Great
Britain is not in the nature of a subsidy at all, but is assistance to be given
in order to enable the curing industry

"To
sum up, the reorganisation proposals fall into three main
divisions: first, the reintroduction of

I feel that the points raised by the

knows that to-day all industries are
suffering in this area, and he is also

I feel that the Minister himself got
over very little of the sixteen pages of
Estimates. It was the shortest presentation of an Estimate amounting to
£212,467 I ever had the pleasure of
listening to. Sixteen pages were got
over in the short space of about twenty

the Members of the Committee possess.
That may be true of those on the Government side and it may not be necessary for the Minister to go into detail
as to the reasons for the money being
asked, but that cannot be said of the
Opposition side. There are very few
agriculturists on our side.
We are
mostly industrial Members, and we
would like to know the whys and wherefores of the large sums that are being
asked. We would also like to know why
we are being asked to pay such high
prices for our foodstuffs in retail establishments.
The Minister of Agriculture-I presume for reasons best known to himselfhas made no reference to the increased
cost of living, but I know that his heart's
delight is in rising prices, because they
bring kudos to him from those who are
receiving those high prices. High prices.
also bring heart-breaking to those who
have to meet them without adequate
purchasing power. I do object strongly
to the reduction of the purchasing power
of the working classes in regard to a commodity which is being produced under
sweated conditions from the labourers'
point of view. To-day we have in
Northern Ireland that sweated industry,
which refuses to pay a living wage to its
labourers. I can give instances where
12s, 14s and 15s a week are being paid
to labourers with wives and two, three
or four children. I call that industry a
sweated industry, and one that is not
worthy of being assisted to the extent of
£212,000 by the general taxpayers of
Northern Ireland.
Until that position is remedied and
until the farmers realise that the labourer
is worthy of his hire, I shall speak in
similar terms of the agricultural industry.
If the same conditions of labour were
put into operation in any industrial concern, whether affecting one man, two
men, or a dozen, there would be a revolution inside of 24 hours. For the last 17
years, while this Government has been
in power, we have had this vicious system
of giving the agricultural labourer any.
thing from 12s to £1 a week. Where do
the labourers come in in regard to equal
rights with the British workman? We
are supposed to go step by step. I
remember that in the year 1921 men who
to-day are leading politicians in Northern
Ireland said that the citizens of Northern
Ireland would not suffer to the extent of
one penny by coming in under a Government such as we have at the present
moment. I can tell this House, and I
can tell those outside, that the working
people both in agriculture and in industry have suffered by the establishment of
this House.
In
In England to-day the labourers have
the Agricultural Wages Board to protect
them against exploitation. We in
Northern Ireland have received no such
consideration up to the moment.
Scotland they have a Linen Wages Board,
which we had under the Imperial
authority in the old days, but which has
disappeared without any explanation
having been given. Of course, I am not
putting that down to the right hon.
Gentleman. I think I am justified in
criticising the expenditure of this amount
of money in an industry that does not
give consideration to its workers, and I
do feel that the time has now arrived
when the Minister will have to put into
immediate operation conditions of employment more in keeping with those of
Great Britain.
The hon. Member for South Tyrone
(Mr. Elliott) spoke about the scarcity
of labour, and said it was due to the
inferiority complex-of course those are
not his words of unemployment insurance. I want to say this to him, because
I believe it is worth saying, that the
party he supports was responsible for
creating that inferiority complex. I
voted against the legislation that caused
it, but his party passed it. The agricultural labourers, with all the hardships
that the Government have imposed upon
them, and with this inferiority complex,
returned the Government to power again.
So the hon. Member's duty now is to go
down to the country and educate the
labourer to support the side on which his
bread is buttered. I want to say that to
the hon. Member, because he has an
independent spirit and speaks his mind.

was
There are many ways in which the
cultivation of flax could be helped-some
of them good, some of them middling,
some of them bad. But no matter what
proposal is put up, sand is always thrown
into the wheels, and the thing will not
work. Whether that is done deliberately
or not I cannot say, but certainly any
scheme put up to the Ministry up to the
present has been turned down, and flax
has become the Cinderella of the crops.
The flax crop of Northern Ireland has
almost totally disappeared within the past
ten years.
The subsidies for other crops
have helped in that disappearance. As
far as I understand, sowing this year
shows a large decrease on the small sowing of last year. If the Government or
the Ministry of Agriculture view the
almost total disappearance of flax cultivation in Northern Ireland with
equanimity, I can assure them that the
vast majority of those interested do not
take that view.
If the Ministry had any knowledge
of what other countries are doing in the
way of subsidising flax production I think
they might follow the example of those
countries. In Germany, France and
Belgium, for instance, there is a good
deal of money spent very successfully in
increasing the cultivation of flax. Personally I know that the cultivation of
flax in Belgium is a highly lucrative and
profitable undertaking for all concerned.
I know that the millions of pounds worth
of flax that comes here from Belgium
passes through five, six or seven hands

hundred have been put down. I know
that the German Government has spent
as much as £30,000 on flax cultivation,
and that during the past few years the
cultivation of flax in Germany has grown
by leaps and bounds.
The policy of this Government has been
to allow flax to disappear, to the detriment of the linen trade, to the detriment
of Ulster, and also, I think, to show the
poverty of the policy of the Government.
I think it is time this policy ceased.
People have come to the conclusion that
something will have to be done. I do not
think the linen trade can allow a crop
they are so dependent upon to totally disappear from this Province, and I do not
think it is beyond the skill of the farmers
of Ulster to grow flax again, both for the
profit of themselves and everybody concerned. I have brought this matter
before the House on several occasions,
but I do not want to over-state my case
and I do not want to weary the Committee, but I do appeal to the Minister
to really consider this question very
seriously, and not, as he has done in the
past, listen to what has been said and do
nothing.
Mr. BAILEY: I also am sorry that
the Ministry has not done something for
the flax industry. As a practical farmer
myself I have an interest in the flax
industry, and I plead that something should
be done to help it. Flax, as you know, was
one of the main industries of our country
for many years, not alone for the farmer,
but for the agricultural worker, and also
the industrial worker. In years gone by
it was the main topic of conversation
amongst the farming community whenever they met, and on coming home
from church on Sunday-what price did
they get, what yield, and so on. But the
most extraordinary fact was that during
the years the flax industry was thriving
farm labourers were able to purchase
farms, and a great number of them are
prosperous farmers to-day. With the
better seed that is now available, and for
which I give the Government every credit,
the more scientific methods of working and
the more modern machinery, there is no
reason why the cultivation of flax should
not again become one of the main
branches of agriculture.
I have been taking a great interest in
this question during the last few weeks,
and I have interviewed farmers who are
not sowing flax this year. When I asked
them why they were not doing so they
said the cost of sowing the seed and working the flax afterwards ran away with
all the profits. I make this suggestion,
that the Government should give a grant
for the pulling of flax, and that the
Ministers of Labour, Agriculture, Finance
and Commerce should get together and
see if something could not be done in this
direction. Farmers have told me, as I
know myself, that the cost of pulling flax
is about £3 per acre, and if the Ministry
could give a grant for this purpose I
think it would encourage farmers to grow
more flax, and I ask the Government to
consider this suggestion.
I also think there should be a fixed
price for flax, because, after all, of every
£100 worth of flax produced in Northern
Ireland £80 is kept in Northern Ireland.
The remainder is spent on seed and
fertilisers. On the other hand, of every
£100 worth of pigs produced in this
country, £90 goes out of the country
for corn and other feeding stuffs. İ
earnestly appeal to the Government to
consider the suggestions I have made.
The PRIME MINISTER: After consultation with my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Agriculture, he agrees that it
is right that, as he was not the Minister
of Agriculture in the early stages of this
movement for assistance for the flax
industry, I should explain, as far as I
can, the situation as the Government sees
it to-day. Of course flax is a speculative
crop, the most speculative, perhaps, that
farmers have to deal with. Some farmers
like a little speculation, and I dare say
they would be annoyed if the Government made the crop and the price
positively certain for them in the coming.
year. They would say, "You have taken
away all the old interest there was in
bargaining with the flax buyers who come
to our markets." I have listened to very
Estimates-
Ministry of Agriculture
27 APRIL 1938
many deputations on this subject for
years past. Having been born in a flaxgrowing district I happen to know a good
deal about it myself.
In the first instance, when a strong
body of agriculturists approached the
Government on the subject, I saw them
along with some of my colleagues, including the late Minister of Agriculture,
and we told them, "Put up a scheme that
will commend itself to the Government
and to Parliament." But nothing
accrued, and I remember-perhaps it
was not in this connection-Mr. Pilkington, who was president of the Ulster
Farmers' Union, saying at one of the
annual meetings, that really it was a
waste of time for farmers to attempt to
improvise a scheme of their own, because
they had not the experience nor had they
the co-operative feeling sufficient to work
together. He concluded by saying it was
much better for the Government to provide a scheme, and somebody at the back
of the hall said, "Yes, and then we can
throw stones at it." Therefore, it is an
extremely difficult and complicated
problem. There is no question at all about
that.
After a great deal of difficulty I persuaded the three parties concerned to
come together, because two of them had
not been living in what you would call
peace and harmony in the years that have
gone by. The buyers were accused by
the growers of flax of having made rings
against them when they went to the
market. It was very much on the same
lines as the complaint that arose when
we first commenced to place the pig
industry on a better plane. The accusation was then made against the pork
buyers that on their way to the markets
-it was a dead pig trade in those daysthey made a ring, and the farmer had
to take any price offered to him rather
than take back his dead meat and store it
in his own premises for a day or two.
Fortunately that difficulty was
was got
over, and now I understand from the
Member for South Tyrone (Mr. Elliott),
who is a member of the Pigs Marketing
Board, that things are working much
better. But it took some years to
smooth over what was originally a very
difficult problem, and I hope that after
the statement made yesterday, and the
promise of help from the British Government, the pig industry generally will go
on and prosper. The same charge was
made against the buyers of flax firms who
were sent to purchase flax in the open
market that they made a ring and that
that kept prices down, and that to-day
the crop no longer pays.
It is a very great mistake for anyone
in Ulster to think that the Government,
or I myself, have any desire other than
to help in every way we possibly can,
within reason. As a preliminary to
taking any further steps I set up a committee, which I believe, even the Member for North Armagh (Mr. Johnston)
will agree, was very representative of the
trade. Perhaps it would interest the
Committee to know that it included representatives of the Ulster Farmers' Union,
the scutch mill owners, who were naturally
very much interested in the subject, and
the Flax Spinners' Association. Those
three bodies were each represented by six
members. The Ulster Farmers' Union
had Mr. Keers, Mr. Brown, Mr. Hazlett,
Mr. Mark, Mr. Maybin and Mr. Nesbitt.
The scutch mill owners are, perhaps, not
so well known, but they were all very
representative men. The Flax Spinners'
Association were represented by Mr.
Louis C. Grey, Mr. J. D. Campbell, Mr.
Malcolm Gordon, Mr. J. B. Morrison,
Mr. C. H. Murland, and Mr. L. Morris,
so I think the Government will be given
credit for having picked out men who
were engaged in the industry, who were
vitally interested in it, and who were as
keen to do something for the industry.
as is the Member for North Armagh.
The committee sat for a long time, and
issued two reports. I need not give the
details of the reports, but they are available to anybody who cares to read them.
I will just read one sentence from the end
of their second report. They say:
The committee regrets that it has
not been able to produce any major
scheme for a substantial revival of the
flax growing industry of Northern
Ireland.
It was a most hopeless position for
us, anxious as we were to help in every
way we could, to get a report from this
combined committee, representing the
various interests concerned, who told us
they were unable to produce any major
scheme for a substantial revival of the
flax growing industry
of Northern
Ireland. From that time on various

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
committees have been set up. On 25th

Hugh O'Neill asked the Minister for

or
Whether in view of the possible

munition purposes the Government

The answer to that was-
An Inter-Departmental Committee
has for some time been carrying out
a thorough investigation into the

That Committee has not yet reported,
but it shows everybody who takes an
intelligent interest in this complicated
problem the difficulties associated with
helping the growing of flax. It is a
most complicated and difficult position.
There have been only two speeches
delivered to-day and they were very
much along the lines of individuals who
come to see me. They know the Government is sympathetic, but have very few
tangible propositions to make themselves.
They feel that the Government
should produce a scheme. That is
the general opinion, that the Government
should produce a scheme. We are still
working on it and we have not given up
hope, but that we will be able to assist in
some way.
The hon. Member for West Down
suggests that it should be possible to
give some help towards the pulling of
flax. When I was a boy-that is much
longer ago than my hon. Friend behind
me- -I used to think it was a very unpleasant job for farmers' sons and
daughters. Many of the girls were employed in the retting and steeping of
flax. I always thought it was a particularly abnoxious sort of work and
time has shown that, even to-day, with
our modern ideas, it is looked upon as a
pretty abnoxious job to have to go down
into these holes and steep the flax. The
hon. Member suggests that something
should be done with regard to the pulling of flax. Just where might that lead
us? I ask everybody to look at it from
the commonsense point of view. Where
would it lead us if we were to give
assistance in regard to the pulling of
flax? Might we not have a demand to
help the farmers to dig potatoes and
do other farming things of that kind? It is
a most complicated matter to help one industry to do so and so, and then not to
have a crowd of bees round you next day
saying, "If you can do that for the
pulling of flax, what about our wheat
because the cost of labour has risen ?"
I am only speaking extemporarily and
am only putting my own views to show
the difficulties the Government are confronted with.
am
Another point I should like to raise.
The hon. Member for South Tyrone
(Mr. Elliott), in his usual emphatic
manner has spoken about officialdom. I
invite him to put forward a suggestion
in regard to flax. I say for those who
are unable to defend themselves that
this Government, or any other Government, could not carry on for any length
of time without the expert knowledge
possessed by officialdom. If a scheme
for flax growing does materialise-I
certain it will not materialise in
my small brain or in the brain of my
right hon. Friends behind me, but
through the same officialdom which
seems to have a sort of weight in the
mind of my hon. Friend. Nearly all
the schemes which have proved of such
benefit in regard to wheat and apple
growing for helping the farmers have
been brought about by officialdom, and
I am perfectly certain that such
officialdom will be most anxious in other
Departments to help us to prepare a
scheme for flax if such a scheme is at
all possible.
I cannot make any further announcement on the subject to-day other than
to say that I want to get it out of
the heads of people that they they can
ask for a subsidy for flax which might
never fall into the hands of the farmers
at all. It might never reach them and
might be a complete failure, but there
may be other ways of helping. If there
are, let the critics come forward and tell
us, but do not let them have always the
same parrot cry. Let them say, "Here
is a way to solve the difficulty.' What
we want in Ulster is to have something
like 100,000 acres under flax. That is
what we are all aiming at. We should like
to double what it is to-day, taking in
round figures 100,000 acres.

If the price of flax on the Continent
rises next year the farmers here will be
very sorry they did not grow it, but, on
the other hand, if the price of flax in

the flax growers would say they wished

Let them put on their thinking caps,

sensible proposition.

do not think that Members of this Committee realise what are the functions of

I think one of the most important
points of policy that we have got in
Northern Ireland is that the officials are
more in touch with the farming community than they are in any other part
of the United Kingdom. I personally
think that is an excellent thing. If you
have a man sitting continually in his

distant, rosy light, whereas if he gets
down to the actual difficulties the farmers
are experiencing it will help his judgment
in working for various economies. I wish

brought about by good administration,
and, I admit, by the soundness of the
