"Between 1933 and 1936 the gross
income of Northern Ireland farmers increased by 40 per cent. In England,
where the effect of the crisis was not
so marked as here, there has only been
an increase of 14 per cent. over this
period."
Surely the officials who work these schemes,
who carry out the orders of their
Minister, and, finally, the orders of this

result has been produced in England and
other countries. Any Minister here is

to make an attack on officers who are

ACCIDENTS IN DUKE STREET,
LONDONDERRY.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
ten accidents have taken place in Duke
Street, Londonderry, within the past.
few years, two of which were fatal;
whether he received a memorial in
November, 1936, and another in October,
1937, signed by fifty persons, petitioning
the Government to urge the Londonderry
Corporation to have Duke Street widened;
whether any action has been taken;
whether he can state what decision the
Government have come to on the matter;
whether the wishes of the citizens, nearly
all of whom were business persons, will
be carried out, and whether he will urge
the Londonderry Corporation to have
this narrow congested leading thoroughfare widened to accommodate sufficiently
present day traffic.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am informed that
within the past
past three
years eight
accidents were reported to the police as
having occurred in Duke Street, Londonderry, and that one was fatal.
In November, 1936, my Department
received a memorial from a number of
persons urging that the street should be
widened, and a second memorial was
received in October, 1937.
The matter was also brought to my
notice by my hon. and learned Friend,
the Attorney-General, and it has been
receiving the earnest attention of my
Department.
The memorials were communicated to
the Londonderry Corporation and have
been given very careful consideration by
that body, but I am sure that the hon.
Member will appreciate that the question
is one for the local authority concerned,
and in the case of the widening of a
city street the matter is naturally of some
magnitude and cannot be undertaken
without very serious consideration by the
local authority who are fully conversant
with all the facts of the case, including
the difficulties to be overcome.
I would remind the hon. Member
that, as in other similar cases, assistance
will be available from Government funds
for whatever widening is ultimately

SOUTH DOWN BLACK SCAB AREA
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he will consider the
question of removing for a trial period
of say five years, with a view to the
permanent removal, the Black Scab in
Potatoes Order in force for the last thirty
years in Newry, Warrenpoint, Rostrevor
and Kilkeel districts, as there have been
no cases of the disease in these areas
for many years.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): For reasons
already given in reply to similar questions
in the past I regret that it is not possible to remove the restrictions applicable
to the area to which the hon. Member
refers. The hon. Member will realise
that the purpose of these restrictions is
to prevent the spread of black scab
disease. There is no known means of
eradicating the disease from ground in
which it has once appeared. Tests have
shown that the disease remains virulent
for an indefinite period of years even
in ground where no potatoes have been
grown since the original outbreak. Control is necessary for this reason, as well
as to comply with the conditions prescribed by the English and Scottish
authorities and other importing countries
in regard to potatoes from Northern
Ireland.
In view of the facts already stated as
to the persistence of the infection in the
soil, the non-recurrence of disease in
recent years in the areas in question
would not be sufficient in itself to justify
the removal of restrictions. Such nonrecurrence may be ascribed to the requirement whereby only potatoes of
varieties immune from black scab may
be grown in scheduled areas.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask as a supplementary question is the Minister of
Agriculture aware that the imposition of
these restrictions, which are a legacy
from the unfortunate past of thirty years
ago and for which I do not propose to
blame the present Ministry, impose a
very grievous hardship upon the potato
producers within the areas, inasmuch as
they restrict the sale-
Mr. SPEAKER: Order, order. If

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): As stated by the noble
Lord, the Prime Minister, yesterday, in
the course of his remarks in the debate
on flax cultivation and notified by him
to the President of the Flax Spinners'
Association in consequence of letters received from him, this matter has been
receiving the very serious consideration
of the Cabinet for some time past. But
in view of the question appearing on the
Order Paper and of the Notice of Motion
which also stands on the Order Paper it
is perhaps more convenient that an
earlier disclosure should be made of the
Government's intention on this matter
than had originally been intended.
I, therefore, have to state that I am
fully aware of the anxiety with which
the question of flax supplies is regarded
by the linen trade, who have on a number of occasions been in touch with me
and my Department on this matter.
Notwithstanding the lack of success
which has been experienced over a period
of many years in obtaining any substantial measure of agreement between
the growers, scutchers and members of

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
the linen trade as to the best means of

of farmers and from the Flax Spinners'

ex-
The Government are anxious to assist
these organisations to put into effect
such means as they may consider best
designed to achieve this end. The Government fully appreciate the desirability
of enabling the linen trade to secure as
ample a supply as possible of its necessary
home-grown
raw material. They also
realise that
linen firms are
many
periencing at present poor demand for
their products and that, accordingly, the
trade would find it difficult to provide
the necessary funds to bring about an
end which they so urgently desire. The
Government feel, however, that those
concerned would not have put forward
the representations they have unless
they believe there is a real solution and
are prepared to give it substantial
support.
The Government, therefore, in response
to these appeals have decided to recommend to this House that for the financial
year 1938/1939 a grant be made of 90
per cent., not exceeding £50,000 in any
one year, of any expenditure incurred
in this connection, leaving only 10 per
cent. to be raised by those interested in
agriculture or in the linen trade, and
that a similar grant be made in each
of the succeeding two years, by which
time it should have been effectively
demonstrated to what extent flax capable
of competing in quality, handling and
price with supplies coming from elsewhere, can be remuneratively produced
in this country.
As to the best means of helping the
trade, the Government have decided to
entrust the preparation of plans to those
vocationally engaged in the trade, and
propose that a Committee
be set up
composed as follows:-
Three members appointed by the Flax
Spinners' Association;
Two members appointed by the Farmers' Union ;
Two members appointed by the Ulster
Agricultural Organisation Society;
One member appointed by the Scutch
Millowners' Association;
One member appointed by the Linen
Industry Research Association;
One member appointed by the local
branch of the Institute of Chartered
Accountants.
The Committee would select one of its
members as chairman, and would also
appoint its own secretary and staff,
whose remuneration and expenses would
be met out of the funds placed at the
disposal of the Committee.
In this period, limited to three years,
it should be possible to introduce and
establish modern equipment and improved methods of handling, designed to
enable the growth of flax to be selfsupporting for the future.
I hope, in view of the statement I
have just made, that those hon. Members
associated with the Notice of Motion on
the Paper will tender their advice to
the Committee to be set up and help in
any way to solve the difficulties inherent
to this problem.

5. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he is aware that notwithstanding the fact that the Belfast
Corporation has just reduced the prices
charged to consumers in Belfast for
electrical current, the Electricity Board
for Northern Ireland has just increased
the charges to consumers throughout
Northern Ireland by abolishing the five
per cent. cash discount in operation for
many years, thus making provincial consumers pay for city price reductions;
whether he is aware that almost every
public body in Northern Ireland has
passed a resolution of protest against this
inequality and discrimination against
provincial centres; whether he is aware
that the present flat rate for electricity
for lighting in Newry, for instance, is
by reason of the abolition of this
cash discount now higher than when
the Electricity Board took over the
Newry undertaking almost six years ago,
when lower prices were promised to consumers to compensate for the compulsory
acquiring of the undertaking, and if he
will have the whole present unsatisfactory
position investigated and the anomaly of
higher provincial prices synchronising
with lower city charges removed.
Mr. BARBOUR: I would remind the
hon. Member that the rates charged to
consumers by the Electricity Board are
governed by the provisions of the
Electricity (Supply) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1931, Section 26 of which requires the Board to fix its charges at such
a level that its revenue will be "sufficient
and only sufficient" as nearly as may be
to pay all salaries, working expenses and
other outgoings. The hon. Member will
appreciate, therefore, that in fixing its.
charges the Board must act in accordance
with the principles laid down in the Act,
and that, moreover, there is a wide
difference between the position of an oldestablished electricity undertaking, such
as that of the Belfast Corporation, which
caters for a densely populated and highly
industrialised area, and a newlyestablished undertaking, such as that of
the Electricity Board, engaged in the
development of electricity supplies over a
wide and sparsely populated area.
As regards the charges for lighting in
the Newry district, I am informed that
the flat rate for lighting charged by the
Urban District Council was not altered
on the transfer of the undertaking to the
Board, and that the withdrawal of the
discount will, in fact, result in a slight
increase of this charge, but that the
Board's alternative two-part tariff for
domestic consumers will still be more
favourable than that offered by the Urban
District Council.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask the Minister
whether he is aware that the Belfast Corporation, who have reduced the price of
current, supply the Electricity Board in
bulk, and is he also aware of the extraordinary situation which exists whereby
the Belfast Corporation are able to reduce
their price while the Electricity Board
are unable to pass on the reduction to the
provincial consumers?
Mr. NIXON: Is it a fact that the
Electricity Supply Board obtain this
Electricity from the Belfast Corporation
at the cost of production?
Mr. BARBOUR: Yes, sir.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it a fact that the
Electricity Supply Board refuse to pay
the standard rate of wages to its employees, and is it not a fact that a halfpenny an hour has been conceded by the
Electricity Joint Council, which the
Electricity Board has refused to apply to
its workers?
Mr. BARBOUR: No, I am not aware
of the fact.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): In presenting
the Estimates of the Ministry of
Labour, in the absence of my
right hon. Friend, the Minister,
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
28 APRIL 1938
whose illness we all deeply
all deeply deplore,
and to whose return to the House we
eagerly look forward, I do not propose to
go minutely into the work of the various
Departments of the Ministry, but will
refer briefly to the principal activities, as
has been the practice since the Ministry
was established. I feel it is due to the
Committee to say that our policy has consistently followed that of the Imperial
Ministry, and though our problems have
been many and varied we have maintained
our social services on the same basis as
Great Britain, and have administered
those services in a reasonable, humane
manner, without discrimination and
affording equal treatment to all.
The extent of the work of the Department is signified by the total net Estimate
of the Ministry, which amounts to
£5,673,770. This figure appears on page
86 of the Estimates. The year 1937 has
not been altogether a happy one for
industry. I wish I were in the position
to report a steady forward trend in employment. During the first quarters of
1937 there was an encouraging improvement in employment, which, unfortunately, was marked by a sharp decline in
industrial activity during the closing
months of the year. World conditions
have had a blighting effect, especially
upon one of the main industries of our
country. Unsettled conditions abroad
have had evil effects upon our exporting
industries.
It was not until February of this year
an appreciable upward movement
took place in employment. Our live
register, I am glad to say, has fallen
steadily during the past three months,
and almost 5,500 more persons have been
placed in employment. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Unfortunately, employment in our linen industry shows no improvement, but there has been a steady
movement in the shirt and collar trades,
hemstitching, making-up trades, agriculture, road and quarry work, and building
work. The set-back which we have experienced has been most disappointing,
because it began just when the volume
of employment in the insured industries
had been steadily increasing until it
reached a record figure in September,
1937.
Our principal industries manufacture
their commodities for export, and every
movement which affects the stability of
conditions in foreign markets has an
adverse effect upon our exporting industries, with consequent unemployment.
The Government is doing everything
possible to stimulate employment, to encourage the establishment of new industries, and to extend those already
established.
The Ministry of Labour recognises the
necessity of assisting local authorities and
public bodies in carrying out works of
public utility to provide employment.
This is a great social responsibility, and
I would like to pay this tribute to local
authorities all over the country-they
have embarked on schemes which meant
an increased load upon their rates, but
they have willingly undertaken the responsibility in order to give employment
and improve the amenities of their
districts.
We have increased substantially the
rates of grants from the Vote of the
Ministry for relief schemes approved on
and after the 3rd March last.
We are
giving 85 per cent. of the wages cost to
revenue and non-revenue producing
works, and for street works in urban
areas dual grants may be paid of 75 per
cent. of the wages cost from the Ministry
of Labour, and 15 per cent. of the
balance of the total approved expenditure
from the Road Fund. To provide for
these grants I am asking the Committee
to approve the provision of £150,000,
which is set out in the Estimates for
this work. Should our expenditure on
this head exceed this sum we shall not
hesitate to ask Parliament to sanction a
Supplementary Estimate for this purpose.
The average unemployed figure over
the past twelve months has been 72,000.
This does not indicate that the same persons have been continuously unemployed
during the whole year. The fact that
255,000 fresh and renewal claims were
received during the year shows the
enormous extent of the turnover in our
live register-

Under the agricultural scheme a
further concession has been given.
waiting period of six days has now been

in line with Great Britain and in the line
of social reform. Previously the law
required that when a man had drawn all
the agricultural benefit to which he was

his contributions, he could not re-qualify

statutory conditions, he could show the

since the exhaustion of his benefit rights.
The law now confines the application of
this requirement to the case of a man
who has drawn the maximum allowance
of 300 days in his preceding benefit year.
It is also proposed to reduce the contributions of agricultural workers over
18 years and of their employers by one
halfpenny per week as from the 4th July
next.
As well as all these concessions both the
general and the agricultural insurance
schemes have been extended since the 4th
April. Chauffeurs in private employment have been brought into general
insurance and also certain classes of
domestic servants employed in clubs,
hospitals, and other institutions not
carried on for gain. Under the agricultural scheme certain classes of outdoor
domestic servants have been included,
such as gamekeepers, coachmen, boatmen, lodge-keepers, and others following
similar occupations.

and
Trade Boards have proved of immense
value as a means of adjusting industrial
relations in the trades to which they
apply. The gradual increase in the cost
serof living has been responsible for a considerable amount of activity amongst
Trade Boards, generally, and nine
Boards recommended increased rates of
wages to the Ministry for confirmation.
Though wage rates are increased by
agreement, sometimes we find it necessary to enforce the decision by taking
proceedings for breaches of the statutory
provisions. During the year the
vices of the Department have been freely
sought in adjusting industrial differences.
These problems arise intermittently, however well organised the workers or employers may be. The existence of powerful organisations is not in itself a guarantee of industrial peace. There is, however, a growing tendency on the part of
employers and workers to recognise the
danger and waste of leaving the settlement of industrial disputes to the
arbitrament of industrial warfare.
I am glad to say that both the workers
and employers in Northern Ireland recognise that a great deal more can be accomplished by a joint conference of those
engaged in the industry than a trial of
strength, either by a strike or a lock-out
of workers. A pleasing feature is the
development of voluntary machinery for
negotiating wages and conditions of service established by certain trades and
industries. The Department is always
willing to give any assistance in its power
to promote this object.
The Government of the United Kingdom has set up Training Centres in Great
Britain to train young men in a variety
of skilled occupations, principally the
engineering and building trade groups.
The British Ministry of Labour has now
arranged to accept volunteers from
Northern Ireland as candidates at their
Training Centres. We are watching the
progress of this experiment very carefully, and we are encouraged by the
results up-to-date. As one would
naturally expect, Northern Ireland
volunteers and I emphasise the word
volunteers to make it plain that no compulsion is placed on any person to go to
one of these Centres-are fully up to the

the United Kingdom. One hundred and
eighty-nine unemployed young men from

gone to these Centres, and I am glad to

placed in suitable employment as im-

over last year of about £3,400, or something like 8 per cent of last year's total.
Part of the increase arises by reason of
the Civil Service re-grading scheme, but
it is mainly due to the necessity of providing the Board with some additional
staff to meet the increased duties that
have fallen within its scope.
The total amount of these Estimates
which I have the honour to submit for
the current financial year is almost
£5,700,000, which represents the contribution of the Exchequer of Northern
Ireland to those of the social services
which fall within the purview of the
Ministry of Labour. That a charge of
such magnitude should be carried on our
revenue in the interests of those less forunate members of the community for
whose benefit this money will be expended is, I feel, no mean tribute to
the social conscience of the Government
and the country, and it is in that spirit.
I confidently recommend these Estimates
to the Committee and ask their support
and help in passing them. I beg to
move.

a green card job in Beresford Street.

I would call the special attention of

I am going to make. It is a point I
should not have to make. It is a reflection on the administration. This particular man I have referred to was unemployed for five years except for the four
weeks the Department got him work in

he became unemployed was in one of the

He got married and has a family. As

Public Assistance Board says that the
last wages earned by a man is what is

earned was £2 8s for the work in Beresford Street. When the authorities got
him off the job in Beresford Street they
ignored the fact that he had got four
weeks' work and went back to the wages
he got while in the mill. The result is
that he is getting for the upkeep of himself, his wife and three children 21s a
week. I give that as an illustration of
what often occurs. They should have
based his public assistance on the wages
he earned during the four weeks he
worked in Beresford Street. It is not his
fault that he is not working. This man
has been after me and asking me to help
him. You would not have known him
after he had worked those four weeks he
was so well improved. Work does improve a man. When you meet young
men who have never worked you know
it because they have no physique. They
are, if I may use the expression, a string.
If you got them into work you would not
know them. There is a terrible problem
arising in that respect.
Now, as regards the means test there
is a great deal of apprehension about it
on the part of some people including
Members on that side. I do not object to
the means test at all so long as it is confined to the applicant and his wife and
immediate family, but I do object to it
when the wages of the brother or brotherin-law are brought in. I will give you
the case of a man and his wife. The ages
are from 54 to about 63. This man and
his wife went to live with her sister and
brother. The man could not get work.
He was getting public assistance. He
went there because he was not able to
keep a house of his own. Although he
was occupying separate apartments he
had under the means test to give the
wages drawn by his brother-in-law. The
latter was under no obligation to tell the
man what wages he was drawing. The
brother-in-law is a man over 60 years,
and what right had he to tell the wages
he receives because these people happen
to be living under the same roof? Wrong
information was given. The correct
information could not be got. Even if it
had been got it is an abuse to bring such
a thing into the means test. That man
is likely to get into trouble because he
did not give the correct wages his
brother-in-law was getting. What
obligation is my brother-in-law under
to tell me what he is earning? The thing
is ridiculous. I say again that so long as
the means test is confined to the individual concerned and his wife and
immediate family it is all right. There
is nothing wrong with that, but when
you poke into what the brother-in-law,
or sister-in-law or brother, who are out
on their own, are receiving in wages you
are going too far. I venture to say
there is hardly one man could tell what
salary his brother or brother-in-law is
receiving. I do not think the heads of
the Department want anything like that.
I give them credit for that. I would ask
the Parliamentary Secretary to look into
cases like that and put them on a proper
basis in conformity with the sympathy I
know the Minister and the Parliamentary
Secretary usually show.

There is another thing I have a word to
say about. I think the Parliamentary
Secretary told us that the visits of inspectors to factories came to something like
7,000 a year. It is not much wonder
that a lot of factories are closing down
with inspectors poking their noses into
business. It would be impossible at the
present time for any man to start in a
small way and build up an industry
owing to these inspectors. When
industries were built up some years ago
the people were not persecuted with
inspectors to the same extent as now. It
is generally the little places they
prey upon. There is a man on the
Shankill Road who was doing well as a
draper. He has a couple of shops now.
Over one of his shops he started a shirt
making industry and employed a number
of girls. He was doing well enough but
he got so much persecution from these
inspectors that he closed the place and
the girls went on the dole. Another man
on the Shankill Road did the same thing
in respect to dress-making on his
premises.
There was
another shop on the
Shankill Road which was doing a good
business. Being too big I could not get
shirts ready-made, and I had to get
someone to make out-size shirts for me.
This man used to get a woman to make
shirts for me and a few more like me.
The poor woman was glad to make them
for the money. The man had no profit
on it, at all. The poor woman had a
family and the money was useful to her.
One inspector one day discovered what
was going on,' and he came up the next
day with two other inspectors.
The
three stayed there nearly the whole day.
They told the man he would have to
put up notices round the shop. He was
not in the manufacturing line at all. He
was giving out work to oblige people outside. At all events when the inspectors
began to visit his place he thought it
time to stop that business and he did.
It was no inconvenience to me, but it

was to the poor woman who made these
shirts in her spare time and got an
existence such as it was. That was all
because of these inspectors.
I was in a little shop one day myself.
Two girls have it and they carry on a
dressmaking business at the back and a
little drapery at the front. A great
inspector came along one day. He was
wearing glasses. I was there when he
came in but he did not know who I was.
If he had known me perhaps he would
not have had so much ground under him,
not that I should say it. In any case,
he endeavoured to see what was being
done there and poked through everything. If the same inspector went to
one of the great big firms controlled by
right hon. Gentlemen who sit there,
there would not be a squeal out of him.
You are not improving the position at
all. You may stand at the box and
make speeches to doomsday, but you
cannot get over the fact that there are
94,000 unemployed in Northern Ireland.
That is the test of the whole thing. Notwithstanding all the talk we hear about
new industries no new industries of any

nominees? Supposing the Parliamentary

which would be safe and give him a good
No man is going to put down

return.

Lieut.-Colonel MITCHELL: I rise to

the House. I intimated to the Minister

caused me to ask that question. It is

The Ministry went to the doctors and said

reduced, or they must accept 18d less
than the figure definitely fixed for the
remuneration of a doctor doing panel
work. I do not believe for one moment

clause in it:
"The arrangement to which statutory
effect was given was made at the request
of the dispensary doctors themselves.
as thev preferred it to a revision of
their dispensary salaries."
What really happened was that they were
distinctly told. "You must take one or
the other." Now, the reduction of the
dispensary salaries of the older men
approaching the age for retirement would
be a very serious thing indeed, because
their pensions would be based on the
amount of money they were receiving
from the board of guardians.
After consideration the younger dispensary doctors, who were many years
away from the pensionable age, agreed
when it was insisted upon, as they had
no option, to support the older men by
agreeing to accept the reduction in remuneration. Let us be clear about that.
That is what actually happened, and it
is not fair to say they requested a reduction. No intelligent body of men would
go to a board of guardians and request
a reduction. Nine shillings was fixed
in consultation with the Council of the
British Medical Association as a right and
fair figure for panel work. Now the dispensary doctors who were approached had
to do exactly the same panel work as
any other doctor on the panel. I hold
there was never any justification for saying to them, "We will pay you less for
the definite panel work than is being paid
in England or is paid to any other panel
doctor in Northern Ireland.”

accuse boards
guardians of paying anything excep

They say, "Our opinion and our work

and have come in amongst us."
I am

Mr. BROWN: I entirely endorse all

the more experienced a man is the less
payment he will get.
Even more grotesque are the regulations under which a man who, if he is
out of employment, can draw 33s a week
for himself and his wife and family, but
if he has the misfortune to become ill
he is transferred to the National Health
Insurance Act and may get as low as 9s
a week to live on. I want this Committee to think for a moment what that
means to a man and his wife and two
children, when the man may be lying
in bed for a month, or two months, or
six months, or even years. His absolute maximum is £1 a week. But
he would get 33s a week if he were well,
and if he was well he would not require
so much money as when he was ill. That
inflicts great hardships which the framers
of these Acts never intended. The
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Labour will probably tell me, and
quite rightly so, that this is the law
in Great Britain.
Mr. BEATTIE: It is not. There the
wife and child would get public assistance

Mr. BROWN: The Leader of His

Next, I want to mention that the Ministry of Labour are going to erect a new

I cannot refrain from saying that I

if in the very unfortunate event of the

Mr. HENDERSON: If it is not your

In view of the Parliamentary Secretary's statement that it is not his

What has happened during the past
two or three months has proved that.
At the recent General Election the cry
raised by the Prime Minister was not
about the starving people, and about

unemployment. Can nothing be done to

eight years? Nothing is being done. All
the Government have to boast about is
the spending of four millions in dele. My

contention is that if the Ministry of
Labour were alive to the needs of the
people there is no earthly reason why

virtually every idle person in Northern.
Ireland. I notice that there is a saving
in this Vote. That saving is to be

given to persons who have been unemployed for the past ten or twelve years.
The plight of the unemployed is
absolutely deplorable. A division could
hardly be found in Belfast in which
poverty and destitution do not exist
owing to unemployment. Take the case
of a man who has been unemployed for
seven years. He draws unemployment
benefit for so many months; then he is
given transitional benefit, and finally unemployment assistance. In many homes.
the father, mother, and two or three
sons are idle. Immediately one member
of the family gets employment the
amount of unemployment assistance
going into the home is reduced, with the
result that the condition of the unfortunate family is in no way improved.
That is a terrible state of affairs. I feel
that the sooner the present crowd who
are running Northern Ireland are cleared
out of office the better for the citizens.
It is estimated that there are 90,000 unemployed persons in this area. The hon.
Member for Woodvale (Mr. Nixon) has
pointed out that at least 10,000 or 12,000
of our people are working in various
parts of England, Scotland and Wales.
If they were to return home they would
increase the number of unemployed to
nearly 120,000. Then we have to add to
those figures the number of unemployed
persons who do not sign at the Exchanges, because they are not entitled to
unemployment benefit. There is also a
large number of persons in employment
who are receiving a pittance equal to
the dole. I believe it is part of the duty

Mr. GORDON: We do that.
Mr. HENDERSON: If they do not
act, why not do as the Minister of Home

The unemployment figures are rising. It

if a contractor in Corporation streets

on every day for the past 17 years, and

closed for ten or twelve days at the Easter

do their utmost to give work to their employees. I feel that something extraordinary will have to be done to cope
with the problem.
One matter that gives me great concern is that of pensions for the widows
and the aged. The Ministry of Labour
have given no indication that they hope
to increase the pension of 10s. The
Ministry are satisfied to continue the
a miserable pittance
pension of 10s,
which enables the recipients to exist only

ance, and buy clothing. Is that the best

There is another matter of vital importance not mentioned in the Estimates.
During the past seventeen years many
men who had been unemployed for a considerable time died, and because they had
not sufficient stamps on their cards their
widows and orphans were not entitled to
receive pensions. Even one stamp has
been responsible in many cases for widows
and orphans not being able to receive a
pension.
I wish to protest against the fact that
the pensions of widows and orphans have
not been increased to an amount equal
to the rise in the cost of living. The
latter has gone up by 30 per cent., while
the widows and orphans are expected to
keep up a respectable appearance and be

10s per week. It was stated by the ex-
Minister of Labour, now the Minister of

Mr. GORDON: I will take a note

Mr. HENDERSON: I would rather

are paying out dole without any useful

the widows and orphans to starve, due

10s per week. Take a note of that and

represent a working-class constituency.
You are entitled to give grave consideration to statements made on this side of
the House.
Another point I wish to raise is in
connection with the reduction of transitional benefit when a member of the
household secures employment. That is
not fair. It is the duty of the Parlia
mentary Secretary to do something.
Instead of that you are going on and
on, until some day your finances will be
in such a position that you will not be
able to pay unemployment benefit.
On looking through the Estimates I
find that the policy of the Ministry of
Labour is apparently to go on constructing new labour exchanges. Is that all
you can do? I want to see labour
exchanges abolished, wiped off the slate.
I want to see new buildings going up
which will be used for giving employment to the people. Is there any cure
for unemployment? Are you attempt.
ing to find a cure? No. The Ministry
are not attempting to find a cure for
one of the greatest evils that could exist

where there is so much distress caused

Ireland. I regret to have to say that.
I would appeal to the Ministry to try

create work for our people instead of continually paying them dole. I am quite
satisfied that 99 per cent. of the men,

any scheme be adopted whereby girls in

commodity connected with the textile
industry? Why not give the employers
a subsidy? The Ministry of Labour is
in the same position as the Ministry of

hunger, suggest
suggest giving the people
physical jerks. A large sum of money

agree it is better to teach these

wrong. The Ministry is also training
them to become boxers and gymnasts

I want to protest against the tactics

the homes of the workers in Northern
Ireland. They go into the home to find

I know an ex-Serviceman with a disability pension of £2 2s per week.
Because he receives this amount his
brother only gets 3s 6d and his son 3s.
If it were not for that ex-Serviceman
giving his money into the home to keep
his brother, wife and family God knows
what would happen to them. This is
only one case of many hundreds.
The Government of this country is
hopeless and useless. If you were competent and knew your jobs instead of
fighting an election on the question of
partition and the Border bogey, which

industries. You did not do that. You

Mr. AGNEW: I listened very patiently

They now find themselves in the unhappy

When we

with the very serious consideration of

I say the Government should go into this

very important issue on the same lines

and

We come to the question of old-age
pensions. We sincerely hope the pensions will be increased to a decent
standard because, after all, the rate of
pensions paid to-day is inadequate to provide food and clothing and shelter.
Under the Unemployment Assistance Act
as it stands to-day the issue of unemployment assistance is barred simply
because there is applied what is known
as the means test. The only solution to
the problem is to have a uniform scheme
of benefits. The amount of benefit paid
is based upon the actual wages paid in
the locality which I think is very unfair,
because as you know some employers pay
very low wages and the applicant for
assistance suffers. I would like to see the
department concerned going into this.
question of unemployment assistance so
far as the means test is concerned to see
that a uniform scale should apply
throughout Northern Ireland. The overriding maximum should be abolished in
so far as wages are concerned because
wages in our district do not bear any
comparison with the rates of wages paid
in the city of Belfast and other centres.
Where there are low wages there are low
benefits. That is a very serious hardship.
We have had advisory committees set
up under the Unemployment Assistance
Board and I am not certain as to
whether the workers are represented on

another matter under unemployment
assistance and that is "not normally
insurable" under the Widows' Orphans'
and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act,
which means that unless a person can

I notice from the Parliamentary Secretary's statement that we have started an
exporting industry, exporting the youth
of Ulster to Great Britain and keeping the
old-aged. If that goes on we will in the
near future become an area populated
with old people. We are sending the best
of our youth to Britain. Would it not be
much better in the interests of the Six
Counties if the work was brought from
Britain to Northern Ireland and the youth
of this Province kept at home? There
would then be some benefit to be derived
by the parents of these boys and girls.
At the moment there is none. I do not
blame the Parliamentary Secretary.
I
blame the Minister of Commerce and the
Prime Minister. They are as guilty, if
not more guilty, than the Minister of
Labour. The Ministry of Labour to-day
are in the front-line trenches. They have
the whole burden of unemployment to
bear, and they have no material to work
upon because neither the Prime Minister
nor the Minister of Commerce has made
an effort to bring work to Northern Ireland which would suit the class of labour
available.
We have been told that one aircraft
factory is likely to come. They might as
well keep it away altogether. If Members
of this Committee were prepared to say
they would proceed to London and argue
our case for the establishment of five
factories there would be prospects of getting some naval contracts. I have before
me a very nice document setting out the
conditions in England, what England has
received, what Scotland has received,
and what Northern Ireland has received.
I was greatly surprised and shocked to
learn that we get as little as some countries with no claim on Britain at all.
The £3,600,000 quoted for battleships
was got because the price was suitable.
We have got a battleship, but that, in
my opinion, is nothing to be jollified
about. We should have had more of
that class of work. Have we got the aircraft work we are capable of turning out?
We have Short & Harland's started.
had no previous experience of aircraft.
manufacture, and I challenge any man

We could do with a factory in Londonderry, and we could do with another in

Mr. BEATTIE: A trade board. I am
sorry. Since took over it disappeared, and no reason was given for its
disappearance. I noticed documents in
the Scottish Linen Workers' Guild on

Northern Ireland. We have been told
in a very able manner by the Parliamentary Secretary that he is prepared
to give 85 per cent. grants to revenue
and non-revenue work, and he is setting
aside £150,000. That is only a drop in
the ocean when there are 110,000 people
unemployed. You say the total unemployed are only 72,000, and that there
are some casually employed and intermittently unemployed, but I claim there
are 110,000 people unemployed in Northern Ireland. About 30 per cent. of the
total have been unemployed for the last
five or six years. In Belfast alone there
are upwards of 3,000 people who have
been unemployed from two to eight years,
and what are you going to do for them?
You are doing nothing now. The whole
position of unemployment should be
tackled more seriously than in the past,
and I hope the Parliamentary Secretary,
if he gets an opportunity to reply,
which is very doubtful, and I know he
does not want to reply, will deal with
the point I have put forward.
Dealing with the question of the Richhill farm mentioned by the hon. Member for South Armagh, are you aware
that that farm has won prizes throughout Northern Ireland for its products.
It has been stated that it is necessary
to maintain that farm so that it could
be used for the purpose for which it
was used in the past. At present the
farm is paying a good wage to its
labourers. It is producing a good
article, and I do not see why we should
make any sacrifice by disposing of it.
If there is a prospective buyer in this
House, we will have to consider increasing
the price. I approve of this place being
used only for the purpose for which it
is used now, that is, production for home
use, and not production for export in
the way of sending boys to Canada and
elsewhere. I want it to be used for
training boys to remain on the land.
I think the time is now opportune to
consider the question of widows' and oldage pensions. I want to put this point
before you. How is it that in England
the Unemployment Assistance Board
can give assistance to persons at the age
of 65? You
may tell me that they
have no power to do so. I may be told
that the assistance to which I refer takes
the form of parish relief; it does nothing
of the sort. I should like the Parliamentary Secretary to elicit information
on that point, because we cannot obtain
it here. We cannot get a halfpenny
here from any quarter. The pensioner
here has to depend solely upon the
pension.
I have read the correspondence in the
Press about the training of boys for the
mercantile marine. It is a good thing to
train boys for the mercantile marine, and
I approve of it; but I do not see any
reason why we should send them to
Gravesend. We can train boys for the
mercantile marine in Northern Ireland as
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
28 APRIL 1938
well as they can train them at Gravesend.
This reminds me of engineers who have
to go to London or Edinburgh to sit for
their ticket; no arrangements are made
for them to sit for the examinations at
home. We could apply ourselves usefully
to the establishment of a college for this
purpose, and thus provide boys with the
ambition to go to sea with facilities for
studying at home.
I know that you will
have public opinion with you if you decide
to establish a school for the education of
these boys whom you are now sending to
Gravesend.
National health insurance is the last
subject with which I wish to deal. Of
course it is owned by the Prudential
Assurance Company, one of the biggest
insurance organisations in Great Britain.
The Government only run it for them;
they own it. The Prudential millions are
referred to in a little paper that you
know well, "Forward.”
This money is
all taken from industrial assurance and
national health insurance. Where is it
invested? I cannot mention any notable
firms in Northern Ireland in which it is
invested. I do not see any of it in Ulster
Savings Certificates. I cannot find very
much in war bonds because the interest is
going down. I find that a very large proportion of it is lent to Germany and to
Poland. That is where our money is
going.
I think we in Northern Ireland should
consider the advisability of making
national health insurance a national service. The funds of that national service
would then be at the disposal of this
House, and not at the disposal of foreign
countries as they are to-day. It never
was the intention of the founders of this
scheme of national health insurance that
it should be run by friendly societies or
trade unions. It never was intended that
those organisations should have the right
to interfere with the administration of
this insurance. It was intended to be a
national service controlled and administered by the nation, and the benefits
accruing from the moneys collected were
intended for the nation. Through circumstances over which there was no control at
the time, the Prudential and other societies
were so powerful that the Government
of the day had to give way, and allow
them to enter the national health section
of the insurance scheme. From that
time onwards they have been making
huge sums of money from it, and they
have now a sum of 33 millions odd invested abroad. I feel that that justifies
my argument that there should be
national control of the National Health
Insurance scheme. We have national
control of unemployment. Why not have
national control of National Health Insurance? Let the people who contribute
to these funds receive the benefits
accruing from their contributions. I feel
that in this way the Northern Government could give a valuable lead to Great
Britain, where they could follow step by
step. From that source we could obtain
funds to sink in industries in Northern
Ireland. Before closing I should like
to express the hope that the Parliamentary Secretary will bear in mind my
remarks about the Unemployment
Assistance Board, and I can assure him
that this is not the last he has heard
of it.

Oral Answers to Questions.
HOUSING CONDITIONS IN
CROSSMAGLEN.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can give any
information regarding housing conditions
in Crossmaglen; whether he can state
how many houses have been condemned
by the authority concerned as unfit for
human habitation; what action has been
taken by the local sanitary officer on this
matter and how many of such unsanitary
houses have been inspected by the sanitary officer for the year ending 31st
March, 1938.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am informed that
the Newry No. 2 Rural District Council
received only four applications from persons living in Crossmaglen for houses in
connection with the scheme of labourers'
cottages which they are preparing. The
houses of two of the applicants were
condemned by the Medical Officer of
Health as unfit for habitation. In the
other two cases, the houses were too
small for the families occupying them.
The Council is providing in their scheme
for the occupants of these four houses.
The local sanitary sub-officer made 145
house inspections during the year ended
31st March, 1938.
OUTDOOR RELIEF IN
CROSSMAGLEN.
now
2. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can
give any information as to any increased
allowances granted to recipients of outdoor relief in Crossmaglen district;
whether this area was visited by an
inspector and certain cases interviewed;
what report has been issued by the
Relieving Officer in Crossmaglen, who
accompanied the inspector, in regard to
outdoor relief; and whether, in view of
the distress prevailing in that district, he
will make further investigations.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The action
taken by Boards of Guardians on applications for relief is not communicated to
this Ministry and I am not, therefore,
in a position to state whether the allowof outdoor relief have been
increased in any cases in the Crossmaglen district.
ances
Oral Answers
Oral Answers.
3 MAY 1938
My Ministry's inspector did, however,
visit this district recently and, with the
Relieving Officer and the Secretary of
the local Labour Party, discussed eight
cases which were brought to his notice.
If it is these cases which the hon. Member has in mind I may inform him that
I understand that of these eight cases,
only four were considered to call for
further investigation or inspection. Of
these, two appeared to be more suitable
for indoor relief than for outdoor relief,
and with regard to the other two, the
inspector was of opinion that there
appeared to be a prima facie case for
further consideration by the Guardians,
but the Ministry is not aware whether
these cases have as yet been reconsidered.
With regard to the latter part of the
question, I would point out that the
administration of relief is a matter for
the Guardians, and the Ministry is precluded from directing them to grant
relief. So long as the Guardians carry
out their duties in a reasonable way it
would be quite outside my province to
interfere, and I may add in this connection that my Ministry's inspector
informs me that applications for relief
receive very sympathetic consideration
at the hands of the Newry Guardians.
Mr. AGNEW: Will the Ministry
make further investigation into the conditions prevailing in that area?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Certainly. I
am quite prepared to do that.

of an adequate water supply for the

by my Ministry.
During the latter part of last year
the Council decided to take steps to
obtain the necessary powers to improve
the existing water supply which
obtained from Clea Lake, but in view
of the opposition to the scheme by the
is
ratepayers it was decided to postpone
the scheme.
With regard to the latter part of
the question, there is no fund at the
disposal of my Ministry out of which
assistance could be afforded to sanitary
authorities for work of this kind, but the
Council are, no doubt, fully aware of the
assistance given by the Ministry of
Labour towards the cost of labour in
connection with schemes approved for
the relief of unemployment.

in Keady make representations to you,
in view of the conditions prevailing regarding a water supply, will you give
it serious consideration?

Home Affairs aware of the fact that

CONDITION OF BESSBROOK
STREETS.
5. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can give
information as to the condition of certain
streets in Bessbrook under the control of Newry Rural (No. 2) District
Council, the reason why the Council
refused to consider this matter at a
recent meeting, and, in the event of
residents in these streets being injured
owing to the deplorable conditions
mentioned, can he state who is liable.
Sir DAWSON BATES: All the
streets in Bessbrook which are under the
control of the Newry No. 2. Rural District Council are in a good state of
repair. I understand that certain streets
in the village are not under the control
of the Council, and in the event of any
person being injured as a result of the
condition of such streets, it would be for
the courts to decide any question of
liability for such injuries.
It is open to a Rural Council, if they
see fit to do so, to take over privately
owned streets and charge their maintenance to public funds, but obviously
all relevant circumstances have to be
carefully considered before this course is
adopted, and so many considerations
arise in a matter of this kind that it
is quite impossible to record specific
reasons for the decision reached.
I understand the Council have not
refused to consider the matter, but have
decided to take no action on it at
present.

when it is intended to introduce the

Sir DAWSON BATES: I hope to circulate the heads of the proposed Housing
Bill to local authorities within the next
few days. As soon as their observations
are received the preparation of the Bill
will be proceeded with forthwith.

CRIMINAL INJURIES IN COUNTY
ARMAGH.
12. Mr. JOHNSTON asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state why the
ratepayers of the County of Armagh
should be called upon to pay, under the
heading of criminal injuries, for damages
sustained by private persons in Northern
Ireland on the occasion of the visit of
Their Majesties the King and Queen on
the 28th July, 1937, seeing that the outrages out of which these damages arose
were committed by persons living outside Northern Ireland, and whether the
Imperial Government claimed for telegraph and telephone lines and Customs'
huts destroyed on that occasion.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The matter
referred to by the hon. Member has been
the subject of very careful consideration
by the Government, and the suggestion
of the hon. Member as to the origin of
the outrages in question has not been
overlooked. The Government cannot,
however, admit that the circumstances
would warrant the abandonment of the
principles of the Criminal Injury Code,
and it may be pointed out, moreover,
that there is no proof that residents of
Northern Ireland were not at any rate
aiders and abetters of the outrages in
question.
With regard to the latter part of the
question, claims were made by the
Imperial Government in respect of the
matters mentioned, but this Government
thought it would be undesirable that His
Majesty's Government should appear as
claimant in respect of damage arising on
the occasion referred to, and urged the
Imperial Government to withdraw its
claim.
The consent of the Imperial Government to this course was obtained on the
undertaking by the Government of
Northern Ireland that the cost of replacement of the property destroyed should
fall upon Northern Ireland Government
funds and would not be regarded as an
Imperial charge.
The same considerations did not, however, apply in the case of private
property, and the Government came to
the conclusion that no sufficient grounds
existed to justify any further acceptance
by the Government of the liability which
is imposed by statute upon the ratepayers.
Mr. NIXON: Is this action on the
part of the Government another
surrender? Why did the Government
not see that the Imperial Government
did this?
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman inform the House under what
practice or custom he has the right to
authorise the erection of huts outside the
jurisdiction of this Parliament ?
Sir DAWSON BATES: That is going
very far.
I used to think that individuals or Governments, lawfully exercising their rights, had a perfect right to
erect any houses in any place in Northern
Ireland.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
it is the bounden duty of the Imperial
Government to meet your claim, and
what right have you to commit this
House to anything which is the responsibility and right of another Parliament?

PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

county borough of Belfast on the 1st
April, 1924, and from that date to the
31st March, 1937, the expenditure out
of the capital account on the erection and

alteration, extension and equipment of

The total amount of the loan charges met

Towards the total net expenditure on all

was about £1,304,000, towards which the

During the year 1936-37 the amount
expended by the Education Authority in

£223.
The cost of the administrative staff in
1936-37 (exclusive of school attendance
officers and the administrative staff of the
College of Technology) on salaries, wages
and insurance was £3,755.
The salaries, wages and insurance of
the education architect and staff
amounted to £3,316 in 1936-37, and the
rent, rates, taxes and insurance of office
premises to £111.
When the position of education
architect was first created in 1924 it was
assumed that, pending experience, the
appointment would be of a temporary
nature. On the resignation of the officer
first appointed representations were made
to the Ministry that men with qualifications and experience necessary for this
important position could not be obtained
and retained for a temporary post, and
the Ministry offered no objection to the
post being regarded as permanent in the
same manner as for other whole-time employees of the authority, if it was desired
to do so; I may mention that the post
is terminable by three months' notice on
either side.
The appointment of an education
architect was first made in June, 1924.
In view of the building programme of the
Belfast Education Authority it is not
possible to say how long the employment
of a whole-time education architect will
be necessary.
Most of the information in respect of
the items of expenditure has been
obtained from the Belfast Corporation's
abstract of accounts for the year 1936-37,
which are the latest accounts at present
available.

COMMUTATION OF LAND
ANNUITIES.
Mr. MINFORD asked the Minister of
Finance whether any representations have
been made by him to the British Government to commute that part of the land
annuities payable by the Ulster farmers
to the Imperial Exchequer, and if not,
whether he is prepared to make representations so as to place the Ulster farmers
in the same financial position as the
farmers of Eire under the recent arrangements made between the British Government and the Government of Eire.
Mr. ANDREWS: As the hon. Member's question indicates some misapprehension of the effect of the recent financial
agreement between the Government of the
United Kingdom and the Government of
Eire, it is desirable for me to reply at
some length.
Under the financial agreement made
between the United Kingdom and the
Irish Free State in 1923 the Irish Free
State Government was to collect the
annuities then existing and pay them
over to the British Government. Annuities arising out of subsequent land purchase schemes were the subject of Irish
Free State finance and were no concern
of the British Government.
The recent Agreement settles for a sum
of £10,000,000 all financial claims
between the Government of the United
Kingdom and the Government of Eire,
and included in such claims is the payment of annuities due to be made to the
British Government under the 1923
Agreement. The recent Agreement has
nothing to do with the relations between
the Government of Eire and the tenant
purchasers, nor has it any concern with
the post-1921 annuities, which never
affected the British Government in any
way.
The position in Northern Ireland is not
similar. The Government of Northern
Ireland has never had to make any payments to the British Government in
respect of annuities existing in 1921.
The money has accrued to the Exchequer
of Northern Ireland, and farmers in
various ways have had returned to them
more than the equivalent amount. As
regards annuities subsequent to 1921, the
amounts collected have been handed over
to the British Government in accordance
with the provisions of the Government of
Ireland Act.
It will be clear from this comparison
that there were no grounds for our
Government making representations to
the British Government, because under
the Government of Ireland Act of 1920,
which the South of Ireland rejected, we
already had been given what is now given
to the Government of Eire.
It is a fact that in the year 1933 the
Government of the Irish Free State (as
it was then called) passed an Act of
Parliament halving the amount of the
land purchase annuities payable by
tenant purchasers to the State, and the
resultant burden on the Free State Land
Purchase Funds and Guarantee Funds
has been accepted by their Exchequer,
but this concession was entirely a matter
of local concern and did not interest the
Government of the United Kingdom.
A mere comparison between the
annuity position here and in the rest of
Ireland would be misleading, because to
arrive at a true relative position of the
farmers in both areas one would have
to take into consideration not only the
Written Answers

annuities but also such matters as the
effect of full derating of agricultural land
and farm buildings in Northern Ireland,
marketing subsidies and grants for the
fertilization of land as compared with any
corresponding reliefs or assistance which
may be given in the rest of Ireland.

The investigation of the cause and

but if the

Superannuation (Teaching Services)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Lieut-Colonel GORDON: This Bill
deals with several unrelated matters,
and therefore it will be convenient to
take the Clauses one by one and give an
explanation of each. Clause 1 provides
for the carrying out of the undertaking
given in the Minister of Finance's Budget Speech of last year, under which the
pension of teachers who suffered cuts as
a result of the reductions in salary are
recalculated as from the 1st July, 1937,
as if no economy cut had taken place.
a
The partial restoration of pensions on
partly restored salary cut took effect, of
course, a year previously. The lump
sum payment which is made to teachers
on retirement in addition to their pension is also payable on the full restored
salaries, not only from the 1st July last
but also for the prior year.
Clause 2 provides in the case of Northern Ireland teachers for the application to them of an arrangement which
was brought into operation last year in
Great Britain in the case of teachers and
which is already in force in Great Britain
and in Northern Ireland as regards civil
servants, that is, to allow a teacher on
retirement on ordinary pension to allocate part of his or her pension to a
dependant. This arrangement has been
asked for by the teachers' organisations
in Northern Ireland and will not inwolve any additional charge either on
the Exchequer or the Teachers' Pension
Fund as the amount surrendered
actuarially equivalent to the amount of
pension to be granted to the dependant.
The subsidiary pension can take either
of two forms-first, a pension payable
for the period, if any, during which the
dependant survives the teacher; or
second, an annuity payable during the
joint lives of the pensioner and his wife
and a pension payable to the wife if she
survives the teacher.
is
The pension allocation scheme, which
is necessary to bring the scheme into
operation, will be promulgated as soon
as possible, and a code of directions explanatory of the provisions of the scheme,
and setting out in tables exactly what a
teacher can receive when he or she
allocates his pension, will be available.
How far the terms of the Bill will be
availed of is highly problematical. The
Civil Service experience does not indicate any great enthusiasm for the adoption of its terms.
Certain
Under Clause 3 it is proposed to

Mr. BEATTIE: The Parliamentary
Secretary has clearly set out the contents of this short Measure. I do not
grumble about what it contains. My
grumble is directed more to what it
evades. It is trying to relieve the
Government of their responsibility to the
serving teacher, and to get them out of
a difficult position in reference to their
claim to follow step by step. In England and in Scotland, when this matter
was brought forward, it applied to all
serving teachers, irrespective of the
period of time during which they had
been teaching. In Northern Ireland
the Government are by statute restricting the right to claim this superannuation and lump sum to teachers serving
only from July, 1937, onwards. But
they have omitted to give any consideration or attention to past services.
I do feel that this is a matter to which
the House will have to give serious attention-whether they are going to continue
the preference to the younger element
who entered the service since last July,
and fail to recognise their responsibilities
to the older teachers who have carried
through the 1923 Act so successfully,
and who have been classified throughout
the British Isles as the cream of the
teaching profession. I ask the Minister
of Finance to give this point of view
serious consideration. If this passes, a
grave injustice will be imposed upon the
teachers who were in the service prior to
July last. The Government will be
creating an injustice that was not imposed in England or Scotland. I hope
to have from the Minister the pleasant
news that this will apply to all teachers
in the service.
The Parliamentary Secretary has
stated on the question of allocation that
this has not come off so well in the Civil
Service. This is not by any means a
thing that one should jump at. I have
gone into the matter. I asked the
reason why the Civil Servants of Northern Ireland have not taken advantage
of the allocation, and I was informed
that the reason only one-third had
availed themselves of this provision is
that better terms can be had from
private companies. I think the Government should set themselves up as model
employers, and should make the terms so
attractive that not only every teacher

Physical Training and Recreation

Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
Motion made and Question proposed,
That for the purpose of any Act of
the present Session "to provide for the
development of facilities for, and the
encouragement of, physical training
and recreation, and to facilitate the
establishment of centres for social
activities," it is expedient to authorise
the payment out of moneys provided
by Parliament of—
(1) all expenses incurred by the Ministry of Education, for the purposes
of such Act, including the amount
of any grants paid or payable
under or by virtue of such Act in
accordance with arrangements
approved by the Ministry of
Finance or in accordance with the
provisions of sub-section (1) of
section ten of the Education Act
(Northern Ireland), 1930;
(2) any payments which the Ministry
of Education may,
with the
approval of the Ministry of
Finance, make in respect of—
(a) administrative expenses of the
Advisory Council to be established under such Act and of its
committees, and of the grants
committee to be so established;
(b) allowances to members of such
Council, committee and grants
committee;
(c) remuneration to the chairman
of the grants committee.-
(Governor's Recommendation
signified-Mr. Andrews).
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: The first
part of the Resolution on the Order
Paper covers the grants which will be
payable by the Ministry of Education,
subject to the approval of the Ministry
of Finance, on the recommendations of
the grants committee which is to be
established under the Act. These
grants may be classified under two
headings:-Firstly, for the provision by
local authorities, managers of schools
(not being elementary schools), or voluntary organisations of various facilities
for physical training and recreation, such
as gymnasiums, playing-fields, and SO
forth; and, secondly, towards the expenses of local authorities in employing
staff to organise physical training.
The total amount which it is proposed
to allocate from Voted moneys for the
provision of facilities under the first
head is £65,000, while towards the expenses of personnel under the second
head the amount voted will be comparatively small. In both cases the grant
will not exceed one-half of the total expenses to be incurred by the local
authority or voluntary organisation concerned.
I should like to make it clear that the
portion of the expenditure remaining on
the rates will not in addition rank for
the usual Exchequer grant in aid of the
annual educational expenditure of a
local education authority.
This part of the Resolution also covers
the expenditure resulting from the
amendment of Section 10 of the Education Act of 1930; that amendment
enables the Ministry of Education to include in the capital expenditure
voluntary schools ranking for grant expenditure on such items as are
vided for the purpose of physical
training and recreation.

Mr. BYRNE: I beg to move the
Second Reading of this Bill, and commend it to the support of the House for
the following reasons. The object of
this Bill is to promote public health by
having all hairdressers' premises registered with the local authority in whose
area they are situated, with a view to
Hairdressers Bill-
Second Reading
3 MAY 1938
having the local authorities make and
operate such bylaws as will, in an inexpensive way, provide for the cleanliness.
of such premises and all apparatus used
therein, and thereby safeguard the public against infection with disease.
This Measure is to operate only in
those areas where the local authority
concerned apply to the Ministry of
Home Affairs for it to be applied to
their area, and, where it applies, only
within such premises as are registered
for the purpose can the trade of hairdressing be carried on. Apart from
this, the text of the Bill is easily understood, and is self-explanatory.
To show further that the House can
support this Bill without any fear of its

to spend money to provide utensils for
the proper cleansing of the tools
apparatus they use in their work of hairdressing, I will now submit to the House
a communication received from the

So far as the registration of hairdressers is concerned the following
local Acts of Parliament contain
provision requiring every person who
carries on the trade or business of a
hairdresser or barber to register his
name and place of abode and the
premises in which the trade or business is carried on in a book to be kept
at the offices of the Council. The
maximum penalty for carrying on the
trade or business without first registering is 40s, and a daily penalty not
exceeding 20s. A court of summary
jurisdiction may order the suspension
or cancellation of the registration.
That applies to Middlesbrough, Wolverhampton, Newcastle-under - Lyme,
Rotherham, Southampton and West
Ham.
On the bylaw aspect the following
local Acts contain provisions enabling
the local authority to make bylaws for
the purpose of securing the cleanliness
of any premises used for the purpose
of carrying on the business of a hairdresser or barber, and of the instruments, towels, and materials used in
such premises.
That applies to Essex, Middlesbrough,
Middlesex, Hertfordshire, Stoke-on-
Trent, Surrey, Wolverhampton, Newcastle-under-Lyme, Rotherham, Southampton and West Ham. The letter
concludes:
The Essex, Middlesex, Hertfordshire, and Surrey Acts enable all local
authorities in those countries to make
bylaws. The maximum penalty for
offences under the bylaws is, in the
case of Essex, 40s, and a daily penalty
not exceeding 20s, and in the other
cases £5, and a daily penalty not exceeding 40s.
The following are the bylaws applied
by these local authorities:-
1. For the purpose of securing the
cleanliness of the premises used for the
purpose of carrying on the business
of a hairdresser or barber, every person carrying on such a business shall
in every part of the premises so used.
cause-

These are some of the conditions under
which the business is carried on across
the water. That communication and
the copy of the draft bylaws which are
operated in the case of very many of
the cross-Channel centres show that this
Bill will enable local authorities here
to do what cross-Channel authorities are
doing to promote public health so far as
it is affected by the work of those in
the trade of barber or hairdresser.
When a Bill similar in object to this
one was before the House all parties
approved of it in principle, because, like
the Public Health authorities who support the principle of this Bill, its object
had their approval. That Bill was withdrawn by consent, in order that the
promoters might arrange with the
Ministry of Home Affairs to discuss the
matter and then submit an agreed Bill.
This is an agreed Bill, because it was
drawn up by the Home Office.
Here is a letter from the Home Office
to the Secretary of the Hairdressers'

With reference to your letter of the
22nd instant and conversations which
we have had regarding the proposed
Hairdressers Bill, I now enclose copies
of a Bill which might be presented
by some Member of Parliament on
behalf of your Association when Parliament reassembles for the opening of
the new Session. You will see that
what is proposed is an adoptive Act
which local authorities can take up if

not in accordance with your request
that the legislation should be compulsory and apply to the whole of Northern Ireland. If your Association does
not like this draft, it is, of course,
open to them to amend it in any way
they like, but the Government takes
no responsibility for its contents.
I am informed that the Association
approved of this Bill, and I trust there
will not be any opposition to it. This
letter shows that the promoters have
made every endeavour to meet the wishes
of the Ministry of Home Affairs in
regard to this Measure.

Mr. MAGINESS: I rise to oppose this
Bill, which I think is a deliberate attack
against the few remaining liberties of the
citizens. From the moment of birth
until the moment of death the lives of
people are harried from morning to night
by hordes of inspectors and other officials.
From the moment a man arrives at his
office in the morning until the moment he
goes to bed at night he is largely occupied
in filling up forms. Up to the present
one of the few remaining refuges a man
had was the barber's shop. He could
slip in there for a few quiet moments and
escape from the conditions under which
he has to live. It is only necessary to
compare the feelings of a citizen going into
a barber's shop now with what they will
be if this Bill is passed in order to realise
how seriously we in this House should
contemplate the Measure brought forward.
At the present time we can slip into a

We can lean back in the chair and
visualise the prospect of Aston Villa
getting up into the First Division, and
for ten or twenty minutes we can forget
the troubles and worries of this life.
We are encouraged, indeed, to go out
and face our responsibilities in a

Now, if this Bill is passed, the first

form, and having studied that we ask to

and have a white cloak put round our

authority that
that his shop has been

shop, but I speak as an ordinary citizen
who does not want to spend his time
inspecting the various forms and certificates in any barber's shop. I go there

When we
