Oral Answers to Questions.
TRAINING OF ROMAN CATHOLIC
TEACHERS.
.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether she can state how
many Roman Catholic public elementary
school teachers have been trained for
Northern Ireland since the opening of
the Ministry's own college at Stranmillis; what is the financial difference in
the cost of training a teacher in Stranmillis and in other training colleges in
which Roman Catholic teachers are at
present being trained; what is the loss
to the Exchequer (if any) owing to the
fact that these Roman Catholic teachers
are not trained in the Ministry's own
training college at Stranmillis.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): Since the
date of opening of Stranmillis Training
College, 234 Roman Catholic men
students and 521 Roman Catholic
women students have been trained for
the position of public elementary school
teachers in Northern Ireland.
In the case of women students, the
capitation grants payable to Stranmillis
Training College and
College and to St. Mary's
Training College, Belfast, are the same
and there is therefore no difference in
the cost to the Exchequer.
In the case of men students the capitation grant payable to Stranmillis
Training College is £70 per annum,
and that to St. Mary's Training
College, London, for Roman Catholic
men students, is similar to the
rate fixed from time to time by the
English Board of Education in respect
of English students attending that
college. The rate in operation for the
last completed session (1936-37) was
£72 7s.
With regard to the last part of the
question, any estimate of the possible
difference in cost to the Exchequer of
the establishment of a combined training
college in lieu of the present arrangement would necessarily be largely conjectural. As additional premises would
have to be provided at Stranmillis
Training College for the accommodation
of Roman Catholic students certain
capital expenditure would be necessary,
and it will be appreciated that this
factor would have an important bearing
on the cost per student to the Exchequer.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the hon. Lady is it not a fact that the
cost of the training of male Catholic
teachers to the students and the students'
parents is a heavier financial responsibility that it is to the parents of the
students who attended Stranmillis; and
is it not a fact that it was due to the
lack of college accommodation that the
agreement was entered into with the
clerical managers for the training of
teachers for their schools in 1923, and
in view of that position is the hon.
Lady Member prepared to recommend
the establishment of a Roman Catholic
training college in Northern Ireland?
Mrs. PARKER: I think so many
questions are involved that the hon.
Member had better put down another
question so as to give more notice.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
4 MAY 1938
POSITION OF CONVENT AND
CHRISTIAN BROTHERS' SCHOOLS.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether she can state if the
teachers in convent and Christian
Brothers' schools are trained and qualified according to the standard required
by the Ministry in the case of teachers
in other public elementary schools;
whether these schools are subject to the
same inspection by the Ministry as other
public elementary schools, and whether
the salaries for these teachers are paid
direct to the teachers themselves, and,
if not, to whom are these salaries paid.
Mrs. PARKER: On 31st December,
1937, the public elementary schools in
Northern Ireland recognised by the
Ministry included 44 convent and seven
Christian Brothers' schools. Of the convent schools eight are staffed under the
regulations applicable to ordinary public
elementary schools, and the teachers
receive personal salaries. The remaining
36 convent schools and the Christian
Brothers' schools receive grants on a
capitation basis in respect of the teaching services of the members of the
religious community or order concerned;
in most of these schools, however, lay
assistants are also employed who, in
general, possess the usual qualifications
of public elementary teachers, and they
receive the appropriate salaries.
Prior to 1st January, 1937, it was
not a condition of the recognition of
schools which received capitation grants
that the teaching members of the community or order should be trained
teachers. Those appointed subsequent to
that date, however, must, as a condition
of permanent recognition, possess the
qualifications required in the case of
ordinary lay teachers, and, in addition,
some members of the existing staffs at
that date were already fully qualified.
Convent and Christian Brothers'
schools are inspected by the Ministry's
officers in the same way as other public
elementary schools.
In reply to the latter part of the
question, personal salaries, where payable, are paid direct to the teachers entitled to receive them, but where capitation grant is payable it is paid to the
community or order.
Mr. BYRNE: Would the hon. Lady
admit that these Nun teachers are very
highly qualified and that the greatest
tribute has been paid to them from time
to time, and is the hon. Lady aware
that the Catholic community are prepared to make any sacrifice in order that
the religion to which they belong should
be taught in Catholic schools under
Catholic management?
ASSISTANCE TO PIGS AND BACON
INDUSTRY.
3. Mr. J. JOHNSTON asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he is yet in a
position to make any statement with
regard to assistance to the pigs and
bacon industry in Northern Ireland on
lines similar to those announced for
Great Britain.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): I am happy
to be able to inform the hon. Member
that the Government has decided during
the next three years to provide a
measure of financial assistance to the pigs
and bacon industry in Northern Ireland.
This assistance will, as far as possible,
be on lines similar to those contained in
the Bacon Industry Bill at present
before the Parliament at Westminster.
As the hon. Member is aware, the assistance in Great Britain is designed not
as a subsidy but as a scheme of reorganisation, having as its object the establishment of an efficient pig producing
and bacon curing industry in Great
Britain, capable of meeting foreign
competition. It is clearly essential that
during the next three years a state of,
at the very least, equal efficiency shall be
secured in Northern Ireland. The problem is full of real difficulties and will
require the utmost goodwill on the part of
both producers' organisations and curers
in the interests of establishing a prosperous industry in the Province. I hope
to be able to present my proposals to
the House during the present session.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: Arising out
of that reply, may I ask whether the
right hon. Gentleman will give this
House an assurance that any legislation
which may be considered necessary for
the administration of such assistance will
not be introduced until fully discussed
and agreed to by the representatives of
the interests concerned?
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Yes, Sir. I will
discuss the matter, as I have always
done, with those concerned.
DEE STREET AND HOLYWOOD
ARCHES.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state on
what date the Belfast Corporation proposes to commence work on the widening
of Dee Street Arch, and the Holywood
Arches.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As I informed the hon. Member on a previous
occasion, the widening of the Dee Street
Bridge is being undertaken by the Government in conjunction with the by-pass
road and will be carried out in connection with that work. It is not possible to say at present how soon the
work can be commenced, but it will be
undertaken without avoidable delay.
I understand that at its meeting on
the 1st day of last month the Belfast
Corporation decided that, having regard
to the need for stringent economy, it
would not proceed, at present, with the
widening of the Holywood Arches, but
that the question would be reconsidered
when money is available.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman is he not
aware that the widening of Dee Street
and the Holywood Arches has no connection whatsoever with the making of
the by-pass road, and is he aware that
the loss of life that has taken place at
these two points is of such a kind that
economy should not be given any consideration by the right hon. Gentleman?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid
the hon. Member misunderstands the
situation. As I pointed out before, the
by-pass road and Dee Street Bridge are
the same problem and are being carried
out by the Government. As regards the
other bridge at the Holywood Arches,
that is an ordinary matter in which the
Government are prepared to subscribe to
the Belfast Corporation, provided they
do the work. The Belfast Corporation
originally intended to do the work with
the Government assistance promised, but
since that time the Corporation decided
not to carry out the work.

Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
the right hon. Gentleman has full power
to sack the Belfast Corporation from the
work at the Holywood Arches and get the
work expedited in view of the danger to
pedestrians on that part of the road?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would not
like to deal with that by question and
answer.
Mr. GRANT: Is it a fact that the
Minister has been approached by the
directors of the Glentoran Football Club
not to start this job in Dee Street until
the football season is over, and now that
it is over will he see that the work is
expedited?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, I cannot
allow sport to interfere with public
business.
BELFAST-HOLYWOOD BY-PASS
ROAD.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
total number of men employed on the bypass road and by what method does the
engineer in charge select the workmen
required.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The number
of men employed on the by-pass road is
at the moment 41.
Apart from the filling of certain jobs.
for which special qualifications are
necessary, the workmen employed
are recruited from the Employment
Exchange.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it a fact that this
scheme was opened by the Minister with
a view to getting employment for the
unemployed, and is he in a position to
say that a reasonable time has expired
and that the numbers in employment are
too low?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The only
thing I can assure the hon. Member
about is that the engineer is only too
anxious to expedite the work as rapidly
as possible, but the hon. Member will
appreciate that there are certain technical
engineering works and surveys to be carried
out before an additional staff of men can
be put on the job.

TRANSPORT BOARD AND FORMER

6. Captain PATRICK asked the Minister

full compensation; and whether he will
see that in such cases the value of the
vehicles taken over is paid to the previous
owners immediately.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am
informed by the Transport Board as
follows:
The hon. and gallant Member is presumably referring to a case in which he
has been in communication with the
Transport Board. In this case untrue
information was furnished to the Board
by the owners, who represented that
they had started business some considerable time before the 1st June, 1934.
The owners have already been paid the

EXPENSES OF UNSWORN
MEMBERS.
7. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Prime
Minister whether the Government intends
to introduce legislation to make it illegal

taken the Oath of Allegiance to continue

The PRIME MINISTER: No, sir,
the answer is in the negative.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask the Prime
Minister whether it is a fact that some
of these abstentionist Members who are
not attending to the business of this
House have not hesitated to attend committees in the House for which they
receive two guineas per sitting, and will
he take steps to prevent such while these
Members continue to disfranchise their
constituents?
The PRIME MINISTER: That is a
matter for the constituents to a large
extent, and it would involve us in great
difficulties if we differentiated between

House for other reasons and those to

Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask the Prime

to constituents, of which I am one, being
in a constituency the Member for which
has disfranchised me what steps does
he think I can take?
The PRIME MINISTER: The hon.
Member might urge the people in his
constituency to vote next time for someone who will attend.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I inform the
Prime Minister I did that, but it was
no use?

House will refuse to give a Second Reading to this Measure.
In the first place I should like to
protest very emphatically against the
way this Measure has been introduced
into this House. This Measure has been
introduced into the House without any
consideration being given to the interests
concerned. That is in direct conflict

with the statement made by the Prime

to put their money into creameries it is

Ministry's

The undertaking was that creameries

Minister introduced this new concern in

What the creameries want to-day is
more milk, not more ways of manufacturing it. There is not a creamery in
Northern Ireland to-day working to
capacity, and what the Ministry ought
to be doing to-day is devising ways and
means for helping the farmer to increase
the cow population and to increase his
production of milk for the creameries
that are at present working at half
capacity. We do not want any more
ways of manufacturing milk until our
creameries are going full steam ahead.
Not a creamery in Northern Ireland,
as I have already stated, is operating at
anything like more than half capacity,
and some even less than that. Surely
we might take an object lesson from the
bacon scheme in Great Britain, where
there is to be a revision owing to the
fact that there are too many factories
operating at less than 40 per cent. of
their capacity. If a revised scheme is
necessary in regard to the bacon industry it is just as necessary in the dairying industry. What we want is not more
machinery but more milk to operate our
existing plant.
Might I suggest to the Minister that
the proper procedure and the proper
policy for the Government to adopt
would be, first of all, to increase the
quantity and improve the quality of the
milk. Secondly, they should help
towards increasing the butter fat of the
milk. Thirdly, they should increase the
gallonage per cow, and last, but not least,
encourage the producer to retain marketing control. Up to the present the
Minister and the Ministry have been cooperating with the agricultural community in order to get more and more
control of the sale of their products. We
have a new system introduced to-day by
the Minister, whereby a proprietary
money-making concern is to be brought
into Northern Ireland, and the farmers
are going to be asked to supply milk
to it. They may pay as good a price
as the creameries are paying at present
and even more than the latter can afford
to pay, but if they manage to put the
creameries out of existence have the
agriculturists any guarantee that they
will continue to pay the enhanced price?
Then the farmers who have invested
their money in the creameries, when the
creameries are put out of existence, will
lose their money and will have no market
but Nestlé's or some other concern out
to make money. They will then be back
under the conditions which existed under
the old pig marketing days, when the

creameries are down and out, and we
expect you to do the best you can for
us."
That is the position the Minister
and the Ministry want to put the agriculturists in after trying for forty years.
to get the farmers to co-operate and to

to put back the hands of the clock and

money-making concerns. We know what

in producing Red Hand butter to go by

Ministry on the help it has given to

We are told that the Ministry are perturbed about the outlook for the butter
market; that they are afraid that the

rising until to-day our Red Hand butter
stands at the top of the market. In
1934 it was 66s per cwt. In 1935 it was
77s per cwt. In 1936 it was 94s
cwt. In 1937 it was 117s per

that the price of Red Hand butter has

for Red Hand butter the Ministry and

Some of the arguments against the Bill
I confess I frankly fail to understand.
I have seen in the literature supplied to
me and I have heard even from the hon.
Member for South Tyrone the suggestion
that a milk processing factory, if and
when established, will not be a new
industry. I find it impossible to understand the arguments that are advanced in
favour of that proposition. I ask myself what possible argument is there in
favour of that suggestion. As I gather
it is sought to be argued that because
the milk processing factory will use the
raw product, our milk, and because at
the moment a certain quantity of the
milk produced from cows in Northern
Ireland is treated in the creameries and
is turned into butter in the creameries
or into cream, that therefore the factory
that uses the same raw material, uses it
in a different way and applies it to a
different purpose cannot be described
as carrying on
new industry.
That form of argument may appeal to
some hon. Members but, personally speaking, with absolute respect to the hon.
Members who have used it I entirely fail
to understand it.
a
I do understand the reasoned objection to this Bill that was put forward
with such force, if I may respectfully
say so, by the hon. Member for North
Tyrone and the hon. Member for North
Derry. I naturally view with
with the
greatest respect any opinions that they
may give to the House on any question
affecting agriculture. I gathered from
the speeches both these hon. Members
made when this debate was first opened
in the House that the main objection to
the Bill is based upon the apprehension
that if a factory such as Messrs. Nestlé's
or a factory in Londonderry or both were
established there might not be or as
the hon. Member has assured us there
will not be enough milk produced in Northern Ireland to enable the present
creameries to carry on their work. I am
quite certain that in that respect I
should be in agreement with any other
hon. Members who oppose this Bill.
It certainly would not be my wish in
supporting this Bill to put an end to the
good work the creameries have been
doing in Northern Ireland. The Minister in explaining this Bill to the House
has assured the House that his intention
was not to do any harm to the existing
creameries. It seemed to me in listening
to this debate that hon. Members in
opposing this Bill have punctuated their
speeches by praise for the policy of the
Ministry in the past, for the support the
Ministry have given to the creameries,
for the assistance that the creameries
have derived from the Ministry, and yet
suddenly the Ministry, according to hon.
Members, have devised a measure which
must necessarily result in disaster to the
creamery industry. It certainly would
appear that that would be a very remarkable change of front on the part of the
Ministry. I venture to suggest that one
would be slow to imagine that the Ministry, which has in the past done so much
admittedly for the creamery industry,
has suddenly changed its purpose and is
at the present moment engaged in promoting a Bill the result of which will be
the destruction of that industry.
On this question of the supply of
available milk in Northern Ireland
might I say that statistics have been
produced. I can quite understand hon.
Members saying that while the Ministry show from statistics that there is a
large surplus of milk available in the
district of Ballymoney, that these

matter, I suggest, does not depend on
statistics. On the one side it is said
that only one out of nine of the farmers
in the neighbourhood of Ballymoney
at the present moment send their milk
to a creamery. That I heard asserted.
It is a matter that is capable of being
proved. I have heard it asserted, and all
hon. Members have heard it asserted, that
there is at the present moment available round Ballymoney and neighbourhood a very considerable surplus of milk,
which can and will be supplied to a
factory when established. I know that
so far as the city of Londonderry is concerned there is a source of supply that
certainly I for one would wish to see
brought once again into Northern
Ireland. I refer, of course, to the milk
that formerly came from the farmers
of East Donegal, which milk can be
utilised in Northern Ireland in such a
factory as is suggested, and I have no
doubt would be utilised if there is any
shortage of milk.
Apart from statistics and from debatable questions, I suggest to the House
that one fact, as I understand it, is not in
Milk Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Murphy]
dispute, and that is that there has been
of late years a considerable diminution
in the cow population in
in Northern
Ireland. I have never in all the course
of argument for and against this Bill
heard any hon. Member assert that the
actual number of heifers and cows now
is as great as some years ago. Why the
reduction? One has heard that farmers
now find it more profitable to fatten
heifers for slaughter, and hence a reduction in the cow population. I suggest
that the reduction in the cow population
of Northern Ireland is capable of a very
obvious explanation. The explanation is
that farmers are not finding a sufficient
outlet for the milk they formerly produced. If farmers, who have on their
farms maintained a very large number
of heifers and cows, will in the future see
that their chance of disposing of their
milk is greatly increased-if they see
another outlet for that product, it will
not be long before they realise that they
can, and that they will again make money
out of milk, and they will increase the
population of cows and heifers. The
supply of milk we may naturally and
reasonably expect will greatly increase in
the future.
It seems to me from the point of view
of farmers that, perhaps, the most important requisite for their success and happiness is to have assured markets for their
products. If a farmer has presented
before him the possibility of two competing outlets for this milk, the creamery
and a milk processing factory, he will
certainly say, if he considers the matter,
"It is far better for me and more in my
interests that I should have these two
outlets for my milk products than that
I should be confined to the existing outlet, namely, a creamery or creameries,
which in the past, at all events, has not
induced me to maintain the number of
cows that formerly I maintained on my
farm." That is only one aspect of this
question. The real question for the
House is this: Here we have now practically for the first time the prospect of
one or two factories being established in
Northern Ireland to deal with one of our
main products to deal with milk, one
of the agricultural raw materials which can
be produced in large quantities, and which
can be produced in still greater quantities.
Are we now to say to an English firm
or English firms, as has been said in some
of the speeches, "We do not want you,
we do not want to encourage you, we
will not extend to you the same facilities
that we extend to our creameries." Are
we to say, as has been said among other
reasons, "You are proprietary firms
because you are profit-making firms." If
that reason is to be used can any hon.
Member think that we are going to get
any new industries in Northern Ireland?
Is there the slightest hope of attracting
new industries if that is the way in which
a prospective new industry is to be
approached? I do not wish to be in any
sense controversial in my remarks, but
are the creameries not profit-making concerns? I recognise that to some extent
at all events the creameries are concerns,
the shares of which are held in very small
quantities by individual farmers, but do
not these farmers expect to make a profit
out of their shares? Do they not make a
profit, and are not the creameries proprietary concerns? If that be so, as I
believe it to be, where does the argument lie against any English firm which
chooses to come over here and establish a
factory avowedly with the object of
running it as any business concern is run
for profit?
This is a matter, as I have said, of the
greatest interest and consequence to my
constituents. I quite recognise that if
the gloomy views put forward by certain.
Members are to be taken as necessarily
correct the House, no doubt, would
hesitate to give a Second Reading to this
Bill. I also suggest that the House
would be and should be very slow to accept
these gloomy views as a reason for
definitely refusing to treat a new concern
or two new concerns in the same way that
the creameries to-day are treated. The
House would be slow indeed to say, as
those who seek to reject this Bill ask the
House, that farmers who supply their
milk to a milk processing factory are not
to get the same benefits as their neighbours who supply milk to a creamery.
Speaking on behalf of my consituents I
certainly support this Bill, and sincerely
trust that the House will give it a
Second Reading.

suggest that this Parliament of Northern Ireland write in imperishable letters

National Health Insurance
(Amendment) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): Section 2 of
the National Health Insurance (Amendment) Act, 1938, which was recently
passed in Westminster, and of which
hon. Members have received a copy, provides that that Measure shall extend to
Northern Ireland if an Act of this Parliament SO authorises. Members will
recollect that Health Insurance is in
many respects a United Kingdom service and that the principal Act is an
Act of the Parliament of the United
Kingdom. The Bill before the House
proposes, therefore, that the amendment
recently made in the law in Great
Britain shall be extended to Northern
Ireland.
To explain the purpose of the United
Kingdom Act it is necessary to refer
to a practice which began to be adopted
in certain quarters when the benefits of
the contributory pensions scheme came
to be generally appreciated. A number
of persons in business on their own
account saw that it would be to their
advantage to transfer their business to
a relative and to become employed in it
in order to qualify for a contributory
pension at 65. In 1935, therefore, the
health insurance and pensions schemes
were amended so as to provide that
persons who transfer their business in
this way should not become insured
persons within the meaning of the Acts.
Owing to the form of words used in
the Act, which declared the person not
to be insured rather than the employment not to be insurable, the effect of
the amendment was more drastic than
was anticipated, and the persons
affected by it were in consequence denied
LER FOR THE NOES-
Mr. Elliott.
any title to voluntary insurance or to a
free period of insurance which they
might otherwise have had. The United
Kingdom Act restores the position in
this respect with retrospective effect, and
a number of claims to pension which had
been disallowed in Great Britain on
account of the Amendment of 1935 will
now be admitted.
In Northern Ireland no claim has been
disallowed on account of the provisions
of the Act of 1935, but it is conceivable
that cases exist in which the person concerned has not yet reached the age of 65.
It is obviously desirable, therefore, that
the law should be amended in the same
way here as in Great Britain.
The Bill also provides for a minor
amendment of the provision relating to
the scheme for the visitation of sick or
disabled insured persons, so as to enable
the scheme to be modified at any time in
the light of experience. I accordingly
move the Second Reading of the Bill.
Question, "That the Bill be now read
a Second time," put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.
Weights and Measures Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. BARBOUR: The Bill to which I
have to invite the attention of the House
this afternoon is purely an administrative measure. The administration of
weights and measures is of necessity a
rather dull and prosaic matter, and one
with which few Members of the House,
I imagine, are familiar. Nevertheless,
the weights and measures service affects
the interests of every member of the public and although in our daily transactions
with the retail trade we are no doubt apt
to overlook the existence of this service,
we are, as consumers, continually deriving considerable benefits from it, whether
it be in the purchase of a pound of meat,
a gallon of petrol, or a pint of beer.
909 Weights and Measures Bill-

4 MAY 1938
Second Reading
So far as the existing standards of
weights and measures are concerned this
Bill does not, of course, embody any
change in the existing law. The State
began the task of introducing uniformity.
into the various measures in common use
as far back as-or even earlier than-
Magna Charta, when it was provided that
"one measure of wine shall be throughout our Realm and one measure of ale
and one measure of corn."

being present—
Mr. BARBOUR: I was just saying
that uniformity in measures was introduced as far back as the days of Magna
Charta in respect of various commodities,
and, although it may have been necessary to add to the list of beverages and
commodities as public taste has changed,
there is no question at the present time,
nor, in fact, has this House the power of
modifying in any way the basic principle
of uniformity throughout the Kingdom.
There is, however, another aspect of
the weghts and measures administration
which has exercised the minds of legislators from the earliest times and which is
affected so far as Northern Ireland is
concerned by the Bill now before the
House. I refer to the method of the
enforcement of the laws relating to
weights and measures. From the
earliest times responsibility for the
enforcement of the law has devolved
upon local bodies and this system of
devolution has, I understand, been on
occasion carried so far that at one period
local administration was made the
responsibility of a single university
which, having been defeated by the
townsmen in what would now be known
as a "University rag," was granted compensation in the form of a "most large
charter which included the supervision
of measures and weights." Although
the weights and measures service is not
now entrusted to academic control, the
principle of devolution is still followed,
and in Great Britain local authorities
are still responsible for local administration. In Northern Ireland, as hon.
Members are aware, local administration has always been in the hands of the
local police, and there is thus already a
greater measure of centralisation in Northern Ireland than in Great Britain.
The present Bill proposes to carry this
centralisation still further. While in
such a service as that relating to weights
and measures local control may be suited
to conditions obtaining in Great Britain,
experience goes to show that in an area
the size of Northern Ireland the devolution of control is not essential and an
efficient and economic service could be
best administered by a single central
authority.
When the Government of Northern
Ireland was established the powers and
duties of the Board of Trade in relation
to weights and measures in the Province
were allocated to my Ministry. The Inspectors of Weights and Measures, as I
have explained, have up to the present
been supplied from qualified men in the
police force who have had to be relieved
from ordinary police duties so that they
might apply their whole official time to
their duties as Inspectors of Weights and
Measures.
The recruitment of Inspectors of
Weights and Measures in Northern Ireland has involved the setting up of classes
of instruction and the withdrawal from
time to time of a number of constables
from normal police duties for a period
of six months or upwards. The cost of
this system of recruitment has been substantial. The standard of the qualifying examination is high and the special
subjects which have to be mastered have
little relevance to ordinary police work.
Accordingly it is not surprising that
there have been many failures to reach
this standard. Moreover, there has not
been any avenue of promotion for
Inspectors of Weights and Measures, as
such, beyond the rank of sergeant, and
this being so an ambitious officer has to
seek his promotion through the exercise
of ordinary police duties.
In Great Britain the local administration of weights and measures services is
entrusted to the local authorities and,
while in some areas the duties are
carried out on a part time basis by the
local police, in the great majority of
a special civilian inspectorate is
cases
employed.
After a careful review of the whole
position the Government decided to seek
the authority of Parliament to substi-
911 Weights and Measures Bill-

Business of the House
[Mr. Barbour]
tute a civilian service under the direct
control of the Ministry of Commerce and
proposals to that end are put forward
in the Bill which is now before the
House.
Concurrently with this change the
Government propose that the financial
responsibility for the provision and maintenance of standards of weights and
measures, scale beams, and other equipinent as well as the travelling expenses
of inspectors and the expenditure for
office accommodation should be met by
the Ministry of Commerce instead of by
County and County Borough Councils as
heretofore. On the other hand it is proposed to take the sum of £1,000 a year
from the Dogs Acts Account as a contribution towards the expenses of the
Ministry.
As regards the personnel of the new
inspectorate, it is intended that existing
inspectors shall be free, to volunteer their
services to the Ministry of Commerce in
a civilian capacity without loss of pension
rights. It may perhaps prove necessary
to recruit a few inspectors from other
sources in the first year or two, but
thereafter it is anticipated that trainees
recruited within the Province will be
available and will qualify themselves for
appointment as Inspectors.
I need not dwell upon the other provisions of the Bill. They are mainly
matters of machinery to give effect to
the change of administration which I
have outlined. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

Education the number of the denominational schools classified as provided and
transferred schools and the number of

equipment of provided schools and the

and improvement of transferred schools;

in respect of schools under Catholic
management and the total contribution
made by the managers to secure such
public aid, and whether the decline of

of the area by 12,000 since 1933 has led
to any modification of the school building
programme of the educational
authorities.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): On 31st
December, 1937, there were 653 provided
and transferred public elementary
schools under local education authorities,
with an enrolment of 93,936 pupils.
These schools are not denominational.
At the same date there were 661
schools under Roman Catholic management (including nine under "Four and
Two" committees), with an enrolment of
71,330 pupils.
Up to 31st December, 1937, the expenditure, under the provisions of the
Education Act of 1923, upon the building and equipment of provided schools,
and the enlargement, improvement and
equipment of transferred schools was
approximately £1,560,000.
In respect of the building and equipment of new, and the enlargement, improvement and equipment of existing,
voluntary schools under Roman Catholic
management, the total grants sanctioned
up to 31st March, 1938, amounted to

CURING FACTORIES.
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether a Wholesale Cooperative Society was granted a licence
over a year ago to open a Wiltshire Pork
Factory at Collin's Glen, Belfast;
whether nothing has since been done in
the matter; whether the Pigs Marketing
Board of Northern Ireland are not in
agreement as to the suitability of this
site; whether a much more central site
could be obtained in Newry, which has
had the largest pork market and the
largest sales of live pigs for pork of
any centre in Northern Ireland; whether
he will state the quotas allotted to the
two Wiltshire pork factories to be erected
at Collin's Glen, Belfast, and Dunmurry,
Belfast, and that to be erected at Cookstown, Co. Tyrone; whether it is the intention to adhere to these quotas in the
event of the pig population increasing to
such an extent as to more than meet
these quotas, and support the provision
of further factories at Newry and elsewhere instead of extending the two
factories at Belfast, and that at Cookstown, and depriving other areas of their
fair share of industrial development.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): No licence for
a Wiltshire Curing Factory has been.
granted to the Co-operative Wholesale
Society, although the Society has been
in communication with my Ministry
with regard to a licence for some time.
The site for the erection of this factory
was not, however, at Collin Glen, Dunmurry, Belfast, where a Wiltshire Curing
Factory has been established by the Pigs
Marketing Board in conjunction with an
English firm. A similar factory has also
been established by the Board at Cookstown, also in conjunction with an English firm. The quota allotted to the
Collin Glen Factory will at present not
exceed 41,600 pigs per annum, and to

With regard to the erection of

POLICE PROTECTION AT
CARNLOUGH.
4. Captain PATRICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he has
received any representations from the
inhabitants of Carnlough regarding
inadequate police protection, and, if so,
whether he will consider establishing a
police barracks in that town.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): A memorial was
received from the residents and ratepayers of Carnlough in 1935, praying for
the establishment of a police barrack
there. At the time, however, it was not
possible to accede to the request, and, in
any event, I was not satisfied that the
expense involved in the establishment of
a police barrack would have been justified, as Carnlough is only 3 miles from
Glenarm Barrack, from which place all
necessary police supervision and protection is given.
However, representations were again
made to me in the following year and
as an experiment I arranged for the
establishment of a temporary station at
Carnlough in the summer months. From
the experience gained by this experiment
I am satisfied that there is no urgent
necessity for the establishment of a permanent barrack at Carnlough, as adequate police attention can be, and will
continue to be afforded from the nearby
barrack at Glenarm.

VACCINATION AGAINST
SMALLPOX.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether, in view of a
general desire, he will take steps to have
the law in regard to vaccination against
smallpox brought into conformity with
that across the Channel, so that parents
in Northern Ireland may have the benefit
of a Clause of exemption on conscientious
or other grounds such as exists in Great
Britain.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir. I
am not aware that there is any general
desire for the amendment of the law suggested by the hon. Member, which I am
advised would not be desirable in the
interests of public health of Northern
Ireland.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask the Minister
if he is aware of the fact that there have
been deaths from vaccination and no
deaths from smallpox ?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, I am not
aware of that. All I can say is this, that
in England, where the vaccination laws
are of a different nature to ours, there
have been several deaths from smallpox,
and in Northern Ireland there have only
been two serious cases of smallpox.
Mr. GRANT: Is it not a fact that
the reason we have no deaths from smallpox is because we have vaccination laws
in Northern Ireland?
Sir DAWSON BATES: That is so.
SUGGESTED EXHIBITION IN
NORTHERN IRELAND.
7. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether, in view of the great
advantages to the tourist industry and
trade in general of such Exhibitions as that
held some years ago at Wembley and that
now being held at Glasgow, and in view
of the desire to spread the benefits of
these and of the fact that the taxpayers
of Northern Ireland must contribute their
share of any deficits, he will make representations to have the next such great
Exhibition held in Northern Ireland.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply.
The hon. Member appears to be under
some misapprehension in regard to the
liability of the Northern Ireland taxpayer in the financing of Exhibitions
such as that now being held at Glasgow.
This Exhibition has been financed in the
main by a guarantee fund raised in Scotland by the Exhibition Association, and
should any deficit occur it will be met
out of this fund and not out of Government funds. In these circumstances the
hon. Member will appreciate that the
organisation and financing of an Exhibition of a similar character in Northern
Ireland would primarily be a matter for
local interests.

"A"
CLASS SPECIAL
CONSTABULARY.
8. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime Minister whether he can state the terms on
which the "A" Class Special Constabulary were recruited in so far as pay
and bonus, etc., are concerned; whether
the contract so far as Northern Ireland is
concerned was broken by the reduction of
the men's pay from 10s per day to 7s per
day and the bounty from £25 to £20;
whether the answer of the Minister of
Home Affairs replying on behalf of the
Prime Minister to a question on 21st
October, 1937, repudiating the suggestion that the contracts made with the
Special Constabulary were in any way
broken or that the members have been
unfairly treated represents the opinion of
the Government, having regard to the
definite and admitted reduction of the
men's pay and bounty; and whether the
Government would even now do justice
to this loyal body of men.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked to reply to this question. The
"A" Special Constabulary was formed by
the British Government in November,
1920, the terms as to pay and bounty
being as follows:-
Whole-time service for a minimum
period of six months-pay 10s per day.
Bounty for approved service at the rate
of £25 per annum in lieu of pension
rights.
A bonus of 6s weekly was guaranteed
up to the 31st March, 1921.
The payment of the bonus referred to
ceased with effect from the 1st October,
1921, but otherwise the men were retained on six-monthly engagements up to
November, 1921. From that date the
contracts of service with the members of
the Force were made by the Northern
Government for three-monthly periods.
only. In September, 1922, a notice was
issued to the Force announcing that,
owing to financial exigencies, on any
future re-engagement the rates of pay
would be reduced from 10s to 7s per day,
and that the bounty in lieu of pension
would be reduced from £25 to £20 per
annum. These reductions duly took
place on the 1st October, and the men
who accepted the new conditions and reengaged did so on a monthly basis at the
new scale of pay.
The reply which I gave to the question
asked by the hon. Member on the 21st
October last represents the opinion of
the Government that the members of the
Class "A" Special Constabulary have not
been unfairly treated.
Mr. NIXON: Did the men sign any
new contract on the reduction of their
pay or did they not?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member really tries to misunderstand
my answer. I tried to point out that on
a certain date the men's contract terminated. They were offered a new contract which they accepted.
Mr. NIXON: That does not answer
the question. Did they sign a new contract form, because if they did they were
wrong, and if they did not they were
right.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Really the
hon. Member is trying to put words into
my mouth which I did not use.
Mr. NIXON: You did not answer the
question.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
explained that on a certain date the contract came to an end. The men were
asked whether or not they desired to enter
into a new contract, which they did.
Mr. NIXON: Was there a form presented to the men to sign, and did they
sign it?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The whole
thing was entirely a matter for the men.
If they chose to come in again they could
do so, and if they chose to stay out they
could do so.
Mr. NIXON: Will the Government
consider the advisability of reducing at
few salaries this afternoon?

Estimates, 1938-39.
Considered in Committee.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
Class II. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF FINANCE.
Motion made and question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £108,678 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1939, to
defray the salaries and expenses of the
Ministry of Finance."-(Note-£50,000
has been voted on account.)
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon): There is a gross
increase of £5,883 on this Vote, which is
mainly attributable to additional staff in
the Works Division. This increase is,
however, accompanied by increased payments for services rendered by the Ministry in the main to the Imperial Government, and as a result a net decrease of
£362 emerges.
The additions to the
works staff are due to a more intensive
building programme, including, it is
anticipated, extensive works on behalf of
the Post Office and accelerated barrack
construction. Provision has been made
for an increase in the number of clerks
of works engaged on services on behalf
of the Imperial Government and for
additional engineering staff. The balance
of the increase is spread over the
architects and quantity surveyors'
sections. The extent of the works programme has also necessitated the addition
of £250 to the provision for travelling
expenses. An item of £550 is also
included in respect of architectural
services the Vaughan Agricultural
Institute established under the Vaughan
Charity Act of 1936.
A new item appears under Sub-head D
-Legal Charges. This represents the
cost of legal agency work taken over by
the Ministry as from 1st January, 1938,
on behalf of the Post Office in connection with the acquisition of sites for new
Post Offices. It is not possible at this
early stage to estimate the cost of such
services with close accuracy, but £250
has been provided with a corresponding
recoupment under the Appropriationsin-Aid Sub-head.
The decrease of £2,400 in the provision
for census staff is due to reductions in the
amount provided for temporary clerical
assistants and tabulation, as the major
part of the work in this connection has
been completed. Some time must unavoidably elapse, however, before the
results can be marshalled in report form,
printed and published. It is hoped that
the first of the county volumes will be
published in July of this year, and the
general report may be available about the
end of the financial year.
A further edition of the Ulster Year
Book is in course of preparation and will
be published about the middle of the
calendar year.
The sum of £1,000 is
provided under Sub-head L to cover the
cost of the quinquennial actuarial investigation of the Teachers' Superannuation
Fund.
In conclusion, I would like to make a
few general remarks on this Estimate.
The total expenditure seems large for a
Ministry of Finance, but when one takes
into consideration that the Ministry is an
amalgamation of many offices and covers
numerous activities and is not merely a
controlling Treasury Department, the
picture takes on a different aspect. In
addition to Treasury control, both
financial and staff, there are the services
relating to the collection of revenue and
land annuities, the granting of loans and
collection of repayments, the calculation
of pensions in particular teachers'
pensions questions of land sub-division
and turbary, the control of certain
branches of charities, Stationery Office
services and the services of the Registrar-
General, all works expenditure, whether
our own or those for which the Ministry
acts as agent. From this list, which is
by no means exhaustive, one can judge
that a substantial number of staff is
bound to be required. I beg to move.

who looks one way and walks another

To get on to the Estimates. I notice
that the expenses are still going up, and
that the salaries are also going up. I
recollect that when complaints about high
salaries were made in this House the
Prime Minister always made the point
that if the salaries were not paid the
money would revert to Great Britain,
and that, as a matter of fact, it was to
the benefit of Northern Ireland to have
high salaries, so as to keep the money
here. That argument no longer applies.
That argument led to revaluation for the
purpose of balancing the Budget, that
in turn led to unemployment, and that
to the many vacant shops and other
premises that we have in this city at the
present time.
Some very serious things have occurred
in the Ministry of Finance. Take, for
instance, the drainage of Lough Neagh
and the Bann. There was an increase
of £200,000 over the contract price. I
know all about contracts and the giving
of contracts, and where a contract has to
be increased by £200,000 there is something radically wrong in administration.
How can other firms be expected to exist
when as a result of the way the administration was carried out the firm getting
the contract at £500,000 or £600,000
had to go in and get £200,000 added to
it? Such a thing is unknown to any
business firm in any part of the world.
The Ministry should look after that.
Then a Cabinet Minister here gets as
much as ten ordinary Members. My
hon. and gallant Friend who was in
Australia will tell you that a Cabinet
Minister there gets very little more than
one Member. We were elected to this
House on 9th February, but our little
allowance did not commence until about
30th March. The Cabinet Ministers drew

If you look through the Book of Estimates you will see that if things go on
the way they are going on at present the

at the present time. I have been struck

page 32-

As regards the balancing of the Budget, we are always told that the Government balance their Budget. I know

I will have
have another opportunity of

without any

trouble. This is the only country in the

Mr. HENDERSON: Yes, as the hon.
Gentleman says, I would find him at the

I wonder does the Minister of Finance
ever go into the question of how much
per minute the Cabinet Ministers and the
Financial Secretaries cost the country. I
suppose it would work out at £50 a
minute. I think that is monstrous.
None of our Cabinet Ministers, except
the Minister of Commerce, can be called
a patriot. Then, there is a sum of £450
for the Parliamentary Secretary's office
and office expenses. Where is this
office? The office is in Glengall Street.
I demand from the Minister of Finance
a
return showing who receives this
money. Is it fair that the taxpayers of
the country should be asked to pay for
an office in Glengall Street? I feel that
the Minister of Finance is in duty bound
to tell the Members of the Committee
who receives this £450. If it is used to
pay servants for looking after this office,
then it is generally wrong. As a general
rule, the office of the Chief Whip is in
Glengall Street. We have the most
reliable information that this office is in
Glengall Street.
That sort of thing would not be
tolerated by the British Parliament.
Just imagine an English Financial Secretary having an office outside, and using
it for political purposes. If this office
were giving any useful service to the
country, I would not object, but some of
the things that originate in this office are
doing Ulster no end of harm.
I can refer in this connection to a
speech that recently emanated from the
Chief Whip. When we pay the
Financial Secretary of this Ministry a
sum of £1,000 for carrying out certain
work, it is our duty to protest if he does
anything to injure the country. He has
just made an utterance outside this
House; it would have been better if he
had made it inside this House. The
speech that he made at an Official
Unionist mothers' meeting the other
night should have been made at Westminster. He was denouncing a British
Statesman, one of his own kith and kin,
and that will do Ulster no end of harm.
Speeches of that nature are bound to
react upon
Ulster. We allow him to
draw £1,000 a year, and then go out and
injure the citizens of Northern Ireland
by making these ill-advised speeches,
which originate in an office maintained
at a cost of £1,450 to the taxpayers of
this country. Is there anyone here who
could justify this? Even the learned
Attorney-General, one of the ablest legal
gentlemen in the country, could not
justify the payment of £1,000 to the
Chief Whip. The only thing this man
has to do is to get up and move "That
this House do now adjourn" until such
and such a date. His duty starts there,
and ends as soon as he has completed
that sentence. He gets £1,000 for doing
that for six or eight weeks in the year.
If the unemployed could get a job at only
one-fourth of that figure they would be
more than delighted. I could get you
any number of men who would be prepared to do this work for £200 a year
and consider themselves well paid. It is
deplorable to compare this payment of
£1,000 with the pittance paid to the unemployed.
I want to protest against these huge
salaries paid in the Ministry of Finance.
I would not like it to get out that I
thought the Ministry's officials were not
competent. I think the officials are
wonderful-they are competent, kind,
and courteous to Members of Parliament,
and I am glad to know that the Minister
of Finance rules over men who are doing
such great work. But there are too
many cushy jobs, to put it bluntly. I
think the right hon. Gentleman could
have reduced these Estimates by £3,000
or £4,000 if he had started off with the
head of the Department.

feel that the least our Government could

I now want to refer to the grading of
the under-dog, the messengers and attendants. It is rather surprising to find in

been established as officers of the House.

conditions under which these men

service and are entitled to be considered

is not sitting.
As I have SO often criticised the

will not say anything in regard to them.

save
not exist in any Parliament similar to

mentary Counsel in Great Britain are

About seven years ago the late Minister of Finance, in reply to representations of mine, said that he would have
shelters erected on the Stormont Estate.
The Government have erected shelters on
the Knock golf links side and the Ballymascaw road side. A more ridiculous
situation for the shelters was never
chosen than those selected on the Processional Road. Before you could get off
the main road to shelter you would be
drenched. The thing is ridiculous expenditure. The shelters have been put
right into the bushes and are from five
to ten minutes' walk off the Processional
Road. There is a shelter at the back
gate and another near Mr. Speaker's
house. When I asked for the provision
of shelters on the Processional Road I
meant shelters of a decorative kind into
which you could step off the footpath
and when the rain ceased proceed on
your journey up the hill. This is a waste
of money and a waste of the time and
labour of those who erected the shelters.
I will be told that the amenities of the
Processional Road would be destroyed.
They would not, provided you had
picked the right sites and put the shelters
in the most convenient places. People,
years after this, will be wondering why

pedestrians. That is all I wish to say on
this Estimate.

which ought to be cleared up. If Parliament passes legislation which requires

directed for the benefit of the people of
Northern Ireland. I cannot see that
there is any complaint whatever in that

VALUATION AND SURVEYS.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a sum not exceeding £33,700 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending on 31st March, 1939, to

(Note.-£17,000 has been voted on

Estimates-
Valuation and Surveys
5 MAY 1938
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: As regards
individual items of expediture this Vote
calls for very little comment as the variation in the totals between this and the
previous year is negligible. I should
perhaps explain that the increase in the
travelling cost under Sub-head B is more
apparent than real. The provision made
for last year proved too small as the work
on annual revision and subsequent appeals
was much heavier than had been expected. A safer Estimate has, therefore, been taken for the present year.
There is one item in Sub-head H which
might call for comment, namely, the drop
in receipts from local authorities in
respect of provisional valuation services.
This is due to quieter conditions in the
building trade and the number of new
houses in respect of which such provisional valuations are sought by the Belfast and the Londonderry Corporations
shows a corresponding decrease.
As
there is so little to comment about in the
detail of the Estimate I propose, firstly,
to make a few observations generally on
revaluation and, secondly, to give
somewhat longer account of the work on
which the Ordnance Survey Branch of
the Valuation Office is engaged.
With regard to revaluation it will be
remembered that the lists in connection
with the first general revaluation were
issued early in 1935 and came into operation on the 1st April, 1936. Under the
Valuation Act of 1932 the lists in connection with the second general revaluation are due to be issued not later than
1st March, 1941, and will operate from
1st April, 1941. While a certain
amount of indoor work has been proceeding in connection with this second
general revaluation little has so far been
done as regards outdoor work, but this
will begin immediately. It will not, of
course, involve the detailed house to
house examination which the first
general revaluation necessitated but
rather a survey of particular classes of
property whose rental values appear to be
most liable to frequent change and, in
particular, whose values may have been
affected by the first general revaluation.
I now turn to the Ordnance Survey
Branch and the work on which it is
engaged. The first and principal duty of
the Ordnance Survey is to carry out the
revision of the 25-inch maps and to keep
them up-to-date by publishing revised
editions. The next principal duty is to
publish new editions of the 6-inch maps
by a reduction from the 25-inch, and the
third principal duty is to revise and publish new editions of the small scale maps,
the one-inch, half-inch, and quarter-inch
-these last being the maps used by
motorists and pedestrians exploring the
by-paths of Ulster. Minor duties include valuation surveys and mapping and
turbary survey and allotment.
Northern Ireland was first surveyed
on the 25-inch scale between the years
1903 and 1908. Previous to that time
the largest scale map of the whole area
was the six-inch, but towns were surveyed
on the 5-ft. scale. It was at first intended that new editions of the 25-inch
and 6-inch maps, except in the case of
sparsely inhabited mountainous districts,
should be published every 20 years.
This period was extended later to 25
years. The intention has not, however,
been carried out, and the programme is
in arrears. One half of Co. Tyrone, the
whole of Co. Armagh, and Co. Fermanagh, now overdue five to ten years, are
still unrevised. Besides cyclic 25-year
revisions of the rural areas county by
county, more frequent revisions of town
areas were sanctioned and between 1930
and 1933 the revisions of most of the
towns in the counties of Antrim,
Armagh, Londonderry, and Tyrone was
carried out and new editions of the 25inch maps were published, together with
enlargements on larger scales. This type
of map is that used by land surveyors,
solicitors, and, generally, for all legal.
purposes.
This interim revision of towns set back
the cyclic 25-year revision of the counties.
When the Ministry of Finance in 1933
took over charge of the survey from the
Ministry of Agriculture, the plans of
Co. Londonderry, which had been revised in the field between 1922 and 1929,
still remained unpublished and their
publication was further delayed by revaluation for which practically the
whole survey staff was commandeered.
Towards the end of 1934 Ordnance Survey work was started again and new
staff was engaged. The first work undertaken was the clearing up of arrears of
publication of Co. Londonderry. At the
same time the field revision of Co. Tyrone
was started. All the 25-inch and 6-inch
Estimates-
Valuation and Surveys
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lieut.-Colonel Gordon]
maps of Co. Londonderry have since been
published. One half of Co. Tyrone has
been revised in the field, and the work
of drawing the new editions is well in
hand.
In future it is intended to employ
approximately one half of the staff on the
cyclic county revision and one half on
urban interim revision. The interim revision of Belfast, Holywood, Greencastle,
Dunmurry, and Finaghy has been carried
out in as far as the field work is concerned during the last six months, and
it is expected that the 25-inch plans of
this area will all be in the printer's hands
before the end of 1938. Six-inch maps
of the area will also be published before
the end of the year. The interim revision of the other towns of Northern Ireland will be undertaken in the order of
urgency, and it is estimated that all will
be revised by 1946.
I now turn to the small scale maps,
which I have explained are largely used
for touring purposes. No new editions
of the one-inch, half-inch, and quarterinch maps were published and no field
work for this purpose was carried out
between 1912 and 1935. These maps
are therefore seriously out of date.
new series of one-inch maps is now in
course of publication following a one-inch
Revision Survey which started in the
Mourne Mountains area and has now
covered over one-half of the territory of
the Six Counties. The Mourne Mountains sheet and the Belfast sheet have
been published. Four others are in the
hands of the printers and a fifth is
almost ready for the printers, so that
towards the end of the month seven of
the eleven sheets which will cover the
whole Province will be either published
or in course of publication. The publication of the revised editions of the corresponding sheets of the half-inch map is
also in hand.
As regards the actual volume of publication, it is of interest to note that
during the last 3 years new editions of
568 plans and maps on various scales
have been published and manuscripts for
78 more are in the hands of the printers.
Including reprints and new editions the
number of prints received into stock during the last 3 years is upwards of
64,000. The number of maps sold during the same period is nearly 48,000. I
hope that this résumé of the work of the
Ordnance Survey Branch will prove of
interest to the Committee and show something of the lesser known activities of the
Ministry of Finance. I beg to move.

The CHAIRMAN: I am sorry to

Mr. CAMPBELL: I was sympathising
with the Financial Secretary, and I
thought you would not interrupt me in
view of the attack made on him. However, if I have transgressed the rules for
standing up for the hon. and gallant
Gentleman I will leave him alone. Some
Members to-day are very keen and thirsting for a general revaluation. Some are
delighted that in this Estimate we are
paving the way for it. The Chief Whip
was a keen apologist for the last general
revaluation. I wonder is he satisfied
with the result of that? He seems to be
keen now for a second general revaluation.
I wonder will he be satisfied with the
second general revaluation when it comes
along. I think the people do not like
general revaluations. We had one in
Belfast in 1906 or thereabouts, and it
resulted in very substantial and sharp
rises in valuations. We had another
under the Act of 1932, which resulted
in a sharp, steep rise in Belfast and the
Six Counties. Now confronted with
these two general revaluations we find
the Chief Whip and Members on both
sides thirsting for a third general revaluation, which will have equally disappointing results.
These general revaluations do not mean
general reductions in valuations, and
never will. I would ask the Financial
Secretary as a matter of information for
the Committee does he pretend to hold
out to this Committee the least prospect
of any general reduction in valuations
following the next general revaluation?
I venture to say his answer would be,
"Emphatically I do not." That is the
reason why I say that I think it would
be wise to take breathing time and consider the grave hardships caused by the
last experiment in revaluation, and see
if they cannot be readjusted and redressed
rather than let loose, within a matter of
two and a half years, a flood of officials
over the Six Counties who will not be
starting on the work with the idea of
pulling down valuations. They will be
doing their duty according to their light.
I say that those who have hopes as to
the results of the next general revaluation-poor tenants in Belfast, businessmen and shopkeepers-are living in a
fool's paradise. There may be vacant
shops in many streets to-day, due to the
last general revaluation, but I believe
their number will be increased as an outcome of the next general experiment of
that kind.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: In reply to

I say that they have tried to draw me
on the question of a new revaluation.
I am afraid they will not succeed, because
revaluation will be carried out in accordance with the Act of Parliament passed
by this House. I would like to inform
the Member for Mid-Antrim that the

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: A new subhead, "D," appears in this Estimate,
"Grants for restoration and repairs under
Section 5 of the Ancient Monuments Act,
1937."
This is put at the more or less token
figure of £100. It is intended to exercise this power to supplement the efforts
of local bodies or private individuals,
especially where a monument, though of
value or interest to a locality, is not of
sufficient merit or importance to deserve
its acquisition and complete maintenance
by the State. Last year one monument
was thus dealt with near Newtownstewart in Co. Tyrone, repaired under
the direction of a member of the Ancient
Monuments Advisory Council. Other
applications are at present under consideration by the Ministry for grants.
It is expected that archæological excavation (Subhead I) will be stimulated
by the recent concession, under which
such projects will receive a Government
contribution of 85 per cent. of the
labour costs of unemployed men engaged
for the work, instead of 75 per cent. as
formerly. This will reduce by an appreciable amount the burden on learned
bodies and individuals promoting such
excavation.
During the past year an application
was received from Dr. Van Giffen, of
Holland, to excavate an important monument in the Ministry's charge-Ballynoe
Stone Circle, near Downpatrick, one of
the largest monuments of this kind in
Ireland. In view of his European reputation as
a scholar and excavator, the
Ministry gladly acceded to his request,
which it assisted by defraying the whole
cost of the labour employed.
I should like to take this opportunity
to express my deep regret for the loss
which has been suffered by the death of the
first Chairman of the Ancient Monuments
Advisory Council, the Very Rev. Dean
Carmody, who for ten years had given
devoted voluntary service in that capacity
for the increase of archæological knowledge in Ulster and indeed retained to the
very last his association with this work
even when the failure of his health had
forced him to relinquish all other forms
of activity. I would also like to express
deep regret at the recent death of the
Right. Hon. H. M. M'Causland, Chairman of the Northern Ireland Branch of

THE WATER SUPPLY.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Captain Dixon).
Mr. BROWN: Before the House adjourns I desire to call the attention of
the Ministries of Agriculture, Home
Affairs, Commerce, and Finance, to a
matter of urgency, which has all the elements of dire disaster slowly but surely
creeping upon us. I refer to the alarm
that is felt all over Northern Ireland at
the havoc that is likely to be caused by
the present drought to agriculture and
industry which are dependent upon
water supplies. I want to remind the
House that we are experiencing at
present the driest spring since 1893 and
the lowest average rainfall for very many
years.
Mr. SPEAKER: Does the hon. Member suggest that that is a matter for
administration on the part of the Government?
Mr. BROWN: I will proceed to show
that it is. It is a matter not only for
administration but for urgent and immediate administration. We have in this
Province the largest lake in the United
Kingdom, Lough Neagh, an area of water
so large that a whole city is buried
beneath its waves. I suggest that it
would be possible to convey supplies from
Lough Neagh to the whole of Northern
Ireland.
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid the hon.
Gentleman has now ruled himself out of
order. It is obvious that if any such
action were undertaken by the Government it would be necessary to introduce
legislation to carry it into effect. Therefore, the hon. Gentleman will see that he
is out of order.
Q
Adjournment
The Water Supply
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. BROWN: I suggest that these
Ministers should come together for the
purpose of formulating a scheme to meet
this situation, which is becoming
desperate, and is a matter of real urgency.
Mr. SPEAKER: The merits of the
case have nothing to do with procedure.
If the hon. Member wishes to discuss a
subject of this kind he must put down
a Motion on the Order Paper. Such
Motions come up for debate on Tuesday
afternoons at 4-30. It is within his rights
to put down such a Motion if he wishes
to do so, but on the Motion for the
Adjournment only matters of administration can be discussed. Matters which
must be carried out by legislation cannot
be raised.
Mr. BROWN: Would I be in order in
asking any of these Ministers to give the
House some information that would allay
public anxiety in this matter?-information as to the steps that are being taken
by them to cope with the situation? I
do not suggest there has been any dereliction of duty on the part of the Government.
Mr. SPEAKER: As a matter of order
there are two ways in which the hon.
Member can carry out his intention-one
is by putting a Question down, and the
other by putting a Motion on the Order
Paper, which would enable the whole
matter to be discussed.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that
some communities have what is known as
rainmakers, who go out and perform
certain evolutions when there is drought,
and thereby invoke rain? Would it not
be a matter of administration for the
Government to endeavour to employ some
of those people? Lough Neagh itself
actually covers a city, the people of which
are not in need of rain. I should not like
to go too far in invoking the aid of Lough
Neagh lest history should repeat itself.
The waters might flood us out altogether,
as they did the ancient city that now
lies submerged under it.
The PRIME MINISTER: In answer
to my hon. Friend, the Member for South
Down-
Mr. NIXON: What about me?
The PRIME MINISTER: I am afraid
you are out of order.
Mr. NIXON: Oh, no.
The PRIME MINISTER: I can assure
him that we all sympathise very deeply
with the situation created by the possible
shortage of water, but it is always for
the local authority to make the initial
move. If the people in the neighbourhood would make a move steps would be
taken to deal with the problem. The
Government cannot go down to the
various areas to start schemes of that
kind. I can assure my hon. Friend that
if he will only bring the matter before
the local authorities in his own constituency he will find the Government most
sympathetic and helpful in every way in
helping to solve the difficulties to which
he has drawn attention.

ment on the subject at the recent General

The PRIME MINISTER: As the hon.
Member will be aware, services relating
to broadcasting are reserved to the Government of the United Kingdom, but
through the courtesy of the Northern
Ireland Regional Director of the British
Broadcasting Corporation I have been
supplied with
with the following information:
The work in connection with the building of the new B.B.C. Station is being
carried out in two stages, firstly the
piling of the site and, secondly, the
erection of the buildings.
The present
position is that the B.B.C. has now
received tenders for the piling of the
site, one of which will be accepted almost
immediately. The piling, therefore, is
expected to start at the beginning of next
month. It will take approximately three
months to complete the piling and
preparation of the site and the building
proper is, therefore, expected to start
about the beginning of September.
TO SAFEGUARD ULSTER.
4. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Prime Minister whether he can state
what steps the Government are taking to
safeguard Ulster's position in the event
of another agreement being reached between the British Government and the
Eire Government to have Partition
removed.
The PRIME MINISTER: None, Sir;
bearing in mind, firstly, the full assurance given by the Government of the
United Kingdom, that the new Constitution of Eire does not affect in any
way the position of Northern Ireland as
an integral part of the United Kingdom
of Great Britain and Northern Ireland;
secondly, Mr. Chamberlain's statement
on Thursday last at Westminster that on
their side they took the view that the
question of Partition was not one for
them.
Any question of the United Kingdom
Government putting pressure on Northern Ireland to come into an arrangement
did not commend itself to them; they
could not even think of such a thing,
and, thirdly, that Government's reiterated declaration that the question of
Partition was one for Northern Ireland
and Eire themselves to determine; and,
in view of Ulster's emphatic pronounce-
He will doubtless have observed that,
in an analogous case, Partition is the
policy of His Majesty's Government,
which has just despatched a Commission
to Palestine to endeavour to partition
that country and delineate a boundary
between two irreconcilable peoples with a
view to establishing and maintaining law
and order in the Holy Land. Moreover,
it must be apparent to everyone that far
from any idea of disintegrating the
United Kingdom, His Majesty's Ministers are engaged in drawing even closer
together all the component parts of the
British Empire.

Money Bills Procedure.
The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to
move the following Notice of Motion,
with which I am sure the House will
agree:
"That a Bill (other than a Bill which
is required to originate in Committee
of Ways and Means) the main object
of which is the creation of a public
charge may either be presented, or
brought in upon an Order of the
House, by a Minister of the Crown,
and, in the case of a Bill so presented
or brought in, the creation of the
charge shall not require to be
authorised by a Committee of the
Whole House until the Bill has been
read a Second time, and after the
charge has been so authorised the
Bill shall be proceeded with in the same
as a Bill which involves a
charge that is subsidiary to its main
purpose."
manner
Hitherto a Bill which is essentially
a Money Bill has been introduced after
the Money Resolution has been passed
in Committee. This means that the Committee have to pass the Money Resolution before they have seen the Bill to
which it refers. It also means that in
some cases the Second Reading debate,
which should be the full debate on the
principle of the Bill, is stultified by the
previous debate on the Money Resolution.
The purpose of this Amendment of
Standing Orders is to enable a Bill
which is essentially a Money Bill to be
introduced in the ordinary way, and to
receive a Second Reading in the House,
during which the principle of the Bill
can be debated. After the Second
Reading and before the Committee stage
the House will go into Committee on the
Money Resolution, when Members have
full knowledge of the Bill, and the
debate will then take place on the Money
Resolution. This is, of course, the rule
which at present exists in respect of
Bills which contain financial clauses subsidiary to the main provisions of the Bill,
and it is now proposed to make this rule
apply to Bills which are mainly finanical.
In conclusion, I should like to say that
the Government has issued intructions
that the Money Resolution is to be
drafted in such a way as to give to the
Committee the utmost freedom for the
discussion and amendment of details,
while at the same time ensuring that the
Government is safeguarded in the discharge of its general responsibilities relating to public expenditure.
the

with this change of procedure. The old

Members of this House from really getting their point of view brought forward
owing to the Money Resolution limiting
scope of the debate. I think that
this change in regard to the Money
Resolution is for the benefit of Members

responsibilities. I think this is long

of the House as a whole, and especially
for private Members.
