Weights and Measures [Money].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair].
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session being an Act "to provide
for the transfer to the Ministry of Commerce of certain powers and duties of
local authorities under the Weights and
Measures Acts and otherwise to amend
the said Acts; and for purposes connected with the matters aforesaid," it is
expedient to authorise the payment out
of moneys provided by Parliament of—
(1) such salaries or remuneration to
the Inspectors appointed under
such Act
as the Ministry of
Finance may from time to time
determine; and
(2) the expenses of the Ministry of
Commerce attributable to the
carrying of such Act into
execution up to such amount
as
may be sanctioned by the
Ministry of Finance."—(Governor's
Recommendation signified. Mr.
Andrews).
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: In order
that the Committee may appreciate the
financial position, I will briefly set out
the present arrangement in regard to
weights and measures inspection work
and the position that will arise under
the Bill.
The expenses at the present time are
met as follows:-The salaries of the Constabulary inspectors of weights and
measures are paid from the Royal Ulster
Constabulary Vote. That vote shows
that 14 sergeants are employed on the
work at a salary cost of about £4,000
per annum. In addition they receive.
the usual allowances paid to members of
the police and a special weights and
measures allowance of £20 per annum,
bringing the actual cost up to about
£6,000 per annum. Their pensions also
are ultimately a charge on the Exchequer and the pension of a policeman
is proportionately a heavier charge on
the State than the pension of a civil servant.
Apart from a small expenditure on
travelling and subsistence in the case of
the verification of standards, the cost of
their travelling and subsistence does not
finally fall on the Police Vote, but is recouped by the local authorities. The
amount per annum is about £1,200 under
this head. To relieve the Government of
portion of the cost certain fees
charged for the inspection work and
these appear as an appropriation-in-aid
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary Vote
at a figure of £1,400 per annum.
are
What the Bill proposes to do is, firstly,
to substitute civilian inspectors under the
control of the Ministry of Commerce for
the police, and, secondly, to relieve local
authorities of the expense which at the
present time they incur in recouping the
travelling expenses of the inspectors, and
in maintaining local standards and prothe
viding office accommodation for
inspectors. The relief to them will
amount in all to about £2,000 per
annum.
I now turn to the Resolution itself.
The first part covers the item of the
salaries and travelling expenses of the
civilian inspectors; the cost of this is
estimated at £5,000 per annum for
salaries and £1,200 for travelling expenses. The second part of the Resolution covers the expenses of the Ministry
of Commerce, which include such items
as the cost of the time of headquarters
staff engaged in supervising the service,
the cost of office accommodation in Belfast and the counties, and the upkeep of
equipment. It is estimated that £1,700
will cover this type of expenditure.
The total, therefore, of the foregoing is
£7,900 per annum.
As against this there will be the usual
receipt of about £1,400 in respect of fees
taken and the £1,000 contribution to be
made to the Exchequer from the Dogs
Act account as a partial set-off against
the expenditure of which local authorities are relieved. The net cost of the
service to the Exchequer under the new
conditions is therefore estimated at
£5,500.
Hon. Members are entitled to ask
whether this expenditure will be less than
077 Weights and Measures (Money)—

Committee
the cost of the service to the Exchequer
as at present administered. The Ministry is satisfied that there will be an
actual saving to the Exchequer despite
the fact that it is taking over portion of
the burden which at present is borne by
the local authorities. This arises in the
main from four factors; firstly, the
heavier pension liability in the case of a
policeman, secondly the withdrawal of
police candidates for these posts from
their duties for six months or more when
examinations are imminent; thirdly, the
cost of classes held for these candidates,
and fourthly the greater fluidity which
a civil organisation will allow. I beg to
move.

their job I will sit down. There has

work done? The man who qualifies for
this weights and measures certificate must
first pass a stiff examination for promotion on literary subjects. In my time it.
was known as the "P" examination,
which was held before the Civil Service
Commissioners. That examination, or
one equivalent to it, still is held, and
very properly so. The man who passes
that examination if he has ambitions to

has to study by correspondence in his

lectures and special illustrations are
given. The result, generally speaking, is
that he knows all about it. The men
must know all about it because there
have been no complaints about how the
Royal Ulster Constabulary did this
duty.
When a man is appointed an inspector
he gets a district, but all the time he is
in that district he is available for
ordinary police duty if he is required. I
worked about Lisburn, where some of
my friends come from. One of my districts was Crumlin. There is a period
set apart for verification. The local sergeant lets the shopkeepers know there is
going to be a verification and the
respectable traders bring in their weights
and measures and scales to be tested.
For this they pay a nominal fee. The
inspection period follows. The member
of the force doing that generally lives in
the local barrack and drives round.
Remember that if there is an emergency
requiring every member of the force for
public duty he is recalled. He is
generally a sergeant, a responsible man,
and he does not want to be recalled
because he goes to his station wherever
that is. The inspector for the town of
Lisburn lives in Lisburn and is stationed
there. He is a sergeant. I do not know
him but I believe he is doing his duty
well. All the time he has to have a grip
on his other duties. He has control of
his men.
He has to tell off their duties.

But if anything happens in Lisburn he

All that is to be done away with
because they do not do it in England.
One reason for this is that every police
force in England is a separate establishment, whereas in Northern Ireland the
police force is under one authority. You
will allow me to tell you the work was
not done as well in England as it has
been in Northern Ireland. I will give
you an illustration. A man who is a
member of an English local authority
may have a shop. He has a vote in the
appointment of the inspector. It may
be that inspector's duty to go round and
inspect his weights and measures a week
after the appointment has been made.
In those circumstances it could not be as
well done as it is in Northern Ireland.
I am making this attack to try to stop
the Government from running to legislation about things that are all right as
they are. The minute this is set up
someone is going to be put at the head
of this department. I know that neither
the Minister nor anyone else is a party to
anything that is not fair or square-I
am not insinuating that-but there will
be someone for the job and he will gather
a big staff about him until he will have
inspectors going over the whole country.
He will have his staff at headquarters.
If the £4,000 or £5,000 allowed is not

get the money. The fees for verification

There should be no politics in a matter

It is tabled on the instruction of someone

money. You can imagine the inspection of weights and measures in Fer-

managh, Tyrone, and Antrim.

we are left in the dark as to their provisions. Before a Measure of this sort
is brought before the House I feel that
if possible a written statement should be
circulated to Members, who would thus

Mr. BEATTIE: I was absent on the
day on which this Estimate was passed
and I take this opportunity of expressing one or two views which will be of
benefit to the Minister of Education and
to the Parliamentary Secretary. The life
of a teacher in Northern Ireland to-day
is not a very pleasant one. That is due
to many causes. First, it is due to the
falling average in the schools. Last
year we had 3,000 fewer children than
we had in 1936, while the figure in 1936
was less than in 1935. There is a declining child population in Northern
Ireland, but the old hard and fast law
still remains so far as the retention of
teachers is concerned. We should set
ourselves to reorganise the conditions
under which teachers are employed.
This is a heart-burning question to
many teachers in Northern Ireland, and
has actually been the means of breaking
down the health of a large number of
teachers. A teacher who is on the verge
of dismissal cannot have very much consideration for the education of the
children. In Northern Ireland we are
lagging behind in this respect, because
our first duty should be the consideration
of the children. Our second duty is to
see that the children have suitable buildings wherein to be educated, and our
third duty is to see that the teachers get
all they require so that they may be
in a position to give the necessary instruction to the children.
What happened last year? We were
placed in a very unfortunate position.
We had teachers who lost their positions,
teachers who lost status, teachers who
lost category, teachers threatened with
the loss of their positions and vacancies
which were not filled owing to a declining average. Altogether 145 teachers in
Northern Ireland were subject to uneasiness of mind due to the declining child
population. Eire has already met this
question by giving the teachers security
of tenure. Northern Ireland to-day
only gives two quarters. If the average is
not up at the end of the second quarter,
away goes the teacher's position. We are
lagging behind in this respect.
What is the reason why the teachers
in Northern Ireland have not got the
same security of tenure as those in Eire?
Why are large classes being maintained
in schools here? No one in this House or
outside it could impress me by stating
that a teacher is competent to deal with
fifty children in one class. In England
the number is from 35 to 40. Why are
we not going step by step with England!
Forty-five is the number in Northern
Ireland, and in a large number of cases
you get an average of 60 or 65, while in
isolated cases it is 70. We have a large
number of trained students unemployed,
and at the same time you are actually
compelling trained teachers in the
schools to carry out the work of two
people each. We in Northern Ireland must
put our house in order and give the
necessary equipment to the schools. It is
necessary that we should apply ourselves
to the reorganisation of the teaching staff
and give security of tenure to all trained
teachers under the Ministry.
Stranmillis College is producing more
than sufficient trained teachers every year
to supply the nine Ulster counties. I
want the House to realise that we represent only the Six-County area. Why
we should produce sufficient trained
teachers to man the nine counties of
Ulster is more than I can comprehend.
The supply is greater than the demand.
I think it is a waste of public money
and there should be a drastic reduction.
There should be a reduction of at least
twenty-five per cent., and we should only
train sufficient teachers to meet the
demand and leave us with a small surplus. Instead of that, although we
require only on an average, over a period
of five years, 85 teachers each year to meet
all the requirements, we actually turn out
in each year anything from 110 to 120.
That is the position. You are making
unemployed teachers.
It may be argued that that amount
would not be sufficient to keep up the
supply, but I can say this, that if we
were training 100 teachers-80 to fill the
places of those who retire, get married,
or break down in health or go on pension,
and giving a surplus of 20-that would
be a very good figure for the training
college to turn out each year. Instead
of that, we have an abundance of trained
teachers each year who fail to find employment. I have actually known an
unemployed teacher who was out of training for the last five years. One recently
Ministry of Education 990
Supply-
10 MAY 1938
placed was out of training for the past
eight years. We have large numbers of
girls whose parents have endeavoured to
put them through for the teaching profession and who come out of college and
fail to find employment, but find a man
instead. That does not give much satisfaction to the parents who spent money
on them.
I ask the Parliamentary Secretary to
expedite the reorganisation of the school
conditions in regard to the appointment
of teachers. Our classes are put at above
35. No teacher who has to give of his
best to the child should be asked to teach
more than 35 pupils. The second thing
I want to ask the Parliamentary Secretary to do is to try, if possible, to get
these classes reduced immediately so as
to bring into employment those who are
now out of employment. Again, I may
be told the accommodation would not be
sufficient to bring the classes down to
that extent. It is very easy to make
temporary accommodation in the meantime and to get proper results from the
money that is spent on education.
Then there is another point I want to
bring forward. It is very humiliating
for a young teacher just out of college
to have to tramp round the countryside
knocking at doors of members of regional
committees seeking their influence and
vote to get an appointment in a particular school, a position for which every one
of them is highly qualified. They have
to go round and be able to speak about
crops, and about the weather, and about
various shows and things that have
absolutely no connection with teaching.
In every town, village and city, if these
young teachers fail to go round and canvass they have no earthly chance of
getting employment. I say this canvassing must be stopped, and it can be
stopped on these lines. The Minister of
Education should establish a select committee representative of all the educational authorities, with teachers in the
majority, so as to give every teacher an
equal opportunity of being judged on his
merits when he comes forward for
appointment. It would mean the abolishing of the school committees which, up
to the moment, in my opinion, have
given no useful service.
Some of the regional committees have
no knowledge of the requirements of a
school teacher. It is all by influence and
friends who have known Mary or John,
or whoever it may be applied. It is not
on the merits of whether they were in
the first, second, or third division. The
merits of the boy or girl are not taken
into consideration. It is whom you
know, not what you know. We will
have a Bill here from a profession asking
for a statutory right to say who shall
come into the profession and who shall
not. I claim on behalf of an honourable
profession, through whose hands each
Member of this House and outside has
passed, that it should also be entitled to
say who is a fit and proper person to
enter that profession. To-day they have
no voice as to who shall come into the
college or who shall come into the profession as a trained teacher. You have
to get the appointment basis changed,
and the Minister of Education is, in my
opinion, the only person who should be
responsible for the appointment of public
elementary school teachers.
That does not apply to voluntary
schools. The difference is this. In the
voluntary schools you have an educated
manager, a man who understands the
proper qualifications of a teacher. He is
a better authority for making appointments than a committee of laymen who
know nothing about the qualifications
required. I have stood for public control of education all my life. But after
seeing it working in Northern Ireland as
it is to-day I am absolutely ashamed to
think that I was an advocate of public
control of education or giving into public
custody the appoinment of teachers. If
I still am for public control of education,
I certainly withdraw all I said about
appointments, because these local authorities are not fit to make appointments in
respect of schools.
The other point I want to bring to the
Parliamentary Secretary's notice is that
there is no provision whereby, if a
teacher's health breaks down, he or she
has a right to retire. To-day we have
teachers suffering from the effects of
sleepy sickness. If they went out on disablement pension it would hardly be
worth while drawing that pension. Why
cannot a teacher have added service in
such a case, the same as the police or the
same as civil servants? In the Civil
Service one gentleman retired with an
added amount of service so that he got
full pension. The Royal Irish Constabu-
Ministry of Education
Annual Holiday Bill
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
lary were disbanded and had years added
to their service. In a case such as I
refer to, in exceptional circumstances,
teachers should be allowed an added
number of years, and pensions should be.
based on that period of service. To-day
you have large numbers of teachers whose
physical fitness could be challenged.
You should make it easier for them to
retire on pension when their health
breaks down so that they might recuperate
and become fit citizens.
The Parliamentary Secretary might
want to know what I would put in the
place of the present system of appointing teachers. Eire has got a scheme
which was submitted to the heads of
departments for their consideration.
Here is the scheme submitted to me by
one who has given the matter a life
study. This is what he says: The
average on the rolls shall be used instead
of the average attendance. The teacher
shall not lose his position owing to a
fall in the average on the rolls until, in
the case of teachers up to 10 years service, the end of six quarters of low
average. That is, to change the average
from two quarters to six. In the case
of teachers of 10 to 15 years, at the end
of seven quarters; in the case of teachers
of 15 to 20 years, at the end of eight
quarters; in the case of teachers of 20
to 25 years, at the end of nine quarters,
and in the case of teachers of 25 years'
service and over, 10 quarters low average.
These averages would be on the rolls, not
the average attendance.
I want to make this quite clear. Every
school day in Northern Ireland 30,000
children are absent from school. That is
the reason why these 145 teachers are
standing in jeopardy of losing their
positions. The School Attendance
Acts are supposed to operate, yet
every day in Northern Ireland 30,000
children are absent from school. If
there is one dead letter, the School
Attendance Act is that dead letter. It is
surprising to me how these Acts were
administered, but I can assure you that
if all these 30,000 were compelled to
attend school these 145 teachers now out
of work would be in work, and instead
of my asking for a reduction in the
trainees of the college I would be solidly
behind the Parliamentary Secretary in
asking for an increase in trainees from
the college. It is the failure of the Act
being put into operation that is one
of the causes of SO many teachers
being unemployed, and the declining
child population helps. I wish to make
these comments and I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will give them sympathetic consideration.
Mr. BROWN: It was stated in this
House by a Minister that he does not
consider his Estimate successful unless it
provokes some criticism. I wish to complete the circle of comments and to assure
success to the gracious Lady who represents the Ministry by offering some
constructive criticism. I wish to bear

In other words, five teachers were being
compelled for nine months to do the work
of six teachers. That is happening
repeatedly. Further, on this question of
averages, this period of six months may
very often be an epidemic period-

Mr. CAMPBELL: I beg to move,
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time." Since a Measure of this kind was
last before the House, a matter of a
year ago, agreements on a very large
scale have been come to in Great Britain
embodying the principle which underlies
this Measure. These agreements cover
great trades like engineers, shipyardmen,
railway shopmen, and iron and steelworkers. Very large numbers have been
brought in under the schemes arrived at
by agreement. The coal-mining interests,
which is rather peculiar in view of their
vicissitudes of lean years, have adopted
the principle in large areas of England.
The result is that this year as far as
Annual Holiday Bill-
Second Reading
10 MAY 1938
Great Britain is concerned tens of
thousands of workers will have happier
holidays than ever they had before.
Strange to say, barmen in licensed publichouses have enjoyed this right for a
matter of almost 26 years.
Under the
Shops Act of 1912 they are entitled to a
fortnight's holiday without any deduction in wages.
It is a remarkable fact
that the licensed trade, which is so very
often decried and despised, should be a
pioneer in the matter of this very worthy
reform.
In Great Britain 450,000 civil servants
now enjoy this right as well as several
hundred thousand servants of local
authorities and some 270,000 workers in
the co-operative movement. In Northern Ireland the number of persons
fortunately circumstanced in a similar
way comes to about 20,000, and in the
other part of Ireland-Eire-the concession has been made in most big branches
of industry, and in a very short period
it will embrace all branches of industry
in that part of the country. In the coal
industry in Lancashire it is estimated
that the cost of seven days' holiday, free
from any deduction in wages, per year
to every man, woman and child employed
in the trade will work out at 23d per ton
per annum. That is a very unappreciable burden. At the present time, as a
result of voluntary agreements, about
5,000,000 British brain and hand workers
now enjoy this right.
Two years ago
almost half that number would have had
to forfeit part of their weekly wages in
order to enjoy the call of the seaside or
countryside in England or Scotland.
Some 12,000,000 workers still wait enfranchisement.
Other countries are very far ahead in
this matter. It is surprising that we
should lag so lamely and so far behind.
Belgium, a small but highly industrialised country, adopted in 1936 this
scheme of wages being paid during
holiday time for all occupations except
agriculture. Denmark proposes to give up
to 12 days' holidays-a day for every
month of employment-to its workers.
Bulgaria in 1936 extended the principle
to all employed people in its area. The
great neighbouring country of France in
1936 provided by law that every worker,
salaried employee and apprentice employed in industry and commerce or in
the liberal professions or in co-operative
organisations, and every journeyman or
apprentice in a handicraft workshop
should have an annual holiday with pay
for at least two weeks without any deduction in wages.
That was a remarkable
stride for that great Continental nation.
In Norway, Holland, Switzerland and the
Union of South Africa they are on the
march. New Zealand rightly gives four
weeks' holidays without deduction of
wages. Germany and Italy are ahead of
democratic lands. It edges the gibe that
totalitarian States move more quickly
than democratic States. Italy treats
these holidays as an inalienable right.
Is it not?
At the International Labour Conference in Geneva in 1936, thirty-eight
Governments voted for a convention for
six days for workers and twelve days for
apprentices and young people. Twelve
Governments abstained from voting and
of this number-I cannot understand
why, but it is a remarkable fact-three
abstentionists were Great Britain, Japan,
and India. What does this Bill seek? It may
not become law to-day or to-morrow, but I
venture to say that as sure as the light
streams through those windows it will be
law in Northern Ireland and also in Great
Britain within a period of five years.
The Bill seeks by law to secure this right
of workers to a full fortnight's holiday
each year without loss of wages. That is
the basic principle. It may be said that
a great deal has been done by voluntary
arrangement, and I am sure that fact
will be duly emphasised when the Minister who will reply comes to speak. At
Westminster the principle of the Bill has
been adopted. Legislation alone will
bring the backward employers into line.
I submit that legislation will be needed
in order to bring the bad employers into
line with the best employers. Can it be
said that people living in working-class
areas in Belfast, Derry, Lisburn, Lurgan, Portadown, and other urban
centres, do not need holidays? Could
any member stand up and defend that
position?
The vast proportion of these people
who need a holiday never have the chance
of getting away for a full week from
their drab environment. Their wives
and children live hard penurious lives.
This reacts on their health to a degree
that it is unwise to underestimate.
Annual Holiday Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Campbell]
There is wear and tear in machinery.
There is likewise wear and tear in the
human machine also. It wants repair
from time to time. It craves rest from
time to time. This House sits and works
from 40 to 50 days in the year. When
any hon. Member is going for his holidays he does not like to feel that decent
workingmen cannot go too, because they
are minus the cash to eke out a few days
change and rest. For them family holidays of a week are virtually debarred
altogether. Others do enjoy that
privilege but not for the working people
in Northern Ireland is there the care-free
holiday which is needed after periods of
long strain and strong endeavour to
restore the wearied frame and jaded nerves
and overwrought muscles. It is no wonder
that so many workingmen and women in
Northern Ireland, to use an expressive
Northern Ireland phrase, are "done"
before their day.
The labourer is worthy of his hire.
He is also worthy of a period of leisure.
I submit that in each industry in this
area wages are inadequate for people
living at a reasonable standard during
the ordinary periods of the year to make
provision for holidays, I submit further
it is against humanity to force them to
economise out of their miserable earnings
to live through a holiday. The people
that need the holiday most of all, free
from anxiety, are manual workers.
They need the holidays most to recruit
their exhausted strength, unclouded, as it
is at present clouded by a sense of injustice and wrong.
Last year when a Bill providing for
seven days' holidays in the year was
before this House it was suggested from
the Ministerial side, not by one of the
Ministers but, I think, by the hon. and
gallant Member for Clifton (Major Hall-
Thompson), that it was an economically
unsound proposition. I hope I am not
doing him an injustice in my recollection of his argument. I submitted then,
and I repeat now, that there is no justice
and no strength in that argument. It is
the Gradgrind philosophy. Against the
Factory Acts as against the Old Age
Pensions Acts, dyed-in-the-wool reactionaries ever cry out that it would ruin
business. Might I quote wise, apt words
from Dickens's "Hard Times"?
"Surely there never was such fragile
chinaware as that of which the millers
of Coketown were made. . . They
were ruined when they were required
to send labouring children to school,
they were
ruined when inspectors
were appointed to look into their works,
they were ruined when such inspectors
considered it doubtful whether they were
quite justified in chopping people up in
their machinery; they were utterly undone when it was hinted that perhaps
they need not always make quite so
much smoke. Whenever a Coketowner
felt that he was ill-used he was sure
to come out with an awful menace that
he would 'sooner pitch his property
into the Atlantic.' This had terrified
the Home Secretary within an inch of
his life on several occasions."
I hope that argument will not terrify
the Minister of Finance out of his life
to-day. I proceed :
"However, the Coketowners were SO
patriotic after all that they never had
pitched their property into the Atlantic
yet, but on the contrary, had been kind
enough to take mighty good care of it.
So there it was in the haze yonder,
and it increased and multiplied."
Now I say that when this reform comes
along the prosperity of the employers,
far from being hampered, or hindered,
or reduced, will be increased and
multiplied also. Is an argument against
a great reform of this kind based on
£ s. d. not a sordid argument, even
though the account is a little on the
debit side? Is that the be-all and end-all
of this question? Is that the fatal and
final answer so far as the welfare side of
industry is concerned? It is reckoned by
competent authorities that two hours a
week less labour is the measure of the concession that the employer would make by
giving a fourteen days' annual holiday. It
would involve restricted labour on the
part of the workman to the extent of
only two hours a week. Is that a terrifying figure?
The costs of production are made up
not only of wages but dividends, rent,
rates, income tax, lighting, heating,
transport, advertising, and so forth. The
wages paid in many industries are a
relatively small percentage of the cost of
production. I submit to the House with
some confidence that the highest possible
Annual Holiday Bill-
10 MAY 1938
Second Reading
increase of the wages bill would be onetwenty-sixth of a pound, less than 4 per
cent., but the percentage would be even
less, because the additional burden would
not apply to every employee of a firm,
as there are all sorts of employees already
getting holidays with pay. The result
is that the increase would not be 4 per
cent., but might be a little over 1 per
cent.
One gratifying feature of the advance
made is that firms which have accepted
the principle have benefited in their
balance sheets, as the returns show.
Why? Because of the better health, the
greater contentment, the higher efficiency
and the finer self-respect of their workpeople. Surely these gains are assets of
great price. The big industries which
made this experiment would not go back
on it. They have found it simple and
easy to make district and general agreements. The best employers to-day in
these isles are whole-heartedly on the side
of this reform. They would not go back
on it. I admit that covetous employers
would not be willing to make this concession. There have always been such
and there always will be such. They
should be let see that they cannot get
rich in a hurry at the expense of their
fair-minded competitors.
I ask the House to remember that
backward employers, if they were
free, would not recognise their responsibilities under the Factories Acts or the
Workmen's Compensation Act. To continue the voluntary system would encourage such men to refuse to do their
duty and to make it hard for good employers to continue as they are doing
when they would be confronted with the
meanness of grasping rivals. A generation or so might pass before this reform
came into force if we left it to a purely
voluntary system.
I ask the House not to sabotage this
Bill. It may be said that we had better
wait a headline from Westminster. We
have the verdict of the Amulree Committee, which was a long time at work.
At that Committee there was agreement
on the basic principle underlying this
Measure. I ask the House by a ratification of that verdict to affirm the basic
principle at stake by giving this Measure
a Second Reading. Too long this right
has been deferred. It is undoubtedly the
right of the masses who toil for their
bread. Superficial expressions of goodwill are cheap and do not advance matters.
They butter no bread. Lip service to
this reform is a mere sham.
Great Britain's total wages bill is
roughly £1,500,000,000 a year. This
concession would cost at most £60,000,000
a year. In all probability it would be
much less. The cost for the Six Counties
would be 1 per cent. or 11 per cent. of
that sum. Multitudes of workers when the
boon comes to them will circulate
millions of money to the good of trade in,
say, recreation and transport. A workman given a fortnight's holiday in rural
Ulster or seaside Ulster will be a better
and a fitter man for the rest of the working year. Common justice to him
demands "paid" holidays instead of
"paid for" holidays. I ask the House
to remember that it is only since the
industrial revolution that the worker has
come to be a bond-slave of work, and his
fetters have not yet been altogether struck
off. They are being struck off one by one.
By this Bill we would give him zest in
the dignity and worthiness of labour.
Very briefly may I refer to the Clauses
in the Bill? The first Clause gives the
employed person's title to a holiday of
not less than two normal consecutive
working weeks or two periods consisting
of one normal working week in each year.
The title of Clause 2 is "Title to wages
during holidays." It may be said there
is an element of compulsion in this
Clause, because it says:
"Where a person is having a holiday
by reason of the provisions of this Act
he shall be deemed for the purposes of
this Act to continue in the service of
his employer and his wages shall be
paid to him without deduction as though
he were at work full time subject
only to the deduction of any sums he
may have earned in any other employment during such holiday."
I think it perfectly fair and right that
wages earned by a workman during that
time should be deducted. The idea is
that compulsion should be exercised and
must be exercised to prevent a man
sacrificing his own and his family's welfare by an evasion of the Bill.
Clause 3 prescribes the penalty for
non-compliance with the Act, and Clause
4 enables the Ministry of Labour to make
Annual Holiday Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Campbell]
regulations for carrying the Act into
effect. Clause 5 prevents contracting
out. It says:
The provisions of this Act shall have
effect notwithstanding any agreement
to the contrary, written or oral, express or implied, whether made before
or after the commencement of this Act,
and any such agreement shall be void.
Clause 6 provides for the calculation of
earnings, Clause 7 relates to the saving
for customary holidays, Clause 8 deals
with a matter in connection with which
there is great difficulty, namely provision
for broken periods; Clause 9 is the interpretation Clause, and Clause 10 gives the
Short Title.
Mr. BYRNE: I have very great
pleasure in seconding the Motion for the
Second Reading of this Bill. The Mover
has put the case for the Measure so
strongly that very few words will be
required from me. We know that a
workingman requires money to enjoy a
holiday. Unfortunately the wageearners spend their money as they go
along. When a man gets a week's or a
fortnight's holiday, without pay, he is
unable to go away, and the result is that
he thinks he has not had a holiday at all.
We all know that this concession of an
annual holiday with pay has been voluntarily given by many people. In the
trade to which I belong this has been
done for many years: the employees get
fourteen days' holiday with pay. The
workers in the service of the Belfast Corporation have been getting their holiday
with pay for some time past: they get
six days with full pay, and then they get
two days at July, two at Christmas, and
two at Easter. That makes twelve days
with full pay.
In many other business establishments
the employees are given two weeks' holiday with pay. There is no reason why
those employers who are niggardly
enough to refuse to give justice to working people should not be compelled to
grant this concession. The object of this
Bill is to put each and every employer
on the same footing. That is all that the
Bill seeks to do. There is no doubt that
sooner or later the principle of this
Measure will be put into operation. I do
not see why we in this country should
lag behind other parts of the world. It
would be a generous and a creditable
thing for the Government to pass this
Bill, and make its provisions compulsory
on all firms. If a workingman gets a
holiday, he should be enabled to go away
to see his friends or to the seaside. He
would come home a much better and
stronger man, he would appreciate the
concession granted by his employer, and
he would take far more interest in his
work. I honestly believe it would be to
the advantage of the employers to grant
14 days' holiday with pay.
The Bill provides that the holiday may
be divided to suit the convenience of employers. If it does not suit the employer
to give a man 14 consecutive days, he can
divide the holiday. A week at a suitable
opportunity would not inconvenience any
employer. I appeal to the Government
to pass this Bill to-day. I believe that
the scheme will be in operation in a very
short time, but it is desirable that ungenerous and unreasonable employers who
will not follow the good example of other
employers should be compelled to conform. There is no reason why there
should be any distinction between employers; they should all be treated in the
same way. I think the provisions of this
Bill are fair and reasonable. I say it
deserves whole-hearted support, and I
sincerely hope that the Government will
support the Motion for the Second Reading to-day.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
I am
Major HALL-THOMPSON:
entirely in agreement with the principle
of holidays with pay, but it is another
thing to suggest that this should be made
compulsory in Northern Ireland when it
is not compulsory in the rest of the
United Kingdom, or to say that it should
be compulsory in Northern Ireland when
it is not compulsory in the markets of
the world in which Northern Ireland has
to compete. The hon. and learned Member for Central Belfast has said that
5,000,000 employees already enjoy the
privilege of holidays with pay, but that
there are 12,000,000 who do not enjoy
that privilege. I think that when the
time comes that 12,000,000 enjoy holidays with pay, and 5,000,000 are still
without that benefit, then we should consider making the scheme compulsory.

While quite in agreement with the statement that lackadaisical and indifferent
employers should be made to conform to

relation to its competitors. I am also

contemplates starting a new industry here.
will hesitate to do anything if there is the

does not exist elsewhere. Again, to repeat my previous argument, he would
hesitate to start a new industry here if
he felt that he would be handicapped in

world. I hope the day is not far distant
when a large majority of employers will
adopt what has already been adopted by
a great number of employers. In the

As soon as a large majority has adopted

Let us see how industry has benefited
by men of science and invention. Take
iron and steel. Is the hon. and gallant
Member for Clifton aware that seven men
now do the work that was formerly done
by sixty men in casting pig iron? Has
he forgotten that the elimination of the
human element in the pig iron industry.
has involved a very great sacrifice on the
part of the workers? Has he forgotten
that science has helped the pig iron industry to reduce the number of employees
from sixty to seven, without reducing
the output? Notwithstanding that fact,
that industry cannot see its way to give
the seven survivors 14 days' holiday with
pay.

man does the work which it formerly

bricks per hour, while formerly it took

brick industry could afford to pay at

A
new forging machine has doubled the

This work would formerly have taken

it a very exorbitant demand.
Ministers receive their salaries whether

Some of the leading industrialists in Great Britain pay their

New Zealand, a new State, with a

They applied themselves to this question
and to-day the working week in industrial concerns is one of 40 hours, for
which the employees receive £4 per week.

I should like the hon. Member for

1919 I was one of the big five which

of forty hours. A firm, which at that

They are setting up a Committee to

may never finish its deliberations. We

I had an opponent at the recent

with pay. One of my agents reported

the
assurance of the Prime Minister

The Prime Minister has been too long in

The House may turn down this

was not customary for the Government to

when it is done in Great Britain it will

In the shipbuilding and engineering

to face than holidays with pay. They
have to meet keen competition from the

quote for a ship of 40,000 tons they have
got to say that there will be £40,000

that charge is not applicable, because

hand, whereas the firms in Belfast have
to pay £1 per ton freight charges. Since
the introduction of iron and steel ships
we have met those charges and have
survived. We are at the top of the
ladder so far as shipbulding is concerned,
and we have a very prosperous industry
in Harland & Wolff's.
If this House decides by Statute the

physical condition of the industrial

their brethren on the other side of the
Channel, but as the powers of the Society
rest very largely on the statutes, it is
right and reasonable that they should
expect from Parliament that those powers
should be kept up to date. As they find
both in Scotland and England that
recent statutes have conferred additional
powers on the corresponding bodies in
those countries they have promoted this
Bill in the hope of furthering the best interests of the profession and through the
Government advancing public interest.
Solicitors Bill—
Second Reading
10 MAY 1938
At this late stage I do not propose to
go through the Bill in any great detail.
I will say, however, that this Bill has
already had some Parliamentary experience, because last year it was introduced
in another place. It passed through the
various stages there, but was unable to
be dealt with fully in this House owing
to the Dissolution. It comes here really
in the form in which it left the other
House, and it is presented so far as
possible in a manner which will not give
rise to controversy. I should also say
that Members must not be unduly impressed by the bulk of the Bill. It is
to some extent a partial codification, and
legislation by reference has been avoided
as far as possible. A large part of
the print of the Bill is taken up with
re-enactment of existing
existing provisions,
subject to certain modifications, which
in many cases are not very material. I
think it will serve the purpose of the
House if I go through the Bill and
indicate here and there new matters
involved, which depart
from existing legislation by raising some question
of importance or principle.
-
The first part of the Bill covers Clauses
1 to 17 and relates to education, apprenticeship and qualifications. Hon. Members will appreciate that as far as the
intending solicitor is concerned his
education falls into two parts the
practical part which is provided for by
apprenticeship with his master the practising solicitor, and the theoretical part
which is provided for by law lectures.
Between these two a balance is necessary,
and this part of the Bill strives to regulate the legal education so as to maintain
that balance. This part of the Bill is
almost a complete codification
on the
subject. If I say a word or two about
the first Clause and Clause 4 it should
suffice to indicate the main variations
which this part of the Bill proposes.
In Clause 1 there are two alterations
proposed. In the first place, it is proposed
that power should be given to the society.
to make regulations which will provide
for some pre-apprentice courses.
At present an intending solicitor becomes an
apprentice on
on passing a preliminary
examination, which is really little more
than a general knowledge test. There is
nothing to enable him to form an opinion
or to enable those who may have to look
after his education to form any opinion
as to the aptitude of the student for the
profession. Power is given here to enable
the society to arrange some preliminary
course to let students satisfy themselves
and those who are to be their masters in
law of their capabilities and aptitude for
the profession. The other matter which is
new in this Clause is that whereas as at
present there are three statutory examinations the preliminary examination, the
intermediate examination and the final
examination-it is proposed that it should
no longer be obligatory to hold the intermediate examination and instead power is
taken to hold a series of tests. The object
of that change will be obvious because in
order to avoid the cramming which was
usual before examinations the learning
which is necessary should spread more
evenly during the course of apprenticeship with advantage to the apprentice
concerned and ultimate benefit to those
members of the public who will be his
clients when he becomes qualified.
It
I pass on to Clause 3, which makes an
alteration which illustrates the intention
lying behind this part of the Bill.
provides that whereas at present a practising solicitor may have two apprentices he
should in future only have one except in
certain circumstances when he may have
two. It is thought that this provision
will enable an apprentice to receive a
better chance of proper tuition. Clause 4
Ideals with another matter which is new.
At present the maximum term of apprenticeship is five years, and in various
statutes certain remissions are permitted
in respect of university qualification.
These remissions are provided for in a
somewhat stereotyped and inflexible form.
For instance, if a person before becoming
an apprentice has a university degree he
is allowed off with three years instead of
five. It does not matter whether it is a
pass or honours degree the Statute makes
no distinction. Again there is a provision
in the principal Act which governs the
society the Act of 1898-that if an
apprentice obtains a degree after he has
become an apprentice his period of five
years can shrink to four. Again, the
Statute makes no distinction between the
good degree and the poor degree, and,
strangely enough, it relates in this regard
only to a degree in arts and ignores a
degree in law.
There are other provisions in this part
of the Bill empowering the society to make
Solicitors Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. MacDermott]
regulations as to what various lengths
of apprenticeship should be required
having regard to the qualifications of the
apprentice. This is a matter which touches
existing university facilities for legal
education. In proposing the Bill I am
not speaking on behalf of the university
I can with
I represent. While that is so,
safety say that the intention underlying
this part of the Bill is simply to give more
flexibility and is not to shun the advantage of university education. The greater
flexibility which this Clause would confer
could be the means of drawing students
more closely to the university and enable
them more than before to share the privileges and benefits of university education.
With regard to the rest of this part of the
Bill, there is very little which I need
comment on. Nearly everything else has
already a foundation in existing legislation subject to some reasonable and small
variations which do not raise any principle.
Part II deals with the all-important
matter of discipline. The situation at
present is that in matters of discipline
any complaint against a solicitor relating
to his professional conduct is made to the
Statutory Committee of the Law Society.
The Statutory Committee considers the
matter, and if it finds a prima facie case
the matter is then transmitted to the
Lord Chief Justice. This part of the Bill
provides a complete code regarding discipline. The situation at present is very
much the situation as it was in England
until the year 1919. What is proposed
will make the position similar to that
which has existed since 1933 in Scotland.
Shortly put, the most important
the
change made in this part of
Bill is that power is given, subject
the Lord
to a right of appeal to
Chief Justice, to the Statutory Committee
of the society to deal summarily with a
solicitor whose conduct, although it has
been a departure from what might be
expected of him, at the same time does
not amount to anything so serious as to
warrant striking him off the roll or suspending him from practice. It is felt
that that procedure which at present
obtains in Scotland would inure to the
benefit not only of the profession but of
the public, because as things are at present it is felt that persons who otherwise
might make complaints refrain from doing
so owing to the fact that if the complaint
is proved it exposes the solicitor concerned, even in a matter of carelessness,
to a public hearing before the Lord Chief
Justice and the possibility of suspension
or being struck off the roll.
That carries me to Clause 33 of the
Bill which commences Part III. This
Clause and the following Clauses up to
Clause 37 relate to regulations as to keeping of accounts and professional conduct.
That is a new provision as far as Ireland
is concerned. The provision shortly put
is that the society may make regulations
as to the opening and keeping by solicitors
of accounts at banks for clients' moneys;
as to the keeping by solicitors of accounts
containing particulars and information as
to moneys received, held or paid by them
for or on account of their clients; and as
to the professional practice, conduct and
discipline of solicitors.
It is felt that this part of the Bill, if
it is passed into law, will give much
greater public confidence and security,
and will minimise the chances of money
being lost through carelessness. It will
be in the interest of the profession and
It is not a new
every member of it.
provision in the sense that it is experimental, because this part of the Bill
follows closely the corresponding provisions of the English Solicitors Act of
1933. It was felt the matter should be
dealt with by way of regulations,
because it may be necessary to obtain
some little experience before the best
form of regulation is discovered. Nothing
of any outstanding importance arises on
the rest of that part of the Bill.
Part IV deals with restrictions and
offences in connection with practice. Very
little arises on the Clauses in that Part.
It is partially a codification of the existing law, and, generally speaking, I think
I may describe it as an attempt to bring
the law of Northern Ireland in this respect up to the level of that now obtaining in Great Britain. Clauses 40 to 45
aim at restraining the activities of unqualified persons, and that is a matter
which will redound, I think, to the
interest not only of the profession but of
the public at large.
Clause 46 deals with the winding up
of the estate of a deceased solicitor. At
present it has been found in some cases
that on the death of a solicitor some
other person may keep his practice
Solicitors Bill-
Second Reading
10 MAY 1938
going for a long time. It is proposed in
this Clause that a duly qualified solicitor
shall be appointed to carry on the practice
of the deceased solicitor for the purpose
of the beneficial winding up thereof for
a reasonable period. This also will be
in the interest of the public and of the
particular estate concerned.
Clause 47 deals with the absence of a
solicitor from Northern Ireland, and is
aimed at stopping the abuse which arises
when a qualified solicitor who has paid.
his licence duty leaves the country and
allows his business to be carried on by
some person not really qualified.
I may pass over the rest of this Part
to Part V. Clause 50 makes provision
that in certain cases where a client has
become bankrupt, or is likely to become
bankrupt, or seems to be making arrangements to leave the country, the solicitor
may obtain an order from a judge of the
Supreme Court, that, notwithstanding
that one month has not expired from the
delivery of his bill he shall be at liberty
to commence an action to recover costs.
This Clause used to have effect in
Ireland, but it was repealed, I think
really by mistake, by the Statute Law
Revision Act, 1883, and the present
Clause follows closely upon the recent
English Act of 1933.
I then come to Clause 53, which is a
matter of some importance, because it
provides as to the regulations under this
Bill which give flexibility of control to the
society. It is important, I think, that
in delegating power by regulation one
should look to the manner in which the
regulation will be made effective. One
finds in this Clause that after the regulation has been made it must be transmitted
to all the judges of the Supreme Court,
and if a majority of the judges, including
the Lord Chief Justice, dissent then the
regulation, or the part of it dissented
from, ceases to have any effect. One also
finds, and this is a very substantial safeguard I suggest, that after a regulation
has become effective a majority of the
judges, including the Lord Chief Justice,
may break it by expressing their subsequent dissent. The Bill in general does
not in any way diminish the powers or
authority of the Supreme Court or the
Lord Chief Justice who exercises particular jurisdiction over solicitors.
The other parts of the Bill are more
or less formal, and I do not propose to
trouble the House with them. In my
submission it is a Bill which may be
commended to the House with a good
conscience, and I should perhaps say
that the fact that it is moved as a
Private Member's Bill should not be
allowed to cast any great shadow upon
it. The balance of precedent is in favour
of this procedure. The existing principal
Act of 1898 was, I understand, moved by
Serjeant Hemphill in the House of
Commons and by Lord Macnaghten in
the House of Lords. I trust that the
House will give a Second Reading to this
Bill, and I beg to move accordingly.

should like to compliment the Mover on

There is one part of this Bill which

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 11th May, 1938.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
PRIVATE BUSINESS.
Belfast Harbour Bill.
It was reported from the Joint
Opposed Committee on the Belfast
Harbour Bill as follows:-That they had
considered the said Bill and examined
the allegations thereof, which were found.
to be true, and that the Committee had
gone through the Bill and made some
Amendments thereto.

Mr. NIXON: This Vote includes the
Cabinet Offices and this building and the
allowances paid to Members of Parliament and various other items of that
sort. Now, before I come to the
allowance to Members of Parliament, I
want to say that it is laid down in the
Scripture that the love of money is the
root of all evil. Well, that is so, for
the love of money arises from selfishness,
and selfishness in this world is the root
of all evil. The ordinary M.P.'s get
£200 a year. They were elected to this
House on 9th February, but their
allowances did not come into operation
until near the 1st of March-I think
about the end of February. That would
be all right if that was the rule of the
House, but it is not. Cabinet Ministers
who get £2,000 a year-one gets as much
as ten ordinary Members drew their
salaries during all that period. They
got their full salaries at the end of the
month. And then when you talk about
it I can tell you the excuse that is going
to be made. "Oh, they do that in the
Imperial Parliament." I do not know
whether they do or not, but having
regard to some statement about £94,000
of error, and some other things, I am
not going to swallow a financial statement like that.
But even if they do we cannot claim
to be following the Imperial Parliament,
because I find here that there is a sum
of £250 payment, at the rate of two
guineas per day, for Members, and so
forth, attending certain committees.
That does not follow the Imperial Parliament. You can cut all that out about
following the Imperial Parliament, for
you only follow the Imperial Parliament
when it suits you. That sum of £2 2s
a day works out at something like £250
a year, and that is the gift of the Chief
Whip's Department. There are Members on this side of the House who never
were on one committee in their lives
and never will. I never was, and I do
not care if I never am. I do not care
one twopenny ticket. And the reason of
that is simply this, I am economical and
I never want that two guineas and I
never miss it. Five pounds would be
as good to me as £30 to some Members

The next thing is that this House has
never been managed properly. There is
no House Committee, and there ought to
be. There is too much responsibility
when there is a party as strong as that
sitting opposite if there is no House Committee to regulate the rights of each

be paid for attending committees. I

committees were paid I ceased to be a

Kitchen Committee and the Public
Accounts Committee. I was eliminated.
I was actually rushed out from the committees on which I served for eleven
years as a voluntary member. We could
save this amount of money, and I believe
there would be less discontent amongst
the Members if they were unpaid.
This House has been established for a
great many years, and it has been

If that is so, why are some of the officials

Commonwealth-in the Dail, in the
British House, in Canada, in Australia,
or New Zealand. I have heard many
compliments paid to the way the business
of this House is carried on. Of course,
I was omitted from those compliments.
Nevertheless I say, without being egotistical, that Members of this House do
sometimes try to get to the real cause of
certain complaints. Although the Members of this House give that highlyefficient service, the Minister of Finance
has never considered the advisability of
giving them free travelling to and from
their respective divisions. We are £400
Estimates-
Houses of Parliament
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
below the amount paid to the Members
of the British House of Commons, and
£200 below the amount paid to the Members of the Dail.
The Members of both those Houses also
enjoy first-class travelling vouchers. I
think the least we have the right to
demand from the Minister of Finance is
the provision of free vouchers for
travelling to and from our constituencies.
My voucher would cost him only 3d for
tram fares, but I do not think tram fares
would be included. The vouchers would
only apply to rail and bus journeys. The
city Members would get no allowance,
but an allowance should be given to those
Members who reside outside the five-mile
radius. I think that is a reasonable
claim to make. I am putting this forward because I will not receive any
allowance, but I am trying to get this
concession for the provincial Members,
and I believe they are entitled to it. I
hope the Minister will give sympathetic
consideration to this request. This Estimate does not show any substantial
increase, and I have dealt with all the
points that I wished to raise.
Mr. ANDREWS: The hon. Member
for Woodvale must know that when
Parliament is dissolved there is a great
difference between the position of hon.
Members and Members of the Government.
Mr. NIXON: I do indeed.
Mr. ANDREWS: In those circumstances the work of Members of Parliament as such ceases, but the work of the
country must go on, and therefore the
Members of the Government are responsible for controlling the affairs of their
Departments, notwithstanding the fact
that Parliament is not sitting. As
regards Committees of the House, these
are appointed by the Chief Whip's
Department in consultation with the
various Parties in the House, and with
the desire to give reasonable representation to each Party. The hon. Member
for Pottinger, I think, mentioned the
fact that he was not now serving on as
many Committees as formerly. I understand that he is serving on three.
Mr. BEATTIE: Two.
Mr. ANDREWS: I think he is a
Member of the Committee of Privileges.
a Member of the Kitchen and Refreshment Rooms Committee, and a Member
of the Public Accounts Committee. As
regards the allotment of rooms in the
Parliamentary part of this building, that
is entirely a matter for Mr. Speaker. As
regards the allocation of rooms in the
other parts of this building, I readily
admit that I have something to say in
connection with that matter.
I am sure the hon. Member for
Pottinger did not intend to misrepresent
the conversation which he and I had in
connection with the allocation of a
particular room, but I think it is only
right that I should state, in my view,
what exactly took place. The hon. Member asked me if I could give a room which
is occupied by the Press, and I said
"No," that I did not think that would
be fair to the Press. The hon. Member
said, "Well, I suggest that another room
could be made available for the Press,
the Visitors' Dining Room," but my
reply to that was quite candid, that I did
not think that would be fair to our visiting friends. As a matter of fact, I
happened to see that that room was
occupied to-day by those who were here.
many of them members of the legal profession, performing responsible duties.
As regards the Empire Parliamentary
Association, that is a very important
organisation. It exists for the purpose
of promoting close association among the
various Parliaments of the Empire.
The hon. Member for Pottinger desires
that we should belong to that body in
the same way as the Dominions, and he
referred to the fact that I opposed our
having that position. I did so, I readily
admit, and will do so again if necessary,
because I feel that as we are part of the
United Kingdom our proper place in that
important organisation is as a branch of
the Great Britain portion of the Association.
The hon. Member also raised a point.
as regards the position of messengers and
doorkeepers. I am sure he will be glad
to know, if he does not know already.
that six of these officers are permanent,
and the other four, I am informed, are
those whose services are only required
when Parliament is sitting, and that is
the reason for the discrimination.

CABINET OFFICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £7,300 be

which will come in course of payment
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: This Vote
shows a decrease of £66, due to the fact
that in 1937/38 the provision was increased to cover incidental expenditure
on official travelling and so forth in
connection with matters relating to the
Coronation. For 1938/39 provision has
been reduced to the normal level, but
a little more scope for contingencies has

Mr. NIXON: I think there should
be some effort to bring some of the items
in this Vote into harmony with the
economic position in Northern Ireland
at the present time. The Member for
West Down told us that the unemployed
people in his constituency were living on
sixpence per day. That was not contradicted. Without any personal disrespect to the Prime Minister, I think his
salary and allowances are altogether in
excess of what they should be, having
regard to what other people are allowed,
and to the economic position in Northern
Ireland.
The Prime Minister's salary is £3,200.
In addition to that he is getting an
allowance for contingencies of office
amounting to £1,750. That allowance is
free of income-tax. There are various
other items appearing in other parts of
the Estimates for the upkeep of the
Prime Minister and the Prime Minister's
establishment. The two main arguments
the Prime Minister himself puts forward
in support of this are, first that it is
not himself personally; it is the dignity
of the position which he says demands
this salary and allowances. Well now,
supposing it is the dignity of the office.
Surely the M.P.'s have some dignity. I
think that if you go through these Estimates and add up the items for
architectural alterations, fuel, light, and
cleaning, furniture, £900 for a car, the
upkeep of the car, gardeners, and various
other things, you will find that the office
of the Prime Minister costs practically
as much as all the private M.P.'s put
together.
Estimates-
Cabinet Offices
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
It cannot be argued, and I am sure it
will not be argued, that the dignity of
the Prime Minister and his establishment
is equal to the dignity of all the private
Members put together. I remember the
Prime Minister inviting and encouraging
the Nationalist M.P.'s to come in here,
and they came in and went out again.
I am not commenting on whether they
come in or stay out because I do not
care, but when they did come in the
Prime Minister's own salary was twice
as much as all theirs put together.
Another argument the Prime Minister
put forward was that it was fixed and
recommended by a committee set up at
the time. This is correct so far as it
relates to the salary, but it is not correct so far as it relates to the £1,750
that was stuck on some years afterwards
and was not in the original recommendation of the committee which fixed the
Prime Minister's salary. I could move
a reduction in the Prime Minister's
salary if I liked, but I will not do so.
I will simply move that that allowance
of £1,750 which was stuck on and which
was not included in the original recommendation be deleted. That is my
Motion.
If it is a question of dignity, the Lord
Mayor of Belfast must have no dignity
at all, because he receives no salary and
he spends £5,000 or £6,000 a year on
the office. If it is a question of the
recommendation of the original committee, then we will take that recommendation after you take away that sum of
£1,750. I told you a short time ago-
I was called to order at the time, but
I am in order now-that the salary of
the Prime Minister of Queensland is
£1,500 a year, and the salary of private
Members is £750. The Premier is a
Scotsman named Forgan Smith, and he
can come over to Coronations and other
functions in London and have as much
dignity as anyone there.
I say that in view of the economic
condition of Northern Ireland the salary
and allowances of the Prime Minister
and the Prime Minister's office are entirely excessive; that they are a bad
example for public administration, and
are calculated to cause unrest and dissatisfaction amongst the 94,000 unemployed people and the 200,000 or
300,000 who are dependent on them, not
to mention all the people who are living
on sixpence a day. That information
has come from the Government side of
the House. I am not saying anything
against the Prime Minister personally.
He claims to be a superman.
The PRIME MINISTER: No, Sir;
that is quite wrong. I am one of the
most humble Members in the House.
Mr. NIXON: The Prime Minister
does not claim to be a superman. I
accept that. But, standing there not
long ago, you told us that when anyone
touched Ulster he touched you.

hear.
MINISTER:

Mr. NIXON: I did not say the Prime

Mr. NIXON: Am I not entitled to

Do not for one moment imagine that

The CHAIRMAN: As long as I am
in the Chair no one on either side of the

Mr. NIXON: I am satisfied on that

Now that I am put to it I say the allowance paid to the Prime Minister is
beyond that given in any Parliament in
the world for a position of similar responsibility and for all he has got to do.
There is no precedent for it anywhere.
It has been stated that there are two
classes of loyalists. One class is composed of those who live for their loyalty.
Nobody need take that to himself if it
does not suit him. I am not referring
to anyone. The other class live by their
loyalty. There are thousands who feel
the same as I am saying now, but they
have not the courage to express their
feelings.
By what law of dignity or anything
else can the Prime Minister of a Parliament like this claim that he should get
as much as all the private Members put
together? It is contrary to commonsense; contrary to logic; contrary to
justice, and contrary to the economic
position of Northern Ireland at the
present time. It is a hardship not so
much financially but on the conscience
and feelings of the people who are suffering through unemployment, the people
suffering from excessive taxation, and
the people who have had to close their
houses, shops and businesses because of
the way they are being crushed and bent
down with taxation. An example should
come from the top. That is all I am trying to show. I am not trying to take
from the Prime Minister anything that
the Committee, which considered what he

trying to take away the allowance of
£1,750 paid to him free of Income Tax.
That amount was stuck on after the
question of what the Prime Minister
should be paid had been definitely settled

the matter and whose report was confirmed.
The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Member
has moved as an Amendment that the

of £1,750 stand part.
Mr. BEATTIE: On a point of order.
The hon. Member for Woodvale has
moved that the sum of £1,750 be
deducted from the total Estimate. That
does not specialise one item.

expense to which the Prime Minister is

Mr. BEATTIE: I was present when

I opposed it when the late Chancellor

the Members of this House considered
when invitations are sent out? I have
no grievance, because as a matter of fact

of Parliament Buildings. Owing to
technical and other difficulties it was not
found possible to commence building
operations under the scheme until August
of last year.
The arrangements were
complicated by the situation and circumstances of the work, and also by the steps
necessary to obtain the requisite supplies
of fabricated steel in view of the state of
the steel market. Progress, however, has

Alterations in the plans were effected in

in building costs, has resulted in an

of
The next item of interest is the Royal
Ulster Constabulary Depot at Enniskillen.
Experience has shown that some
the sleeping accommodation is cramped
and that there should be greater facilities
for recruits for study. It is, therefore,
proposed to erect a new two-storey building within the precincts of the depot,
embodying a canteen, reading and writing room, and billiard room, and to
utilise the rooms thus vacated as lecture
rooms and for additional sleeping accommodation. The cost of this new building is £4,000.
The Malone Training School has been a
matter of much concern, as juvenile crime
has, unfortunately, taxed the accommodation to the utmost limit. A large scheme
of alterations and additions has been in
hand, and the works are expected to be
completed in the summer of this year.
The provision includes the cost
modernising the fire-fighting equipment.
of
The policy of providing an improved
standard of accommodation at employment exchange premises is being continued. Last year the erection or adaptation of exchanges was completed at
Bangor, Carrickfergus and Cookstown,
while a new building at Newtownards is
almost ready for occupation. Sites have
been acquired at Dungannon, Omagh,
and Strabane, and negotiations for a site
at Newry are in train.
There is a bulk provision of £9,300 for
other exchanges, as improved accommodation is urgently required in several other
provincial towns. The work, however,
is contingent in most cases on the acquisition of suitable sites, and as negotiations
for these are sometimes protracted, it has
been thought advisable to include
general figure to cover the probable expenditure for this programme.

detail on pages 32 and 33 in Sub-heads
B, C and D. There is a small increase
of some £1,300 over last year's figures.
Reductions in the provision for architectural and engineering services and for
rent are offset by increases in the figures
for furniture and fittings, rates and fuel.
The cost of new surveying equipment for
the Ordnance Survey Office accounts for
the increase of some £500. The increase
of some £500 in the provision for the
Prime Minister's residence and Cabinet
offices is due to the renewal of the lead
on the turrets, which is necessary for the
preservation of the fabric.
Turning to Sub-head F, drainage
schemes, it may interest the Committee
to know what the progress on the Bann
Drainage Scheme has been up to March
24th of this year. With the exception of
certain reaches betwen Carnroe Weir and
Kilrea Road bridge and the upstream
end of the Gorge, which, owing to their
difficult nature, have been deleted from
the contract works, and will be carried
out by direct labour, the only contract
dredging remaining to be completed is
immediately downstream of the Toome
sluices. All contract rock excavation is
completed as well as the sluice-gates at
the Cutts, Portna and Toome, with their
accompanying fish passes and other
fishery protection works, and these works
are now being operated for drainage purposes by the Ministry's engineers.
During part of the year the Ministry's
dredger has been operating on the removal of shallows and hard fords on the
Upper River Bann, while on the Lower
Bann channel improvements upstream of
the Cutts sluices have been decided upon
in order to provide a better run-off for
the flood waters to the Cutts sluices, and
to reduce flood levels in the Agivey River
district. The material to be removed in
these reaches is practically all rock, and
it will be necessary to drill and blast
under water and to dredge by a specially
designed dredger, which has now been
delivered from the makers and will start
work at once.
As regards the effect of the works on
flood levels, the past winter can be regarded as a dry one, although there were
three wet periods with maximum river
discharges. The floods which did occur
were handled without the flood level of
Lough Neagh being reached, and during
the winter the Lough has been controlled
at summer level, with the exceptions of
the three short periods mentioned; but
even then the maximum level did not
exceed ten inches above the summer level.
During the progress of the Bann Drainage Scheme material dredged from the
river has been deposited in the form of
dumps along the banks between the Cutts
at Coleraine and Toome. The areas used
for this purpose have, as far as possible,
been chosen with a view to minimising
interference with the local amenities.
The Committee will be aware that to
prevent these dumps becoming a permanent disfigurement of the landscape
a scheme of planting trees on the areas
effected has been undertaken. Some four
hundred acres have already been planted,
and the area to be planted will be in
the neighbourhood of six hundred acres.
It is anticipated that the cost of the
scheme will be about £10,000, and it is
hoped to complete it about the end of
the year 1939. Before leaving this Subhead I should refer to the drainage works
on the River Quoile. Though unexpected difficulties occurred connected
with the stability of the road bridge over
the river, these were overcome, though at
a considerably enhanced cost of the
scheme. The effect, however, on the
flooding at Downpatrick has been entirely
satisfactory, and the money has been well
spent.
Hon. Members may be interested in
sub-head I, which involves merely a
token amount, and is inserted in order
that Members may be aware that land
purchased for a particular purpose is now
being leased for another object. A full
explanation appears on the face of the
Estimate, and I am sure that hon. Members will be pleased to know that it has
been found possible to make such
central site available for our new Ulster
Territorial Association. The drop in the
receipts shown
in
Sub-head J, as
appropriated in aid of the Vote, is due
to the fact that moneys can no longer be
drawn from Capital Fund No. 2, which
I mentioned earlier in this speech, as this
Fund is now exhausted. I beg to move.

proper explanation has been given about
