GRANTS TO FARMERS FOR LAND
IMPROVEMENT.
1. MINFORD asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he has given consideration to the representations which
have been made from time to time by
farmers for a modification of the scheme
of grants to farmers for land improvement and unemployed relief, and, if so,
whether he is now in a position to make
a statement.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): I have much
pleasure in stating that, after consultation with my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Finance, it has been found
possible to make substantial modifications.
in the scheme for the relief of unemployment in rural areas by grants for the
improvement of agricultural holdings.
Such grants will now be available for
bona fide farmers whether they possess
a subsidiary source of livelihood or not.
It has also been arranged that in future
grants will be available in respect of
holdings with poor law valuations of not
more than £200 on the following scale:
Poor law valuations of £100 or
under-grant of 85 per cent. of the
wages of men specially engaged for the
work.
Poor law valuations between £101
and £150-grant of 75 per cent. of the
wages of men specially engaged for the
work.
Poor law valuations of between £151
and £200-grant of 50 per cent. of
wages of men specially engaged for the
work.
Grants under the scheme will, as in
the past, be given in respect of land
drainage and reclamation, stubbing of
whins, improvement of ditches, watercourses and river or sea embankments,
construction of farm roads, construction
and improvement of flax dams, and well
sinking.
I feel sure that the scheme as now
amended will be of the utmost benefit
whether it be regarded from the point
of view of the improvement of farm
buildings or of the relief of unemployment in rural areas.
PROTECTION OF THE YOUNG.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether the Government intends to bring forward legislation
this Session for the protection and welfare of the young and the treatment of
young offenders.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The recommendations of the Committee appointed to
inquire into the existing provisions of
the law in Northern Ireland for the
protection and welfare of the young and
the treatment of young offenders are at
present receiving the earnest consideration of the Government, and the
preparation of the consequent legislation
will be undertaken at the earliest possible moment.
The hon. Member will, however,
appreciate that the questions involved.
are of an
intricate and complicated
character, and although I am unable,
therefore, at the present time to give
any definite assurance as to the date
when it may be possible to introduce
legislation, he may rest assured that I
am just as eager as he is that the matter
should be pressed forward as expeditiously as possible.
THE "A" SPECIAL
CONSTABULARY
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he and the Prime
Minister called a meeting of the "A"
Special Constabulary, through the Inspector-General, in the Exhibition Hall,
Belfast; whether the Prime Minister
addressed the men and asked them to
stick to the Force and the Government
and that everyone would be retained in
the Royal Ulster Constabulary; and
whether six weeks after this meeting
1,500 were in fact disbanded.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
12 MAY 1938
Sir DAWSON BATES: In answer to
the question, which is a somewhat
garbled account of what actually took
place at a meeting of members of the
"A" Special Constabulary, which was
addressed by the Prime Minister in the
Exhibition Hall, Belfast, on the 21st
October, 1922, I may say that the opportunity was then taken of explaining to
that Force the reasons which had necessitated the reduction in the rates of pay
and also the necessity for reducing somewhat the strength of the Force. No
such promise as that referred to by the
hon. Member was given by the Prime
Minister and, in fact, the disbandment
of a portion of this Force to which the
hon. Member refers had taken place
prior to the date of the meeting.
I am glad to be able to record that,
after that meeting, a letter was received
by the Inspector-General from a member of the Special Constabulary who had
acted as chairman of the "A" Specials
Committee, expressing the thanks of the
Committee to the Prime Minister and
to him for the courteous treatment which
the members of the Special Constabulary
received and for the Prime Minister's
speech.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of that
reply was that letter received before the
Government disbanded and dismissed
1,500 of the men addressed by the Prime
Minister?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, Sir; I
prefer to accept the statement of the
Prime Minister rather than that of the
hon. Member.
Mr. NIXON: Does the Minister
wish us to believe that the survivors of
the men at that meeting, upwards of one
thousand, would make a different statement to what the Minister might hear,
and when he states what is inaccurate
is it a sample with the statement made
a short time ago when he made a misstatement of £94,000 on the bus
question?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not
think that question arises. The Prime
Minister was present at that meeting and
the hon. Member was not. For that
reason I prefer to accept the statement
of the Prime Minister.
SPECIAL CONSTABULARY
AWARD FUND.
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether there existed in
connection with the Special Constabulary
a Special Constabulary Award Fund,
and the total amount of such fund;
where the money is now and how it is
to be disposed of.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer
to the first part of the question is in
the affirmative, and the amount of the
fund is approximately £2,000. This
fund is governed by the terms of the
Special Constabulary Reward Fund
Regulations (Northern Ireland), 1929,
and full particulars are given annually
in the Appropriation Accounts.
Mr. NIXON: What does the Government intend to do with that fund?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am rather
surprised at the hon. Member, who used
to be a member of the Police Force, not
knowing that the Award Fund is used
for the purpose of helping in hard cases,
funeral expenses, and also of rewards for
good police service.
Mr. NIXON: How does the Minister
express surprise at any mistake any
person might make in a financial statement in view of his mis-statement of
about £94,000.

Mr. BEATTIE: I had
opportunity in Committee of making a
comment on this Estimate. I wish to
do so on the Report stage. At one period
we had ground at Newtownards rented
for a training depot for the R.U.C. We
had it at a reasonable fee, but for some
reason which I am not aware of we
bought the old military barracks at
Enniskillen. This building cost
upwards of £52,000. I understood that
was to include the all-in requirements
for the training of recruits for the
R.U.C. When it is realised that only
65 members are called each year it will
be seen that this was a very costly building. So far so good in reference to that
charge. We also rented a place named
Sprucefield. Why we paid rent for that
place is more than I can tell. According to the Estimate presented yesterday,
we have decided now to purchase this
place. I do not know what you want
that for because I have been advocating
for years to clear out all the goods and
chattels that are in that building.
Every year the goods stored there are
depreciating in value. We have wireless
sets, lighting sets, ammunition, rifles,
battery sets, and everything of a perishable kind-things that are going out of
use. They are a very heavy charge.
We have also to provide a guard and
storekeepers, and each year there is an
audit. All this expenditure could, in
my opinion, be done away with provided the Minister of Finance decided
immediately to clear out all these things
that are stored at Sprucefield. I can
see that we are going to have this item
as an everlasting patch upon our Estimates. This is going to be our own
property. I thought when the £52,000
was being granted by the House for
Enniskillen that that place would
accommodate everything that was at
Sprucefield. We have purchased
Sprucefield and some poor landowner
has got a few thousand pounds and has
been made rich out of a little bit of
ground that at one time would not have

(Bill 18.)
Milk and Milk Products Bill.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): I beg to
move, "That it be an instruction to the
Committee that they have power to
amend the Bill so as to provide for the
registration of premises used for manufacture of milk products."
The purpose of the Motion is to enable
certain Amendments to be made during
the Committee stage, which would not
have been possible as the Bill was
originally drafted. The object of these
Amendments is to make provision for the
registration of premises other than
registered creameries, that is to say,
factories which are processing milk and
in other ways carrying on work not done
at the creameries. It would also empower
the Ministry to refuse to register premises
not in use at the time of the passing of
the Bill. The Ministry may also refuse
to grant a licence in a case where they are
not satisfied there is a sufficient supply of
milk to justify the establishment of a
new factory. They may also, under the
Amendments which will come before the
Committee make it a condition of
registration that milk shall be drawn from
certain determined areas.
Hon. Members who heard the debate
which took place upon the Second Reading will appreciate the reason why I have
adopted the unusual course of introducing a Motion of this kind. The reason
is that I was most anxious to meet all
the legitimate criticism of the Bill. If
the Amendments are passed the Ministry
would be empowered to afford creameries
and other milk-producing undertakings
the measure of support which some Members considered was necessary. It
appeared in the course of the debate on
the Second Reading that any factory had
power to come into Northern Ireland and
establish itself without let or hindrance,
and there was a fear expressed by hon.
Members that that might jeopardise the
position of other factories. I am myself
satisfied that that would not take place,
and that there was no real danger to these
other undertakings, but in order to meet
the criticism and to go as far as I can in
satisfying the desires of hon. Members,
we propose to bring in the registration
at present in force in regard to creameries.
Machinery will be provided to prevent the
purchase of milk by such factories in
areas where, having regard to the existing outlets, a sufficient supply is not
available. I beg to move.

NEW CLAUSE. (Registration of
premises used for manufacture of milk
products).
(1) Any premises (not being
premises registered as a central
creamery or as an auxiliary creamery
under Part I. of the Marketing of
Dairy Produce Act (Northern Ireland), 1929), which are used for the
manufacture of milk products from the
milk supplies of several cow-keepers
shall be registered by the owner or
occupier thereof with the Ministry of
Agriculture in such manner as the
said Ministry may prescribe, and any
person using or causing to be used for
the said purpose any premises not duly
registered for that purpose shall be
guilty of an offence under the principal Act.
(2) The Ministry of Agriculture
shall, on application being made in
the prescribed manner by the owner or
occupier of any premises to which this
section applies, and on payment of the
fee specified in this section, register
the said premises upon the prescribed
conditions:

of premises

on

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I can assure
the hon. Member that the only interest

for the calculation of the sum payable
under sub-section (6) of section four
of the principal Act, which rates are
in this Act referred to respectively as

rate."

be higher than five
five shillings per

(3) The reduced rate shall apply in

has been purchased for manufacturing

Agriculture may require in order to

A person who fails to comply with

(5) Sub-section (2) of section ten of

conviction to any such penalty as is
imposed by the said sub-section (2).
(6) In this section the expression

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have already,

therefore, propose formally to move the

SCHEDULE (Modifications of the
Milk and Milk Products Acts in their
application to processed milk factories).
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Under the
Milk and Milk Products Act of 1934
licence fees were payable in respect of
milk sold on the liquid milk market,
and this was expressed by saying that
fees should be payable in respect of milk
sold or delivered otherwise than to
creameries. It is now proposed, in view
of the fact that there will be a new
class of undertakings engaged in the
manufacture of milk products, to exempt
milk sold to such undertakings, also
from the provision relating to licence
fees. The Act of 1934 also provided that
the determinations of the Joint Milk
Council relating to milk prices should
not apply to milk delivered to a
creamery. It is now proposed that shall
not apply to milk delivered to a processed milk factory. I beg to move, at
the end to add:
6. The following modifications shall
be made in the principal Act, that is to
say:
--

Committee

(a) In paragraph (a) of sub-section
(5) of section two after the word
"creamery" there shall be added

at a processed milk factory."
(b) In paragraph (a) of sub-section
(4) of section six after the word
"creamery" there shall be inserted the words "or to a processed milk factory."
Amendment agreed to.

"A Bill to provide for payments into
and out of the Milk Fund established
by the Milk and Milk Products Act
(Northern Ireland), 1934, in respect

engaged in the manufacture of certain
milk products, and for allowances out

the said Act to sell butter and margarine; and otherwise to amend the
Milk and Milk Products Acts (Northern Ireland), 1934 to 1937."
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I beg to move
after "certain milk products" to insert

Oral Answers to Questions.
EXPORTS OF COAL AND OTHER
MERCHANDISE TO EIRE.
1. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he is aware that
great uncertainty prevails amongst coal
merchants and other merchants regard-
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
17 MAY 1938
ing their position as to the exports of
coal and other merchandise from Northern Ireland to Eire; and whether he is
prepared to make a full and comprehensive statement to the House on the
whole position.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The position in regard
to exports of coal to Eire, to which the
hon. Member particularly refers, is set
out in Article 16 of the Agreement. The
hon. Member will be aware that the
Agreement has not yet been ratified and
in these circumstances it is not possible
for me to state how Article 16 will be
operated in practice. I have no reason
to anticipate, however, that there will
be any difficulties in the way of the
export of British coal to Eire by Northern Ireland merchants.
As regard the tariff treatment of other
types of commodities exported from
Northern Ireland to Eire, the position in
which they will be placed subsequent to
the ratification of the Agreement is
governed by the Articles of the Agreement and the Schedules thereto. I
would suggest that if any trader anticipates difficulties in the application of
the Agreement to the particular commodities in which he is interested he
should get into touch with my Ministry,
which is at all times ready to render
every assistance possible in such matters.
P.E. SCHOOLS UNDER SEPARATE
ROLL NUMBERS.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether she can state the
number of instances in which adjoining
boys' and girls' public elementary schools
are recognised under separate roll numbers, distinguishing between schools
under-
(a) the management of a local education authority,
(b) Roman Catholic management,
(c) Protestant management,
and if she will further state what alteration it would make in the total staff
employed if each girls' school was amalgamated with the corresponding boys'
school.
PARLIAMENTARY
SECRE-
The
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): In the unavoidable absence of the Parliamentary
Secretary I have been asked to reply.
At 31st December, 1937, there were
about 80 instances in which adjoining
boys' and girls' public elementary
schools were separately recognised by the
Ministry, representing a total of 160
such schools. Of this total, 4 schools
were under the management of a local
education authority, 146 under Roman
Catholic management and 10 under Protestant management.
The amalgamation of boys' and girls'
schools is not always practicable, and
this is more particularly so in the case of
the larger schools. It is difficult to
estimate what difference there would be
in the total number of teachers employed
if adjoining boys' and girls' schools were
amalgamated as in some instances the
amalgamated schools would have an
attendance in excess of 365 and would
be staffed under different regulations
entitling them to a staff larger than the
combined staffs of the separate schools.
If all schools are included it is calculated that about 30 fewer teachers might
eventually be employed but, if schools in
which the average daily attendance on
amalgamation would be over 365, are
excluded, this number (30) would be
increased to 46.
I would point out, however, that the
present regulations require that where
the average daily attendance of pupils
at one of the schools for the preceding
calendar year has been less than 50
amalgamation shall take place on the
occurrence of a vacancy in the staff of
either school unless for special reasons it
shall be otherwise directed by the
Ministry.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask whether
any pressure has been exercised by the
Ministry or regional committees on
Protestant managers to compel them to
unite their boys' and girls' school, a
pressure which has not been brought to
bear on the managers of Roman Catholic
schools or schools under Roman Catholic
management?
Mr. GORDON: Much as I would like
to reply to the hon. Member, I think
this is a matter he should raise when
the Parliamentary Secretary is present.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. ELLIOTT: Thank you.
LAND ANNUITIES IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he is aware that when
previous efforts were made to have the
land annuities in Northern Ireland reduced, the finances of Northern Ireland
were not in so strong a position as at
present, and the rate of interest on
money was much higher than at present,
and whether in view of the altered circumstances he will reconsider the easing
of the burden on the farmers of Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): The Government of Ireland
Act requires the Government of Northern Ireland to collect the land purchase
annuities, old and new, and by virtue
of the Northern Ireland Land Purchase
(Winding Up) Act, 1935, the payment
and redemption of the annuities remains
a reserved matter. It is not therefore
competent for this Government or this
House to alter the amount collectible.
Our financial position does not affect the
matter.
The hon. Member is well aware that
in recent years this Government and the
Imperial Government have assisted
farmers in Northern Ireland to a much
greater degree than a mere adjustment.
of the annuity payments would bring
about. Examples of such assistance are
the derating of agricultural land and
buildings; beef, milk and other subsidies;
and the restriction of agricultural imports by means of the quota system.
Mr. BROWN: Is the Minister aware
of the fact that the position could be
substantially eased by carrying out a
loan conversion scheme for the deduction
of the interest and extension of time
such as was carried out in the year 1933
by the Down County Council of which
the Minister was then and is still a
member?
Mr. ANDREWS: I do not think the
two positions can be compared.
Mr. NIXON: If another Government,
to wit, the Government of Eire, can
persuade the British Government to
alter the 1920 Act and other Acts in
favour of the farmers in that country,
why cannot the Government of Northern
Ireland procure the same concession for
farmers here?
SUGGESTED ULSTER AGRICUL-
TURAL COUNCIL.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state how many
general meetings have been held by the
Ulster Development Association since its
inception and the number of committee
meetings; whether he is aware that in
the appointment of committees no committee was set up to deal with the greatest
industry in Northern Ireland, that of
agriculture, and whether, in view of the
fact that agriculture provides the greatest
volume of employment and the largest
output of industry in Northern Ireland,
he will set up an Ulster Agricultural
Council to do for farming what the
Ulster Development Council was intended
to do for other industries.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply. The
Ulster Development Council has held
two general meetings. At the second of
these meetings the Council set up two
sub-committees, one, an Information
Sub-Committee, and the other a Publicity Sub-Committee.
The Information Sub-Committee met
on the 3rd January and formulated a
programme for the collection of information which is at present being carried
out. The Publicity Sub-Committee has
held six meetings.
In addition to the formal meetings of
the Council and sub-committees, I have
had from time to time discussions with
the chairman and vice-chairmen of the
Council whenever occasion arose.
The Ulster Development Council was
established with the object, first of coordinating the activities of the various.
organisations engaged on publicity work
on behalf of Northern Ireland industries,
and, secondly, of disseminating information regarding the facilities available for
the establishment of new industrial undertakings in Northern Ireland. The
hon. Member will appreciate that it
rests with the Council to decide what
sub-committees shall be set up, but I
Oral Answers
17 MAY 1938
Oral Answers
understand that it is not the intention
of the Council to set up separate subcommittees for individual industries,
and, accordingly, the last part of the
hon. Member's question does not arise.
B.B.C. NEW HEADQUARTERS.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he will make representations to the British Broadcasting Corporation to have the new £150,000
B.B.C. headquarters in Belfast built of
Newry or Mourne granite, and thus assist
employment in the oldest existing industry in Northern Ireland, which produces
building materials and gives more and
better paid employment than any other.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply.
Immediately following upon the
announcement of the B.B.C.'s intention
to construct new premises, my Ministry
took up with certain granite-producing
interests the question of the possible use
of Mourne granite in the proposed new
building. At that time, however, I was
given to understand that local granite
merchants did not appear to be interested,
as they had a substantial number of
orders already on hand.
If, however, producers of Mourne
granite are now desirous of having an
opportunity of submitting tenders in
connection with the new B.B.C. building,
I am quite prepared to bring the matter
to the notice of the British Broadcasting
Corporation.
EXPENSES OF JURORS.
7. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether, in view of the
expense to which jurors are put in connection with criminal prosecutions, in
travelling to Assize and County Courts,
he will introduce legislation into this
House to reimburse those who perform
the duties of jurors their travelling expenses, as well
as allowance for subsistence while so engaged.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The obligation of
jury service has, from the earliest times,
been regarded, especially in criminal
cases, as one of the duties of citizenship
to be discharged by the citizen without
payment.
The Government is fully alive to the
desirability of minimising the inconvenience caused by the necessity of jury
service, and I would remind the hon.
Member that as a result of the alterations
in the law embodied in our Jury Law
Amendment Act of 1926 a substantial
measure of relief was afforded in this
respect, both by way of a revision of the
rating qualifications, which exempted a
considerable body of persons of small
means, and also by ensuring a more even
distribution of the burden of jury service,
so that in general the obligation of any
person liable for jury service to attend
as a juror only recurs at long intervals,
whereas formerly in many instances
jurors had to attend several times a year.
The suggestion of the hon. Member
would impose a heavy charge upon the
taxpayer, but apart altogether from any
financial consideration, I do not think it
would be desirable to depart from the
practice which obtains throughout the
United Kingdom and which is based
upon such a well-established principle of
British law.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask whether,
in view of that reply, the Government
would be prepared to give their support
to such a Bill if it were introduced by a
private Member?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
explained the views of the Government
in regard to this matter, and when I
tell the hon. Member that so far as his
own county is concerned the average
attendance of jurymen is only once in five
years he will realise there is not such a
great hardship as he imagines.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware of the fact that jurors
are the only people who are unpaid?

which he based his statement on 1st

that the accounts of the Transport Board
for its first year to 30th September, 1936,
then almost ready for publication, would,
it was expected, disclose that the revenue

Sir DAWSON BATES: The information on which the statement referred to
by the hon. and learned Member was
based, was given to me by the chairman
of the Transport Board in the course of
an informal conference on the general

There is, consequently, no report in

The first intimation I had as to the

HOURS OF BARMEN IN COMBER
DISTRICT.
9. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware of
the conditions prevailing in the Comber
district amongst barmen who do not enjoy a weekly half-holiday or annual
holidays with pay as provided under the
1912 Shops Act; whether the Newtownards Rural District Council have any
powers to enforce the law under the
Shops Act of 1912; and whether he will
cause investigations to be made to find
out the actual situation which not only
applies to barmen but other employees
in other stores.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
17 MAY 1938
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Ministry
has received representations from the
Amalgamated Transport and General
Workers' Union with regard to the conditions of employment of barmen in the
Comber district.
No rural district council in Northern
Ireland is a "local authority" within the
meaning of the Shops Acts, and the
Newtownards Rural District Council has,
therefore, no power to enforce those provisions of the Shops Act, 1912, which
apply in such districts.
The whole question of the law as to
shops in Northern Ireland is at present
under the consideration of a committee
appointed by me, and I understand that
their report will shortly be submitted
to me.
DISPLACEMENT OF LABOUR BY
TRANSPORT BOARD.
10. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he will consider
the position of persons deprived of employment by the taking over of buses and
lorries by the Transport Board; whether
this displacement applies to persons employed as painters by private concerns
on the painting of buses and lorries, and
whether such persons will obtain a share
of the work given out by the Transport
Board, or will receive compensation for
loss of work.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The position
of persons in the employment of transport undertakings was considered when
the Bill was before this House, and the
hon. Member will find the provisions
dealing with the matter in Section 36 of
the Act.
It was, of course, quite impossible to
cover all persons whose business or employment might be indirectly affected in
some way under the provisions of the
Act, but obviously the general volume
of work of the nature referred to by the
hon. Member that is available in the
Province would not be greatly affected
by the transfer of these undertakings to
the Board.
WORKING-CLASS HOUSES IN
ARMAGH.
11. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether in view of the
acute housing situation and the small
number of houses built in Armagh, he
will consider the advisability of setting
up a Commission of Inquiry into the need
for working-class houses, SO that
immediate action may be taken; whether
a number of houses have been condemned
and closing orders issued by the Commissioner, thus placing tenants in an
awkward position without the provision
of alternative accommodation; whether
representations have been made by the
building trades to the local Commissioner
regarding housing, and if so, what action
did he take; whether, in view of this
housing situation, the appointment of a
Commission will be treated as urgent, as
serious unemployment exists amongst
workers in the building trades of Armagh,
and would he be willing to accept
evidence from the National Federation of
Building Trades Operatives if a Commission is set up.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government has already intimated that it proposes to introduce legislation to encourage
the building of houses for the working
classes, and the proposals have been prepared and will be circulated to local
authorities within the next few days for
their observations. In the circumstances
matters would only be delayed by the
appointment of a Commission of Inquiry
as suggested.
It is a fact that the Commissioner for
Armagh urban district has condemned a
number of houses, but I am not aware
that in any instance closing orders have
been enforced where no alternative
accommodation was available. I am unable to say whether the Commissioner
received any representations from the
building trades, but at the request of the
Ministry he caused a survey to be made
of housing conditions in Armagh and
furnished my Ministry with a copy of the
report as evidence of the need for the
building of new houses.
In view of what I have said, the considerations referred to in the last part of
the question do not arise.

STAFF AT BELFAST HARBOUR
BOARD'S NEW AERODROME.
13. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether there are about eighty
men working for the Belfast Harbour
Board on the new aerodrome; whether
fifty-three of these men were placed on
the job by the Ministry of Labour and
are paid £2 7s per week; whether the
balance of the men receive £2 9s per
week; whether the men are all doing the
same class of work, and if so, whether
the Ministry will see that the men placed
on the job by the Department will receive
exactly the same wages and conditions as
the men working alongside them on that
job.
Mr. GORDON: The hon. Member will
be glad to learn that arrangements have
already been made by the Harbour Commissioners, with the approval of the
Ministry of Labour, for the men engaged
through the employment exchanges for
work on the new aerodrome to be paid
the same wages, namely, £2 9s a week,
and as from the same date as the Harbour
Commissioners' own employees.
Following a recent agreement between
the Harbour Commissioners and the
Amalgamated Transport and General
Workers' Union, under which an advance
of 2s a week was given to men in receipt
of 47s a week and over, the Harbour
Commissioners were able to pay the

whose instigation the remuneration paid.

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): The Ministry of
Agriculture is empowered to determine

dealers, and such determinations cannot

given by the Egg Marketing Committee.
Before the price-fixing scheme came
into operation last year my Ministry was
advised by the Egg Marketing Committee that the price payable to Class B
dealers by Class A dealers should be

Recently the Egg Marketing Committee has again had this question under
consideration, and has tendered advice to

that for the remainder of the year the
margin should be seven-sixteenths of a
penny per lb. The question of approval
by my Ministry does not arise since, as

on the recommendations of the Egg
Marketing Committee. The total service
margin remains unaltered; this is solely
a question of the proper division of the
margin between A and B merchants.

Financial Statement, 1938-39.
Mr. ANDREWS: I feel that I am
probably correct in saying that Ministers
of Finance the world over invariably
look forward to their Budget Day with
a considerable amount of anxiety, for it
is the occasion beyond all others when
they are called upon to give an account
of their stewardship-to unfold how the
"out turn" of the past financial year
has corresponded with their Estimates
made at its beginning, and further to
enter again the dangerous domain of
prophecy as regards the financial year
that lies ahead.
It will be appreciated that estimating
is a particularly difficult task here, due
to the fact that over eighty per cent. of
our tax income is regulated mainly by
the rates of taxation fixed by the British
Chancellor, whilst our expenditure is
largely decided by the fact that the
Government feels that our Ulster people,
as citizens of the United Kingdom, are
entitled through their social services to
the same advantages as are enjoyed by
our kith and kin who live in Great
Britain. Further difficulty in estimating arises owing to our being so largely
dependent on three industries for our
prosperity, with the result that a slump
in any one of the three affects our unemployment expenditure to a greater degree
than would be the case in Great Britain.
This disadvantage the Government hope
will be gradually overcome by the
establishment of new industries of
various kinds.
Following the usual practice of my
distinguished predecessor, to whom Ulster
will always owe so much, I wish at
this stage to say a few words as regards
our industrial position because of its
close association with our financial
position. The welfare of our native land
is the wish of us all, although we may
differ widely as to the methods by which
this can be best brought about. Up to
last September trade, generally speaking,
was fairly satisfactory and more of our
people were in work than probably ever
before, and the number of unemployed
was below normal. In the latter months
of the year a very regrettable set-back
took place due to circumstances quite
beyond the control of this Government.
The most important adverse influences
have been the war between China and
Japan, the Spanish Civil War, the
financial difficulties of almost every
country in Europe, the general depression in the United States of America,
and the regrettable delay in bringing
about the new Trade Agreement between
that country and the United Kingdom.
Unfortunately our linen trade was also
seriously affected by the substantial fall
in the price of raw cotton, with the
goods manufactured from which our
staple industry has to compete.
Notwithstanding these adverse influences, it is satisfactory that the
tonnage of goods passing through the
Port of Belfast in 1937, including the
Minister's Financial Statement 1110
The Budget-
17 MAY 1938
tonnage of vessels cleared at the Port,
equalled the record figure attained in
the previous year. The trade of the
Port of Londonderry, too, was well above
the average of previous years.
The
value of our exports of linen showed an
improvement, and it is also encouraging
to know that the manufacture of aeroplanes, our principal new industry, is
now giving employment to over two
thousand persons, and that this number
is likely to be considerably increased in
the near future. Our shipbuilding
industry is enjoying a considerably
increased degree of activity.
Our people's investments in Trustee
Savings Banks and in the Post Office
have shown year after year a very important increase, and I think it will be
admitted that, speaking generally,, social
standards have been raised, and through
our ever extending social services and in
other ways it is gratifying to know that
poverty is being gradually and substantially reduced.
Agriculture, our chief industry, is
undoubtedly on a sounder basis than for
many years, largely due to the Imperial
Government's tariff and quota policy and
the substantial subsidies and assistance given in various ways to encourage the production of crops and the
rearing of cattle. The various pricefixing Boards which have been
established by my friend the Minister of
Agriculture ensure as far as possible that
farmers get a reasonable return for their
capital and labour.
As regards industrial prospects for the
current financial year, it is difficult to
say anything very definite. If peace and
security can be established throughout
the world and the nations influenced to
appreciate that the welfare of each is for
the good of all, that instead of being
bitter and suspicious rivals they should
be helpmates, and that the human race
is one wherever domiciled, a secure
foundation would be laid upon which
increased prosperity the world over could
be gradually built and in which we, as
a large exporting country, should fully
share.
May I, however, at this stage sound a
warning note? I feel that as a community the belief is being fostered to too
great an extent that we should rely on
the State instead of on ourselves for the
development of our industry and the promotion of our trade. (Hon Members:
Hear, hear.) The industries of Ulster
were not built up by State financial
assistance or by Government Departments. They were established by the
courage, enterprise, diligence, devotion
to duty and skilled craftsmanship, of
individual Ulstermen and Ulsterwomen,
and I am convinced that it will only be
through the display of these high qualities that this portion of the United Kingdom will continue to play its part in the
world of commerce and in promoting the
progress and welfare of mankind. It is
true that the State has its proper sphere
of co-operation and in the prevention of
injustices. Unwise State interference
with industry and its too wide-spread
activity would become thoroughly
demoralising and destructive of personal
initiative, and would consequently be
liable, in my opinion, to do more harm
than good.
In preparing my second Budget I have
had more time to examine the intricate
nature of our finances than was the case
last year, and as this is the first Budget
of the new Parliament and as we have
many new Members present, I should
like to take the opportunity of referring
to certain suggestions and criticisms
regarding our finances which have been
made during my first year as Minister of
Finance. This will, however, increase
the length of my statement to-day, and
I would therefore ask for the indulgence
of hon. Members.
The Government is frequently urged,
as all Governments are, to reduce taxation and at the same time to spend more
in many directions. It should be
remembered, as I have already said, that
more than eighty per cent. of our
taxation is levied and collected by the
Imperial Government on a United Kingdom basis, and it must be a relief to our
taxpayers to know that we have not the
power to raise income tax and super tax
above the British standard level even
if we wished to do so. It is true, however, that we have the power to grant
certain refunds in connection with these
two taxes if we considered we were justified in doing so. The Government has
never, however, used this power because
it has been our policy, for the past
seventeen years, to provide for our people
similar social services and, generally
Minister's Financial Statement 1112
The Budget-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
speaking, the same level of the standards
of life as are enjoyed in the other parts
of the Kingdom. Through our interlinking with British finance we have, in
connection with unemployment, agriculture, and in other ways, received considerable advantages, and besides it gives
us a meausure of security and credit,
which is of the greatest value to us
financially and economically. Hon. Members will appreciate, however, that we
could not expect to enjoy this position.
if we were not prepared to shoulder the
same obligations as regards taxation as
our fellow citizens in the rest of the
United Kingdom.
I am sometimes asked why, if our
finances are in a satisfactory condition,
it is necessary for the Ministry to
borrow. In order to clarify the position,
I have for the first time included in
the White Paper which hon. Members
have in their hands a statement of our
Public Debt-Table IV.
Our major borrowings are for three
purposes. First, for the Government
Loans Fund, out of which we lend to
local authorities for capital works such
as water supplies, housing and so forth,
as well as to the Exchequer for such
Government expenditure as Parliament
may decide is to be financed out of
borrowed money; examples are-
-the payment of housing subsidies, the cost of
constructing or rebuilding police barracks, and of the Bann Drainage Scheme,
the loan repayments being spread over
a period of years. These improvements
obviously result in the creation of
tangible capital assets, and, therefore, it
is reasonable that the cost should be met
by gradual repayments, which are con-

The second purpose for which the

ceased; the amount outstanding, however, is substantial but is being repaid
gradually, and these repayments are met

The third main purpose of our borrowing is to meet temporary shortages in
which

revenue
The third question which is sometimes.
put to me is "Why are we creating
Capital Funds? Why not relieve the
taxpayers instead?"
There are four such Funds. The first
is a Reserve Fund, which is not earmarked for any particular purpose, but,
as its name implies, is held in reserve for
the Exchequer much as a commercial
house holds a reserve: it consists of our
Budget surpluses in recent years, and
its value at 31st March last was
£107,573.
The second is a Capital Fund, amounting to £1,310,145, of which the interest
is paid to the Exchequer. It represents
our apportioned share of All-Ireland
Funds in existence before our Parliament was established, and as the services
formerly met from those Funds are now
financed in Northern Ireland out of
voted moneys, it is proper that the
apportioned capital should be held intact
and the interest on it go to relieve the
Exchequer, which is now charged with
the relative expenditure.
The third is a Sinking Fund, which
amounted to £1,288,958 at the 31st
March last, designed to meet the interest
payable to holders of Ulster Savings
Certificates. Prudent finance demands a
provision of this sort, and, in fact, Mr.
Pollock wisely adopted this safeguard
in advance of the corresponding provision in Great Britain for the Savings
Certificates of the United Kingdom Government.

view of the amount of revenues derived

The two Funds together were valued at
31st March last at £2,319,518.

Now I can arrive at my balance sheet
for the year.
The estimated expenditure is £14,662,000. The estimated
revenue is £15,922,000. Leaving me
with a provisional balance of £1,260,000
on the credit side of the account.
I now come to certain proposals affecting both the revenue and expenditure of
the year. In presenting my Budget last
year I was able to announce certain concessions in regard to motor vehicle duties,
which became operative from 1st January
last. The rates of tax on private cars,
motor-cycles and agricultural goods
vehicles were reduced to the same levels
as those obtaining in Great Britain. The
fee for driving licences was also reduced
to the amount payable in Great Britain.
The difference in the rates of duties
between Great Britain and Northern
Ireland on goods vehicles was reduced by
one-half, and the difference between the
rates on hackney vehicles by approximately one-half. Notwithstanding these
concessions, which were estimated to cost
£93,000 in a full year, of which £82,000
would represent the loss to the Road
Fund, the revenue from the motor vehicle
duties has continued to expand although,
of course, the full effect of the reductions
made last year has not yet been felt.
The duties last year yielded actually a
sum of £26,000 in excess of the Estimate,
mainly due to a very substantial increase
in the number of private cars.
The
number of annual and quarterly licences
issued for private cars increased from
72,734 during the year 1936-37 to 83,291
in the year 1937-38.
While it would be imprudent to assume
any continued expansion of the revenue
from motor vehicle duties at anything
like the rate which these figures indicate,
I have decided, after consultation with
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Home Affairs, that in the present state
of the Road Fund finances I am justified
in making further concessions by way of
bringing the Northern Ireland rates of
motor vehicle taxation into line with
those prevailing in Great Britain. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Accordingly,
as from 1st January
next, the remaining difference between
the rates of duties in Great Britain and
Northern Ireland on goods vehicles will
be abolished. The cost of this concession in a full year is estimated at
£26,000 and in the present year at
approximately £15,000.
The rates of duties on hackney
vehicles, that is to say, omnibuses, and
such like, will also as from 1st January
next be reduced to the rates operative
in Great Britain. The loss of revenue
entailed by this proposal is estimated in
a full year at £9,000 and in the present
year at approximately £8,000..
Again, as from 1st January next, the
fee of five shillings in the case of motorcycles and ten shillings in the case of
all other motor vehicles at present
charged in Northern Ireland on an
application for the refund of the surrender value of a Road Fund licence
will be abolished. This remission is expected to cost approximately £2,000 in a
full year.
The loss in the present year
will be relatively small.
The total cost of these motor taxation
concessions is, therefore, estimated at
£37,000 in a full year and £23,000 in

I should mention that there is a type
of motor vehicle in respect of which the

paid in Great Britain. I refer
certain classes of electrically-propelled

The additional tax of £2 a year
charged on private cars used for drawing
trailers will remain. My right hon.
Friend and myself have given very careful consideration to the representations
which from time to time have been put
forward in favour of the removal of this
additional tax. Our decision to retain
it has been taken, not on account of
the revenue involved, which at present
is some £2,200 a year, but on account
of the much more important consideration of road safety. No step should, in
our opinion, be taken which would lead
to any substantial increase in the use of
these conveyances. In any case it is, I
think, only fair that these vehicles,
which are responsible in some degree for
the wear of the roads, should pay a
small contribution towards the cost of
their upkeep.
I come now to a proposal which affects
to a minor extent the revenue from

benefit of dependants are chargeable
with estate duty if they exceed in value
£25 a year. I propose to extend the
limit of this exemption to £52 a year in
order to bring our law in this respect
into line with the law in Great Britain,
in which a similar amendment was made
in 1935. The resulting loss of revenue
will, it is expected, be rather less than
£1,000 a year, but the concession will,
I believe, be welcomed by a very deserving class of persons-mainly the widows
and children of men of comparatively
Some hon.
Members may recollect
that in our Finance Act of the year
1936 an amendment was made in the

of the £2 annual licence duty
persons hawking goods in motor vehicles.
The 1888 Act only referred, for obvious

scope
While no opposition was offered to the
amendment at the time, the demand for
the first payment last year evoked protests from certain grocers, who objected
to being brought within the scope of the
hawkers' licence duty, and also from oil
distributors. I set up an Inter-
Departmental Committee to investigate
the matter, and I received their report
a short time ago. They obtained evidence from interested parties, including
Chambers of Trade and Commerce,
grocers' associations, and so forth, and
found the position bristling with difficulties and, indeed, I may say, anomalies.
It is, for example, difficult to justify a
person who hawks vegetables being
exempt from licence duty, while
who hawks cheap manufactured goods,
such as men's shirts or ladies' underwear, should have to pay.
one
I propose, therefore, to recommend to
Parliament to abolish present hawkers'
licence duty with retrospective effect
from 1st April last. The loss of revenue
which this involves is comparatively
small, amounting about £1,750
a year.

I am hopeful that the independent committee of the various interests concerned

For some time past the Government
has been giving careful consideration to
the question of what further steps might
usefully be taken to assist the objects
which the New Industries (Development)
Act of last year was designed to achieve.
The Government fully recognises the
advantages which from this point of
view would accrue from having permanently resident in the Capital of the
Empire a Northern Ireland trade representative. (Hon. Members: Hear hear.)
It is, therefore, proposed to proceed at
the earliest possible date with the establishment of a Northern Ireland office in
London under the control of an officer
appointed by the Minister of Commerce,
and with an appropriate staff.
During recent months I have had
several conferences with representatives
of the Belfast Harbour Commissioners
regarding the need for the deepening of
part of the channel of the harbour to
an extent sufficient to enable the shipyard to undertake the construction of
the very largest size of merchant ships
and battleships. The cost of the work.
necessary for this purpose is estimated at
£400,000, a sum which the Harbour
Commissioners state could not be provided out of their own resources.
In considering this matter the
Government and the Harbour Commissioners have had in mind not only the
immediate employment created in undertaking a work of this character, but also
the benefit, from the point of view of
future employment, of attracting to the
shipyard orders for the construction of
certain of the largest types of vessels,
for which at present the harbour does
not offer adequate facilities.
As a result of the conversations to
which I have referred, the Government
has undertaken to provide assistance
towards the cost of the work on a very
generous scale, namely, to the extent of
£225,000. I have every reason to expect that the Harbour Board will shortly
confirm the agreement reached by me
with their representatives, and that,
when they have done so, the work will
be commenced without delay. In view
of the magnitude of the amount, it is
intended that the Vote charge shall be
spread over a period of years by means
of an annuity arrangement. A Bill to
give effect to this, and a Supplementary
Estimate for such portion of the charge
as may arise in the current year will be
introduced in due course.
I am glad also to announce that the
Government has arranged to assist in the
financing of extensive harbour deepening works at Londonderry up to a sum
of £20,000 to enable ships of deeper
draft to reach the port, and at Coleraine
up to a sum of £6,000 for a similar purpose. The work at Londonderry has
already begun.
I come now to a matter to which
during the past year I have given a
great deal of consideration, that is the
amount of the grants out of our Exchequer to the Queen's University. On
the Vote for Educational Services our
Parliament provides each year for
this purpose, in pursuance of various
statutory enactments, grants totalling
£40,000, including the grant of £10,000
formerly charged on the revenues of the
Church Temporalities Fund. In addition,
the Agricultural Services Vote bears a
substantial charge in respect of the
University's Faculty of Agriculture. Of
the total revenue of the University,
which amounts to rather less than
£100,000 a year, Government grants,
therefore, account for £47,000-not an
ungenerous contribution by the State.
My Colleagues and I have nevertheless
been impressed by the arguments which
have been put before me as to the
University's needs in regard to both
staffing and accommodation, and that,

The Government are satisfied that this

£1,000.
There is another matter to which I
desire briefly to refer. It will be
remembered that, when the medical
benefit system was introduced, the feeling was very general that as existing dispensary doctors would be relieved of a
substantial portion of their dispensary
work by the medical benefit system,
while continuing to receive the same
salaries from the Boards of Guardians,
they should not be paid the same rate
for their panel patients as the doctors
who had not dispensary salaries to
depend upon. That arrangement has
been continued until now, but after
giving the matter careful consideration
I have come to the conclusion that the
position has so altered, both as regards
the work at the dispensaries and in other
directions, that its discontinuance can be
justified. The cost of this concession in
a full year will at present be about
£6,500, but it is, of course, a diminishing amount. Legislation to give effect to
this proposal from 1st October next will
be introduced in the autumn by my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Labour.
Finally, I come to one proposed new
item of expenditure which, though
relatively small, will perhaps not be
without interest for Members of the
House. It is my intention to submit
to-morrow a Resolution authorising, with
effect from the commencement of the
present Session, the payment out of
voted moneys of the expenses of
private Members of this House, incurred
in travelling between their homes and
Belfast for the purpose of attending
meetings of this House or of Committees.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) In addition, the Resolution will include provision for a flat rate allowance of £10 a
year for all private Members of the
House of Commons to cover their additional expenses in travelling between the
City and Stormont, and for an increase
from two guineas to £2 5s in the daily
allowance payable to Members of the
Senate in respect of their expenses for
attendance at meetings of the Senate
or at meetings of Select or Joint
Committees.
I have now completed my review of
new expenditure unprovided for in the
Estimates already presented. The total,
although it cannot at the moment be
definitely stated, is a large one. Moreover, most of the items are recurrent and
will impose additional burdens on our

con-
I hope that, as a result of what I have
said this afternoon, the soundness of our
financial position will be apparent to all.
The anticipated increase in the yield of
our reserved revenues in the present
year, owing partly to the recent increases
in taxation levied by the United Kingdom Government, has of course
tributed to that position. Tax reductions in a future year would, on the other
hand, reduce the margin of revenue.
Owing, however, to our recent arrangement with the United Kingdom Government we are now, I am glad to say,
given complete security against periods.
of depression in our finances—a security
which we did not formerly possess, and
the lack of which often caused me considerable anxiety. I feel that I am now
entitled to say definitely that on the
basis of equal rates of taxation the people
of Northern Ireland can at all times
depend upon enjoying the same conditions as their fellow-countrymen in other
parts of the United Kingdom. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)

then did so in support of the principle
of the Bill, and the opposition came from
the legal Members of the House. Sometimes lawyers take a conservative view on
many matters in the way of progress, and
the motto of the Inns in which most of
them studied is "nolumus mutari." A

Bill by this House, a similar Bill found

Thereupon, the Solicitor-General for

Bill the help of the Parliamentary

thrice the House of Commons at Westminster had shown a disposition to right
the wrong under which a father can
dispossess a child or dispossess a wife.
under his will without just cause. That
Bill was amended by a Standing Committee of the House of Commons. That
Bill in its present form, of which this
Bill is mainly a replica, is really the
drafting of the English law officers.
I do not intend to cover the ground
I covered last year, but I must again
submit to the House that it is a manifest
breach of duty by a father or husband
who knows what his duty is towards a
wife or children who are dependent on
him to dispossess them at death, to cut
his
them off either through caprice or callousness. A wise and just father would never
do such a thing. A wise and just
husband would never do such a thing.
He would make, as in duty bound,
adequate provision for the maintenance
of his widow and for the maintenance,
education and advancement
of
children. Is it right that an unjust or
unwise father or husband should have
the opportunity at death to divest himself of all responsibility towards wife or
children, that a mother who has worked
for very many years, and worked well,
for the welfare of the family, should be
treated as an outcast, and that the children
should be cut off without a penny and
denied all reasonable opportunity of
education and a proper livelihood? I
submit it is not right that we should continue to legalise capricious disinheritance.
It is an iniquitous exercise of power that
ought to be regulated. The state of the
law at present allows it. One peculiarity
is that that arbitrary power can be exercised without the least notice to those who
are most concerned. In many cases they
never know until after death and when
the will becomes public.
A good will is a thing to be respected.
A vindictive will, striking without just
cause and disinheriting those nearest and
dearest to the testator, is a thing not to
be respected, and possesses no claims to
respect. It is a peculiar fact that the
law is now about to be altered in England.
This principle has been ratified within the
last few weeks by a unanimous decision
of the British House of Commons. It is
also remarkable that there should be no
division in that authoritative assembly
on this question. All parties were agreed,
and within the past few weeks a similar
Bill passed the Third Reading in the
House of Commons without a dissenting
voice. If it becomes law in England in
the next few months what will the result
be? It will be that Northern Ireland
will be one of the two or three countries
in the world which are continuing this
unjust law. Surviving spouses and
children of a testator cannot be cut off
capriciously in Scotland, Australia or
New Zealand or in a number of the
Canadian provinces. In fact they cannot
be cut off in most European countries.
The general sentiment of civilised
nations is manifest and unmistakeable on
this point. The law of Scotland says
where there are no children the wife of

[Mr. Campbell]
the testator takes half of his moveable

children take one-third of the estate of

Under this Bill the share to the surviving parent or children is not rigid or
fixed. It is left to the wise discretion
of the court within strict and welldefined limitations, and to a court which
will have due regard to all the circumstances of each particular case. No one
under this Measure gets any right to any
money unless the court is satisfied that
it is right and reasonable he or she should
get it.
Some critics will say that we
ought not to interfere with the liberty of
the individual. To-day in every domain
of life, in every department of activity,
the State is interfering with the liberty
of the individual for the common good.
Other critics say that a Measure of this
kind once it is law will bring grist to the
legal mill. I venture to say it will not.
That is not the experience of countries
where the law is actually in force. I
took the trouble to investigate the circumstances with regard to New Zealand, and
I found that there in one year there were
only seven cases in court under an Act
similar to this Bill. In the next year
there were only four cases in the New
Zealand courts, and all told since the law
came into force there were 40 cases heard
in court. In Australia the litigation is
negligible and so also in Canada. There
are now few unjust wills. They are not
numerous at the present time. I submit
they will be fewer if the law is altered.
A competent solicitor would advise a
testator against the folly of making an
unnatural will, cutting out a wife or
children, and point out that he is running a risk which ought to be guarded
against. Then again, it is said that this
may lead to the washing of dirty linen
in court. That objection can be easily
met, because provision can be made for
the hearing of cases under the Bill, when
it is thought right and proper by judges,
in chambers, which will avoid publicity.

I believe this reform will come in due
time, if it does not come at once. It will
work best in the case of small estates and
in the case of poor people. It has few
enemies. It has many friends. I think
the fact that there is no hostility on the

measure is indicated by the decisive

the water. The hostility among the lay

venture to say further that there is no

Where he has undertaken responsibilities as husband or parent, is it right
that in this present year he should be
allowed to get rid of all that responsibility at death? When he has worked
with a good wife and good children
should he at death be able to fling them
to the winds, to throw them upon the
world, to throw them upon the rates or
upon the alms of charity? That is our
law and it is a law that ought to be
remedied. Is it right when a wife's day

out that the husband by a cruel will,
for some reason or whim we cannot
ascertain at the moment, should be able
to expose her to poverty and humiliation and to feel in the evening of her
days how cruel this world's law is?
This Bill is simple and workable. It
provides for the maintenance of a widow
during widowhood out of income and
not out of capital. The same applies in
the case of a child. It is limited to that,
and to nothing more. In the case of
children it is limited very precisely and
very strictly to children under twentyone years of age or who, if they are over
age, are either daughters who are
spinsters or disabled sons. Surely those
are a class most deserving of consideration at our hands. I admit that in the
case of a quite small estate the Bill recognises the desirability of giving discretion
to the court to make provision by allotment from either income or capital.
There will be a maximum allotment of
income. The courts have not a free hand
in the matter. There can be a maximum
allotment of income amounting to onehalf in the case of a childless widow
during widowhood, to one-third in the
case of a widow with children and onethird to the children, and one-half in
the case of children left unprovided for
without a mother.
It may be said that we are invading
the freedom of uncontrolled testamentary
disposition of freehold property, but this
freedom is of comparatively recent
growth. The widow had her right of
dower in freehold land until 1933. This
freedom of testamentary disposition, you
may say, came into vogue during the past
hundred years.

Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state under what
Regulation or Act of Parliament Mr.
Cooke, a civil servant in the Northern
Ireland Civil Service, has been able to
retire on full pension although he completed only 25 years' service; whether
he can state if this position has been
done away with or has someone else been
appointed.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): I think that this question is,
in an amended form, the one put by the
hon. Member last week to which I
handed him a reply which I understood
would be published in Hansard.
In reply to the present question, the
authority for the retirement of this
officer is contained in the Government
of Ireland Act, 1920. He wished to
retire, and as the period within which
he could exercise an option in that
regard had expired in 1928, arrangements were made, in view of the outstanding character of his services in the
Ministry of Finance, for his retirement
under the provisions of the Eighth
Schedule to that Act.
The pension awarded was less than the
maximum amount payable under the
provisions of the Superannuation Acts.
had he remained until the normal retiring age.

been granted in Northern Ireland by

Just let me say what actually happens
in England and Scotland in regard to
this matter. The English teachers
secured the lump sum with full recognition of past service in 1917. The
Scottish teachers secured their lump sum
also with full recognition of past service
in 1918. In the following year, 1919,
the Irish Education Bill was introduced
in the Imperial Parliament by the then
Chief Secretary, Mr. Ian Macpherson,
M.P. This Measure, which never
reached the Statute Book, proposed to
give the lump sum on similar terms to
Irish teachers. Ever since the establishment of the Northern Government the
teachers here have been claiming that the
promise of lump sum given in the
Macpherson Bill should be implemented;
but no notice was taken of their claim
until the Budget of 1936, when the lump
sum was granted as from 1st July in that
year, but with no recognition of past
service.
Since that date numbers of old
teachers who have borne the burden and
heat of the day, have retired on pension,
with little or nothing in the shape of a
lump sum. For the privilege of getting
the lump sum, serving teachers have had
to pay an additional one per cent.
pension premium. The sum thus paid
for the lump sum amounts to £13,000
per annum, but owing to the refusal of
the Government to recognise service
rendered before 1936 for the lump sum,
the amount that is being paid out each
year as lump sums to teachers retiring
is only a fraction of the amount accruing
from the extra one per cent., namely,
£13,000. At the present rate, if no
recognition is given for past service the
award of the lump sum will not cost the
Government a penny for years to come.

nothing of the sort if you unbalance
other people's budgets in order to balance
your own. It is not a sign of prosperity
if, in order to do so, you close hundreds
of shops and business houses in the city
of Belfast through the operations of the
Valuation Act and also by making an
education levy. That is not a sign of
prosperity, it is the reverse. I noticed
while passing along Bridge End to-day
that half the shops in that thoroughfare
are vacant.
If your revenue was a genuine revenue
it would be something to boast about, but
since a rather substantial amount of your
revenue is obtained through a levy of 1s
in the £ on rates it is nothing to boast
about. You increased the valuation
before you put on that levy of ls. That
is not legitimate taxation at all.
the taxation was on the same basis as

I totally disagree with the observations

that such an office is bound to be useless.
Such an office is not bound to be useless.
Such an office may, on the one hand,

On the other hand, if it is not rightly
established and rightly run, it may be of
very little service to the Province.
The great Dominions-Canada, Australia, South Africa-think it worth while
to keep buildings in London. The
Canadian Government, the Australian
Government, and the Government of the
Union of South Africa keep imposing
offices in London with the object of bringing before the people of England their
countries, the nature of their countries,
the features of those countries, the products and industries of those countries.
If they find it of value to keep offices in
London, Ulster may well find it of value
too. For some time past it has been
suggested in the Press that such an office
is likely to be established by our Government, but among people, both inside and
outside this House, who have discussed
the proposition of establishing an Ulster
Office in London there has been a certain
amount of disquiet because it has been
said time and again that the office that

the nature of a department of the Ministry of Commerce, with a civil servant at

servants.
An office of that kind, I am afraid,

to the Province. What you want in
London is not a sub-office of the Ministry
of Commerce, with perhaps an Assistant-
Secretary or a Principal at the head of it.
Such an office suggests itself as merely
a sub-department of the existing Ministry of Commerce. The function of such
an office suggests itself as being the
function of the ordinary Civil Service,
the collection of statistics and the filing
of information, an office girt about with
red tape. Anything of that nature, I
think, will be of very little value.
What we want in London-and I
think it is recognised inside and outside
the House is something of an entirely

Solicitors Bill.
Considered in Committee.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the chair.]
CLAUSE 1 (Power of the Society to
make provision as to education,
apprenticeship, and qualifications).
Question proposed: "That the Clause
stand part of the Bill."
Mr. BEATTIE: This Clause is going
to give statutory powers to an organisation to rule and control a profession
which they claim to have a right to
control without first and foremost giving
safeguards to the public against exploitation of charges. If the Clause is
accepted you are going to have further
claims made upon you. Are you prepared to accept the claims of other
organisations for equal treatment? The
Clause sets out the power of the Society
to make provision as to education.
Imagine the Law Society being asked to
be the authority of what class of education will be required before a pupil can
enter the profession as an apprentice. Is
not the duty of the Minister of Education
to say what class of education will be
provided for the children of Northern
Ireland? Perhaps when we are being
replied to we will hear a definition of
what is meant by the words "power to
decide the class of education necessary
before one can be accepted as an entrant
into the solicitors' profession." Then
the Society seek to be empowered
to regulate the apprentices and
their qualifications. What is meant
there? Is it to keep control of the profession for a class in the community
known as the old school-tie class? If
that is so, I think that is a preserve that
I at least am not going to consent to.
I feel that this first Clause is going to
be a menace or obstacle to the working
class ever being hopeful of entering the
solicitors' profession. If we had an
authority like an appeal tribunal regulated by those outside the solicitors'
profession to adjudicate on claims when
presented before it, I would say we might
risk giving this authority to this Society,
but without these guarantees in the
Clause, I, as one representative of the
working class, am not prepared to give
this preferential treatment to this class
in the community, which we sometimes
feel greatly displeased with. I understand the Bill got its Second Reading.
It would not have got it unopposed if
I had been here. The Clause says:
The Incorporated Law Society of
Northern Ireland (in this Act referred
to as "the Society") shall have power
to provide facilities for education and
to make regulations for ascertaining. . .

[Mr. Beattie]
I want to know who is going to examine
the entrants to the solicitors' profession.
Will it be an educational body, or the
ordinary educational committees who
operate, say, for the Civil Service, the
teaching profession, or the medical profession, or is it going to be the solicitors

will be the parties concerned. I do not

you will get what I call the family line

a member of the
solicitors' profession my son, or daughter,
or other relatives, would have
a preference of entry. Again, I say the working class are being deprived of their
right to pursue their claim to become
members of this profession equally with
other persons.
Then the sub-clause goes
on to say:
(b) a final examination, that is to say,
an examination of persons applying

What does that mean? Regulations
are to be made which will not be subject
to the House of Commons. We will have
nothing to say in this matter at all, and
we will find it very difficult when we get
entangled in the net which is now being
woven round this class in the community.
We as Members of this Committee should
have some more clarification of this paragraph before we actually pass it.
There is so much wording in this Clause
that it savours of a legal document, but
the legal profession live on words. I
presume they have got an example of how
they live and they have inserted in this
Clause all the words necessary to meet six
or seven different ways in which they feel
difficulties may arise. To give the Society
power to make regulations is something
which I would not stand for. It is autocracy at its extreme. There is no democracy in a measure of this kind. This
upholds the right of the privileged few
to the detriment of the masses of the
people. I am not going to accept Clause
1 because of the vicious principle contained
in it. Until the father of this measure
is prepared to mete out to other units
of the community the same rights for
their organisations as he is claiming for
his, and until he makes a declaration of
justice for all and privilege for none, I
could not possibly support this Clause.

Solicitors Bill-

This Society wants this Clause-
A person shall not be capable
of being bound by indentures of
apprenticeship to a solicitor unless that
person has obtained from the Society,
or from such person as the Society may
authorise in that behalf in writing, a
certificate to the effect that the person

with such provisions with respect to
admission to apprenticeship as may be
in force by virtue of this Act or regulations made by the Society thereunder.

Oral Answers to Questions.
MARKET TOLLS AND STALLS.
1. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether in the legislation to be introduced regarding market
tolls and stalls he will make provision
for dealing with the whole problem of
itinerant trading in general.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The problems
arising out of itinerant trading are
essentially different from those connected
with markets, and could not be oppropriately dealt with in a Bill dealing
with markets and fairs.
Mr. BROWN: Does the Minister propose to deal with the matter in another
Bill?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have
already told the hon. Member that the
matter he raised is not one for this Bill.
Mr. BROWN: I asked does the
Minister propose to deal with this matter
in another Bill-a separate, distinct, and
different Bill.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No.
CIVIL AUTHORITIES SPECIAL
POWERS ACT.
2. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can give any
information as to the powers of police,
under the Civil Authorities Special
Powers Act, as to entering of houses or
other premises; whether a warrant is
required in order to
to obtain entry;
whether if articles of a private nature
are taken away by the police it is necessary to give a receipt or return same
intact; whether the Minister is aware of
an incident which took place in Portadown on 17th April, 1938, when worshippers were coming out of Divine.
service and a number of young men held
up; on whose instructions were the District
Inspector and Head Constable acting,
and what was the reason for the action
they took; and whether he will, in due
course, approve of the abolition of the
Civil Authorities Special Powers Act.
Sir DAWSON BATES: In reply to
the first part of the question, I would
refer the hon. Member to the regulations
made under the Civil Authorities
(Special Powers) Acts (Northern Ireland), 1922 and 1923, all of which have
been laid upon the Table of the House,
which set out the conditions under which
the police are empowered without warrant
to enter premises and to seize articles
suspected to be in possession in contravention of the Regulations.
In reply to the next part of the
question, I may say that it is not the
practice to give receipts in respect of
articles so seized and the return of any
such article depends entirely upon the
circumstances of the case and the nature
of the article.

I have had a report of certain action
which the police found it necessary to

of

The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I am aware of
the circumstances in which lace is made
and sold in the Crossmaglen district.
As already explained to the hon. Member in my letter to him, dated 13th

and the lace maker would appear to be
that of buyer and seller, rather than
employer and employee. If the hon.
Member can furnish me with evidence to
the contrary I shall be glad to have it
investigated.

CLOSING OF MILLS AND
FACTORIES.
9. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Prime Minister whether, in view of the
serious industrial situation in Northern
Ireland, due to the closing down of mills
and factories all over the Province, resulting in severe business depression in which
traders large and small, and all types of
industrial workers alike, are suffering
great hardship, he is prepared to set up
a committee, drawn from all those classes,
to advise the Government as to what
methods should be adopted to remedy
this growing evil.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply. Whilst
I am at all times willing to take any
step likely to alleviate the present unemployment situation in Northern Ireland,
I am not satisfied that the setting up of
a committee, as suggested by the hon.
Member, could effectively supplement the
efforts at present being made by the
Ulster Development Council, the Ulster
Industries Development Association and
the Irish Linen Guild to develop and expand the industries of the Province.
Accordingly, I regret that I am unable
to act upon the hon. Member's suggestion.
Mr. HENDERSON: In view of the
failure of the Government, which has not
been able to cope with the serious situation that has arisen, why can the Minister not set up a committee of sound
business men in Northern Ireland to
bring prosperity to the country?

with complex financial

Mr. CAMPBELL: I cannot allow this
Bill to go through without directing
attention to some of the recent utterances
of the Prime Minister, some utterances
of recent date, which were jarring at a
time when everybody having responsibility in England and Ireland was speaking words of appeasement and goodwill,
and utterances which in my humble
judgment unnecessarily tended to create
friction between the North and South of
Ireland, and were hurtful to the best
interests of both the Irish and the English
The Prime Minister speaking
peoples.
in this House compared the people on
this side of the Border and their fellow-
Irishmen on the other side in irreconcileability with the Arabs and Jews in
Palestine.
I do submit that that comparison is
very remote from the truth. I do submit that it was a blazing indiscretion.
The Prime Minister suggested that that
was the view also of Conservative statesmen. A very distinguished Conservative
statesman, the present Prime Minister of
the United Kingdom, said recently that
the two countries have a community of
interest. Judging by his statements, the
Prime Minister of Northern Ireland looks
askance upon any suggestion of the growth

of England. Mr. Chamberlain has just
acclaimed
The intangible, imponderable, but
nevertheless valuable fruits
of magnanimity in politics. The Prime

bouquets upon the minority in this part
of Ireland. He delights in beating a
defiant drum and in singing a hymn of
hatred. The fact is that our Prime

The Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, on the contrary, judging by his
recent utterances, is trying to live in the
