his ship by reckonings taken in the year
1690.

of that area, and I am glad to see from

distrust is ineradicable. May I remind

The Prime Minister of the United

"A friendly Ireland is worth more

Appropriation Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Campbell]
That is between Ireland and England.
He said that the friendship of Ireland is
of more value to them in peace and war
than any mere paper rights. I do not
suggest that the Prime Minister of
Northern Ireland should go about during
times of diplomatic talks and negotiations.
trying to find means of reconciliation and
goodwill, or that he should go about
with an oil-can in his hand to lubricate
the wheels. I do not suggest that. I do
suggest, however, that he should not go
about with a spanner in his hand ready
to fling it among the wheels when they
are in motion. I venture to think that
the people in Ireland and the people in
England owe very little thanks-I say
this with all deference-to the Prime
Minister for ill-timed remarks such as we
have had in recent times from him.
British statesmen, of course, have grave
anxieties and weighty responsibilities with
war clouds rolling up from the Continent.
They must be concerned, naturally concerned, with the safety of Great Britain,
and I think it is no flight of the
imagination to say that they must have
in their mind's eye that long stretch of
Irish coast from Lough Foyle, in the
extreme north of Donegal, along the west
and southern coast coming up on the
eastern coast as far as Carlingford Lough.
They may have in their minds, too, the
statement, a short but pregnant statement, made by Lord Macaulay in 1844. I
will quote him to the House. His words
sound grandiloquent to-day and remote
from realities. He said:
Till Ireland is tranquil England can
never hold her proper place among the
nations of the world. To the dignity,
to the strength, to the safety of this
great country, internal peace is indispensably necessary. England can do
many things which are beyond the
power of any other nations in the
world. She could again sweep from
the ocean all commerce but her own.
She could again blockade every port
from the Baltic to the Adriatic. But
in this gigantic body (that is the
Empire) there is one vulnerable spot
near to the heart. At that spot 46
years ago a blow was aimed which
narrowly missed and which, if it had
not missed, might have been deadly.
The Government and the legislature,
each in its own sphere, is deeply responsible for the continuance of a state
of things which is fraught with danger
to the State.
To-day that is the peril of partition and
scientific sectarian discrimination under
partition.
The PRIME MINISTER: I always
hesitate to follow a distinguished Member of the Bar, in this case, indeed,
almost the father of the Bar in Northern
Ireland. However, I have had to do so
before and I will do so again and give
the best answer that occurs to me on the
spur of the moment to the various points
that the hon. and learned Member has
put to the House. In the first instance,
he accuses me of living rather in the past
instead of in the present. Well, the 9th
of February last is not very much in the
past. If I were representing the feelings
of the people of Ulster up to that date.
and if a couple of months ago they showed
their approval of the action which I had
taken, I do not think he can blame me
for not relying upon Macaulay or anybody else marking out the path which
Ulster should take at the last General
Election.
I gather, although it was hidden away,
that the hon. and learned Member wants
Ulster to go into the Free State. I presume that is what he was suggesting, and
that I was the bogey man blocking the
way. I said at the General Election-I
do my utmost at all times to represent
the feelings of the people of Ulster-that
it was an opportunity for them and not
for me to give an answer to the hon. and
learned Member. They gave that answer in a most emphatic voice which nobody could misunderstand. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Surely that is so.
The hon. and learned Member quoted
some remarks made by certain bishops.
I presume he refers to the remarks of
some bishops of the Church of Ireland.
I would point out, however, that during
his lifetime the late Lord Primate did
me the honour of consulting me from
time to time. I recommended His Grace
in 1921 not to allow the Boundary that
had been established to make any
boundary in the Church of Ireland, and
I do not see that the bishops have got
anything to complain about, because the
Government has never interfered in a
matter of that kind. The Church of
Ireland, like the Presbyterian Church,
Appropriation Bill-
Second Reading
19 MAY 1938
holds sway over the whole country, and
any weight which they carry must be in
a religious sense and not in a political
direction. The public return us to Parliament to represent them from the political
point of view, and the vast majority of
the people in Northern Ireland are
desirous that partition should remain.
Personally, I hope it will remain for ever.
I cannot put it stronger than that.
I have always kept steadily in mind
the utter impossibility of mixing irreconcilable people. That is why I used the
expression the other day, which I hold is
perfectly true, that we should not ask
people to mix who do not want to mix.
It would only raise trouble in future
years. At the present time law and
order prevail in the North, and in the
South, I believe, they are also maintaining law and order and peace.
While you
have these peaceful conditions, surely it
is more satisfactory from the British point
of view to allow them to continue rather
than run the grave risk of forcing anything either on the South or
on the
North which would be antipathetic to
the personal feelings of the people.
Therefore, so far as the hon. and learned
Member's appeal in that direction is concerned, and so far as I am concerned, I
am sorry to have to put it in such a crude
way-it cuts no ice, none whatever.
The hon. and learned Member went on
to say something about the Council of
Ireland. Who did away with that
Council? Who was it passed the resolution and the Free State Acts which did
away with that Council? The truth of
the matter is that the Free State started
off with ideals which we here did not hold,
ideals which we thought were wrong.
What has happened? As time passes
they are apparently finding out that they
were wrong themselves, and, according to
the hon. and learned Member, they are
drawing closer and closer to Great
Britain. We in Ulster never separated
from Great Britain; we are associated
with Great Britain and form part of the
United Kingdom. Therefore, it is not
necessary for us to look at the picture in
the same way as the followers of the hon.
and learned Member look upon it. In
his own words they are beginning to
recant and regret what they did in the
past, and are trying to shuffle back to
the position which existed in 1920, when,
if the South had accepted the 1920 Act,
they would not have all the trouble they
have to-day.
The hon. and learned Member referred
to the important question of war. Well,
he will find Ulster ready if there is a war,
and she will probably show the South
where loyalty really lies. If what has
taken place brings Great Britain-the
United Kingdom-and Eire closer and
closer together it will only be what we
have been preaching all the time. We
will say, "God bless them and more
power to them, and hope that in the
event of hostilities the South will flock to
the assistance of Great Britain and the
Empire. Where do we come in? What
is it that the hon. and learned Member
wants? He is not very clear. I do not
think it matters very much, because the
suggestion underlying all his remarks was
that Ulster, and myself particularly,
were standing in the way of an agreement
between the North and the South, and he
suggested that we should walk into their
domain and be governed from Dublin
instead of from Stormont. The thing is
utterably preposterous.
This Parliament has been functioning
for 17 years.
We have our own establishments, which are working smoothly. Our
ideals and our views are clear to every
Ulsterman and every Ulsterwomen. I
have not heard of any great desire from
any part of our population that they
would like to leave the British flag and
live under the flag of Eire. Remember
that there are other minorities in the
North besides the minority represented
by the hon. and learned Member, and
those minorities are perfectly happy
under the British flag. Nearly all the
grievances put forward from time to time
are manufactured for the purpose of casting aspersions upon the people of Ulster.
It is difficult, of course, to be always on
the spot to answer the charges made
against us.
I am
a very critical judge, and because I am backed up by such a large
majority of the people of Ulster and of
this House, I feel my responsibilities all
the greater. Therefore I am particular,
and my colleagues are meticulously particular, that nothing should be done to
cause any minority in the Ulster area
to feel that they are left under a
grievance.

I am alarmed at the costly administration of the Ministry of Home Affairs.
I want to say quite candidly that the
sooner this House takes notice of that
Department the better for the country.
The existing state of affairs is due, in
my opinion, to not having a competent
Cabinet Minister at the head of affairs.
I venture to say that it is very seldom
he attends to his duties at all. Considering that we pay the Minister of
Home Affairs £2,000 a year, and his
travelling expenses, I think we should
get great service from him. I cannot
understand why no action is taken to
reduce the right hon. Gentleman's salary
by 50 per cent. You can never get the
Minister at his post no matter on what
day of the week you ring up. I think
he is the worst offender in that respect.
For that reason I want to protest against
this extravagant Department.
I feel that the policy of the Minister
of Home Affairs in bringing Englishmade uniforms over to Northern Ireland
is altogether wrong. In the past Northern Ireland was able to manufacture
these uniforms. If a lead were given by
the Prime Minister and the Minister of
Home Affairs surely some person in

Ulster Constabulary. In view of the

19 MAY 1938
[Mr. Minford]
To-day we have arrived at the stage
when his House should take some step.
During my election campaign I made.
speeches stating that if possible I would
see that no persons should live in houses
unfit for human habitation. Therefore,
I ask this House to take steps to make
the local authorities move in the matter.
Consider the work that could be provided
by the building of these houses. Work
would be provided in brickyards, timber
yards, cement works and other places.
Mr. HENDERSON: Newry granite.
Mr. MINFORD: We could put into
work thousands of people. The Minister
of Home Affairs should now force the
local authorities to build houses.
I
I agree with my hon. Friend, the
Member for South Down, that something
should be done for the small farmers, who
are unable to make their houses fit for
the present-day standard of living.
hope the Minister of Home Affairs will
take some steps to give the urban
authorities the same powers as the rural
authorities possess. The small farmers
ought to get a grant to enable them to
make their homes fit for human habitation. I often think that we should put
ourselves in the position of the people
who are living in these hovels. I speak
with experience of my own constituency.
I think the time has arrived when this
House ought to take steps to see that the
laws are put into operation. There is no
use in having these laws passed, and permitting the rural authorities to laugh at
them. I believe that good houses make
happy homes. The local authorities have
neglected the opportunities which this
House has provided, and I hope the
Minister of Home Affairs will see that the
Acts that we have passed are not allowed
to lie dead for years.
Mr. BEATTIE: Why do you not pay
good wages?
Mr. MINFORD: We always pay good
wages. I have invited the hon. Member
for Pottinger to come down to my constituency on several occasions, but he is
too busy a man to accept my invitations.

be willing to consider the advisability of
giving this deputation his blessing and

THE LUMP SUM PAYMENTS TO
TEACHERS.
Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the amount
received from the teachers of Northern
Ireland by deduction from their salaries
of the additional one per cent. for lump
sum payment on retirement, from 1st
July, 1936, till 1st March, 1938, and the
total amount of lump sum payments
made to teachers retiring during this
period.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY (Lt.-
Col. Gordon): I have been asked by the
right hon. Gentleman to reply.
The figures required are respectively.
£23,697 and £1,117. I would, however,
remind the hon. Member that as the
maximum liability on the Teachers'
Superannuation Fund in respect of lump
sum payments will not be reached for
another 30 to 40 years, the one per cent.
contributions are, in accordance with
Statute, treated as capital and do not go
to relieve the annual charge on the
Teachers' Superannuation Fund in respect of superannuation payments.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the Parliamentary Secretary is it not a
fact that 30 years will expire before one
penny-piece will have to be met by the
Government. In view of that period of
time, and in view of the funds that will
be accumulated, is he prepared to recommend the step-by-step policy in applying the lump sum conditions to serving
teachers in Northern Ireland from 1922.
Lt. Col. GORDON : That is a
question of which notice would be
required.

Mrs. PARKER (by leave of the
House): I think the hon. Member has
somewhat misunderstood the Amendment
which was introduced in another place.
The local authorities have certain compulsory powers for the acquisition of land
for certain purposes, such as labourers'
cottages and other matters of that kind.
In the original Bill, as passed by this
House, there was also compulsory power
for the local authority to take land for
the purpose of a holiday camp or camping site. The Amendment simply means
that that compulsory power for this particular purpose will not exist, and that land
can be acquired by the local authority
only by agreement. The hon. Member
must know that when it is necessary to
take land for, say, labourers' cottages if
agreement cannot be come to-and, in
fact, agreement is practically always
arrived at there can be a public inquiry
and land can be taken compulsorily. I
think, as he merely asked for an explanation, that is the explanation of the
amendment. In this particular instanc
it will not be possible to take land unless
agreement is reached between the owner
and the local authority concerned. I
think I have answered all the hon. Member wished to know as clearly as I can.

I take it that unless there can be agreement arrived at no ground can be

and women with the object of taking

in the town of Dundee.
Then there is the weaving of sheets, a

hundreds of sheet weavers unemployed,

sheet weaving to be ready in a certain

we have looms for this class of work lying

has been set up is only a make-believe

position is so serious that I, with the

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Expiring Laws Continuance Bill,
Order for Second Reading read.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
Bill to which the House is asked to give
a Second Reading proposes to continue
for a further period of one year certain
Acts-three Acts of the United Kingdom
and one Act of this House-which, were
it not for the proposals in the present
Bill, would expire on 31st December of
the present year. The present Bill is
identical with the Act that was passed
a year ago in this House, but as hon.
Members may wish to have some
reference made to the actual Acts whose
operation it is proposed to extend, if
they would look at Part I of the Schedule
of the present Bill they will see that the
first Act whose operation it is proposed
to extend is the Glebe Loan (Ireland)
Act, 1870.
As many hon. Members may know, under
the provisions of that Act the Government was enabled to advance up to twothirds of the amount of money which
was to be expended on the building or
repair of houses for ecclesiastical persons
or ministers, as they are described in
the Bill, of any denomination, and the
Act also provides for loans for the purpose of purchasing lands to be occupied
with these houses, the loan, as in the
case of the loan in connection with the
construction of a house, not to exceed
two-thirds of the purchase money, and
the loans to be secured on either a
mortgage or a rent charge for certain
limited periods.
The second Act is the Harbour, Docks
and Piers Temporary Increase of Charges
Act, 1920. Under that Act the Ministry of Transport in England and the
Ministry of Commerce in Northern
Ireland is enabled to modify the statutory provisions regulating charges. There
are certain provisos which very markedly
secure the interests of any persons who
might be affected by the increased
1309 Expiring Laws Bill-

4 OCTOBER 1938
Second Reading
charges, and I may only say that that
Act, passed in the year 1920, has been
continued not merely in Northern Ireland, but also in the rest of the United
Kingdom by the Expiring Laws Continuance Acts in this country, and also
in the Parliament at Westminster from
year to year.
The third Act is the Unemployment
Relief Works Act of 1920, and that
short Act provided machinery by which
land could be acquired for the purpose
of road construction or other works of
public utility, and as applied in Northern Ireland, lands for those purposes can
now, under the provisions of this Act,
be acquired compulsorily as under the
Housing of the Working Classes Acts,
1890 to 1919.
The last Act which it is proposed to
extend is an Act passed in this House
in the year 1921, the Local Government
Emergency Powers Act of 1921, and, as
I am sure all hon. Members are aware,
under the provision of that Act the
Ministry of Home Affairs, if satisfied
that any local authority has refused or
failed or is unable to perform all or any
of the duties imposed on that local
authority by statute or Order, is enabled
to dissolve the local authority for any
prescribed time and to appoint some
person to discharge the duties of the local
authority.
As I have said, all these four Acts
which it is now proposed to extend for
another period of one year were the subject of an Act passed in this House one
year ago. It is
necessary that the
operation of these Acts should be continued for a further period of one year.
Accordingly, I beg to move.
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Mr. BEATTIE: I do not see the
necessity for this annual review of the
Glebe Loans Act. I understand it has
been the practice of the Northern Government to make the concession to the
clerical profession in Northern Ireland
whereby they can have two-thirds loan
on parochial houses or residences for
ministers and can also have the right to
a loan on land adjoining these homes.
I take no exception to that law. What
I do take exception to is-and this is
now becoming an established fact in
con-
Northern Ireland-that this is a law
pertaining to the clerical profession.
Why should we each year be asked to
confirm this law? Why should we not
make it a statutory condition applying
to the clerical profession? The
tinuation of this review every twelve
months will otherwise go on for as long
as we live and as long as those who follow
us live. The condition of the clerical
profession has been established by precedent, and that precedent should now
become law. Let us dispose of this
matter for all time.
As
The second matter deals with the
powers given to the Belfast Harbour
Board and other harbour boards. I
totally disagree with the principle of
these powers, and I will give my reasons.
Two-thirds of the population of Northern
Ireland have no voice in the administration of these harbour boards. They have
no say as to who should represent a particular class of people on the boards.
I am a believer in the principle of bringing democracy here into line with other
democratic countries, I am opposed to the
extension of the powers contained in this
Measure. It would take me some time
to read over the Harbour, Docks and Piers
(Temporary Increase of Charges) Act.
It would take me some time to see how
far the powers given to the various
harbour boards regulate the cost of stuffs
coming into the ports. I have heard
many grumbles in regard to the heavy
dues charged. It is put forward that the
harbour boards, having plenary powers,
are all-powerful in that respect. I do
not agree that these boards should have
these powers extended further than the
present year.
The third Measure is the Unemployment Act, which deals with the reclaiming of land for the purpose of starting
unemployment relief schemes and other
useful works to absorb into employment
all those who are unemployed. There
is no Department in Government circles
I have more respect for than the
Ministry of Labour, and before
proceeding
to make my comment
I would like, with your permission, Mr.
Speaker, to congratulate the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Gordon) who is now
occupying the very important position
of Minister of Labour. I want to remind
him of his early days when he and I and
others did believe that Cabinet rank
caused one to lose sight of the unemploy-
Expiring Laws Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
ment question. As he is one who has
risen from the lower ranks I expect to
get very big things from his Department
in the future. I wish to give him my
wholehearted support in respect of all
Measures in that direction which are
brought before the House. I would also
like to pay a tribute to the Parliamentary
Secretary (Mr. Grant). He is one who,
like myself, had to go through the school
of adversity. He knows the disastrous
effect of unemployment on working-class
homes. He also knows how unemployment affects the lives and wellbeing of
the younger ones in the home. I am
satisfied that if he makes use of and
applies the knowledge he possesses, then
we shall have big and startling things
brought out under the Ministry of
Labour in a year or two. I wish him,
also, well in the position to which he has
been appointed.
In connection with the reclaiming of
land for useful work, I would like to
know how much of this Act has been
used by the Ministry of Labour in the
past. They have not taken advantage of
all the power that they possess under the
Measure in order to try to do something
in regard to the establishment of
factories and the creating of employment. I would like to know how often
this Act has been used in the past five
years?
Mr. NIXON: Once every four years.
Mr. BEATTIE: I question that very
much. I would like to see it used at
least four times every year. I have just
returned from a tour of Scotland and
England, where I studied the conditions
of relief work, the establishment of
munition factories and the reorganisation of industries that were once very
successful but had gone back, as well as
the amount of money spent there on the
revival of these industries. I want to
tell the right hon. Gentleman that he is
now in a position to cater for new industries for Northern Ireland under this
scheme in an abler way than they are
being catered for in England or Scotland.
I hope the extension of this Act will be
granted, and that it will be used. It
should not be left lying as a dead letter'
on the Statute Book, serving no useful
purpose. I would like to see the
Measure made a permanent fixture, but
as the Cabinet only require it as a temporary Measure I will give it my wholehearted support.
Now we come to the Minister of Home
Affairs, the man who can make or unmake democracy, the man who has
deliberately cut down the democratic
rights of the people, although his chief
has stated time after time that we are
a democratic Government, elected by the
people for the people. The Minister of
Home Affairs gets an extension of power
under this Act. What does he do? He
appoints Commissioners. I question very
much whether the services of the Commissioner in Donaghadee benefited that
town as they should have done.
Donaghadee has got its Council restored,
and I hear very good stories about the
councillors appointed. I have heard that
if it had not been for the action of the
Minister of Home Affairs in wiping out
the Council, Donaghadee might have
been one of the best seaside resorts in
Ireland. Owing, however, to the Minister clearing the Council off the slate, the
town is now a backward area as far as
seaside resorts are concerned.
It is, therefore, a very dangerous thing
to give this power into the hands of any
one Minister. We should wipe this law
off the statute book. If cases arose in
Northern Ireland where the elected representatives of the people failed to recognise
the demands of the people concerned the
Minister should have the right to come
to this House and ask permission to wipe
out the particular Council and set up
some other form of administration. But
to give him the right he has under this.
Act is a principle that is wrong and we
should not be parties to it.
Let me take the case of the Armagh
Council. I have heard good reports from
my colleague who represents South
Armagh, and he can speak for the area
better than I can. Very high opinions
have been expressed about the gentleman
appointed as Commissioner in Armagh,
but notwithstanding his ability and the
highly efficient manner in which he is
carrying out the work allotted to him he
is still there and acts as an irritant to
the democratic voice of the people.
Things in that area are coming to a point
when a demand will go forth for the reestablishment of the Council. I think
that demand could be justified because of
the failure of certain things being done
that would have been done if the Council
had been operating.

I hold in high respect the gentleman
who is Commissioner in Armagh because
he has done good work-much work that
he receives no fees or reward for. I have
given my comments on this law. There is
more in this law than I have outlined.
Yesterday we heard of a case where a 93
years' old Act was brought into being
against a very able civil servant in the
Ministry of Home Affairs. We have too
many of these laws lying on the statute
book. Some people say they are dead.
Some are dead I know, but they can come
to life when required just the same as one

Finance Bill.

The
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): This short Bill is designed to
give effect to the taxation concessions
which I announced in my Budget statement in May last, and which were
approved by Money Resolution.
concessions fall under three headsmotor vehicle and hawkers' licences, and
estate duty. The provisions relating to
motor taxation are intended to take
effect from 1st January next, the beginning of the motor licensing year; the
provision relating to hawkers' licences is
retrospective from 1st April last; and
the amendment in estate duty law will
take effect as soon as this Bill becomes
law.
The motor taxation changes are dealt
with in Clauses 1 and 2, and the Schedule
of the Bill. The effect of Clause 1 and
the Schedule is to reduce the rates of
motor vehicle duty on goods vehicles and
hackney vehicles to those already in
force in Great Britain. The rates of
duty on agricultural goods vehicles were
brought down to the level of the British
rates by our Finance Act of last year,
and this type of vehicle is not, therefore. referred to in the Schedule. The
reduction in the taxation rates for
hackney vehicles affects only the larger
type of hackney vehicle, such as omnibuses and chars-a-bancs, because the rates
for taxi-cabs and vehicles seating not
more than eight persons in addition to
the driver are already the same as those
in Great Britain. The cost of these
additional concessions this financial year
is £23,000, and in a full year £35,000.
Clause 2 provides for the abolition of
the fee of 5s in the case of motor-cycles,
and 10s in the case of all other motor
vehicles, which is at present charged on
any application for the refund of the
surrender value of a Road Fund licence.
Clause 3 provides for the total repeal
of the Hawkers Act, 1888, which
originally imposed a licence duty of £2
a year on persons hawking goods in
horse-drawn vehicles, and similarly for
the repeal of Section 1 of the Finance
Act (Northern Ireland), 1936, which extended the scope of the tax to persons
hawking goods in motor vehicles. When
speaking on the Budget Resolutions I
mentioned that my decision to abolish
this tax had been taken after considering the report of an Inter-Departmental
Committee which had investigated the
whole question, and mainly in the light
of the anomalous position arising under
the present law, whereby persons hawking certain types of commodities
exempt from duty, while those hawking
other classes of goods have to buy a
licence. Moreover, it is not always
simple to determine what is hawking and
what is not.
are
The effect of the amendment of estate
duty law in Clause 4 is to increase from
£25 to £52 a year the limit of exemption
from liability to estate duty of annuities
left by deceased persons for the benefit
of their dependants. The second part
of this Clause provides for giving
modified relief on a diminishing scale in
the case of annuities between £52 a year
and £104 a year, at which point the
normal rates of duty become chargeable.
This concession has recently been given
in Great Britain. It will cost the
Exchequer £1,000. I beg to move.

Mr. BEATTIE: I have a question to
raise of which I have given notice. It is
in regard to the cramping of the law in
the Courts of Northern Ireland. Statements have appeared in the Press to the
effect that the resident magistrates in
Northern Ireland are being cramped in
their work because of the fact that the
use of certain standard works of law is
being denied to them. These standard
works are a very high price; they are too
expensive for a resident magistrate to
buy them. I understand that they are
necessary and essential for the good
administration of the law, and that without them no resident magistrate can have
a full knowledge of every law which he
is called upon to administer. He has
to refer to standard works.
There was a case in our own courts
yesterday in which Maxwell's standard
work was quoted, and the magistrate who
heard the case said that he had never
read the work referred to, as he could
not obtain it owing to the heavy cost.
He said that the resident magistrates
had, as a body, applied to the Minister
of Home Affairs to have Maxwell's
volume placed at their disposal, and that
the Minister had refused to give the
court the assistance asked for. I claim
that all those who are coming before the
courts are entitled to the full opinions of
those who are entitled to express opinions,
and I also say that the magistrates in
Northern Ireland should be supplied
with these books, just as the legal
advisers of the Ministry of Home Affairs
are supplied with this particular work in
their own Department. I may be told
by the Minister that the reason why his
Department has refused to supply this
book to the courts is the high price of
the work. How many courts are operating in Northern Ireland at the moment
that would require to be supplied with
this volume? I should say about twelve.
I understand the price of the volume is
about £2, and it would serve for at least
25 years.
There are highly-efficient minds interpreting the laws passed by Parliament.
We in this House pass the law, but we
cannot interpret it; it takes somebody
else to interpret the law as it is passed
here. We imagine that we know what
the law means, but if we ever get into
the hands of the law that we have passed
we realise that it means a different thing
from what we thought when we were
passing the legislation. I ask the Minister of Home Affairs to supply the courts
with this volume of Maxwell's, so as to
give the magistrates an opportunity of
administering the law as it should be
administered. This has arisen out of a
case brought under an Act of Parliament passed 93 years ago. I understand
that an Act of 1934 has smothered up
that old Act. If that is so, then we
should make it known to the public, and
the resident magistrates should be placed
in possession of the information that
appears in this work. I ask the Minister of Home Affairs has he definitely
refused to supply this volume to the
courts sitting in Northern Ireland, and,
if so, why.

The PARLIAMENTARY
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Warnock): I
think it is a fact that some request was
made by the resident magistrates in
Belfast for certain works of reference.
Whether or not Maxwell's Interpretation
of Statutes was one of those works I cannot at the moment say. It has not, I
think, at any time been the custom for the
Government to supply the resident magistrates of the country with a law library,
and it is a mere coincidence that in this
particular case to which reference has
been made one individual's work was
asked for. In the course of our work in
the practice of our profession we have a
law library of several thousand volumes,
and I do not know where we would stop
if any suggestion were made that a law
library should be provided for every
court in which resident magistrates sit
throughout the Six Counties. Volumes
dealing with the interpretation of
statutes alone would make a fair-sized
law library. The Law Reports, of which
there are roughly one thousand volumes,
deal with the interpretation of statutes
as laid down by the judges. It has never
been the custom, and I do not think it is
necessary, that these standard works of
reference should be supplied to these
courts. In the particular case to which
reference has been made to-day, the
learned resident magistrate was within
one hundred yards of a library which has
every book necessary for the purpose of
his work.

CLASS VII. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF COMMERCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £10,120 be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1939, to defray the salaries and
expenses of the Ministry of Commerce."
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): Hon. Members will
recollect that in introducing the annual
Estimates for my Ministry in March last
I informed the House of the steps which
were being taken to broaden the basis of
the industrial life of the Province under
the powers conferred by the New Industries Development Acts. With the aid
of the Ulster Industrial Development
Council, which, as hon. Members are
aware, is composed of representatives of
the entire business community under the
able chairmanship of Senator Sir Roland
Nugent, valuable work has been done in
making known to industrialists, not only
in Great Britain but elsewhere, the
attractive facilities which are available
under the Acts, for the establishment of
new industries and also for the extension
of existing undertakings. The results of
these efforts have, so far, given hope that
substantial progress can be achieved.
Up to the present 63 formal applications have been received by the Ministry
and considered by the Advisory Committee set up under the principal Act, and
definite offers of assistance have been
made in 20 cases. Of the remainder, 27
have been unsuccessful and 16 are still
the subject of negotiation. One of the
main objects of the legislation was the
diversification of the industrial structure
of Northern Ireland and good progress towards this desirable end may
be
seen from the variety of the
new industries to which assistance
has been offered; such as, for
example, the production of preserved
apples, carpets, dried milk products,
veneered plywood panels, staple fibre
yarn and viscose, industrial solvents,
ready-made clothing and flax retting.
Up to the present only a few of the
successful applicants have commenced
production, the others being engaged in
the erection or adaptation of premises
and the installation of machinery, but it
is estimated that new work has already
been planned for approximately 2,000
people, and it is hoped that when the
assisted firms are in full production this
number will be substantially increased.
As a result of these activities it has been
found necessary to augment the staff of
the Ministry by the appointment of an
assistant secretary, an assistant principal,
and a clerk.
As Members of the Committee will be
aware the Weights and Measures Act
which became law in June of this year
provides for the allocation to the Ministry of certain powers and duties of local
authorities under the Weights and
to
Measures Acts and for the transfer of
inspection duties from the Royal Ulster
Constabulary to the Ministry. In this
connection I am happy to be able
inform hon. Members that it
has been found possible to form
the new civilian inspectorate by transferring to the Ministry of Commerce all
those members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary who have hitherto acted as inspectors of weights and measures. The
transfer is to take effect on 1st November
next. The sum of £3,055 provided in
the Estimate includes £200 for temporary clerical assistance, a proportion
of which is required in connection with
weights and measures.
1337 Supplementary Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce 1338
5 OCTOBER 1938
Following the announcement made in
this House prior to the summer_recess,
when the proposal to establish in London
the office of an agent for Northern Ireland in Great Britain was generally
approved by hon. Members, considerable
progress has been made with the preliminary arrangements, and the office will
be equipped and working normally at an
early date. The Government was fortunate enough to secure, in the capacity of
agent, the services of Sir James Cooke-
Collis, a distinguished soldier and
administrator, who had only recently
relinquished the post of Commander-in-
Chief of His Majesty's Forces in Northern Ireland. The premises selected form
part of the building, 21 Cockspur Street,
known as Norway House, and are within
a stone's throw of Trafalgar Square.
They stand, moreover, in one of the principal arteries of traffic linking the East
and the West of London. They include
spacious ground-floor accommodation together with effective window display space
not only within the premises themselves,
but also in the main vestibule of the
building. The offices of many of the
great trans-oceanic shipping companies
are located in this street, which is, in
consequence, one of the first points of
call of Dominion and foreign visitors to
these islands. The principal groundfloor room in our premises will, therefore, be largely devoted, in collaboration
with the Ulster Tourist Development
Association, to the publicising of the
attractions which Northern Ireland can
offer to the holiday maker. In collaboration also with the Ulster Industries
Development Association displays of
Northern Ireland products and manufactures will be on view and the public
office will serve as a general information
bureau. Another room, also on the
ground floor, is being designed as an
Ulster Reference Room, where Northern
Ireland newspapers, directories and
general works of reference will be
available. The administrative offices will
be on the upper floors.
One of the main tasks of this new
office will be the intensification, not only
in the Metropolis, but throughout Great
Britain of
the campaign for the
attraction of new industrial enterprises
to Northern Ireland. I am happy to
say that the agent has already received
offers of collaboration and assistance from
many quarters, and I can assure hon.
Members that he will gladly welcome the
co-operation of everyone interested in the
promotion of the prosperity of the
Province.
I cannot conclude this reference to the
new office without paying a tribute to
H.M. Office of Works, and in particular
to the Director of Lands, Buildings and
Accommodation, and his staff for the valuable assistance so readily given not only
in the negotiations involved
involved in the
selection and leasing of the premises, but
also in their decoration, adaptation and
equipment.
The committee, to which reference is
made under subhead G of the Estimate is
now engaged in the investigation of the
ways and means by which tourist traffic
may be developed in Northern Ireland.
As chairman of this important body, I
was fortunate to secure the hon. and
learned Member for the University. I
am glad to have this opportunity of conveying, on behalf of the Government, to
him and his colleagues an expression of
appreciation of the readiness with which
they acceded to my invitation to assist in
this matter. I beg to move.

Regrets of Belfast Chamber of
Commerce.
At a special meeting of the Council
of the Chamber of Commerce held in
the Boardroom yesterday the report of
the deputation to the Prime Minister
in regard to the appointment of Sir
James Cooke-Collis as Ulster agent in
London was received, and, after discussion, the following resolution was
adopted :-
"That this Council of the Chamber
of Commerce regrets that the whole
scheme for the establishment and
staffing of a Northern Ireland office in
London was made public before it had
been submitted to Parliament for its
approval, as such a procedure would
have enabled commercial and trade
organisations interested to make any
necessary representations on the
matter.'

CLEANSING OF RAVERNETTE
RIVER.
1. Captain PATRICK (on behalf of
Mr. Maginess) asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state if an
application for a grant under the Ministry's scheme for the improvement of
agricultural holdings was made by a
farmer resident in County Down in respect of the cleansing of the Ravernette
River running through his farm;
whether such application was refused on
the grounds that the Down County
Council had served notice on farmers
through whose lands the said river runs
requiring them to cleanse the bed of the
river where it runs through their lands;
whether it is the policy of the Ministry
to refuse to make grants under the said
scheme where such or similar notices have
been served and if the Ministry
differentiate between "necessary" and
"desirable" works, refusing grants in
the case of the former and making grants
in case of the latter, and will the Minister reconsider the question of making
grants under the said scheme in cases
similar to the above.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): The scheme of
Land Improvement and Unemployment
Relief does not extend to such works as
would normally fall to be carried out by
County Councils under the Drainage
Acts (Northern Ireland). In the case
to which the hon. Member refers inquiries are being made as to whether the
drainage of the river is a matter for the
County Council. If it is shown that this
work is the responsibility of the individual farmer, the Ministry is prepared
to consider giving him a grant under the
scheme.

-persons wholly or mainly engaged in

of Agriculture is the authority for deciding upon all questions concerning grants

part of his question.

a

BLOOD TESTS FOR OFFENDING

7. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether, in view of the

that the drivers had partaken of intoxicating liquor, he would introduce legislation making it compulsory for all
motor drivers who are charged with this
class of offence to undergo a blood test.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The hon. Member's question appears to be based on a
fallacy as it assumes an increase in the
number of traffic accidents which are due
to drivers having partaken of intoxicating liquor.
His assumption is not supported by
fact, for although the number of persons
licensed to drive motor cars during the
past four calendar years has increased
very substantially, the number of accidents attributed to intoxication has not
increased.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
University and Collegiate and Scientific
Institutions Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon): The principal
provisions of the Bill which I am now
privileged to move a second time give
Under Clause 1, which will form the
subject of a financial resolution, it is
proposed to make a substantial increase
in the existing annual Parliamentary
grant to the Queen's University. The
present grant which is contained in the
Estimates for Educational Services
amounts to £40,000 per annum, and is
made up of four sums; firstly, £10,000,
which was formerly paid out of the
Church Temporalities Fund (a fund of
which the share apportioned to Northern
Ireland no longer exists as a separate
entity, having been merged in our
Capital Fund); secondly, £18,000, which
was the original grant under the Irish
Universities Act, 1908; thirdly, an
increase of £8,000 conferred by the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, and,
lastly, a further increase of £4,000 under
the Queen's University Act, 1928. The
Minister has very carefully considered the
present circumstances of the university,
and has satisfied himself that an
additional grant of £20,000 per annum is
fully justified, having regard to the
important developments
in staffing.
accommodation and equipment which it is
desirable to undertake. The increased
grant operates as from 1st April last, and
accordingly permission has been included
in the batch of Supplementary Estimates.
now in hon. Members' hands, for a sum
of £20,000 in respect of the current
financial year.
Clause 2 provides for a grant of £2,500
per annum in aid of the funds of Magee
University College, and as hon. Members will see, this grant is to be applied
exclusively for the purposes of the literary
and scientific side of the college.
This condition is essential in view of
Section 5 of the Government of Ireland
Act, which lays down that the Parliament of Northern Ireland must not
legislate so as either directly or indirectly
to endow any religion. It was this fact
which prevented an earlier recognition of
the services of the college to education.
Happily the endowment scheme of the
college was so amended in 1934 as to pro-
Universities Bill-
Second Reading
6 OCTOBER 1938
vide for the maintenance of two separate
departments, the literary and scientific
on the one hand, and the theological
on the other. The former is entirely undenominational, and at present numbers
about eighty students. The segregation
of the two departments has thus opened
the way for a grant from public funds.
Clause 3 provides that the accounts of
the two departments shall be kept entirely
separate. In this way the legal requirements of the situation are fully satisfied,
and there can be no possible suggestion
that the grant is being misapplied.
Clause 4 provides for the representation of the Government on the body of
trustees in accordance with Section 3 of
the amending endowment scheme, which
makes such representation the condition
of any grant. This Measure reflects the
increased interest of a Government which
is to become a substantial contributor to
the funds of the college. Provision is
likewise made in the Supplementary
Estimates for the current year's grant.
Clause 7 provides for a grant in aid
of Armagh Observatory. The amount of
the grant is purposely not specified in the
Bill, but hon. Members will recall that
my right hon. Friend indicated in his
Budget speech that it would be fixed for
the next five years at £300 a year. This
observatory was established by Act of
Parliament in the reign of George III.,
and in the course of its 147 years of
existence has held a prominent place in
the scientific life of the United Kingdom.
Armagh is now the only observatory
in Ireland, and as such is consulted by
scientists from all parts of the country.
Since 1927 the observatory has been in
receipt of an annual grant of £100 from
public funds, but it has become clear
that this sum is inadequate if the
observatory is to be of real as contrasted
with sentimental value to the Province.
I am sure that there is ample scope for
this, both from the point of view of
popular interest in astronomy and of
research.
The governing body as at present constituted consists of the Archbishop, Dean
and Chapter of Armagh, together with
two laymen whom the governors have
power to co-opt. The governing body
have agreed to Clause 7, which provides
that the number of lay members shall be
increased to five, one of whom shall be
appointed by the Government and one by
the Queen's University. It is both
fitting and desirable that a scientific
institution such as this observatory should
be linked to the university, for by such
co-operation its increased usefulness can
be turned to the best account. I have
noted with pleasure that since the Minister's announcement of this grant was
made the distinguished director of the
observatory has been appointed by the
university as a lecturer in astronomy.
Clause 7 grants to the governors power
to sell or lease land belonging to the
observatory when it is in the interests.
of that institution. Hon. Members will
see that following the lines of the Charity
Acts the assent of the Ministry of
Finance is to be required. This is the
normal method of safeguarding the
interests of the public. The governors
have asked for the inclusion of this
Clause in the Bill. I beg to move.
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

Lieut. Colonel MITCHELL :
behalf of the authorities of Queen's
University I would like to express their
appreciation of the generosity of the
Government in making this grant to the
university. I have heard people
occasionally say that it is a very big
grant. That is not so. Facts as to the
position of Queen's University have been
put forward in irresistible form, and they
show that the annual income is less than
half, or practically half, that of any
university in the United Kingdom with
similar numbers and standing. They
have been labouring there under very
great difficulties, and some of the
lecturers have had to give their lectures
two or three times over on the same day
in order to meet the number of students.
The original figures were settled at a
time when the University had very little
more than half the number of students
it has now, and the additional students
have involved the appointment of a considerable number of assistant lecturers,
demonstrators, and others in order to
teach these young men the rudiments so
that they may thoroughly understand
the subject on which they are working.
The buildings of Queen's University are
now insufficient for the large number of
students we have. It may amaze hon.
Members to hear that at the present
time we have 500 medical students on
the list at the University. The men
who are turned out from Belfast have
such a good reputation that within three
weeks of their getting their degrees
practically every one gets an appointment of some kind or other.
It is not unusual for us to receive
letters from across the water asking us
to send an assistant or locum tenens.
They want men who know their work
and are prepared to work. That is the
reputation these young men have got.
They are real Ulstermen. When you
give them an opportunity they take
every advantage of it and are a credit
to Ulster. The only pity is that we
have to train so many for export. They
hold prominent positions in every part
of the United Kingdom, in the military
services, and in the Colonies. I am sure
that every Member will feel that the
Minister of Finance is entirely satisfied

indulged in. The first is recreation that

saw in my Division-healthy recreation.
The third form of recreation is found in
a lazy, ne'er-do-well atmosphere, in
which people lose sight of all around
them and do not see the beauties of the
earth as they should see them.
I disagree with the hon. and learned
Member in regard to the first form of

Under the terms of this scheme, as
now revised, a grant is payable on the

where the holding does not exceed £100
valuation, 75 per cent. for valuations
between £100 and £150, and 50 per cent.
for valuations between £150 and £200,
whereas grants were formerly made on
the basis of 50 per cent. of wages with a
valuation limitation of £75. It has been
found necessary to employ additional staff
to
carry out inspection of schemes of
work which applicants propose to promote. A greatly increased volume of
work in connection with payment of
grants in respect of completed work has
also necessitated the employment of
additional staff.
It has been found necessary also to
employ additional staff for work in connection with the Oats and Barley Subsidy
Scheme under the Agriculture Act, 1937.

are, however, being recovered under an
agency agreement from the Ministry of
Agriculture and Fisheries. A further

recoverable under the Milk and Milk
Products Act (Northern Ireland), 1934.

RETARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Grant): Before moving
the Second Reading of this Bill I
should like, with your permission, to
thank hon. Members on both sides of the
House for their congratulations to me on
my appointment. These congratulations are divided into two parts. Some
came from hon. Members who shook me
by the hand, wished me well and left it
at that. I appreciated their kindness
very much indeed. Other congratulations came from hon. Members who
wished me well, and then asked me for
something. I did not appreciate their
congratulations in just the same way.
The hon. Member for Pottinger-I do
not wish to suggest that he was less
sincere in his remarks than any other
Member-after extending his congratulations told the Minister of Labour and
myself what our responsibilities should
be in the future. His first suggestion
was in regard to reclaiming land. When
he said this, I had a horrible vision of
the Minister and myself in our shirt
sleeves, our trousers hitched up to the
knees, and with picks and shovels, or the
other necessary working tools, reclaiming
land in Northern Ireland, on which to
build new industries. I did not, then, feel
quite so enthusiastic about the position
I have been called upon to occupy. The
hon. Member for Falls (Mr. Byrne),
who I regret is not in the House at the
1451 National Insurance Bill-

Second Reading
[Mr. Grant]
moment, stated that he and I did not
agree on many things. He, however,
wished me well. If he were in the
House, I would tell him that if he
promised to mend his ways, he and I
would be better friends in the days that
lie ahead.
Coming now to this Bill it implements
the promise made by the Minister of
Finance in his Budget speech on 17th
May last and provides for the payment to
all dispensary medical officers as from 1st
October, 1938, of the full capitation rate
of 9s for their work in connection with
insured
persons under the National
Health Insurance Medical Benefit Scheme.
Hon. Members may be anxious to know
why dispensary doctors have been receiving less than the full capitation rate, and
I think it is desirable, therefore, that I
should deal briefly with the history of the
matter.
Medical benefit was not introduced in
Northern Ireland as part of the National
Health Insurance Scheme until 1st
October, 1930. Before then insured persons had either to pay for their own
medical treatment or to have recourse to
the dispensary service which, as hon.
Members are aware, provided, and still
provides, free medical treatment for the
poor. The dispensary medical officers
were and are paid by boards of guardians
with the assistance of a substantial grant
from Government funds.
When the introduction of medical
benefit was under consideration the question naturally arose as to the extent to
which it would reduce the work of the dispensary doctors. In order that information
might be obtained the doctors were invited to keep a record for a short period
of the persons to whom they gave treatment so as to show insured and uninsured
separately. It was found that the proportion of insured to uninsured varied
greatly as between different districts, but
taking Northern Ireland, as a whole, it
appeared that about half the persons
treated under the dispensary scheme by
dispensary doctors were insured under the
National Health Insurance Acts.
Once medical benefit was introduced the
doctors would cease to be liable to treat
these insured persons under the dispensary
scheme. They had been receiving payment for them under that scheme and,
obviously, they could not be paid for them
twice over. The Government proposal
was that there should be a reduction in
dispensary salaries proportionate to the
reduction in dispensary work.
This proposal did not commend itself to the
doctors, partly, I understand, because
they were afraid it might prejudice their
conditions of service, and their superannuation rights, and they preferred, as an
alternative, that their dispensary salaries
should be left untouched, and that the
adjustment should be effected by a reduction in the capitation rate payable under
the medical benefit scheme. Accordingly,
by agreement with the representatives of
the dispensary doctors, a reduced capitation fee of 7s 6d was fixed for dispensary
doctors joining in the medical benefit
scheme, and the amounts deducted were
paid over to the Exchequer, which was
thus placed in the position it would have
been in if the dispensary doctors' salaries
had been reduced and the grant made by
the Ministry of Home Affairs to the
boards of guardians had been reduced
correspondingly.
was
The House will appreciate that the
adjustment had
had nothing to do in
the
principle with
National Health
Insurance Scheme, and that it

doctors in consequence of the reduction
in their dispensary work, and as the total

the Ministry of Labour Vote, there was
no saving to the National Health
Insurance Fund.
A new situation, however, gradually
arose. The reduction in dispensary

medical benefit, was not maintained.
After a few years a steady growth in the
number of persons seeking treatment
from dispensary doctors began to be
apparent, and to-day the work is very
little, if any, less than it was in 1929.
understand that the increase is attributed

earner has led others, if eligible for

A second factor has also been

The cost of this Bill to the Exchequer

therefore amount to about £3,000. I beg

the Committee appointed to deal with
juvenile crime, and whether he is aware
of the great necessity for an increased

Sir DAWSON BATES: The report to
which the hon. Member refers is at
present under consideration, but I am
not yet in a position to make any definite
statement as to the date when it may be

RENT ALLOWANCE FOR R.U.C.
5. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of

has had the effect of forcing up the rents
of houses throughout Northern Ireland;
whether he will look into this matter,
and, if necessary, consult the representative body of the Royal Ulster Constabulary to see whether a more satisfactory

could not be devised.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not
aware that the present system of payment of rent allowance to the R.U.C.,

LAND PURCHASE ANNUITIES.
9. Mr. BAILEY asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he included
mountain and waste land when at a
recent meeting he quoted the average of
7s 6d per acre payable for land annuities
by the farmers of Northern Ireland, and
whether he can give the average annuity
payable per acre for arable land.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): The acreage to which
the average figure of 7s 6d refers does
not include mountain and waste land.
The figure was arrived at by dividing the
total land annuity receipts for the
financial year 1937-38 by the acreage
under crops and pasture only. If the
total annuities are divided by the area
of arable land alone, i.e., the area under
crops and rotation grass, the figure would
amount to approximately 17s 6d per acre,
but that does not mean that arable
farmers are paying on the average 17s 6d
per acre.
MARKETING BOARD'S LEVY ON
PIGS.
10. Mr. BAILEY asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he will make
representations to the Pigs Marketing
Board to have the levy or marketing
charge of 4s per pig carcase reduced;
whether he can state the reason for the
losses of the Pigs Marketing Board which
gave rise to this levy; whether he can
state who appoints the live pig graders
on the Pigs Marketing Board, and where
they are trained to do this work.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The levy of
4s per pig at present payable by pig
producers consists of two parts. First of
all, there is a levy of 1s per pig to pay
the administrative expenses of the Board
-that is, to pay salaries, etc. The
amount raised by this levy in the year
ended 30th September, 1937, was
£38,037 17s. In addition there is at
present a levy of 3s per pig to cover trading losses sustained by the Board. These
losses amounted to £23,900 at 23rd July,
1938, and the Ministry had, therefore,
no option but to impose this levy at the
request of the Board in order to enable
the Board to recoup itself for its trading
losses. The live pig graders are
appointed by the Board itself. Their
work relates, of course, only to live pigs
sold to the Board and disposed of by the
Board outside Northern Ireland. There
is no special training given to graders
before they are appointed, but the Board
endeavour to appoint persons who have
experience of the live pig trade.

provided.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): The cost
of supplying milk to school children
would depend upon the price determined
by the Joint Milk Council for Northern
Ireland. At present the Council has
authorised education authorities to obtain
supplies at the producers' prices, which
is under the most favourable terms
possible. Based upon the prices fixed
for the year beginning 1st October, 1938,
it is estimated that the annual cost of
supplying free half-a-pint of milk, on
each school day, to every child in attendance at a public elementary school
would be, approximately :-
......
for Grade A milk
£148,000
for Grades B and C ... £129,000.
I understand that in Great Britain
there are schemes under which milk is
supplied at a reduced rate, or free to
children below a certain standard of
necessity, and in general it may be
stated that about half of the children
attending the public elementary schools
in England, Wales and Scotland take
advantage of these arrangements. This
is only possible, however, by means of
financial assistance from the Government. School medical officers testify to
the good effects of the milk upon the
children.

this
We hope that to-day when
measure passes an important forward
step will be taken in educational history,
but perhaps, in order to understand its
significance, a glance at past history
might be advisable. Hon. Members need
not be afraid that it will be necessary
to go back further than 1892 when the
Imperial Parliament made
made education
compulsory for all children between six
and fourteen, with the important
exception that any child of 11 and upward who had reached a certain standard was no longer required by law to
continue at school.
In those days pupils were exempt from
prosecution provided they made a minimum of 150 attendances in a year of
about 200 days, and besides there were
numerous allowances for chidren absent
through farm work and other reasons.
In those days the procedure in enforcing
attendance was slow and full of loopholes, and the working of the Act was
very defective. The percentage of
regularity was extremely low, and when
the Ministry of Education took charge
in Northern Ireland the attendance was
so unsatisfactory that the daily average
attendance was only 76 per cent. of
enrolled pupils.
At first pupils had been exempted.
from the Act if they had passed 4th
but
standard,
the National Board
gradually raised this to 6th standard, a
degree of attainment within reach of a
normal child of 13. This being the
situation in 1922, it is only natural that
the Lynn Committee of which I was a
member in their Report should have
urgently recommended a reform in compulsory attendance. In Lord Londonderry's Education Act of 1923, which
was the result of the Committee's Report, the arrangements were considerably tightened up and every child was
required to attend until the age of 14.
At this time 14 was the statutory age
in England and Scotland, but any
education authority there had the power
to make a by-law raising the age in its
area to 15. As a matter of fact, only
four local education authorities in England and Wales used this power up to
a year or two ago.
Here in Northern Ireland our Education Act of 1923 made an immediate
improvement in school attendance. The
percentage of regularity increased from
76 to about 86 and pupils remained
longer at school than before. But in
spite of that school attendance, especially
in some areas, is far from being satisfactory and there still is much room for
improvement in the enforcement of the
Act, as those who have read the latest
Report of the Ministry will realise.
In 1936 Acts applying to England,
Wales, and Scotland were passed in the
Imperial Parliament to enforce attendance up to 15, but these Acts are not
to come into force until three years
later, that is to say in 1939. In passing
I may say that the reason for this postponement was to give time to education
authorities and school managers to provide the additional school accommodation which might be necessary owing to
the expected increase in attendance. I
will revert to this a little later.
Now I turn to Northern Ireland and
to the Bill which I am now submitting
to the House for its approval. I would
say, at the outset, that we have not
slavishly followed the terms of the
English Measure in all respects. Our
reasons are that our education system
has not grown up in the same way, that
there are differences in policy and working, particularly in financial provisions,
and we felt that any new measures
should be prepared to fit into the existing framework. I think I can say with
confidence that we have produced a
better Bill, and I hope to convince hon.
Members that I am right by drawing
attention in my speech to the main
points in which we have departed from
the English Act.
The English Act requires pupils who
are not exempted under its provisions to
remain full time at the day school until
they are fifteen. Here in Northern Ireland in our Bill we offer an option. We
say you must remain at school full time
until you are 15-but you can, if you
or your parents prefer, attend at
technical classes for half time, namely,
a minimum of 15 hours weekly, and in
the rural parts of the country some of
these classes may be agricultural classes.
By this attendance you will satisfy the
obligations of the Bill. It really means
that the adolescent or his parent has the
alternative of a period during the week
free from education in which he might
be able to earn some small sums towards
his maintenance or he might assist his
Al
Education Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Parker]
parents at domestic work or on the farm.
For boys and girls who have used their
opportunities well up to 14
14 at the
elementary school this alternative of
attendance at a technical school for the
next period may be of more advantage
to them than remaining on at the
elementary school.
This provision has also the advantage
of, in many cases, obviating the need
for any new accommodation being added
to the elementary school. The attendance at the technical classes will be free
from school fees. This will obviously
throw an additional responsibility on the
regional education committees, but we
look confidently to them and to the staff
of the technical schools to assist in what
is clearly bound to be of great advantage
to the coming generation.
I would like now to deal with what
was a controversial subject in England,
that is the question of exemptions. In
England an education authority may
when granting a Certificate of Exemption lay down a condition to the employer that the child is to have certain
opportunities for continuing its further
education whilst in employment, but
such a condition is not obligatory and
may be dispensed with by the education
authority.
In this Bill we propose that no Certificate of Exemption can be given unless
the education authority is satisfied that
arrangements are made for the child to
attend some suitable school or classes
where such facilities are available for at
least six hours in each week and in the
day time.
By this means we hope to secure that
even where we give an exemption and
the child under 15 does enter employment, he will not be completely divorced
from any contact with education as he
so often is to-day. I am
sure hon.
Members will agree that when we spend
such very large sums on education it
does seem, I might almost use the words,
a waste when we reflect that in so many
cases school work is entirely dropped
when the children leave and little
remains of what it has cost the country
so much to impart. In my opinion,
from 14 to 18 years is the age when
education sinks in much more
than
previously, and takes far deeper root.
Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Mrs. PARKER: I know the hon.
Member opposite will agree with me in
that, and I think I am only stating
what is absolutely true when I make
that assertion. Anything that will prevent this waste of money and also of
effort on the part of the pupil must
necessarily be of tremendous importance
to us all. To-day I think we are taking
another step in the right direction. It
is possible that some employers of
juvenile labour may, at first, find the
loss of the young employees' services on
one day in the week embarrassing or
inconvenient, but I do believe that with
good-will this difficulty may be obviated
by reorganisation. But if the child's
absence for six hours weekly would really
dislocate the working of a factory then
surely it would be better, where this
occurs, for children under 15 not to be
employed at all.
This would also have the advantage of
relieving to some extent the unemployment among juveniles of 15 to 18 years.
In this connection I would point out
that many of our largest employers of
juvenile labour do at present release
their boys and girls in order to enable
them to attend technical classes, and an
extension of such arrangements is certainly most desirable. A large number
of prominent English industrialists
adopt a similar policy and the practice
is spreading to an increasing degree. For
example, I read in the "Times" of 29th
August last that "arrangements have
been made by the Lancashire Associated
Colleries, Limited, for pit boys between
14 and 16 years of age to receive education on one day a week. Two hundred
boys will be accommodated at the Leigh
Municipal College, and batches of 40,
beginning in October, will attend one
day each batch. While they are at
school the colleries will pay the boys
their pit wages. I believe that cases
of this kind are becoming more common,
and there is an increasing body of educational opinion in favour of the principle
of compulsory part-time attendance at
technical classes up to 18 years of age.
The English Act provides exemption
for "domestic necessity" circumstances
in which exceptional hardship would be
caused if the child went to school. Here
our Bill contains this provision with
Second Reading

Education Bill-
11 OCTOBER 1938
modification. We do recognise and I
want to make this very plain-the
special position of farmers on small holdings of which we have so many in
Northern Ireland-where the help of
the younger members of the family is
required at special seasons-in gathering of crops, etc.-and we give exemptions in these cases, but limited to a
maximum of three months for any individual child, and this, of course, may be
extended on further application. The
condition of exemption is that whenever
practicable the child shall continue its
education by part-time attendance at
classes. I recognise that this provision.
is somewhat more lenient than the English Act, but I know that Ulster rural
life is different, particularly on account
of the many small holdings in this
country, and we felt-and rightly feltthat this must be taken into account.
Then I come to the question of
accommodation. Much of the English
Act deals with proposals to enable
voluntary school managers to obtain
grants for necessary enlargements of
school houses to meet the needs of extra
accommodation. In England this is an
entirely new departure, because hitherto-unlike Northern Ireland-all voluntary schools are debarred by statute
from a share in building grants. Here
there has been no necessity for legislation under this head, as voluntary
schools do receive a share of building
grants. But we do realise that an influx
of an additional age-group of children
may present accommodation difficulties.
We have considered the matter very
carefully, and for two reasons we
of opinion that there will be little need
for enlargement through the operation
of the Bill, and consequently we have
made no special provisions for it.
are
Our two reasons are (1) the regrettable
decline in the ordinary school population-a loss of some 10,000 enrolments
in the past five years-and (2) the fact
that a great many of our country schools
have at present surplus accommodation.
While on the question of accommodation I would refer hon. Members to
Clause 8 of our Bill. Here we have a
clause in this connection which is not in
the English Act, and which enables
exemptions to be granted to children if
the education authority are satisfied that
there is not suitable school accommodation available within a reasonable distance of the child's home. But-and I
lay stress upon this-exemptions under
this head are not to be given until the
Ministry has been consulted and its consent obtained.
Under the same Clause exemptions
may also be given in any exceptional
case where it is clear that the special
attainments of the child, or the standard
of education in the school or schools
available, is such that the child would
not be likely to derive advantage if it
did attend. This exempting power also
requires the approval of the Ministry.
To pursue my comparison with the
English Act, in England if parents are
dissatisfied with the action of a local
authority they have no right to appeal
to the Ministry. Here they have this
right of appeal in Clause 9. I think
this provision ought to give a feeling of
confidence, and ought to help to ensure
uniformity in the operations of this
Measure. I look upon that as most
necessary and important. A question
which loomed very largely in the debates
on the English Bill was that of uniformity.

there is an option given to pupils to

expected that a considerable proportion

In the case of the proposed technical

and grants will continue; that is to say,

and paid on the scales of salary prescribed in the Ministry's regulations for

technical teachers. The basic salary

This system of financing the classes is

administrative kind. There will, however, be some additional expenditure
thrown on the education authorities
through the upkeep and maintenance of

not give any help to education authorities whose present expenditure exceeds.
the margin of the shilling rate.
Generally speaking, it is estimated
that the cost of technical classes under
the Bill will be borne by the education
authorities in the proportion of about
£4 from the rates to £3 from the Exchequer. On the other hand, the
increased cost of pupils over 14 at public elementary schools will fall almost
wholly on the Parliamentary vote, inasmuch as it will consist almost entirely
of the salaries of the additional elementary teachers employed on the teaching.
staffs to deal with the pupils over 14. It
is, as I have already stated, practically
impossible to give any estimate of the
proportions in which the increased
amounts will be shared between the
different types of school, but a rough
guess has been made to the effect that
the total cost may in the first year
amount to £25,000, rising in five years
to £50,000. This is based on the Bill
coming into effect from 1st July, 1939.
These are some of the main features
of this Measure, which it is hoped may
initiate a considerable improvement in
our educational system. It will,
doubt, like other Measures, be largely
no
dependent on the interest shown by the
community generally, and, of course, by
the education authorities.
It is hard to realise that less than a
century ago, in 1847, a debate took
place at Westminster as to whether education was a matter in which the State
should interfere. In that debate Lord
Macaulay said that it was unanimously
acknowledged that the duty of every
Government was to give security to persons and property and suggested that the
education of the people was an effectual
means of bringing about this result.
It will be seen that the idea that every
individual has a right to educationthat no ground can be allowed to lie
fallow, and that it is the duty of the
State to safeguard this aspect of a citizen's life-even against some citizen's
inclinations, is one of comparatively
recent growth.
I personally believe, and I am sure
my belief is shared by many hon. Members, that no reforms can be of lasting
benefit if they come so suddenly that
they are far in advance of public opinion.
Public opinion must be moulded, and
that takes time. Gradually, imperceptibly education for the masses has
improved, the children and the State
have benefited and the parents are satisfied-all this without running counter
to parental and public opinion.
To-day I am presenting for Northern
Ireland another instalment. I believe
from the bottom of my heart it cannot
fail to be of benefit. I do not claim
perfection for it, but I do say that it
recognises that it is a crime to stop a
child's education at 14, and that it
provides for a continuation of that education, without, I hope, imposing hardship on anyone. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be

her clear presentation of this Education

House understand the real purport of
