is no difference in the principle of the
Measure, and there is very little difference in the way it will work out.
The hon. lady Member comes forward
here on behalf of a Tory Government
propounding the idea of extending the
school age for working-class children. It
is heartening to me to know that in the
year 1938 the hon. lady Member has
wakened up to her responsibilities,
because in my lifetime I never heard from
the Tory Benches that that party stood
in favour of the extension of the schoolleaving age for the working-class child.
It was consoling to me to hear the hon.
lady Member agree that education is
only grasped at the age of 14, and that
prior to that the child is being ground
in to receive the education that it should
receive from 14 to 16 years of age. She
has not gone to the sixteenth year yet,
but circumstances will compel this
Government and other Governments of
same make-up, to recognise that
education is a factor in the world of
to-day, and that the sooner working-class
people are provided with an equal opportunity to receive that education the sooner
the people in the world will come to learn
and to understand one another as they
have not done in the past.
What are the principles omitted from
this very important year's extension?
Working-class children cannot go to
school after the age of 14, because of the
economic position in their homes.
The
advocates of education for working people
have always laid it down that if there
is going to be a lengthening of the school
life of the child, there must accompany
that an allowance for the maintenance
of the child while it is at the continuation school. Why have the Ministry not
brought in a maintenance allowance for
the additional year? Only for the action
of the Tory Government in the 1924
year
there would have been an Education Bill
passed for the working classes of England,
Scotland and Ireland, with a maintenance allowance, but the House of Lords,
that noble Assembly in London, cast it
into the wastepaper basket. Parents
cannot be expected to continue the schooling of their children on wages that are
inadequate to keep their homes in decency
and comfort.
I say that the best thing in this Bill
is the realisation by the Tory Party of the
necessity for a Measure of this kind, and
although they are doing it in a piecemeal way, it is a step in the right direction. This Bill proposes to give the
education authorities power to grant

caused. Let us see if that is in accordance with all educational authority. Has
the principle of exemption been accepted

Does the hon. lady Member believe

or she comes along to have a child exempted? They will do nothing of the
sort. There is no more fruitful ground
for exemptions than Northern Ireland.
The hon. Lady has not told the
House the likely number of children who
will attend school for the extra year.
An estimate was submitted in the British
House of Commons, but the hon. Lady
has omitted to give an estimate
here of the percentage that she expects
to take advantage of the extra year.

Mr. BEATTIE: Why did you not

6 years? That is the most important year

That is not a job for the teachers at all;
it should be the task of the Ministry.
Why was not that factor in the life of
the children considered? That is a very
important thing left out of this Measure.
The children should be compelled to
attend school when they attain the age

a proper education. If that were done,
when the children went out into the
world they would not be left with the
doubt in their minds that they were not
up to the standard of children educated
in another country. Our educational
system is I know this and the local
authorities also know it-one of the best
in Great Britain or Ireland, but the
children when they leave school are
afraid that they are not just as good as
the children educated in England or
Scotland. That is not the fault of the
educational machine; it is the fault of the

matter which the teachers are compelled
to impart inside the schools.
In my opinion the children best suited

Land Annuities.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I beg to move, "That
this House, in view of the hardship incurred by farmers in the payment of
land annuities, is of opinion that the
Government should grant some form of
financial assistance in order to relieve
this burden which bears so heavily on
the agricultural community."
I should like, in the first place, to
make my position clear by stating that
this Motion is not to be taken as a vote
of no confidence, or of lack of confidence,
in the Government, because I am taking
this opportunity of bringing before the
Government as forcibly as I can the
deplorable state in which the agriculturists of Northern Ireland find themselves to-day.
I should also like to explain to the
House why this Motion appears on the
Order Paper to-day in an amended form
You, Sir,
in your ruling-and I am not questioning your ruling for a moment-decided
that the Motion I had originally handed
in was not one within the jurisdiction
of this House. Consequently, I had to
bring it inside that jurisdiction and
while the Motion as set out on the Order
Paper to-day limits me and my Colleagues very much in our efforts to have
this burning question of Land Annuities
brought forcibly before the Government,
I feel rather more the fact that your
ruling also prevents me putting forward
a suggestion I intended making, which,
if carried into effect by this Government,
and if approved by the Imperial Government, would have immediately given
relief to the extent of 33 per cent. to
all those who pay land annuities.
At the outset, however, I am quite prepared to admit that a reduction of 33
per cent. on the amount paid in land
annuities would not in itself have
brought back prosperity to that industry,
but it might, I think, have been a means
to that end. The total amount of land
annuities, payable by the agriculturists
of Northern Ireland amount to the round
figure of £990,000, of this sum about twothirds is claimed by our Government, and
used, I understand, not only for adminis
trative purposes here, but portion of the
amount so claimed is used to establish a
sinking fund, which will be a valuable
source of income to this Government when
the annuities are no longer payable. The
remaining one-third or about £320,000
which is also collected and remitted
annually to the Imperial Government,
would, if it had been possible to get the
Imperial Government to forego their
claim to this sum, have given immediate
relief to our agriculturists to the extent
of 33 per cent. and perhaps I might be
permitted to say, this would have been a
very small Imperial contribution to
Northern Ireland agriculturists when
compared with the concessions given to
the Government of Eire, a concession
which must be shouldered by all Imperial
taxpayers. As we are included in that
number, we must now pay not only our
own annuities, but help to make good
the 140 millions handed over to the Government of Eire. However, as I am,
from your ruling, treading now on very
thin ice, I must, as you would perhaps
say if I did not say it for you, get back
to the motion before the House.

I should like to preface my further
remarks by saying that I am not at all
unmindful of or ungrateful for all the
help that we as agriculturists have
received, not only from this Government
but also from our Imperial Government.
We have, I am glad to say, a Government in office here, as well as at Westminister, that have already shown
themselves to be in sympathy with the
agricultural industry, and it would be
most ungrateful of me not to say how
much we appreciate all that has been
done for us. I know that farmers are
classified by some people, who perhaps
know nothing of the difficulties with
which they have to contend, as a lot of
lazy, indolent, grumbling, unthankful
people who never were satisfied and who
never will be satisfied with anything that
is done to help them. I can assure you
that this is not the case. No class of
people work harder or work longer hours
and contend with so many difficulties, and
get so little return for their efforts. No
person going through the country for
the past two or three weeks and looking
at the harvest fields in their present
condition could, I think, have anything
but sympathy for those who see the fruits
of their year of toil deteriorating in value
and becoming, I am afraid, in a good
many cases more of a liability than an
asset; for in how many cases do these
same farmers see the crops with which
they intended discharging all their
liabilities become less and less capable of doing so. No, if we cannot give
the agriculturists at the moment any
financial assistance let them, at any rate,
know that in these trying times they at
least have our sympathy.
It has been stated so often that I need
hardly reiterate it that agriculture is our
basic industry. We are proud-and have
every reason to be proud-of our other
great industries- shipbuilding, linen,
tobacco, and all the rest. I should like
to remind the House that without agriculture these great industries would cease to
exist. It has been truly said that more
people are engaged in agriculture than in
all these other great industries put together. When I have stated that more
people are engaged in agriculture I must.
also say that many so engaged to-day are
not in remunerative employment. In all
my experience of agriculture, and I speak
not only as a representative of a constituency which is mostly agricultural, but
also as one extensively engaged in it, I
think I can truthfully say that in a succession of lean years the present one is
about the worst. In fact, I believe that
the present year has been the worst we
have had for the past twenty. Agriculture,
as we once knew it, is passing out of existence, and all around our countryside we
see large tracts of land, which once produced crops of various kinds in abundance, now nothing more or less than
overgrown and barren wastes. Whether
we realise it or not agriculture is in a very
bad way and despite all the assistance
it has received. Unless something further
can be done to re-establish it, the drift
from the land will continue and our cities
and towns, already teeming with unemployed, will find many more added to
those ranks. We often hear it stated that
the agricultural labourer is the worst paid
worker we have. With that I thoroughly
agree. Many agriculturists to-day, however, although not paying their labourers
as much as they would like to do, are
paying more than they are able.
By all means let us improve the conditions under which the agricultural
labourer works and lives. Let us give
him a house worthy of the name, and
let him be paid a wage sufficient to keep
him and his family in comfort. This
can only be done, however, by, first of
all, putting the agriculturist himself in
a position to do so, and then, if necessary,
seeing that he does it. Many farmers
to-day, even although they are only paying what some people would call an inadequate wage, find that when wages are
paid they have nothing left for themselves. I like to read the writings of that
well-known agriculturist and writer, A.
G. Street, and I would commend his
literary contribution to any person who
wants to get a clear insight into practical.
agriculture. In a recent article by him
and published in the "Farmers' Weekly,"
he said if when passing through the
country you come to a place where you
find on one side of the road a neglected
farmstead, a very poor crop, land overgrown with rushes and whins, and on the
other side a neat farmstead with a bountiful crop and good grazing, carrying a
big stock of healthy looking cattle, do not
immediately jump to the conclusion that
in the farm which appears to be neglected
you have a lazy, indolent farmer, and in
the other a hard-working, efficient farmer.
Rather you must, he says, if you know
Land Annuities
Land Annuities
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Elliott]
anything at all about agriculture, come
to the conclusion that the farmer who
appears to be down and out is one who
has spent all the capital he had in trying
to make good and has failed, while the
other man, who seems to be prospering, is
one who has still some capital left to lose.
That, to my mind, explains, the real
position of the agricultural community
to-day. Whatever is to be done to restore
prosperity to it must be undertaken at
once. One of the greatest benefits ever
conferred upon the agricultural community was the derating of land and farm
buildings. Many people, however, have
the idea that the farmer now pays no
rates. I have no intention of belittling
in any way the benefit the farmer has
received from derating. To those who do
not understand the true position and who
say they pay the rates for the farmer, and
does the farmer also want them to pay his
land annuity as well, I would say that, in
the first instance, agriculture is not the
only industry that was derated. What
about all the other big industries which
benefited from the Derating Act? The
farmer, in common with his fellow townsman, pays rates on his dwelling-house. A
shopkeeper pays rates on his shop, but he
does not pay rates on his stock-in-trade.
Derating has put the farmer in the same
position as any other householder-he
pays rates on his dwelling-house, but not
on his stock-in-trade, his land.
The benefit of derating to the agricultural community is not, however, as real
to-day as it was when derating first came
into existence. I should like to point out
that shortly after the Derating Act was
passed a Valuation Act was also passed.
Agricultural land and farm buildings
were left outside the scope of that Act,
but the dwelling-houses were included. In
County Tyrone the revaluation increased
the valuation of the county by £90,000.
Some portion of that amount fell on the
dwelling-houses occupied by farmers.
do not know of a single case where revaluation caused a reduction. Then subsequent legislation increased the rates.
The tendency of all recent legislation has
been, I am sorry to say, to save the
Exchequer at the expense of the local
authorities.
I
Some people would go the length of
saying that the benefits of derating have
disappeared. I do not subscribe to that
doctrine, but I do say that with the increasing demands that are being made on
local authorities, due to fresh legislation,
the time is coming when, even with derating, the farmers' rates will be a very
serious matter. At the present time the
education levy of 1s in the £ takes no
less a sum than £10,163 7s annually out
of County Tyrone. The farmers' dwelling-houses contribute to this sum, that
is, according to their valuation.
Unfortunately, the numbers occupying our mental hospital are increasing.
More humane methods are being used in
the nursing and in the care of these unfortunate people. As a result the cost
per head has been almost doubled. The
contribution made by the Government
has not so far been increased. While its
contribution in by-gone days represented
about 60 per cent. of the total cost of
these institutions the contribution to-day
only represents about 25 per cent. The
additional burden has to be carried by
the ratepayers, and the farmers have to
pay their share. Therefore, in the
country we are gradually losing the
benefits of derating. I would ask the
Government to pass legislation which
would protect the rate-paying community,
not only in the rural districts, but also in
the cities and towns.
I could give many more instances to
show the rising tendency in regard to
local expenditure. The agricultural community have to bear their share of this
expenditure. Wild statements are sometimes made about the money which is
being spent on agriculture. Not long
ago in this House a
hon. Member
stated:-
We cannot go on as city representatives and city people throwing
out money in shovelfuls to agriculture.
As I said before, I do not intend to
compare the city with the country. I
believe that one hangs on the other. If
we have a prosperous city, then the
country will benefit. If, on the other
hand, we have prosperity in the country
districts that prosperity is bound to react on the city.
I should now like to refer to the
Estimates for the current year. The
Estimate for unemployment amounted to
£3,375,000, while there was a supplemental Estimate for £300,000. That

gives us a total of £3,675,000. I am not
quarrelling with the amount spent on
unemployment, nor am I quarrelling
with the provisions the Government has
made for unemployment. Until some
better provision can be made for the unemployed, I say the Government would
be lacking in their duty if they did not
make ample provision for them. I will
now take the Education Estimate. On
educational services we are spending
£2,158,677, which, with a supplemental
Estimate of £27,850, makes a total of
£2,186,527. An additional sum of
£69,634 has been spent on education,
which raises the amount we are spending
on education to nearly £3,000,000.
When I come to agriculture I find the
Estimate amounted to £91,273, which,
with £121,194 for agricultural services,
makes a total of £212,467. An additional
sum of £40,000 was passed in this House
a few days ago, which makes the total
spent on agriculture £252,517. About
£3,750,000 is being spent on unemployment, while the agriculture Estimate is
about a quarter of a million. I should
like to add to that quarter of a million
the derating grant of about £800,000.
Even with this £800,000 added we are
only spending £1,052,517 on agriculture,
while £3,750,000 roughly is being spent
on unemployment.
I am a great believer in new industries,
but I am just as strong a believer in old
ones. If the Government can see its
way to spend three and three-quarter
million pounds-I am not quarrelling
with the amount-in establishing a new
industry of unemployment, then I
should like to see the old industry
of agriculture getting more money.
Agriculture is the basic industry on which
all the others are built. I do say that the
Government if they put their heads together and consider this great question
of unemployment could surely find ways
and means whereby a great deal of the
money spent on unemployment at the present time could be diverted not only to the
agricultural industry, but to all the other
industries. I say it would be much better
to subsidise all industries rather than to
continue to foster and establish for all
time the unemployment industry and
carry an unemployed army of 80,000
perpetually in our area.
It is easy to state the disease; it might
be more difficult to prescribe the remedy.
I am not SO sure that this matter of
*improving agriculture can be done just in
a moment. I know that subsidies have
helped agriculture very materially, and
although I do not believe that that is the
way that agriculture is going, in the end,
to be brought out of the morass in which
we find it, until we can find some better
plan than that of subsidy we must continue to help agriculture in that way.
The present subsidies are not enough
and the farming community to-day are
groaning under a load they can no longer
carry. They cannot continue to carry on
agriculture under present conditions. I
have sympathy with the Government. I
believe it is only necessary to bring that
matter forcibly before the Government to
get them to take steps to help the industry. Farmers are crying out about
the annuities. I have great sympathy
with those who cannot pay. But I believe
that the total wiping out of the annuities
would not put farming on its feet again.
At the same time any concession given
along that line would be a help to the
great industry.
I want to touch on one point, but I
will keep within your ruling, and that is
the collection of the annuities. Reference
has been made to the harsh and ruthless
way in which the Ministry of Finance
collect these annuities. I do not subscribe to that doctrine. The present
Minister of Finance and his predecessor
were both most sympathetic in the collection of these annuities. I am here to say
that I appealed to the Ministry more than
once to give some of my constituents some
extension of time and never
was that
appeal of mine refused. I want to express
my gratitude to the present Minister of
Finance and to the officials of the Department who were there in the time of his
predecessor. I say also that the farmer
who got the concession always agreed to
the bargain and lived up to it.
A great deal of capital has been made
by some people I know about the number
of farmers prosecuted and taken to court
over the annuities. I have taken the
trouble to get some particulars from the
Ministry of Finance about the number of
farmers brought to court for their annuities. There are 120,000 people in Northern
Ireland who pay annuities and only 1.4
per cent. of these people were ever taken
to court. I can say this for the farming
community that they are a very honest

Mr. ELLIOTT: I am glad to have that

the farming community are, after all, an

not treated these annuity payers
with any
undue harshness or severity. I must refer
to a speech which the right hon. Gentleman the Minister of Agriculture made on
the 12th August at the famous town of
Enniskillen. It was made on a Black day.
It looked at first to me to be a very black
speech from the agriculturists' point of
view. But I must confess that on rereading it I cannot see anything but
sympathy from the Minister. Let me
read, just in case I might misquote, a
report from the Press. After dealing with
the annuity question from different standpoints he says:-
Now let me tackle the question from
the point of view of the tenant purchaser or, in practice, the farmer. He
is the person who actually pays the annuities, and his position must be considered. Are the annuities a crippling
burden on his farm? If they are, then
a case might be stated for their being
reduced or remitted altogether, just in
the same way that rates on agricultural
land have been remitted, for we all
agree that, with rising labour costs and
with prices as they are, his position is
precarious enough. The reduction of
the annuities would then rank as an
ordinary agricultural subsidy, which is
the proper way in which the matter
should be approached. The Anglo-Eire
Agreement has nothing to do with it.
What the Government must ask itself
is whether the state of the agricultural
industry is such as to make the grant-

ing of another subsidy imperative, and,
if so, whether this subsidy would take
the form of a reduction of the
annuities.
The Minister of Agriculture put the
case better than I could put it. He
made a very good case for the Govern
ment to consider this matter. I do not
care whether you call it subsidy, or
whether you call it remission of land
annuities or financial help or anything
else. I ask the Government to take
serious cognisance of the position agriculture is in and the suggestion of the
Minister, and to devise some scheme or
some plan whereby the farmer will be
helped or put in a position by legislation
or by guaranteed prices for his produce,
or whatever it is, to pay the annuities
if he cannot get rid of them in any other
way. By doing so, I think the Government would be doing a great deal to
relieve unemployment in our area and
bring about prosperity, not only in
agricultural communities, but in other
areas. I appeal to the Government not
to turn a deaf ear to the appeal that
agriculturists are making. I know
many to-day are making a grim struggle
for existence and holding on by a thread.
Farmers to-day are in a very precarious
condition. Agriculture is going out of
existence. I appeal to the Government
to do what they can to help to restore
prosperity to the industry. I feel that
the appeal will not fall on deaf ears.

to those who represent agricultural constituencies, is only given to those who
finish their cattle for beef. We find in
districts of Tyrone and Fermanagh they
are doing nothing in that way and only
rearing stores. We find that those who
are rearing two or three calves are very
apt to forget that there is such a thing
as a beef subsidy. We have passed through
a year when beef cattle got a big drop in
price. Those farmers who, unfortunately,
held on to store cattle in the spring, and
did not take the price then prevailing in
the market, find now that they are
getting £2 or £3 less per head. Then
again look at the result of the labours of
farmers owing to the wet weather in the
back end of the season. We see oats
standing out in stook, and plenty of hay
not yet in. We see the ground saturated
with flooding. The lot of the agriculturist is hard. I am sure every 'Member
who has friends similarly fixed, would do
his utmost to give much needed help.
I do not intend to occupy the time of the

Motion from going before it. I beg to
second the Motion.

reducing the annuities or having them

to enable him to maintain his child at
school. In my opinion it is a class Bill.
There is a privilege given to the rich to
educate their children to any age but no
privilege is given to the worker who must
only send his child to school under certain conditions until he reaches the age
of 15. That is ridiculous. Unless there
is compulsion in this Bill it will be a
hopeless failure. In the case of the
worker who will send his child to school
there is no provision in the Bill for books
or meals, which are a very important
matter and should be included in it.
If I may quote the Glasgow Corporation I would point out that during the
last four years they have spent
£3,000,000 on education. They have
through their efforts reduced illness and
disease amongst the school children.
They have been the means of supplying
meals which on the average cost only
1s 5d per week. Yet in Northern Ireland we have no provision whatever for
the workers' children, whether necessitous or otherwise, attending school.
Then in the city of Glasgow 35,000
children are provided with boots and
clothing. That is a splendid effort on
the part of the Glasgow Corporation
which should be followed in Northern
Ireland, seeing we are part and parcel of
the United Kingdom and should go step
by step in everything that is to the benefit or welfare of the workers.
We see cultural education defined
here, but it has not been defined too
clearly. In Great Britain it is developed
in each school for the benefit of the
children. There is no distinction made
there.
I am at all times in agreement with
the raising of the school age, because,
after all, the worker's child is entitled
to pass from the public elementary school
to the university. That is his birthright,
but under this Bill how many children
will be able to take advantage of this
raising of the school age. In the rural
districts I am afraid that the regional
education committees will grant exemptions as high as 90 per cent., because,
from my own experience, I know they
are not in sympathy with working-class
education. The Government should
make the raising of the school age compulsory; otherwise it will become a farce
so far as the regional education committees are concerned. It is not just
that, through no fault of his own, but
solely on account of his parents' lack of
income, a working-man's child should
have to seek exemption from attending
school until he is fifteen.
I maintain that it is the duty of the
State to take full control of education
and take it out of the hands of regional
committees. It is the duty of the State
to see that every child attending school
is guaranteed the highest degree of
education, free of interference from any
outside body. In order to make this extension of the school age possible the
Ministry should give consideration to the
question of making allowances to children
on the same scale as in Glasgow, and
particularly in cases of destitution. We
have absolutely no provision for such
allowances. Why send a child to school
hungry and ill-clad, particularly in the
winter time. If we are sympathetic and
considerate we have a duty to perform,
not alone in giving children a decent
education, but in ensuring that no child
shall attend school inadequately clothed
or under-nourished.

During the period they are attending

another year at least at that time

1561 Holiday Pay Bill-

12 OCTOBER 1938
Second Reading
Holidays With Pay Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): The Bill which comes before
the House to-day for a Second Reading
follows the text of the Holidays With
Pay Act recently passed at Westminster.
It may, accordingly, be helpful to Members if I recount briefly the circumstances in which this advance in social
reform has now become practical politics.
The principle of holidays with pay was
accepted in Great Britain so long ago as
1929, when a Private Members' Holiday
Bill secured a Second Reading, but had
to be dropped owing to lack of time.
In 1936 and 1937 Private Members'
Bills were again introduced, and in the
course of the debate on the latter Bill the
Minister of Labour intimated that he
proposed to appoint a Committee to look
into the matter, and as a consequence a
representative Committee, under the
chairmanship of Lord Amulree, was
appointed to examine the whole subject
and report their findings to him. After
hearing comprehensive evidence the Committee in April of this year presented
their report, in which they recommended
unanimously a paid holiday of at least
one week for all insurable employees,
adding that such holiday should be
established as part of the terms of the
contract of employment.
The Committee also urged that during
the next two to three years voluntary
holiday agreements should be encouraged
in every possible way, and that after that
probationary period general legislation
should be introduced. As an exception
to this procedure it was further recommended that trade boards, agricultural
wages committees, and any other wage
regulating authorities should be
powered to consider and determine
whether the provision of a paid holiday
should be granted in their industries, and
that enabling legislation covering existing wage boards should be introduced at
an early date.

It was in accordance with this recommendation that the Imperial Ministry of

Having given the trade boards power
under Clause 1 to provide for the granting of holidays, Clause 2 is designed to
ensure that all such holidays shall be
holidays with pay. I would like
specially to emphasise this point, that
under the Clause a trade board will not
be in a position to require holidays to be
given without pay. This is, undoubtedly,
the foundation principle of the Bill. If
a board decides that the workers under
its jurisdiction should have a holiday
it must then make provision for securing
that they shall receive pay for the period
of the holiday. Sub-section 2 of Clause
2 empowers a trade board to lay down
the times at which, and the conditions
under which, holiday pay shall become
payable.
Experience of the many voluntary
schemes of paid holidays has shown that
there are numerous methods of doing
this, and clearly each trade board should
be enabled to make the most suitable
arrangement for the industry which it
covers. It is assumed that in general the
trade board will direct that the payment
shall be made when the worker, in fact,
has his holiday.

schemes similar to that in the engineering industry, the sub-section also pro-

I have outlined briefly, though I
trust clearly, the proposals embodied in
the Bill, which, I hope, will mark the
beginning of a new era in the relationship of industrial employers and workers.
The Bill which is before the House may
be looked upon as an experimental one,
yet all our schemes of social reform which
have proved a boon and a blessing to

our people engaged in industry have had
their initiatory stages. Pioneer work is
always attractive and arresting to those
engaged in it though it may not always
attain the ideal in view.
I feel sure hon. Members on both sides
of the House are agreed on the desirability and value of an annual holiday,
and for the continuance of pay during
the holiday. In these days of increased
mechanisation health and efficiency demand a periodical rest from the onerous
conditions of modern industrial life. I
would go further and say that a holiday
free from the anxiety that must follow
a cessation of income is an investment
not alone to the individual, but also to
production.
A holiday without pay, therefore, is a
contradiction in terms. Such a "holiday" merely adds to the strain of
making domestic ends meet, and totally
fails to achieve the valuable effects which
a proper holiday could bring.
On the other hand, a paid holiday is
capable of effecting a mild revolution in
the social life not only of the family but
of the community, while at the same
time removing the distinction which now
exists between the black-coated and the
manual worker.
Paid holidays arranged by voluntary
agreement are most likely to be operative first of all in those industries where
employers and workers are best organised. At the other end of the scale are
those industries where the degree of
organisation is poor, and where, accordingly, the Trade Boards Act has been
applied for the regulation of wages.
Obviously it was because these trades
required special treatment that they
were singled out by the Amulree Committee for statutory action in regard to
paid holidays.
The Bill, which I am hopeful the
House will pass this evening, will mean
that each of the eighteen trade boards
at present functioning in Northern Ireland will be afforded the opportunity of
considering and determining the propriety of granting a week's paid holiday
for the 50,000 or so workers employed by
about 2,500 employers covered by the
boards.
As each board is composed of an equal
number of
of employers' and of employees' representatives, with an independent chairman, their discussions, as
well as the ultimate result of such discussions, will be extremely valuable in
creating a public opinion among the
other industries which now have no paid
holiday schemes on a voluntary basis.
Voluntary arrangements on the subject of paid holidays in our Northern
Ireland industries are progressing, and
I am glad to say that at the present
moment there are over thirty agreements
of this nature which have been reported
to the Ministry of Labour. These include shipbuilding and engineering, sawmilling, provender-milling, the printing
industry, transport, the cinema industry,
and municipal employees in Belfast and
Londonderry.
I trust these are but the indication of
a general tendency, and that in the near
future we shall hear of many more such
voluntary agreements resulting from the
desire and the ability of those associated
with our industries to make their contribution in the matter of holidays with
with pay. I beg to move.

SENTENCE ON A BOY OF 15.
8. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether a boy of
fifteen years of age is serving a sentence
of twelve months' imprisonment in Belfast under the Special Powers Act.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): It is a fact that
a youth, now 16 years of age, but who
at the date of conviction on 22nd June
last was aged 15 years and 10 months,
is at present serving a sentence of 12
months' imprisonment in Belfast Gaol.
The offences of which this youth was
convicted were of a very serious nature,
and the magistrate in convicting him
found it necessary to certify, in accordance with the provisions of the Children
Act, 1908, that the prisoner was of so
unruly a character that he could not be
detained in a place of detention provided
under Part V of the Act, and accordingly sentenced the prisoner as already
stated.
The youth is, of course, kept with
the juvenile adult class in the prison.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask the
Minister what kind of a boy he was
at 15?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think I was
better than the boy in question.

any action
has been taken by the Government in

likely to need them in the near future.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sure no
one in this House who has had the
privilege of acquaintance with Dr.
Wilson, and who knows his genial and
kindly disposition, could for one moment
believe that the statement which he is
alleged to have made on the occasion referred to could possibly be taken literally.
I think everyone-even the Members
opposite will recognise that if in fact
Dr. Wilson did make use of any such
expression, this must have been merely
one of these exuberant oratorical flights
which are not uncommon at political

perhaps the hon. and learned Member

in its strictly literal meaning.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not
understand the question
the question my learned.

BOMB OUTRAGE AT NEWSPAPER
OFFICE.
11. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether the offices of
the "Daily Mail" and Associated Papers
in Rosemary Street, Belfast, were
bombed and damaged; whether any steps.
have been taken to clear up this and
other bombing outrages; whether the
Minister was referring to a newspaper of
the "Daily Mail" group in his speech
in Londonderry as reported in the
"Northern Whig" on 20th July, 1938,
in which he is reported as having said
among other matters, "You will find
that the English Press, and particularly
one paper, represents the Orange celebrations as taking place amidst riots, and
as though a campaign of terrorism had
broken out"; whether the Minister will
give the House of the name of the paper
which he particularly referred to, and
what official action, if any, he has taken
in the matter.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer to
the first part of the hon. Member's question is in the affirmative; every effort
has been made by the police to render the
offenders amenable, but without success.
The newspaper to which I referred on
the occasion mentioned by the hon. Member was the "Daily Mirror." Immediately my attention was drawn to the
statement in question I communicated
with the proprietors of the journal,
calling upon them to publish a correction
and apology, and I received a reply, explaining the origin of the error, and
enclosing a subsequent copy of the paper
containing an apology for and retraction
of the statement which had been made.

not prepared to take one solitary word

Gordon): No, no.

responsible wage regulating authorities.
has resulted in a large percentage receiving holidays with pay. The English

Mr. YOUNG: I would like to get

Labour on the question of what this week

Bill visualises that trades which do not

The old Factory Acts laid down that
workers should be allowed six holidays in each year. It was definitely
laid down that these six days must
include Good Friday and Easter Monday.
In place of Good Friday a worker could
take Easter Tuesday. It was also laid
down that two of the other days must be
Christmas Day and Boxing Day. The
trades were to arrange on what days they
would have the remaining two. Of
course, in this country the days chosen
were the 12th and 13th July.
What I want to get from the Minister

it would be most natural in the North
of Ireland if any scheme for holidays

If six days with pay were given in a week

Holiday Pay Bill-
Second Reading
13 OCTOBER 1938
The hon. Member for Ballynafeigh (Mr.
Thompson) gave us some idea of the
general advantages to health this Bill
will mean. Since his hands got a
week's holiday they have had better
health the whole winter. There has been
far less for the medical profession to do.
If you gave them a month's holidays the
doctors might have to leave the city
altogether. If a week does so much good
what would a month do? I am not so
sure this is correct because the 100,000
unemployed who have a permanent holiday through no fault of their own are
certainly not as healthy as the people
who are working.
The hon. Member for Bann Side (Mr.
Young) seems to be worried as to whether
these days are to be in addition to the
days the workers have already got. It
is quite plain that they are, and I hope
the Government will adhere to that.
There are special days, including 12th
July, recognised as holidays in any case,
and I believe the Bill means that these
holidays will be in addition, and that a
man who would get his holidays during
the week in which 12th July fell would
be entitled to get a day the next week
or at some other time in lieu of 12th
July. The same applies, I think, to
Christmas Day and Good Friday and the
other days recognised as holidays.
The hon. Member seemed to be greatly
worried. I cannot say what his motives
are or whether he wants to get a day off
the workers in some way or other by
letting them off during Twelfth week. I
sincerely hope-in fact, I feel certainthe Government will not give way on
that point because that would be what
we know as giving with one hand and
taking back with the other. Whatever
holidays the men have at present let
them have, and as the Clause which was
read by the hon. Member for Bann Side
says let them have the additional holidays as well. It certainly can do them
no harm and will do them good.
"
I know of some firms that have given
these holidays with pay. I have never
heard any of them complaining. I think
the plan has been to the general advantage of the firms and of the people employed by them. For instance, if an
employee in a firm knows that if he
works for a year he will get holidays
with pay would you not think he would
take more interest in doing his work well
and retaining his position in that firm?
In addition to earning his living would
he not be looking forward to that happy
time when he would walk away for a

economic conditions, and if they are now

Factories Bill.

Mr. GORDON: The Bill which I am
placing before the House is a consolidating and amending Measure containing
162 clauses and three schedules. The
last co-ordinating Factory Act was that
of 1901, and since that time several
amending Acts, along with numerous
Orders and Codes of Regulations have
rendered factory legislation unwieldy
and difficult to interpret and administer.
Indeed, both employers and workers are
often puzzled to know how the law stands
on a particular matter, and I am sure
it will interest the hon. and learned
Member for Central to know that even
experienced lawyers admit that the
present Factory Code is not only cumbersome, but somewhat of an enigma.
One of the main objects of the Bill is
to simplify the law by gathering up and
welding together into one coherent
whole the best of the bits and pieces of
enacted since the
factory legislation enacted
But
beginning of the present century.
the Bill aims at much more than the
mere provision of a consolidated code.
The Act of 1901 was a great Measure for
its day and generation. It marked a
distinct advance in social legislation and
subsequent extensions of the law fulfilled
their limited purpose. The fact remains,
however, that a general overhaul of the
Factory Acts is much overdue. In view
of the developments in the investigation
of the conditions of health and safety in
industry. Consequently, the main
ideal before the Ministry of Labour has
been to produce a Bill which will reduce
accidents and occupational diseases to a
minimum, carrying out the old adage:

"Where there is no health there is
no energy;
Where there is no energy there is
no output."
The Bill not only breaks new ground,
but adds to the provisions already in
existence. First of all, it makes
additional provision
provision for ventilation,
heating, lighting, cleanliness and medical supervision designed to safeguard the
health of the workers; secondly, it protects more adequately life and limb;
thirdly, it secures a shortening of the
hours of work for women and young
persons engaged in industry. Lastly,
it further encourages the promotion of
those amenities which come under the
general heading of "Welfare." And in
none of these proposals have we gone
to a dangerous extreme.
Such are the underlying principles of
this Bill, and I am certain that the Bill
will commend itself to all sections of the
House. I need hardly remind Members
that the Bill is based largely I use the

which was passed recently by the Imperial Parliament. In this respect I
make no apology whatever for following the example of the predominant

It is a far cry to 1802 when the
Imperial Parliament passed its
its first
Factory Act providing for the cleansing
and ventilation of cotton mills, and for
the clothing, hours of labour and
religious education of the child workers.
employed in those industries. Since
that time the United Kingdom has been
in the van of social progress, and we
in Northern Ireland cannot do better
than take the British Act of 1937 as our
guide, modifying it, as we have done, to
meet certain special conditions in Northern Ireland. The Imperial authorities,
before drafting their Bill, had numerous
consultations with representatives of employers' and workers' organisations and,
so I am informed, secured a very large
measure of agreement on many of the

We,
also, in Northern Ireland have likewise

all interests concerned, taking the Great

of unanimity evinced at the conferences
has been very gratifying to those in the
industry.

accepted unreservedly by every

No, sir! We have
been told by some that we are moving

Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Mr. GORDON: Yet I think I am
safe in asserting that the Bill represents

to what should now be done to bring
the conditions in all factories more into

these
observed that the Bill abolishes the distinction between "factories" and "workshops" and between "textile" and "nontextile" factories. One by one
and other descriptive terms originated
in the earlier Factory Acts of the last
century; protection was first extended
to workers in the spinning and weaving
concerns, then to those in non-textile
factories, and finally to the women and
girls in the smallest dressmaking establishment or other workshop. They have
now served their purpose, and we propose to wipe out these troublesome distinctions which have become artificial
and obsolete, and to replace them with
the one term, "factories." The provisions of the Bill are designed to apply
to all premises coming within the revised
definition of "factory" as set out in
Clause 157.
The first part of the Bill sets out a
number of new general requirements as
to health. Some of these re-enact without change the existing law, while others
contain important modifications and extensions of the Act of 1901. Some important changes are made in the first
Clause of the Bill which require daily
removal of dirt and refuse from floors,
benches, and passages, as well as the
weekly cleansing of floors. In the past
our inspectors have found it most
difficult to enforce a satisfactory
standard in these matters, simply because the existing law makes no precise

that the standard reached in many

of opinion that to lay down a definite

Another important

400, and which will, no doubt, receive

This proposal is not new in industrial

a higher standard than 250 cubic feet is
already afforded, or can be afforded, with
a

It is found that excessive extremes of
temperature cause general physical dis
comfort, and complaints are frequently
received during the winter months from
workers as to lack of proper heating of
their workrooms. This is one of the
matters in which the need for better provision seems to be most strongly felt, and
we have outlined the necessity of enforcing more stringent temperature requirements.
Most important new proposals are
those regarding lighting. The need
for these proposals was established by
the reports of a Departmental Committee in Great Britain on lighting,
which appeared during and after the
Great War. This Committee recommended:-(1) That adequate and suitable lighting should be required in every
part of a factory; (2) that there should
be power to define what is adequate and
suitable illumination; (3) that certain
minimum standards should be laid down
for "working areas"; and (4) that all
external windows should be kept clean
both inside and out. It will, no doubt,
surprise some hon. Members to learn
that the existing law is silent on a subject which has such a vitally important
bearing on the health, safety and
efficiency of the worker. Following a
lighting exhibition organised on a modest
scale a few years ago by the Ministry,
the factory inspectors reported, and continue to this day to report, that many
employers have voluntarily spent time
and money on improved schemes of lighting in their various industries. Clause
5 will give the Ministry power to enforce
generally what has already been done
voluntarily in the more advanced
factories.
Let me now refer to medical supervision. Clause 12 safeguards the
physical, mental, and economic interests
of the workers for the first time. It
gives power to require reasonable arrangements to be made for the medical supervision of the workers in certain circumstances while employed in industry.
Some may be inclined to oppose medical
examination on the ground that it may
deprive persons of employment, but that
is not sufficient reason for rejecting the
constructive principle underlying such
health measures.
This would be but a
precautionary measure to safeguard the
worker. Under the existing law there is
no power to require medical supervision.
in a particular works to meet a special
emergency such as an outbreak of
anthrax, dermatitis, or sepsis; or to meet
cases where there is reason to apprehend
that some substance likely to be injurious
is being introduced; or where young
persons have been, or are about to be, put
on work which it is thought may prove
too much for them.
For example, as regards paragraph (a)
of Sub-clause (1) of Clause 12, which
covers cases of illness due to the nature
of a process, had the powers of this
Clause been available last year they would
have been very valuable indeed in dealing
with a factory in Belfast where the handling of a new material caused a number of
girl workers to suffer from eye trouble
and other sources of pain and loss.
Paragraph (c) of the same sub-section
will be helpful in estimating the effects
on health in the clothing industry, where
the "conveyer system" is becoming very
general. Under this system, a single
operation is performed, minute in and
minute out, throughout the working day,
the speed being dictated by the speed
at which the conveyer is set. It is probably too early to judge of its effects on

the health of the workers, but apprehension is felt that it may be detrimental to health, and the provisions in

Under Part II of the Act the present
law regarding safety has been largely recast. This Part contains a number of
new provisions as to safety devices or
arrangements, and requires additional
precautions in the case of cranes, chains,
hoists and other parts of factory plant.
The
I would like to draw special attention
to Clause 18, which deals with the construction and sale of new machinery.
By throwing the onus on the seller of a
new machine to provide certain minimum
safety requirements, this Clause introduces an entirely new principle.
practical arguments in its favour are,
first, that it tends to ensure safety by
dealing with the matter at the first stage
before the machine is installed; and,
secondly, it meets the reasonable complaint of many factory owners who often
find, after buying new machines, that
rather expensive guards have to be fitted
to comply with the Factory Acts.
In
these circumstances employers, not unnaturally, complain to inspectors that
machines should have been made accident
proof before purchase, and this Clause
is an effort to meet such representations
and remove a real grievance.
When dealing with questions of safety
it might be appropriate if just now I
asked the House to direct its attention to
another section of the Bill, which, by
imposing duties on the workers themselves, is a new provision of considerable
importance. Various codes of regulations for dangerous trades impose the
duty on persons employed to give the
safety plans provided by the employer
a fair chance of doing what they are
intended to do. Unfortunately, many
workers, through ignorance, carelessness,
or other causes, are very remiss in such
matters, with the result that numerous
otherwise preventible accidents are being
reported to the Ministry from time to
time. It is hoped that the insertion in
the Bill of this general Clause 125 on the
lines proposed will have a far-reaching
effect in accident prevention, by placing
a degree of responsibility on the worker.
In particular, it will tend in practice
to grant some relief to the employer from
the rigour of the general principle that
he is formally held liable for seeing that
the Acts are fully complied with in his
works. This onus on the employer often
acts harshly. It is frequently impossible to discharge it when a worker
wilfully removes guards or otherwise endangers himself or others, and, as I have
stated, the sharing of the responsibility
by the worker will, I sincerely hope,
effect a marked change in the Ministry's
accident statistics.
The fact that in 1937 there were 23
fatal and 2,397 other accidents in our
factories proves that the safety of life
and limb is of paramount importance. I
trust that the tightening up of the law
which this part of the Bill indicates will
result in a substantial reduction in the
industrial accident roll of Northern Ireland.
Welfare plays an important part in
this Bill. Part III. of the Bill deals
with general provisions as to welfare.
The Act of 1916, by enabling welfare
orders to be made, gave a statutory basis
for welfare work in certain types of
factories. The aim now is to include
such obvious amenities as drinking water
and washing facilities, first-aid, sitting
accommodation, and the like in the
permanent social code, and I have no
doubt that the House will support me
wholeheartedly in these proposals.
Part IV. contains special welfare provisions in regard to health, safety and
comfort. Here again fresh ground is
broken. Thus the existing provisions as
to the removal of dust are made much
stronger, while new provisions are introduced to control underground workrooms
in factories, and I would draw special
attention to a very important Clause,
Clause 61, which deals with the lifting
of heavy weights. Often thoughtlessly
on the part of a foreman, women and
young persons are sometimes permitted
or required to lift such excessive
loads as to impair permanently their
physical health, and this Clause will, I
hope, go a long way towards mitigating
such a manifest evil.
Part V. makes no radical change in the
existing law, but when we now come to
Part VI. the Bill touches every man,
women, and young person in factory
employment. It is true that men's
hours never have been regulated by
Factory Acts, but a century's experience
Factories Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
has proved that the restrictions imposed
on women and young persons invariably
and inevitably dictate the hours of the
great majority of men in the
in the same
factory. Following the precedents of
100 years, the proposal is to review the
duration of the working day and working week of women and young persons,
and to bring the statutory limits more
into line with those which, during the
war and immediately post-war years,
were hammered out by agreement
between all the interests concerned.
Probably the most important portion
of the Bill is Clause 76. It provides
for a normal 9-hour day and 48-hour
week as against the present statutory 55
hours in textile and 60 hours in nontextile factories. It may be argued that
this is a "Thank you for nothing" concession in view of the fact that 48 hours
is the usual limit now prevailing in
industry, and that, in any case, the proposals are vitiated by the amount of
overtime permitted. The reply is
simple: although a week of 48 hours or
less is now the general rule, many cases
come to the notice of my Department
where, by trade overtime, legal overtime, and sometimes by illegal overtime,
the present daily or weekly limits are far
exceeded.
The only criticism of the proposed 48hour week which the Ministry of Labour
has received up to the present is from one
section of industry which for several
years has been organised on the basis of
a 49-hour week. I had the pleasure of
meeting a deputation, the members of
which did their level best to convince me
that their branch of industry should be
treated exceptionally in view of the
peculiar circumstances in which their
processes had to be carried out.
No one in this House is more sympathetic than myself regarding the difficulties with which industry is burdened
at the present time, and it would have
given me and, I know, the Government
much pleasure if it had been possible for
us to meet the views of the spokesmen
for this old-established trade. We found
it, however, quite impracticable-nor
would it have been fair to other sections
of industry-to single out one branch of
industry for a 49-hour week, while imposing a 48-hour week on all other
factory employers.
Apart from all other considerations,
such an exception would have been a
complete departure from the principle of
the Government for the last seventeen
years that our workers will be accorded
at least the same rights and privileges
as those in Great Britain, where operatives for many years past have all
enjoyed a 48-hour week.
Another provision which deserves more
than passing notice is that contained in
Clause 77, which proposes to reduce the
weekly hours of juveniles under sixteen
to 44 per week. In the last few years
opinion has become manifest that for
young people just leaving school the
immediate jump from the short and
elastic school hours to a rigid 48-hour
week in a factory is far too abrupt, and
imposes a physical and mental shock
which, in many cases, must have ill
effects in after life.
This aspect was very fully developed
during the Committee Stage of the
Factories Bill at Westminster, when all
sides of the Committee pronounced in
favour of a shorter working week for
these young people. We fully share
this view, and I trust that the Clause
will commend itself to the whole House,
after noting that industry is being given
a year from the date of the commencement of the Act to adjust itself to the
change, and that reasonable provision is
being made for exceptions under sub-
Clause (2).
This sub-clause leaves it open to employers in any particular industry to
make a case for a longer week than 44
hours on the grounds that the young
workers form part of a team composed
of men, women and older juveniles; that
any increased hours would not be
injurious; and that the employment in
itself is not likely to be a blind alley one.
Great Britain will have had considerable
experience of the working of this Clause
before it becomes operative in Northern Ireland, and we here will benefit
by the examples set us there as to the
appropriate types of cases to take advantage of the exception.
Now I come to the question of overtime-always an irritating question, and
difficult to deal with, especially in peak
periods of trade. Clause 79 makes provision for up to six hours' overtime in
the week, in not more than 25 weeks in
the year, and subject to a yearly maxi-

This Clause is put forward on the
basis that some overtime by
workers beyond the 48-hour limit is
necessary in almost every industry at
some time or other in the course of the

Clause for the first time permits of overtime by persons over 16 years of age,

18 at present.
This elasticity has been decided upon
because of the interdependence of the
work of men, women and young persons
in many cases, and of the great difficulties which would be caused if overtime
beyond 48 hours were confined to persons
over 18 years of age.
As regards the amount of overtime,
the maximum figure fixed must necessarily be somewhat arbitrary. Inquiries
made by the Ministry, however, indicate
that while the figure of 100 proposed in
the Bill is less than the amount now

sufficient in most industries with proper
management.
I trust that the House will recognise

hardship on the worker, has done its best
to meet the differing needs and the
emergencies which are always cropping
up in industry.
It is proposed to permit no overtime
by workers under 16, and those between
16 and 18 may also be precluded from

be shown that overtime employment is

During the Committee stage I have no
doubt that opportunities will be afforded.
for further developing the various considerations regarding hours of employment. Meanwhile, let me assure
House and especially any hon. Member
who may be critical of the present proposals on the ground that they are excessive-especially at this juncture when
there is a great deal of unemployment,
I am fully alive to the folly of overburdening one worker when another is
idle because no man is in a position to
hire him.
Part VII of the Bill, in addition to
continuing the limited application of the
present law to docks and warehouses,
casts the legislative net wider in several
important respects. For example, Clause
110 removes the anomaly of ship fitters
being factory employees when in dry
dock, but not when in wet dock.
The succeeding Clause deals with the
present irksome position of persons working on building operations being in the
morning within the protection of the
Factory Acts, and outside them in the
afternoon merely because a crane has
been moved away from the site during
the dinner adjournment.
These occupations, as well as that in
works of engineering construction now
dealt with for the first time in Clause
112, all produce their quota of health
and safety problems, and it is good to
know that the interests most affected are
in favour of the advance outlined in the
Clause to which I have referred.
The remaining parts of the Bill call
for little comment at the moment. For
the most part they re-enact existing
legislation, sometimes with minor modifications or amendments designed to
better facilitate the smooth working of
the Measure as a whole.
I have now endeavured to give the
House a brief outline of the main provisions of a Bill which will make factory
legislation at once more comprehensive
and simple. The overriding intention
is that the tightening up of the law
should create a more pleasant, healthy,
and a safer working environment for all
factory employees.
At a time of falling birth-rate there
is a special obligation on the Government to protect adequately the lives and
limbs of the living. Better health,
greater freedom from accidents, and
more attention to "welfare" amenities
among the working population are,
therefore, among the chief objects of the
Bill, and I believe that its passage into
law will have beneficial results not only
for the workers but for the community
at large.
The reforms indicated in the Measure
will cost money to some firms. On the
other hand, many employers have little
Factories Bill—
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS

to fear, because their conditions in many
respects are already in line with, if not
ahead of, the demands of the Bill. But
even where outlay is involved it will
ultimately prove a profitable and satisfying investment in increased safety,
lessened absenteeism, greater contentment at work, and higher standards of
workmanship and output.
I have already informed the House
that before drafting the Bill we took
into our confidence representatives of all
interests likely to be affected. Before
sitting down, therefore, I would like to
express my appreciation of the helpful
and, on the whole, constructive criticism
which the Government received from the
representatives of employers and workers.
Except as regards the point or two I
have already indicated, practically all
employers joined with the spokesmen for
the workers in acquiescing in the view
that our operatives should have the same
rights and privileges as their fellows in
Great Britain. This has been our aim
throughout the drafting of this long and
rather complex Bill. I am sure the
House will forgive me if at this stage
I diverge to say that I am under a deep
obligation to our Chief
Chief Inspector of
Factories, Mr. McCaghey, and his very
able assistant, Mr. McWilliam, for the
very able advice and the great help they
have given me in presenting this Bill
to the House to-day.
Once it becomes law, I feel confident
that the factory owners of Northern Ireland will co-operate in the most hearty
manner with the factory inspectors in
bringing their factories into line with the
new demands which will be made upon
them. For, it must again be emphasised,
there is no single requirement in the
Bill-I think I am correct in making
this statement-which has not already
been tried out voluntarily and proved
in one factory or another by an employer who has not been content to limit
himself to the compulsory rule as regards amenities for his workers.
Away back in 1833 the first factory
inspector who officiated in Northern Ireland made use of these words in his first
annual report:—
"I have met with the most
courteous attention on the part of the
mill owners . . . All my intercourse
with them has satisfied me that . . .
they will give their cordial assistance
to promote the objects of the legislature, and, without that concurrence
any Measure that could be devised
must prove only very partially effective
in practice.'
That was more than a hundred years
ago, but the employers of to-day are
the sons of the men who impressed the
first factory inspector with their vision
and public spirit.
I look with confidence to these sons of
their fathers to ensure that, once Parliament has signed this new Magna Charta
of the workers, the factory inspector of
a few years hence will be again impelled
to report that the Northern Ireland
factory employers have left no stone unturned to make the new Act what the
Government intends it to be a wellordered social code reflecting the public
conscience on the duty to one's neighbour. I beg to move.

Adjournment.
Motion made, and Question proposed:

(Capt. Dixon).
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the Prime
Minister kindly inform the House of the
order of business for Tuesday?
The PRIME MINISTER: I am able
to give the House details of the business
to be carried through next week. The
Factories Bill (Second Reading), and the
Education Bill (Committee) will be taken
on Tuesday. In addition there are
three Motions down by private Members.
On Wednesday the Air Raid Precautions
Bill (Second Reading), Holidays with
Pay Bill (Committee) and the Appropriation Bill (Second Reading) will be dealt
with. On Thursday we will take the
Factories Bill (Committee) and the
Second Reading of the Marketing of
Potatoes Bill.

pursuant to the

1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware of the
treatment meted out to an applicant for
assistance who appeared before the
Appeals Tribunal as not available for
work and discovered that his allowance
was reduced from 30s to 23s; whether
the Chairman of the Appeals Tribunal
can reduce the allowance as stated seeing
that the claimant was brought before
this tribunal under a different reading as
quoted above.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I have made inquiries from the
Unemployment Assistance Board, and I
am assuming that the case referred to in
the hon. Member's question is that of an
applicant residing in Blackwatertown.
The reduction of the allowance was not
made by the Chairman of the Appeal
Tribunal, who decided that the applicant
was available for work, but by the area
officer of the Board subsequent to the
hearing, on the ground that the previous
allowance did not reflect the applicant's
normal earning capacity. Against this
decision the applicant had a right of
appeal, and although he did not exercise
his right within the prescribed time, the
Board is prepared to allow him all the
facilities in its power to have his case
heard.
Mr. AGNEW: When this claim was
brought before the Unemployment Assistance Board-the tribunal at Portadown
-there was no mention made of a reduction in the allowance.

not in order. He must not give information when asking a supplementary
question.

not informed of the reduction prior to
the hearing at the Appeals Tribunal?
Mr. GORDON: It became known to
us that the information given by the
applicant was not proper information,
and consequently we had to reduce the
amount he was entitled to.
Mr. NIXON: Under what law, rule,
or regulation is an area officer allowed
to reverse the court, and reverse it without reference to a higher court or higher
authority?
Mr. GORDON: I do not think I said
the area officer reversed the decision of
the Appeals Tribunal.

the Appeals Tribunal?
Mr. GORDON: When the Appeals
Tribunal gives a decision and any new
information comes in regard to the applicant, then the Appeals Tribunal again
examines the case, or the Chairman of
the Appeals Tribunal examines it.

UNEMPLOYMENT
ASSISTANCE
ADMINISTRATION.
2. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware of reductions in the awards to claimants for
unemployment assistance where no
change of circumstances is shown from
the first determination issued; whether
area officers reduce the amount of allowances without consulting the Unemployment Assistance Board, and, if not,
whether he can state who is responsible
for such reductions.
Mr. GORDON: The duty of assessing
unemployment assistance allowances has
been placed upon the officers of the Unemployment Assistance Board by Parliament. In carrying out this duty
these officers act under the general super-
The regulations provide that, in assessing the amount of an allowance, regard
should be had to the potential earnings
of the household, and when, owing to
any cause, the earning powers of an
applicant have diminished, it is sometimes necessary to reduce the amount of
the allowance on that account. Conversely, allowances have been raised in
cases where it was thought that the earning powers of an applicant had increased
since the first assessment.
An applicant has a right of appeal
against any alteration of the amount of
an allowance.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
is it not a fact that according to Statute
the applicant has also a right of appeal
against the decision of the Appeals
Tribunal to the right hon. Gentleman
himself?
Mr. GORDON: That is a difficult
question, but at the moment I rather
think that the Appeals Tribunal is, by
Parliament, the final and deciding voice.
Mr. BEATTIE: I do not want to take
the right hon. Gentleman at a disadvantage, but does he not act as umpire on the
insurability claims of persons under the
Unemployment Assistance Board?
Mr. SPEAKER: The question can
be raised on the adjournment if the hon.
Member so wishes.

Factories Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Factories Bill.
Order read for resuming adjourned
debate on Question (13th October):
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time." (The Minister of Labour.)
Question again proposed.
Mr. BEATTIE: In considering the
Factory Bill as presented by the right
hon. Gentleman, one has to deplore the
many omissions from a Measure of this
kind which, if included in it, would have
been of great service to the unemployed
of Northern Ireland. I understood a
Factory Bill was to regulate the conditions under which workers should be
asked to follow in the various classes of
industry in which they are engaged. That
was the purport of the first Factory Act
established. I would like to dispute the
right hon. Gentleman's statement as to
the effect of the first factory inspection.
The inspector was certainly not received.
as an
angel in disguise. He was
hounded from pillar to post, and
absolutely refused admission into the respective works he was delegated to inspect.
The employing classes of that time
strenuously opposed any legislation in
regard to the conditions under which the
workers should be employed. They
resented it very much. Up to this present
year of 1938 conditions have been perpetuated which have always been resented.
To-day we are providing for the
future regulation of industry in a Bill
which, we are told, is similar to the
English Act. Allow me again to refute
that statement. This Bill is not exactly
the same as the Measure which passed
through the British House of Commons.
This is a Bill designed, I presume, to
meet the conditions existing in Northern
Ireland. I say that Northern Ireland
is not stabilised so far as industries are
concerned. Are we not hoping through
our new Industries Act to establish new
industries in Northern Ireland, industries which are already established in
England and Scotland but which, for
some reason of which I am not aware,
are not to be found in Northern Ireland? For that reason this Bill should
have been an exact duplicate of the English Act.
Take the glass-blowing industry.
There will never be a glass-blowing
industry in Northern Ireland again.
The last glass-blowing industry was in
my Division, and if it had received the
assistance it should have received from
this Government it would have been still
in existence and would be producing
sufficient glass for the requirements of
Ulster. That industry was allowed to
die out. There is no provision in this
Bill for a glass-blowing industry
although in the English Act it is set out
an English industry. I might be
accused of saying that cotton will never
come into Northern Ireland as an industry owing to the elements, but I would
remind the House that the most
prosperous industry Ireland ever had
was the cotton industry, and that
because of its prosperity it was transferred from Ireland to England.
as
Mr. JOHNSTON: Blethers!
Mr. BEATTIE: The hon. Member
for North Armagh says "Blethers."
He should read history. He is the biggest blether and nuisance in this House.
The cotton industry which was once very
prosperous in Ireland was taken away
from Ireland and planted in England.
Ireland was then given the linen industry, which enabled the hon. Gentleman's
class to sweat the workers and draw the
life's blood from them by paying them
low wages and making them work long
hours. It cannot be disputed that the
linen industry has served its day and
generation in that direction, as we were

Mr. NIXON: I beg to move :
"That, in the opinion of this House,
in order to relieve unemployment and
make better provision for the care and
happiness of old and blind people, the
Government should take steps to increase
all Old Age, Insurance, Widows, and
Blind Persons Pensions to £1 per week,
and in the case of old age and insurance
pensions reduce the age limit by five
years."
I will endeavour to be as brief as possible. A great many Members of the
House expressed sympathy with pensioners during the last election, and I
hope this afternoon to give them an
opportunity of giving practical effect to
that sympathy by their votes. I say at
the outset that this Motion does not
pretend to contain everything that might
be worked into the scheme if and when
it becomes law, and I only want the
House to accept the principle. In the
first instance, no one will pretend that
10s a week is enough for a widow, or
an old man or an old woman, and I am
as sure as I am standing here that the
time will come when the amount given
will be increased.
New Zealand is a country that the
Prime Minister and the Government are
very fond of holding up as a model, and
the other day the people there gave their
assent by popular vote to a pension of
30s a week. I am not asking for 30s; I
am only asking for 20s. I know that it
will be argued from that side of the
House, as it was argued before, that the
country cannot afford to pay £1 a week.
They will say that £1 a week would
bankrupt the country, but I wish the
House to recollect that when the 5s a
week was first granted it was argued by
the predecessors of the present Members
of the Imperial Parliament that
country would be made bankrupt. That
was argued on platform and in Press, and
if you go back to the files of the "Telegraph," "News-Letter," and "Whig" of
those dates you will find it was argued
that 5s a week would bankrupt the
country. Well, it did not, nor did 10s,
and £1 would not bankrupt it.

Mr. BEATTIE: I wish to support the
Motion, although, perhaps we should be
considering a proposal to confer even
greater benefits upon the old-age
pensioners. We have at our disposal the
experience of a very voung State-New
Zealand. Every Member of this House
is aware that a Labour Government has
been in power in New Zealand, and in
their few years of office they have made
great strides with the social services.
The hon. Member for Woodvale, I understand, has already referred to the Social
Security Act passed by the Labour
Government of New Zealand. It is a
contributory scheme similar to the one
that has been established in Northern
Ireland and Great Britain, but is on a
different basis. It provides that all
citizens of New Zealand shall be secure
during times of infirmity and sickness
and in old age.
The figures seem very
high, but when they are worked out it
will be found that they are not such a
high contribution for the benefits that
will be conferred.
Under the Security Act each citizen of
New Zealand must register by paying a
fee of £1, and then, in addition, he has
to pay a levy of 1s on each pound he
earns. A man earning £3 a week would
pay a levy of 3s a week, plus £1 per
annum as a registration fee. If he is a
married man he has, in addition, to pay
a registration fee of 5s for his wife.
That entitles his wife and himself to a
joint pension of £3 a week when they
attain the age of 60. If they are single
persons they pay the same annual registration fee and the same levy on their earnings. This contributory pensions scheme
has a means test. If a former Minister
of Labour were in the House at this
moment he would doubtless ask the Member for Woodvale if he was prepared to
have a means test. There is a means
test in the New Zealand Security Act,
but it is applied in a case where a person
has a fixed income which is likely to
maintain him and his wife and family in
decency and comfort for the remainder
of their lives. Such a person also has
to pay his contribution to the pension
scheme for the benefit of the other citizens of the country.
If we could fashion our Acts dealing
with the social services-old age, unemployment, sickness, and infirmity-into a
composite Act like the Security Act of
New Zealand we would be giving a lead
to the British Isles. Under our present
social laws the people are never going to
