Another point is the cost of the proposals. On the 30th September, 1938,
the total number of old-age contributory,
non-contributory, widows' and blind persons' pensions in payment in Northern
Ireland was 89,444, made up
follows:-65-70 old-age pensions, 15,716;
70 contributory old-age pensions, 25,238;
70 non-contributory old-age pensions,
31,253; widows' pensions, 15,776, and
blind pensions, 1,461. The reason I am
differentiating between the different types
of pension is because I want to point out
what the savings might be and the number
of people who are likely to be absorbed.
into employment as a result of the proposals. The pensions paid to these 89,444
persons amount to about £2,310,000 per
annum, and the adoption of the proposal
to increase the pensions to £1 per week
would mean an added charge of £2,310,000
per annum.
Mr. BEATTIE: How do you make that
up?
Mr. GORDON: I am explaining how I
make it up.
We have 89,444 persons getting 10s
a week. That represents
£2,310,000. If we give another 10s a
week it will represent another £2,310,000.
The adoption of the proposal to reduce
the existing qualifying ages for old-age
pension by five years would, it is estimated, qualify an additional 40,000 persons for pension. This figure, on the
basis of £1 per week, would mean a
further increase in pension costs of
approximately £2,100,000. That, added
to the £2,310,000, would be somewhere
in the region of £4,400,000 as an added
charge on the Exchequer. There would,
as the Motion suggests, be some saving in
unemployment benefit and assistance if
the proposals were adopted.
I should like to deal with the people
whose age for qualifying for a pension
was reduced from 70 to 65. Those people
are largely small shopkeepers, farmers,
or spinsters of limited means. It would
not be possible to put young men in the
jobs of those people. I am not in a position to show there would be any saving
to the Unemployment Fund for those
people, and I do not know the number of
young people likely to be absorbed into
jobs held by persons between 65 and 70
years of age, but I have some figures of
the extent to which persons in receipt of
contributory pensions remain in insurable employment. About 7,000 people
over 65 are at present employed, but their
average employment is not high, and if
they were replaced by younger persons it
is doubtful whether, in the result, there
would be full-time employment for more
than 5,000 people. Assuming, therefore,
that these 7,000 retired, on the pension
being raised to £1 a week, the saving in
unemployment insurance benefit or assistance would not exceed £260,000 a year.
It is unlikely that increasing the pension
to £1 a week would induce these people
to retire, because there are numbers of
men who probably earn £3 or £4 a week
between the ages of 60 and 65 and they
would not wish to retire from industry
to receive £1 a week.
Now we come to the other classes of
pensions. If the age limit for insurance
pensions were reduced to 60 it is
estimated that the number of new
pensions granted would be in the
neighbourhood of 22,000. These are
included in the Estimate of 40,000 which
I have mentioned for contributory and
non-contributory pensions. Of this figure,
7,000 would represent women pensioners
whose title derived from their husbands'
insurance, SO that the 22,000 would
actually represent not more than 15,000
in the industrial field. There are about
3,500 persons unemployed in the age
group 60 to 64, and as it would
presumably be made a condition that
pension and unemployment benefit could
not be drawn at the same time, the benefit
and assistance at present received by
persons in this group would be saved, the
estimated total being £180,000 per
annum.
Of the 11,500 persons at present in
employment, who would qualify for contributory pensions under the proposals,

Mr. BAILEY: I congratulate the
right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of
Labour, and the Parliamentary Secretary not only on the way they have
framed the Bill, but on the way it has
been presented before the House. I can
assure them it will be well received in
the Division I represent. The factories
around Banbridge I claim are amongst
the best linen factories in the world.
They have always been careful of their
employees, both as regards health and
accidents. Speaking at a meeting some
time ago I suggested that when this
Factory Bill would become law they
would not have to make a six o'clock
start as they could be asked to do as
the law stands. I was subject to a good
deal of criticism both by employers and
employees at the time. They both agreed
that the six o'clock start had not been
in operation since 1912 in these districts.
I knew that perfectly well and also that
this Bill applies to other parts of Northern Ireland, but the people who offered
that criticism forgot the fact that, may
be, there were other factories in Northern Ireland not so kind to the workers
as they were in Banbridge and district.
I also welcome the amalgamation of
the laws relating to factories and workshops as a step in the right direction.
But I would like to see the Bill go still
further. I wish to refer to Clause 108,
Part 7, with regard to institutions. The
Minister of Labour did not deal with this
Clause when presenting the Bill to the
House, and I would like to hear more
about it, as there are many institutions
where work is being carried on in competition with factories, workshops and
laundries which are complying with the
Act and which will have to comply with
the new Act in future. These institutions, and there are many of them, are
making, altering, repairing, ornamenting, and not only adapting goods for
sale, but are selling them cheaper than
other factories which have to comply.
These places have no wages to pay nor
hours to keep, and certainly no holidays.
The hon. Member for Woodvale has
referred to some women who made outsize shirts being put out of business
owing to the number of officials and inspectors who visited her. This may be
all right or it may be all wrong, but I.
would ask the Ministry of Labour to
send some of these inspectors to the
institutions which I am going to refer
to, to examine the inmates not only in
the presence of the managers of the
institutions, as it says in this Clause, but
also privately and personally. I am referring to convents where labour without
wages is being carried on in competition
with other factories that have to pay
wages, and I want an undertaking from
the Ministry of Labour that these places
in future will be made to comply with
the Factory Act. I also hold that the
present Clause which we have in the
latter part of 108 will not be complied
with by them.

Northern

Factories Bill-
Second Reading
19 OCTOBER 1938
I am
a little surprised at the hon.
Member for Pottinger asking "What is
new in the Bill? There is quite a lot
of new things in it. I am informed that
the right hon. Gentleman who is now
Minister of Finance, when introducing
legislation, adopted the procedure of letting Members of the House get a
memorandum explanatory of what the
Bill really stood for. That procedure has
been followed in connection with this Bill.
For the convenience of the Member for
Pottinger I will read over one or two
of the outstanding new items which the
Bill contains. He will appreciate that I
am not trying to be comprehensive now,
but just having a shot at forestalling
history-if I may say so-and trying to
visualise what future generations will
remember about the 1938 Factories Act.
It was the Act, people will say, that
first laid down requirements, hitherto unmentioned in the Statute Book, for the
proper lighting of work places. It was
the Act that saw an entirely new principle
laid down, the principle of placing the
onus on the seller of a new machine to
provide certain safety requirements. It
was in 1938, people will say, that the
great advance was made in industrial
welfare, when drinking water and washing facilities, first-aid and sitting accommodation-the ordinary amenities of
civilised life-took their place in the permanent social code. This year will be
remembered, I hope, as the year in which
clearly defined and acknowledged normal
working hours were established; a normal
week of 48 hours, a normal day of nine
hours, and a one o'clock finish on Saturday became the minimum standards of
industry in Northern Ireland, below
which it was illegal to drop, and up from
which many good firms progressed. It
was in 1938 that control was first
exercised over the hours of work of young
persons in "unregulated" occupations,
messengers and van boys.
It is not in any way a revolutionary
piece of legislation. It is, however, a
progressive Bill, and it is my firm conviction that it will prove a practical
working Measure. In it, be it clearly
understood, the Government are striving
to establish a minimum standard, not an
ideal State.
The hon. Member for Windsor, whom I
congratulate on his maiden speech, said
the Bill had his approval, but he would like
to see uniformity of wages. I am entirely
at one with him on that point, and anything that can be done to assist him in
the matter will have my wholehearted
support, but, unfortunately, within the
confines of this Bill I am not able to help
him in that particular matter. I would
remind him that the Factory Acts never
attempted to regulate wages; they have
always been confined to conditions of
labour and have left wages to wages
boards, trade boards and the like.
The hon. Member for South Armagh
was very half-hearted in his congratulations on the Bill. He started off by saying that it had its good points and spoiled
the effect of his remarks by saying that
it had its bad points. He said child
labour should be abolished. I think he
will agree that this Bill goes a long way
at any rate to make child labour a more
humane matter than it has been in the
past, and we are moving in the right
direction. I suppose he has hopes, and
I share in them, that we will live to
see the day when child labour will be
abolished in the country altogether.
The next point is one that the hon.
Member for Pottinger and other Members raised, that was the abolition of
overtime. This is a point that I think
probably the hon. Member for Pottinger
and I know more about than most other
Members. If he and I were talking outside this House we would agree that the
obstacles in the way of the abolition of
overtime are not just as easy to get over
as he mentions. In the first place, I am
convinced that no employer will have any
unnecessary overtime, because the fact
remains that he will have to pay an
increased rate for that overtime, either
time and a quarter or time and a half.
I think the hon. Member for Pottinger
would privately agree with me that the
villains of the piece in regard to overtime are not in many cases the employers
but the workmen. I myself have had the
painful experience of dealing with members of trade unions who were trying to
solve this question of the abolition of
overtime.
We know that inside our own ranks
there are men who are so fond of money
that they would sleep in the shipyard
and other places if they got an opportunity. They have no thought or care for
their more unfortunate brethren who
cannot get employment. No matter
Factories Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
what regulations trade unions or anybody else try to bring into operation the
greatest obstacle to the abolition of overtime is the workers themselves. No
matter how we legislate we cannot overcome that difficulty, and the only satisfaction we can get in connection with
this Bill, if there is any satisfaction, is
to make the working of overtime as
costly as possible. Then the employers
will not have any unnecessary work of
that description.
The question of medical examination
was raised by the hon. Member for
South Armagh (Mr. Agnew). I would
remind him that Clause 103 provides
that a young person under 16 must be
medically examined and certified fit
before he or she is allowed to be employed in a factory; and I might add
that last year about one hundred
children were rejected by the certifying
surgeons, some for medical reasons, some
for legal and other reasons. The hon.
Member for South Armagh also referred
to the question of malnutrition. Unfortunately in this Bill we are not
legislating for anything in that line.
All we are trying to do is to carry out
legislation similar to that passed across
the Channel.
The hon. Member then mentioned the

this work. I know the hon. Member is
very interested in the people in his district and I would suggest to him that he
should approach the local authorities on
this matter. After all, it is in their

men engaged in this dangerous work.

necessary.

women
after childbirth so that they

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In introducing
the Second Reading of this Bill
relating to Air Raid Precautions
may I say, and it is perhaps a commonplace remark but its truth is very
important, that the carrying into effect
of the provisions of this Measure cannot
stop an air raid, but it can prevent
the consequences of a raid from spreading and doing infinite damage. If there
is a fire in a theatre and everybody loses
his head a catastrophe may result, but
the presence of even a few persons in
the audience who, by reason of previous
training and experience, know what to
do will, in most cases, be sufficient to
avert panic and enable the building to
be cleared in an orderly and safe way.
This analogy underlies the whole principle of air raid precautions organisation.
Those who have studied the provisions
of this Bill and who have been interested
in the working of precautions in Great
Britain will have noted that one of its
basic
is
principles
the voluntary
character of its provisions. It is, in
fact, the duty and responsibility of
every citizen to take his own share in
ensuring his safety and that of his
neighbour. It is, therefore, fitting that
the duty of preparing air raid precaution schemes should be placed upon the
local authorities, who are best able to
give effect to the wishes of the inhabitants of their respective areas and who
are obviously in a position to adapt their
schemes of precaution to meet the
requirements of their area in the way
best suited to local conditions.
Of course I fully realise that all local
authorities will not have the same
Air Raid Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
problems. The precautions to be taken
by the county borough of Belfast can
have little similarity to those taken in
some remote rural area, and the Bill
makes ample provision for the schemes.
of various authorities differentiating in
this manner.
The decision to organise these precautions on a voluntary basis was also
deliberate. It must be part of the policy
of all free and democratically governed
countries to show that they are capable
of organising themselves by free methods
and of displaying a sense of responsibility, which will produce results at
least as good as those in countries where
greater authority and more severe restrictions are exercised, over the lives of
the people.
I have now explained that all air raid
precautions are, in the first place, voluntary, and, secondly, carried out by local
authorities. It is a commonplace historical experience that administration by
local authorities in this country often
begins rather slowly but steadily gathers
momentum, and it has rarely failed in
making a job of anything it has set out
to do. I have no doubt that we in
Northern Ireland will take advantage of
the provisions contained in this Bill and
make a success of our air raid precautions.
Many handbooks and memoranda have
been published in Great Britain on the
various aspects which the precautions
may take, such as, the preparation of
schemes, the
the reinforcement of firefighting services both in boroughs and
urban and rural areas, the establishment
of first-aid posts, the decontamination of
personnel and property which may have.
become impregnated by gas, and the
treatment of casualties. Similarly,
handbooks have been issued to assist
employers of industry in taking precautions for the safety of their staff; to
help public utilities, such as, harbour
boards, gas undertakings, et cetera; and
lastly, and perhaps the most important of
all, to advise the ordinary man what steps
he make take in his own house to safeguard his family. Many of these publications have been circulated already, but
they may nearly all be obtained from the
Stationary Office and I commend the
very helpful advice which they give to
local authorities and undertakings who
have to consider the various matters to
which I have referred.
In time of emergency the defence
forces of the country-the Navy, Army
and Air Force-are engaged in their
own specific tasks and the police force is
clearly inadequate to deal with all that
might happen under air attack, and so it
becomes necessary to raise a volunteer
defence force which would take on the
major task of helping the civil population if they were subject to air attack.
The foundation of the precautions
scheme is, therefore, the enrolment and
training of this civilian defence force.
Undoubtedly, other parts of the scheme,
such as shelters, et cetera, are important,
but development of them is not a substitute for the organisation
the organisation of the
civilian defence force. One hears criticism-I have heard it myself that we
in Northern Ireland are comparatively
safe from attack from the air, but I must
say at once that in my view this is both
a misleading and dangerous statement.
Geographically we more happily
situated than England or Scotland in respect of a European enemy, but with the
ever-increasing range and speed of aircraft
I can say quite definitely, and I have been
advised by experts to this effect, that
attacks on our territory are very far
from being out of the bounds of possibility, and it behoves us, therefore, to
take this problem-one which, unfortunately, I fear has come to stayseriously.

No doubt the first objective of a hos
tile air attack would be places of naval
or military importance, but there is

on business or industrial centres.
this disorganisation panic might well
result, leading to a sapping of the morale.
of the country, and a breakdown which

organised.
It is sometimes said that far too much
attention is being paid to anti-gas
measures and not sufficient to the other
two forms of aerial attack-that of high
explosives or incendiary bombs. All I
can say is that against the latter forms
of attack every precaution that can be

taken should and will be taken, but we

What is to be done as to the recruiting
of this civilian personnel? In the first
place, I am glad to say that during the
past eighteen months many thousands of
people have attended the admirable

of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem
and the British Red Cross Society at
centres in Northern Ireland. Then
again, many, including doctors and professional men, have attended an intensive course arranged by the Order of St.
John in London. Certain officials of
local authorities have, under an arrangement with my Ministry, been able to
attend a course at the Government Anti-
Gas School in England, and these men
in turn have, on their return, formed
and trained classes. Within the past
few weeks my Ministry arranged a week's
course of instruction in order to train
civilians and thus decentralise local
instruction, and I am glad to say that
the interest which was shown in this
course was evidenced by the high percentage of marks obtained by the great
majority of those who were present.
Many of those who attended this last
course came from local authorities, and it
is to them now that the local authorities
must look for guidance and help in formulating their schemes.
Respirators have now arrived sufficient
to meet the needs of the city of Belfast,
and I believe it will not be long before
further consignments come along, and
these will be distributed first to local
authorities in the more vulnerable parts
of Northern Ireland. I anticipate that
within a comparatively short time we
will have in Northern Ireland respirators
for every member of the civil population.
A system of warning for Northern
Ireland of approaching raids is being
organised by my Ministry in conjunction
with the authorities in Great Britain,
and here again we may perhaps be in
better position owing to our geographical situation resulting in a slightly
longer period of time between the warning and any attack which may follow
in which to get the air raid precautions
personnel into action.
May I now say a word to local authorities who are faced with the formation of
schemes a task very far from their
ordinary duties of local government but
one which I can count on their fulfilling,
as they do all their other duties to the
public.
In the case of the more vulnerable
parts of Northern Ireland a comprehensive and full scheme dealing with the
various aspects of air raid precautions
will be necessary, but I want to say at
once that I don't expect any elaborate
arrangements to be made in outlying
urban or rural areas. The latter will
have three main provisions to incorporate in their schemes. First, to
arrange storage accommodation for the
stock of respirators which they will be
sent without cost by my Department.
Respirators have to be stored in a proper
manner, otherwise the rubber perishes.
I am prepared sympathetically to consider any proposals which adjoining
authorities may agree upon to have a
joint storage for the respirators of such
authorities. Secondly, the duty of providing first-aid posts. These could conveniently be set up with little cost at
dispensaries, or perhaps schools could be
earmarked for this purpose. The medical requirements of such posts will again
be provided without cost by my Department. And,
And, thirdly, local auhorities
must ensure that there is within a
reasonable distance some efficient firefighting appartus, on the services of
which they may call.
It is only appropriate that I should.
mention here that many local authorities
have already prepared draft schemes and
have shown that they do not take a
light view of this problem, but realise
their duty to the members of the community in their area. Local authorities
must bear in mind that in an emergency
many of those now living in their midst
will join the Services or may perhaps be
engaged in munition works or in shipyards in areas far more vulnerable and
liable to attack than those in which they
reside. Is it not only right and proper
that these men and women should have
received the benefit of instruction as to the
wearing and maintenance of respirators

In connection with the medical

Northern Ireland. This Association has

medical practitioners who are willing to
offer their services in an emergency. I believe that by utilising the services of
the small Emergency Committee of the

I should like to add that the air raid

suggestions would be found most useful.
May I now say a few words on the
financial aspect of this question. Respirators, sand-bags, protective clothing, and
medical requirements will be provided by
my Department without cost to local
authorities. The Government will give a
grant as set out in the Bill, that is, 70
per cent. in the case of the city of Belfast,
and 75 per cent. elsewhere, in aid of the
cost of any expenditure undertaken by
local authorities in connection with a
scheme of precautions previously
approved by my Ministry. This follows
strictly on the financial lines of the
English Act, and the percentage calculation is based on exactly similar considerations. Should, however, it be found
necessary for a local authority to incur
expenditure which, after payment of the
grant to which I have referred, involves
the raising of a penny rate, then any expenditure beyond this amount will earn
a grant at a rate of 85 per cent. I think
it will, therefore, be obvious to everyone in Northern Ireland from what I
have said that these precautions which I
am now urging should be taken will not
involve anything but a minute increase in
the rates.

that this room, which it is intended

Much has been written and spoken in
recent times on air raid precautions in
Great Britain, and I am sure that everyone must realise that every country in
Europe is dealing with this situation in
its Own way. We in the United
Kingdom believe that the voluntary
system is the best, and that this duty will
be efficiently carried out by local authorities. We in Northern Ireland are considerably behind-hand in taking precautions against air attack, but recent events
have brought home to every one of us, I
think, how swiftly a danger may come
upon us and how necessary it is for us
to have our arrangements made in
advance. I do, therefore, most seriously
urge local authorities to draw up their
schemes now so that standing arrangements may be made for the safety of
persons and property in their respective
areas.
Lastly, I would urge on the public
generally that it is their essential duty to
come forward, be enrolled and trained by
the local authorities, and if this is done,
not only will each member of the air raid
precautions force learn his own contribu
tion to the whole scheme, but the public
will recognise what has been steadily
created in their midst-a civilian defence
force for their own protection. It may
be necessary to introduce certain Amendments in the Committee stage, following
the discussions that are still going on in
Great Britain. Therefore, the Government would be very glad to consider any
suggestions which would make this
Measure more secure. This is in no way
a political Measure, and I hope that I
can count on the House helping to make
it as good as possible. I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: The Minister of Home
Affairs has outlined the precautionary

Counties. I thought his opening remarks

I hope before I have finished to give him
some home truths in regard to the saving
of life in Northern Ireland. In the year
1937 I belonged to the working-class
movement. We in our day thought that
the authorities were carrying out a protective measure capable of saving the lives
of the working-class people. We decided

air attacks, and I am satisfied in my

measures which this Bill is attempting to
put into operation. I use the word
attempting, because this Bill is only an

take place in this part of the world.
This scheme, I believe, points the way
to a system of A.R.P. which literally may
save thousands of lives in Belfast. While
it does not claim to be a fully detailed
report, it lays the foundation for security,
and consequently must be accepted as a

Belfast, because it is the dangers that
Belfast will be exposed to that we have
deliberately set ourselves out to deal with.
The nature of the dangers has been
described by the right hon. Gentleman.
What is the nature of the dangers with
which we will have to contend? High
explosive bombs. Although the official
Government plans have paid but scant
attention to the menace of high explosives,
there is little doubt that this is the
gravest menace we have to face.
The chief effects of high explosive
bombs are: Penetration, the ability of
the bomb to penetrate downwards due to
its weight and explosive powers. It is
obvious that an exploding bomb can
create destruction, due to shock, at a
lower depth than that to which it penetrates. The British Government do not
appear to have compiled any data regarding the penetrative powers of different
weights of bombs, but the following
figures compiled by the French Ministry
of the Interior agree with those of other
foreign countries, for example, the Swiss
Federal Commission on A.R.P.

working-class movement, myself included,
with a view to getting the authorities to

attacks; cwt. bombs require 10 inches

earth. The next danger is from splinters.
When a bomb casing bursts the scattered
fragments cause destruction over a wide
area. In Spain, people have been killed
by splinters 400 yards away from the
actual explosion. The British Government recommends the following thicknesses for protection from splinters from
a 500lb. bomb at 50 feet: -Stock brick,
13 inches solid; mass concrete, 12 inches;
reinforced concrete, 10 inches, and earth
2 feet 6 inches. The next point is blast.
This is the result of the actual explosive
power of the bomb and is the most
destructive effect of all. In Spain a
650lb. bomb has demolished a building
with a frontage of 200 feet, while in the
crowded districts of Belfast, such as Dock
Ward and Ballymacarrett, a whole street
of our miserably constructed houses might
well be reduced to ruins. Windows
would be smashed over a still wider area.
I now come to incendiary bombs.
These will ignite any inflammable material
with which they come in contact and
generate so much heat that they will
burn through most metals. As these
bombs weigh but two or three pounds
each, one aeroplane is quite capable of
starting two or three hundred fires inside
a very few minutes.

may be divided into three categories.
I need not define them, but there are

I now want to analyse the proposals

House to understand that the Air Raid
Precautions Bill is free and unfettered
and has no political taint. It is for

to take any political kudos for the Party
I represent.
In Belfast we are offered only one
form of protection against high explosives, namely, trenches. These should
be about seven feet deep and it will
usually be necessary to brace the walls
with wooden props or corrugated iron.
In addition, they should be covered with
corrugated iron or other suitable
material and a three foot layer of
earth. Where possible they should be
30 or 40 feet from the nearest building.
No one, however, can claim that these
trenches would offer protection against
anything but splinters. In the event of
a direct hit, everyone in that section of
the trench would be blown to pieces and a
bomb falling up to 150 feet away would
probably bury the occupants alive. In
addition, it is very obvious that the districts most needing protection are the
very districts where no trenches could be
built. The densely populated areas
along the river banks and near the
centre of the town have no free space for
trenching. Dock Ward, which is one of
the districts most liable to attack, has

On the other hand the Government
advises us on the merits of "dispersal";
that means we are to sit in our own homes
until the raid is over. They argue that
concentrating people together will mean
a higher number killed than if they are
scattered over the district. It is quite
true that if a bomb falls in the middle
of a crowd of people many will be killed,
but the Government apparently fails to
realise that if people are crowded
together at one spot they will avoid
bombs falling elsewhere in that area.
Professor J. B. S. Haldane, who has
done extensive work in the theory of
probability, explodes this fallacy in his
book "A.R.P." In a dangerous area
it does not matter whether we "disperse" or stay together; we enjoy the
same chances of being killed.
Our houses afford virtually no protection against high explosives. From
the figures which we have quoted it is
obvious that not one working class house
in one hundred has a wall sufficiently
thick to keep out even a splinter, while
houses which are almost falling down of
their own accord would collapse like a
pack of cards if a bomb burst anywhere
near.
The Lord Mayor of Barcelona
probably has more first-hand knowledge
of air attacks than anyone living. He
says:
Instead of the small gas and incendiary bombs, for which officials are
trying to prepare the British public,
the real danger in Barcelona, just as
it would be here, came from large
high explosive bombs. The only way
to provide anything like adequate
protection is to build enough underground shelters to house the majority
of the population. These must be
deep and soundly built. Cellars
under houses are no use at all.
If we leave this matter to the local
authorities-we have had experience
during the past eight months-we will
have no shelters at all. Major Eastwood, Belfast's A.R.P. Officer, told a
Press Reporter that:
No bomb proof shelters are to be
built in Belfast, primarily on account
of expense. It is possible that
trenches would be made in public
parks, private grounds, gardens, etc.
This method of protection will probably be adopted at the Queen's
Island and other big industrial concerns where ground is available.
That paragraph appeared in the "Belfast
News-Letter" of the 17th August, 1938.
Apart from the fact that trenches would
be death traps in the face of an attack,
such as the Island and aircraft factory
may be expected to receive, Major Eastwood does not tell us what is to be done
for the women and children of York
Street, where no ground is available.
He tells us that it is normally impracticable to provide effective protection against high explosives, and,
consequently, proposes to concentrate on
"protection against blast, splinters and
gas." How he proposes to prevent a
building being demolished by blast we
will be eager to learn. Also we are not
clear as to what he means by "normally
impracticable." We are glad that he
did not say impossible because the Lord
Mayor of Barcelona could prove him
wrong on that point. From all this it
emerges that Belfast will not receive
protection from its greatest danger,
namely, high explosives.
I now come to incendiary bombs.
These constitute a danger to property,
but very little danger to life, except, of
course, in the resulting fires. The
official plan for coping with these bombs.
is to buy a bucket and a shovel with a
long handle, together with a small hand
pump to prevent the house being burned
down. This method has not been tested
under conditions such as would exist in
an air raid. At A.R.P. exhibitions,
for example, the demonstrator has his
shovel ready before the bomb bursts and
has little trouble in lifting it into the
bucket and smothering it with sand. In
practice it will probably be found that
by the time the father of the house
reaches the bomb-he may have to look
for it first if it has passed through
several stories-a fire is likely to be
raging in all the surrounding woodwork
and he may find difficulty in approaching the bomb itself. And then, of
course, it may be a phosphorous bomb,
which is quite unapproachable at all
times. In addition, we are asked to
buy these fire-fighting implements ourselves. It will be difficult to persuade
an unemployed man with an undernourished family to spend at least thirty
shillings on apparatus, which may, or
may not, save his landlord's property.

designed to give the people of Belfast
something to occupy their attention and
create that feeling of false security
which we so much deplore.
The Government has given us full and
detailed instructions on how to make a
room gasproof. We are to fill all chinks
in the floor, etc., with soaked newspaper.
The chimney is to be blocked and the
windows sealed. The door is to be
covered with a wet blanket and so on.
We will only make three comments on
this procedure. The first is that the
room in which this document which I
am reading from was written, like many
other working class houses in Belfast,
could not be made "gas proof" even
according to Government specifications
without complete reconstruction. The
second is that most working class homes
in Belfast cannot afford to devote a
spare room to be converted into a refuge
room. Two thousand three hundred
and four persons in Belfast live in single
room tenements with two or more persons to the room. The third point is
that since the middle of last century it
has been an acknowledged fact that
nearly three quarters of the air which
leaks into any room comes, not through
the obvious chinks in the floor, etc., but
through the actual walls and ceilings.
Regarding gas masks which the Minister
spoke of and which are to be supplied
to us, we are told by one group of
experts that they are 100 per cent.
efficient and by another that they are
worse than useless. We would like
something more than official reassurances
on this point. We ourselves have blown
cigarette smoke through a civilian gasmask, and this may indicate that the
gas-mask would be unsafe in the presence
of arsenical smoke. We have had no
opportunity of testing this mask. We
believe it would be well to have
chamber in which the public could test
them so that they may become proficient
in the handling of them. To be effective masks of the civilian type should
fit the face perfectly. We have not been
told that masks have been made to fit
facial deformities. Young people and
children cannot wear ordinary respirators. No masks for babies are supplied
although we have heard of masks for
horses, dogs and cattle.
a
Much that has been written makes
very depressing reading, but here we
offer constructive suggestions for the protection of the people of Belfast. We do
not suggest that the scheme we outline is
in any way complete. In fact there are
many important omissions, particularly
in regard to the staffing and organising
of the necessary services. But we believe
that it lays the basis of a plan of A.R.P.
which would not only allay tendencies to
panic among the civil population, but
would serve the much more important
function of saving valuable lives that
may otherwise be lost. No organised
schemes for transferring sections of the
population out of the danger zone appear
to have been considered by the A.R.P.
authorities. We have already emphasised
the danger of air raid attack in congested districts. The presence of women
and children in time of war would mean
unnecessary danger both to themselves
and to those whose duty it would be to
look after them. We consequently propose that arrangements should be made
for two stage evacuation, the first stage
to be carried out on the outbreak of war
and the second stage if a succession of
raids is expected. In the light of present
knowledge final stage or complete
evacuation of the city should not prove
necessary, but the question should be
kept in mind as it is possible that our
essential services might become so disorganised as to render occupation of the
city impossible.
For the purposes of evacuation we
have divided Belfast into two zones which
are clearly defined on the map at the
end, which I will give to the Ministry
of Home Affairs. Zone 1 consists of all
districts within a 7,000 foot radius of
Queen's Bridge, together with certain
districts outside this radius, namely, all
Victoria Ward and that portion of
Duncairn Ward south of Fortwilliam
Park.
Zone 2 would be all other districts inside the
the city boundary. In
arriving at this definition we have largely
been led by consideration of proximity
to legitimate military objectives and of
population density. We would point out
at this stage, however, that in modern
warfare a very good case has been made
out for regarding ordinary residential
districts as military objectives, and the
bombing of such districts has been a
noticeable and lamentable feature of warfare in Spain and China.

Inside Zone 1 we find four entire
wards, Dock, Court, Smithfield and St.
George's, which are the most densely
populated wards in the city, ranging
from 95.5 to 165.4 persons to the acre.
It also includes the most densely populated portions of every other ward in
the city and such obvious military
objectives as the harbour and docks, the
shipyards, the aircraft factory, three
railway termini, military barracks, power
station, gas works, etc. The presence of
the aircraft factory renders most of
Victoria Ward and Pottinger Ward
dangerous in time of war, while the
eastern portion of the ward adjoins the
Parliament House, which is likely to be
attacked if only for the moral effect
which would
be produced by its
destruction. We do not believe that we
are exaggerating the gravity of the
position when the area we have
delineated contains so many objects liable
to attack.
By laying emphasis on the danger to
inhabitants of Zone 1 we do not suggest
that the rest of the city is safe from
attack. Many densely populated districts lie outside this area, and those
adjoining railway lines must consider the
possibility of heavy bombardment. We
would suggest as first stage evacuation on
the outbreak of hostilities that all inmates of hospitals and nursing homes,
institutions, etc., should be evacuated,
together with the following classes:-
Compulsory evacuation, first, of all
school children between the ages of 5 and
15 from Zone 1. There would probably
be 56,000. Then, second, teachers to
look after them, totalling about 3,000,
and, third, invalids, blind persons, etc.,
from Zone 1, about 5,000. Then, voluntary evacuation, of all persons over 70
years of age, together with their
wives or husbands where these
below that age, say about 5,000; nursing and expectant mothers, 2,000;
children under 5 years from Zone 1, say,
10,000; and those in Zone 2 listed as
compulsory, 18,000. The total evacuated
at the first stage would be 99,000.

It is obvious that evacuation on this
scale cannot be carried out in a haphazard manner. A Home Office publication "The Protection of your Home
against Air Raids," states: "If you live
in a large town think whether you can
make arrangements for your children,
invalids and elderly persons and pets to
be sent away the moment danger
threatens, so that they may be in a place
of greater safety." It will be noticed
that the pets of those who can make
arrangements, in other words, those who
have money, will receive greater consideration than the children whose
parents have not got the money. This is
not our idea of evacuation. Neither do
we believe in an indiscriminate flight
from Belfast of those who can make
arrangements. Our organisation must
be carefully planned in advance so as
to ensure that panic-stricken mobs
streaming along the roads leading to the
country will not interfere with our
normal social and defence services. We
realise that it is concentration of people
under these circumstances of disorganisation and panic that offer the most perfect target for attacking air planes
Under conditions such as this machinegun fire could be used with deadly effect,
as, indeed, it has been in Spain.
must decide in advance not only where
the sections of the population will be
evacuated, but also the means by which

We propose that all inmates of hospitals, together with those who will
attend to them, be evacuated to inland
country, hotels where possible. Dangerously ill patients, however, will require
special facilities, which will only be
available in already existing hospitals.
Special arrangements will be necessary
for these, together with those who are
so ill that they cannot be moved in
safety. School children will be billeted
in large country houses. This proposal
is likely to cause dismay to the owners of
such property, but our A.R.P. authorities will have to decide whether the
safeguarding of the lives of thousands of
workers' children is more important than
avoiding inconveniencing the owners of
large country houses.
As far as possible we would aim at small colonies,
rather than the large encampments which
are sometimes suggested. Using existing
property will be more economical and
will be less likely to draw attack from
the air. The remaining classes will be
lodged in other country houses. There
are few farmhouses, for example, which
could not find accommodation for three
or four persons.
We realise that this proposal will
necessitate much immediate investigation

Certain districts in
Down and Antrim would need to be

Evacuation is to be carried out by Corporation buses and Transport Board
buses and lorries. Private lorries and

the various railways be approached

be able to handle in a given time. If
a succession of raids is expected we propose that the following classes
evacuated: All remaining children, old

All remaining children under 5 years of

Evacuation on this scale will offer
certain difficulties regarding accommodation. To overcome this we suggest that
immediately first stage evacuation takes
place those so evacuated will gradually be
transferred to other districts in the Six
Counties, leaving the Counties of Down
and Antrim in a position to receive those
evacuated at the second stage. Churches
and public halls will also be available.
With the exception of our larger seaports little evacuation will be necessary
from other towns in Northern Ireland,
and so there is little danger of our plans
clashing with those of other districts.
Certain modifications of our existing
social services will be necessary to cope
with an influx into otherwise sparsely
populated districts, but at the moment
we are not in a position to deal with this.
Detailed plans have been worked out for
the evacuation of Paris and we believe
that tickets have already been printed
giving the routes and destinations of
those concerned. We suggest that
Belfast's A.R.P. authorities investigate
these arrangements, which would act as
a guide for the steps which require to
be taken here and which prove conclusively that evacuation of most of the
population of Belfast is a feasible,
practicable and urgently necessary procedure.
Having evacuated approximately 99,000
at the first stage, there remains in the
city 339,000 persons. Of these 129,000
will be evacuated in the second stage,
leaving 210,000. We consequently propose that work be commenced immediately on the construction of bomb proof
shelters to accommodate 210,000 and
trenches for 129,000. These shelters and
trenches would be distributed throughout the city in relation to the figures
which we have already set out for the various classes and the two zones. In addition,
shelters will be necessary in all factories
and business premises and in the shopping centres for those who are too far
from home to reach their local shelter
inside the twenty minutes' warning
which we may expect to receive.
cost of shelters for employees will be
borne by employers of labour and be a
first charge on their profits. Legislation may be introduced to provide for
the granting of loans to those employers
who can prove they are not in a position
to safeguard the lives of their workers.
I know that will be an important factor
in the carrying out of this scheme, but,
nevertheless, money is of no value where
life is concerned.

We have already pointed out that the
present emphasis on precautions against
gas attacks and incendiary bombs tend to
distract attention from the more important dangers. It is important, however,
that adequate steps be taken to protect
the population from the effects of these
menaces. Protection against the effects
of gas would be automatically afforded by
the provision of underground shelters.
We believe, for reasons which already
have been advanced, that the safeguarding of property against fire on the basis.
of each tenant acting as his own fireman
is doomed to failure. The responsibility
of dealing with outbreaks of fire will
naturally fall on the existing fire-fighting
service. In the event of war our present
service will be found to be completely
inadequate to deal with the number of
fires which even one airplane may be expected to set alight. A considerable
increase in the staff and equipment of our
existing fire brigade will be necessary,
together with additional depots scattered
throughout the city.
be
In the event of a raid contact will have
to be maintained without interruption,
and for this purpose the ordinary telephone service is likely to prove unsatisfactory. It is extremely likely that
telephone wires and cables will
damaged and it is essential that a system
of short wave wireless be installed to keep
in touch with the various districts. Steps
will also have to be taken to ensure that
private calls do not interfere with
essential A.R.P. communication on the
telephone circuits. Sirens must be
liberally dispersed throughout the city to
give warning of approaching airplanes
and ensure that civilians have adequate
time to proceed to their shelters. Provision must be made for the positioning
of anti-aircraft guns, especially on the
hills surrounding Belfast.
While not attempting in this short
memorandum to deal with the organisation of the various departments and
warden areas, I wish to offer a few comments. As to wardens, the Government
handbook states that "a warden should be
a responsible member of the public,
chosen to be a leader and adviser in a
small area in which he is known and
respected." There is only one way to
ensure that a warden is respected by
those for whose safety he is responsible,
and it is that he should be elected by
the people. Any "approval" or "recommendation" of wardens by the Government or police authorities is an infringe-

Now we come to the question of finance,
and I know in that respect I will shock
the susceptibilities of Members. I estimate that Belfast can be adequately protected from an attack for £5,593,000.
Individual items are detailed in a statement which follows. We realise that this
is a considerable sum of money, but point
out that this is capital expenditure and
not a recurring liability. I estimate that
for a sum of approximately £15,000 per
annum it should be possible to maintain
this organisation at a high level of
efficiency. This sum could be provided
by the Belfast Corporation without hardship on the taxpayers, but it is obvious
that the capital cost cannot be met by the
citizens of Belfast in the ordinary
manner. I propose, therefore, that the
Corporation should press for the entire
expenses of Belfast's necessary protection from the Government. This could
easily be raised by taxing the rich, who
are at the present time reaping large
profits from the armament industry. An
alternative is that the Corporation should
seek powers from the Government to
levy a municipal income tax on incomes
exceeding £350 a year. Assuming that
similar protection were given to all other
comparable towns in the British Isles,
I estimate that the cost of the complete
scheme would be in the region of £10 per
head of the entire population. To those
who complain that this is an impossibly
high figure I would point out that the
cost of the Government rearmament programme will certainly run to a minimum
figure of £40 per head. To this argument there can be no answer. If
£2,000,000,000 can be found for the
destruction of human lives then quarter
of this sum should be immediately forthcoming for the saving of lives. It can
be done. It is the duty of the people of
Belfast to see that it is done.

We believe that that charge is too
heavy for the local authorities ever to
attempt to carry out. We believe that
they will evade their responsibilities

Mr. MacDERMOTT: I am sure the
prayer and hope of us all is that the day
will never dawn when the Bill now before
the House will be of any practical use,
but while that is so and while our situation here is, perhaps, one of the most
favourable in the United Kingdom, we
must none the less treat this subject with
seriousness. We do not know what a day

may bring forth, and we must all realise
that here, very near us, we have the
nerve centre of the whole of Northern
Ireland. Within a square mile we have
the power station, which supplies light
and power to a large part of Northern

To any person who has seen the effect
of bombardment or has witnessed a civil
population in flight, it is obvious that this
House will not be doing its duty unless
we forge this Bill into an instrument as
perfect as we can make it to meet the
menace of air raids when they may come

here as a bogey or to say anything that
would engender panic about them, but
while that is so the matter is one that
must be faced by every Member of the
House quite apart from any consideration of party or party politics. This was
stressed by the Minister, and it also was
stressed by the hon. Member for Pottinger
in his opening remarks. While I do not
intend to touch on anything controversial,
I think I am entitled, after listening to
this memorandum, to say that having
declared that this was a non-party subject it is strange that he should inflict on
this House a long memorandum which has
"party" written all over it.
This Bill, in my submission, is a very
imperfect instrument to accomplish what
it sets out to do. I say that not in a
spirit of captious criticism, but because
having considered the Bill to the best of
my ability I think the House would be
ill-advised to pass it in its present form.
It may depend on the provisions of this
Measure whether the people of Northern
Ireland will remain safe or not, and so
this is not the time to shirk criticism
which seems to be well founded.
The criticism I first offer about this
Bill is that it places the whole burden
of air raid precautions upon the local
authorities, excluding the county councils.
I understand the exclusion of the county
councils is on account of experience
gained in England. Excluding the
county councils, under this Bill the
administration of air raid precautions will
be placed in the hands of a multitude
of local bodies-rural district councils,
urban councils, boroughs, and county
boroughs. It is right that those authorities should take their part in dealing
with a matter such as air raids, but when
it is considered that this Bill is aimed
to meet what is nothing less than a
national emergency and the result of war,
one begins to doubt whether there is any
excuse whatsoever for attempting to put
the necessary powers in the hands of local
authorities.
When one considers that the very
nature of an air raid will demand not
only adequate preparation and adequate
anti-aircraft defence, but the necessary
amount of executive authority-in other
words, police arrangements-then
seems to me there can be no excuse for
leaving the administration of the Act in
the hands of local authorities who, in the
ordinary course, have no police authority
whatever.
it
The memorandum that has been read
and a good deal of what has been said
appear to me to bear the mark of lack
of imagination. One does not deal effectively with an air raid simply by providing shelters, or gas masks, or extra
fire engines. That is generally realised,
and the events of the last few weeks have
served to emphasise that one of the
matters which have to be dealt with
in case of an air raid is the avoidance
of panic on the part of the population.
If an emergency has to be met there has
to be preparation made not only by
accumulating the necessary materials and
by way of training people in first-aid,
and so forth, but there has to be provision made for the power to say to a
man, "You must keep clear of the
street," power to say, "You must report
to such and such a person," and power
to say that every other citizen will be a
special constable.
From the beginning to the end of this
Bill there is not a word which would
clothe the local authorities with any
power of a coercive or executive kind.
Until the danger comes it may not be
necessary to use such power, but if this
Bill is to be worth the paper it is written
on it must contain not only provisions
for precautionary measures, but it must
contain the necessary provisions so that
when the time comes, if it ever comes,
there will be sufficient authority and
Air Raid Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. MacDermott]
power in the authorities responsible to
deal with the situation that arises.
The Bill is absolutely silent on that
important matter. It is a matter which
in my submission is one for the central
Government. I almost go the length
of saying it is a matter not merely for
this Government but for the Government
of the United Kingdom, which has the
exclusive power of dealing with matters
of war and peace, and the results of war.
It is very hard to distinguish the air
raid precautions which are envisaged by
this Bill from air raid defences, and I
do think it is a matter of serious consideration as to whether representations
should not be made to the Imperial
authorities as to how far they are prepared to take steps to alleviate for the
civilian population here the effects of war.
For those reasons I would suggest that
the Bill should provide for what it is
really aiming at, that is, a state of
emergency. The central controlling
authority should be some department of
the Government. It may be said that
that would mean a host of extra officials,
but that is not necessarily the case,
because it would not follow from a central
administration that the local authorities
would have nothing to do. For instance,
it might well be that the central administration could provide more effectively for
the marshalling and training of air raid
wardens. I do not believe for
moment that under any local authority's
scheme one will find a sufficient number
of air raid wardens volunteering. Those
wardens could be given by a central
authority an executive power which they
could not be given by a local authority.
They could be made special constables.
one
It might still remain with the central
authority, if I might take an illustration, to say to the local authorities that
they have to co-operate. They could
say, for instance, to the Surveyor of the
city of Belfast, "You are in charge of
the roads. It will be for you to arrange
for decontamination. We will supply
the plant and foot the bill, but it is for
you to prepare the scheme for the carrying out of that particular work." Again,
the central authority might say to the
local authority, "It is for you to see that
new buildings erected have at least roofs
which will turn incendiary bombs."
So the work in effect would be split
between the central authority and the
local authorities, and this is the point of
my remarks, the scheme I have in mind
would ensure a central co-ordinated
authority clothed with sufficient executive
power. Again, I say that as far as I
can see there is nothing in this Bill
which gives the necessary executive
power to the authorities, and, therefore,
I cannot see that it can be an efficient
instrument to meet the dread purposes
which it is intended to meet.
There is one part of the Bill which is
urgent. It provides for the legalising of
expenditure already incurred by local
authorities during the recent crisis. I
can understand the need for passing that
into law as soon as possible, but I do
suggest most respectfully to the Minister,
who has asked for criticisms, that the rest
of the Bill might very well await the
digesting of the experience gained in
England in the last three weeks. I do
not think we would lose anything by a
little delay in this matter. It is abundantly plain that this Bill is going to be
the gateway of a great deal of expenditure out of public funds. That is my
main objection to the Bill.
There are two other matters to which
I wish to refer. One is in reference to
Clause 4, which provides for the acquisition of land by a local authority. That
is all well and good for the local authority
to have the power which is proposed
under this Bill to acquire land, but some
provision should be made for the providing of materials such as sand-bags,
timber, and so forth. The Minister has
told us that those things will be supplied
free of charge to the local authorities, but
if that is so it should be stated in the
Bill. The matter is of some importance,
because in an emergency a local authority
may have to provide itself with material
of this kind. We have seen within the
last few weeks the disgraceful situation
which arose in England where local
authorities, when buying sand-bags,
which ordinarily cost 1d, had to pay as

Adjournment
Queen's University of Belfast Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mrs. PARKER: The Bill which I
have the honour to present to the House
is being introduced by the Government
at the request of the Queen's University.
It is entirely a non-controversial Measure
and the only effect of its enactment will
be to ensure that the honorary treasurer
of the university and the secretary of the
Academic Council, if a member of that
body, shall be members of the Senate of
the University. Under the present constitution of the university it is purely a
matter of chance whether the persons
occupying these positions are or are not
members of the Senate.
The Senate is, as hon. Members are no
doubt aware, responsible for the administration of the university, and clearly it is
most important that they should have the
expert advice in their deliberations of the
honorary treasurer of the University and
of the secretary of the Academic Council.
I beg to move, "That this Bill be now
read a Second time."
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
whole House for to-morrow.

postponed.

DELAY IN ACCEPTING TENDERS.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether she is aware that the
building of new schools is being seriously
hindered through the length of time
taken to obtain sanction from the Ministry for
the acceptance of tenders;
whether it is true that on 5th May, 1938,
the Ministry was asked to approve of the
acceptance of the lowest of seven tenders
for the erection of a new school in Ballyveamore, County Down, and that the
Ministry sent no reply until 21st June,
1938, when sanction was refused ;
whether, owing mainly to the failure of
the Ministry to give a reply one way
or the other, the summer of 1938 was
lost so far as work at Ballyveamore was
concerned; whether in future steps will
be taken to see that in the case of
schemes for which plans have previously
been approved by the Ministry, requests
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Brown]
for approval of the acceptance of tenders.
are dealt with within one week of
receipt, and whether she can inform the
House why granite was not specified for
this building in the heart of that industry in Mourne.
Mrs. PARKER: The Ministry's
approval of the plans for the erection of
new schoolhouses as a rule includes
approval of the estimate submitted and
where the tender proposed for acceptance is the lowest received and is within
this approved estimate, the Ministry's
further sanction to the acceptance of the
tender is unnecessary. Where, however, the tender exceeds the approved
estimate the Ministry is again consulted,
and its approval or otherwise to the
acceptance of the tender can only be
given after full consideration has been
given to the case, for which, of course,
reasonable time must be allowed.
With regard to the second part of the
question, the facts as regards the Ballyveamore school are as stated. In this case
however, the lowest tender exceeded the
approved estimate by nearly 50 per cent.
and the Ministry declined to sanction the
acceptance of the tender. Following on
conferences which then took place between the committee's architect and the
Ministry's advisers, at which careful and
exhaustive examination of the plans
in conjunction with the Bill of
Quantities was made, it was eventually found possible to effect savings
in the scheme to the extent of
nearly £600 and the Ministry's approval
of the reduced tender was given on 18th
August. Having regard to this saving
of £600 to public funds, the Ministry
cannot agree that the time spent on the
consideration of this matter either constitutes delay or is a cause for dissatisfaction.
In reply to the third part of the
question, the Ministry has no information as to the date on which work on
the
new school at Ballyveamore was
begun, but it is understood that the
building is already well on the way
towards completion.
The Ministry cannot give the undertaking sought in the fourth part of the
question. As already pointed out, if the
tender proposed for acceptance is the
lowest, the Ministry's sanction is necessary only in cases where the tender exceeds the approved estimate, and in such
cases the Ministry and its advisers must
be allowed reasonable time to examine
the details of the tender, if due regard
is to be had to the exercise of economy
in the expenditure of public funds. The
Ministry will, however, continue to make
every effort to avoid delay in dealing
with these cases.
In reply to the last part of the
question, the Ministry is not aware why
granite was not specified for the Ballyveamore Public Elementary School, but
it may be stated in general that the
materials to be used in school buildings
are a matter primarily for the committee
or manager on the advice of the architect
who is employed.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask is it a fact
that the hon. Member for South Down
resides in a house which is not built of
Newry granite?

5. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether she can state the
number of pupils on the public elementary school rolls on the 31st December,

Catholic pupils, (b) Protestant pupils.
Mrs. PARKER: Separate statistics
are given in the annual reports of the
Ministry of Education for those
denominations with relatively large
numbers of adherents, but it has been
necessary to include under the general
heading of "Others" information in
regard to the less numerous Protestant
religious bodies and the Jewish community.
It may, however, serve the hon. Member's purpose if I give him the total
number enrolled and the number of
Roman Catholic pupils. On 31st
December, 1923, the total number of
pupils enrolled was 196,015, of whom
67,925 were Roman Catholics; on 31st
December, 1937, the total number of
pupils was 194,347, of whom 72,259 were
Roman Catholics.

CONTROL
OF LIGHTS IN
NORTHERN WATERS.
the
11. Mr. HENDERSON asked
Prime Minister whether it is a fact that
the light buoys in the water around
Northern Ireland are controlled from
Dublin, and which Government controls
the waters around Northern Ireland.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply.
Navigation lights on the coast of
Northern Ireland are subject to the control of the Commissioners of Irish Lights,
whose headquarters are still in Dublin.
This body, as the hon. Member will be
aware, is in a position analogous to that
of the bodies responsible for the lights on
the other coasts of the British Isles, the
general administration in respect of all
of which is connected with the Mercantile Marine Department of the Board of
Trade.
The territorial waters around Northern
Ireland are under the jurisdiction of the
Imperial Government and the Government of Northern Ireland according to
their respective powers.
Mr. HENDERSON: Will the Minister state whether any of the waters in
the North of Ireland are controlled by
our Government?
Mr. BARBOUR: No.

NEWRY GRANITE FOR SCHOOL
BUILDINGS.
13. Mr. BROWN asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether she intends seeing that
a position similar to that which arose at
Ballyveamore, County Down, where
granite was not specified for a new school
there in the home of that industry in
Mourne, is not allowed to arise in the
case of the new class-rooms to be added
to Windsor Hill P.E. Schools, Newry, at
a cost of £4,000 odd; and whether she
will see to it that Newry granite is
specified at least for part of this work.
Mrs. PARKER: I reply to the first
part of the question, as I explained in
my reply to the hon. Member's previous
question this afternoon, the materials to
be used in school building are a matter
primarily for the person or body erecting
the school, who will doubtless be guided
by the advice of their architect.
Provided that the materials proposed
are suitable, and that they are satisfactory as regards cost, the Ministry
would not be disposed to interfere. The
last part of the question does not, therefore, arise.

SPEED LIMIT FOR MOTORISTS.
16. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether, in
view of the number of serious motor
accidents in Northern Ireland in built-up
areas, he is prepared to recommend a
speed limit of 25 miles per hour in builtup areas, and so minimise the number of
accidents.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
given long and careful consideration to
the question of whether speed limits
should be imposed on motorists in builtup areas, but I am not satisfied that the
object desired can best be attained by
such a method.
It is already an offence to drive a
motor-car on a public road at a speed
which is dangerous to the public, having
regard to all the circumstances of the
case, including the nature, condition,
and use of the road, and the amount of
traffic which is actually at the time, or
which might reasonably be expected to
be, on the road.
The penalties which may be inflicted
on conviction for such offence are drastic,
and can be imposed on any motorist who
endangers another road user by driving
at an even lower speed than that
mentioned by the hon. Member.
I am sure the hon. Member will agree
that this law affords a much more useful means of preventing accidents than
one fixing a maximum speed irrespective
of any circumstance other than that it
applied in a built-up area.
MARKETS AND TOLLS.
17. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is now in
a position to state when the Government
intends to proceed with legislation dealing with markets and tolls, and whether
this legislation will be on the lines embodied in the report of the Markets and
Tolls Commission.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government has given very careful consideration to the question of proceeding to
give legislative effect to the recommendations of the Committee on Markets and
Tolls, but I regret that such divergent
views have been expressed in regard to
the proposals by local authorities and
other interested bodies and persons, that
it is clear a Measure on the lines suggested would not be acceptable, and the
Government has, accordingly, come to
the decision that it would not be opportune to proceed with legislation in the
matter at present.
POOR LAW MEDICAL SERVICE.
18. Mr. MAGINESS asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether his attention has been called to an article in the
current issue of the "British Medical
Journal," and written by a well-known
medical practitioner in Northern Ireland;
whether the allegations contained in the
said article are substantially correct, and
if so, whether he can state if it is the
intention of the Government to introduce
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
20 OCTOBER 1938
the necessary legislation to remedy the
defects in the poor law medical service,
to which the said article calls attention,
and whether it is the intention of the
Government to establish a Ministry of
Health.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have seen
the article in question, and I must
apologise if my answer appears somewhat
lengthy. It appears that Dr. Kidd would
like a complete reconstruction of all
public health and medical services under
the control of one central Ministry
specially established for the purpose.
There may be a great deal to be said for
such a proposal, but I am afraid it is
more an ideal for the future than an
immediately practical proposition. Our
health services have evolved gradually
out of our practical needs, and as new
wants have been felt, new methods have
been devised to meet them. In this way
a number of specialised medical services
have grown up under which, admittedly,
there is a certain amount of overlapping.
But the overlapping is, perhaps, more
apparent than real, as in practice each
local authority tends to leave the special
work to the ad hoc authorities which
have been set up to deal with it. Moreover, it will always be possible to make
adjustments from time to time so as to
avoid unnecessary overlapping.
With regard to the number of local
authorities, I would point out that the
administrative services for a population.
scattered over a large rural area, with
many separate towns, is quite a different
matter from that of administering the
services for a compact mass of people in
one city like Glasgow.
The proposal to establish a new Ministry of Health is, I am afraid, not possible
for financial reasons. The Government
is often criticised for the number of
Ministries already existing, and if it was
to set up another one the taxpayers
would have something to say about it.
I should like to add that Dr. Kidd's
picture of the existing hospitals is rather
misleading. In the last twenty years
twelve of the old workhouse hospitals
have been converted into district
hospitals, usually after being completely
reconstructed, and the medical and nursing arrangements and the equipment are
of a high standard. The thirteen (not
fifteen) remaining workhouse hospitals
have all been improved also, and in some
of them the standard is not appreciably
lower than in the district hospitals.
While I am not prepared to agree with
Dr. Kidd's implied suggestions that gas
cannot be an adequate illuminant for
hospital purposes, it may be of interest
to note that all but four of these hospitals
already have electric light or are having
it put in, and two of the four have it in
certain parts of the institution. The
only two hospitals which had oil lamps
are now having electric light introduced.
The dispensaries, which receive some
prominence in Dr. Kidd's article, are
not, I would point out, intended for
operations. They are merely consulting
rooms, and improvements are constantly
being made to old premises or new
premises are being obtained.
I do not say that our existing system
is incapable of improvement, but it is
adapted to our requirements and, on the
whole, works very well.
I need hardly add, however, that
every opportunity will be taken to effect
improvements.
Mr. HENDERSON: Arising out of
the reply, is the right hon. Gentleman
aware that in Enniskillen to-day in
some of the institutions mentioned they
are burning candles?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would
refer the hon. Member to my answer,
which I stand over.
Mr. SPEAKER: The replies to the
remaining questions will be circulated
in the Official Report unless hon. Members wish to postpone them, in which
case will they please give notice at the
Table?

"We, His Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Commons of

-(Sir Dawson Bates.)
Mr. NIXON : I thought perhaps
that the Minister was going to give the
House some information.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid
I lost my opportunity.
Mr. SPEAKER: If the right hon.
Gentleman wishes to make a statement

Mr. NIXON: I give way.
Sir DAWSON BATES (by leave of
the House): The purpose of this
Resolution is to provide for the application to Northern Ireland of the Architects (Registration) Act, 1938, which
was passed at the end of last summer
by the Parliament of the United Kingdom. The Act as it stands does not
apply to Northern Ireland, but provision is made in Section 6 (1) whereby
it may be extended to Northern Ireland by an Order of His Majesty in
Council, made in pursuance of a
Resolution passed by both Houses of
this Parliament. The Act has been
drafted in close co-operation with the
appropriate authorities here, and it is for
the purpose of having it extended that
I now submit this resoluton to the
House.
Hon. Members will recollect that a
similar procedure was followed in the
case of the Architects (Registration)
Act, 1931, which is the principal Act
in this particular code of legislation.
The 1931 Act, as the House is aware,
set up an Architects' Registration
Council for the United Kingdom, and
with the application of that Act to Northern Ireland the registration of our
architects was merged with that of the
United Kingdom architects, a procedure which this House decided was
in the best possible interests of the public and the profession.
Hon. Members will recollect, further,
that the Act of 1931 protected the use
of the title "registered architect."
The object of this provision was to provide such guidance for the public as
would protect them from unwittingly
employing as architects persons not
properly qualified to undertake architectural work, but there is little doubt
that this provision failed in its object,
and in the light of experience since the
passing of that Act it became obvious
that it could never succeed so long as
it was open to unqualified persons to
style themselves architects at all.
No one but a duly registered person
may call himself or herself a solicitor,
physician, surgeon, dentist, veterinary
surgeon, chemist, or even a midwife,
and there would appear to be no
essential characteristic common to these
professions which is absent from the
architectural profession.
It cannot be seriously contended that
the relations of the public with the
architectural profession are of a less
intimate and indispensable nature than
they are with, say, the veterinary profession, or that the prospective loss or
injury to the client is greater in the
case of unskilled veterinary advice than
it is in the case of unskilled archi-

The Act which I now propose we
should apply to Northern Ireland protects the title of "architect" by providing that no person shall practise or
carry on business under that title unless he is a registered person, just in the
way, as I have explained, that the
titles of physician, surgeon, dentist,
etc., are protected under their respective Acts.
I should, however, make it clear that
it does not in any way hinder any person from designing or supervising the
erection of buildings. It merely
secures that a person shall not hold
himself out to be an architect, and
invite the public to employ him as one,
unless he is properly qualified as such.
Throughout the passage of the Bill
this Government has been closely in
touch with the promoters and with the
Department of the Imperial Government
concerned, and the Ulster Society of
Architects-which, of course, has been
deeply interested in the matter was in
close co-operation with them. It was
carried in all its stages in the Imperial
House by overwhelming majorities and
received the support of all substantial
interests concerned.
The Act is a very short one and I
feel I need but refer very briefly to it.
Apart from its main provision, it

harshly affected by it. Persons who are

practising, and in the event of any

Act. This tribunal will be under the
chairmanship of a person appointed by
the Lord Chancellor, and will have six
other members, of whom two will be
