ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Marketing of Potatoes Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Before endeavouring to explain the proposals
embodied in the Bill now before the
House, it may be desirable to indicate
briefly the existing position. First of
all, I need hardly remind Hon. Members that the potato is our chief tillage
crop the back-bone of our system of
arable farming-that the average
annual output for export and human
consumption in Northern Ireland is
478,000 tons, valued at £1,294,000, and
this is apart altogether from the large
quantity used for feeding stock on
farms. In a recent year our exports
reached 243,000 tons, worth £816,000.
It is consequently essential that such a
valuable branch of the agricultural
industry should be preserved and
developed in every practicable way. It
was a realisation of this fact that
prompted the House to pass the Acts of
1928 and 1934. The standard of
quality, the grading and packing of
potatoes have helped the shippers and
the producers to a very great extent.
Existing legislation has secured that
our potatoes reach the British market
in the best possible condition, with the
result that even in times of glut we have
been able to effect sales when local British
supplies were often unsaleable. That
position has been maintained and this
year I might call it a surplus year—we
have sent no fewer than 175,000 tons.
It must be admitted, however, that the
price has not been up to the standard we
should have liked. We have reached the
top of the market in regard to quality,
but up-to-date we have not, on all
occasions, received the highest or, perhaps, an economic price. Obviously we
cannot guarantee a price, but what we
1769 Marketing of Potatoes Bill-

20 OCTOBER 1938
Second Reading
hope to do, if this legislation is passed,
is to see that the producer gets a reasonable price, and that there will be no
undercutting to undermine the price.
We have for many years been giving
this price problem our attention, but
it has been practically impossible to do
anything except to see that the potatoes
are properly graded and sent out in a
proper way. Since the inauguration of
the Potato Marketing Board on the other
side of the water a gleam of light has
appeared, and by orderly marketing it is
hoped that the position will be improved.
We founded the Potato Marketing
Association. The association is composed of gentlemen interested in the
shipping industry, with the addition of
two farmers' representatives and a representative of the Ministry. They have
discussed with the Potato Marketing
Board in England the measures to be
taken to procure orderly marketing.
They have sat once a week to consider
the prices prevailing on the other side,
and compiled a list which they circulated
to the various shippers. They also suggested that the prices which they fixed
should be adhered to. They came to
what I might call a gentleman's agreement with the Potato Marketing Board
in England that the exports from
Northern Ireland should be limited to
200,000 tons, provided, however, that if
foreign potatoes were coming into Great
Britain there should be no limit whatever. I should like to emphasise that
there is no statutory power behind this
gentleman's agreement. For the information of Members of the House I may
state that the average exports of potatoes
from Northern Ireland have not exceeded
200,000 tons.
It is now felt by the producers and
shippers that the association should be
given statutory powers. The association has done excellent work, and I am
certain had it not been for their
knowledge and foresight the whole of the
potato trade might have fallen into complete disorder. Under this Bill, when it
becomes law, the Ministry will be given
power to assist in various ways the formal
organisation, and the association will cooperate with the Potato Marketing
Board on the other side.
I think it is only right for me to avail
myself of this opportunity to state that, notwithstanding many difficulties, the Board
has, on the whole, brought a measure of
stability and confidence. In answer to
a question I explained to the House that
it was probably one of the most difficult
marketing schemes to work, because it
was necessary, over a number of years, to
obtain data sufficient to work it. I hope
that the Board will pay particular attention to those parts of Great Britain
where Northern Ireland potatoes are sold,
namely, Lancashire, South Wales and
South-West England.
The scheme embodied in the Bill comes
within the Marketing Act of 1933, which
was passed by the Parliament of the
United Kingdom and also by this Parlia-
It enables co-operation to take
place between the scheme in this country
and a similar scheme on the other side.
ment.
Briefly, the Bill provides for the framing of a scheme by the Ministry for
regulating the marketing of potatoes
sent from Northern Ireland to Great
Britain. The scheme will be drawn up
in consultation with the association, and
it is proposed that the Potato Marketing Committee shall be composed of
representatives of licensed merchants,
producers, with the addition of persons
appointed by the Ministry. The Ministry retain the power to appoint an
increased number of producers' representatives if at any time plans for fixing
the prices to be paid to growers, as
distinct from shippers, are brought into
operation.
Under Clause 2, sub-clause (6), the Bill
provides that the Ministry shall have
access to the accounts of any shipper.
That, of course, is being done to provide against undercutting, which is detrimental to all concerned. The scheme
may also provide for the constitution of
an agency for receiving and disbursing
moneys payable in respect of potatoes
shipped to Great Britain, and for requiring consignments to be invoiced
through a central agency. It is further
proposed that the Potato Marketing
Committee shall advise the Ministry on
all matters appertaining to growing,
selling and other matters of interest to
the trade. Naturally the advice will be
most valuable, because it must be remembered the committee will be composed of
gentlemen who know all sides of that
particular trade.
Clause 4 provides that the Ministry
may regulate the removal of potatoes

In its financial aspects the scheme will
provide, first of all, for the establishment
of a fund to be administered by the
Potato Marketing Committee, and for the
payment into the fund of all moneys
received under the provisions of the
scheme, and the payment out of the fund.
of any moneys required for the operation.
of the scheme; thus the Marketing Committee will have full financial autonomy.
It also provides for the payment by licence.
holders of contributions to the fund of
such amounts as may be necessary for
the operation of the scheme. Such contributions would be on the basis of tonnage shipped, and would probably be at
the rate of 1d, or at most 2d a ton.
I am sure the House will be glad to
learn that the cost of operating the
scheme will be borne by the trade and
not by the Exchequer. In addition to
providing for a scheme on the lines which
I have indicated, the House will observe
that Clause 5 provides that all applications for licences must be received by the
Ministry on or before the 30th September in each year. That is being done to
prevent what I might call the in-and-out
trade. It occurs quite frequently that
a man will not come into the trade until
he has made up his mind that it is a
good year to deal in potatoes. He probably has no technical knowledge of shipping or selling, and it is practically
impossible to control what he does. Such
a person is a source of danger to the
whole of the potato trade. Under this
Bill, if a man wishes to enter the potato
trade he must make up his mind before
the 30th September, otherwise he will
not be able to obtain a licence.
Clause 6 provides that if at any time
the Ministry, after consultation with the
Potato Marketing Committee, is satisfied
that the then existing merchants are
sufficient to carry on the trade, the granting of further licences to new men may
be discontinued for the time being. That
covers the point I have already referred
to. In order to have an efficient trade it
is essential that only a sufficient number
of shippers should handle it. If a
number of small men-I have already referred to this matter—are allowed to deal
with this very technical question, it will
cause damage to a most important trade.
The Ministry may, in addition, cease for
the time being to grant further licences,
and this arrangement might apply to the
whole of Northern Ireland or only to a
part or parts thereof. I wish to make it
quite clear, however, that any shipper
who held a licence on 1st July, 1938, will
not be prejudiced by the suggested
arrangement.
Clause 7 provides that any person disclosing information, that is to say information he may acquire while carrying
out his duty of inspecting books, will be
guilty of an offence, except in so far as
such information is disclosed for the purpose of a prosecution or legal proceedings.
In conclusion, I wish to inform the
House that the whole of this legislation
has been discussed with the Executive
Committee of the Merchants' Association and with the Ulster Farmers' Union.
They are satisfied and support the
Measure wholeheartedly. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

Mrs. PARKER: With regard to the

order to give a certain percentage of

That would be a burden which could

I also pointed out to the hon. Member
that under our financial arrangements
with Great Britain it is absolutely
necessary for us to go step by step with
Great Britain, particularly in this

The hon. Member said that under
this Bill education for the workingclasses was going to be limited. It is
quite impossible for me to follow that
argument. Under this Bill education
for the working-classes is going to be
extended, and I think it is obvious that
even though there might be a certain
number of exemptions the Bill will be
of the very greatest benefit to the class
which he claims to represent, but which
we all represent, because we all stand
for the working-classes.
Mr. BEATTIE: Do not the rich get

Mrs. PARKER: I can only say that
I am quite confident that under this

think the hon. Member would realise
that if he were not so determined to
try to pick some flaws in the Measure.
There are very few flaws he could pick
and naturally he concentrates on this
point which I have tried to explain.

POISONING OF FISH BY FLAX
WATER.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he is aware of the
serious destruction of fish in the Claughy
River, Ballymoney, which took place in
the month of September through the
discharge of flax water; whether many
flax growers in the townland of Claughy
were warned by the police prior to the
discharge of this poisonous matter in
accordance with instructions issued to the
police by the Ministry of Commerce;
whether many flax growers in the townland have been prosecuted by the police
or will be prosecuted; what steps he proposes to take to ensure that flax growers
in this townland are warned of the
seriousness of this offence.
Mr. BARBOUR: I am informed that
no prosecutions were instituted this year
in respect of the Claughy River as there
was no evidence that flax water had been
discharged into that river. Convictions,
however, were obtained in September
against four defendants charged with the
offence of allowing flax water to enter
the Lade and Eden burns which are also
in the Claughy district. In regard to
the issue of warnings, I would inform the
hon. Member that, as in previous years,
steps were taken early in August,
through the medium of the Press, the
B.B.C., the Ministry of Agriculture
bulletin and the police, to bring to the
notice of all flax growers in Northern Ireland the serious danger to fish life
attendant upon the discharge of flax
water into any river or water-course.
Moreover, I am assured that flax growers
in the Claughy district have been
sufficiently warned against this danger to
leave no doubt in their minds as to the
precautions to be taken in retting flax.
It is my intention to take similar action
each year so long as circumstances appear
to warrant my doing so.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
has the right hon. Gentleman made
arrangements for the draining off of this
water on future occasions when necessary.
Mr. BARBOUR: No, Sir. Instructions have been given to flax growers
as to how flax water should be disposed
of.
INCREASE IN BREAD AND COAL
PRICES.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether his attention has been
called to the increases that have taken
place in Northern Ireland in the prices
of coal and bread; whether he has seen
a resolution unanimously adopted by the
Newry Board of Guardians calling on
the Members of Parliament for South
Down, Mourne and South Armagh to
take this matter up in the House;
whether he has seen a resolution unanimously passed by the Newry Urban District Council on the same subject; and
whether he has taken any action or proposes to take any action in the matter,
and, if so, what line this action has
taken or will take.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have seen Press
reports of the resolutions to which the
hon. Member refers.
The price of bread in Belfast was reduced from 10d to 9d per 4lb. loaf in
June last, and, so far as I am aware,
there has been no subsequent rise. I am
given to understand that the price.
applies to Newry as well as to Belfast.
The hon. Member will be aware that
there is always a rise in the retail prices
of coal in the autumn months and I have
had no evidence that the general price
situation is abnormal. In view of the
fact, however, that certain representations have been made to me by the Newry
Urban District Council with regard to
the price charged in that town, I have
instituted inquiries into the matter,
which are still proceeding.
AN ARDGLASS FISHING SCHEME.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he is aware that it
has been stated in the Press that more
than 1,100 jobs are to be provided in
Northern Ireland by a £400,000 fishing
scheme comprising every unit of the industry, with Ardglass as the chief centre;

whether he can give the House any information about this project; whether the
figures given are substantially within the
facts; whether a grant has or will be
made by the Government to help to

in the developments contemplated.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have seen reports
in various organs of the Press to the
effect mentioned in the first part of the
question. Beyond the information given.
in those reports, however, my knowledge
of the project is confined to an outline

As regards the question of a grant, the

undertaking sought by him in the last
part of the question.

LAND PURCHASE ANNUITIES.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he is aware that in the
case of the land purchase annuities
collected by his Department a very grave
injustice is being perpetrated by reason
of the fact that many Northern Ireland
tenants, who bought out immediately
under the Wyndham Act of 1903, by
which the payment of the money was
extended over a period of sixty-eight
years, and have paid their annuities ever
since, were credited with their instalments only from the time that the owner
received his final payment from the
British Government, which in many cases
was in 1919, with the result that farmers
paying for about thirty-five years are
to-day only credited with 19 or 20 instalments; whether the Government when
a somewhat similar position arose in 1929
dealt with the situation more fairly, and
whether he will take steps, or make
representations to the proper quarters to
have steps taken, to have this grievance
of purchasers under the Wyndham Act
whose annuities the Ministry of Finance
is collecting remedied along the lines of
the Northern Ireland Land Act, 1929.
Mr. ANDREWS: It is true that many
of the tenant-purchasers under the 1903
Act, owing to the congestion of cases,
had for a considerable period to pay
interest without any payment towards
sinking fund in lieu of rent. This
situation was inherent in the Act itself,
and the interest was less than the former
rent.

DUNGANNON BRICK COMPANY.
8. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he is aware that the
failure of the Dungannon Brick Company to honour their contract has been
responsible for the dismissal of 31
labourers and 10 bricklayers; whether
this company are only delivering 5,000
bricks per day, whereas they contracted
to deliver 14,000 bricks per day, and
whether this company has dismissed ten
prominent members of the trade union
and threatens to dismiss as many more;
and whether any reason has been given
for their dismissal.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply to this question.
Since receipt of the question, a joint
conference with the parties concerned
has been held under the auspices of my
Ministry, with the result that a satisfactory solution of the differences between the employers and the union
concerned has been reached. In these
circumstances, I feel sure that in the
interests of harmony the hon. Member
will agree that the specific matters
referred to in the question should not be
pursued further at the moment.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask the right
hon. Gentleman whether his attention
has been called to the enormous quantity
of foreign brick that is being imported
into the city of Belfast, and whether he
will use his influence to induce the
builders to use local brick?
Mr. BEATTIE: Am I to understand
that through the good offices of the right
hon. Gentleman the relationships that
should exist between employer and men
have now been restored?
Mr. GORDON: I would like to say
that the position I occupy is to endeavour
to maintain harmonious relations between
employer and worker, and those relations
have been restored most satisfactorily in
the present case.

Home Affairs whether he can state the
amounts paid to the five veterinary
inspectors in County Antrim for the past

instead of merely giving the amount

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The amounts paid to
the five veterinary inspectors for the past
financial year were as follow:—(1) £6 9s ;
(2) £3 2s; (3) £3 14s; (4) £4 5s; (5)
£4 19s. These amounts include travelling expenses.

PROTECTING THE SILENT VALLEY
WATER SUPPLY.
18. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state if any steps are being taken under
the air raid precautions to protect the
Silent Valley water supply.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The question
of the protection of the Silent Valley
water supply is one for the Belfast Water
Commissioners who, I am informed, have
the matter in hand. Arrangements have
already been made by the Board, under
which a large reserve supply of pipes of
all sizes is available for use in the event
of damage, and provision is also being
made for the establishment of a repair
corps, who will be specially trained and
will be readily available to effect any
necessary repairs with the least possible
delay.

19. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister

why the amounts paid to each of seven
rate collectors in County Antrim were not
given in the Secretary's statement for

them and ensure that they are given in
future instead of a quotation of their
poundage rates; and whether he can also
state why the poundage rates to these
collectors varies from 10d to 2s 6d in
the £.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Secretary's statement, to which the hon. Member refers, is simply a record of the
officers of the local authorities and their
rates of salary, which is prepared by the
clerk to the local authority and submitted
to the local government auditor for his
information. The information in it is
that specified by Statutory Order.
Of the twenty-three rate collectors in
County Antrim, fifteen are paid an
annual salary and eight are paid by
poundage rates.
The actual amounts paid to each of
these eight collectors for the year ended

VICTORIA HOMES,
BALLYSILLAN.
Mr. HENDERSON asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether she is aware that the
children in the Victoria Homes, Ballysillan, have to walk from the Homes to
Wolfhill P.E. School during the winter
months in all weathers, and that the
children are often drenched with rain
when going to school; whether the
Ministry are prepared to assent to the
provision of transport for these children
from the Homes to the school and back.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): In reply
to the first part of the question I understand except on very wet days or in the
case of very young children it is the case
that the pupils of the Victoria Homes,
Ballysillan, walk to and from the Wolfhill Public Elementary School, which is
distant about a mile from the Homes.
I understand also that the authorities
of the Victoria Homes do not consider
the provision of transport facilities
either necessary or desirable in view of
the shortness of the distance and the
benefit to the children's health from a
daily walk.
I am aware that it is desired to obtain
a concession for free travel by tram to
and from the school in the case of the
very small children but this would seem
to be a matter between the authorities
of the Homes and the Tramways Committee of the Belfast Corporation.
With regard to the last part of the
question, I could not give a categorical
answer unless detailed proposals had
been submitted for the Ministry's
consideration, but from the facts as I
understand them I think that the hon.
Member may take it that the Ministry
would not be prepared to approve the
expenditure of public funds upon transport facilities for these children who
have not on the average to travel a
greater distance to school than many
other children.

Mr. AGNEW: I beg to move:

the Government should introduce legislation to bring the able-bodied unemployed under the same regulations for
outdoor relief as applies in Britain,

outdoor relief as provided for under
Exceptional Distress Order, compulsory legislation should be introduced in
order to instruct Poor Law Guardians
to grant relief to able-bodied unemployed as carried out in Britain under
heading of Public Assistance admisistered by Local Government bodies."
This Motion which I am placing before
the House is one to which I have given
very serious consideration because it
affects the lives of many of our citizens,
and it is of the utmost importance that
the Government should also give it their
serious consideration from every aspect
which will be put forward. The Government must realise that able-bodied unemployed who are denied the right to work
are justly entitled to maintenance
adequate to guarantee security. We find

no guarantee of security, or even food,
clothing and shelter. It is a matter
of serious concern in this year 1938 that

that the present system of maintenance
is bound up with unemployment benefit,

the breadwinners who have been denied

force to-day which, if brought into being,

able-bodied workers who are denied the

It says:

When one is dealing with a Notice of

of some difficulty. There has not been
for some considerable time past any procedure by Exceptional Distress Order.
The Exceptional Distress Order came in
first in the Local Government Act, 1898,
and in 1928 under the Poor Law Relief
(Exceptional Distress) Act power was
given to the local authorities to make
orders for particular areas where exceptional distress existed. Two such Orders
were made one in respect of the city of
Belfast and the other for Newry.
It was found between 1928 and 1937
that the procedure of the Ministry making Orders was inconvenient, and this
House passed an Act which virtually did
away with the Exceptional Distress
Orders because under that Statute the
poor-law guardians did not have to apply
for an Order at all, but were by the
Statute authorised to give relief. There
is not any scale laid down. In the
Orders up to 1937 the standard scale was
indicated by the Ministry, and that scale
goes from 20s to 32s.

Oral Answers to Questions.
TRANSPORT BOARD LOSSES.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether, having
regard to the heavy losses of the
Northern Ireland transport system since
its commencement, he proposes to reappoint the present Transport Board on
the expiry of its term of office.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The question of
what reorganisation may be necessary in
regard to road transport in Northern
Ireland must depend upon the result of
the consideration of the McLintock
Report, but I resent most strongly the
implication contained in the hon. and
learned Member's question that the
members of the Transport Board have
failed in their duty, and I should like
to take this opportunity of expressing
my gratitude for the public spirit which
has at all times actuated the Board in
carrying out their extremely difficult
responsibilities.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the responsibility for the Northern Ireland transport rest on the Minister or on the
Transport Board?
Sir DAWSON BATES: It rests so far
as road transport is concerned on the
Board.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Are the losses
running into thousands per month?
Sir DAWSON BATES: If the hon.
and learned Member will wait he will
soon see.
PRESERVATION OF SCENIC
BEAUTY.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can state
what effective steps have been taken by
the Ministry or the local authorities for
the preservation of the Ulster countryside or the control of the epidemic of
bungalows, bill-boards, petrol pumps and
gimcrack villas now disfiguring places of
scenic beauty in this area; and if the
legislation passed for these purposes has
become a dead letter.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The preservation of the amenities of the countryside rests with the local authorities,
which have been given powers for the
purpose under the Housing and Planning Act, 1931, and the Advertisement
(Regulation) Act, 1937.
Planning resolutions have been passed
by the Belfast and Londonderry County
Borough Councils for the whole of their
areas, and by the Castlereagh and
Armagh Rural District Councils for
portions of their areas.
I share the hon. and learned Member's regret that local authorities have
not availed themselves more freely of the
powers conferred on them by this Act,
but I can assure him that my Department is doing everything possible to encourage greater activity in this respect.
Under the Advertisements (Regulation) Act, by-laws for the control of
advertisements have been made by the
County of Tyrone, and by-laws proposed
by the Counties of Antrim, Armagh,
Down and Londonderry, and the Urban
District of Banbridge, are under consideration.

adopting schemes for the separation of

their theological studies.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): I have been asked by the hon.
Lady to reply.
The answers to the first two parts of
the question are in the affirmative.
With regard to the third part of the
question, I am not aware of any denominational colleges of similar standing in
Northern Ireland, but if the hon. and
learned Member has any particular case
in mind I shall be happy to look into
the matter. I would stress, however, the
three conditions which are applicable to
the Magee University College grant, and
would have to be equally applicable in
any other case-
Firstly, the separation of the administration and the accounts of the arts and
the theological sides; secondly, audit of
the entire accounts by the Comptroller
and Auditor-General; and lastly, the
nomination of Government representatives to the governing body of the
institution.

CLAUSE 1 (Amendment of 8 Edw. 7,
c. 38 and 16 & 17 Geo. 5, c. 13).
Question proposed, "That the Clause
stand part of the Bill."
Mr. CAMPBELL: I submit to the
Committee that this Clause should not
stand part of the Bill. I anticipated
that certain Amendments, which I put
on the Order Paper with a view to
broadening the constitution of the
University Senate, would be challenged
having regard to the framework
of the Bill and also having regard
to the Irish Universities Act, 1908, and
the Government of Ireland Act, 1920.
It is interesting to notice that there
could be no challenge to the competence
of this Committee to vote, as it did vote
on a recent occasion, £20,000 annually
to the general purposes of the University,
but I bow to the ruling that it is not
competent for this Committee to alter
this Bill to the extent of a single comma.
This is a Government Bill. It is brought
forward by responsible Ministers of the
Government. My objection to it is that
it is not right that the constitution of
the University should be altered in this
piecemeal way.
The Preamble of the Bill says and
recites that it is a Bill to alter the constitution of the Senate of the Queen's
University of Belfast. I very respectfully and very deferentially agree that
that is expedient. I submit the time has
come when it would be right and proper
that the constitution of the Senate should
be altered in the sense of widening the
foundation upon which the Senate, as
the responsible body of the University,
rests. The Senate should be put on a
more wide and more representative
foundation. This Bill adds two gentlemen of undoubted learning and integrity, but they are gentlemen from inside
the household of the University.
What is needed at the present time in
this University, and, indeed in any
University, is an influx of fresh minds
from the outside world who would perhaps on many points not see altogether
with the usual official or highbrow minds
who are accustomed very often to work
in hidebound grooves bereft of initiative.
I am fully conscious of the priceless boon
a University is to any community, and
especially to this community. If it were
nothing else and nothing less than a
corrective of the widespread prevalence
of narrow and conceited ignorance a
University is a priceless boon. I
sometimes think when listening in
this House what a chastening restraint
a University training would have on the
fiery nonsense that is often poured forth
from the Benches opposite.
Captain DIXON: What about your
own Benches?
Mr. CAMPBELL: You do not recognise the fiery nonsense on your side, you
are so accustomed to it. I suppose it
becomes a matter of routine and causes you
no surprise. I see hon. Members there not
yet elevated to the Front Bench or the
Bench immediately behind it with
ambitions-whether they will be satisfied
in time or not I cannot tell-but I think
sometimes that a University education
even in their case might be very useful.

Again, a University education would be

the Six Counties, habits of frank, and

That is the end-all and be-all of University life. Even in this mercenary age,
when we are discussing money from day
to day and the whole trend of life seems
to be commercialised, a University

who, make what sail they can in life,

The annual income of the University
up to a week or two ago was £95,000.
Now under recent grants made by this
Committee the income will be £115,000.
Would it not be wise when such a large
sum of money is being voted that the
Senate should be broadened out in a way
that would give the entire community,
not any section of the community, not
any learned section or the learned professions, but the community at large, a
sense of confidence in regard to the
proper disposition of the moneys given.
Is that £20,000 to go to the medical
faculty or is it to be spread among all
the faculties of the University? Is it to
go in erecting or modernising buildings,
or in creating new Chairs and Lectureships?
The existing exodus of medical
graduates of Queen's University from the
Six Counties is going on at an alarming
rate. I believe that of the 1,200 medical graduates who finished their courses
in Queen's during the past fifteen or
sixteen years only 400 have settled down
in the Six Counties and that 800 have
gone elsewhere and have settled down
in other countries. What does that
mean? It means that all the money, all
the toil, and all the time devoted to the
training of those young medical gentlemen is lost to this area and goes to the
benefit of other countries. To what is
that due? Is it due to the fact that
openings in this circumscribed area for
efficient medical graduates are too few
and too unattractive? I believe that
there also an influx of fresh minds to the
Senate would be desirable.
I hear a scheme has been mooted for
the removal of the Clinical Chairs of the
University to where they would be an
adjunct to another institution. That
would be a blow to the prestige of the
University, and the University truncated
would no longer be the old Queen's
University. For another reason I regret
that opportunity was not taken in this

the gifted children of the working people.
The doors of the University should be
wide open to talent, no matter from what
class of the community that talent
springs.

question. First of all, I think the hon.
and learned Member for Central Belfast
is somewhat under a misapprehension
when he complains of the way in which
this Bill purports to change the constitution of the University. The only way
in which the constitution of the University can be changed is by the method
adopted in this Bill. As the hon. and
learned Member knows full well, under
the Government of Ireland Act of 1920
the constitution can only be dealt with
by this House after the proposed changes
have been before the three bodies
referred to in the Preamble of the Bill,
and if there is any cause of complaint
about the method of alteration that is a
matter beyond the control of this House;
it rests entirely upon the principle of the
Act of 1920.
I should like to refer to one other
matter which the hon. and learned
Gentleman mentioned. He has paid a
very glowing tribute, for which I must
thank him, to the effects of University
education, and I trust that very
pointedly he will not indicate me as the
exception to the rule. When he refers
to the representation of the body for
which he speaks here to-day I think I
am entitled to say that there is ground
for believing that the complaint which
he has made is not based on any suggestion of that body, but is made for
the purpose of making political capital
out of a situation which should never
have been allowed to develop in that
direction.
The reason I say that is
this: As soon as I learned from the
Order Paper of the hon. and learned
Gentleman's proposal, I made inquiries
and I found that the Mater Infirmorum
Hospital has never approached the
Senate for the purpose of suggesting to
the Senate that it should be directly
represented thereon. The hon. and
learned Gentleman knows that, as a
matter of good sense as well as of law,
the only body that could deal with any
alteration is the Senate. I am not saying anything as to whether it is right

Mr. HENDERSON: I do not think I

that every creed and class in Northern
Ireland is represented on that body.
The students consist of Roman Catholics,
Protestants, Socialists, Communistsevery conceivable sect that could be
mentioned is represented at the University. Each of these sects has the right
to nominate a man to represent it on the
Senate. They do that, I think, yearly.
I am quite satisfied that the rights of
every student at the University are
protected.
I agree with the hon. and learned
Member for Central Belfast in this
respect. I feel very much the fact that
a large number of the students cannot
secure employment in their own country.
I suppose the industrial depression has
a good deal to do with that state of
affairs, but if the students of the
University are not doing something for
Northern Ireland they are adding lustre
to its name in the British Dominions.
Therefore, I think the University

Death of Sir Robert James Johnstone.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report to
the House with the deepest regret the
death of Professor Sir Robert Johnstone,
late Member for the University. In all
corners of the House he was extremely
popular, and the Members recognised to
the full the great ability and the great
sincerity with which he uttered his views
on the floor of the House. I am sure
the House would wish me to convey to
Lady Johnstone, on their behalf, their
deepest sympathy and deep sense of
having sustained an irreparable loss.

A MINISTRY OF LABOUR

1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether Mr. Samuel Milligan,
Ballyskeagh House, Newtownards, was
recently appointed canvassing and investigating officer (Agricultural Section)
under the Ministry of Labour; whether
he would state if this is a full time
position and give the salary and allowance attaching to the post; whether this
gentleman is also collecting agent for the
Pigs Marketing Board in the Newtownards area and what is the salary attached
to this post; and whether, in addition,
the gentleman is also a substantial
farmer.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): Yes, Sir. On his application
for the position in the Ministry of
Labour, Mr. Milligan stated that he held
a part-time employment under the Pigs
Marketing Board, for which he was remunerated on a commission basis, and
before he was appointed to the Ministry
of Labour he was informed that the
Department would require his full-time
services.
The Department felt that it was
reasonable to allow Mr. Milligan a
reasonable opportunity of making alternative arrangements in regard to his
work for the Pigs Marketing Board, and
he has now been informed that, in the
Department's view, sufficient time has
elapsed for him to do so.
The salary attaching to his post in
the Ministry of Labour is 60s a week,
with travelling expenses on the Civil
Service scale.
I am informed that Mr. Milligan does
not himself own a farm, but that before
his appointment to the post in the
Ministry of Labour he was engaged on
his father's farm.

temporary ex-Servicemen for posts in the
Ministry of Labour? I would like an
answer.

some importance that required local
knowledge of agriculture, and, consequently, in the various districts we had
advertisements in the local papers asking
for some person with a knowledge of
local conditions and a knowledge of

NUMBER OF UNEMPLOYED.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the total
number of unemployed in Northern Ireland in 1938 as compared with 1923.
Mr. GORDON: The average number
of persons registered at the employment
exchanges in Northern Ireland over the
year 1923
was 47,000. The average
number registered over the first 10
months of this year was 92,000.
The two figures are not, however, comparable. In the interval there had been
an increase of almost 100,000 in the
insured population. The conditions for
the receipt of benefit had been relaxed
and the inducement to maintain registration consequently increased, while
other factors, for example the franking
at the exchanges of National Health
Insurance cards under the new Arrears
Scheme, have contributed to make the
enumeration of unemployment to-day
much more comprehensive than it was 15
years ago.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.

be less than the following month and I

know.

Mr. BROWN: I rise to oppose this
Clause, as I have done in regard to preceding Clauses, because it contains a provision imposing a fine of £50 on anyone
who discloses any information obtained
by him in the exercise of any power conferred on him. I suggest that the only
effect of such a Clause will be to
increase the number of inmates in jails,
and surely that should not be our object
here. I cannot conscientiously vote for
a Clause that is going to hold over the
heads of farmers the threat of a fine of
£50. If you examine the penalties laid
down in the criminal code for certain
offences you will find a great variation
between those penalties and the penalty
set
out in this Clause. In the

nature as this? Farmers are to be prosecuted and jailed just as they have been
prosecuted for the recovery of land
annuities. Are we going to impose a

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: With
regard to Clause 10, as hon. Members
will see this Clause requires a little legal
explanation. It is sought to be provided
that the scheme shall only operate
if and so long as there is in force such
certificate of a Secretary of State as
may be given under section twentyeight of an Act passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom and
entitled "the Agricultural Marketing
Act, 1933."
That is to say, it shall only operate in
so far as it involves or may involve a
matter in respect of which there is a
limitation on our powers of legislation.
Hon. Members will recollect that our
powers of legislation, under the Act of
1920, are in some respects limited. One
of those limitations extends outside our
jurisdiction. As far back as 1933 a
Statute passed in the Imperial Parliament, the Agricultural Marketing Act of
1933, dealt with this point. A difficulty
might arise in connection with agricultural marketing schemes which were
contemplated by the Imperial Statute of
1933 as well as our Statutes in Northern
Ireland. This difficulty which might
arise in view of the limitation of the
legislative power of the Northern Ireland
Parliament was provided for by Section.
28 of that Imperial Statute of 1933.
I do not propose to trouble the Committee by reading the whole of a somewhat long section, but that section
enabled this Parliament for the purpose
of schemes, of which this is one, to legislate notwithstanding the limitation
imposed by the section to which I have
referred in the Act of 1920. The only
limitation on such legislation is that
any scheme made under such legislation,
in so far as the scheme involves, or may
involve, a matter in respect of which any
limitation is so imposed, that is to say,
imposed under the Act of 1920, shall
have effect only after and so long as
there is in force a certificate given by
a Secretary of State concerning agriculture in Northern Ireland certifying that
it is expedient that the scheme or regulation, as the case may be, shall have full
effect.

move that these words be inserted for the

a more effective measure for encouraging

raids. The object of the Clause is to

the protection necessary for all members.
of the community, be they workers or

I have already expressed myself on the
principles of the Bill. On the question
of rating all one can do is to make the
Bill in such a form that whether an air
raid takes place or not every person who
might possibly supply protection should
be encouraged to do so. The Measure as

of buildings. First of all, buildings which
consist of rooms or passages or portions
of a hereditament capable of occupation
are provided for to the extent that if they
are provided solely for the purpose of airraid protection, and are not used for any
other
there shall be relief of
rates in respect of them.
purpose,
In the Amendment which I have not
moved I endeavoured to widen that relief
by adding the words "used to any substantial extent." That point raises so
many complications in regard to income.
tax that it would be impracticable, and I
have therefore abandoned it. The other
kind of building to which the Clause
refers is one which must necessarily
be used for the ordinary purposes of everyday life. For instance, if an employer or
the owner of a house puts on a specially
prepared roof for the purpose of avoiding
the results of incendiary bombs he has
altered the hereditament which is used
for purposes which have nothing to do
with air-raid precautions, but he has provided air-raid protection. The Bill
encourages such a person to do so.
There
is provision for a person who alters or
improves an old building, but there is
none for a person who erects a new building providing some feature which will
enable those in it, be they workers or
employers, to benefit in the event of an
air raid. I think that is an omission which
should be rectified and, therefore, I move
that the words in the Amendment should
be added. I believe if they are inserted
this Clause will apply not only to those
who alter an existing building, but also
those who provide for air raid precautions in new premises. The words in the
Clause "alterations or improvements"
would only relate to premises already
erected.

valued as buildings. I think I might

Suppose that two builders build a

street, the same kind of houses so far as

would be at present. The other is a row

but having a roof which will be impervious
to incendiary bombs, and windows so
designed as to become gas proof. As

stands drafted the position is undoubtedly
that the houses designed against air raids
will have a better money value and the

in a public spirit will find himself with a

the other side of the street who provided
houses with no protection whatever. If
these words are not put in it would mean
that the person who builds better houses
so far as air raid protection goes is mulcted

"(4) Where, solely for the purpose of

The object of this Amendment is really
to relieve the ratepayer. As the law
stands at the present time where a person
makes any addition to his property it
goes on the Town Clerk's list for revision,
and not only is the new property added
liable to be valued, but the entire property is liable to be revalued by reason of
that addition. The object of this subclause is if for the purpose of air-raid protection the property owner makes some
addition to the property. While that
addition will be liable to valuation, it
does not give the Commissioner of Valuation the right to value the entire property. That is the object.
Amendment agreed to.

any young person up to 16 years of age
may not work after six p.m. will be a
great inconvenience to a number of
firms. Quite a number of firms find

no
Mr. GORDON: Firms wishing to
work later than six o'clock will,

During the discussions that took place at

same discussions would take place herethe feeling was strongly expressed that

should get away early in order to continue their education at evening schools.
Mr. BEATTIE: I hope the Minister
will not accede to the hon. Member's
request. I agree that hardship could be.
imposed on any employer because of

be done to the children by asking them

I am pleased that the Minister and Parliamentary Secretary stood out for
children of this age being relieved from

Mr. MAGINESS: The Minister may
have seen a letter in the papers on this
particular Clause. I have received a
further communication asking for some
little information as to how this Clause
affects bleach works. The Minister may
have seen that the employers in 1919
agreed to a 49 hour week with regard
to bleach works. They complain that
under this Clause they cannot have continuous working by means of shifts and
cannot have a five-day week. They
complain also that the English Act gives
the Secretary of State power to allow the
period of employment of young persons
to be extended.
Mr. GORDON: I am glad that the
hon. and learned Gentleman raised those
points. Hon. Members, no doubt, observed
that during the course of my speech in
the House, I referred to no industry. I
had a specific industry in my mind at
the time, but I determined that I would
make my points without referring to any
particular industry. As the hon. and
learned Gentleman has raised this question with regard to the 48-hour limit laid
down I would like to explain. We are
merely asking that women
and young
persons should have a 48-hour week the
same as applies to every industry in the
country. My argument is that I do not
see how it would dislocate industry in any
way to ask employers whose workers have
a 49-hour week to allow women and
young persons to cease work a quarter of
an hour earlier than other workers in the
industry.
The operatives in the cotton and bleaching trade in Lancashire have enjoyed a
week of 48 hours for many years by agreement. Henceforth under the Great
Britain Act they are to continue to enjoy
that privilege. Previously it was enjoyed
by agreement. Now they will enjoy it by
Statute. I want to thank Members
for the great help they have given me.
Every Member intimated to me the points
he desired to raise in the House. They
have come to my office, and we have discussed these points in conjunction with
our inspectors in order to see whether we
could give way on anything. I am not
giving way with regard to the 48-hour
week. They came to see whether there
was any point on which we could give
way. Every Member was perfectly satisfied with the explanations we were able to
offer them. My hon. and learned Friend
referred to the point raised in the newspapers. Exception has been taken to our
attitude.
One of the points raised was that because an agreement was come to 20 years
ago with the trade unions that that agreement should still remain in existence.
There is nothing static nowadays. We are
living in times of changes and improvement-an improvement not only in the
working conditions in factories, but in the
welfare conditions in these places. As a
result of that arrangement made at that
particular time, is it likely that any
organisation is going to allow its members.
to work a 49-hour week? There are
other things I would like to say. I am
not entering into an argument with any
person. My position as Minister of
Labour is, and will be, not to argue with
those outside or inside, but to endeavour
to reason with them so that we may come
to an amicable and satisfactory settlement
of any disagreement there may seem to
be.

We have undertaken that there shall be
an inquiry to find out first if it would
be injurious to their health; second, if
it would likely lead to permanent employment. That inquiry will be held by
an independent chairman, and we would
have to be satisfied before an extension
from 44 to 48 hours was permitted.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would be opposed
to any inquiry or conceding that request.
No inquiry could say whether a child
would be competent to work the
additional hours.
Mr. BEATTIE: In the words of the
Prime Minister, "Not an inch." The hon.
Member for Iveagh has made reference to
two letters of Mr. Cowdy in the "Belfast
News-Letter." I am given to understand that the trade union who conceded
14 hours to the bleach and dyeing industry
also had a letter in the Press.
At one
period the workers were working anything
up to 60 hours a week. In 1919 we
brought in a shorter working week, and
from that onwards we were endeavouring
to reduce the hours. I have been told
by representatives of the dyeing industry,
that it is going to be impossible for them
to get through their work satisfactorily.
I asked why? I was told that if a worker
was engaged in the process of dyeing an
article blue, and he had to knock off
before the process was completed, it
meant that the product was spoiled.
That was an impossibility in the dyeing
industry, and it meant that the Government wanted to close the industry down.
I am not a supporter of the Government,
but I would not accept dictation like
that. I ask the Minister to hold fast to
the 48-hour week for women and
children. It is right that they should
have that protection under the Clause.
The industry will go on the same in the
future as in the past. If the firm has to
close down, well, I am sorry.

CLAUSE 129 (Powers of inspectors).
Question proposed, "That the Clause

Mr. MAGINESS: I do not object to
the first part of the first sub-clause
which gives the inspector power to examine
either alone or in the presence of any
other person any person whom he finds
in a factory, but I object to the last part
of the sub-clause giving the inspector
power
to require every such person to be so
examined and to sign a declaration of
the truth of the matters respecting
which he is so examined; so, however,
that a person shall not be required
under this provision to answer any
question or to give any evidence tending to criminate himself;
I suggest that that gives the inspector
powers far exceeding the powers given to
any other inspector under any Act or, indeed, a member of the police force. Not only
can he examine a person, which is only
right and proper, but he can require the
person to sign a document and state that
that document is true. That is giving
him inquisitorial powers. Moreover, if at
person refuses to sign that document and
refuses to make the statement he is com-
Factories Bill-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Maginess]
mitting an offence under this Measure,
and can be heavily fined, and, in some
cases, sentenced to imprisonment for a
short period.
Those are powers which no inspector
should have, and while I am informed
that they have been sparingly, if ever,
used-I accept that statement implicitly
-it is not a question of how the power is
used so much as a question of whether the
power ought to be there or not.
A policeman taking a statement from
a person whom he afterwards summons
can ask questions, but if the person does
not answer he does not commit an offence.
I suggest that a factory inspector is given
more power under this Bill for the purposes of this Measure then a policeman
has in the course of his ordinary duty.
The inspector is being given extraordinary
powers, powers which it is most unusual
to give persons in the capacity of police
or inspectors of factories. I would ask
the Minister to withdraw the latter part
of the sub-clause. The first part gives
sufficient powers because if a witness does
not answer he can be summoned to the
petty sessions court and there he can be
forced to answer. To give an inspector
power to go to a person's house and force
him there and then to sign a declaration
is going further than there is any necessity for and is going further than is wise.
Mr. GORDON: We have to be very
careful that no person is employed in a

would be very anxious to meet the request

virtue of his
age. If a person is working

been employed on overtime during the
past number of days and how many hours
he has been so employed. In order to get
a report the inspectors have a right to
obtain evidence.
I would like to draw the hon. and
learned Gentleman's attention to the concluding portion of sub-clause (1) (f):
A person shall not be required under
this provision to answer any question or
to give any evidence tending to criminate himself;
Therefore, there is no necessity for him to
give evidence that would criminate himself. I hope the hon. and learned Gentleman will not press me to withdraw such
powers from the inspectors because it
would leave them rather weak in
endeavouring to carry out their duties in
connection with this comprehensive Measure.
Clause ordered to stand part of the Bill.

always been a constitutional axiom in

This sub-clause means that a man
guilty until he is proved innocent. This
is
is a Clause that should be inserted very

large extent the credit and reputation.

""
a
Take the case of a young person who
obtains employment and has no birth
certificate. The inspector comes along
and says to the employer, "Prove to me
that this employee is over 16 years of
age. The answer of the employer is, “I
cannot do it because the employee has no
birth certificate." He is then summoned
and if the young person appears to the
resident magistrate to be younger looking
than 16 the onus is cast upon the employer
to prove that he is not. He must produce
documentary proof that he has not got
and can never get, but the onus is cast
upon him to prove that the appearance of
the child is deceptive. I submit that no
such burden should be cast upon a citizen
of Northern Ireland. If it were impossible for the prosecution to prove that the
employee was under 16 it would be equally
impossible for the employer to prove that
she was 16. If there is documentary
evidence for the defendant then there can
be documentary evidence for the prosecution, but this Clause lays it down that in
case there is no documentary evidence
then the onus is cast upon the defendant.

Mr. GRANT: I beg to move:
"That the Order in Council made by the
Governor of Northern Ireland on the 30th
March, 1938, under Section 65 of the
Unemployment Insurance Act (Northern
Ireland), 1936, for increasing the maximum number of additional days of
benefit, other than agricultural benefit,
payable in benefit year,
and for
augmenting the increase in the weekly
rate of benefit other than agricultural
benefit, payable in respect of adult dependents, be hereby approved."
a
It is the duty of the Unemployment
Insurance Statutory Committee to report
to the Minister of Labour in Great Britain
on the financial condition of the Unemployment Fund there at the end of each
calendar year.
In their report on the
state of the fund at the 31st December,
1937, the Committee estimated that there
was a surplus which they recommended
should be spent in the following way:-
(a) By increasing in benefit years beginning on or after 1st January, 1938, the
number of "additional days" of benefit
which may be drawn under the general
scheme by claimants with good industrial
records, and (b) by increasing from 9s to
10s per week the rate of benefit payable
under the general scheme in respect of
an adult dependant.
With Parliamentary approval an Order
giving effect to these recommendations
was made by the Minister of Labour in
Great Britain on the 25th March, 1938,
and the provisions of that Order were
made applicable to Northern Ireland by
the Unemployment Insurance (Additional
Benefits) Order (Northern Ireland),
1938, for which the approval of the House
is now sought.
In accordance with the provisions of the
Unemployment Insurance Act (Northern
Ireland), 1936, under which the Order
was made, it would cease to have effect on
the expiration of twelve months from the
date on which it came into operation unless at some time prior to the expiration
of that period it had been approved by
Parliament.
Question put, and agreed to.
Unemployment Insurance (Additional

while the experience of the Agricultural

not yet sufficient to enable precise conclusions to be drawn, there was a surplus
in the finances of the Scheme that might

week in the rate of agricultural insurance contributions payable respectively by workers over the age of
18 years and their employers.

per week in the agricultural benefit
rate payable to young men between
18 and 21 years.

March, 1938. The provisions of that
Order were made applicable to Northern

(Additional Benefits and Reduction in
Contributions) (Agriculture) Order (Northern Ireland), 1938, which is the subject
of the present Motion.

date on which it came into operation unless approved by Parliament in the meantime.

Oral Answers to Questions.
UNEMPLOYMENT ASSISTANCE
ALLOWANCES.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware of the
drastic reduction in allowances that is
being put into operation by the Unemployment Assistance Board in Northern
Ireland, and whether he is prepared to
issue an order cancelling these reductions during the winter months.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): The Unemployment Assistance
Board is not making any general reductions in allowances as suggested by the
hon. Member. On the contrary, in accordance with the Unemployment Assistance.
(Winter Adjustments) Regulations (Northern Ireland), 1938, which were made
recently, the Board is preparing to increase the allowances of certain claimants
to meet winter conditions. It is true
that from time to time allowances. of
individual applicants are revised either
upwards or downwards if such adjustments are found to be required for any
reason, but in all such cases the applicant has a right of appeal against the
new assessment.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
an unemployed deputation met the right
hon. Gentleman two days ago and stated
to him the large percentage of reductions.
that have taken place in the allowances
as granted by the Unemployment Assistance Board? Is it not a fact that the
Unemployment Assistance Board is now
regulating assessments in accordance
with the poverty wage which the worker
was in receipt of at the time of last
employment, and is it a fact that upwards of 90 per cent. of the claims now
being assessed are reduced to allowances
far below the poverty line? If the right
hon. Gentleman wishes proof of my
statements I am prepared to table them
for him.
Mr. GORDON: The questions raised
by the hon. Member are debatable ones.
It is true a deputation did come to see
me and did offer some criticism, but at the
same time they admitted that they were
treated fairly by the Board. Each individual stated that in his application he
was treated fairly and with due courtesy,
and so far as the Board is concerned he
had no objection to offer. As to the
other points raised by the hon. Gentleman it would be exceedingly difficult to
examine them now.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
the unemployed deputation is coming in
a fortnight's time to table proof of their
statement in regard to the very drastic
cuts that are taking place during the
winter months?
Mr. GORDON: I think it would be
better if I did not anticipate their
coming. I will deal with the questions
raised in a sympathetic manner.

3. Mr. BROWN asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether the detailed consultations with the architect referred to in
recent answer with regard to Ballyveamore School could not have been initiated
by the Ministry at least a month earlier
than they actually were, and within a
week or fortnight of the original application for approval; whether she is aware
that in case of prolonged delay in dealing with tenders there is grave risk lest
the cost of schools should be forced up
by the withdrawal of those who tender at
keen prices on the assumption that work
will proceed at an early date; whether
attention was called to the risk of loss
through withdrawals by the Down County
Regional Education Committee at a time
when the acceptance of a tender for the
£15,000 school at Dromore was held up,
and whether, in all the circumstances, the
Minister will direct that applications for
the approval of tenders be given precedence over certain other business and
dealt with in the least possible time.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): It is
necessary to explain that not only was
the tender for the new Ballyveamore
school about 50 per cent. in excess of the
approved estimate, but that had it been
accepted the cost of the school would have
been approximately £8 per school place
higher than in the case of another public
elementary school recently provided by the
same Regional Education Committee.
The original Ballyveamore tender had,
therefore, to be considered in a specially
detailed way
and from more than one
point of view. In the circumstances,
and having regard to the number of
building cases then under consideration
by the Ministry
Ministry and its
its technical
advisers on behalf of the Down County
Regional Education Committee alone,
the answer to the first part of the hon.
Member's question is in the negative.
The answer to the second part of the
question is also in the negative; the
position visualised by the hon. Member
appears to be based on the assumption
that prices would rise, whereas it is
possible that on the other hand they
might fall; in any case, I am not prepared to regard as a "keen tender" a
tender which materially exceeds the
approved estimate, nor do I agree that
reasonable time spent upon the examination of such a tender-which in the case
of Ballyveamore, resulted in a saving of
nearly £600-can accurately be described
as delay.
The reply to the third part of the
question is in the negative; what is suggested by the hon. Member in the last
part of the question is already being done
as far as possible.

Lady if it is a fact that Down County

5. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he is aware that in
the case of grants under the Physical
Training and Recreation Act the total
that can be obtained in each case is
50 per cent. of the expenditure; whether
the taxpayers are being asked to bear
100 per cent. of the expenditure in the
case of the new playing fields to be provided for Civil Service staff at Stormont
at a cost of £9,000, and whether such
preferential treatment in the case of the
latter expenditure can be reconciled with
the oft repeated statements in the House
that city and provincial interests receive
equal treatment.
The PRIME MINISTER: The reply
to the first two parts of the question is
in the affirmative.
As regards the last part, the hon.
Member will appreciate that as the
Government is in the position of the
employer to the Civil Service, it is important that it should set an example, which
it is hoped that other employers will
follow. I cannot follow the hon. Member's suggestion that this is an example
of preferential treatment to the city;
firstly, the Civil Service represents the
whole of Northern Ireland; secondly, the
greater part of the Stormont estate,
including these playing fields, is situated
in County Down, and not in the Belfast
urban area; and, thirdly, the persons
who will use the grounds do not by any
means all live in Belfast.
Mr. BROWN: Can the Prime Minister tell us under what Statute this grant
of 100 per cent. was given, if it is a fact
that it was not made under the Physical
Training and Recreation Act?

whether it is the intention of the Government to bring in legislation to have the

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The Shops Act
Committee has not yet submitted its

8. Mr. MINFORD asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he is aware
of the fact that 52 houses in the town
of Antrim were condemned by the
medical officer of the Ministry of Home
Affairs, and what steps he proposes to
take to see that suitable accommodation
is provided for the people who occupy
them.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The use of
the word "condemned" in the hon.
Member's question may, perhaps, give
rise to misunderstanding. In the
statutory sense of the word a house is
not condemned until declared by the
medical officer of health for the district
to be unfit for human habitation.
Actually only three houses in Antrim
have been so condemned. It is, however, a fact that an investigation made
by a medical inspector of my Department, on the request of the Antrim
Town Commissioners, would suggest that
there are about 52 houses in the town
which are definitely below the presentday standard for working-class houses.
Antrim, being a town under Town
Commissioners, the housing authority is
primarily the Rural District Council,
although the Commissioners themselves
have, or can obtain, powers under the
Housing of the Working Classes Act, and
the whole question of housing in Antrim
is at present under consideration by the
Rural District Council in connection
with their labourers' cottage scheme.
The draft scheme, as it stands at
present, provides for about 27 labourers'
cottages in the neighbourhood of the
town, 15 close to it, and the other 12
within two miles, and it is possible that
the Council, as a result of further facts
which have been put before them by the
Ministry, may consider the provision of
some further houses necessary and
justifiable.
The hon. Member will, however, I am
sure, appreciate that there are large
numbers of working-class houses throughout the Province that are below presentday standard, some of which may require
to be replaced, and some of which would
be capable of being dealt with under the
repairs provisions of the new Bill, if, and
when, these provisions are given statutory effect, and while we all hope that all
these houses will be eventually dealt with

Mr. BROWN: I have no intention
of occupying the House at any length

brought into it. Now I want to point
out that the Committee to be appointed
under the Bill will include men chosen
to represent the producers of potatoes,
in other words, farmers may be members of the Committee. The Clause to
which I object sets out that any person
removing or attempting to remove
potatoes from Northern Ireland to Great
Britain would be liable on conviction
to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months or a fine of £100, or
"to both such imprisonment and fine."
Once more I defy contradiction of the
fact that the fine of £100 and the
imprisonment of three months can be
made applicable to farmers, as they are
in fact and in law in every respect
applicable to farmers.
Furthermore, there is the question of
the fine of £50. I was told once more
that that was not applicable to farmers.
I say farmers can come under this. The
Clause says:
Any person who discloses any information obtained by him in the exercise
of any power conferred on him or on
the Potato Marketing Committee or
on the Ministry of Agriculture by or
under the provisions of this Act shall
be guilty of an offence against the
principal Act and be liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding fifty
pounds:
A farmer can be a member of that
Potato Marketing Committee. Therefore, in regard to both these Clauses the
farmers of Northern Ireland are liable
to be fined.

Major PANTER: I noticed in this
House on the afternoon of October 26th,
and also in Hansard, that the hon.
Member for Antrim has mistaken me
for the hon. Member for South Down
(Mr. Brown) and has therefore accused
me of denouncing this Bill in toto and
in globo. I want to say at the outset
that I have been trying for a week or
more to address this House on the Bill
before us, but have not had the opportunity owing to the effusive speeches of
other hon. Members. Not only do I
support this Bill, but I welcome it as
a definite step forward in the right
direction.
A very great number of farmers in
my constituency are potato growers, and
I consider that they have a legitimate
grouse with regard to the price they
receive and what the consumer pays, as
the difference is very considerable and
to my mind altogether unwarranted.
In making this statement it is only right
that I should prove it to the best of my
ability. In order to do this I have personally visited several potato growers in
my constituency and asked them what
they received for one cwt. potatoes. They
said ls 9d. I went to Stewart's Cash
Stores on my way to this House and
asked them what they wanted for one
cwt. potatoes, and they said 3s 6d.
This morning I telephoned from Newcastle to Turners, in Belfast, and they
said they wanted 4s 6d a cwt. If the
farmer only gets 1s 9d and you pay 3s 6d
in the shop, that is an addition of ls 9d,
or a difference of 100 per cent. The
poorer people generally buy potatoes by
the stone and pay 9d or 10d, which
works out roughly at 6s a cwt. That
means a difference of 200 per cent.
There is, I maintain, something wrong
with such a system.
The Minister of Agriculture must, I
think, be congratulated on recognising
this fact and on having the vision to
produce a Bill in order to obviate this
discrepancy in price between grower and
consumer. Two points in the Bill are,
to my mind, of outstanding importance,
and as they will benefit the grower and
certainly not increase the price to the
consumer, I believe that both sides of
this House will acclaim this Bill.
What are these points to which I
allude? The first is that all losses
due to incompetent marketing or undercutting will ultimately
ultimately benefit the
grower; in other words, the Bill before
the House will make it possible for the
incompetent merchant to be eliminated
and undercutting to be prevented. The
second point contemplates the direct
fixing of growers' prices.
Naturally if growers' prices are fixed,
excessive middleman profits will be
eliminated and presumably a working
margin fixed for dealers, in the same
way as has been done with eggs. Here
then we see a constructive policy being
advocated which I am convinced that
the hon. Members of this House and the
farmers in general will agree is preferable to a destructive policy as always
evinced by the hon. Member for South

In New Zealand they have a population of 1,000,000 compared with
1,350,000 in Northern Ireland. The
Government here has been in office for
17 or 18 years without any opposition.
From the day it took over office until
now it has been going from bad to
worse. What does the future hold?
The position is going to get worse. The
Government do not consider the needs
and requirements of industry. A
Labour Government came into power in
New Zealand in 1935. They had an
unemployment problem just the same
as we have, but on a larger scale.
What did they do during their first year
of office? They reduced the unemployment figure by 50 per cent. The next
thing they did was to increase the relief
to those who were still unemployed.
They granted £1 per week to single
persons, £1 15s to married people, and
8s for each child. To-day, after three
years, they have again been returned to
power, not by an increased number of
representatives but by an increased vote.
They are working towards the elimination of unemployment from their midst.
This evil of unemployment and
poverty should not exist in any State.
That is one of the things any
Government should set its mind to

been proved by the New Zealand Government in its three years' work. This

There are, to my mind, five Ministries

might also add that these Acts were

Rev. Professor CORKEY: I rise to
second the Amendment which has been
so ably and so wisely moved by the hon.
Member for Dock. The Motion before
the House calls our attention to one of
the greatest social evils which have ever
befallen our country or any other
country. There are, it seems to me, two
great problems before the world at the
present time. One is the problem of unemployment and the other is the problem
of war. I do not think it improper that
either of these great subjects should be
brought before this House.
I have no criticism to make of the
spirit behind the words of those who
moved the Motion and seconded it, indeed I am in agreement with many of
the things they said. I feel, however,
that in its present form this Motion is
not very satisfactory and stands in need
of amendment. That is why I have
agreed to second its amendment. First
of all, the Motion is purely negative, but
in addition there is a suggestion behind
it which seems to me to be unfair and
untrue. It is implied in this Motion,
which has been described by one of the
speakers as a vote of censure, that the
Government of Northern Ireland have
power to solve the unemployment
problem.
I think that is not a fair suggestion
to make, and it is unreasonable to
criticise the Government on the ground
of a suggestion. The Motion ignores the
limitations of the Government and also
the wide ramifications of the unemployment problem. It is not caused by any
circumstances or any fact under the
immediate control of our Government,
and consequently it is not in the power
of our Government to deal with the circumstances which have brought this great
misfortune upon us. They are worldwide and we in Ulster are suffering to
some extent from the effects of worldwide events over which we have no control. The war in China has reacted very
seriously against some of our industries in
Northern Ireland, and, consequently,
while I am in agreement with a great
deal that has been said by the Mover
and Seconder of the Motion, I feel it calls
for amendment, and I am thus seconding the Amendment which has been
drawn up.
It is very easy to make statements
which are verbally correct and yet which
have in them suggestions which are incorrect. Clever people can do that quite
well. A Member of the Opposition, for
example might table a Motion to the
effect that in the opinion of this House
the Northern Government has done
nothing to improve the climate of the

absolutely true verbally. I can imagine
some of the speakers in the Opposition-

I feel I am justified in qualifying it in

As well as want of heart.

ings, and their moral dangers and

We pride ourselves upon our social

compared with the standards set up in
most other countries of the world; but I
venture to say that anyone with a

situation with which we are faced in this

We are faced with a new situation in
the world to-day. We are all familiar
with the causes, or with some of the
causes, of this situation. It is easy to
name some of them. We have, for
example, the increasing introduction of
labour-saving machinery, which to some
extent makes for unemployment, or we
are accustomed to the idea of the increasing competition for our export trade
throughout the world, which depresses
industries that are engaged in this export
trade and makes it more difficult for
them to carry on, and consequently tends
to increase the number of unemployed;
or we think of the obstruction of trade
that is presented by the increasing tariff
walls throughout the world, another new
circumstance in the present age with
which we have to deal. It is not
generally known that the Great War
resulted in the extension of tariff walls
in the world by 10,000 miles. Tariff
walls are always very fine for the individuals who get the benefit of them, but,
looking at the world
as a whole,
economists believe that they hamper
trade, tend to make people poor, and
create unemployment.
Another factor which is often cited as
a cause of unemployment, and to which
importance is attached by those who
have studied the subject, is the excessive
tendency of some people to save money
for the purpose of investing it.
Occasionally sums are set aside for
investment that cannot be invested;
industries cannot absorb all the money
that people possess, with the result that
a
there is a jam in machinery and there
are those periods of slump and depression which make for unemployment.
All these are circumstances which create
new situation that has presented us
with a tremendous standing army in
unemployed people, whose position is not
enviable, and many of whom are in semistarvation, especially when there are
families.
Our unemployment insurance system has
been devised to deal with this matter.
It is a great system, it is a splendid
system, and the people who criticise the

hostility, who criticise what they call
the dole, ought to remember that if it

that many people in receipt of unemployment benefit are indeed in very great
necessity.
Perhaps you will allow me to mention
a couple of other facts. In a survey of
conditions in Bristol, undertaken
recently by the students of the University
there, it was discovered that in families
where there were four children or more
52 per cent. of such households were
living below what is called the poverty
line, a line fixed by the British Medical
Association as suitable for the physical
needs of the people. The second fact is
more interesting still it concerns a
survey made recently in an area in
Belfast, and the facts disclosed by this
survey in our own city are even more
alarming than those which are disclosed
by the survey that was made by the
students of Bristol University.
May I say that this survey was made
by a number of good-hearted young men
and women belonging to the Methodist
Church, and that they made it in our
own city in order that the facts might be
known. They investigated carefully the
position in some 705 households in a
district in a city which is not a slum
area. They discovered that 58 per cent.
of those households were living below the
poverty line, and the standard which they
fixed was 6s a week for food and clothes
for an adult, and 4s a week for a child.

Other countries that were carrying out

we carry on are now formidable rivals

only to reflect for a moment on these conditions to understand how extremely delicate trade is and how easy it is to transfer
from country to country operations which

country. Countries which pay lower

low, aggravate competition, and adversely
affect the markets where we sell our products. These are realities we have to
face.
Take shipbuilding, which was referred

and Pottinger. We are told by shipowners that the cost of building a ship
is so high that they must postpone their
