SPECIAL CONSTABULARY
RESIGNATIONS.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will state the
number of "B" Special Constabulary
attached to the Whitehouse Sub-District
who have resigned, or who have otherwise severed their connection with the
Special Constabulary during last summer;
whether a "B" Sergeant with 15 years'
service was discharged for alleged "unsatisfactory service," and whether he
will state what the unsatisfactory service
consisted of; whether the County
Commandant called a meeting of the
men at the Legion Hut, Whitehouse, at
8 p.m., on

Tuesday, 31st May, 1938;
whether he will state what the Commandant said to the men when so
assembled, and whether as a result of
that meeting practically the entire men
of the Station, about 25, left or were
obliged to leave the force.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The facts of the
incident to which the hon. Member
refers are, briefly, as follows:
On the appointment of a Sub-
District Commandant of the "B"
Special Constabulary in succession to
the former Sub-District Commandant
who had resigned, 21 members of the
sub-district (including an Acting
Sergeant, to whom possibly the hon.
Member refers in the second part of
his question), who desired the appointment of an officer of their own
selection, were unwilling to continue
to serve. In these circumstances the
County Commandant arranged a
parade in order that he might have
an opportunity of explaining to the
men the reasons for the appointment
of the officer in question. The men,
however, persisted in their attitude,
and in these circumstances there was
no option but to discontinue the subdistrict. A new sub-district has,
however, been established at Glengormley under the Sub-District Commandant in question and is working
most satisfactorily.
I may add that such an instance of
indiscipline on the part of members of
the "B" Force is, I am glad to say,
entirely unprecedented, and is altogether
foreign to the loyal spirit which
actuates the Force generally.
Mr. NIXON: Would the Minister not
think that perhaps a little more tact on
the part of the authorities would have
avoided the whole thing and have retained these men?

authorities have shown tact, because the
men and

Sir DAWSON BATES: Lieut.-Col.
Sargent's salary is at the rate of £950
per annum, and he is in receipt of
uniform allowance of £5 per annum. He

Written Answers.
TRANSPORT BOARD AND
RAILWAY COMPANIES.
Mr. NIXON asked the Prime Minister
whether he can state what business was
discussed at the meeting of the Transport
Board and Railway Company representatives recently held at Stormont, and
presided over by the Prime Minister;
whether he can state the total loss incurred by the Transport Board up to
date; whether he is aware that there is
widespread apprehension that the Government contemplate restoring the railway
monopoly by merging the over-riding
control of all public transport in the
Railway Companies; and whether the
Prime Minister would make any statement to allay this apprehension.
The PRIME MINISTER: In reply to
the first part of the question, I am not
prepared to give any information as to
the matters discussed. With regard to
the remainder of the question, I have
nothing to add to the statements which
have already been made by the Government in this House except to repeat that
hon. Members will be given ample opportunity to discuss the findings of the reports, which will, I anticipate, be in the
hands of hon. Members to-morrow.
TREES ON STORMONT ESTATE.
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if trees
were cut on the Stormont Estate near
the Newtownards Road in the spring of
1937; whether two loads of these trees
were stolen; whether any report of the
larceny, and the names of the culprits,
was made to the Estate authorities.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): The reply to the first part of
the hon. Member's question is in the
affirmative.
After the receipt of tenders a contract
with a timber company for the purchase
and removal of six trees was entered into
in January, 1937. When the trees had
been removed I personally gave directions that the branches which were left
over, instead of being burned on the
spot, should be given away free as firewood to any person asking for them.
A complaint was received at the time.
that two cartloads had been removed
from the site without authority, but after
full investigation I am informed that no
such removal took place.

Written Answers
23 NOVEMBER 1938
KING'S VISIT-STORMONT CASTLE
DECORATIONS.
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he will state the name
of the firm which supplied the silk used
in decorating Stormont Castle on the
occasion of the King's Visit in 1937; the
cost of the silk; whether the silk was
returned to or bought back by the firm
which originally supplied it; whether
four webs of this silk were missing;
whether there is any information as to
where this silk went, and generally, what
is the position so far as the security of the
property in the Stormont Buildings and
Castle is concerned.
Mr. ANDREWS: In June, 1937, a
contract was placed with Messrs. Flags,
Ltd., for the decoration of various
Government buildings, etc., in preparation for the visit of Their Majesties to
Northern Ireland. The decoration of the
pavilion which was erected in the grounds
of Stormont Castle for Their Majesties'
was included in the contract, and
artificial silk was used for the interior
covering of the roof.
use
It was a condition of the contract that
the necessary materials should be supplied
by the contractors, and at the end of the
contract all the materials used in the
decorations, including the silk referred
to, were re-sold to the contractors, who
were responsible for dismantling.
The contractors did not report loss of
any materials to the Ministry and the
Ministry has no knowledge of any silk
being missing.
With regard to the last part of the
question, the furniture in all Government
buildings, including Stormont Castle, is
recorded on inventories which are in the
custody of responsible officers, and are
kept up to date.
BANK INTEREST ON
BILLS.
GOVERNMENT
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether bank interest on Northern Government Bills has recently been
almost doubled; whether the Joint Stock
Banks decided that certain Bills formerly
accepted as security for many market
loans are no longer acceptable; and
whether this action on the part of the
banks may be regarded as a want of con-
"
fidence in the economic policy of the
Government.
Mr. ANDREWS: The hon. Member is
correct in saying that the rate of interest
on Northern Ireland Treasury Bills
tendered for at the close of October was
considerably higher than has usually been
the case, the rate of the accepted tender
being 24/8 per cent. per annum.
I may add that the London Discount
Houses are very eager to secure Northern
Ireland Bills, but no doubt found themselves handicapped by the sudden decision
of the Joint Stock Banks not to rediscount Bills no matter by whom issued
other than those rediscountable at the
Bank of England. The temporary increase in the discount rate was, therefore,
due to a technical reason. I am in touch
with the interested parties, and I feel
confident that the matter will be satisfactorily adjusted. The answer to the
last part of the question is in the
negative.
LAND PURCHASE ANNUITIES.
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he would state the
number of civil bills issued in respect to
the non-payment of land annuities in
Northern Ireland during the years 1933,
1934, 1935, 1936, 1937, 1938, and the
number of farms put up for sale by the
Ministry in order to recover the outstanding land annuities during the same
periods, and the number of such farms
actually sold; the percentage of costs in
relation to the amount sued for, and
whether any such costs were borne by or
fell on the Ministry.
Mr. ANDREWS: The number of civil
bills issued for the recovery of arrears of
land purchase annuities during the six
years 1933 to 1938 inclusive is approximately 30,000, varying between a maximum of 5,900 in 1935 and a minimum of
4,436 in the present year. During the
same period of six years 449 holdings were
put up by the Ministry for sale by public
auction and 315 were sold.
The costs incidental to the civil bill
proceedings represent on the average
approximately 10 per cent. of the amounts
sued for, of which about nine per cent.
represents costs recovered from the
defaulters and one per cent. costs borne
by the Ministry.

Message from the Senate.
The Senate agree to McMullan's
Divorce Bill and Marks' Divorce Bill as
reported from the Joint Committee without amendment.
They agree to the Education Bill, the
Queen's University of Belfast Bill, the
Appropriation (No. 2) Bill, the Factories
Bill, and the Holidays with Pay Bill
without amendment.
They agree to the Hairdressers Bill, the
Marketing of Potatoes Bill, and the Air
Raid Precautions Bill with some amendments, to which they desire the concurrence of the Commons.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Hairdressers Bill.
Order for consideration of Senate's
amendments read.
CLAUSE 1 (Premises to be registered
with the local authority).
In the district of any local authority
in which this Act is in force any
premises in which the trade or business of barber or hairdresser is carried
on shall be registered by the owner or
occupier thereof with the local
authority in such manner as the
Minister of Home Affairs may by
regulations prescribe, and any person
using or causing to be used for any
such purpose as aforesaid any premises
not duly registered for that purpose
shall be guilty of an offence under this
Act.
Senate amendment: Leave out "owner
or" ("registered by the owner").
Mr. BYRNE: I beg to move, "That
this House do agree with the Senate in
the said Amendment.'
The effect of this Amendment is that
only the person carrying on a barber's
business will be held responsible for any
offences that may occur under the Bill.
This seems reasonable, as the owner of
the premises very often will have
nothing whatever to do with the business.
Mr. BEATTIE: The time has now
arrived when Members of this House
should make up their minds in regard to
their standing as legislators. Also,
private Members bringing forward
measures should clearly understand that
Members will not be led at all times by
the interpretation of words in amendments coming from the Senate in a light
fashion. The hon. Member for Falls
says it would not be fair for the owners
of premises to be held responsible for any
act or misconduct that might take place
on those premises. I am not a lawyer,
or the son of a lawyer, but I understand
that the owner of premises is held responsible under all Acts of Parliament.
The owner of premises let for a barber's
business, I am sure, would also be held
responsible in law. That is a layman's
view of the law as it applies to the
ownership of premises.
I would ask the Member for Falls what
he means when he asks the House to
delete the words "or owner" and leave
in "occupier." His interpretation of the
Senate's amendment does not convey the
real meaning of the deletion of the two
words. I have in my possession the Bill
as returned from the Senate, and certainly it is not a private Member's Bill
I would like to support on the Second
Reading. Having given a fair measure
of support to the Bill I must now oppose
these words being deleted. If the amendment is accepted there is going to be an
innovation in the lives of the people of
Northern Ireland which is unknown in
any other country. Therefore, I move
that this amendment which the Member
for Falls has accepted be rejected by this
House.
Mr. SPEAKER: The remedy the hon.
Member has is, of course, to go into the
Lobby against it.
Mr. HENDERSON: If a crime is
being committed by persons who are
tenants of property it would not be fair
that the owner should be prosecuted.
Take a barber's shop. Revolutions have
been preached in barbers' shops, and the
owners knew nothing about them. Even
Unionists own barbers' shops in Belfast,
and revolutions are being preached in
them day in and day out against the
atrocities of the Government. Supposing
a crime is committed in a barber's shop,

Mr. CAMPBELL: I am extremely

This Bill has no parallel in any other
legislature I do not know of any other

Act and I think that this new Subclause is also very uncommon. What does
it do? It authorises the officer of a local
authority to enter and inspect at any
reasonable time on production of his
warrant any premises-that is to say, a
factory, or shop, or private dwellinghouse-which he has reason to believe are
used for the purpose of carrying on the
trade or business of a barber.
It does not even say any reasonable
time by day. It may be by day or night,
and, therefore, under this new Sub-clause,
which is exceptional in Northern Ireland
and without parallel in any other community, an official, not a member of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary wearing
uniform, but an official vested by the
local authority, will have power at any
time of the day or night to enter any
private house which he of his own volition
believes to be a barber's shop. The House
may agree to it, but I wish to point out
that we are doing something which goes
a great deal beyond any power of entry
given to any authority, either police or
private, of entering a private house.
Quite recently the Minister of Labour
and the Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Labour piloted through this
House a Factories Bill. I may say that
they both belonged to the working class
at one time. They did their work exceedingly well and skilfully, and they are
a credit to their class. In that Bill you
find power of entry. Clause 129 of that
Bill gives an inspector, who is a recognised officer of the Ministry, the power of
entry by day. There are not many of
those inspectors. They are men of responsibility, culture, and standing. The
Minister and the Parliamentary Secretary
were careful to provide that even in the
case of a factory the power of entry should
only be by day, but this Sub-clause

THE PROCLAIMED MEETING AT
NEWTOWNBUTLER.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adourn."-
(Sir Wilson Hungerford.)
Mr. CAMPBELL: On the adjournment of the House I wish to raise a question of administration dealing with
the department of the Minister of Home
Affairs. I hope to speak with brevity and
also with restraint. I do hope my speaking with restraint is not to be taken as
an index of want of strong indignation
with regard to this act of administration.
Last week the Minister of Home Affairs
issued an order proclaiming a meeting of
Nationalists fixed for last Sunday in
Newtownbutler, County Fermanagh. It
was a meeting fixed to be held in an overwhelmingly Nationalist district. There
was not the slightest danger of any peril
to or breach of the peace. The theme of
the meeting was perfectly legitimate-the
impolicy and injustice of the Government
of Ireland Act, popularly known as the
Partition Act. That Act is an Act of
the Parliament at Westminster. The
Parliament which made it can unmake it.
That Parliament is the supreme overriding authority in this area. It legislates
for this area and administers in this area.
It supplies the funds and the force for the
carrying on of a subordinate Parliament.
Matters have now come to this pass for
the Nationalists of Northern Ireland that
in this area under Imperial rule a peaceable meeting called for the redress of
grievances inflicted by an Imperial Act is
met with violent repressive action on the
part of the Executive. The pretext of
the proclamation was specious and
spurious. It was a threat of undisclosed
agents provocateurs to hold a counterdemonstration. The Minister of Home
Affairs seized on the pretext with eagerness and alacrity. The Nationalist meeting was to be crushed. The Special
Powers Act was ready to hand as always
for opponents. It was to be addressed by
Members of this House and Members of
the House of Commons at Westminster.
It was not a meeting of irresponsibles. It
was a meeting duly, peaceably and lawfully convened, and would have been
perfectly orderly. There was not even
the colour of probability of any disturbance being caused until this counterdemonstration idea was launched. I know
that featherheads at Stormont and elsewhere are crowing over this proclamation
as a masterstroke. It reminds me of the
story of a distinguished poet who when a
minor poet was appointed Poet Laureate,
said- I wonder what he was thinking
of when he got his appointment."
friend said " It is very hard to say what
a bantam is thinking of when it is crowing."

side is concerned it is directed with the

think that by this lying propaganda.
directed from Dublin, they may accomplish this object through England, having

matters of administration, that is,
whether a Minister is properly administering the law passed by this House.
Mr. HENDERSON: There is a case
in point, where a man's unemployment
assistance allowance was reduced to such
an extent that he found himself in the
plight I have described. The allowances
paid to the people are being reduced
every day, and the cost of living is going
up. I do not want to embarrass you,
Mr. Deputy-Speaker. We have sat here
for about 27 hours, at a cost to the taxpayers of this country of tens of
thousands of pounds, and we are leaving
this House to-day without one solitary
means of solution of the problem having
been brought forward.
Minister.
Mr. HENDERSON: I am criticising
the Minister of Labour in this respect,
that the grants made to the unemployed
at the present time are not sufficient to
keep them, and that thereby the morale
of the people is being lowered. The
pittance that these people get is absolutely terrible, and could not possibly
give them an opportunity of living in
decency. I am speaking now on behalf
of thousands of men all over the country
who have been reduced to such an extent
that they receive no unemployment
benefit at the present time.
-
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER: That,
again, is going outside the matters which
the hon. Member knows he can raise.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not within the
right of a Member on the Motion for the
Adjournment to raise the question of the
disqualification of insured persons?
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: We cannot discuss any Act of Parliament. We
can only discuss the methods by which
a Minister administers an Act.
Mr. HENDERSON: Is the Minister
of Finance going to reply for the Minister
of Labour, or is he going to see the fights
at the King's Hall? Where is the
Minister of Labour? He is the only one
who can say whether or not my statements
are correct. I warned him, and he ought
to be in the House. If something be not
done to assist the people whose means of
livelihood has been reduced by the
Government there will be a revolution,
not a religious revolution, but a revolution for bread and butter, which is more
important. Old-age pensions and blind
persons' pensions have also been reduced.
How can the Government expect old
people to live on six shillings a week just
because they happen to have two or three
shillings coming in from other sources.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: That is the
law as passed by this House, and the hon.
Member can only criticise its administration. He has been warned three times
already.
Adjournment
Adjournment
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. HENDERSON: I do not want to
run across the Deputy-Speaker of this
House.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: It is not
a question of running across me. It is a
matter of keeping within the rules of
order.
Mr. HENDERSON: You put me out
when you were not altogether correct. We
will argue that out some time; we will not
argue it now. It does not make any
difference in our friendship. The House
will rise to-morrow, and it will be March
before anything is done. The Minister
of Labour has £2,000 a year, £40 a week,
and he is not here. May I ask the
Minister of Finance to convey to him my
appeal to do something for the starving
men, women and children of this country.
I am anxious that something should be
done for them between now and March,
and if anything is done to increase their
miserable pittance it will earn my special
thanks on their behalf.
In the meantime I protest against the
way the workers of this country are being
treated. I hope the day is not far distant
when an alternative will be found for
those who do not do their duty. I do
not want a revolution, but I do want
something done. If something is not
done I will lead a fight to transfer this
Parliament, bag and baggage, back to
Westminster. That would save the cost
of administration here, and the unemployed would get better conditions than
they are getting at the present time.
appeal to the Minister of Finance to convey my message to the Minister of Labour
on behalf of the 94,000 unemployed
persons.
I
Mr. ANDREWS: There are not 94,000
persons unemployed.
Mr. HENDERSON: There are well
over 80,000 and the number will be increased to 90,000 in a week or so when
the shipyard and mills become slack.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: I have
been very patient with the hon. Member,
but he must realise that he cannot go on
in this way.
Mr. HENDERSON: May I ask the
Minister of Finance to convey my appeal
on behalf of my fellow-loyalists in Northern Ireland to the Prime Minister before
he goes away? I am most anxious that
something should be done in the way of
increasing the amounts granted to those
in distress during the winter, and that
special efforts should be made to find work
for as many as possible.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I can appreciate that the hon. Member is anxious
about bulbs and cut flowers, but, as Mr.
Deputy-Speaker said quite rightly, the
question is one for the Imperial Government. This Parliament can do nothing
to prevent the entry of goods of that
type. I am very closely in touch with
the horticultural associations and nurserymen, but I have not had any complaints
about this matter. If the hon. Member
has a particular case in mind and will let
me know about it I will go into the matter
and see what can be done about it.
Perhaps the hon. Member will let me
know privately.
Question, "That this House do now
adjourn," put, and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at
Twenty minutes before
Six o'clock.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.

on Adulterated Wine, That they had
made progress in the matters to them
referred, and directed that a Report
thereof be made to the House, together
with the Minutes of Evidence taken before
them.
Royal Assent.

Transport Inquiry Report.

the McLintock Committee's Report?
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to inform the
hon. Member there can be no debate.
Mr. HENDERSON: The scandal must
go on for another ten days.
PROROGATION.
A Message was delivered by the
Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod as
follows:-
I am commanded by the Senate to inform this honourable House that the
Proclamation of his Grace the Governor
of Northern Ireland proroguing this present Session of Parliament is to be
communicated forthwith, and, further, I
am commanded to invite this honourable
House to attend in the Senate in order to
hear the said Proclamation.
The House went, and, having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in the
Clerk's place at the Table): I have to
report that the House has this day
attended in
the Senate, when the
Proclamation proroguing this present
Session of Parliament was read by the
Speaker of the Senate as follows:-
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION
For Proroguing the present Parliament
of Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by section.
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said Act,
that the Governor of Northern Ireland
shall, in his Majesty's name, summon,
prorogue and dissolve the Parliament of
Northern Ireland.
Prorogation
End of Session
HOUSE OF COMMONS
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that
this present Parliament of Northern
Ireland should be prorogued to the sixth
day of December, one thousand nine
hundred and thirty-eight:
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
DUKE OF ABERCORN, KNIGHT OF
THE MOST NOBLE ORDER OF THE
GARTER, KNIGHT OF THE MOST
ILLUSTRIOUS ORDER OF SAINT
PATRICK, Governor of Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation do publish
and declare his Majesty's Pleasure that
the said Parliament be, as from the reading of this Proclamation in the Parliament
of Northern Ireland, prorogued
Tuesday, the sixth day of December, one
thousand nine hundred and thirty-eight.
to
AND I do hereby further declare his
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to be
that the said Parliament shall on the said
sixth day of December, one thousand
nine hundred and thirty-eight, assemble
and be holden at Stormont for the
despatch of divers urgent and important
affairs, and the Senators and Members of
the House of Commons of Northern
Ireland are hereby required to give their
attendance accordingly.
Given this Twenty-fourth day of
November, one thousand nine hundred
and thirty-eight.
(Signed by his own hand),
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
End of the First Session (opened

Tuesday, 1st March, 1938) of the Fifth
Parliament of Northern Ireland, in the
second year of the Reign of His Majesty
King George the Sixth.

NON-CIRCULATING DOOA
YD 08452

Tuesday, 6th December, 1938.
The Second Session of the Fifth
Parliament of Northern Ireland appointed
to meet 6th December, 1938, in the
Second year of the Reign of King
George VI, was opened by the Governor
(His Grace the Duke of Abercorn, K.G.,
K.P.) in person.
The House met at Five Minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(Right Hon. H. G. H. Mulholland) in
the Chair.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod
(Major T. Dalby Hackett, D.S.O.) was
announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman Usher said:
His Grace the Governor of Northern

SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Election for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return or Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such bribery or other corrupt
practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any persons hath been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,
the same is declared to be a high crime
or misdemeanour; and this House will
proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in
any case before this House or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Question proposed, "That the Commissioner of the Royal Ulster Constabulary
do take care that, during the Session of
Parliament the passages through the
streets leading to this House be kept free
and open, and that no obstruction be
permitted to hinder the passage of Members to and from this House, and that
no disorder be allowed in the precincts of
or in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts, and that the Serjeant-at-
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that,
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear his Grace's Speech on
behalf of His Majesty to both Houses of
Parliament, of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The Speech
is as follows:-
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
It is a source of general satisfaction
that on the occasion of the inauguration of the Second Session of this
present Parliament the international
position has considerably improved.
The critical situation, which has
happily passed, called forth from our
people a manifestation of their constant readiness to respond to any call
which may be made on them to assist
in the defence of the Realm.
It is a matter of profound regret to
my Ministers that, owing to the unsettled conditions in many countries,
unemployment remains at a high level.
It is, however, gratifying that the
number of persons unemployed in
Northern Ireland has steadily declined
since July. My Ministers are hopeful
that the present downward trend in
the unemployment rate will be maintained, although, unfortunately, the
disturbing factors in world affairs may
prevent any substantial improvement
in the immediate future.
I trust, however, that the resumption of overseas purchases of our
manufactures on a normal scale, particularly in the United States of
America, will not be long postponed
and that, in view of the satisfactory
Trade Agreement concluded between
the Government of that country and
His Majesty's Government in the
United Kingdom, the position of our
linen industry will thereby be
improved.
I am gratified that the stimulus
provided by the increase in the rate of
Unemployment Relief Grants has
resulted in the promotion of a large
number of schemes of public utility
by local authorities. Since the 1st
January last, fifty schemes, involving
a total expenditure of approximately
five hundred and fifty thousand
pounds have been sanctioned, as have
also a large number of agricultural
improvement schemes which have from
their inception provided spells of employment for more than seven thousand
unemployed farm labourers. I am
pleased to learn that the Government
is carrying out works of public utility
such as new and improved police
barracks, employment exchanges, and
King's Speech
King's Speech

new Post Offices, which are providing
substantial employment to the building and allied industries.
I note with satisfaction that the
facilities provided for the physical
training of unemployed persons have
met with a gratifying response on the
part of the unemployed, and have also
obtained a large measure of public
approval. I am gratified, too, that the
opportunities of training afforded by
the Government Training Centres in
Great Britain, and in the case of those
wishing to enter the British Merchant
Service by the Gravesend Sea School,
continue to be appreciated by young
men in Northern Ireland, and that
those who complete the courses of
training are highly successful in
obtaining employment.
The Measure sanctioned last Session
for the encouragement of physical
training is now in full operation, and
local authorities and voluntary organisations may therefore qualify for substantial financial assistance towards
the promotion of schemes designed to
provide new or increased facilities for
physical training and recreation. I
feel confident that full advantage will
be taken of the opportunity afforded
to the appropriate promoting bodies of
making so important a contribution to
the physical well-being and general
happiness of our people.
Noteworthy legislation of the past
Session in connection with our social
services included the passing of the
Factories Act and the Holidays with
Pay Act; two Measures which will
have far-reaching, and, I trust, beneficial effects on the lives of our industrial workers. The Factories Act will
favourably influence their health,
safety and general welfare conditions in
a marked degree, and will preserve the
uniformity of the Factory Code
throughout the United Kingdom.
The statutory means now provided for
enabling a week's paid holiday to be
given annually to employees in industries covered by Trade Boards will be
much appreciated, and no doubt will
encourage the extension of the movement
to establish such schemes by
voluntary agreement in industry
generally which has become a prominent feature in recent times.

dealing with the pig and bacon industry and providing for the establishment of an Agricultural
Wages

In order that full opportunity might

this Measure will again be brought

Members of the House of Commons.

Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I am gratified to learn that the steps
taken by the Government to attract
new, and to promote the extension of
existing industries are providing a
stimulus to industrial enterprise in
Northern Ireland.
I am pleased to observe the continued activity of the local education
authorities in the construction of new
school buildings, which has shown no
relaxation during the past year. The
new works are not confined to
elementary schools alone; much has
been done to improve the buildings
used for secondary and technical
education. The passing of the
Education Act in the last Session for
the raising of the school leaving age
to fifteen is confidently expected to
lead to valuable results in the further
education of the young.
I earnestly trust that the appointment of an Agent in Great Britain will
serve to further Northern Ireland's
interests in the commercial and industrial fields and so ensure the continuance of that participation in the
reciprocal trade between the various
centres of the United Kingdom which
Northern Ireland has always enjoyed
through its happy position as a full
partner in one economic and fiscal
entity.
I pray that the blessing of Almighty
God may rest upon your deliberations.
Debate on the Address.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: I beg to move:
"That a humble address be presented to his Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland as followeth:
"Your Grace
"We, His Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Commons of
Northern Ireland, in Parliament
assembled, beg leave to offer our
humble thanks to your Grace for the
Speech which your Grace has addressed
to both Houses of Parliament."
The Gracious Speech which has just
been read refers at some length to the
work of the past Session. It affords,
and I am sure is intended to afford, an
opportunity of considering what
what the
tendency of our legislation has been, as
it were to take stock of our position and
to ascertain if possible whether the trend
of our law is in the right direction.
That question raises another, and that
is what should be the duty of this
assembly with regard to legislation. I
am sure it will not be denied that the
first duty of any Government is to
govern and to protect its people and
their institutions from hostile attack.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) But
over and beyond that any democratic
Parliament must have another duty ever
present to its mind. It must be alert
to promote and foster the common weal,
not by any violent or disruptive methods,
not by revolution, but by a steady process of evolution working justice to all.
The
is,
question then
have we
honoured that obligation in the Session
which is past? I venture to say that
when one regards the legislation that has
been passed during this present year he
can answer that question with assurance.
When one considers even the titles of
the Acts which were passed into law
during the last twelve months he can
say that the trend of legislation in this
place has been in fulfilment of that
duty. There have been passed such
Acts as the Factories Act, the Holidays
with Pay Act, the Blind Persons Act,
the Education Act, and the Physical
Training Act.
I think we should not pass from this
review without some expression of
thankfulness that it has been possible
to legislate on those lines notwithstand-
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. MacDermott]
ing the present international situation. With stress on all hands, with
trade depression, with unemployment,
with a paralysing black fear affecting every nation in their world it
is something to be thankful for that we
can legislate as we have done. We owe
thanks to the right hon. Members who
those
have introduced legislation on
lines, but I am sure they would be the
first to agree that we also owe thanks
to the fact that owing to our Constitution we are still part and parcel of a
country big enough and great enough
to uphold the torch of progress while
maintaining her defences. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
What of the future? The Gracious
Speech forecasts legislation along
different lines, but so far as it relates
to the social services I think we may
well say that the trend of the past will be
continued in the Session to come. It is
not possible to deal with all the
Measures referred to in the Gracious
Speech but there is one outstanding
Measure which I think should be
mentioned, and that is the Housing
Bill which is to be considered in the
present Session. As hon. Members will
recollect, it was referred to in the last
Gracious Speech, and I sure its
chances of becoming sound law will be
all the better for the mature consideration which the delay has enabled it to be
given.
Bad housing is a disgrace in any
civilised community, and the conscience
of any people is best judged in its back
streets. The problem has been dealt
with on previous occasions with partial
success, but if I understand this Measure
aright it is designed to provide a decent
house for the poor man, it is designed
to provide a house for the man who can
only afford to pay a small rent, and if
it succeeds in that we will have placed
upon the Statute Book a Measure well
worth while. I trust that when this
Measure becomes law it will give an
opportunity for the construction of good
houses in the town as well as in the
country, and that the local authorities
will not only be alert but enthusiastic
in their adoption of it.
In dealing with social matters the
Gracious Speech makes reference to the
question of unemployment. The ray of
hope which follows upon the recent
trade agreement with the United States
is one of the brightest pieces of reading
in the Gracious Speech. The Speech
holds, and can hold, no remedy for
unemployment, but it does refer to at
least one of the palliative remedies which
have been tried with considerable
success. I refer to the unemployment
relief grants. I am glad they are to be
continued with as much energy as in
their past and I appreciate the large
percentage-85-of the Government contribution. But I look forward to the
day when this matter of providing the
necessary work for those who have none
will not rest entirely on the local
authorities. I look forward to the day
when there will be at periodic intervals.
a national survey of all the work that is
worth doing, and when the doing of that
work will not depend upon the mood or
caprice of the local authority concerned.
The Gracious Speech turning from the
social evils of unemployment and bad
housing makes reference to the life blood
of our community, trade and industry.
It makes reference to the experiment
which has been prosecuted with so much
energy since the last Session commenced.
I refer to the establishment of the Ulster
Agent in London. It is too early to
measure yet the value of what has been
done in that direction, but I venture to
think from all we see and read that there
is no reason why the high hopes
expressed last Session should be regarded
as dimmed in any way, and I look
forward to a story of increased usefulness
as the establishment of that house makes
itself felt throughout the length and
breadth of Great Britain.
There is another matter affecting
trade and commerce, and I cannot pass
from the Gracious Speech without
mentioning it. I refer to the Transport
Act. I understand it is a tradition of
this speech not to touch upon controversial matters, but I think there are
several matters in relation to transport
which are altogether beyond party
or controversial considerations. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) The problem is
not only one of importance for every
member of the community, but it is one
of the utmost urgency. I need not
dwell on that in view of recent events,
but I would proceed to say that while
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
6 DECEMBER, 1938
it is urgent there is every need for
patience and calm deliberation of the
matter.
I can imagine no more difficult
problem, not only in its technical and
legal aspects but in its practical aspects.
In truth, it is not one problem but
many, and it is well to remember that it
is not merely the problem of the Act
passed three years ago but that it is still
the problem of transport in Northern
Ireland. If all the loss which has been
incurred could be paid off and if everything could be undone that was done
under that Act, we would still have a
problem to face, and one of the first
magnitude. We still have the problem
which is now confronting every country
where transport has reached a developed
stage, and so when we read the Reports
which have been tabled-I think I am
expressing the view of all those who
have read them, that they are documents
about which it is impossible to form any
hasty opinion-they must be read and
digested with care and when that is done
every effort must be made to ascertain
as far as is possible what the results
of the recommendations would be.
There is another matter in relation to
transport which I would mention. It
would be unfair, I believe, to any of the
great carrying bodies to say that the Act
of 1935 was a failure because of their
lack of co-operation. That may have.
been an important element, but it is
hardly correct to say it was the only
element. I think it will have to be conceded, and we had better face it, that
in some measure the failure of the Act
was due to the failure of the public to
co-operate in working out its provisions.
I cannot measure the extent of failure
due to that cause, but I believe that if
the new Measure is to be a success ultimately it will have to be supported by
co-operation on the part of the public
at large. The problem is not beyond.
solution, but the eyes of the world are
upon us, and I trust that when the new
Measure is placed on the Statute Book
every member of the public will do his
or her best to make it a success. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
May I go further?
further? It is not merely in
the realm of transport that co-operation.
between Parliament and the people is
needed. I venture to think that there
never was a time in the history of democratic institutions when it was more vital,
more essential, that the people of Northern Ireland should co-operate and show
a united front in respect of every
Measure which has reached the Statute
Book. There is not a Measure mentioned
in the Gracious Speech, or a Measure to
come before Parliament in this Session,
which would not be enriched in its usefulness by a willing co-operation on the
part of those for whose benefit it is passed.
When I think back over what has been
done in recent years I am astonished at
the number of beneficent Measures which
have the dust thick upon them. Take one
example. A few years ago this Parliament passed an Allotment Act. I can
conceive of no Measure more likely to
alleviate the results of prolonged unemployment than that Measure, but except
for one or two small aids which have been
given, I think, mostly by Belfast Corporation, the Measure has not been
worked. I believe that many Acts passed
in the last Session will suffer a similar
fate unless they have the hearty cooperation of the people behind them.
It is almost a common doctrine nowadays that legislation can accomplish everything. One would be almost led to
believe that there are those who think that
a man's soul, as well as his body, can be
redeemed by the passing of an Act of
Parliament. It is time for the public to
realise that that is not so, that Parliament can only go part of the way, and
that the rest is for them, that co-operation, that unity as between Parliament
and people, or to give it a short description, that community spirit is needed, not
only to enrich what we do here, but for
another, and, perhaps, greater reason,
having regard to the world as it is to-day.
We have only to look at the papers to
realise that democracy is on its trial.
There are rival systems, and we must
admit that a dictatorship would probably
solve such a problem as the transport
problem in half-an-hour. But
believe the price would not be worth paying, and for that reason it is essential,
if we are to protect our democratic
institutions, that we in Ulster should play
our part, and, should be alert and united
in order to realise what democracy is and
can be.
we
At this present time we are looking to
the Trade Agreement with the United
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. MacDermott]
States to relieve our unemployment and
to promote prosperity here, and when we
consider what is to be done for democracy
I venture to think it will not be out of
place to go back to that great and plain
man, the first American, Abraham
Lincoln. The other day I found in a
speech of his an expression which seemed
to me to typify all that democracy stood
for then and still stands for. At the
close of one of his great speeches he used
this simple sentence:
Let us have faith that right is might,
and in that faith let us to the end dare
to do our duty as we understand it.
Those words, plain words, spoken not to
a Cabinet and not to a Government, but
to the hearts of every man and woman,
may sound strangely to-day, but I venture
to believe that if Parliament and people
in Northern Ireland lay them to heart
and enter into this common enterprise
with energy we have little to fear from
present difficulties or future perils. I
beg to move. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Captain PATRICK: I rise to second
the Motion for the Address, which has
been so ably proposed by the hon. and
learned Member for the University (Mr.
MacDermott), and I should like to
acknowledge at once the honour that has
been done to my constituency by my
being permitted to undertake the task, a
constituency second to none in its loyalty
to the Empire, and one which I am proud
to represent.
The Gracious Speech refers to the improved international situation, and I am
sure we are all grateful for that improvement. The crisis came upon us suddenly,
and some of us, who had not thought
seriously about war since 1918, when we
reached the very edge of the abyss, were
horrified and surprised at what we saw.
Others of us whose calling it was to think
more deeply about the subject were
equally horrified, but not so surprised,
as the deficiences that have been brought
to light in our capability for defending
ourselves have been apparent for a long
time.
This is not the time or place to go into
those deficiencies, but I should like to say
that to my mind there is only one real
cause for this state of affairs, and that
is public opinion. Parliament, under a
constitution such as ours, is but a reflection
of public opinion, and until very recently.
no Minister since the war, whatever his
party, could have presented estimates to
Parliament which would have made good
our deficiencies and carried them through.
Every year the demand was for reduction.
It has been suggested recently in this
House that the money spent on the gates
of Stormont would have been better spent
on an anti-aircraft gun. I am not going
into the question of the relative merits of
guns or gates, but I do say that if the
Government had purchased anti-aircraft
guns in large numbers at that time their
action would not have been supported by
public opinion, and they would have been
generally stigmatised as war-wongers.
We once had an ancient car in which
a visitor was being taken to the train.
Time was short, and she inquired from
the driver if he couldn't go any faster.
"Maybe I can," came the reply, "but
I've to stay with the car." (Laughter.)
In the same way Government action must
stay within range of public opinion. It is
their duty to lead it and mould it, but
they cannot be too far ahead of it, they
must take it along with them.
As regards the people of Ulster
Province being ready to assist in the
defence of the Realm, I think I might
say that the response from the Province
to the recent appeal for officers for the
anti-aircraft units to be raised here has
been magnificent. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) It shows that the spirit of
Ulster is the same as it was in 1914.
to say.
I do not want at this stage to say much
about transport. Hon. Members on all
sides, I know, have got all sorts of things
Both reports emphasise that
goodwill is essential to any successful
scheme, and lack of goodwill contributed
to the failure of the present Act. That
the scheme has failed there is no doubt
in anyone's mind, and, of course, when
anything fails, blame is bound to be given

But let us be quite clear what the primary

anyone to pat himself on the back and
say, "I told you so." It is not even to

it is to produce an efficient scheme at the

never be done in an atmosphere of

recrimination about the past. We can
profit by the mistakes of the past; we
have now a certain amount of experience
to guide us. In the process of hammering

we do not look on it exclusively from the

I am quite sure that the postponing of
the Revaluation Act, due in 1941, will
give general satisfaction, as will the
setting up of a committee to consider the
machinery of valuation. Personally I
was not in the country at the time
of the last valuation, but I think it
was generally unsatisfactory, and the
machinery can be overhauled with
advantage.
As the House is probably aware, a
Bacon Bill has been passed recently in
the Imperial House, the provisions of
which came into effect across the water on
1st December last. In general it affords
protection to the trade across the water
from low bacon prices.
For reasons which it is unnecessary to
go into here, this Government has found
it is unable to introduce equivalent legislation so far, and the North of Ireland
trade at the moment has not got the same
protection as is afforded to the trade
across the water. As the output of bacon
from Northern Ireland is roughly onethird of the total home production, it
will be seen how serious the position is,
and I hope it will be possible to take
action at a very early date to put this
matter right.
Finally, I note with great satisfaction
the good work that has been done by our
recently appointed Trade Commissioner
in London. I think I may claim to have
had as much experience as most Members about English public opinion in regard to this country. In my view the
average person in England rarely gives
us a thought. In the old days Irish
affairs were continuously in front of
English people. Irish battles were fought
on the floor of the House of Commons at
Westminster, but nowadays the debates
are not published in the London Press,
and I am afraid that very many people
do not know of the existence of this
House. I am sure every hon. Member
has had the annoying experience of going
into a shop in London or elsewhere and,
after ordering goods to be sent to a
person in this country, or to his home
address, of being presented with a
Customs declaration form. It infuriated
me on several occasions to be presented
with such a form, and when I protested
I was met with a polite remark as if I
were going to smuggle something in unawares.
I should like to pay a tribute to the
General Post Office for its efforts in helping us to overcome this difficulty. I have
with me a proof of a pamphlet which it
is proposed to issue to all post offices in
the United Kingdom in the very near
future. It sets out quite clearly the
counties of Ulster and the counties of
Eire, gives the postal rates to each place,
and mentions the counties where
Customs declaration form is necessary.

Captain PATRICK: The pamphlet
will be available at every post office very
shortly and should receive the widest

I say I am convinced that the more the
British public know about Ulster the
more sympathy will they have with us.

The PRIME MINISTER: I must at
the outset echo the sentiment of the hon.
Member who has spoken subsequent
to the Mover and Seconder of the
Address. I should like to say how very
much the House appreciated the speech
of the Mover (Mr. MacDermott) of this
humble Address. It was, I think, one
of the most brilliant speeches we have
heard on a similar occasion in this House
since it was established-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and I am quite
certain that the weighty words used by
him will be given the careful consideration to which they are entitled. What
gives me additional pleasure with regard
to the hon. and learned Member's
remarks is the fact that his father was
one of my lifelong friends and one of the
most distinguished clergymen in the
Presbyterian Church. It is delightful
to see one of the ability of the hon. and
learned Gentleman joining our ranks
here and giving us the benefit of the
great knowledge he has of the Ulster
people. With regard to the Seconder
(Captain Patrick), who is a worthy
successor to the Member who so long
represented Mid Antrim in this House,
we were all charmed with his remarks.
I personally tender my heartiest congratulations to both of them.
Before I answer the very reasonably
presented remarks of my hon. Friend
the Member for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie),
I would like to say with what gratification we have learned of the visit of their
Royal Highnesses the Duke and Duchess
of Kent. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I merely mention their visit at
the outset because it is doubly significant
that his Royal Highness really invited
himself a unique experience and afterwards, obtained, of course, the approval of
His Majesty the King. He has announced
that it is to be an official visit, and
echoing the views of all sections of this
House, I may say that I am sure that
he and the Duchess will receive that
welcome which Ulster always extends
to any member of the Royal Family.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I may
mention that I have put forward a
proposition that if he can spare the time
his Royal Highness might come to see
us here in session at work. That would
be a great compliment to the Parliament
of Northern Ireland. I have every hope
that he will be able to accept that
invitation.
On the occasion of the opening of a
new Session one is always in the position
of having to listen to the first speech of
the Opposition and just on the spot to
answer in a superficial way some of the
questions that are asked and reply to
some of the problems suggested. It is
not always
always easy to do that, but
fortunately I am in the position of
possessing the knowledge which will at
any rate satisfy the hon. Member for
Pottinger for some time to come.
Before doing that I would like to
mention one other thing referred to by
the hon. and gallant Member for Mid
Antrim. He spoke of the response of
the people to the demand for volunteers
for the service of protecting the Realm,
and I wish to congratulate him
personally on the efforts he is making
in this direction. But he knows, as
everybody in the House knows, that
when Ulster is asked to make sacrifices
in the interests of the defence of the
Realm, or, if the necessity ever arose, to
go even further, the request is always
honoured at a moment's notice and to
the fullest extent within the power of
the people. Therefore it has not surprised me, though I am happy to have
the information, that he has not found
any difficulty in starting off the work
to which he has set his hand.

I think that some
people are missing a very great chance.

that are continuing to be sent out, in
the form of a pamphlet, they are miss-

public may have forgotten that this

Outstanding at the present moment

I myself, I can assure the hon. Member-it is admitted by those in the
know-have been hand and glove with
the Belfast Harbour Commissioners and
with Messrs. Harland & Wolff for years
past in doing everything that possibly
can be done by the Government in order

With regard to the Belfast Harbour
Commissioners, I have to say that owing
to the close connection between Mr.
Pollock, our late Minister of Finance,
and our present Minister of Commerce
and the Board, I undertook a great deal

I wish to say that I do not think a more
farseeing, long-sighted Board exists in
the United Kingdom. They, and if I
may say so their forefathers, have shown
an appreciation of what the development
of the Belfast Harbour may come to in
the long years that lie ahead. They
have laid the foundations soundly, and
the result is that in some respects the

Kingdom. Moreover, they showed

property lying beside the Harbour Commissioners' estate.
That was entirely outside the scope of
their original charter, which is to look

shipping, and so on, but their plans were
so laid that they were able to acquire
as quickly as possible-and I am glad
that the Government were able to help
them the property which brings them.
down practically to the point of the
Kinnegar at Holywood, and to fill up a
sufficient area to enable them to make
a successful beginning with the airport,
which we hope will go on developing
until it is one of the best-I was going
to say in the United Kingdom, I hope
in the Empire. All the possibilities are

What has happened? The question

of such a large patriotic scheme in order

What was the proposition? We are

After long negotiations-I may say
naturally very friendly negotiationswith the Minister of Finance an arrangement was come to whereby he promised
that this House would pass a Vote

receive from the Government 25s for
every 20s that they put up. I am not
referring to the cost of labour only, but
to the cost of the whole scheme. The
Government are prepared to put down
25s for every 20s provided by the Commissioners, and I understand that the
Commissioners expressed themselves as
satisfied with the effort that has been
made by the Government. That, I
hope, will satisfy the hon. Member for
Pottinger that something really substantial is being done to help the
Harbour Commissioners and also the
firms of Harland & Wolff and Short &
Harland.
Now I come to the question of the
Transport Board, which is mentioned
here. I thank the hon. Member for
Pottinger (Mr. Beattie) for making the
suggestion that we should segregate that
subject from the other matters mentioned
in the Gracious Speech, and devote
another day, two or three days, or whatever length of time is required, to deal
with it. I should like to re-echo briefly
the words that were used by the hon.
and learned Member for the University
(Mr. MacDermott) on this question.
We want all the help we can get.
Recriminations are of no value whatever
in a matter of this sort. The moment
that any shock reaches an individual in
any class of life, I think his very first
thought, which comes like lighting, ishow does this affect me? Then, after
he has thought the matter over he says
to himself, "Well, that is so; but how
can I get it both ways?" That is a
very natural thing to do.
a
But the Government cannot take that
view of any shock, no matter how
sudden it may be. Their very first
thought naturally is what effect will this
have upon the people of the country?
The second thought is that we know well
there has never yet been invented
common formula whereby people can get
the best of matters both ways. Therefore a solution must be found, and the
Government have to consider not the
effect it would have upon themselves
individually or collectively-they have
to consider the best way to provide what
is required for the Ulster people. I can
only say that that will be done. How it
will be arrived at, of course, is a matter
that will require the careful consideration of my Colleagues and myself. As
soon as the Debate on the Address is
over, the Government will put a short
Motion on the Paper, and will take it
as the first Order on the first day after
the Debate on the Address has been
concluded, so that there will be ample
time for hon. Members on both sides to
give this matter that concentrated attention which the gravity of the case
requires. I am sure I can count upon
the support not only of the Members of
this House, but of the whole people of
Ulster still to persevere and still to carry
on-we may be pioneers in the matteruntil we have solved one of the most
complicated and difficult problems that
this or any other Government has had to
face. If we have the courage to carry
it through, then I feel it will be one
of the greatest accomplishments of this
Assembly. With these few words I am
content to leave the matter for a few
days, and we can then enter upon a discussion of the subject in all seriousness.

One would think, listening to his

is not one solitary ray of hope in the

country. The hon. and learned Member

words:
The critical situation, which has
happily passed, called forth from our

which may be made on them to assist
in the defence of the Realm.
Ulster people have always done that. The

be meted out to the men who will fight

to some of those who fought in the Great
War. One hundred ex-Servicemen are
in the workhouse-the poorhouse as it
should be called-on the Lisburn Road.
They work seven days a week, and at the
end of the week, after working from.
7 o'clock in the morning until 7 o'clock
at night, they are given a chew of
tobacco. They are, of course, given their
food. There is no work for them. Not
one ray of hope is given to them by the
Government.
It says in the Gracious Speech that the
critical situation is past. That is rather
strange, because every nation in the world
is working night and day for war. In
the light of that, how can you say, "The
critical situation, which has happily
passed." Even the greatest experts in
international affairs admit that war might
come like a thief in the night. The
critical situation is not past; in fact, it
is prophesied by Members who are, if I
may say so, vastly superior to me and
have a greater mentality than I have,
that within six months we may have war.
Some of the statesmen in the Dominions
say that. It may come at any time, and
I hope that those who serve their country
will be better looked after than the men
who fought in the last war.
Has the Minister of Finance thought fit

- who are at present in the workhouse?

get very little in return when they return
home.
I say here and now that the speeches

Debate on Question (7th December).
"That an humble Address be presented to His Grace, the Governor of
Northern Ireland, as follows": :-
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland, in Parliament assembled,
beg leave to offer our humble thanks
to Your Grace for the speech which
Your Grace has addressed to both
Houses of Parliament.-(Mr. MacDermott).
Question again proposed.
Mr. MINFORD: I would like to join
with other hon. Members in congratulating the Mover and Seconder of the
Address. Turning to the King's Speech,
I am glad there will be a Bill for the
better housing of the working classes, but
may I say to the Minister of Home
Affairs that I hope when this Bill passes
through Parliament the local authorities
will take better advantage of it, because
in Northern Ireland we know that the
need for houses for the working classes
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Minford]
is very urgent. I am rather surprised
that some of the rural authorities have
not yet taken advantage of the Labourers
Act, and I would like to ask the Minister to adopt some steps where the rural
authorities will not take advantage of it,
to have these houses erected.
I want to make some remarks on agriculture and the land fertility scheme.
Under that scheme we in Northern Ireland had a share with Great Britain of
the subsidy on lime and basic slag. The
figures given in the report from the
Ministry show that Northern Ireland is
getting a very small amount of that subsidy. Last year only 1,500 tons of slag
were brought to Northern Ireland. That
was not the quota and was the lowest
for ten years back. I was amazed when
I found that Great Britain had half-amillion tons of basic slag, while the
Ulster farmer was deprived of this cheap
manure. The Free State is getting 5,000
tons of basic slag from British manufacturers, while we in Ulster have only
got 500 tons. I should like to know
whether Northern Ireland is going to get
any more or not.
The Minister of Agriculture has probed
this thing to the bottom, but I should
like to see the Minister of Finance taking
an interest in it. I was one of a deputation that approached him, and a letter
was sent to the other side, but all I have
heard of that letter since was that it was
acknowledged. I feel that in these depressed times for agriculture in Ulster
the farmer is entitled to a fair share of
basic slag available for the production
of grass.
We have to compete in the
same markets as Great Britain, and if
we cannot get British slag, the Ministry
of Agriculture or the Treasury in Great
Britain should allow us to get some substitute, such as North African phosphates.
The half-million tons in Britain is, I
think, 70 per cent. more than Great
Britain received prior to the introduction
of this Act and Northern Ireland has
only got 50 per cent. of her needs prior
to 1936. I hope the Minister will press
on and take some steps so that farmers
in Ulster will get this cheap manure.
Why should the British manufacturers
be allowed to send 5,000 tons to the Free
State which does not participate in the
subsidy? We have an outlet for it in
Northern Ireland. I am speaking within reasonable figures when I say we want
3,000 tons in Northern Ireland, and we
only get a few tons. The price of cattle
and the prices of sheep and lambs have
gone to a very low level and we are going
to be deprived of this artificial manure.
It is only fair we should get at least our
quota of basic slag. This is supposed to
be a subsidy for farmers. In my opinion
it is a subsidy for the manufacturers of
basic slag. Why does the British Government not allow the Ulster farmers to
get Belgian basic slag or slag from our
own factories in Belfast, or phosphates,
when he cannot get British?
The
There is much misapprehension.
farmer thinks we are not sufficiently
pressing this matter in the House. This
manure is useful to farmers, large and
small, in Ulster. I am not going to cast
any reflections on the Minister, because
I brought this matter to his notice last
year, but I call upon the Minister of
Finance to take some steps with the
Financial Secretary on the other side. I
understand the whole thing lies there,

I have no objection to the British farmer

State under this scheme, while the land
in Northern Ireland is suffering.
Regarding the other parts of the
Speech, I am delighted that we are going
to have a Wages Board, because I feel if
we are going to stop the drift from the
land we must give the workers on the
land a wage which will compare with
that of other workers in industry. I
do not blame the Government in regard
to the housing question. The Government has done a great deal in that connection, in fact it has done a lion's share,
but, unfortunately, the rural authorities
are not taking advantage of the Acts.
While I welcome the Wages Board,
which will regulate the wages of farm
labourers, I do think, considering
the present condition of agriculture and
the low prices received by farmers, it
would be impossible for the farmers to
pay these wages. I, therefore, suggest to
the Government to do what is done in
Australia, and that is subsidise the
farmer for part of his labour costs. The
drainage scheme introduced by the Minis-
Debate on the Address
7 DECEMBER, 1938
Debate on the Address
try of Agriculture has been a great
success. Farmers have taken advantage
of that scheme, and are now getting
their lands drained and ditches cleaned
with all speed. That is due to the action
of the Ministry. If that Drainage Act
could be extended to include harvesting
and planting it would be of great advantage. Owing to the low prices received
at present for agricultural produce, I
believe the farmers will employ few men.
We have a large number of unemployed in Northern Ireland, and if the
Government could see its way to give
the farmers a subsidy to help them to
pay their workers a large number of unemployed could be absorbed for farm
work. We cannot expect men to work
hard on the land for a worse wage with
longer hours than men working in
factories receive. As one private Member of this House I believe if we are to
reduce unemployment it is only through
the production of food by farmers. I
have figures here showing how many
workers are now on the land compared
with 1914 and how many acres are under
cultivation now as compared with 1914,
and they are evidence that if things go
on as at present farming in Northern
Ireland will be a thing of the past.
know the Government have done well
for farmers. They have allowed subsidies for beef and have established a
Pork Board, also a Milk Board, which
is a big success. There is a crying out
for an extension of the payment of land
annuities, as farmers are finding it
difficult to carry on every year. We
want our labourers to stay on the land
and we want to stop the drifting away
to the towns. I suggest that when the
Wages Board is established the Government should give the farmers some return
for their labour-some help that will
enable them to pay their men a decent
wage. Farmers are facing a very dark
year-one of the darkest for many years
past.

Now he comes along and blames the Government for providing decent labour exchanges. I give credit to where credit is

Mr. BEATTIE: Ten per cent.

pay that
wage and carry on their agricultural pursuits. We are spending millions

be.

Let us look at our unemployment problem. This is not a matter of party
politics. The problem of diminishing our
number of unemployed is one that should
be tackled by everyone. I fear that at
this season of the year the number of the
unemployed, particularly in the provincial areas, will be greatly increased.
We all know what unemployment means.

made. The most energetic steps should

Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I do not
know where the hon. Member got the

I understand, some provision whereby, if
a proper agreement is entered into between the employer and the employee a
concession is made in regard to the unemployment contribution. Could something further than that not be done,
because there is no comparison from the

worker a farmer gets at the employment

who will engage with him for six months
or twelve months and who knows the
general working of the farm and what
is expected of him.
If farmers are to be induced to maintain even the present level of cultivation
they will have to be given some safeguards of that kind. No farmer will put
in a crop in the springtime if he does

to enable him to harvest it. I would

on this subject. However, I agree that

I thoroughly agree with the points
made by the hon. Member for Antrim
in regard to basic slag. Something ought
to be done to get the farmers in Northern Ireland something like a fair proportion or percentage of the total amount
of slag manufactured in Great Britain
and available for distribution generally.
We have not been getting anything like
a fair percentage of that slag, and, consequently, the scheme has been, to that
extent, a failure in Northern Ireland.
With regard to the use of lime, it is my
opinion that it is not being availed of

Mr. BEATTIE: Go all the way.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I sympathise up to a point. I may be quite
wrong, but I see something of what goes
on in certain homes throughout the
country. A good deal of foolish agitation is going on to-day with regard to
children. That is the result of our
boasted democracy. We find a tremendous amount of what I call sloppy
sentiment in the home and the want of
ordinary discipline. It is in the homes
that a tremendous lot of trouble arises.
On every side we have an outcry against
corporal punishment or physical punishment of any kind in the schools. I do
not know that we should regard children
as angels. Personally I am in favour of
giving them every privilege and every
opportunity, but I still regard them as
children with a great deal to learn. Their
parents should have some control or some
discipline over them and should COoperate much more with the teachers.
The parents ought to be doing that,
and I am afraid they do not. I hope
whenever legislation is brought in along
these lines we will not be led away by
what they did in Great Britain.
I do not wish to detain the House
further. The Gracious Speech certainly
gives us plenty of material for thought.
I would have thought that after 17
years' legislation in this House there
would be practically nothing further to
legislate upon. There are, however,
questions raised in the King's Speech
that will take up a good deal of the time
of the House and require all the ability
which Members can bring to bear upon
them.
Mr. MAGINESS: I should like to
compliment both the Proposer and
Seconder of this Motion. In particular
I should like to compliment the Proposer on his most able speech, and also
on the democratic tendency shown in
that speech. When he made a plea for
co-operation between the Government
and the people he struck a responsive
chord in the hearts of all. We know that
co-operation between the people and the
Government promotes good will. The
Government is willing to co-operate, if
the people on their part are willing to
co-operate. We feel that that happy expression by the hon. and learned Mem-
COber for the University will be realised
and that more and more, as time goes
on, there will be that close co-operation,
that equal co-operation-because
operation must be implemented by a coequality between the Government and
the people.
The hon. and learned Member
described democracy as being on its trial.
It seems to me that in Europe at the
present time it is on the retreat. We
must see to it that it does not retreat
in Northern Ireland. There must be no
interference with democracy here. There
must be a continuous and unrelenting
offensive, and, as it appears the lamps of
democracy in Europe are going out one
by one, we must take care in Northern
Ireland to see that the lamp is kept going
so that the beams from it may lighten
the twilight creeping over Europe at the
present time. To accomplish the fulfilment of democracy in Northern Ireland we must be continually on our
guard; we must be continually on the
watch so that in the future, as has happily
been the case in the past, there will be
this co-operation between the Government and the people. We must save
ourselves by our own energy, and it may
be that we can save Europe by our
example.
In the Gracious Speech there is a
reference to the Housing Bill. I regard
that Bill as very admirable in itself, but
even more admirable was the method in
which it was introduced to the House. I
should like to pay a sincere compliment
to the Minister of Home Affairs for the
way in which he has managed what I
might call the pre-introduction stages of
the Bill. A rough draft was sent to
every Member of the House. It was also
sent to the local bodies. He asked for
and obtained suggestions so that almost
everybody in Northern Ireland not only
knew of the proposals of the Government,
but also knew that the Government was
prepared to consider any counter proposals in a most favourable light. Suggestions which were made have been
adopted by the Government and introduced into the Bill now before the
House. I hope that in future there will
be more legislation of that kind-that
before a Measure is introduced the feelings of the various bodies and the feelings of the Members of this House will
be consulted.

Rev. Professor CORKEY: We are
faced with dictators in Europe who have
abandoned every principle of morality
except the principle of self-interest, and
they are prepared to act upon that
principle of self-interest regardless of compassion, regardless of treaties, regardless
of truth, regardless of anything whatsoever. I feel that the Government is
