Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Rev. Professor CORKEY: I believe
the people are prepared to defend themselves. That is a major fact in the
situation. I believe they will defend themselves if Great Britain is attacked or if
any of our Colonies are attacked, whether
armed adequately or not, whether with
allies or not. They will stand up for
what they consider their just rights and
they will fight. That is a fact which I
may say leads me to the conclusion that
pacificism is absolutely hopeless-
Mr. BEATTIE: Those who did not go
last time can go this time.
Rev. Professor CORKEY: There are
thousands jumping to go. Those in the
University who are voting that they will
never fight will be the first to jump forward when the trumpet sounds and the
drum beats. That is a fact we need not
ignore. Everyone will not go. Neither
did all go in the last war. What I want
to say is more important than that, the
people will fight, it is that this readiness
to defend oneself is not enough, although
perhaps at the moment it is about the
only thing we can do. Nurse Cavell
stated a very profound truth in a classic
way when she said patriotism was not
enough. We will have to learn if we
want peace to be prepared not only to
defend ourselves, but to defend the cause
of justice everywhere by collective action.
We will, it seems to me, have to learn
the duty of going to the help of the
victims of unprovoked attack in any part
of the world. The world has become one.
The world needs institutions to match
that increasing unity, and if civilisation.
is not to go by the board altogether we
will have to educate our people up to this
point, that they will know the principle
of self-defence is not enough. They will
have to defend a court of justice. The
fatal error, it seems to me, made by
leaders-I am not referring to any particular leaders-was made in 1931, when
they did not set their faces very firmly
against the unprovoked and universally
condemned attack by Japan upon China.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
knows that under the terms of the 1920
Act we are precluded from discussing
foreign affairs. I think, perhaps, he has
made some reference to matters outside
the King's Speech, and now he might
pass on to another point.
Rev. Professor CORKEY: Thank you.
The matters to which I referred, I agree,
do, perhaps, deal with Imperial affairs
more directly than with the affairs we are
concerned with in this House. I am sure
everyone will applaud the determination
to go through with the Housing Bill,
which has been introduced. I heard it
stated that the conscience of a community
may be judged by its slums, and I feel
that the conscience of this community
may be judged to some extent by the
desire on the part of the representatives
of the people to do away with any
remnant of slums we may have.
There are many features in the Speech
that appeal to me very much. For
example, the control of the rent of these
new houses. But there is one suggestion
I would like to make to the Government,
and that is in future Housing Bills they
should prohibit absolutely the building
of any more houses within the boundary
of Belfast. Belfast is big enough for
health. It is big enough for happiness,
and in view of the possibility of air
raids, it is big enough from the point of
view of safety. The ideal which I think
the Government ought to hold before its
mind in future is the ideal advocated by
the town-planning associations at the
present time, the idea of satellite towns
in the neighbourhood of great cities,
where the homes of the people would be
built, and where they would enjoy more
health than in a crowded city. Every
possible bit of ground in the city, all the
places that might be used as playgrounds
for children and for parks, are being
rapidly built over.
I have observed that all those who have
spoken while I have been in the House
have avoided one matter that is dealt
with in the Speech, a thorny matter,
perhaps, in the opinion of some people
and delicate. It may not be inappropriate if I make a passing reference to
it, however dangerous it may be. The
laws governing divorce have been modified
in England, and I have read the matrimonial clauses of the Act adopted in
England, and in my opinion there is
nothing in the Act that threatens in any
way the morals of the people. I have no
desire myself to take advantage of any
extended privileges that may be given in
any Divorce Bill. Shall I call them
privileges or possibilities?

At the same time, I am one of those
who think that neither on Christian nor
rational or historical or social or moral
grounds can you condem divorce in all
cases as immoral. I think that that is
going too far. At the same time, I feel
that the Government in handling a difficult subject such as this, about which
people are very sensitive, should take all
possible precautions to safeguard the home
and the security and sanctity of the home,
which is the central educational institution in our midst. Anything which
threatens the home threatens the wellbeing of the community morally and
spiritually. The Russian people have
discovered of late that their great hopes
in national nurseries were ill-founded.
They have been sadly
been sadly disillusioned,
because they have discovered that children
brought up in these national nurseries do
not compare either physically or morally
with children brought up in homes. I,
therefore, will support the Government
if they introduce a Bill on this subject
along the same lines as the Bill which has
been adopted in England.
Reference has been made by several
speakers to the possibility of legislation
based on the Report that deals with child
welfare and young offenders. We have
had an excellent report. I have read it
all with great interest, and I am confident that the legislation that will be
based on such a report will be for the good
of the community. May I make an
observation somewhat bearing on this
subject. The legislation that will be
introduced will deal with young offenders
who, of course, are only a minority in the
community. I think something more
might be done in the way of getting at
the causes of juvenile delinquency. Much
is said about the carelessness of parents
at the present time, and the speaker
before me charged the people generally
with a great deal of sloppy sentimentality
in regard to child welfare. It seems to
me that we have been so keen in the
North of Ireland upon the question of
religious education that we have largely
ignored, perhaps, a more fundamental
necessity, namely, moral education, about
which there will be no great disagreement. There are great principles and
sentiments lying at the very basis of our
democracy-moral sentiments which lie
near the heart of our Christianity.
It seems to me we have handed over the
care of these tremendously important
moral principles to the hands of the
parents, many of whom are not themselves great examples of loyalty to these
moral principles. I think if we believe.
in our democratic principles we should
teach them, and if we believe in Christian
moral sentiments we should teach them.
The dictators have their own peculiar misconceived ideals and everyone knows how
they are hammering these ideals into the
very soul of every child who is subject to
their authority. I believe the teachers
in the elementary schools not only by
courses of instruction, but incidentally by
their example, are doing a great deal,
outside even the times set apart for
religious instruction, in giving the
children some appreciation of their duties
to their neighbours, and of the value of
sincerity and honesty and the other
moral principles in which we all have
faith. In our secondary schools we must
provide a handbook on the principles of
Christian morality and Christian citizenship. In our University we have a
lectureship on moral philosophy.
these days, when the foundations of our
morality are being questioned, I think it
would be a good thing if the lectureship
were raised to the status of a professorship, and every student who wants an
arts degree were required to take a course
in moral philosophy. It would not
necessarily make him any more moral,
but if he happened to have any morality
it would help him to take in the principles
bearing on the subject.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I was delighted to hear the
hon. Member for the University address
the House here this evening and to listen
to his inspiring, and, if I may say so,
optimistic speech, even though it was
dealing with war. I have listened to the
pessimistic utterances of Members on
both sides all evening. Some painted a
gloomy picture of the conditions of agriculture and low wages. Others painted
a worse picture of the industries of the
country. Some had a suspicion of the
physical training of the unemployed.
Others thought we were making a great
mistake and their criticism was very
severe-in sending boys for industrial
training on the other side of the water.
Others saw the lamp of democracy-
Mr. BEATTIE: Going out.
Mr. GORDON: Yes; going out. They
hoped that the lamp of democracy would
remain lighted here, and then suggested
that the Government should take steps,
if the local authorities failed to take
charge of certain operations, to extinguish the lamp of democracy here.
I just want to refer to a few points
made by Members on both sides. Some
were talking of world unrest. I do not
think I will venture too far on that subject, because Mr. Speaker might pull me
up if I discussed world unrest. It is
outside the purview of the Gracious
Speech from the Throne, but when
Members paint a gloomy picture of
world conditions to-day-a gloomy
picture of the trade of the country-I
would remind them that only a few
days ago a German-French agreement
was arrived at. There was also an
Anglo-Italian agreement come to. These
may not help trade to a very great extent so far as Northern Ireland is concerned, but another agreement was
made some time ago, and that was the
Anglo-American agreement, which is
bound to give a great fillip to the industries of the country. I have reason
to believe that the pessimistic utterances
of some Members to-day will within a
very short period of time be changed.

opportunity of developing themselves.
physically so that if a job turns up they
will be able to undertake it.
I have answered the few points raised
with regard to the Department of the
Ministry of Labour. Other points were
raised such as subsidising wages and
matters of that kind. It would be a
serious matter for me to tackle them at
the moment. It would open up a very
wide discussion if we were to talk about
subsidising wages. You could not confine yourself to one particular industry.
If you began to subsidise the wages of
one section of industry every other
section would make a demand for the
subsidy and that demand would have to
be conceded. Consequently I will not
deal with that question. But I want to
say that the Government have done and
are doing a great deal for agriculture.
I am hopeful that the efforts put forth
will bring again into life and vigour the
industry which is the foundation industry of our country.

Prime Minister's Statement 94
Transport Act, 1935-
8 DECEMBER, 1938
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Road and Railway Transport Act, 1935.
Prime Minister's Statement.
The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to
move, “That in the opinion of this House
the Government should immediately
devise measures to deal with the evasions
of the provisions of the Road and Railway Transport Act (Northern Ireland),
1935, and to assist to secure the improvement of the provisions of the existing
Acts relating to hours and conditions of
wages in the transport industry; and that
the Government do further take into
consideration the matters dealt with in
the Reports of the Recorder of Belfast
and Sir William McLintock's Committee, with the object of securing that
such arrangements will be made for transport as will be in the best interests of the
people of Northern Ireland."
In opening the debate on this very
important matter, I do not intend to go.
very far back except to say that during
the last twenty years, roughly speaking,
the situation in regard to transport, not
only in Ulster but throughout the world,
has been gradually becoming more and
more acute. Although we may claim, I
think rightly, to be pioneers in attempting to solve this very complicated
problem, and although we may possibly
have been a little premature in attempting the task, I do not believe that any
body of men, or indeed any House of
Commons, could have given more careful consideration to the problem before
it was launched. I do not believe that
those who have been attempting to work
the Act passed by this House could have
acted more zealously than the gentlemen who accepted the invitation of the
Government to act on the Board. It is
a great pleasure to me to be able to say
that.
We are faced with a colossal problem,
and naturally we are bound to suffer
from almost day-to-day criticism of a
very severe nature. I need hardly repeat
the fact that the Ulster people are
splendid in that way. They have a good,
upstanding fight, and having fought their
fight in nine cases out of ten, whether
they win or lose, they are prepared to
shake hands and carry on. I have always
found in my long experience that that is
a characteristic of the Ulster people.
There was, undoubtedly, during the
passage of the Bill, and after it became
an Act, a violent attack from time to
time on the Government and on the
Board. Well, I think it was all worth
it. We have learned a lesson. The
Government on its part watched jealously
the progress that was being made, and I
think we were right in allowing an ample
opportunity for the Board to settle down.
to its real work.
It had to fashion a new system all over
the country. It had to go into every
yard of our Ulster area in order to see
how it could best be served, and it had
to start on what was, undoubtedly, a
most complicated business with regard to
compensation. As there was no precedent the compensation that was paid was,
I may say, very ample, more than ample
in some cases. But one must remember
that the difficulties were added to by the
fact that most of the undertakings then
in existence were of a very varied nature,
and in order that the country would
accept the Measure at all it required that
full justice, indeed a little more than
justice, should be meted out to them. In
the case of purchases by the Government
-that is what this amounted to reallycompensation is very often fixed by a
tribunal, and after taking the real value
of the estate, that is passing hands, there
is always compensation for the compulsion
necessary for the Government to acquire
whatever asset they may be acquiring.
In this case that was fully carried out,
and I think that when one looks back
upon that compensation one may be
satisfied that this House has not imposed
any great wrong upon the former proprietors of the vehicles taken over. I
I would not like to stand here and think
that we had been niggardly, or that the
Board had been niggardly, and made it
more difficult for everybody by stirring
up more trouble than we had to face.
That is my first reference to that in order
to show the difficulties under which the
Board were placed in the initial stages.
Over and above that there was considerable pressure brought to bear from
practically everybody to give cheaper
fares and better services than there were
before, and the Board, from my knowledge of them, have pursued a line of
action most conscientiously with the desire
to help in every way the public, and
Prime Minister's Statement
Transport Act, 1935-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
especially the farming community. Blame
is attached in the McLintock Report to
practically all those who had anything to
do with the original Act and with its
carrying out. I am sure that from men
of such eminence and distinction in the
realm of finance and road and rail transport those observations were deserved.
I myself and my colleagues are quite prepared to take the strictures passed upon
us, and I am sure that all who have been
doing their best in very difficult circumstances will also follow that line.
We find ourselves to-day face to face
with a crisis-there is no use using a milder
term-and certainly there is no intention
on the part of my right hon. Friends or
myself to shirk in any way our responsibility for solving the difficulties with
which we are now presented. But if I tell
the House the steps the Government propose to take I hope I will be able to get
a unanimous acceptance of the plan.
That is saying a good deal, but I believe
that that is what I will be able to obtain.
It will take at least six months-probably eight-to prepare an alternative to
the present Act, an Act which in its main
objects was intended to secure co-operation between rail and road. If that Act
has broken down, as it has, because to
my mind there is practically no co-operation and never has been any, it is
principally due to the fact that, instead
of bringing the two bodies principally
involved together and reaching harmony
and agreement, the attempted dual control has brought about a situation of such
a kind that the Government feel it
necessary to evolve a scheme under which
dual control will be dispensed with and
an attempt made to have single control
and single power in regard both to railway and road transport.
We are, taking the matters in sequence,
first of all proposing to introduce in the
course of a few days a Bill dealing with
two things which will be of very great
importance under whatever scheme is
carried out. The two points that the
Emergency Bill will deal with are the
questions of preventing the illegalities
which are at present almost widespread
throughout the country, and of improving the wages which are paid outside the Transport Board. The
Transport Board has to work at a
disadvantage, as compared with those
who are privately working their vehicles,
in regard to the hours, which I am informed should undoubtedly be improved,
and also in regard to the wages which are
paid to the drivers of the vehicles. It
will be agreed by the House that this
great question is not a political one; there
is no politics in it. If there were, being
accustomed to dealing with matters of
that kind, I would know exactly what
steps to take, but this is a business matter
affecting the whole community.
It is a matter that I feel confident
can be solved, but there is no use in
a Government like ourselves, most of us
with no experience whatever in regard
to transport matters, and certainly no
experience with regard to road transport,
undertaking the task without careful
preparation. We did find before the
absolute necessity of guiding ourselves
and the House by taking advantage of
the experienced knowledge of the
personnel of the McLintock Committee
and of the prior advice on certain
matters of the learned Recorder of Belfast. Their two reports were presented
to the House. They contained a great
deal of very valuable advice. But my
colleagues and I are very anxious to
meet the House on all sides as far as
we possibly can in the framing of the
new Measure, and therefore, I hope
with the approval of everybody in the
House, we propose to set up a comprehensive Committee of all parties in the
House and in the Senate, and to allow
them, with the most capable chairman
that we can secure and we have plenty
of brains to pick from-to take
this volume, and in view of the results
of the past working of the present
Board, go into the whole matter and
then report to the Government.
I
The Government will then endeavour
to embody in a Transport Bill their
recommendations, wholly if possible but,
if not, in part. My colleagues and I
are taking this step for two reasons.
was very much impressed by the speech
of the hon. and learned Member for the
University (Mr. MacDermott) on the
Address. He let fall a sentence with
regard to the requirements of democracy.
In a State where there is a dictator, he
said, a scheme of transport can be
devised and carried out whether the
people of the country like it or not, and
it then becomes very simple for the
97 Transport Act, 1935–—
Prime Minister's Statement 98
8 DECEMBER, 1938
Government, if there is one, or the
dictator as the case may be, to say "Let
it be,' and it is. I felt very strongly
that if those few remarks of the hon.
and learned Member were carried into
effect there would be many difficulties
especially in political matters. But
when it comes to a matter entirely of a
business nature, such as this, affecting
not one side of the House but both sides
and all parts of the country I feel it
would be a wise thing to give a trial to
a committee and to obtain a report to
the Government covering the whole
ground.
Some of the Members here represent
the towns, some the University, and the
majority, of course, come from the
country. They will have in view the
advice of their constituents; they will
be able to hold meetings on the spot,
to go into the matter meticulously, and
then make a report which has behind
it the whole sense of the people of
Ulster. On the other hand, they might
say to us, "Go on with the Bill that
you suggest, based upon the reports of
the McLintock Committee and the
learned Recorder of Belfast." Some
people are very fond of asking a thing
to be done as long as they have no
responsibility whatever; that is easy
enough. I am sure that the amount of
destructive criticism in the past would
form a volume compared with the constructive criticism which I think should
be tendered to a Government. In other
words, you will get 99 out of 100 people
to criticise and you will get about one
out of 100 to make suggestions that are
so valuable that they can be carried out.
This will prevent all that.
I have noticed in the papers, whether
the reports are authentic I cannot say,
that certain Members are already
beginning to form a small party with
a view to taking certain action. It will
be far better, I am sure, that those
Members should be incorporated in the
Committee of both sides of the House,
in order that they may give it the
benefit of all the knowledge that they
have of their own countryside, and be
able to embody it in some sort of report.
If they can produce a scheme for an
efficient transport system on a sound
economic basis, the Government will be
only too delighted to do what they can
to embody it in an Act of Parliament.
I
may say, though perhaps the
necessity for it hardly arises, that every
Member of the Government will help
this Committee if that is their desire,
and do all they can to fashion a Measure
which will meet not only all the requirements of our people, but be economic
in its working, and prove to the outside
world that Ulster can do this for itself
and at the same time give a lead to
others in overcoming difficulties. I
may say that even since this Report of
Sir William McLintock was placed in
our hands there have been signs of a
considerable amount of difficulty in
England and in Eire, and in other
parts. They have had to set up committees to begin to study the whole of
this complicated question, with a view
to preventing the losses that are taking
place at the present time.
There are one or two very broad
points. My right hon. Friend the
Minister of Home Affairs will, I hope,
have an opportunity of dealing with
matters that I am leaving entirely to
him. I want to assure the House and
the country that far from desiring in
any way to dragoon anybody into
accepting the views of a few Cabinet
Ministers, we wish to associate the
whole of the people of Ulster in a
scheme for their convenience, not for
the convenience of the Government-it
will have to be a proper proposition
from the financial point of view-and to
assure them that the Government have
no desire whatever, and never had, to
make a profit for themselves or to add
to their revenue out of the proceeds of
the Board.
Then I come down to another point,
and that is, that I cannot impress too
strongly upon the people, and upon the
hon. Gentlemen who, I hope, will act on
the Committee, the necessity of coordination, and secondly the necessity
of seeing that we do not lose our main
line railways. It is to me lamentable
that some people should put up the idea
that the railways are of no use
nowadays. I can realise that those who
live quite adjacent to our larger towns,
like Belfast, Derry, and Enniskillen,
and so on, and who do not use the
facilities of the railways very much,
may treat this matter in a rather careless way, because they have short

of Derry, what would happen there if

by rail, was done away with? Take the
amount of passenger traffic and goods
traffic. My right hon. Friend (Sir
Dawson Bates) will, I hope, be able to
supply the House with the actual
figures. Take Enniskillen, what would
happen there if the railway were cut off
and cattle and goods had to be conveyed
by road vehicles? Take my own childhood's town of Bangor, if I may so
describe it. How would the population,
which is increasing every year, be dealt
with only by motor traffic?
I am sure that eventually redundant
parts of the railways must be cut off-
I feel that that is coming fairly
rapidly-but I hope that our main line
railways will be maintained in the
scheme which is put forward by the
Committee which I propose to set up.
That is the ordinary every-day work of
those companies. The three companies
are involved the Northern Counties,
the Great Northern, and the County
Down. Where would we be in the
summer months, with all the visitors
whom we encourage to come across the
Channel and from abroad, if we lost the
services of the railways on occasions of
that sort? The problem is a very
important one, and my strong view is
that it should be tackled from the point
of view of the co-ordination of the two
systems of transport, and of doing what
they can to reconcile them, which up
to the present has not been found
possible.
I do not think I may refer to any of
the details because I do not wish to
prejudge what the hon. Members of
this House and another place may feel
fit to report. It will take, I presume,
some considerable time. We had aimed
at having a Bill prepared and ready to
place before the Members in about six
to eight months, but if it is found
necessary I am sure it will be well worth
waiting a little longer if the Committee find it impossible to conclude
their work in that time.
In conclusion, I would make an
earnest appeal, if I may, to the outside
public. This will be to all intents and
own Bill, their own
purposes their
ideas their joint ideas embodied in a
Measure intended entirely for their
benefit. That appeal is also an appeal
to those who are always inclined to go
against what I may call law and order
in the more modified way-that instead
of blocking the way they give the provisions to be made their serious consideration, not for their own individual
help but for the assistance of the whole

of Parliament unless the people are

done.
I know it is a difficult task. Full
opportunity will be given for expressions
of opinion. Local authorities, Chambers
of Commerce, and of Trade, anyone,
indeed, who can give help to this Committee will be at liberty to do so. I
ask the House with confidence to accept
this proposal. It is an attempt at all
events to solve the difficulties which at
the present moment are extremely
severe. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

been recorded in Hansard. My attitude
on the Railway Commission Report of
1922 in regard to road and rail transport is also on record. Since I entered
public life my contention has been,
especially in regard to Northern Ireland
more than in any other part of the
world, that national ownership of road
and rail is essential and important for
the well being of the community. I
read the speech of the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates), and I listened
to him delivering it on the Second Reading. He gave a résumé of the building
up of road transport, and he also gave
an historical review of the position of
the railways at that time. I found that
that position was bound to arise sooner
or later, and it did arise.
When it did arise representations
were made to the right hon. Gentleman
and he and his Government introduced
a Bill. I opposed that Bill on the
grounds that it was only meeting the
case as presented half way. I wanted
a fully fledged national ownership of
road and rail transport as that was the
only service that would meet the
requirements of Northern Ireland. I
am quite satisfied that if this Committee which is to be set up realises its
responsibility to the nation, to trade and
industry it will have to come in with
a fully fledged Bill for the complete
control of road and rail transport.
Having said that I want to dilate for
a moment or two on the remarks made
by the Prime Minister. It is a difficult
position for the Government, who have
been the pioneers of the transport board
system, to find themselves in. I admire
the Government in their day and
generation for having the courage to go
one step in the direction which I felt
they would have to go the whole way.
They went that one step in 1935. They
had nothing to guide them, with the
result that anomalies appeared in the
Act. After it was placed on the
Statute Book certain things appeared on
the horizon to destroy the scheme as
outlined in the Bill. I know the nature
of the bullets used; I know there was a
deliberate plan to destroy it, and I
know that no other country in the world
would have allowed the abuse and the
destruction of public money in the same
way as has been done here for the past
number of years.
I say that the Board and the railways
are subject to the same piracy as they
were previous to the passing of the Act.
We had keen competition to our tram
and bus undertakings in the City of
Belfast by pirate buses, and we had to
take strong measures to stop them from
taking the streets of the city. We had
to build up the service for the
municipality, and it was up to us to see
that outsiders who did not give a helping hand to build up that service were
not to be allowed to destroy it. That
is what I blame the Government to-day
for. They tried to the best of their
ability to build up a road transport
system by an Act of Parliament, but
they left it there. They did not look
after the offspring they brought forth.
People who I understand received.
compensation from the Board afterwards
invested that money in private lorries
or posed as merchants and are still
plying on the roads in Northern
Ireland. My advice to the Government is this. The Report is a very
severe one, but it does not tell you
to drop the idea of national transport.
You have the basis of a system and I
trust you will hold to that basis and
improve upon it. If you improve it in
the direction which I will give you
advice upon I am satisfied that in ten
years there will be no complaints in
regard to road and rail transport.
I have been told that it would be
better to give the whole undertaking
into private hands again. God help
trade and industry in Northern Ireland
if we revert back to where we were
previous to the introduction of this Act.
A high standard of working conditions
has been applicable to all workers in
road transport. That is one thing they
have done, and it is one of the things
we are going to fight to retain. I give
the Government due warning that if

from the Road Transport Board being
made applicable. We are not going
back to the 70, 80 or 90 hours per week
for 30s or £2.
It may be argued that the railways
are trying to create a monopoly. There
is a fear in the minds of many people

8 DECEMBER, 1938
Transport Act, 1935

Transport Act, 1935
passed a further Act, which gave the railway companies power to provide road
services for passengers and goods, thereby putting them on a basis of equality
with other operators on the road. It is,
however, unfortunate that the railway
companies did not at once proceed to take
greater advantage of this Act than they
did.
Looking back now it is, perhaps, hard
to realise that prior to the war motor
traffic was of little importance in the
economic organisation of the country. It
had proved, it is true, a most dangerous
rival to horse transport, but so far as the
railways were concerned no one imagined
for a moment that it would prove to be
anything but complementary to the railways, and that, in fact, it would simply
serve as a feeder to the railways. It was
not long, however, before the motor began
to abstract from the railways much of
their most valuable goods traffic, this
being a class of traffic which was of small
bulk and could be handled by road
operators with expedition and ease, and
it is interesting to note that it is one of
the most important factors in the problem of to-day that the class of traffic
which the road is abstracting from the
railways is the most profitable traffic, so
that the railways, with their heavy overhead charges in the way of railway lines
and so forth, are left with the less profitable freight.
It was not until 1923 that regular
services of omnibuses between points in
Northern Ireland first began to make
their appearance, and having once made
their appearance this type of vehicle.
gained such immediate popularity that
in 1923 Parliament was obliged to pass
the Char-a-banc Regulation Act, with a
view to enabling local authorities to
regulate the new road passenger services.
It was not long, however; before experience showed that any purely local control
of this kind was hopelessly inadequate.
and, accordingly, three years later-in
1926-the Motor Vehicles (Traffic and
Regulation) Act was passed, which entrusted the Ministry of Home Affairs
with the duty of supervising motor traffic
as a central authority.
no
At first the Ministry's supervision was
mainly directed towards ensuring the
suitability and proper maintenance of the
vehicles. The Act provided that
omnibus might be operated until it was
first licensed by the Ministry, and no
licence was granted until an examination of the vehicle showed that it was
suitably constructed and in a proper state
of repair.
By the following year the railway
companies began to appreciate the serious
menace which road transport offered to
them, and in 1927 Parliament accordingly.
In the following year-that is to say,
in 1928-something like 800 omnibuses
were in use in Northern Ireland. Their
competition with the railways was serious,
but it was in the city of Belfast that it
was most felt, for the rival omnibus firms
were racing one another in the streets
and competing with the Corporation
tramway undertaking, and there is no
doubt about it that if the Government,
through the Ministry of Home Affairs,
had not stepped in, the Corporation's
tramway undertaking would have been
reduced to very dire financial straits.
The Ministry, even as far back as this
time, appreciated that co-ordination in
transport was essential for the good of the
community, and it took advantage of the
opportunity presented by an inquiry
which was being held into the confirmation of Corporation traffic bylaws to deal
with the matter in the city. An arrangement was accordingly reached, by which
the Corporation was given a monopoly of
the tramway and omnibus services within
its area, so long as it continued to provide adequate and satisfactory services,
and I think that this House will agree
that that monopoly has in no way
injuriously affected the public.
At the same time similar protection.
was given to all omnibus operators who,
on the 27th August, 1928, were providing regular services outside the city.
This, in fact, was the quid pro quo which
the private operators received-in consideration for which they agreed to
abstain from operating in the city.
Under this arrangement no new omnibus
services could be commenced without the
approval of the Ministry, and the Ministry approved of no new services so long
as the existing ones were satisfactory.
The routes over which the different
operators were authorised to provide
services were strictly defined, and the
Ministry insisted on adherence to time
tables, which, in the greatest degree
possible, secured co-ordination between
the different services, as well as the

passenger services run on the railways.
This arrangement, of course, was only
possible by an agreement that had been
reached with the omnibus operators, for
I think there can be little doubt that the
Ministry was stretching its powers under
the 1926 Act in using them to control the
use of omnibuses in this way. It proved,
however, in practice, eminently satisfactory, and in 1929 a further Motor
Vehicles and Road Traffic Act was passed,
which placed matters on a more strictly
legal footing, and made various other
provisions which experience had proved
to be desirable-as, for example, the
establishment of a Tribunal for the fixing
of fares. The fixing of these fares gave
rise to a very considerable amount of

throughout the greater portion of the

since been generally accepted
satisfactory.
as
Towards the end of 1928 almost every
road in the Province which could support an omnibus service had one, and
after that year few new services were
commenced. In the first instance there
was a very large number of operators,
but after five years the number was reduced from something in the neighbourhood of 200 to about 52 in the ordinary
commercial course of absorption of small
services by the larger operators. No protection was, however, afforded to vehicles
used solely for tours, etc., and in 1933
there were round about 80 vehicles
licensed for this purpose.
It will be seen from the foregoing that
no effort had been made to deal with the
transport of merchandise by road. The
number of vehicles in use for this purpose
had steadily increased from about 1,600
in 1921 to about 7,300 in 1933, and
tests made by the Ministry revealed the
fact that a greater amount of merchandise
was actually being carried by road than
by the railways and canals combined.
It was now becoming evident that if
something were not done on the lines of
co-ordinating road freight services in the
way that the road passenger services had
been co-ordinated, the transport of our
Province was in serious danger of breaking down. The road services, themselves,
it was perfectly evident, were not being
run on an economic basis, and, moreover, the conditions under which they
were being used were such as to constitute a grave menace to public safety, and
in the other direction the railway companies were rapidly being reduced to such
a condition that it would be impossible
for them to carry on.
I think the public generally are a little
apt to jump to the conclusion that the
railways are an out-of-date form of transport and are no longer necessary. It is
a conclusion that I submit a very little
thought will dispel. Farmers in particu-
│lar, I think, are apt to allow themselves
to be led into this fallacy, for there is
no section of the community that would
suffer more severely from the collapse of
the railways than the farmers, although
they do not think so. In the remoter
districts the railways are essential to the
farmers for their services in the conveyance of bulk traffic and produce, and
nearer the industrial centres the railways
are equally essential to the farming
community, for without the railways it
can not be doubted that the tourist traffic
which does so much for the seaside towns
of Northern Ireland would practically
come to an end. It can not be doubted,
further, that if all this bulk traffic which
is at present conveyed on the railways
was to be diverted to the roads the expense to the community would be greatly
increased, and a new series of problems
would arise.
I would not go so far as to say that
the very expensive railways system that
we have in Northern Ireland to-day must
at all costs be maintained, but that a
substantial mileage of railway line is
essential to the well-being of the Province
I think no intelligent person, who has
given the matter any consideration, will
deny, and I think it will further be
admitted that the only way of maintaining this necessary amount of railway is
by the co-ordination of road and rail. It
was in an attempt to create this coordination that the 1935 Act, which has
now come in for so much criticism, was
passed.
I am not going to attempt to argue
about the faults that have been found
with the 1935 Act, nor am I going to
enter into any defence of the Government
for departing from certain recommendations of the Pole Report, but I will just
say this, that one must walk before one
Transport Act, 1935
Transport Act, 1935

can run, and one can only direct oneself
on sound principles and go as far towards
the ideal as it is practical for the time
being to go.
The principle of co-ordination remains.
the same, whether you secure it one way
or the other, and I do not think that
anyone will say it is foolish to try to
secure it in the simplest way, and the
way that will result in the least disturbance of existing arrangements, before
adopting an alternative and, possibly,
more scientific course. That co-ordination
has not been secured I do not attempt
to deny, but I am not one of those who
attempt to explain this failure by resorting to personalities. The simple fact of
the matter is that road and rail interests
are, ex-facie, opposed to one another, and
in order to unite them some common interest must be provided. In the 1935 Act
we tried the common interest of a pooling
system. Hon. Members will, no doubt,
recollect that this was not put forward
by Sir Felix Pole in his Report as the
ideal or most effective arrangement, but
simply as one that might be expected to
work, and it was adopted by the Government for that reason. It has not worked
very well, at all events up to the present.
We recognise that. We must just see
whether it will be possible to make it
work, and if it is not possible to do so,
then we must find some other method to
bring about co-ordination.
The difficulties of the Government and
the Board were greater than we anticipated, but when you are obliged to
acquire by compulsion a vast number
of small businesses
which keep no
proper accounts; when the purchase
price must contain an element of
compensation; and when it is necessary
to temper strict justice with a very great
deal of mercy, then surely it is unreasonable to expect that as good a bargain
from the point of view of the concern
taking over can be made as if the transaction were an ordinary commercial one
between a free buyer and seller.
At the same time, I think, also, the
initial financial results of any such
scheme as this must depend upon the
amount of support it receives from the
public, and the extent to which it gets,
what I may call, a fair crack of the whip.
I suggest that the Board has not got a
fair crack of the whip at the hands of
the public. When persons have received
generous compensation for the undertakings and the goodwill they have sold, and
when they utilise the money they have so
received to start, under one disguise or
another, competition with the concern to
which they have sold, that is certainly
not fair play, and that, as this House is
aware, is a proceeding that has taken
place to a very widespread extent, and
that system has got to stop.
The scheme of public transport which
it was the object of the 1935 Act to provide was not introduced for the benefit
of railway shareholders. It was intended
to assist the railways in meeting their
heavy overhead expenses, but that is an
entirely different matter from providing
dividend for railway shareholders, with
whom everybody will have the greatest
sympathy. The railways are simply a
part of the general transport of Northern
Ireland, and as such, and as a part of
the general transport which is working.
under grave economic difficulties, they
must be supported by the remainder of
the Northern Ireland transport. The
principle is exactly the same as that
which applies in any public service, as
for example, the Post Office. Anyone
would be willing to take over the postal
services in the big centres of population,
and could safely undertake to run them
at a very big profit, but you would not
find much competition for the Post Office
services in the wilds of Scotland, where
it would be out of the question to afford
services on a paying basis at anything
like the ordinary postal fees that are
charged throughout the service, and it is
hardly necessary to point out that it
would not be to the interests of the business undertakings situated in the large
centres of population that there should not
be an adequate postal service throughout
the country. It is exactly the same with
transport. A satisfactory system of
transport cannot be provided by dealing
only with the most remunerative part of
the traffic and allowing the remainder to
be neglected. It is all very well to talk
about private enterprise, but you cannot
expect private enterprise to provide
transport services which cannot possibly
pay, nor can you expect a controlled
monopoly to carry on if they are subject
to intensive competition in their
munerative traffic and left to bear the
whole burden of their unremunerative
traffic.

Get out, clear out, every one of you.
Nothing that the Government have done

since the Government took over the reins

seaside trips now for the working people

I want to call attention to the fact
that some time ago a Free State bus came

unholy state of affairs. A Northern

I do not want to say anything hurtful
about the men who constituted this Road
Transport Board, but I must say that
what has been done has not been a credit
to anybody. Those people got cushy jobs.
A great many of them got £2,000 or
£3,000 a year. They were out for blood.
They were quite ready to milk the cow
that was giving them the "hardy." They
milked the cow until the poor old cow
ran out of milk. Then the cry went out
that the Board was on the verge of bankruptcy. I trust that when the next
Board is constituted it will consist of men
who know their jobs. I ask the Government to consult every local authority in
Northern Ireland in order to ascertain
if they have any men with a knowledge
of transport. They should also consult
the Chambers of Commerce and the
Chambers of Trade. I see that the Prime
Minister has adopted some of my ideas,
so there must be some good in me after
all. He suggested the very thing that I
mentioned a week ago.
The Government should get into touch
with the men who ran the road transport
in days gone by if they want to make a
success of the undertaking. Let them
cut their losses just as any business man
would do. Let us go back to private
enterprise and then we will get service
again. That is the only way the transport undertaking can be made a success.
It cannot be said it was not a success
before the existence of the Road Transport Board. The Government's only
excuse for what they did was that if they
did not take road transport from the
hauliers and omnibus owners those people
would become bankrupt, but none of them
did go bankrupt. The best thing is to
think seriously over handing road transport back to Ulstermen who know what
the Ulster people want. If the Government hand the transport system over to
an English railway company I may tell
them that there will be wigs on the green
in many parts of Ireland.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I am glad that the
Prime Minister and the Government have

men were asked by the Government to

It is all very well for the McLintock

are responsible for the chaos in which they

HOUSE OF COMMONS

I do not hold any brief for the members of the Transport Board; I am here
to say that the Government ought to take

Act.
We have now got into a mess and
we are making history to-day. I have
been a Member of this House since 1925,
and this is the first time that the Government have ever suggested that back
benchers or the community ought to have
a say in legislation.
To-day the Prime Minister said he
wants representatives of all parties in
this House to come together and help to
frame legislation. Is it not a strange
thing that it is only after the Government have made a complete mess of this
business that they are willing to ask the
Back Benchers to come to their assistance? I have been here since 1925. I
have always been willing to help the Government to put legislation on the Statute
Book that is suitable for the people, but
never, until to-day, would the Government listen to the Back Benchers or to
the people outside-I want to bring this
charge home to the Government-or they
never would have passed this Transport
Act through this House. I have heard
a great deal from the Government to-day
and from other people to the effect that
the people of Northern Ireland did not
give that enthusiastic co-operation to the
Transport Act that the Government expected. The Government, when this Act
was passing through this House, would
not heed the Farmers' Union or any
other organisation or any individual
Back Bencher. Their attitude was,
"Our duty is to lead and your duty is
to follow." That is the reason they have
landed themselves in the mess they are
in to-day.
I want to say that this is the first time
that the Government have taken the
Back Benchers into their confidence, and
that is a step in the right direction; it
is a pity it did not happen long ago
for it would have saved the Government
from a great deal of the odium to which
they are being subjected to-day. A great
deal has been said about the best procedure to adopt in connection with this
transport business. Some people say that
the best way to mend this Act is to end
it. I do think it is the duty of everyone to give what constructive help he can
to try to bring about a new scheme which
will be suitable for the people of Northern Ireland.
I want to say, in reply to the hon.
Member for Shankill, that if I were one
of the rebels to whom he referred I would
not be muzzled either in Committee or out
of it. I am going to express my opinion.
in any place that I have the opportunity
of doing so, and I am going to give my
suggestions which I believe are in the
best interests of the people who sent me
here to represent them. When the Act
was passing through this House I made
the statement that I believed it was
being placed on the Statute Book in
order to bolster up the railways. I may
have been wrong because it has not
bolstered up the railways. The Transport Act has not done what the Government believed it would do, and the
Government have realised that at last.
It has taken them a long time to do so.
A good deal of money has been taken out
of the taxpayers' pockets before the Government realised they had made a mistake. Even yet I do not think the
Government have admitted that they
made a mistake. They have made the
admission that the Act did not operate
as they would have liked it to operate,
and as they thought it would operate.
I do hope now that the Government in
their efforts to cope with the situation
will not enact any hasty legislation
which, perhaps, would only make the
situation worse than it is at the present
time. We must try to see that any
amending Act passed here will improve
the situation rather than make it worse.
The McLintock Report is to be taken
into consideration by this Committee
formed by Members of both Houses of
Parliament. I do not intend to go into
that Report to-day further than to say
this, that I would never accept completely or wholeheartedly suggestions
conveyed in the McLintock Report.
There are suggestions contained in that
Report that very few Members of Parliament could accept.

8 DECEMBER, 1938
At any rate there is sufficient in the
McLintock Report to give food for
thought upon the part of the Government and people of Northern Ireland for
many a long day. It seems to me
strange that when the Government was
setting up this Transport Board they did
not ask for the co-operation and the help
of those who were engaged in the transport business, and who would, I am sure,
have been quite willing to give their
assistance in carrying out the Transport
Act. Those people had made a success
of their own business, but when the Government took over transport they simply
said to those men, "You know nothing
about the way the business ought to be
run; we will show you the way the business ought to be run; we will appoint
our own Board to run the business, and
we will make the transport system of
Northern Ireland the envy of the whole
world." It has been well said that instead of being the envy of the whole
world the transport system to-day is the
laughing stock of it. I am sorry to have
to say that. I want to say that, although
I opposed the Act, I was not one of those
who said that as it was put on the
Statute Book without my assistance, and
against my opinion, I I would have
nothing to do with it. I co-operated
with the Transport Board and I made use
of it to do my work. I am glad to say
that the Board have carried out that
work well and have done it efficiently.
They have given me good service.
If the Government is going to get the
co-operation of the people they will only
get it by listening to the representatives
of the people putting forward their views
as best they think fit. I am prepared,
so long as I am in this House, to give
the Government that assistance provided
they legislate along lines which will
help my constituents. I am reminded of
a story which I heard some time ago in
connection with the Transport Act. Two
men went into business, one had the
money and the other had the experience.
They traded together for five years and
at the end of that time the man who had
the experience had the money, while the
man who had the money at the beginning
now had the experience. The Government went into this transport business
with the money, but the men who were
in the transport business previously had
the experience. To-day, the men who
were in the transport business previously
have got the money, at least paper
money, while the Government have got
the experience which, I hope, will be a
lesson to them in regard to any future
legislation.

A very startling announcement was
made in the Press a short time ago.
was stated that the Transport Board
were not going to pay interest to the

Many of my own constituents who are
stockholders were looking forward to the

half-yearly dividend. When I see that
announcement in the paper it looks to me
as if the Government have not only made

they are going to leave these people without any money. The Government ought
to come out with a bold statement and
say, "We are not only going to put a
Transport Act in operation that is going
to be the envy of the whole world, but
we are going to pay every stockholder
the full 20s in the £ and interest up to
date."
I want the Government to make a
clear declaration on this matter so that
the minds of the stockholders may be
put at rest and that they may be
reassured, as I have tried to reassure
them that they are going to get their
stock not only paid in full but that the
dividend will be paid up to date.
I am
not raising the question as to whether
they got too much or too little; that
is not my object. The Government,
through the Tribunal, told them they
were going to give them so much for
their undertakings. They have not
given them money, but scrip. Up to six
months ago they got interest on that
scrip, and many men are looking
forward to getting money in January.
The Government should tell these people
from whom they took businesses that
they gave them stock, and that
they are going to give them interest no
matter what blunder has been made. I
will stand behind them in paying every
stockholder 20s in the £ and interest
up to the time the stock has been paid.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 13th December, 1938.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Paper Presented.
Ministry of Commerce:
Report of the Registrar of Friendly
Societies for Northern Ireland, Part B,

(By Act).
Oral Answers to Questions.
PRICE OF HIGH GRADE
NORTHERN IRELAND EGGS.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state
whether under his new Egg Marketing
Scheme the price of Northern Ireland
super-inspected highest grade eggs were
last week 1s 2d per lb. or for two-ounce
eggs ls 9d per dozen, whereas the
average price (as announced by wireless
Friday, 18th instant) the English producer obtained last week for
noninspected eggs was 2s 3d per dozen-a
difference of 64d per dozen now, whereas
previous to these Acts the difference was
ld per dozen.
The MINISTRY OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): The price
fixed by the Ministry, on the advice of
the Egg Marketing Committee, for eggs
delivered by producers to licensed wholesale dealers during the week ended the
19th November was 1s 2d per lb. If the
eggs were delivered by the producer to a
Class A dealer's packing store 1s 2d per
lb.
was payable; if the eggs were
delivered to a retailer who was not also
a wholesale dealer, the retailer was empowered to pay a price not exceeding
1s 3d per lb. The price payable to producers who retail their eggs to consumers
directly is not controlled, and such producers would normally receive the
current retail price which for the week
mentioned by the hon. Member was 2s 6d
per dozen.
The price of 2s 31d per dozen referred
to in the question is the price payable
to producers in England and Wales, and
is not comparable with the prices I have
quoted for Northern Ireland. Moreover,
since the bulk of eggs sold in Northern
Ireland must ultimately find a market
in Great Britain, it will be evident that
the prices received by producers here
must approximate to the current British
price, less carriage charges and the costs.
of handling the eggs. It is the function
of the Egg Marketing Committee, on
which producers and merchants
represented, to advise the Ministry with
regard to the appropriate price payable
to producers in Northern Ireland having
regard to the prices realised for Northern
Ireland eggs in Great Britain.
COST OF FRUIT INSPECTORS.
are
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether it is a fact that
there are six fruit inspectors; whether
he can state the cost in salaries and expenses for the years 1937 and 1938;
whether it is a fact that three inspectors
motored from Belfast to Annaghmore
daily during the strawberry season to inspect strawberries and that often there
was not as much fruit there as when sold
would have covered the cost of the inspection; whether a member of the Fruit
Advisory Committee on complaining that
there was no use their attending meetings as their advice was ignored was told
by the Ministry that any member of the
Advisory Committee dissatisfied with the
Ministry's action was at liberty to withdraw from the membership of the committee; and whether he is aware that the
English fruit buyers visiting the recent
show in the King's Hall were commenting on the volume of dissatisfaction expressed to them by growers on all sides
at the Ministry's prohibition of apples
and packages for export.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: If the hon.
Member suggests that six inspectors are
regularly engaged in operations under
the Marketing of Fruit Act, the answer
is in the negative. The position is that
we have three inspectors employed on
horticultural work generally, including
educational work, supervision of county
staffs, enforcement of the Destructive
Insects and Pests Acts and Orders made
Oral Answers

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke]
thereunder, and the Marketing of Fruit
Act. From time to time, when shipments of fruit are heavy we reinforce the
normal fruit inspection staff by inspectors
from other branches in order to facilitate the trade. At the moment only
one inspector is engaged on work under
the Marketing of Fruit Act. It is not
a fact that three inspectors motored to
Annaghmore daily during the strawberry
season. The number of inspectors who
attend at this or any other centre is
regulated by the quantity of fruit likely
to be displayed, and normally our officers
would endeavour to fit in such inspection
work with other duties in the same neighbourhood, thus killing two birds with
one stone. The total salaries and expenses of the horticultural staff in the
years mentioned were:

GRADE OF IRISH GROWN APPLES
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether there are apples
going out as "Extra Fancy" or
"Fancy," and whether the regulations.
for the grades made by his Ministry are
so stringent that it is impossible to attain
them in Northern Ireland; whether all
the apples are (and have been for years)
going out as "C" (third) grade and the
remainder go as "Culls" and "Ungraded."
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Apples are
going out this season as "Extra Fancy"
and "Fancy.". The grades laid down in
the regulations have been and are being
attained in Northern Ireland and I
would like to point out here, as showing
what our apple-growers can do, that at
the recent Imperial Fruit Show at
Bristol Northern Ireland growers
obtained three second prizes and one
third prize for Bramley apples in competition with the best British growers.
The answer to the second part of the
question is in the negative.
USE OF APPLE BUSHEL BASKETS
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state if,
under the Northern Ireland Fruit
Marketing Act, the bushel basket is prohibited from being used for export of
apples to Great Britain since 1931;
whether this is the most common package
used by British growers and merchants;
whether the Minister has granted permits or licences to certain British fruit
merchants or salesmen to ship Northern
Ireland apples in these bushels; whether
he can state the names and addresses of
those who are able to obtain such permits; whether it is a fact that other
British apple buyers were refused liberty
to use these bushels; and whether he will
see that there is no discrimination
practised in future in these things.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The bushel
basket is not prohibited nor is it the
package chiefly used by British growers
and merchants. Permits for its use for
the shipment of apples from Northern
Ireland have been granted both to
British and Northern Ireland merchants,
as well as to Northern Ireland growers.
If the hon. Member wishes I can hand
him a list of those who obtained such
permits last season. We have no record
of the refusal of applications for such
permits for graded fruit.

THE CIVIL SERVICE PLAYING
GROUNDS.
6. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the position
of the playing grounds for the civil servants for which £9,000 was recently provided in the Estimates, the exact area of
these grounds, the price paid, the total
legal expenses including assignments, the
name and address of the person or persons from whom the grounds in question
were purchased or will be purchased, and
whether the service playing hours have
been fixed or will be fixed by the
Ministry.
Mr. ANDREWS: The playing fields
are situated on the south-east side of the
Stormont Estate adjoining the Newtownards Road. The area is between six and
seven acres. Play will not, of course,
take place during office hours, and apart
from this the Ministry does not interfere
with the clubs' discretion. As the ground
was already the property of the Government, having been handed over many
years ago by the Imperial Government,
who purchased the Stormont Estate, the
remainder of the hon. Member's question
does not arise. The Civil Service Clubs
have no legal tenure of the area, only
permission to use it.
I may add that the carrying out of
this scheme is giving useful employment
to from 40 to 50 persons, mostly ex-
Servicemen, for a period of from six to
eight months, whose unemployment
benefit is being consequently saved.
Mr. NIXON: Why is it the Minister
will not fix the playing hours for civil
servants when he has given the playing
grounds?

Member's question, they are not prepared to furnish any further information
in the matter, but if the hon. Member

Sir DAWSON BATES: I have

FRUIT GROWING IN ULSTER.
12. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if, in view
of the deep-seated discontent amongst the
fruit growers and the serious financial
loss they have suffered as a result of the
Fruit Act and the imminent danger of
Ulster losing one of its formerly prosperous industries, he will redeem his
promise made to this House and repeated
to the Ulster Fruit Growers' Defence
Association on December 21, 1934, to
settle this matter in accordance with the
growers' wishes.
The PRIME MINISTER: In reply to
the hon. Member, I am satisfied that
there is no foundation for the suggestion
that there is deep-seated discontent and
serious financial loss due to the operation
of the Marketing of Fruit Act. On the
contrary, there is ample evidence to show
that but for that Act the apple export
trade of Northern Ireland would by now
have virtually ceased to exist on account
of competition from other countries where
strict attention is paid to grading and
packing. One of the best tributes to the
utility of the Act is the fact that in the
six years preceding its operation the
exports of apples from Ulster averaged
2,054 tons, whereas in the six years subsequent to the passing of the Act the
average was 7,040 tons. Furthermore,
notwithstanding unsatisfactory seasons,
the apple acreage has, I am glad to say,
been well maintained. There can, therefore, be no question of modifying existing legislation on this subject.
Mr. NIXON: If the fruit growers are
as satisfied as the Prime Minister has
stated, why ther are they here protesting
and writing protests all the time?
The PRIME MINISTER: I really
cannot tell. All I can say is they must
be in a minority who are dissatisfied.

INDUSTRIAL CONDITIONS IN
NORTHERN IRELAND.
17. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Prime
Minister whether he had any recent communications with the Imperial Government as to Northern Ireland being classified as a distressed or special area;
whether there was any need so to classify
this area, and if so, whether anything
could be done to provide special relief
works here; whether linen exports to
China formerly amounted to millions of
pounds and are now almost nil; whether
hundreds of thousands of pounds due from
the Continent to traders for linen goods
are irrecoverable; whether only one-third
of the working capacity of the local shipyards is occupied; whether in Lurgan,
out of a population of 15,000, between
4,000 and 5,000 are idle; whether the conditions in Lurgan are equalled in many
industrial centres here; and whether any
distressed or special area in Great Britain
has a higher percentage of unemployment
than Northern Ireland.
The PRIME MINISTER: As the
answer is rather long I will, with the hon.
and learned Member's permission, circulate it in the Official Report.
to:
The following is the statement referred
-
In the opinion of the Government,
Northern Ireland is not an area comparable with those scheduled under the
Special Areas legislation in Great
Britain. In any event, the determination of that question would be one
primarily for this Government, and it
has not, therefore, been the subject at
any time of communications with the
United Kingdom Government.
It has been the policy of this Government for many years to provide moneys
for works of public utility, and the rate
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
13 DECEMBER 1938
of grant for this purpose was increased
early this year to 85 per cent. of the
wages cost. As a result of the Government's action in this matter, and in the
other directions indicated in the Gracious
Speech at the opening of the present
Session, a large amount of employment.
has been, and will continue to be,
provided.
Furthermore, the United Kingdom.
Government extends to our manufacturers
the preference that is given, other things.
being equal, to tenders for Government
contracts received from firms in areas of
heavy unemployment, which are not
necessarily depressed or special areas.
Linen exports to China have at no
time amounted to millions of pounds.
There was a steady increase in the value
of such exports over the decade 1926 to
1936, the figure for 1936 being £475,000,
as compared with £181,000 in 1926. The
final figures for 1937 and 1938 are not yet
available, but the unhappy war in China
has, unfortunately, dislocated the whole
trade of Northern Ireland with that
country.
I have no information such as would
lead me to the conclusion that Northern
Ireland linen firms have now large irrecoverable debts in Europe. On the contrary, agreements concluded in recent
years with certain Europen Governments
have been instrumental in liquidating the
major portion of any debts formerly outstanding. If, however, the hon. and
learned Member is aware of any important unliquidated debts, I suggest that
he should bring them to the notice of my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Commerce.
Whilst it is the case that the number of
slips occupied in the local shipyard represents only about one-third of the firm's
shipbuilding capacity, the firm is engaged
in most important activities on other
forms of production, and I am happy to
say that in consequence very substantial
employment is being maintained for our
workers.
I regret that the hon. and learned
Member's figures regarding the population and the number of unemployed
persons in Lurgan are not quite accurate.
The total population of the urban
district of Lurgan was under 14,000 at
the last census, and in the Employment
Exchange area of Lurgan, which includes
a number of smaller towns in the vicinity,
the number of unemployed persons
insured under the general scheme is not
between 4,000 and 5,000, but is under
3,000. I regret that the unemployment
rate in that district is high, but I am
glad to say that every other industrial
centre in Northern Ireland, comparable
in magnitude with Lurgan, has a substantially lower rate of unemployment.
Moreover, I am hopeful that the recent
trade agreement with America will
increase employment in Lurgan and elsewhere in Northern Ireland in the future.
I might add that, unfortunately, there
are a number of towns in Great Britain
with a still higher percentage of unemployment than that prevailing in Lurgan.
The answer to the last portion of the
hon. and learned Member's question is
in the affirmative.

of the provisions of the Road and Railway Transport Act (Northern Ireland),
1935, and to assist to secure the improvement of the provisions of the existing
Acts relating to hours and conditions of
wages in the Transport industry; and
that the Government do further take
Transport Act, 1935-
Adjourned Debate
HOUSE OF COMMONS
into consideration the matters dealt with
in the Reports of the Recorder of Belfast and Sir William McLintock's Committee, with the object of securing that
such arrangements will be made for
transport as will be in the best interests

(The Prime Minister).
Question again proposed.
Mr. MINFORD: It is some three
years since this House almost unanimously passed the Road and Railway
Transport Bill. At that time every
Member had high hopes that the best
road and rail services would be in Ulster,
but unfortunately we have been brought
back here to-day to debate this very
important question. It would not be
fair for me to criticise the Road Transport Board or the railways, but it is only
right to say that a Committee was set
up for the investigation of complaints
against the Board and that if the advice
of that Committee, of which I was
Chairman, had been taken, although it
came only from a few back benchers,
we should not be here to-day trying to
overcome this great difficulty.
When the Bill was passed it was the
intention of the Government that there
should be co-ordination between the road
and rail services, but unfortunately competition seemed to be more acute
between the Road Transport Board and
the railway companies than it was
between the private owners and the
railway companies. It is my honest
opinion that at this time, which the
Prime Minister has described as a crisis,
it is the duty of every Member of this
House to give his contribution in order
to make the transport of Ulster one of
the best in any country. When the
Road and Railway Transport Act was
passed it met with hostile criticism, but
as one of those who supported the Second
Reading I was prepared to give the
Measure my utmost and best support.
A Committee is now going to be set
up to thresh out the best method of
transport for Ulster with the idea of
co-ordinating road and rail. We who
live in Ulster, practically an agricultural
country, know the great difficulties that
such a combination will have to overcome. We must recognise that prior to
the taking over of transport in Ulster
even the smallest farmer was served
fairly well. To-day, where the Transport Board, with all its faults, is getting
a chance it is not doing too badly. I
believe it is better to tell the truth and
give honour where honour is due. My
experience of the Transport Board both
in business and in agriculture has been
one of the happiest. It has been most
efficient.
Perhaps in the remote parts of Ulster
some of the small holders who are not
getting as well served as they were under
private ownership. That is not to be
wondered at when you consider that the
private haulier often had a very meagre
income and was most anxious to knock
out a livelihood. Now we have set up
a Transport Board for Northern Ireland
and it has not met with the success we
expected. I believe that if the Committee to be set up had been set in
action at that time the co-ordination of
road and rail transport would have been
better than it is to-day.
I am one of those who believe that
to do away with the railways would be
a mistake. Consider the railway from Belfast to Derry. If we had no railway
what would be the condition of the
roads? As one who travels night and
morning by car I can visualise what the
position would be within ten miles of
Belfast with the loads of timber and the
requirements of builders not to mention
the one hundred other things. Therefore I feel it is essential that the
railways should be kept in being, but
at the same time there are parts of the
railways which have become redundant.
As an agricultural community the people.
of Northern Ireland are determined that
the transport of their goods within a
certain distance of Belfast must be by
road as they must support what is most
economical. If it is more economical to
transport goods by road for a distance
of twenty or thirty miles then it is time
that that part of the railway which is
redundant should be cut off.
This is not the time for any Member
to throw out suggestions, because every
Member will have an opportunity of submitting his views to the Committee,
which will be set up. May I say that
whether I am a member of that Committee or not I am determined to give
what knowledge I have in order to make
our transport a success. The transport
of a country is a matter of the greatest
Transport Act, 1935-
Adjourned Debate
13 DECEMBER 1938
importance, and to-day we are living in
a time when we need to get the cooperation of the general public. That
will be a very difficult thing to do
because no matter what Act comes from
this House you will get members of the
public to criticise it destructively. If
the people are determined to make the
transport of this Province one of the
best systems an opportunity will be
given them.
I for one
can visualise what would
happen if there was a failure. When
you consider that for seventeen years
this House has legislated, and legislated
well, I think it would be unfair because
one Act has not met with the requirements of the people of Ulster to scrap
that Measure and say, "Let us go back
to the old method of transport. The
Transport Board had a very large undertaking. They had to go into the question of compensation for lorry owners,
they had to value the lorries and the
trade, and I think they were generous
to many of these people.
""
I feel this Emergency Act is very
much required. I have no sympathy
with a man who when he has got a handsome sum from the Board for acquiring
his trade disguises himself as a merchant
or something else after a month or two
and begins to compete with the Board.
The time is more than ripe when some
steps should be taken to put an end to
that practice. I can only compare it to
a man selling a milch cow to his neighbour and then milking it night and
morning, allowing the poor neighbour to
keep and feed her.
As regards cheaper freights and fares
in Ulster, it is most important that we
should get the best transport at the
cheapest rate, but there must be a fair
return to the Transport Board. There
is one point which I do not think any
Member has yet mentioned. One reason
for the failure of road and rail transport
in Ulster has been the depression in
trade. We know perfectly well that the
linen trade and agriculture have been
suffering very severely, and that in my
opinion is one of the reasons why we
are not getting the volume of trade.
The people who are carrying on their
businesses in a legitimate way are most
anxious and willing to help this House
to frame a Bill which will be a success.
You can visualise a farmer taking a
load of 35 cwts. of hay to the Belfast
market, and after two hours detention
he has got to pay 35s for the transport
of that hay. He gets the handsome sum
of £2 for it, leaving him the same
amount to produce the goods as the
transport of the hay cost him. I do not
suggest that the Transport Board charge
too much, but I do suggest that it is
impossible for the farmer to pay these
rates of transport when he is getting
such a miserable pittance for his produce.
The agricultural industry is of the
utmost importance to both road and rail
transport, and to take it away would be
equivalent to taking from the railways
and Transport Board at least threefifths of their trade.
Although the members of the Transport Board did not take the advice of
the Committee of which I was chairman,
I do not suggest that the members of
the Board are not good business men and
men of ability, but on the Transport
Board there should have been at least
two members representing agriculture.
While the members of the Board may
know all about business, the only man
who can understand and appreciate the
needs of agriculture is a man who knows
agriculture. There ought to be two
members on the Transport Board who
understand what farmers want, although
I do not say that they should necessarily
be farmers. I hope the Government will
send a message to the farming community in every remote corner of the
Six Counties that they are prepared to
give to every farmer the best system of
transport possible.
Although a farmer may have only a
small holding in the most remote corner
of the Province he has got to make his
living there, and his transport requirements should be provided for. If an
emergency Measure is to be put through
Parliament to do away with the
irregularities that have occurred under
the 1935 Act and we know the irregularities are very numerous-the Government should let the farmers know that
the Transport Board are as anxious to
cater for the small farmer with 10 acres
as they are to cater for the large farmer
with 300 acres, or the big linen merchant.
I hope the Members of this House will
give the best adivce possible to the Committee that is to be set up.
If they
Transport Act, 1935-
