con-
[Mr. Minford]
criticise they should criticise
structively, because it does not require
much brains to criticise destructively.
If we give both road and rail transport
the support it is entitled to, although up
to the moment it has not proved a
success, I am confident that we shall be
able to produce a scheme that will be an
example to the rest of the British
Empire.
Mr. CAMPBELL: As an Ulsterman
I deplore the loss in this disastrous
transport scheme. Up to the present
the loss has been £460,000, and it may
possibly involve the taxpayers of Northern Ireland in a contingent liability
of about £3,000,000. The Northern
Ireland taxpayers alone will bear the
racket this time. It is not a case in
which the taxpayers across the water
can be asked to bear any share of the
burden. It is a very remarkable fact
that the first big experiment of the
Government in which they had not a
British head-line to copy has become all
a muddle. I do say that a more colossal
example of futility and ineptitude has
not been the bitter experience of any
country in our day.
The Nationalists can wash their hands
of responsibility for this collapse. In
vain they challenged the passing of the
Act in 1935. In vain they criticised it
from time to time in its administration.
In vain they sought to throw light upon
its failures. They were not appointed
to posts of importance in the administration of the Act-not one of them. The
Act provided that in making these
appointments the Minister should have
regard, among other things, to the
proved capacity and tried experience of
men in public affairs. That gave the
Minister a master key. Under the Act
of 1935 each member of the Board holds
his office at the pleasure of the Minister.
Over a year ago I had the honour of
moving in this House a resolution
animadverting on the wrongs and
injustices inflicted by this Act, and the
resolution was voted down by the
Ministerial phalanx.
This was supposed to be a masterpiece
of supermen of commerce. When efforts
were made to penetrate the secrecy with
which the Board was conducted-very
remarkable secrecy-these efforts came to
nothing because the cry of "hush, hush"
was raised. The scheme staggered on
from loss to loss. Criticism was stifled.
They contemplated and projected coordination between road transport and
rail services. What did it culminate in?
A long drawn out Kilkenny cat contest.
No co-ordination, no harmony, no sign
of concord. That all disappeared in the
course of the development of this system.
I do not know whether at the present
time the unfortunate holders of "A"
transport stock could not apply to the
High Court for the appointment of a
receiver to wind up this fiasco.
For almost three years the public had
hardly an inkling of the drift of transport finance. On 1st December, 1937,
the Minister of Home Affairs came down
to this House and jauntily said that it
was expected that the accounts for the
first year ending on 30th September,
1936, would disclose that the revenue for
that year was sufficient, or nearly
sufficient, to meet the interest charges.
It was not so at all. There was a dead
weight, stunning liability and loss, and
the House and the public were definitely
misled by that statement. Further, on
6th May, 1936, the Prime Minister said
to this House, "No Act which was ever
placed upon our Statute Book has given
less cause for trouble in this Province.'
And he added, "If there ever was a
Measure which has been fully justified
it is the Road Measures which this House
has passed.'
""
That is a very remarkable declaration
made by the Prime Minister-that no
Act of this Parliament had given less
cause for trouble in this Province than
the Road Transport Act. Where did he
get the facts to justify that statement?
Where did he get the figures? What
information and knowledge had he on
which to base a statement of that kind?
He proceeded to say that if there ever
was a Measure that had been fully justified it was the Road Transport Measures
passed by this Parliament. Who credits
that statement now? Who would
honour it to-day? Not a solitary soul
in the length and breadth of the Six
Counties. I challenge any hon. Member on the other side of the House to
say that that statement was justified.
What information or knowledge had the
Prime Minister when he made a statement of that kind?

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Campbell]
On that point, may I ask is there any
other country in the world where both
road and rail traffic are controlled by
a Government? I do not know of one.
It may be so in Soviet Russia-I cannot
say with certainty. I think it cannot be
denied that Ulster initiative and Ulster
enterprise, which used to be the backbone of Ulster industry, have been
sapped. We must consider the fact that
the area of Northern Ireland is less than
the area of one English county-Yorkshire. We have all the trappings of Government here, all the machinery and
impedimenta of an Imperial State, in the
area in which this scheme has failed,
with all the resources of Government
behind it.
In its origin the Act was a Railway
Relief Act. It has brought them
precious poor relief. It was rushed on
by the Minister at a time when, on his
own showing in the Second Reading
debate, passenger services were being
carried on with regularity and safety.
That Minister does not shine as a Minister of Transport; he is more at home
when signing weekly proclamations banning peaceful meetings of Catholics for
the delectation of his brethren. One
regret to many is that with the
disappearance of private competition
disappeared also many of those excursions of large groups of the working
classes. The cheap services they enjoyed
in this respect belong to the past. What
is the upshot of it all? Loss piled on loss,
confusion worse confounded, a hideous
shipwreck.
The Government, with craft and
cunning, now want to pass on to others
a share of the responsibility which must
be the exclusive glory of their own party.
"We have made a sorry mess of this job,
we are at our wit's end, true we have
boycotted you, but do help us to pull
the chestnuts out of the fire." They set
up a Committee under the chairmanship
of the hon. Member for Antrim, which
will go down to posterity as the Minford
Committee. I congratulate the hon.
Member on achieving immortal fame.
Other Members on the other side of the
House will be forgotten, but people in the
future will talk about the Minford Committee.
Mr. NIXON: They did not take his
advice.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Then we had the
Recorder's inquiry and the McLintock
Committee. Now there is to be a Parliamentary Committee. This device is like
that of the cuttlefish which darkens the
water as it retreats. This fobbing off
of responsibility from the shoulders of
the Government is contemptible; it is not
statesmanship, it is a runaway and a surrender after abject failure. I wish the
Committee success, but its appointment
is a subterfuge. The captain and officers
fleeing from their ship in distress is a
very unheroic spectacle. The responsi
bility, past, present and future, must
rest with the Government, first and last.
Mr. THOMPSON: As one of those
who took part in insisting that the
McLintock Report should be laid upon
the Table of this House, I feel that we
were fully justified in insisting that all
the facts of the Transport Inquiries
should be brought under public notice.
There is no doubt that the Government
are faced with one of the most difficult
domestic problems they have ever had to
face, and those of us who were not in
any way a party to this enterprise feel
we have nevertheless a responsibility. 1
am sure that every Member of this House
is anxious to do his part and to help in

I wish to express my own personal
views on the problem. We must proceed
slowly, and every step taken must be
carefully thought out. I quite agree
that the first step is to make sure we get
what we have paid for, and I hope the
Emergency Bill now coming before this.
House will put that right. Why it was
not done twelve months ago I cannot
understand. The leakage should have
been stopped the moment it was detected,
instead of waiting until it has gone
almost beyond control. If it can be

the road traffic, passenger and goods,
pretty well under control. The passenger end should be paying handsomely;
there is no reason whatever why it should
not now be a real paying concern. Everything indicates that it should be.
The goods traffic is the real problem. I
am one of those unrepentant people who
believe that this end should never have
been taken out of the hands of private
enterprise. It should have been

the railway companies were able to submit, at least as far as has been made

William
delighted to think that Sir

and gave
his reasons for doing so. If

want to know what is going to be the

It will be necessary to have a manager

and also a manager for the passenger
traffic. These should be expert men in
their own end, and should also be above
prejudice and petty misunderstanding.
A chairman with wide and wise administrative ability should be appointed,
together with an arbitrator to decide any
matters that may cause misunderstanding. The undertaking should then be put
on a year's trial. If, in the meantime,
the railways are in difficulty steps might
be taken to help them through. I am
satisfied if we go a step at a time we can
yet make a success of the undertaking.
Rail versus road controversy must cease,
and cease at once. There must be no
further thought of rail control or of road
control, there must be joint control,
harmony and goodwill, with a common
policy for the good of the whole Province.
If the old Act must go unwept, unhonoured and unsung let us build something that will bring credit to all concerned. I am reminded of the words of

of Ireland when he said:
I raised such men as had the fear of
God before them and made some
conscience of what they did, and from
that day forward they were never

It is not my desire to prolong the agony

there is still a basis left on which to pro-

Not only that, but the fact is that
road transport in Northern Ireland had
as its background the great railway
strike. The real development of road
transport dates from that period. The
country people felt that the lorries and
their owners saved the country from a
terrible catastrophe at that time. Therefore the position of these transport
vehicle owners was really due to two
factors, sentiment, and the fact of a very
economic and cheap service. That
created a spirit of ill-will which was
practically fatal to a scheme of this sort
no matter how well conceived it may
have been, but I am not one of those
people who are prepared, as some people

say
it is entirely owing to the antipathy of

has failed. I am of the opinion that it
has in part failed because of the
inefficiency of the Board or the Board's
officials.
A comparison has been drawn between
this scheme and gas and electricity undertakings, the Post Office, and so on.
I do not think there is any true analogy
there at all. In the case of gas or
electricity the individual using it has it
in his own house and simply presses a
button or turns a tap and serves himself. It is only the means of actual
production that is centralised, there is
not autonomous control. There is no
comparison between services of that kind
and services such as the Transport Board
was intended or expected to give.
I will give you an example of the
inefficiency of this Board. I do not often
travel by bus, but I was travelling one
day nearly two years ago by a public
bus owned by the Transport Board
running on a route which used to be one
of the best managed and most satisfactory in Northern Ireland. What did
I find? When we got to a certain point
on that journey into the city here the
conductor had to go among the passengers asking them not only where they
were going but how much they were in
the habit of paying. That all arose from
a notion which the Transport Board got
to change round the conductors in
different districts and on different
routes. Whether they could trust them
or not I cannot say. Under private
management the conductors knew the
routes, they knew every gateway, every
lane end, even in the dark of the night
they knew where to stop the bus to let
Mrs. Jones or Mrs. Brown off
practically at her own doorstep.

got each year in Northern Ireland a certain amount of traffic. The big idea
behind this 1935 Act was to so spread
this available amount of traffic between
road and rail that both of them could
make it pay.
Previous speakers have.
submitted that taking into consideration

the use of road transport. We might

work and number of shifts per dayunder which the railways have been and

Ireland will enable us to keep that sort
of thing going.

end of transport in Northern Ireland is

great deal of the present position is due.
to the public antipathy in the midst of

limit hours in any drastic way with a

for transport, and you are going to

transport system in Northern Ireland.
I do not know how the Departmental
Committee has set about its task at all.
I presume they have been content to
frame this Bill on general principles of
equity. I think it would have been far
wiser to have taken another fortnight
or three weeks, or whatever time be
necessary, and surveyed the different
individuals and companies case by case
to see whether they are legally operating concerns, and take proper stock as to
the functions they are fulfilling in their
different districts. Then base your Bill
on the facts. Whatever you do it will
not be by sitting down and making a
cast-iron mould and trying to force the

have to sit down and carefully survey all
the facts and all the different circumstances in town and country in regard
to both road and rail transport, and then
try to make them meet.

We should ask the people do they

Another thing I want to know is, at

We have no emergency legislation to take

Belfast and the city of Londonderry. No,

successfully without the inclusion of the

I wish to remind the House that half

We know from what has happened that

If I wanted to prove that I could call no

at the meeting of the York Street Flax
Spinning Co. You pointed out that
Northern Ireland could only supply oneeighth of your requirements; in other
words, Northern Ireland is sending about
five million pounds a year to the mass
murderers of Moscow and the butchers of
Berlin for flax which could be grown here.
That is being done in spite of the fact that
our farmers are down and out.
In conclusion, I should like, if I may,

Mr. BYRNE: I should like to say a
few words in regard to this matter.
First of all I wish to point out that the
Nationalist representatives in this
House had nothing whatever to do with
this Act or this undertaking. They can
safely say that they had neither act nor
part in the calamity. We on this side
of the House voted against the Measure.
Personally, I thought it was a very
dangerous thing to take over the transport business. There was, I am aware,
a great deal of competition and a good
many employees who were underpaid
and who had to work very long hours.
That matter could have been remedied
the way other grievances are settled by
having an organisation to fix hours and
wages for the employees. So far as the
hauliers themselves were concerned, they
could also have organised and fixed rates
which would have made their business
a paying proposition. The people in the
country districts were well served and
did not want any change. I have some
experience in regard to the buses and
the lorries, because I have used both
from time to time.
I am strongly of the opinion that mistakes were made when the businesses
were taken over from these men.
Naturally, if people had certain work to
do over again they would do it much
better the second time. On a road with
which I am familiar a bus service was
run, and the people were well catered
for and appreciated the service they
were getting. When the Transport
Board took over that business, instead of
leaving the men who were well acquainted.
with that district on that route they
transferred them to a district of which
they had no knowledge. In my opinion
that cost the undertaking hundreds and
hundreds of pounds. They put on new
men who knew nothing about the
business on that road, and by doing so the
transport undertaking lost money.
In regard to the working of the
Transport Board, I wish to pay tribute
to the officials in charge of the haulage
and bus services. I always found them
very civil, decent and attentive to their
duties. They deserve great credit for
the manner in which they discharged
their duties. If those in charge of this
undertaking had continued to run the
service in the same way as the services
were run previously, and had kept the
employees who had been on a particular
route instead of transferring them to a
strange district, it would have been
wise action. After gaining some experience they could then have effected
a

If by bringing in an emergency Bill the
Government intend to create any greater
monopoly than at present they will be
making a vast mistake. I hope they will
take the views of the county and district
councils throughout the Six Counties.
They should go slowly with any emergency
measure and make sure they have the
confidence of the people behind them. I
speak as one engaged in the old industry
of agriculture, which is passing through
a parlous time owing to climatic conditions
which have allowed crops to lie rotting in
the fields. I feel that the farmers have
a lean time before them. I would ask
that transport traffic be not added to
their burden; that things may not be
made harder for them, but that they may
be smoothed out in the future.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolved: "That, in the opinion of
this House, the Government should
immediately devise measures to deal with

and Railway Transport Act (Northern
Ireland), 1935, and to assist to secure the

and that the Government do further take

in the Reports of the Recorder of Belfast
and Sir William McLintock's Committee,
with the object of securing that such
arrangements will be made for transport
as will be in the best interests of the
people of Northern Ireland."

what steps the police have taken arising

All

the information obtained by the police

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS

DISCHARGE OF SEWAGE AT
NEWTOWNARDS.
5. Mr. GAMBLE (on behalf of Captain Stronge) asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether his Ministry in October,
1935, directed its medical inspector to
make a special inspection at Newtownards of the foreshore and lough bed,
into which crude sewage is discharged;
whether, as a result of the inspector's
report, representations were made to the
Urban District Council of Newtownards
to take steps to provide for the purification of the sewage before its discharge;
whether the Ministry subsequently, in
September, 1936, represented to the
Council that in view of the shallowness
of the water in the upper part of the
lough and the distance to which the tide
recedes it would be necessary to provide
for purification as well as sedimentation
of the sewage; whether it is now two
years since the Council employed a consulting engineer to advise them as to
the carrying out of the Ministry's proposal; and will the Minister say whether
the Council will be allowed to delay the
matter further and when he expects the
new system will be in operation; whether
in view of the fact that the crude
sewage of a population of 10,500 people
is discharged at all times of the day and
tide upon the exposed foreshore, and in
view of the importance of this thoroughfare in respect of tourists and the volume
of industrial and pleasure traffic from
Belfast and surrounding districts, the
Ministry will make urgent representations to the Newtownards Council to
fulfil forthwith an undertaking made
with the Local Government Board for
Ireland 30 years ago which it has failed to
carry out; and, further, will the Ministry
undertake that the proposed scheme of the
Council will provide for bacterial purification and be as efficient and perfect
as present scientific knowledge and experiment can evolve, and whether in the
interests of the public at large no system
will be sanctioned which contains any
element of experiment or uncertainty in
its effectiveness for the removal or destruction of all substances as would be
likely to cause or promote any nuisance
or vegetable growth.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Sir DAWSON BATES: The facts are
as stated in the first half of the question.
With regard to the queries in the second
half of the question, I may say that
my Ministry has made representations to
the Newtownards Urban District Council
concerning the necessity of carrying out
the sewage purification scheme as quickly
as possible, and the Council are now preparing the necessary plans. It is not
possible to state when the work will be
completed, but the Ministry will endeavour to secure that there is no undue
delay.
The question of the methods to be
adopted for purifying the sewage is one
in which the Ministry must be guided
by the expert opinion of the engineers,
but the hon. Member may rest assured
that the Ministry will do all in its power
to secure that the methods adopted will
be those most suitable for the locality.
Mr. HENDERSON: Arising out of the
statement of the right hon. Gentleman,
is it not a fact that thousands and
thousands of people bathe in the foreshore, and in the event of the District
Council not carrying out the scheme will
the right hon. Gentleman take steps himself to see that it is carried out?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I cannot
imagine that condition of affairs arising.
The Urban District Council of Newtownards are a most responsible body who are
prepared to do all they can to serve the
ratepayers.
Mr. HENDERSON: They are not
so quick in carrying out improvements.
Will the right hon. Gentleman give a
promise that there will be more progress
with this scheme than with the by-pass
road?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think the
representatives of Newtownards will see
that they carry it out.
Mr. HENDERSON: That is not correct. The representatives are not here
and they do not care if the people in the
next street are living in filth of every
description.

Order for Second Reading read.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I would like,
in the first instance, to apologise for the
short notice that hon. Members have
been given of this Bill, but they will, I
think, understand, the urgency of the
matter, and it is of course a short and
simple Measure, the terms of which can
be fully examined in a very short time.
The Government are introducing it
following upon the Resolution adopted
by this House. That Resolution, as hon.
Members are aware, called upon the Government immediately to devise measures
to deal with the evasions of the provisions
of the Road and Railway Transport Act,
without waiting for the preparation of a
more comprehensive measure.
I am not going to recapitulate the
reasons and circumstances which led up
to the appointing of the Joint Committee
of our two Houses. The whole of that
matter has been fully covered by the
debate of the past few days, and I think
I may therefore confine my observations
strictly to matters dealt with in this Bill.
The Bill, of course, was framed with
due regard to the wide terms of reference
that has been given to that Committee.
The Government felt it was most necessary that this Bill should do nothing that
would in any way pre-judge the findings
of that Committee or prove an embarrassment to them, and accordingly the scope
of the Bill is somewhat limited.
example, in the matter of licensing it is
proposed to go no further than to provide
for the collection by my Department of
such information as would be necessary in
any scheme the Committee may recommend.
For
On the general question of the necessity for dealing with what is known as
"piracy" I do not think I need say anything. That necessity has been recognised by this House in the passing of
the Resolution, as a consequence of which
the Bill has been introduced.
As hon. Members are aware, the
greater part of the illegal competition
with the Transport Board is being carried

if this Bill is accepted a useful step will

on by persons who have received compensation for their undertakings from the
Board and have used the money they
received to enter into competition with
the Board. When one sells and is paid
for anything-be it a particular object or
be it the goodwill of a business-it is no
more than ordinary straight dealings to
deliver over to the purchaser whatever
has been paid for, and this is precisely
what certain operators have not done.
The Government has therefore included
in this Bill a clause which is not unlike
the covenant that is commonly found in
agreements for the sale of a professional
business or practice-or, indeed, the sale
of any business-to the effect that the
person who sells shall not enter into competition with the person who buys. I
feel sure that there is no hon. Member in
this House who will take exception to a
provision of this kind. I think, indeed,
there is no hon. Member in this House
who would purchase a business or a
practice without some such covenant as
this.
With regard to the third Clause of the
Bill, it simply provides that a limit of
time, i.e., to 1st March next, should be
fixed within which claims can be made
by owners of transport undertakings on
whom will be placed the onus of proof
that the undertaking in question is one
which the Board is required to take over
under the terms of the Act of 1935.
Finally, may I say a word of explanation again as to the short time which
has been available for hon. Members to
study this Bill It may, indeed, seem to
them, at first sight, that the preparation
of such a short Bill as this should
not occupy very much time, and
that the Bill might therefore have been
ready somewhat sooner than was the case.
I would, however, inform the House that
the Government felt that it should not
deal with any matters that might prejudice the Select Committee, and this, of
course, meant the exploration of any
number of suggestions before it was possible to determine exactly to what points
the scope of the Bill should be limited.
Many matters, therefore, were considered
of which there is no mention in this Bill
at all, but I need hardly say that the
Government will most carefully consider
any suggestions which hon. Members of
this House may have to make. In the
meantime, the Government believes that
I desire, on behalf of the Government,
to thank hon. Members who have consented to act on the Committee and assist
in solving this very complex problem, and
I can assure them that every possible
assistance will be afforded them by the
various Government Departments concerned. I beg to move.

With regard to the basis on which compensation was paid to carrying companies
taken over by the Transport Board, there
are many countries in the world which
would never have considered the payment
of compensation for transport services
that were taken over by the Government.
At one time I was a convert to refusing
to recognise the payment of compensation
to private enterprise. The view was put
forth in the British House of Commons
that under no conditions would public
money be given to private enterprise as
compensation for any business or works
or anything else to which a person or
company might claim rightful possession.
But one gets mellowed by age.
times you come to realise that there has
been a certain amount of self-sacrifice and
enterprise, and that there is a just claim
for a consideration or reward for the
years of labour performed by those who
had established something that the
nation requires to take over for the good
of the nation. Therefore, we dropped the
idea of being deaf to the cry for compensation, and we believe now that it is
the nation's duty to give due consideration to the claims of those who have built
up the nation's industries and placed
them in the position they are in to-day.
Hence my reason for now agreeing that
there is a claim for compensation on the
part of the certain transport owners.
I have also got to say that in my
opinion the basis of compensation that
was fixed was very high. I do not think
goodwill value would have been considered in fixing compensation in any
other part of the world. The 1935 Act
and the Board did give a fair and reasonable rate of compensation. If you buy a
tailored suit you expect to get a tailored

You do not want to get the coat and
trousers and not to be supplied with the
waistcoat, or you do not want the tailor

With regard to the customary Motion
on the Paper at the close of the Session,
this follows our formal practice with a
single exception. As hon. Members will
observe, I have put down the hour of
our meeting on 7th March at 3-30
instead of 3 o'clock. The reason for
that is, in case there should be any
misconception, I understand His Royal
Highness, the Duke of Kent, when he is
over will receive the Freedom of the City
of Belfast, and necessarily a large num
ber of Members will probably desire to
be present in their capacity as members.
of the Belfast Corporation. Therefore
we have made arrangements that our
time will be advanced this half-hour, to
allow Members who desire to do so, to
reach the House in time to be able to
be present in their places when His
Royal Highness honours us with a visit.

area
It has been my practice when submitting
these. Estimates in the past to review
briefly the principal items during the
year of agricultural progress and development. It has often been
a point of
criticism with the Committee that the
under cereal crops in Northern
Ireland was declining, and the point was
used in debate as a measure of the inability of the Ministry to safeguard the
welfare of the agricultural industry. It
is, therefore, worth while pointing out
that the agricultural census in June last
showed a welcome increase of 40,000
acres under crops, and that our staple
cereal crop, oats, accounts for this
increase. As hon. Members are aware,
the Ministry, beginning next month, will
be paying out on behalf of the Imperial
Government a subsidy of 13s 2d per acre
in respect of the 1938 crop of oats, which
will mean a sum to farmers of Northern
Ireland of approximately £168,000. But
that is only part of the story. The assistance which is at present being given to
the oat crop is on a much less generous
scale than in the case of wheat. The
position is under review. All that I am
able to say at the moment is that the
rate of assistance will be increased
and that the increased rate will
be made retrospective to the 1938
crop. Whilst, therefore, the subsidy
which will be paid out by my Ministry
next month will amount to £168,000,
there will later in the year be a further
payment in respect of the 1938 crop.
Before I leave cereals there is one
further matter I should mention. In the
past a farmer has only been able to claim
assistance in respect of either wheat or
oats plus barley. In the future this restriction will be removed and assistance
can be claimed on all these crops, and
there will be in operation what is
equivalent to a price insurance scheme for
oats, wheat and barley.
As hon. Members are aware, the
sudden and almost violent collapse of
sheep prices last autumn had a very
serious effect on a large number of our
farmers, both small and big alike, and
was for them and for me a matter of very
considerable anxiety. Although the
position has improved to a great extent
since then I am hopeful that arising out
Ministry of Agriculture 1180
Estimates-
27 APRIL 1939
of the efforts which are, at present being
made it will be possible to devise proposals which will be of very material help
to the sheep industry, and will prevent
a repetition of the. unfortunate position
last autumn. I am hopeful the position
will be improved.
And now may I just say that in
general, as the Committee is aware, during the past few weeks consideration has
been given by the Agricultural Departments, in conjunction with the farmers'
representatives in England, Scotland and
Northern Ireland, to the question of
price insurance schemes which have as
their object the maintenance of the
fertility of the land and the maintenance
of the area under the plough. I would
just like to assure the Committee that the
benefits which accrue. from such schemes
to farmers in England and Scotland will
also apply to Northern Ireland.
And now I should like to turn to one
or two other features of our agricultural
output. I am sure I need say little about
pigs, as Members must be well informed
on this subject. All I need say is that
our output continues to increase, and that
we are within reasonable distance of
securing our objective, that all pigs produced in Northern Ireland will be cured
into bacon and ham in this country, thus
providing the maximum employment and
benefit for our own people. I have confident hopes that within the next twelve
months this desirable object, together
with a further expansion of our output,
will be attained.
There is, however, one other product,
namely, cream, which gives me cause for
some anxiety. Cream may be only a
relatively small item in our agricultural
income, but we have, after great efforts,
built up a steadily increasing trade. It
is, however, only natural that English
and Scottish producers should be turning
their attention to that particular outlet
for their own manufacturing milk, and
I am afraid, therefore, that if we are
to maintain our position it is going to
call for a great improvement in efficiency
in our creamery organisation. The
present situation is that our creamery
organisations are not able to deal with
their manufacturing milk as efficiently
as organisations on the other side, judged
by the standard of the price they return
to the farmers. That is, of course, not
the sole standard of measurement.
Many of the factors involved are outside
the individual creameries' control, and
I do not want hon. Members to be under
the impression that I am casting any
reflection upon our creamery managers.
But the problem is there and it is one
to which, with the co-operation of those
concerned, I hope to give early attention.
Once again the United Kingdom crop
of potatoes has proved a bumper one and
surplus to requirements. As the home
farmer has the home market entirely to
himself the Government can do no more.
unless adopt the fantastic suggestion of
paying producers not to grow.
There remains one other item I should
like to mention. The assistance paid to
beef producers in Northern Ireland
during the past year amounted to no
less than £226,000, a benefit in which
all sections of farmers participated, producers of fat cattle and of stores either
directly or indirectly. There is one
feature I am particularly pleased about
and that is the steady, indeed the remarkable, improvement in the quality
of our beef cattle. Since the inception
of the super subsidy for first quality
animals our percentage drawing the
higher subsidy of 7s 6d per cwt. has
increased from 6 per cent. to 30 per
cent. May I say with all the emphasis
at my command that this increase is not
in consequence of a lowered standard or
easier grading. It is entirely due to a
wider understanding amongst producers
of the standard required and their
success in reaching these standards.
The agricultural year which has just
closed has been, we must all admit, a
difficult one for producers. The element
which no Government can control or
influence, namely, weather, has been
heavily against us, together with certain
price movements of an international
character. There have been very great
difficulties which have caused us all
anxiety, but I feel that with new
methods of helping agriculture, and with
the aid of various farming organisations
and of the Department of Agriculture in
Scotland and my Ministry there is a hope
that things may improve and that we
can look forward to the future with a
greater measure of confidence than has
been possible in the past. I beg to move.

A circular letter was sent to all
registered producers warning them of the

unless sales were carred out through

steps would be taken to inflict penalties

Armaghdown, had an agency with

name was not on the register. Armaghdown continued to ship cream
through that firm. The Minister has
pointed out that they did not cut the
price, and that this was again only a

Cream Board held that as the right hon.
Gentleman's Department had sanctioned

the whole supply it was a breach of the

This firm had previously acted for
Armaghdown, and on 2nd July, 1936,
a contract form was submitted for
registration. They had every right to
put this forward under the terms of the
Butter and Cream scheme. We could
not see our way to register the contract.
Our legal adviser advised us against it,
but on pressure from the Ministry and
the Minister's officials, two of whom were
members of our Board, we decided to
register them, and we were placed in a
very embarrassing position. Naturally
the agent we had appointed took exception to the course which we had pursued,
and if Armaghdown continued to sell
through their agency he naturally held
he could not be responsible for the
collection of bad debts which we had
asked him to be responsible for. He felt
we were not carrying out our part of
the bargain.
In pursuance of this Armaghdown continued to sell cream by regular weekly
deliveries other than through the Board's
agent right up to 13th January, 1938,
when they discontinued. No sales were
then made up to April of this year.
The Board, on legal advice, held that the
contract had now lapsed, and they notified the Armaghdown Creamery to that
effect. They replied that they were not
working on the old contract, and it was
agreed by all the parties concerned-by
the Board, the Ministry, and Armaghdown Creamery-that the contract had
lapsed. Armaghdown Creamery then
asked the Board's permission to carry on
as heretofore, but the Board could not
see their way to agree to that. When
the Board pointed out to the Creamery
that they were wrong, the Creamery
said it would be better to refer the whole
matter to arbitration. The Board imposed a penalty of £20 on them, but it
was not in respect of one offence that
took place after the 6th April. To be
perfectly candid, 22 offences had been
committed.

It has been borne in upon me with

The Minister attended a conference with

Board, and we discussed this question.
He there told us that he intended to take
away from the Board the power of inflicting penalties, and that he would leave
with them only the power of inflicting a
nominal penalty of a shilling. In thus
proposing to take away the powers of the
Board the Ministry made the position of
the old Board impossible. At last it

open to them, and that was to resign. I

That resolution was passed unanimously

unrepentant. I still think

when we are faced with the prospect of

done at this moment, to increase our
very vital tillage.

appeal to the Government even at this
moment to consider seriously whether,
under the heading of war-preparedness,

patriotic need, duty, and vital necessity
of cultivating every acre of land that can
possibly be cultivated, and that they
should back it by some sort of financial
inducement in the way of a slight
subsidy on these two substantial items of

Mr. MAGINESS: It seems to me that
the presentation of this Estimate has
enabled the battle between the Ministry
and the Board to be joined. Perhaps
that was inevitable. I think it
would be a bad thing if the
public believed that there was anything
inherently wrong in either the Ministry
or the Board, or anything peculiar in
their administration in Northern Ireland.
Agriculture is simply passing through that
period of development which must come
at some stage to every industry. A hundred years ago economists held the theory
of laisser faire. Any form of Government interference was a sin, but we have
long since passed from that stage.
essential in the face of foreign competition to have some form of organisation.
Organisation may be internal; that is,
that the producers of the particular commodity may, without any Parliamentary
interference, have an organisation of
It is
their own. But so soon as the element of
compulsion is introduced, and so soon as
Parliament takes a hand in that organisation, you have got a new feature, and
that new feature in the case of agriculture must be the Ministry of Agriculture.
Up to the present time we have had a
form of dual control, necessarily dual
control, because, as I have said, once. you
get the introduction of compulsion all
departments must be interested in the
development of the organisation, and so
for some, years past we have had this dual
control. I have tried to think when dual
control was successful, but in all the
examples which passed through my mind
I found that dual control inevitably
ended in failure. We have had it tried
all through the course. of history, and
the inevitable result came; that one
or other of the parties gave way, and it
ended up with single control. Perhaps
it is better that that is how agriculture
should and must finish up in Northern
Ireland.
I am not suggesting here whether that
individual control should be confined to
the Ministry or whether it should be confined to the producer, but I think it is
only right to submit to the House that
we are now passing through this phase of
dual control, and that it can be only a
temporary phase. It is for hon. Members in this House to decide whether,
when this temporary phase comes to an
end, the control is to be left in the hands
of the producers alone, or whether the
control is to be retained in a department
of this Government.
In any democratic country interference
by Government in the concerns of the individual is to be deprecated, but in this
year of grace, 1939, we say that Governmental control is absolutely necessary to a
certain extent. We see from examples in
other countries that the whole tendency
of the present time is for control by the
Government to increase and go on increasing. In totalitarian States that may be in
defiance of all pre-conceived ideas, but we
in a democratic country elect representatives of the people, and hence the people
themselves retain the final and supreme
control. Departmental control can never
reach the stage or have, the same results
as it may have in the totalitarian States,
and, therefore, I suggest to hon. Members that they should bear in mind that
Ministry of Agriculture-

they are rapidly approaching the crossroads, and a decision must be made as to

fore, if you want to encourage the cultivation of the land and increase employment

Mr. ELLIOTT: I did not say that.

What I meant to say was that the three

the insurance charge. The Minister said
a few days ago that we on the old Pigs
Marketing Board charged the curers 6d
ourselves. May I point out that that 6d
included cover not only for condemnation
for tuberculosis, but also cover for
damage in transit and other damage. We
found that the 6d was necessary to cover
all the risks. The present Board's insurance is simply an insurance scheme to
cover condemnation. I say that if the.
Pig Industry Council had had all the
facts before them they would not have
consented to an additional charge of 3d
for insurance.
The reason I say that is this: the
audited accounts of the Cookstown Bacon
Factory, in which the Pigs Marketing
Board hold the majority of the shares,
show that 19,037 pigs were handled in
the first three months of its working-
28th September to 31st December, 1939.
After deducting T.B. offal and T.B.
pigs condemned, the net profit was
£272 15s 6d. If you deduct all the
damage claims-damage to gamons and
hams and dead pigs-there was still a
net profit of £155 15s 6d. In view of
those figures, which are in possession of
the Board-because they get the accounts
of the company-I hold that this is an
unwarranted addition of 3d for insurance.
Threepence per pig may seem to be a
very small thing, but I have delivered to
the factory this year 2,000 pigs, and if you
take 3d over 2,000 pigs it comes, according to my arithmetic, to something like
£25. A sum of £25 is a good deal to
pay in the way of extra insurance when
that extra insurance is not warranted. I
respectfully ask the Minister to go into
this matter again, in view of this information, and to put the full facts before
the Pig Industry Council. If they are
satisfied that what I have stated is correct, and that the increased insurance
charge is not justified, then I would ask

whether that is so or not, but if it was
done by an official of the Ministry in
order to circumvent the Ministry's own
regulations then I say it was altogether
wrong. Nobody reading the whole of
that unfortunate case of the Butter and
Cream Marketing Board could come to
any other conclusion but that the Ministry were out to thwart them in carrying
out the duties entrusted to them.
The Minister said something about the
heavy fines that were imposed by the
Butter and Cream Board. I am in a
position to say-and the Minister can
deny this if he is able to do so that the
Butter and Cream Marketing Board put
it to the Minister that they were quite
prepared to waive all claims against this
new creamery, to wipe out all those fines,
if the creamery would undertake to comply with the requirements of the Board.
If that is so, then I think it is not fair
to state over and over again that the
fines were iniquitous, seeing that the
Board were quite prepared to waive the
penalties if the creamery would only
come into line. I do not want to penalise the Armaghdown Creamery or any
other creamery, but I would put it to the
Minister that surely this Armaghdown
Creamery ought to be prepared to comply with the requirements of the Butter
and Cream Board's regulations.
In looking at the Estimates before us,
I was rather struck with the fact that
a sum of £100,741 is asked for. I have
searched through and through the
details of this Vote, and I cannot find agriculture coming into
the picture at all. All that I can find
is that we are asked to-day to vote
£100,741 for 419 officials. As far as
agriculture is concerned, I can see no
place where it comes into the picture at
all. It may be necessary to have 419
officials in the Ministry, and to spend
£100,741 upon them, but it does strike
me that the amount is out of the question altogether. This is an increase on
last year's Vote. I hope that when the
Minister is going through these figures
again he will see to it that some of this
£100,741 goes directly to benefit agriculture itself.
We had two officials in the Pigs
Marketing Board for six or seven months,
and since the Board was dissolved there
are three or four additional officials
there. Evidently the work of the Ministry has been carried on without the
officials, and it has occurred to me that
if the Ministry can carry on for eight
or ten months without six of their
officials, how many more officials could
the Ministry do without? If the Ministry have not asked for officials to replace
these six, then it does strike me that
there are too many officials in the
Department. If there are too many
officials, then the only thing to do is to
get the number reduced.
May I say another word before I sit
down? I believe that the Minister of
Agriculture is doing his best, as far as
he knows, for agriculture. I have
always found him quite amenableuntil quite recently. (Laughter.) I believe
that he thinks what he has done is in
the best interests of agriculture. I do
not bear the Minister any illwill. I am
too much concerned with agriculture to
allow personalities to divert me from
doing what is best in the interests of the
agricultural industry. I am going to
help the Minister in any way I can to
develop and improve agriculture. At
the County Committee of Agriculture in
Tvrone we were greatly impressed the
other day with the amount of money
that the Ministry had allocated to us in
order to carry out various schemes. I
think the Ministry have treated Tyrone
Ministry of Agriculture 1216

very generously, and we are grateful to
them for all they have done. Perhaps
they could have treated us more
generously if they reduced the number
of officials and gave us another thousand
or two.
No good is going to come out of the
Ministry of Agriculture to the industry
so long as this antagonistic spirit exists
between the Ministry and the different
Boards and organisations. I would say
that the sooner a kindly harmonious
spirit is brought to bear on the Ministry
and the co-operative societies and the

asked to pass here to-day. I would
appeal to the Minister, all actively
engaged in agriculture. and representatives of different boards throughout the
country to come together at a round
table conference. Let them remove all
petty jealousies, petty spites and anything which is keeping us from getting
together to develop agriculture along the
lines it should develop.
In view of the national position it is

weight. It will never pull its full weight

emergency, if for nothing else, I would

about

agricultural community. I believe the

Estimates, 1939-40.
Resolutions reported:
CLASS II. No. 4.
PUBLIC WORKS AND BUILDINGS.
"That a sum not exceeding One
hundred and forty-five thousand five
hundred and thirty-four pounds be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1940, in
respect of Public Works and Buildings,
including Annuities and other expenses.
in connection with Drainage."
CLASS I.
No. 1.
HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT.
"That a sum not exceeding Seventeen
thousand five hundred and seventy-five
pounds be granted to His Majesty to
complete the sum necessary to defray the
charge which will come in course of payment during the year ending 31st March,
1940, to pay the Salaries and Expenses
of the Senate and of the House of
Commons, including a Grant-in-aid.”
CLASS 1 No
CABINET OFFICES.
"That a sum not exceeding Seven
thousand three hundred and eighty
pounds be granted to His Majesty to
complete the sum necessary to defray the
charge which will come in course
of payment during the year ending
31st March, 1940, to defray the
Salaries of the Department of the
Prime Minister, the Salaries of the
Cabinet Secretariat, and other expenses
in connection therewith, including the
expenses of the Privy Council Office."
Resolutions agreed to.
The remaining Orders were read and
postponed.
Adjournment.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn.".
(Captain Dixon.)
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask the Prime
Minister to inform the House of the
order of business for next week?
The PRIME MINISTER: It is
proposed on Tuesday to take the
Matrimonial Causes Bill, Second Reading; on Wednesday the Estimates of the
Ministry of Home Affairs; and on
Thursday the Estimates of the Ministry
of Finance.
Question put, and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at Twentyfive minutes before Seven o'clock
until Tuesday next, pursuant to
the Resolution of the House of
this day.
